    Chapter 1 · Ancient India

    Stone Age

    113 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Earliest evidence of animal domestication in India: Adamgarh (Narmadapuram, M.P.) and Bagor (Bhilwara, Rajasthan).×2
    2. Latest research: earliest evidence of agriculture in the Indian subcontinent is from Lahuradewa, Sant Kabir Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh.×2
    3. Before this research, the earliest evidence was wheat at Mehrgarh (Balochistan, Pakistan), around 7000 BC.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 31 UPPSC questions

    Periods of history

    • Prehistoric period = period with no documented evidence of its history.
    • Proto-historic period = period with evidence of a script that is still not deciphered; it lies between the prehistoric and historic periods.
    • Historic period = time after which documented description is available.
    • Stone Age comes under the Prehistoric period.
    • Indus Valley Civilization and Copper Age culture come under the Proto-historic period.
    • The historical period starts from around 6th century B.C.
    • Three-age system (Stone, Bronze, Iron), from the collection of Copenhagen museum, was coined by Christian Jurgensen Thomsen.UPPSC
    • Research on Stone Age civilization in India first started in 1863.
    • Stone Age has three parts, based on difference of tools used: Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic periods.
    AgeMatching site
    Palaeolithic AgeSohan/Soan River Valley
    Mesolithic AgeBhimbetka Caves
    Neolithic AgeBurzahom
    Chalcolithic AgeBanas Valley

    Archaeologists and institutions

    • Robert Bruce Foote: British geologist and archaeologist (as per Encyclopaedia Britannica); discovered the first Palaeolithic tool in India.UPPSC
    • Robert Bruce Foote is considered the father of Indian pre-history; he was with the Geological Survey of India and documented Stone Age antiquities.
    • Alexander Rea, A.H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess and Walter Elliot were associated with archaeological excavations; they worked mainly on South Indian history.
    • Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) works under the Ministry of Culture; premier body for archaeological research and protection of the nation's cultural heritage.
    • 1871 AD: Archaeological Survey set up as a separate department; Alexander Cunningham was its first Director-General.
    • 1901 AD: in Lord Curzon's tenure it was centralized and named Archaeological Survey of India; John Marshall became Director-General in 1902.
    • Alexander Cunningham (1814-1893 AD), British army officer with the Bengal Engineer Group, is called the 'Father of Indian Archaeology'.
    • National Museum of Mankind = Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya, at Bhopal (M.P.); autonomous body under the Ministry of Culture; country's biggest museum showing history of human development.

    Palaeolithic period

    • Palaeolithic period has three parts on the basis of tools: Lower, Middle and Upper.
    Palaeolithic phaseTools
    Lower PalaeolithicHandaxe, Cleaver, Chopper
    Middle PalaeolithicPoints, Borer, Scraper
    Upper PalaeolithicBurins, Blades
    • Chopper-chopping pebble tools were first found in the Sohan river valley of Punjab (Pakistan).
    • Hand-axe tools were first found at Pallavaram and Attirampakkam near Chennai (Tamil Nadu); other tools of this culture: cleaver, scraper.
    • Yale-Cambridge expedition led by De Terra did the most important research in Sohan valley in 1935.
    • Belan valley research was directed by G.R. Sharma of Allahabad University; nearly 44 Lower Palaeolithic sites were found there.
    • A bone-made Mother Goddess statue of this age came from Lohanda Nala in Belan Valley; it is now kept in the Prayagraj museum.
    • Palaeolithic people lived a natural life and depended mainly on hunting.
    • Palaeolithic people did not know fire, so they ate raw meat; they did not know farming or animal husbandry.
    • First evidence of man (first human fossil) in India was found in the Narmada valley of Madhya Pradesh, discovered in 1982 A.D.
    • Stone Age people of the Vindhyas migrated to the Ganga Valley in the terminal Pleistocene period, because climate change had made the Vindhyan valley dry.UPPSC
    Archaeological sitePresent location
    NevasaMaharashtra
    IsampurKarnataka
    DidwanaRajasthan
    Gudiyam CaveTamil NaduUPPSC

    Mesolithic period

    • Mesolithic period became known after A.C.L. Carlleyle discovered rock paintings in the Vindhya region (1867-68 A.D.).
    • Excavated evidence shows domestication of animals began in the Mesolithic period.UPPSC
    • Earliest evidence of animal domestication in India: Adamgarh (Narmadapuram, M.P.) and Bagor (Bhilwara, Rajasthan).UPPSC ×2
    • Many implements of bones and horns were found at the Mesolithic sites Mahadaha and Sarai Nahar Rai (Pratapgarh district, U.P.).UPPSC
    • 'Puratattva Vimarsh' by Dr. Jai Narayan Pandey describes pointed objects and ornaments of bone from Sarai Nahar Rai, Damdama and Mahadaha.UPPSC
    • Mesolithic sites from west to east: Mahadaha (Pratapgarh, UP) → Lekhahia (Mirzapur, UP) → Paisra (Bihar) → Birbhanpur (W. Bengal).UPPSC
    • Damdama (Mesolithic site, Pratapgarh district, U.P.): 41 human graves; 5 are double burials; one triple burial (three skeletons in one grave).UPPSC
    • A grave with four human skeletons was found at Sarai Nahar Rai.
    • Lekhahiya rock shelter 1 (Vindhya region) gave 17 human skeletons as per 'Puratattva Vimarsh' by Dr. J.N. Pandey: the most from any Vindhyan rock shelter.UPPSC
    • Some Lekhahiya skeletons were in relatively pristine condition; most others were warped.
    • John R. Lucas of the University of Oregon (USA) says remnants of 27 human skeletons were found in Lekhahiya.

    Bhimbetka

    • Bhimbetka rock shelters are in Abdullahganj, Raisen district (Madhya Pradesh).
    • Bhimbetka is famous for prehistoric rock paintings; it is the best example of rock paintings of the prehistoric era; its rock art is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.UPPSC
    • Bhimbetka has 500 pictures in 750 rock shelters: the most pictures from any rock shelter in India.UPPSC
    • Bhimbetka caves show the earliest traces of human life on the Indian subcontinent; pictures include elephant, sambhar and deer.
    • Bhimbetka was discovered by V.S. (Vishnu Shridhar) Wakankar in 1957 (1957-1958); he first found the prehistoric importance of its rock paintings.UPPSC

    Neolithic period and start of farming

    • Grains were first produced in the Neolithic Age; people were introduced to agriculture then.UPPSC
    • Koldihwa and Mehrgarh are the two Neolithic sites with clear evidence of rice (rice bran) and wheat respectively.
    • Fire was first used in the Neolithic period.
    • Eight main food grains of modern human society: barley, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, mustard, oat and rice.
    • These crops first grew as weeds in different areas; humans later grew them from seed at different places and times.
    • Barley was the first grain cultivated by man, in 8000 B.C., in western Asian countries between the northeast Mediterranean Sea and Iran.UPPSC
    • Wheat was later cultivated in the same area around 8000 B.C.
    • Latest research: earliest evidence of agriculture in the Indian subcontinent is from Lahuradewa, Sant Kabir Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh.UPPSC ×2
    • Lahuradewa: human activity and start of rice cultivation date to around 8000-7000 BC.
    • Before this research, the earliest evidence was wheat at Mehrgarh (Balochistan, Pakistan), around 7000 BC.UPPSC ×2
    • Earliest evidence of rice before this research: rice bran from near the bank of river Belan, district Prayagraj, dated 6500 BC.
    • Rule for the earliest-agriculture answer: Lahuradewa if it is among the options; if not, Mehrgarh.
    • Koldihwa (Belan river valley, U.P.) was long held to be the oldest evidence of paddy cultivation in the world; Lahuradewa now gives the oldest evidence of paddy.UPPSC
    • Oldest cultivated grains barley and paddy come from many excavated sites of U.P.: barley and paddy from Mahagada, paddy from Koldihwa.
    • Mehrgarh (Kachhi plains, Balochistan) gave the earliest evidence of settled (permanent) life, around 7000 B.C.UPPSC
    • Oldest dates: Kile Gul Muhammad 4000 B.C.; Kalibangan 3500 B.C.
    • Cultural remains from the Stone Age to the Harappan Civilization were found at Mehrgarh, Balochistan (Pakistan).UPPSC
    • Burzahom: prehistoric (Neolithic) settlement in a village of the same name in Kashmir valley; famous for pit dwelling and Neolithic tool industry, not for rock-cut shrines.UPPSC
    • Burzahom: bones of dogs and antlered deer were found with human skeletons in many pits.UPPSC
    • Burzahom: human and animal skeletons had trepanning (bored hole) marks; humans were buried in pits in a sitting position along with animal bones.
    • First excavation at Burzahom: Helmut de Terra and Dr. Thomas Paterson, 1935 A.D.
    • Ash mounds were found at the Neolithic site Sangana Kallu (Ballari district, Karnataka); also at Piklihal and Utnur.UPPSC
    • Ash mounds are burnt relics of seasonal camps of the Neolithic herdsmen community.

    Megaliths

    • Megaliths = burials made of large stones, in graveyards away from the habitation area.UPPSC
    • Many megaliths are linked to burial or post-burial rituals, including memorials for those whose remains may or may not be available.
    • Megalith types: Chamber tomb, Dolmens, Stone alignment, Stone circle (cromlech), Pit-circles.
    • Mangadu (Kollam district, Kerala): important excavated Megalithic site; its monuments had 28 hard, compact, uneven laterite blocks.
    • Urn-burials at Mangadu show post-cremation fragmentary burials.

    Chalcolithic (Copper) Age

    • Copper was the first metal used.
    • Copper Age is also called the Chalcolithic Age: copper instruments were used along with stone.
    • Chalcolithic settlements in India: South-East Rajasthan, Western Madhya Pradesh, Western Maharashtra and South-East India.
    • Ahar civilization (Chalcolithic) flourished around the Mewar region of Rajasthan; people used copper tools, knew copper smelting, and metal work was a means of their economy.
    • Ahar people knew rice.
    • Ahar pottery: mostly black-and-red ware with white geometric designs.
    • Ahar-Banas culture (2100-1500 BC) was contemporary with the Harappan Civilisation.
    • Ahar-Banas culture flourished in Mewar (Rajasthan), along the Banas River and its tributaries; main sites: Ahar, Gilund, Balathal.
    • Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture was in Rajasthan; hundreds of copper objects were found at Ganeshwar.
    • Navdatoli is near Khargone district, Madhya Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Navdatoli was excavated by H.D. Sankalia, Professor of Deccan College, Pune.UPPSC
    • Navdatoli was the most extensively excavated Chalcolithic site of the Indian subcontinent; dated between 1500 B.C. and 1300 B.C.
    • Navdatoli had round and rectangular houses: round ones about 1-4.5 m in diameter, rectangular ones 5-6 m long (also printed as 5.6 m).
    • Navdatoli roofs: probably hay, tree branches and leaves, on massive wooden posts 22 cm in diameter, set at regular intervals around the huts.
    • Navdatoli: open spaces between posts had mud-plastered bamboo screens.
    • Navdatoli floors: silt clay and river gravel, surface coated with lime.
    • Navdatoli huts had one or two-mouthed 'chulhas', storage jars and other earthen vessels.
    • Jorwe culture people lived in large rectangular houses with wattle and daub walls and thatched roofs.
    • Jorwe people (Chalcolithic Maharashtra) believed in life after death; they buried the dead under the house floor, adults lying supine with head to the north (north to south).UPPSC
    • Jorwe children were buried in two urns joined mouth-to-mouth, set horizontally in the pit.
    • Jorwe culture sites: Daimabad, Inamgaon, Chandoli, Nevasa.
    • Inamgaon (Pune district, Maharashtra): post-Harappan agrarian village; one of the most intensively and extensively excavated, well reconstructed Chalcolithic sites of the Deccan plateau.
    • Ochre-Coloured Pottery (OCP) was discovered and named (christened) by B.B. Lal in 1950-52 at Hastinapur.UPPSC
    • OCP features: leaves ochre colour on fingers when rubbed (looks badly fired at first sight); porous; always worn out at the edges.
    • Most OCP evidence is found at Atranjikhera and Hastinapur.

    Other sites

    • Chandraketugarh is in North 24 Parganas district, West Bengal (not Odisha); it was an important trading port city with huge walls.
    • In early historic times Chandraketugarh was linked to the Ganga by the Vidyadhari river; it was an important trade centre and possibly a political centre.
    • Chandraketugarh was a major centre of terracotta craft.
    • Finds at Chandraketugarh: coins, pottery, seals and sealings, and figurines of ivory, wood and bronze.
    • Salihundam (Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh): important Buddhist site with Buddhist stupas and a huge monastic complex on a hillock; no rock-cut cave shrines.
    • Salihundam excavations gave relic caskets, four stupas, a Chaityagriha, structural temples and sculptures of three phases of Buddhism: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana.

    Chapter 2 · Ancient India

    Indus Valley Civilization

    216 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Evidence from archaeological excavations is the major source of knowledge about Harappan culture.×3
    2. Rakhigarhi · Haryana (not Rajasthan)×2
    3. Mandi (village in Muzaffarnagar district, U.P.): a hoard of Harappan gold ornaments was found; it became famous after villagers found and looted an ancient treasure in June 2000; ASI says the jewellery is late Harappan.×2
    4. The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro is its most important public place and a well-known structure of the civilization; it seems to have been used for ritual bathing.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 49 UPPSC questions

    Name, nature and sources

    • Human society depends mainly on the economy; as the economy changes, human society changes.UPPSC
    • Indus Valley Civilization is also called Harappa Civilization, because the first archaeological evidence came from Harappa (the site discovered first).
    • With ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, it was one of the three ancient civilizations of the world.
    • Archaeologists use 'culture' for a group of objects, distinctive in style, usually found together within a specific area and period of time.
    • Distinctive objects of Harappan culture: seals, beads, weights, stone blades and baked bricks.
    • The Harappan seal is possibly the most distinctive artefact of the civilization.
    • Historical period is decided by available written literature; the period before the art of writing was known is called early historical age.
    • Indus Civilization is Proto-historic: writing was known but is still not deciphered.UPPSC
    • Indus Valley Civilization was the earliest known urban civilization of the Indian subcontinent; Aryan civilization was rural.UPPSC
    • Pottery found in excavations proves Indus Civilization existed before Aryan civilization: Harappan pottery was red painted with black figures; Aryans used grey painted pottery.UPPSC
    • Script and town planning of Indus Civilization were more developed than those of Pre-Aryans; pottery evidence comes from early settlements of Mehrgarh.
    • Indus culture differed from Vedic culture: it was urban (Vedic was rural), had a pictographic script, and did not know iron (Vedic people used iron weapons widely).UPPSC
    • Evidence from archaeological excavations is the major source of knowledge about Harappan culture.UPPSC ×3
    • First artefact uncovered at Harappa: a unique stone seal carved with a unicorn and an inscription; similar seals with other animal symbols and writing are found across the region.
    • Excavation of the civilization began in 1921; tools, weapons and ornaments were found, but the main source is seals; more than 3000 seals were found.
    • Indus Valley Civilization was a Bronze Age civilization; people did not know iron; gold, silver, copper and brass are found, but not iron.UPPSC
    • In India the Iron Age began from the later Vedic period (about 1000 B.C.).
    • Order of appearance in India: urban culture (Harappan) → iron (post-Vedic period, around 1000 B.C.) → punch-marked silver coins (7th-6th century B.C.) → gold coins (Indo-Greek rulers, 2nd century B.C.).
    • Copper was the first metal used by humans, though the period of its use varies around the globe.
    • Indus Valley Civilization is known for town planning, for Mohenjodaro and Harappa, for agriculture (ploughed field at Kalibangan) and for industry/business (evidence from Lothal).
    • Main sites: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Ropar, Lothal and Kalibangan; cities had roads, proper housing and drainage; Harappans knew metals.
    • Mohenjodaro and Harappa are extinct (dead) cities today; they were discovered through excavations, but that is not the reason they are dead.UPPSC
    • Pataliputra (next to modern Patna) was not an Indus Valley site; Kalibangan, Ropar and Lothal are.
    • Sohgaura is not a Harappan site: village on the Rapti river, Gorakhpur district, U.P.; a Mauryan copper plate inscription found there tells about storehouses.
    • Chanhudaro and Kot Diji (Sindh, Pakistan) and Desalpur (Kachchh, Gujarat) are Harappan sites.

    Dating, extent and people

    • Carbon-14 dating puts the Harappan period at 2600 BC to 1700 BC (widely accepted); the civilization peaked during 2300 BC to 1900 B.C.
    • Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilizations were contemporary to the Indus civilization.
    ResearcherTimeline given
    John Marshall (Mohenjodaro)3250 B.C. - 2750 B.C.
    Ernest Mackay (Mohenjodaro)2800 B.C. - 2500 B.C.
    Madho Sarup Vats (Harappa)3500 B.C. - 2500 B.C.
    C.J. Gadd (trade with Mesopotamia)2350 B.C. - 1700 B.C.
    Mortimer Wheeler (Harappa)2500 B.C. - 1500 B.C.
    Walter A. Fairservis2000 B.C. - 1500 B.C.
    • Harappan culture covered parts of Afghanistan; Punjab, Sindh and Baluchistan in Pakistan; and in India Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, fringes of western Uttar Pradesh, J&K and Western Maharashtra.
    • Boundaries: north Manda (Jammu and Kashmir); south Daimabad (Maharashtra); west Sutkagen Dor (Baluchistan, Pakistan); east Alamgirpur (Meerut, Uttar Pradesh).UPPSC
    • The area formed a triangle of about 13 lakh sq km: larger than Pakistan and bigger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
    • The civilization spread from the Jhelum river to the Hindon river (tributary of Yamuna; Alamgirpur); it had rivers Indus, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej and Jhelum, but not the Ganga.UPPSC
    • Population of Mohenjodaro was a mix of at least four races: Proto-Australoids (Caucasian), Mediterraneans, Alpines and Mongoloids.
    Archaeologist / historianFounders of the civilization, in their view
    Dr. Laxman SwaroopArya
    V. Gordon Childe and WheelerSumerians
    Rakhal Das BanerjiDravidians (Dravid)
    • Origin views: E.J.H. Mackay = migration of people from Sumer (Mesopotamia); D.H. Gordon and Mortimer Wheeler = migration of the idea of civilization from Western Asia.
    • Amalananda Ghosh: pre-Harappan culture matured into Harappan civilization.
    • M.F. Rafique Mughal: Harappan civilization developed in the Ravi river region at Harappa; he rejects the old belief that it was inspired by Mesopotamia.
    • Excavated Indus cities fall in three groups: central city; coastal city and dockyards; other cities and towns.
    • Four major cities (large towns): Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Banawali and Dholavira.

    Discovery and excavators

    • The vast mounds were first reported by Charles Masson in 1826.
    • Alexander Cunningham, head of the ASI, visited Harappa in 1853 A.D. and 1856 A.D.; he made small excavations and reported ancient pottery, stone, tools and a stone seal, but did not recognize its significance.UPPSC
    • Sir John Marshall was Director-General of the ASI from 1902 to 1928; he announced the discovery of a new civilization in the Indus Valley to the world in 1921.
    • Marshall appointed Dayaram Sahni; Sahni's excavation found the ruins of Harappa in 1921 (survey in January 1921); Rakhal Das Banerjee dug out Mohenjodaro in 1922: the two Indians linked with the discovery.
    • Harappa was later excavated by Madho Sarup Vats (1926-27 to 1933-34) and Mortimer Wheeler (1946).
    • Others who contributed to the discovery: K.N. Dixit, Ernest Mackay, Aurel Stein, A.N. Ghosh and J.P. Joshi.
    • V.A. Smith was not linked with Harappa-Mohenjodaro excavation; he was an Irish Indologist and historian.
    SiteExcavator (years)

    • Excavators: Harappa = Daya Ram Sahni; Lothal = S.R. Rao; Surkotada = J.P. Joshi; Dholavira = R.S. Bisht (not B.K. Thapar).UPPSC

    • Uttar Pradesh sites: Alamgirpur (Meerut) and Hulas (Saharanpur).UPPSC
    • Mandi (village in Muzaffarnagar district, U.P.): a hoard of Harappan gold ornaments was found; it became famous after villagers found and looted an ancient treasure in June 2000; ASI says the jewellery is late Harappan.UPPSC ×2

    Harappa

    • Harappa is in Montgomery district (now Sahiwal district) of Punjab province, Pakistan, on the left bank of the Ravi river.UPPSC
    • Stuart Piggott called Harappa and Mohenjodaro "Twin capitals of one United Kingdom".
    • Harappa had two mounds: eastern = city mound; western = Citadel mound.
    • Harappa granary remains: 12 rooms in two rows of six rooms each.
    • Harappa has Cemetery R-37; Lothal the dockyard; Kalibangan the furrowed land; Mohenjodaro the Dancing Girl statue.UPPSC

    Mohenjodaro

    • Mohenjodaro is a Sindhi word meaning "Mound of the dead".
    • Mohenjodaro is on the right bank of the Indus river in Larkana district, Sindh, Pakistan; discovered by Rakhal Das Banerjee in 1922.
    • The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro is its most important public place and a well-known structure of the civilization; it seems to have been used for ritual bathing.UPPSC ×2
    • A large ruined building north-east of the Great Bath measures 70.1 × 23.77 m; perhaps the residence of a very high official, possibly the high priest or a college of priests.
    • Roads were the main quality of Mohenjodaro: the main road (Rajpath) was 9.15 m wide; straight roads cut at right angles, making square and quadrangle blocks.
    • Mohenjodaro finds: mother goddess idol, dancing girl statue, seated male in soapstone (Priest-King), Pashupati (Shiva) seal, skeletons in wells, teeth of horse, evidence of cotton cloth.
    • Mohenjodaro also gave sculptures, seals, pottery, gold and jewellery; the most famous is the humped bull seal.
    • The Dancing Girl of Mohenjodaro is about 10.5 cm high, made of bronze, cast by the lost-wax technique.
    • Clay model boats were found at Lothal; seals with a boat model were found at Mohenjodaro.UPPSC
    • Evidence of human sacrifice was also found in Mohenjodaro.

    Chanhudaro

    • Chanhudaro lies about 130 km south of Mohenjodaro; discovered by N.G. Majumdar in 1931; excavated on a large scale by E.J.H. Mackay in 1935-36.UPPSC
    • Mackay found a bead making factory and furnace at Chanhudaro; some phase cut bricks were also found.
    • Remnants of Jhukar and Jhangar cultures were found at Chanhudaro.
    • Chanhudaro may have been an industrial hub: shell making, bangle making and bead making.
    • Chanhudaro finds: ornamented elephant, toys, vestige (trace) of a dog that followed a cat, lipsticks.

    Lothal

    • Lothal is near Saragwala village, Dholka Taluka, Ahmedabad district, Gujarat; discovered by S.R. Rao in 1954; Harappa and Mohenjodaro are in Pakistan.UPPSC
    • Lothal lies along the Bhogava river, a tributary of Sabarmati, in the Gulf of Cambay.
    • A brick basin on the eastern side of Lothal town is identified as a dockyard by its excavator; Lothal is the only Indus site with evidence of a port.UPPSC
    • Lothal, on the shores of the Gulf of Khambhat, was an ancient trading port and a major harbour for trade with Western Asia.
    • By planning and material goods, Lothal seems a mini Harappa or mini Mohenjodaro.
    • Lothal finds: rice husk, metal workers, shell ornament makers, bead makers, shop, fire altars, terracotta figurine of a horse, terracotta model of a ship, a Persian seal, painted jar.
    • An ivory scale was found at Lothal.UPPSC
    • Three double burials were found at Lothal; double burials were also found at Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi.

    Kalibangan

    • Kalibangan is in Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan (not Haryana), on the bank of the Ghaggar (Saraswati) river.UPPSC
    • Kalibangan was discovered by Luigi Pio Tessitori, an Italian Indologist; excavated by A. Ghosh in 1950-52 as a Harappan site.
    • Kalibangan excavation was started by B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar in 1960-61.
    • Kalibangan's western mound was a fortified enclosure with rectangular salients and towns (as printed).
    • Kalibangan gave the earliest ploughed (furrowed) field ever found in excavation.UPPSC
    • A terracotta plough, along with the ploughed field, comes from the early phase of Kalibangan (as per ASI); a terracotta plough also comes from Banawali.
    • Kalibangan finds: Mesopotamian seals, wheels of a toy cart, fire altars.
    • Kalibangan: a series of 'fire altars' on mud-brick platforms was discovered.
    • A triangular terracotta cake from Kalibangan has a horned deity on one side and, on the other, an animal (goat) dragged by a rope by a human; it points to a sacrificial tradition.UPPSC

    Dholavira

    • Dholavira is in the Rann of Kachchh (Kachchh district), Gujarat; second largest Harappan site in India after Rakhigarhi.UPPSC
    • Dholavira was excavated by R.S. Bisht and colleagues in 1990-91 (also printed as 1992).
    • Dholavira gives important information about a great bath and a rock-cut reservoir, about 79 m × 12 m and 7 m deep, with huge capacity.UPPSC
    • Dholavira town was rectangular and divided into three parts: Citadel, Middle town and Lower town.UPPSC
    • Dholavira people knew an advanced water management system: from the earliest period they built a series of dams and channelled water into connected reservoirs.UPPSC
    • An inscription of ten large-sized signs of the Harappan script was found at Dholavira.

    Other sites

    • Rakhigarhi (Hisar district, Haryana; Ghaggar-Hakra river plain) is the largest Indus Valley site in India; the village lies along the bank of the Ghaggar river.UPPSC
    • Banawali is in Fatehabad district, Haryana, in the valley of Ghaggar and its tributaries.
    • Banawali finds: clay figures of the mother goddess and a toy plough (terracotta replica of a plough).
    • Surkotada is in Kachchh district, Gujarat; discovered and excavated by Jagatpati (J.P.) Joshi.
    • Surkotada gave horse bones and pot burials.
    • Daimabad is on the left bank of the Pravara river in Ahmednagar (now Ahilyanagar) district, Maharashtra; discovered by B.P. Bopardikar in 1958.
    • Daimabad is famous for many bronze goods, some influenced by Harappan culture.
    • Ropar (Punjab) is on the left bank of the Satluj; present name Rupnagar; discovered by B.B. Lal in 1950; excavated by Yagyadatt Sharma in 1953-55.
    • Rangpur is in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, on the bank of the Bhadar river (coast of the Arabian Sea).
    • Rangpur people grew Rice, Bajra and Sorghum, as large vegetative remains show.
    • Dadheri (Kotla Dadheri): prehistoric excavation site of Govindgarh, district Fatehgarh Sahib (Punjab).UPPSC
    • Dadheri is known for painted grey ware culture, thought to be linked to the arrival of the Aryans.
    • Alamgirpur is in Meerut district, U.P., on the Hindon river.
    • Alamgirpur finds: a small terracotta bead-like object coated with gold, evidence of cloth, and utensils with triangle, peacock and squirrel impressions.
    • Hulas (Saharanpur district, U.P.) is a Late Harappan site.
    • Hulas finds: hand-made and wheel-made pottery with geometric or naturalistic designs painted in black, chert blades, bone points.
    • Bhagwanpura is in Kurukshetra district, Haryana, on the southern bank of the Saraswati; excavated by J.P. Joshi.
    • Manda is on the bank of the Chenab in Jammu and Kashmir; excavated by J.P. Joshi and Madhubala (year printed as 1776-77).
    • Manda is seen as a site used to get wood from the Himalayan regions and send it downstream to other Indus towns.
    • Sinauli (Baraut Tehsil, Baghpat district, U.P.): 125 graves of the Indus Valley Civilization (human burials) were found.UPPSC
    • Sinauli graves are oriented North-South; most are primary human burials; some have animal bones, gold, copper and bangles.

    Town planning and buildings

    • Town planning was the unique feature of the civilization; cities and towns were well planned, most on a grid pattern.
    • Drainage was advanced: drains ran along the roads and were covered with slabs (big stones and bricks).
    • Both baked and raw bricks were used; burnt bricks from all Indus towns generally had the ratio 4:2:1.
    • Bricks were not all of one size or kind: ornamental bricks come from Kalibangan and curved bricks from Chanhudaro.
    • Most houses had one storey, but some had two storeys, as stairs found in some houses show.
    • Roads in Harappan cities were generally 10 metres wide.
    • Use of burnt bricks in buildings was a main feature: used in plenty at Harappa and Mohenjodaro; at Lothal used for drainage.
    • Other main features of the civilization: well planned architecture, advanced trade and commerce.
    • Remains of wells and bathrooms are found in almost every major Indus city.

    Economy, metals and crafts

    • Trade and commerce were advanced; there is evidence of both internal and external trade.
    • Harappans knew silver: the earliest evidence of silver in India; its proper use is seen at Mohenjodaro and Harappa.
    • Other sources of silver for Harappa and Mohenjodaro were Afghanistan and Iran.
    Metal / materialSource
    CopperKhetri (Rajasthan), Balochistan and Oman
    LazuriteBadakhshan (Afghanistan)
    TinIran, Afghanistan
    SilverJawar and Ajmer mines of Rajasthan, Afghanistan and Iran
    LeadAfghanistan, Iran and Rajasthan (India)
    ShilajitHimalaya
    Garnet stone (Gomed)Gujarat
    GoldSouth India (Karnataka)
    • Cotton was first cultivated for clothing in India; earliest evidence of cotton cultivation came from excavations in India.UPPSC
    • From India cotton reached Greece, where it was called "Sindon".
    • Cotton cultivation began in India in 3000 BC; in Egypt in 2500 BC.
    • Cotton textiles were made in the Harappan period, as artefacts show.
    • Harappan pottery is bright or dark red, uniformly sturdy and well baked; wheel-made; both plain and painted.
    • Plain ware is usually of red clay, with or without a fine red slip; painted pottery was red and black; black painted ware has a fine coating of red slip.
    • Polychrome pottery was rare: mainly small vases with geometric patterns, mostly in red, black and green, less often white and yellow.
    • Painting colour scheme: light black, chocolate or light red over a buff or greenish-buff background.
    • Art forms found at the sites include seals, pottery, gold ornaments and necklaces.

    Seals and animals

    • Most Indus seals were made of steatite; a few of terracotta, agate, chert.
    • Most seals were square; a few were cube, circle or cylinder shaped.
    • Pipal tree appears many times on Indus seals, showing its sacred value.
    • Elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, deer and sheep are shown on Harappan seals and terracotta art; the cow is not shown.
    • Most seals carry short inscriptions with figures of the one-horned animal (most common), buffalo, tiger, rhinoceros, goat and elephant.
    • Harappans knew the horse, but there is no horse on the seals.UPPSC
    • Evidence of cow and elephant is found; evidence of lion is not mentioned anywhere in Harappan excavations.
    • Evidence of bull and elephant is found (seal of Zebu bull; seals showing elephant); the horse is disputed, though the latest excavation shows evidence of horse.
    • Horses played no major role in the Indus Valley Civilization; BPSC accepted 'horse' as the animal not known to Indus people.

    Religion

    • Pre-Aryan period is taken as the start of idol worship; it was prevalent in Indus Civilization, as coins from Mohenjodaro with the seal of God show.UPPSC
    • Many pieces of evidence of Mother Goddess worship are found; people probably worshipped Mother Goddess along with male and female deities.
    • Marshall identified a figure from excavation (Mohenjodaro; also printed as Harappa) as an early form of the Hindu God Shiva (Rudra) or Pashupati (lord of animals).
    • Pashupati seal: three-faced male god in yogic posture, with a rhino and a buffalo on the right and an elephant and a tiger on the left.
    • Cylindrical stones show that people worshipped the Lingam, symbol of Lord Shiva.
    • No temple or place of worship has been found till date; people worshipped both male and female deities; they did not have great palaces and temples, and did not use horse-drawn chariots in war.
    • The only religious sources are statues of mud and stone, and seals.
    • These show worship of female deities, Shiva or Pashupati, and animals like snake and elephant.
    • Worship of plants and trees, and of stone or other objects as 'Linga' or 'Yoni' symbols, was common.
    • Indus Valley Civilization is considered a secular civilization, with no trace of theocratic or organized religion.
    • Indus people may have performed Yagya (fire pits found at Rajasthan and Gujarat sites); burial rituals show belief in Atma or spirit.
    • The undeciphered Indus script has attracted speculations and hypotheses.

    Decline

    Reason of declineResearchers
    FloodMarshall, Mackay, S.R. Rao
    Attack of AryansGordon Childe, Mortimer Wheeler and Stuart Piggott
    Climate changeAurel Stein, Amalananda Ghosh
    Geological changeM.R. Sahni, H.T. Lambrick, G.F. Dales
    EpidemicK.A.R. Kennedy
    • IIT Kharagpur report: continuous low or negligible rainfall (drought) for 900 years caused the fall of the civilization.

    Other ancient civilizations

    • Ancient Egyptian civilization flourished along the banks of the river Nile for almost 3,000 years.UPPSC
    • Nile is called the 'lifeline of Egypt'; a major north-flowing river in north-eastern Africa, generally regarded as the longest river in the world.
    • Indus Valley Civilization (India) and Mesopotamian civilization (Iraq) were contemporary civilizations.
    • Mesopotamian civilization (present-day Iraq and nearby areas) is considered the world's oldest civilization.
    • Egyptian civilization (civilization of the Nile) grew in the Nile basin and is held to have emerged after the Mesopotamian.
    • Sumerians were the first to develop the art of writing in a proper system; their original script was very simple and primitive.
    • The Cuneiform script of Sumeria is known as one of the earliest systems of writing.
    • Civilizations from north to south: Aztec → Maya → Muisca → Inca.UPPSC
    • Aztec civilization spread over the northern part of Mesoamerica; Mayan over the southern part of Mesoamerica.
    • Mesoamerica = region from central Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and northern Costa Rica.
    • Muisca civilization was in the eastern part of Colombia (South America).
    • Inca civilization spread in western South America, from north of Quito to Santiago in the south.

    Chapter 3 · Ancient India

    Vedic Age

    234 facts · 11 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. "Satyameva Jayate" ("Truth alone triumphs") is from the Mundakopanishad.×4
    2. Boghaz-Koi inscription (Asia Minor, Turkiye), of 14th century B.C., mentions four Vedic gods: Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya; it tells of the Aryans' movement from Iran to India.×3
    3. Upanishads are books of philosophy, for all times and all people.×3
    4. Kathopanishad (Katha Upanishad) has the dialogue of Yama, lord of death, and Nachiketa, a 12-year-old boy who left home to find the meaning of death and beyond.×3
    5. The cow was called "Aghanya" (not worthy to be killed) in the Vedic period, showing how pious it was held.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 64 UPPSC questions

    Aryans and their homeland

    • 'Vedic' comes from the Sanskrit word 'Veda', meaning knowledge.
    • The civilization that grew in India after the Indus Valley Civilization is called Vedic or Aryan Civilization.
    • Arya means great or highborn; in classical Sanskrit Arya means 'a noble man'.UPPSC ×2
    • 'Aryan' (meaning 'noble') was a self-designation of Indo-Iranian people; Vedic people used it as an ethnic label for themselves and for the noble class.
    • Scholars say that even in ancient times the idea of 'Aryan' was religious, cultural and linguistic, not racial.
    • History of Aryans is known mainly from the Vedas; Aryans are generally said to be the authors of the Vedas.
    • Scholars differ on the original home of the Aryans.
    Homeland of AryansScholar
    Kashmir or Himalayan regionL.D. Kalla
    Brahmarshi DeshP. Ganganath Jha
    Seven Indus statesDr. Avinash Chandra Das
    Devika StateD.S. Trivedi
    South RussiaGordon Childe & Nehring
    Central AsiaMax Muller
    North PolePt. Bal Gangadhar Tilak
    TibetSwami Dayanand Saraswati

    GermanyHart & Penca
    • Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his book 'The Arctic Home in the Vedas', said the North Pole (Arctic region) was the original home of Aryans; most historians do not accept this.UPPSC
    • The Indo-Iranian group that composed the Zoroastrian Avesta and the Hindu Vedas called themselves Aryans; the Avesta, written by Zoroastrians, relates to present-day Iran.UPPSC
    • Boghaz-Koi inscription (Asia Minor, Turkiye), of 14th century B.C., mentions four Vedic gods: Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya; it tells of the Aryans' movement from Iran to India.UPPSC ×3
    • Vedic Age has two parts: Rigvedic or Early Vedic Age (1500-1000 BCE) and Later Vedic Age (1000-600 BCE).
    • 800 B.C. to 600 B.C. is the Brahmin (Brahmana) era.UPPSC
    • Sutra period = from 7th or 6th century B.C. to 3rd century B.C.

    Geography and rivers

    • Rigveda mentions four rivers of Afghanistan: Kubha (Kabul), Krumu (Kurram), Gomati (Gomal) and Suvastu (Swat); this shows the Aryans' deep relations with Afghanistan.UPPSC ×2
    • Rigveda mentions seven rivers of Sapta-Sindhu (land of seven rivers): Saraswati, Vipasa, Parushni, Vitasta, Sindhu (Indus), Shutudri and Asakini.
    • Yamuna is mentioned three times and Ganga once in the Rigveda.
    • Marudvridha, a river of Kashmir, is also mentioned.
    • Sindhu (Indus) is the river mentioned most in the Rigveda; it was the most important river of the Vedic period.
    • Indus is called 'Hiranyani' (Hiranyayi) for its link with gold; it ends in the Arabian Sea.
    • Saraswati was the most sacred river: called 'Matetama' (best of all mothers), 'Devitama' (best of all goddesses) and 'Naditama' (best of all rivers).UPPSC
    • Saraswati is believed to be the scene of activities of the Vedic tribes Bharatas, Purus and Kurus.
    Vedic river nameModern name
    Asakini (Askini)ChenabUPPSC
    VipasaBeas
    ParushniRavi
    VitastaJhelum
    KubhaKabul
    KrumuKurram
    GomatiGomal
    SuvastuSwat
    SadaneeraGandakUPPSC
    ShutudriSutlej
    DrishdvatiGhaggar
    • Chenab is also called Chandrabhaga; it rises at Tandi in Lahul Spiti, where the rivulets Chandra and Bhaga meet.
    • Aryans called the Ganga-Yamuna doab and nearby areas Brahmarshi Desh.
    • Area between the Himalaya and Vindhyachal ranges was named Madhya Desh.
    • Later the Aryans spread over the whole of North India, which came to be called Aryavarta.
    • In the Mahabharata period the Mahanadi was called Chitrotpala; the Bhishma Parv praises it as Punayadayini and Paap (sin) Nashini; Indian people drank its water.
    • Mahoba copper plate of Someshwar Dev calls the Mahanadi 'Chitrotpala Ganga'.
    • Vayu Purana names the Mahanadi Nilotapala; Matsya Purana calls it Chitrotpala.

    Vedic literature: the four Vedas

    • Vedic literature is also called Shruti; Vedas are the most ancient literature of India.
    • Four Vedas: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda; Rigveda is the oldest and most important.UPPSC
    • Rigveda, Yajurveda and Samaveda together are called Vedatrayi or Trayi.UPPSC
    • Each Veda has four parts, in this order: Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads.UPPSC
    • Samhitas and Brahmanas form the Karma Kanda of the Vedas.
    • Aranyakas and Upanishads form the Gyan Kanda; they focus on philosophy and spirituality.
    VedaSubject
    AtharvavedaMedicine; charms and spells
    RigvedaGod Grace; hymns and prayers
    YajurvedaSacrifice process; hymns and rituals
    SamavedaMusic; musical hymnsUPPSC ×2
    VedaBrahmana text
    RigvedaAitareya, Kaushitaki
    SamavedaPanchvisha

    Rigveda

    • History of the Rigvedic age is known from the Rigveda; it is the oldest known book in the world, though its author and date are disputed.
    • Rigveda is an ancient collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns by several seers, each hymn averaging about ten verses; one of the four canonical sacred texts (Shruti) of Hinduism.UPPSC
    • Rigveda has 10 mandals, 1028 suktas (hymns) and 10552 verses (Richas / mantras).
    • Mandals 2 to 7 of the Rigveda are the most ancient.
    Rigveda MandalAssociated Rishis
    FirstMaduchchanda, Medhatithi and others
    SecondGritasamada
    ThirdVishvamitra
    FourthVamadeva
    FifthAtri
    SixthBhardvaja
    SeventhVashishtha
    EighthKanva & Angiras
    NinthAngiras and many others
    TenthVimada, Indra, Shachi and many others
    • Gayatri Mantra is in the third Mandal of the Rigveda; written in Sanskrit by Brahmarshi Vishwamitra; dedicated to Savitra (Surya).UPPSC
    • Meaning of Gayatri Mantra: "May the Almighty God illuminate our intellect to lead us along the righteous path."
    • Trishtubh Mantra was prescribed in the Upanayana ceremony of Kshatriyas; it stood for their martial, heroic qualities and warrior duties.
    • All 114 hymns of the ninth mandal are dedicated to 'Soma'.
    • At first three Varnas are described: Brahman, Kshatriya and Vaishya.
    • Shudra is first mentioned in the Purush Sukta of the 10th Mandal of the Rigveda.
    • 'Varna' is first found in the Rigveda: a hymn shows Brahmin (priest), Kshatriya (noble), Vaishya (commoner) and Shudra (servant) coming from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet of the primeval Purusha.
    • Literal meaning of Varna (Sanskrit) is colour or class.
    • Priests of the Rigveda were called Hotri / Hota.UPPSC
    • According to Patanjali, the Rigveda has 21 branches.
    • Basic script of the Rigveda was Brahmi; work on script or 'Bhasa' is said to be started by Brahma, so the script was called Brahmi.UPPSC
    • Iron is not mentioned in the Rigveda but is found in later Vedic literature.

    Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda

    • Yajurveda in Sanskrit means 'wisdom of sacrificial formulas'; compiled a century or two after the Rigveda.
    • Yajurveda has prose and verse formulas spoken by priests doing the manual part of the sacrifice; it gives procedure of rituals and Yajnas using Rigveda hymns.
    • Yajurveda Samhitas have two parts: Shukla (White) Yajurveda and Krishna (Black) Yajurveda.
    • In Krishna Yajurveda mantras are irregular and mixed; in Shukla Yajurveda their order and recitation are more systematic.
    • Shukla Yajurveda has a separate Brahmana text, the Shatpatha Brahmana.
    • Vajasneyi is the Samhita of Shukla Yajurveda.UPPSC
    • Shukla Yajurveda is only in poetic form; Krishna Yajurveda has both poetic and prose form.
    • Shatapatha Brahmana: prose text on Vedic rituals, history and mythology, linked to the Yajurveda; placed after the Rigveda in Vedic literature; also describes social subjects.
    • 'Purushamedha' is mentioned in the Shatpatha Brahmana of Shukla Yajurveda and the Taittiriya Brahmana of Krishna Yajurveda.
    • Many historians discuss the Purushmedh Yajna only with the Shatpatha Brahmana.

    Note from the book The question on which scripture mentions 'Purusha Medha' has no single answer: Shukla Yajurveda, Krishna Yajurveda and Shatpatha Brahmana were all among its options.

    • Shatpatha Brahmana tells of King Videgha Madhava (a king of Videha) and his priest Rishi Gautama Rahugana, carrying the sacred fire to the east.UPPSC
    • The king carried fire (Agni Vaisvanara) in his mouth; on his guru's prompting it fell out and burned the earth towards the east.
    • This story keeps the tradition of how the Kosalas and the Videhas received their culture.
    • Samaveda is the shortest of the four Vedas; closely tied to the Rigveda, from which it took many verses.UPPSC
    • Samaveda was compiled for ritual use; all its verses are meant to be chanted in ceremonies; its hymns are lyrical and melodious.
    • Samaveda Samhita has 1875 verses; all except 75 or 99 are from the Rigveda.
    • In Atharvaveda the priest chanting mantras was called the Brahmana priest.
    • 'Anga' and 'Magadha' are first mentioned in the Atharvaveda, along with Gandhari and Mujavats.
    • The earliest account of magical charms and spells is in the Atharvaveda.
    • Ayurveda ('Science of Life') first appeared in the Atharvaveda; it is an Upaveda (also taken as Upanga) of the Atharvaveda.UPPSC
    • Atharvaveda describes thoughts and superstitions of common people; contents: disease prevention, coordination, loyalty, marriage and love poetry.
    • Yajurveda contains the description of stotras and recitals.
    • Atharvaveda holds much knowledge of the physical world and spirituality.
    • Gopatha Brahmana is the only Brahmana of the Atharvaveda; a prose text on Vedic rituals; linked with both Shaunaka and Paippalada recensions.
    • In the post-Vedic period the Kuru-Panchala region was the axis of Aryan culture, for its achievements in science, mathematics, astronomy, religion and philosophy.UPPSC

    Upanishads

    • Upanishad means pupils sitting near the teacher to learn the secret doctrine.
    • Upanishads are books of philosophy, for all times and all people.UPPSC ×3
    • Upanishadic philosophy opposes no school of thought, religion or reading of scripture, but its method of explaining is unique.
    • The word salvation (Moksha) is not used in the Vedas; it was first discussed in the Upanishads.UPPSC
    • Moksha means 'liberation'; the endless cycle of life and death is not the real aim of the human soul.
    • As per the Upanishads, the core of the self is not body or mind but the Atman (Soul).
    • Kathopanishad (Katha Upanishad) has the dialogue of Yama, lord of death, and Nachiketa, a 12-year-old boy who left home to find the meaning of death and beyond.UPPSC ×3
    • "Satyameva Jayate" ("Truth alone triumphs") is from the Mundakopanishad.UPPSC ×4
    • Satyameva Jayate is India's national motto, inscribed at the base of the national emblem; adopted by the Government of India on 26 January 1950.
    • Satyakama Jabala, a boy and later a Vedic sage, first appears in chapter IV of the Chhandogya Upanishad; the legend challenges the stigma of an unmarried mother.
    • "Tamso Ma Jyotirgamaya" is from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; it means "lead us from darkness to light, from ignorance to truth".
    • The dialogue of Yagnavalkya and Gargi is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
    • Gargi was a philosopher of the Later Vedic/Upanishadic period, not of the Rigvedic period.
    • Shvetashvatara Upanishad, embedded in the Yajurveda, literally means 'carried on a white horse'.
    • Upanishads contain several parables and stories; they were composed mainly in the later Vedic period, much before the Puranas (which began around the early centuries of the common era).
    • A parable is a short simple story teaching a religious or moral lesson.
    • Parable of the two birds (about the jivatma, a blend of human and divine) is in the Kathopanishad, and also in the Mundaka and Svetasvatara Upanishads.
    • Upanishads say some Kshatriya kings, great scholars, taught even Brahmins: Janak of Videha, Pravahan Jabali of Panchal, Asvapati of Kekaya and Ajatshatru of Kashi.
    • King Asvapati, a Kshatriya and a famed learned teacher, ruled Kekaya when Janak was king of Videha.UPPSC
    • Kekaya kingdom lay on the bank of river Beas, east of Gandhara.

    Puranas and epics

    • Puranas are the sacred literature of Hinduism; there are 18 Puranas.UPPSC ×2
    • The 18 Puranas: Matsya, Markandeya, Bhagavat, Bhavishya, Brahmanda, Brahma Vaivrata, Brahma, Vamana, Varaha, Vishnu, Vayu, Agni, Narada, Padma, Linga, Garuda, Skanda, Kurma.
    • Srimad Bhagvatam is called the 'Crown Jewel' of all Vedic literature.
    • Five characteristics of Puranas: Sarga, Pratisarga, Vansa, Manvantara and Vanshanucharita.UPPSC
    • Sarga and Pratisarga = natural creation and renovation (cosmogony); Vansa = history of sages and gods.
    • Manvantara = period of different Manus; Vanshanucharita = genealogy of kings.
    • Vishnu Purana tells of the Mauryan dynasty; Vayu Purana relates to the Gupta dynasty; Matsya Purana relates to the Andhra Satavahana dynasty.UPPSC
    • Shrimad Bhagavad Gita was originally written in Sanskrit; it has 700 verses and is part of the Mahabharata.
    • Mahabharata originally had only 8,800 shlokas; its original name was 'Jaya' or Jayasamhita.UPPSC
    • Mahabharata today has 100,000 shlokas (hence Shatasahasri-Samhita); believed to be written by Sage Veda Vyasa.UPPSC
    • Churning of the ocean of milk (Ksira Sagar): Mount Mandara was the churning rod; Vasuki, king of serpents who stays on Shiva's neck, was the rope.
    • Lord Vishnu, as Kurma Avatar, held the mountain on his back.

    Rigvedic society

    • Family or Kul was the smallest unit of Rigvedic society.
    • Rigvedic society was patriarchal; the Varun Sukta shows a father could sell his child.
    • Pancha-Jana = five tribes named after their founder ancestors: Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu and Puru; Kikat was not among them.UPPSC
    • Dasharajnya ('Battle of Ten Kings'), told in the Rigveda, was fought on the bank of the Parushni river.UPPSC
    • The Dasharajnya story is placed long before the Ramayana.
    • Sudas, a descendant of King Bharata, won a great victory over a confederacy of ten kings.
    • Women who composed Rigveda hymns were called Brahmavadini: Lopamudra, Vishwawara, Sikta, Nivavari, Ghosa.
    • Lopamudra was the wife of Agastya Rishi.
    • Ghosha, Apala and Vishvavara are female seers with hymns in the Rigveda.
    • Vansha, Gotra and Kula are family-system words; Kosa relates to the treasury.
    • Gotra first occurs in the Rigveda, meaning "cow shelter" or "herd of cows".UPPSC
    • The sense "family lineage kin" for gotra is more recent, first recorded around the post-Vedic period.
    • Later Vedic period: four ashramas were recognised (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyasa) and four Purusharthas (Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha).
    • Pancha Mahayajnas were performed in the Grihastha Ashram: Brahma Yajna, Deva Yajna, Pitra Yajna, Bhuta Yajna, Atithi Yajna.
    • Grihastha Ashram was the foundation of society: one earned wealth and supported the other three ashramas.
    • There are sixteen Sanskaras: three before birth, twelve during life, one after death.
    • The 16 Sanskaras: Garbhadhana (conception), Punsavana (foetus protection), Simantonnayana (satisfying cravings of the pregnant mother), Jatakarman (childbirth), Namakaran (naming), Nishkramana (first outing), Annaprasana (solid food), Chudakarma (hair cutting), Karnavedha (ear piercing), Vidhyarambha (starting education), Upanayana (sacred thread), Vidyarambha (study of Vedas), Keshant, Samavartana (return home after education), Vivaha (marriage), Antyesthi (cremation).
    • Upanayana seems the most important and common Sanskara, besides the wedding and the ritual after death.
    • Upadhyaya = one who took up teaching for a livelihood and taught only a part of the Veda or Vedangas.
    • Untouchability took definite shape in the early Christian era, the Dharmashastra era, when Brahmanical religion was rising.
    • In the Dharmashastra era scriptures were being written and social customs were strictly practised; untouchability was one of them.
    Society / periodNature
    Indus Valley CivilizationUrban
    Later Vedic SocietyAgrarian
    Rigvedic SocietyPastoral
    Medieval PeriodLand LordismUPPSC

    Economy and daily life

    • In ancient times the Aryans depended on agriculture and hunting for livelihood.UPPSC
    • Cattle breeding was the most important economic activity of Rigvedic people; prayers were made for more cattle; cattle were a medium of exchange; the cow was the most valued property.UPPSC
    • The cow is treated as a deity in some suktas of the Rigveda.
    • The cow was called "Aghanya" (not worthy to be killed) in the Vedic period, showing how pious it was held.UPPSC ×3
    • 'Yava' in the Rigveda means the food grain barley.UPPSC
    • Crop names: Vrihi = rice; Mudga = mung bean; Yava = millet (in this matching list); Ikshu = sugarcane.
    • 'Nishka' (Nishka-Griva) was a gold necklace in the Rigvedic period; later the word came to mean gold coins.UPPSC ×2
    • "Pani" in the Rigvedic period was a class of traders.
    Rigvedic termMeaning
    VasaLower garment
    AdhivasaUpper garment
    TakshaCarpenter
    KarmaMetal worker
    VeknatMoneylender
    AritriBoatmen
    • Earliest evidence of iron use in India is from Atranjikhera, dating to around 1000 B.C.UPPSC
    • Atranjikhera: prehistoric and historic site on the Kali river, a tributary of the Ganga; first identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in 1861-62; excavated by R.C. Gaur.
    • Atranjikhera digging: trial trench 1962; small-scale digging next year; regular excavation from 1964.
    • Early iron smelting by tribal artisans in India dates to 1300-1200 B.C.; most archaeologists take about 1000 B.C. (around 3000 years ago) as the start of the Iron Age in the subcontinent.
    • Rigveda mentions a coat of mail and helmet of gold and iron, possibly used in war; Indus people left no evidence of weapons and were possibly ruled by a class of merchants.
    • Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper; Indus people knew only copper and bronze; iron spread in North India between 1000 BC and 600 BC.
    • Rigvedic Aryans owed their success in India to horses and chariots; horse bones were found at Bhagwanpura (Haryana, Rigvedic period).
    • Indus horse evidence: from a superficial level of Mohenjo-daro and a doubtful terracotta figurine from Lothal.

    Religion and gods

    • Religion of early Vedic Aryans was mainly worship of nature and performing Yajnas.
    • Early Aryans saw life as a manifestation of nature and believed a divine power works behind fire, water, wind.
    • Sacrifice (Yajna) was the central feature of Rigvedic religion; domestic sacrifice was the rule; community sacrifices by kings were grand festivals; gods were believed to be pleased by Yajna.UPPSC
    • Rigvedic religion was polytheistic: many gods were worshipped; nature was worshipped as having a living soul.UPPSC
    • Vedic gods in three groups: sky = Varuna, Mitra, Surya, Vishnu; space = Indra, Rudra; earth = Agni, Brihaspati, Soma.
    • Treating whichever god is worshipped as the Supreme God is called Ekeshwarvaad; Rigveda supports it with "Ekam Satt Vipra bahudha badanti".
    • Rigvedic Ekeshwarvaad included Advaityavaad, Sarvadevtavaad and Bahudevatavaad; this one-supreme-God idea differs from modern Ishwarvaad.
    • Indra is the most powerful and most important god of the Rigveda; about 250 hymns (the largest number) are devoted to him.UPPSC ×2
    • Agni comes second with 200 hymns.UPPSC
    • Indra is called Purandara (destroyer of forts); he was the Storm-God, Sky-God and God of War, who wields the thunderbolt.UPPSC
    • Indra is the king and Dev of Svarga (heaven): god of heaven, lightning, thunder and rain; some hymns pray to Indra to punish sinners.UPPSC
    • Varuna upheld 'Rita' (the moral/natural order), so he was called 'Ritasyagopa'.
    • 'Rita' = universal principle of natural order (natural law), of Vedic origin; basis of Indian culture, legal theory, politics and philosophy.
    • Dharma and Rita appear as early as the Rigveda; Dharma = cosmic ordinance, natural or divine law; Rita = universal harmony where all things have a proper place and function.
    • Rita means an impersonal law; Dharma means the personal actions that create or keep the cosmic order.
    • Dharma = idea of obligations and doing one's duties to oneself and to others; Rita = fundamental moral law governing the universe and all in it.
    • Brihaspati (Deva-guru) is the teacher or priest of the gods.UPPSC

    Polity and administration

    • The most common system of rule in the Vedic era was hereditary monarchy; some cases of election by the people existed, but people favoured monarchy.
    • 'Sabha' and 'Samiti' are named as checks on the king's autocracy.
    • Sabha = assembly of the learned and elite (a council of ministers); Samiti = assembly of the common people.
    • The two cannot be told apart precisely; Rigveda mentions Sabha at least eight times and Samiti nine times.
    • Atharvaveda calls Sabha and Samiti the two daughters of Prajapati and shows them as two separate institutions.UPPSC
    • The tenth Mandal of the Rigveda also mentions Sabha and Samiti and appeals for unity between them, but their roles are not clearly separated there.
    • Rigveda mentions tribal or clan assemblies Sabha, Samiti and Vidatha; Sabha had the judicial function.

    Chapter 4 · Ancient India

    Buddhism

    232 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Ashoka's Rummindei Pillar inscription (Mauryan dynasty) shows that Lumbini was Buddha's birthplace.×5
    2. From Uruvela (Bodh Gaya) Buddha first went to Rishipattan (Mrigadava / Deer Park; present Sarnath, Varanasi) and gave his first sermon to five Brahmin sanyasis.×3
    3. The Bhumisparsha Mudra Buddha image of Sarnath belongs to the Gupta period.×3
    4. At Kushinagar he gave his last sermon to Subhadda, the last person he converted.×2
    5. Buddha died at Kushinagar (Kushinara), in the Republic of the Mallas, in 483 BC at age 80; this is called 'Mahaparinirvana'.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 66 UPPSC questions

    Birth and early life of Buddha

    • Gautama Buddha, founder of Buddhism, was born in 563 BC.
    • He was born at Lumbini near Kapilavastu (now in Nepal), in the Shakya Kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu.UPPSC
    • Father: Shuddhodana, chief of the Shakya clan.
    • Mother: Mayadevi (Mahamaya), of the Koliya clan.UPPSC
    • Childhood name: Siddhartha.
    • His mother died a few days after his birth; he was raised by his aunt Prajapati Gautami.
    • Married at 16 to Yashodhara, daughter of the Shakya clan; later Buddhist texts also call her Gopa, Bimba, Bhadkachhana.
    • Their son was Rahul.
    • Ashoka's Rummindei Pillar inscription (Mauryan dynasty) shows that Lumbini was Buddha's birthplace.UPPSC ×5
    • As per this inscription Ashoka came to Lumbini after the 20th year of his coronation and worshipped the place where Shakyamuni was born.
    • Ashoka freed Lumbini from Bali tax; it had to pay only an eighth share of the produce.
    • Buddha is also called 'Tathagata' and 'Shakyamuni' (also Siddhartha, Gautama); Parth and Gudakesh were names of Arjuna in the Mahabharata; Mihir and Prachhanna were not names of Buddha.

    Note from the book On 'another name of Buddha' the intended answer is 'none of these', but the Chhattisgarh commission gave 'Prachhanna' in both its initial and revised keys.

    • Tathagata means 'he who has won truth'; the exact meaning is uncertain and Buddhist commentaries give more than one meaning.
    • Buddha used 'Tathagata' for himself after enlightenment (bodhi); it became one of his stock epithets.
    • Shakyamuni = 'Sage of the Shakyas', as he was born in the Shakya clan; Nayaputta is not his epithet.
    • Nayaputta (Son of Nayas) is Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism; the name refers to his clan of origin.
    • Gautama Buddha is known as the 'Light of Asia' (Light Beam).UPPSC
    • Edwin Arnold wrote 'The Light of Asia' (subtitle 'The Great Renunciation') on Buddha's life; first edition July 1879; based on the contents of 'Lalit Vistara'.UPPSC

    Renunciation and enlightenment

    • Four sights deeply affected Buddha: an old man, a sick person, a dead body and an ascetic/monk.
    • Siddhartha left home at age 29, leaving wife and child while they slept, on his horse "Kanthaka", with Channa.
    • Leaving home is called 'Mahabhinishkramana' in Buddhist texts.UPPSC
    • He met Alara Kalama, Acharya of Sankhya philosophy, near Vaishali; Alara Kalama was a teacher of Buddha, famed for spiritual strength.UPPSC
    • Buddha learnt much from Alara Kalama, including meditation, and equalled him; Alara Kalama then asked him to stay and teach his students with him.
    • At Rajgriha Siddhartha met another Dharmacharya, Rudrak Ramputta.
    • After six years of effort he got enlightenment at age 35, on Vaishakh Purnima night, under a Pipal (Bodhi) tree at Bodh Gaya (Bihar); the Mahabodhi temple was built there.
    • After enlightenment he was called 'Buddha'.
    • Bodh Gaya (Uruvela) is on the bank of the river Niranjana.UPPSC
    • Present Bodhi Vriksha at Mahabodhi temple is not the original; as per Hiuen Tsang, king Shashank destroyed the original tree in the 7th century.
    • The present tree was planted on Alexander Cunningham's orders and is called the fifth generation tree; it is a heritage site and only its fallen leaves may be touched and picked.

    Note from the book Another source says the tree was planted twice by Ashoka, once by Pushyamitra Shunga, once by Purvaverma and last by Cunningham, making it the 6th generation; Bihar Tourism calls it 5th; BPSC deleted the question from its key.

    Preaching life

    • From Uruvela (Bodh Gaya) Buddha first went to Rishipattan (Mrigadava / Deer Park; present Sarnath, Varanasi) and gave his first sermon to five Brahmin sanyasis.UPPSC ×3
    • The first sermon is called 'Dharmachakrapravartana' (Pali: Dhammachakkhapavathana).UPPSC
    • The first sermon was about suffering, the cause of suffering and the path to end suffering.
    Event of Buddha's lifePlace
    BirthLumbini
    EnlightenmentBodh Gaya
    First preachingSarnath
    DeathKushinagar
    EventSymbol
    BirthLotus & Bull
    Great Departure (Mahabhinishkramana)Horse
    Enlightenment (Nirvana)Peepal (Bodhi tree)
    First Sermon (Dharmachakrapravartana)Wheel
    Death (Mahaparinirvana)StupaUPPSC
    • In Indian art the wheel with deer stands for the first preaching.UPPSC
    • After Sarnath he went to Koshala, Kapilavastu, Vaishali and Rajgriha to spread his teaching.
    • Of the kingdoms, Buddha was linked with Koshala and Magadha; he visited both to preach.
    • He spent the 2nd, 3rd and 4th rainy seasons at Rajgriha.
    • Bimbisara, ruler of Magadha, built the Mahavihara 'Venuvana' for his stay.
    • From Rajgriha he reached Vaishali, capital of the Lichchhavis, and spent the 5th rainy season there.
    • Lichchhavis built the famous 'Kutagrasala' in Mahavan for his stay.
    • Amrapali, royal courtesan of Vaishali, became his disciple and gave her mango grove (Amravatika) for the monks.
    • In the 8th year of enlightenment Buddha let women enter the Sangha as Bhikshuni at Vaishali, on the advice of his dear disciple Ananda.UPPSC
    • Mahaprajapati Gautami, the aunt who raised him, was the first woman to enter the Sangha.
    • Devadatta, Buddha's cousin, was first a follower and good monk, then an enemy; he tried to remove Buddha and head the Sangha himself, but failed.UPPSC
    • Buddhism became very popular in the Koshal state; most of Buddha's disciples were from Koshala.
    • Buddha gave the most sermons at Shravasti, capital of Koshala.UPPSC
    • Anathpindak, a rich merchant of Koshal, became his disciple and donated 'Jetavana' Vihara to the Sangha.
    • Koshal king Prasenjit and his family adopted Buddhism.
    • 'Pubharama' (Purva-Ram) vihara was built for the Sangha by Vishakha, a disciple of Buddha.
    • Buddha visited Kaushambi in the reign of King Udayana; influenced by Pindola Bharadwaj, Udayana turned to Buddhism and gave Ghoshitram Vihar to the Bhikshu Sangh.UPPSC
    • Buddha did not name any successor; he asked his followers to work towards liberation.

    Last days and Mahaparinirvana

    • Buddha spent his last rainy season at Beluva village, a suburb of Vaishali, at age eighty, with two disciples, one of them Ananda.UPPSC
    • At Pava (capital of Mallas) he stayed in the mango grove of Chund, a blacksmith.
    • Chund gave him 'Sukaramaddava' to eat; it caused sickness with bleeding and violent pains (food poisoning).
    • At Kushinagar he gave his last sermon to Subhadda, the last person he converted.UPPSC ×2
    • Buddha died at Kushinagar (Kushinara), in the Republic of the Mallas, in 483 BC at age 80; this is called 'Mahaparinirvana'.UPPSC ×2
    • Kushinagar was the capital of the Malla republic (first capital city of the Malla kingdom) and one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of the 6th century B.C.UPPSC
    • Mahaparinirvana temple is in Kushinagar district, Uttar Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Its Buddha statue was found in excavation in 1876-77 AD; carved from Chunar sandstone; 6.10 metres; it shows the dying Buddha lying on his right side.
    • Four holy places of Buddha's life: Lumbini (birth), Bodhgaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon), Kushinagar (death).

    Teachings and philosophy

    • Buddha's teachings rest mainly on purity and holiness of conduct.UPPSC
    • Buddha gave the 'Four Noble Truths' and the 'Noble Eightfold Path', accepted as basic tenets by all Buddhist sects.
    • Four Noble Truths (Arya Satya) in order: there is suffering → there is a cause of suffering → there is a cessation of suffering → there is a path to the cessation of suffering.UPPSC
    • Also worded: life means suffering; the origin of suffering is attachment; cessation is attainable; there is a path to cessation.
    • The eightfold path is the theme of the 'Dharma Chakra Pravartana Sutta' (sermon of the turning of the wheel of law); it is the way to end life's miseries and reach Nirvana.
    • Buddha was born near Kapilavastu, got enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, discarded the Vedas and Vedic rituals (favouring noble deeds), and preached the noble truths.UPPSC
    • Buddha believed in Karma, rebirth and attaining Nirvana, but not in the existence or power of God.UPPSC
    • Buddha's previous lives are recorded in the Jatakas.
    • Buddhism sees desire as the cause of all pain; Nirvana literally means 'blown out': the extinction of the flame of desire, a state free from desire, pain and pleasure.
    • As per Buddhist philosophy the cause of Samskara (impression) is Avidya (ignorance).
    • Avidya = absence of knowledge, not understanding reality; ignorance is the root of all suffering.
    • Buddhism preaches Anatmavada (no-self): no permanent self, soul or essence; this follows from Buddha's principle of Pratityasamutpada.
    • Pratityasamutpada is the essence of Buddhist teaching: life arises from interdependent preconditions; one state comes from a previous state.
    • Buddhism rejected the infallibility of the Vedas and the immortality of the soul, yet accepted rebirth and Karma.UPPSC
    • Anitya (impermanence) is an essential doctrine and one of the three marks of existence, given by Buddha himself: all conditioned existence is "transient, evanescent, inconstant".UPPSC
    • All temporal things, material or mental, are compounded objects in constant change, subject to decline and destruction; impermanence is a source of Dukkha.
    • The doctrine of momentariness was propounded by the Buddha; through it he explained impermanence.
    • The seed of Buddhist philosophy lies in Buddha's own teachings; he stressed a moral life to end suffering, not philosophical problems.
    • Later Buddhist scholars built a deep philosophy on Buddha's teachings.
    • Triratna (three jewels) of Buddhism: Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.UPPSC
    • 'Paramitas' = perfections; qualities a bodhisattva perfects to purify karma and kleshas and develop bodhichitta.
    • Upasaka = lay follower of Buddhism (not a monk); Parivrajaka = male renunciant and wanderer; a Buddhist Bhikkhu is primarily a parivrajaka.
    • Shramana = wandering monk in ascetic traditions such as Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivikism.
    • Pavarana: after the four months of rainy season (spent in the Mahavihar without preaching), monks confess their offences and plan future work.

    Buddhism and Jainism; society; spread and decline

    • Common to Buddhism and Jainism: indifference to the authority of the Vedas, denial of the efficacy of rituals, and non-injury to animals (Ahimsa).
    • Avoiding extremes of penance and enjoyment is a Buddhist trait, not a Jain one.
    • Both Buddhism and Jainism believe in Karma and rebirth: past actions affect present and future life.UPPSC
    • Karma idea: one who does evil in this life may be reborn as a worm; afflictions of this life are explained as effects of Karma of a previous life or of earlier misdeeds in this life.
    • Buddhism accepted the caste system to some extent, challenged the top rank of Brahmins, and placed some castes as low.UPPSC
    • Reasons for spread: simplicity (eightfold path, non-violence), appeal to non-Brahmins and lower classes (Dalits), missionary spirit, and preaching in the common people's language.UPPSC
    • Buddhism did not believe in caste distinctions.
    • Buddhism declined in early medieval India because Buddha came to be seen as an incarnation of Vishnu and became part of Vaishnavism.
    • Gupta kings supported the Brahmanical faith but were not opposed to Buddhism.
    • Pushyamitra Shunga (185-149 BCE), founder and first ruler of the Shunga empire, did not help Buddhism; Buddhist texts say he cruelly persecuted Buddhists.
    • Pushyamitra was a general of the Mauryan Empire; in 185 BCE he killed the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha and made himself emperor.
    • Neo-Buddhism (Navayana, "new vehicle") is B.R. Ambedkar's re-interpretation of Buddhism.
    • Navayana rejects renouncing monk and monasticism, Karma, rebirth, samsara, meditation, enlightenment and the four noble truths; it revises Buddha's teachings on class struggle and social equality.
    • Karmapa Lama belongs to the Kangyupa sect of Tibetan Buddhism.UPPSC

    Buddhist councils

    • The Sangha held several councils to reach agreement on doctrine and practice; Buddha's teachings existed only in oral tradition.
    CouncilYearPlacePresidentRuler
    First483 BCRajgrihaMahakassapa (Mahakashyapa)Ajatashatru
    Second383 BCVaishaliSabakami (Subukami)Kalasoka

    • Council places in order: Rajgriha → Vaishali → Pataliputra → Kundalavana.UPPSC ×2
    • First council was held soon after Buddha's Mahaparinirvana at Rajgriha (Rajgir).UPPSC
    • It met in the Saptaparni Cave of Rajgriha.UPPSC
    • Mahakassapa presided over the first council.UPPSC ×2
    • Its patron was the Magadha king Ajatashatru.UPPSC
    • Aim of the first council: preserve Buddha's teachings (Sutta) and rules for disciples (Vinaya); Ananda recited the Suttas and Upali the Vinaya; Abhidhamma Pitaka was also included.
    • Second council: at Vaishali, 100 years after Buddha's death.UPPSC
    • Second council was held in the reign of Kalasoka; Sabakami presided.
    • Third council: at Pataliputra in Ashoka's reign.
    • Fourth council was held at Kundalavana in Kashmir; so it was the one not held in Bihar.
    • Fourth council was held under the Kushan king Kanishka.UPPSC
    • Vasumitra presided over the fourth council; Ashvaghosha was his deputy.
    • The fourth council clearly split Buddhism into Hinayana and Mahayana; Mahasanghikas dominated it.

    Sects: Hinayana, Mahayana and others

    • In the first century, those holding the traditional faith were called 'Sthavira', later 'Theravada'; led by Mahakatyayana.
    • Those who accepted change were called 'Mahasanghika'; led by Mahakassapa.
    • Sthaviravadins belong to Hinayana; the Lokottaravadin sect was an offshoot of the Mahasanghikas; deification of Buddha by Mahasanghikas fostered Mahayana.
    • Basic difference: Hinayana sees Buddha as a great man; Mahayana treats him as God and worships him through idols.UPPSC
    • Buddha was raised to the position of God in Kanishka's period.
    • Buddha's were the first human statues worshipped in India; Mahayana followers began it, so Buddhism laid the foundation of idol worship in the country.UPPSC
