    Literal meaningLesser VehicleGreater Vehicle
    View of BuddhaA great manA god
    NatureIndividualistic: each person gets salvation by own effortSimple and accessible principles; common devotees matter along with monks; believes in soul and rebirth
    Idol worshipNot believed inBelieved in
    PracticeVery strict worship; follows monk lifeIdol worship and rituals
    IdealTo attain 'Arhat''Bodhisattva'
    Major sectsVaibhashika and SautrantikaShunyawad (Madhyamik) and Vigyanwad (Yogachar)
    • Mahayana features: belief in Buddha's divinity and many forms and incarnations; the path of the Bodhisattva; idol worship and rituals.
    • Bodhisattva = bodhi (enlightenment) + sattva (essence, spirit / living being): one who aspires to enlightenment and does altruistic acts.
    • Bodhisattva is the goal and ideal of Mahayana (not Hinayana): a compassionate one who delays his own salvation to help all sentient beings.
    • Avalokiteshvara, Bodhisattva of infinite compassion, is also called Padmapani ("Lotus-Bearer"); the sculpture stands in tribhanga (tri-bent) pose.
    • Maitreya is the 'future Buddha' of Buddhist tradition.
    • Maitreya first appears in the Cakkavatti Sutta of the Pali Tripitaka, where Buddha speaks of a future when dharma is forgotten and Maitreya gains awakening with a Sangha of thousands.
    • This is the only time the historical Buddha is recorded as mentioning Maitreya.
    • Sautrantika and Sammitiya were sects of Buddhism, not Jainism.
    • Sarvastivada = "doctrine that all exist": past, present and future phenomena all have some form of existence; things empirical are transient but dharma factors exist forever.
    • Vajrayana was the main form of Buddhism in the medieval (Sultanate) period; it flourished mostly in the 8th century A.D.
    • Vajrayana principles are in 'Arya Manjushrimulkalpa' and 'Guhyasamaja'.
    • 'Aryamanjushrimulakalpa' is a Buddhist tantric text linked with Mahayana and Vajrayana; it gives instructions on rituals, meditations and practices.

    Scholars

    • Nagarjuna's main contribution was the concept of Sunyata (doctrine of void).UPPSC
    • Nagarjuna wrote "Madhyamikakarika" (Madhyamika school), which has his famous words on emptiness or co-arising.
    • Nagarjuna was an eminent figure in Kanishka's court; Hiuen Tsang called him one of the world's four great guiding powers.
    • In "Madhyamikakarika" Nagarjuna discussed the theory of relativity; he is called the 'Indian Einstein'.
    • Chinese mythology says Nagarjuna travelled to China and preached Buddhism.
    • Aryadeva was a Buddhist philosopher and disciple of Nagarjuna; Dignaga was a Buddhist scholar; Nathamuni was a Vaishnava scholar, seen as the first teacher of the Vaishnava sect.
    • Sanghabhuti, Indian Buddhist monk who went to China at the end of the 4th century AD, wrote a commentary on the Sarvastivada Vinaya.
    • Sarvastivada Vinaya gives rules of monastic life for the Sarvastivada school; it was the most common vinaya tradition in early China; Sanghabhuti's commentary explained the Vinaya rules for Chinese Buddhist practitioners.

    Buddhist literature

    • Tripitaka is the most important holy book of Buddhism: the collection of Buddha's teachings in three parts, compiled after his death.UPPSC ×2
    • Sutta Pitaka: sayings, sermons and teachings of Buddha; the book of discourses on ethics and doctrine; the basic doctrinal part of the canon.
    • Digha Nikaya, a part of the Sutta Pitaka, has 34 long Suttas with doctrinal expositions, legends and moral rules.
    • Vinaya Pitaka: rules for members of the Sangha and monks (monastic life).UPPSC
    • Abhidhamma Pitaka: philosophical exposition of the Dhamma.
    • Abhidhamma Pitaka has seven books: Yamaka, Patthana, Kathavatthu, Puggalapannatti, Dhatukatha, Vibhanga and Dhammasangani.
    • Mahavamsa gives regional histories of Buddhism.UPPSC
    • Jatakas = texts with stories of Buddha's previous births; kept alive orally before being written in Pali.
    • Divyavadana and Aryamanjushree Mulakalpa were written in Sanskrit; Deepvamsa and Mahavamsa (history of ancient India and Sri Lanka) in Pali.
    TextAuthor
    MilindpanhoNagasena
    Buddhcharita, Saundarananda, Sariputra PrakaranaAshwaghosha
    MadhyamikakarikaNagarjuna
    VishuddhimaggaBuddhaghosha
    AbhidhammakoshVasubandhu
    • 'Visuddhimagga' is a treatise on Buddhist practice and Theravada Abhidhamma.

    Centres of learning

    • Main Buddhist centres of learning (Gupta and post-Gupta period): Nalanda, Vikramshila and Vallabhi; Nagpur was not one.
    • They drew students from many Janapadas and from abroad: China, Japan, Tibet and other countries of South-East Asia.
    • Taxila and Nalanda had the status of universities.
    • Nalanda was the main centre for Mahayana education; Vallabhi for Hinayana.
    • Vallabhi (Vallabhipura) was in Gujarat; capital of the ancient Maitraka dynasty.UPPSC
    • Vikramshila Mahavihara was founded by Pala king Dharmapala, who also built temples and monasteries there.
    • Nalanda: large Buddhist monastery in Magadha (Bihar), near Rajgriha (Rajgir); it came up and flourished in the Gupta period.
    • Nalanda was famous for Buddhist religious philosophy.
    • Nalanda, called the world's first international university, was founded in 450 AD in the reign of Kumaragupta.
    • Kumaragupta I first gave donations to Nalanda Vihara; later Buddhgupta, Tathagatgupta and Baladitya also donated.
    • Alexander Cunningham identified the site as Nalanda University (year printed as 1915-16).
    • Kautilya (Chanakya; 4th-3rd century BCE; minister of Chandragupta Maurya and Bindusara; author of Arthashastra) was linked with Takshashila, not Nalanda.
    • By the end of the 12th century Nalanda Mahavihara waned due to Muslim invasion; it had been losing importance as Pala rulers of Bengal gave protection to Vikramshila instead.
    • Nava Nalanda Mahavihara is a modern Pali and Buddhist research centre; foundation stone laid on 20 November 1951.
    • Odantapuri (Uddantapura), in Magadha (Bihar), was a major education centre; founded by Pala emperor Gopala I.
    • Dhanyakataka (present Dharnikota, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh): major Buddhist centre under the Mahasanghikas; key Deccan town and capital of the later Satavahanas.
    • Excavation at Dharnikota has revealed viharas there and nearby.
    • Ashokaram Vihar was built at Pataliputra by Ashoka, under the monk Indragupta, as per the Mahavansh.UPPSC
    • Rajgir is a pilgrim centre for Buddhists, Hindus and Jains, famous for hot water springs.
    • Lion Capital of Ashoka is at Sarnath, not Rajgir; Lothal has an ancient dockyard; Sarnath saw the first sermon; Nalanda was a great seat of Buddhist learning.

    Stupa, Chaitya and Vihara

    • Stupa, Chaitya and Vihara are all related to Buddhism.
    • Chaitya is a place of worship (a meeting or assembly hall used for prayer); Vihara is the dwelling place of monks, their shelter in the rainy season.UPPSC
    • "Chaitya" literally means 'related to Chita (funeral pyre)'.
    • Samadhis built over buried bodies were first called Chaitya or Stupa; relics of great men kept in them made Chaityas centres of worship.
    • Houses built near monasteries or Chaitya Griha were called Vihara.
    • The word 'Stupa' is first used in the Rig Veda, where it means "tree stem".
    • Rigveda speaks of a stupa raised by king Varuna above the forest in a place with no foundation; anything raised like a heap or pile may have been called a stupa.
    • The idea of the stupa is older than Buddhism (word found in Rig Veda, Atharva Veda, Vajasaneyi Samhita, Taittiriya Samhita); stupas were usually repositories of relics and later became votive and commemorative.
    • 'Stupa' literally means 'to pile up': something raised by accumulation; building stupas in memory of the dead existed before Buddhism.
    • The practice grew from old burial customs: tombs over the remains of dead community leaders later became stupas.
    • In Buddhism a stupa is a monument (dirt burial mound faced with stone) to keep the remains of Buddha or his chief disciples; the earliest held portions of Buddha's ashes.
    • Four types of stupa: Sharirik (body), Paribhogika, Uddheshika (objective) and Vratanusthit (worshipping).
    • Sanchi Stupa is not linked to any event of Buddha's life; Bodhgaya = enlightenment, Sarnath = Dharma Chakra Pravartana, Kushinagar = death.UPPSC ×2
    • Bharhut and Sanchi stupas were built in Ashoka's reign; some sources also place Dhamekh stupa in Ashoka's reign.
    • Amaravati stupa was built in the Satavahana period.UPPSC

    Note from the book The book says the order of building of Bharhut, Sanchi and Dhamekh stupas cannot be decided, so the stupa-chronology question should be excluded from evaluation.

    • Devnimori (Devni Mori) is in Arvalli district, Gujarat; remains of a Buddhist monastery and stupa of the 3rd-4th century AD were found.
    • Vishwa Shanti Stupa (World Peace Pagoda) on the hills of Rajgir, Bihar, is called the highest stupa in the world (height printed as 400 metres).
    • Kesariya Stupa (East Champaran, Bihar): about 104 feet high and 400 feet in circumference; called the largest and tallest Buddhist stupa in the world.UPPSC
    • By ASI's 1998 excavation and State Government literature, Kesariya is one foot taller than Borobudur (Indonesia).
    • Early Chaityagrihas and Viharas of Guntuphalli (then West Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh; now NTR district) are rock-cut; Chaityas and Viharas of Eastern Deccan are usually rock-cut.UPPSC
    • The largest and most evolved Chaitya cave of the Hinayana phase is at Karle, Pune district, Maharashtra.UPPSC
    • Kanheri caves (Salsette Island, Mumbai; in Sanjay Gandhi National Park): cave 41 (earlier 23) has an Avalokiteshvara with four arms and eleven heads, the only such statue in India.UPPSC
    • Kanheri, called Kanhashail, Krishnagiri, Kanhagiri in old records, was a main Buddhist centre; it has the most caves on a single hill; built in 1st century B.C., in use till 11th century AD.
    • Worship of the eleven-headed Bodhisattva was current in China, Chinese Turkistan, Cambodia and Japan in 7th-8th CE.

    Images, mudras and paintings

    • Gandhara art flourished under the Kushanas, especially Kanishka, a great patron of art and architecture; standing statues of Buddha belong to the Kushana period.UPPSC
    • Both sitting and standing Buddha statues were carved in the Mathura school.
    • Kushana art of Gandhara is known for the many sculptures found in Buddhist stupas and monasteries.
    • Gandharan Buddha image drew on Hellenistic realism, tempered by Persian, Scythian and Parthian models; its main subject is Buddha's life.
    • Gandharan images show Dharma Chakra, Meditation, Abhaya and Varada postures; the Sarnath first sermon is shown by the Dharma Chakra mudra.
    • First Buddha statue: Mathura as per V.S. Agrawal; Kaushambi as per Hiuen Tsang; other historians credit Gandhara; so it cannot be said for certain where it was first made.
    • Bhumisparsha Mudra: Buddha seated, right hand over right knee reaching the ground, palm inward, touching the lotus throne; left hand in lap, palm up.
    • It shows Buddha calling the earth to witness his enlightenment (purity) despite Mara; Mara tried to frighten him with armies of demons and was defeated.
    • The Bhumisparsha Mudra Buddha image of Sarnath belongs to the Gupta period.UPPSC ×3
    • This mudra stands for steadfastness; Dhyani Buddha Akshobhya is linked with it for keeping his vow never to feel anger or disgust.
    • It also shows the union of skilful means (upaya; right hand touching earth) and wisdom (prajna; left hand in lap).
    • The Giant Buddha statue at Bodh Gaya is 80 feet high, in dhyana mudra, seated on a lotus in the open; built with help of the Daijokyo sect of Japan.
    • It took seven years to complete; made of sandstone blocks and red granite.
    • The painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani is in Cave I of Ajanta.
    • Padmapani in Sanskrit = "one who holds the lotus"; he is shown among devotees (princesses and commoners), with long dark hair under a jewelled crown, a blue lotus in his right hand.

    Chapter 5 · Ancient India

    Jain Religion

    166 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Parshvanath attained Parinirvana on Mount Sammed Shikhar (Sammet Shikhar/Sammeta); so it is a Jain pilgrimage place.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 25 UPPSC questions

    Basic terms and the 24 Tirthankaras

    • Jain comes from the Sanskrit word 'Jina' = conqueror/victor.
    • Founders of Jainism are called Tirthankara; Jain Mahatmas are called Nirgranth.
    • The word Tirthankara is related to the Jain religion; Jainism has 24 Tirthankaras who spread Jain philosophy from time to time.UPPSC
    • The 24 Tirthankaras in order: 1 Rishabhdev (Adinath), 2 Ajitnath, 3 Sambhavnath, 4 Abhinandan(nath), 5 Sumatinath, 6 Padmaprabha, 7 Suparshvanath, 8 Chandraprabha, 9 Pushpadant (Suvidhinath), 10 Sheetalnath, 11 Shreyansanath, 12 Vasupujya, 13 Vimalnath, 14 Anantnath, 15 Dharmanath, 16 Shantinath, 17 Kunthunath, 18 Aranath, 19 Mallinath, 20 Munisuvrata, 21 Naminath, 22 Neminath (Arishtanemi), 23 Parshvanath, 24 Mahavira Swami.
    • Nathamuni was NOT a Jain Tirthankara; Chandraprabha, Nemi and Sambhav were.UPPSC
    • Chronological order: Abhinandan (4th) → Padmaprabhu (6th) → Vimalnath (13th) → Munisuvrata Nath (20th).UPPSC
    • Rishabhdev = first Tirthankara and originator of the Jain religion; other names: Rishabhnath, Adinath, Vrishabhnath.UPPSC
    • Vasupujya = 12th Tirthankara; attained Nirvana (Moksha) at Champapur (Bihar), not Sammed Shikhar.UPPSC

    Parshvanath

    • Parshvanath = 23rd Tirthankara; born in Kashi (Varanasi/Banaras) in 850 BC; mainly associated with Varanasi.UPPSC
    • Parshvanath's father = Ashwasen (Aswasena), king of Kashi; mother = Queen Vama; he belonged to the Ikshvaku dynasty.
    • Parshvanath lived as a prince of Varanasi; at age 30 he renounced the world and became a monk.
    • Parshvanath meditated for 84 days before attaining Kaivalya Jnana; got Kaivalya in Ashrampad Udyan near Varanasi.
    • Parshvanath attained Parinirvana on Mount Sammed Shikhar (Sammet Shikhar/Sammeta); so it is a Jain pilgrimage place.UPPSC ×2
    • Parshvanath's four restraints: Ahimsa (non-violence), Aparigraha (non-possession), Asteya (not stealing), Satya (truth).

    Mahavira Swami: life

    • Mahavira Swami was born in Kundagram (Kundalpur) near Vaishali (Bihar) about 599 BC.UPPSC
    • Childhood (original) name of Mahavira = Vardhaman.
    • Father Siddhartha = chief of the Jnatrika (Gyatrik) Kshatriya Sangh/clan, under the Vajji of Vaishali.
    • Mother Trishala (Videhdatta) = sister (not daughter) of Chetaka, head/king of the Lichchhavi republic.
    • Nandivardhan was Mahavira's elder brother.
    • Mahavira was married: wife = Yashoda (daughter of Kundinya Gotra).
    • Mahavira's daughter = Anojja (Priyadarshana); she was married to Jamali.
    • Jamali, Mahavira's son-in-law, was his first disciple/follower.UPPSC
    • Jamali met Mahavira at Kshatriya-Kundagram (Mahavira's birth village) and took the vow together with 500 of the warrior caste.
    • Mahavira was related to Bimbisara of Magadha, who married Chellana, daughter of Chetaka.
    • 'Kaivalya' = the Jain word for complete knowledge (complete intellect).
    • Mahavira got Kaivalya under a Sal tree on the bank of the Rijupalika river near Jrimbhik village, after 12 years of hard austerity.UPPSC
    • After Kaivalya Mahavira was called Kevalin, Arhat (Yogya), Jin (conqueror) and Nirgranth (free from bonds).
    • After Kaivalya Mahavira began to preach his principles; he propagated Jain philosophy in the 6th century BC.
    • Chetaka, Lichchhavi chief of Vaishali and Mahavira's uncle, greatly helped spread Jainism.
    • Mahavira = 24th and last Tirthankara of the Jain religion.
    • Mahavira attained Nirvana at about age 72 in 527 BC at Pavapuri, near Rajgriha (Rajgir), near Patna.
    • Mahavira did not accept the authority of the Vedas and opposed the related social-cultural traditions and humbugs.

    Jain philosophy and doctrines

    • Leaving the extreme views of selfish people and atheists, Mahavira took the middle path called 'Syadvad' — a Jain doctrine.
    • Syadvad is also called Saptabhanginaya = knowledge is relative.
    • Jain philosophy revolves around two closely connected main doctrines: Anekantavada (core theory, a metaphysical concept) and Syadvada.
    • Anekantavada: every being has numerous properties; permanent property that makes a thing's nature = attribute (guna); accidental property = mode (Paryaya).
    • Syadvada: our knowledge is partial and relative because passion, anger, greed obstruct it; yet we take it as complete and absolute.
    • Sunyavada and Sarvastivada are related to Buddhism, not Jainism.
    • Monks give up all worldly enjoyments and take five great vows (Mahavratas): Ahimsa, Satya, Brahmacharya, Asteya, Aparigraha.
    • Mahavratas are hard for ordinary people, so they follow Anuvratas (Ahimsa, Satya, Brahmacharya, Asteya, Aparigraha Anuvrat) — a Jain concept.
    • Three means to Moksha = Ratnatraya/Triratna of Jainism: Right Belief (faith), Right Conduct (action), Right Knowledge.UPPSC
    • Jain Triratna names: Samyag darshana, Samyag jnan, Samyag charitra.
    • Triratna exists in Buddhism too: the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.
    • Sanvar Tattva = freedom from bondage and stopping the inflow of karmic matter into the soul.
    • Nirjara element = destruction of Karma.
    • When the remaining karma of life is exhausted, the soul attains Moksha.
    • Anant Chattushtya = Anant Gyan (infinite knowledge), Anant Darshan (infinite perception), Anant Virya (infinite power), Anant Anand (infinite bliss).
    • Jain belief: the world is created and maintained by Universal Law; the universe runs by itself on its cosmic laws (laws of nature); no almighty is needed.
    • Jainism: the universe and all its substances are eternal, without beginning or end; so no concept of 'final annihilation of the world'.UPPSC
    • All substances change gradually; old forms give way to new ones without losing their inherent qualities.
    • Jain reality (Tattva) has three characteristics: origination, decay and permanence (Nityata); also described as attributes and modifications.
    • Origination and decay are only changes of form; permanence = essential attributes that stay constant; an entity is real (Sat) when it has both permanence and transformation.
    • Basic point of Jainism = Ahimsa (non-violence); Jainism is called the religion of Ahimsa; Ahimsa is above all concepts, rules, customs and practices.UPPSC
    • Cardinal principles of Jainism: Ahimsa, Anekantvad and Aparigraha.
    • Jainism: every object, even the smallest particle, has a soul — also earth, water, fire, air, plants, rocks, running water.
    • Jain acharya Gurudev Chitrabhanu: "the universe is not for humanity alone; it is a field of evolution for all living beings."
    • Jain doctrine: Karma is the bane of the soul and must be ended; the surest way to annihilate karma is penance.
    • Law of Karma: every action (thought, word, deed) produces an effect that causes another action; this chain of cause and effect = Karma.
    • Karma is also seen as extremely subtle matter that enters the soul and hides its natural, transparent, pure qualities.
    • By its karma a soul transmigrates and is reborn in heaven or hell, or as human or animal.
    • Samadhi Maran (Sallekhana, Sanyasna Maran) = last vow of the Jain ethical code.
    • Samadhi Maran: ascetics and lay votaries slowly reduce food and liquid at life's end; allowed in old age, incurable disease or near death.

    Jain Sangha, split and sects

    • Mahavira set up a Sangh in his lifetime; it had 11 chief followers called 'Ganadhar'.
    • The 11 Ganadhars: Indrabhuti, Agnibhuti, Vayubhuti (three brothers), Arya Vyakta, Sudharma, Mandavya, Mauryaputra, Akampana, Achal, Metarya, Prabhasa.
    • After Mahavira's death Sudharma became the first head of the Jain Sangha.
    • After Sudharma, Jambu was president of the Sangh for 44 years.
    • Sambhutavijay and Bhadrabahu were presidents of the Sangha (printed both as "at the time of the Maurya ruler" and "at the time of the last Nand ruler").
    • Sambhutavijay and Bhadrabahu were the last to know the ancient Jain texts, the 14 Purvas.
    • Fourteen Purvas = earliest (ancient) Jain scripture, preached by all Tirthankaras, given by Mahavira.
    • About 150 years after Mahavira, when Bhadrabahu headed the order, a severe famine raged for 12 years in Magadha (ruler printed as Nand dynasty in one place, Maurya in another).
    • Pataliputra, the capital city, had become the centre of learning and knowledge at that time.
    • In the famine monks could not keep the code of conduct; Bhadrabahu migrated to the South with many followers and spread Jainism in South India.
    • Bhadrabahu's migrant followers were mostly unclad → called Digambars (skyclad).
    • Sthulabhadra and those who stayed in the north covered the body with plain white cloth → Shwetambars; Sthulabhadra = first founder of the Shwetambar creed.
    PointShwetambaraDigambara
    ClothesWear white clothesCompletely naked, perform austerity (Tapsya)
    Moksha for a womanPossibleNot possible
    Food after enlightenmentBelieve in taking foodAgainst it
    Mahavira's marriageWas marriedWas unmarried
    19th Tirthankara MallinathWas a womanWas a man
    • Yapaniya = a Jain sect, believed to have come out of the Digambaras, but it also followed some Shwetambar views.UPPSC
    • Yapaniyas worshipped nude images of the Tirthankaras in their temples.
    • Sthanakvasi = a sect of Shwetambara Jainism; it arose from the earlier reformist sect 'Lonka' founded by Lonkasha.
    • Sthanakvasi belief: idol worship is not essential for soul purification and Nirvana.

    Jain councils and literature

    • First Jain Council (Sabha): Pataliputra, 4th century BC (about 310 BC), reign of Chandragupta Maurya, president Sthulbhadra; 12 Angas compiled and Shwetambara Agama edited there.UPPSC
    • Followers of Bhadrabahu did not take part in the first Jain council.
    • As all the ancient Jain texts had been destroyed, a Jain council was organised in the 4th century BC to recompile them.
    • The Shwetambara canon includes the 12 Angas, the canonical texts based on Mahavira's teaching; they were compiled at Pataliputra, not first at Vallabhi.
    • Second Jain Council: Vallabhi (Gujarat), 6th century AD (512 AD), president Devardhigani Kshamashraman.
    • Second council compiled: 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnas, 6 Chedsutras, 4 Mulsutras, 2 Chulikasutras; the holy books got final form here.
    • Jain literature is called 'Aagam' (principle): 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnas, 6 Chedsutras, 4 Mulsutras, 2 Chulikasutras.
    • All the earliest Jain religious literature, including the twelve Angas, was written in Ardha-Magadhi.UPPSC
    • The 12 Angas: Acharanga-Sutra, Sutrakritanga, Sthananga, Samavayanga, Bhagavati Vyakhyaprajnapti, Jnatrdharmakatha, Upasakadasah, Antakrddasah, Anuttaraupapatikadasah, Prasnavyakarana, Vipaksruta, Dristivada.
    • Each of the 12 Angas has a related Upanga; Upangas describe the universe, classes of beings, astronomy, time division, life after death.
    • 10 Prakirnas = supplements to the major texts.
    • 6 Chedsutras = rules for Jain monks: Jitakalpa, Brihatkalpa, Nishith, Mahanishith, Vyavhar (behaviour), Aachar Dasha.
    • 4 Mulsutras hold Jain sermons, forest life, duties of monks, rules of Yam: Dashvaikalik, Utaradhyayan, Avshayak, Pindniryukti (Pakshik Sutra).
    • 2 Chulikasutras = Nandi-sutra and Anuyogadwara-Sutra: independent Jain texts, a kind of encyclopaedia; they have moral stories for monks.
    • Therigatha is a Buddhist scripture (early nuns/bhikshunis tell their struggles and attainments), not Jain; Acarangasutra, Sutrakritanga, Brihatkalpasutra are Jain.

    Patrons, centres, temples

    • Jain literature calls Samprati, grandson of Ashoka, the patron of Jainism; Ujjain became a major Jain centre in his rule.
    • Mathura = second major Jain centre; many temples, statues and records found there.
    • Kharavela, Chedi king of Kalinga (1st century BC), was a follower and great patron of Jainism; he supported Jain monks and gave for their livelihood.
    • Kharavela cut caves for Jain monks in the Udaygiri and Khandagiri hills near Bhubaneswar.
    • Khajuraho temples are related to Hinduism and Jainism; built under the Rajput Chandela dynasty.
    • Dilwara Jain temples of Mount Abu are made of marble; Vimal Vasahi is the most prominent among them.
    • Vimal Vasahi was built by Vimalshah, Samanta of Chalukya (Solanki) king Bhimdev I of Gujarat.
    • Shravanabelagola is in Karnataka; its Gomateshwara statue is one of the most important tirthas of Jainism.
    • Gomateshwara statue shows Bahubali, son of first Tirthankara Rishabhdev — not the last Tirthankara.
    • The Bahubali (Gomateshwar) statue was built about 981 AD by Chamundaraya, minister of Ganga ruler Rachamalla IV (Panchamalla).UPPSC
    • Mahamastakabhisheka = Jain festival for Lord Bahubali, held at Shravanabelagola every 12 years; the statue is 18 metres high.
    • Tawang Monastery (Tawang district, Arunachal Pradesh) = India's largest monastery.
    • Hoysaleshwara temple is dedicated to Shiva.
    • Kaushambi = famous pilgrimage of both Jains and Buddhists in Uttar Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Present Kaushambi district was carved out of Prayagraj on 4 April 1997; it is 55 km south-west of Prayagraj.
    • Kaushambi is mentioned many times in Vedic and Jain literature; Jain texts: named for its many Kushamb trees.
    • Puranas: Nicakshu, sixth in line from Parikshita, shifted the capital from Hastinapur to Kaushambi after floods, locust invasion and upheavals in the Kuru family.
    • Buddha preached many times at Kaushambi and made many disciples; its most famous monastery = Ghoshitram, built by Shresthi Ghoshit.
    • Ikshvakus of southern India (3rd–4th century) followed Vedic religion but also supported Buddhism — they were not hostile to it.
    • Pala rulers of eastern India were patrons of Buddhism; Bengal became the main nucleus of Buddhism under them.
    • Gautama Buddha's mother Maya, wife of Suddhodana, was a Koliya princess.

    Ajivika sect

    • Makkhali Gosala was first a disciple of Mahavira, then fell out with him and founded the Ajivika sect.UPPSC
    • Sources name Ajivika scholars Nanda Vaccha and Kisa Samkicca even before Gosala; Gosala is credited with first popularising the sect.
    • Ajivika belief = 'Niyativad': everything in the world is controlled by destiny (fate); man is incapable.UPPSC
    • Makkhali Gosala, contemporary of Mahavira and Buddha, was the most important Ajivika leader; central idea "Niyati"; Ajivikas held regular sabhas (meetings).
    • Ajivikas were egalitarian and rejected the rigid caste and class system.
    • Ajivikas believed in determinism (fatalism) and in austerity; they held the rebirth cycle cannot be changed by personal effort.
    • Ajivikas: all joys and sorrows are preordained by an unchangeable cosmic order; no free will or moral effort can change fate.
    • Ajivika austerities: long silence and fasting, seen as part of their predestined path.
    • Ajivikas enjoyed great respect in the Maurya era; they were influential even under Bindusara.UPPSC

    Note from the book Ajivika question on forest-dwelling: UPPSC gave "both statements" as answer, but by the sources "only II" (respect in Maurya era) is more appropriate.

    • Ajivikas were nude wandering ascetics who begged in villages and towns and lived in rock-cut caves; not described as forest dwellers.
    • Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha had caves cut in the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills as residences for Ajivika monks.

    Chapter 6 · Ancient India

    Shaiva, Bhagavata Religion

    120 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Varaha = third incarnation of Vishnu; killed the giant-king Hiranyaksha and freed the Earth from him.×2
    2. Nayanars = devotees of Shiva (Shaivas); they spread Shaivism in South India; number = 63.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 17 UPPSC questions

    Yugas, Astika and Nastika

    • Ancient Indian cosmogony: four epochs (yugas) in order = Krita → Treta → Dvapara → Kali.
    • 6th century BC context: Astika = believed in the authenticity of the Vedas; Nastika = did not believe in it.UPPSC

    Bhagavata (Vaishnava) religion: origin

    • Vaishnava religion developed from the Bhagavata religion.
    • Traditional originator of Bhagavata religion = Lord Krishna (Vasudeva), a Vrishni (Satvat) descendant, basically from Mathura.
    • Chhandogya Upanishad describes Krishna as son of Devaki and disciple of Ghor Angirasa.
    • Earliest form of Vaishnavism = worship of Krishna, son of Devaki; first worshippers of Vasudeva Krishna = Bhagavatas.UPPSC
    • Krishna's early name (Vasudev) was current in Panini's age; Panini mentions Vasudev worship and Bhagavata Dharma and calls Vasudev's worshippers 'Vasudevak'.
    • Rig Veda mentions Vishnu as God of the sky.
    • Three major gods of the later Vedic period: Prajapati, Rudra, Vishnu.
    • Vishnu is considered guardian and protector of the people.
    • Patanjali described Vasudev as a form of Vishnu; in Vishnu Purana Vasudev is also a name of Vishnu.
    • When the Krishna-Vishnu link was joined with Narayana, Vaishnavism became 'Pancharatra Dharma'.
    • The religion was first prevalent in Mathura and nearby areas, then slowly spread to other parts of India.
    • Megasthenes (Greek ambassador): people of Sursen (Mathura) worshipped 'Heracles' = Vasudeva Krishna.
    • Garuda Pillar of Vidisha (Besnagar) = first stone monument and earliest epigraphic evidence of Bhagavata religion.UPPSC
    • The pillar was set up by Heliodorus, Greek (Yavana) ambassador from Taxila (Takshila), who accepted the Bhagavata religion.UPPSC
    • Besnagar inscription calls Heliodorus 'Bhagavata' and Vasudeva 'Devadevas' (God of Gods); it relates only to Vasudeva.
    • Bhagavata cult recognises Navadha (9) Bhakti — nine forms of bhakti — for Moksha.UPPSC
    • Balarama (Haldhar), brother of Krishna, is shown in art holding a plough.UPPSC

    Vaishnavism under Guptas and later

    • Bhagavata/Vaishnava religion reached its peak under the Guptas; they made it the state religion.
    • Most Gupta rulers held the title 'Parambhagavata'; Garuda, the mount (Vahana) of Vishnu, was the Gupta state symbol.
    • Mehrauli Pillar: Chandra (identified as Chandragupta II) set up the Vishnu flag on Vishnupad hill.
    • Bhitari Pillar inscription: Skandagupta installed a statue of Vishnu.
    • Amarsimha gives 39 names of Vishnu in his book Amarkosha.
    • Chalukyas of Eastern Vengi were Vaishnavas; Garuda was their state symbol, like the Guptas.
    • Rashtrakuta king Dantidurg built the Dashavatara temple at Ellora; it tells the story of Vishnu's ten incarnations.
    • 'Dashavatar Charitam' was composed by Kshemendra.
    • Varaha = third incarnation of Vishnu; killed the giant-king Hiranyaksha and freed the Earth from him.UPPSC ×2
    • Purana pictures: Varaha balances the earth on his tusk (teeth) and rises from the sea.
    • Varaha form: boar head on a human body with four arms holding Shankha, Chakra, Gada, Padma.

    Alvars and Nayanars

    • Medieval devotional spirit spread mainly in South India, specially Tamil regions, through two sects: Alvars and Nayanars.
    • Alvars = devotees of Vishnu; they spread Vaishnavism in South India; number = 12.
    • 'Alvar' = one who is immersed in the experience of God, the omnipresent mysterious one.
    • Poigai, Pudam and Thirumangai were Alvar saints; Tirugyan was not.UPPSC
    • Andal = the only female saint among the 12 Alvars.
    • Nayanars = devotees of Shiva (Shaivas); they spread Shaivism in South India; number = 63.UPPSC ×2
    • Notable Nayanars: Tirugyan, Sundar Murthy, Sambundar, Appar, Manikkavachakar.
    • Alvars and Nayanars: personal love and dedication to God is the only way to Moksha; they opposed caste rigidity.
    • Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis made devotional (Bhakti) religion popular in Northern India.
    • Nathpanthis, Siddhas, Yogis criticised ritual, conventional religion and the social order, and advocated renouncing the world.

    Gita, Vedanta, epics

    • Bhagavad Gita gives equal importance to Jnana, Karma and Bhakti as means of liberation.UPPSC
    • Advaita Vedanta: Shankaracharya accepted Brahma as the only truth.
    • Vedanta and Vishistadvaita Vedanta give supremacy to Bhakti; Mimamsa mainly propounds Karma.
    • Main teaching (central theme) of the Gita = Nishkama Karma Yoga; Gita holds it supreme among all yogas.
    • Nishkama Karma = to act unselfishly, without thought of personal gain or expecting good in return.
    • Prasthantrayi of Vedanta = Upanishad, Brahmasutra, Bhagavad Gita; Bhagavata is not in it.UPPSC
    • Upanishad is the prime Prasthan; the other two are based on it.
    • Shankaracharya = oldest of the Vedanta Acharyas who founded sects by writing commentaries on the Brahmasutra.
    • Naimisharanya (Sitapur district, U.P.) = home of 60,000 hermits, where the whole Mahabharata was narrated.UPPSC
    • Sut Goswami narrated the Mahabharata to Saunak and other hermits during a Yagya; earlier Vaisampayana narrated it to King Janamejaya.
    • Valmiki wrote the Ramayana, the Adi Kavya in Sanskrit, with seven Kands.
    • Kishkindha Kand (4th Kand): first meeting of Rama and Hanuman, death of Bali, Sugriva becomes king of the Vanaras.UPPSC
    • Ananga (incorporeal) = Kamadeva, god of human love/desire; wife Rati.
    • Other names of Kamadeva: Kandarpa (inflamer even of a god), Madana (intoxicating), Manmatha (churner of hearts).

    Vaishnava festivals and temples

    • Rathyatra of Puri (Odisha) honours Lord Jagannath (Krishna), with Balram (Balbhadra) and Subhadra; yearly on dwitiya of Shukla Paksha, Ashadha month.
    • Kumbh Mela at Nasik is held on the bank of the Godavari, every twelve years.UPPSC
    • Kumbh is also held at Haridwar (Ganga), Prayag/Prayagraj (confluence of Ganga, Yamuna and extinct Saraswati) and Ujjain (Kshipra/Shipra).

    Shaiva religion

    • Religion devoted to Shiva = Shaiva Dharma; worshippers = Shaiva.
    • Shaiva is the oldest Hindu tradition in India; it goes back to the prehistoric age.
    • Indus Valley people worshipped Shiva: a Mohenjodaro seal shows a three-faced Yogi with trishul-like headgear; Marshall linked it to Rudra Shiva.
    • Rig Veda calls Shiva 'Rudra', famous for ferocity.
    • Shatarudriya Mantra of the Vajasaneyi Samhita calls Rudra the God of the universe.
    • Atharvaveda calls him Pashupati, Bhav, Sarva, Bhupati.
    • Patanjali's Mahabhashya shows Shiva's idol was worshipped in the 2nd century BC.
    • Names of Shiva in the Mahabhashya: Rudra, Mahadev, Girish, Bhav, Sarva, Trayambak.
    • Kushan coins carry figures of Shiva, Vrisabha and Trishul.
    • Udayagiri cave inscription: Virasena, minister of Chandragupta II, built a Shaiva cave on Udayagiri hill.
    • In Kumargupta's time Shiva Lingas were set up at Khoh and Karamdanda.
    • Gupta period: Shiva temple at Bhumara and Parvati temple at Nachana-Kuthar.
    • Kalidas praised Shiva's glory in Kumarasambhavam.
    • Kandaria Mahadev temple of Khajuraho was built by the Chandela rulers.
    • The Kailash temple of Ellora was built under the Rashtrakutas.
    • Chola rulers were exclusive Shiva worshippers; Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswar (Raj Rajeshwar) temple at Tanjore.
    • Kulottunga II, a staunch Shaiva, threw the Vishnu statue of the Chidambaram temple into the sea.
    • Ardhanarishvara = composite androgynous form, half male Shiva (usually the right half) and half female Parvati, split down the middle; shows union of God with his Shakti.UPPSC
    • Ardhanarishvara = synthesis of masculine and feminine energies; Shakti (female principle) is inseparable from Shiva (male principle).
    • Twelve Jyotirlingas: Somnath, Nageshwar (near Dwarka), Kedarnath (Uttarakhand), Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi), Vaidyanath (Deogarh, Jharkhand), Mahakaleshwar (Ujjain), Omkareshwar (M.P.), Bhimashankar (Pune), Trayambakeshwar (Nashik), Ghushmeshwar (Maharashtra), Mallikarjuna (Andhra Pradesh), Rameswaram (Tamil Nadu).

    Shaiva sects

    • Vaman Purana names four Shaiva sects: Shaiva, Pashupat, Kapalik, Kalamukh.
    • Pashupat sect arose in the 2nd century BC; Puranas: founded by a Brahmachari, Lakulish (Lakuli), held by followers to be Shiva's incarnation.
    • Kapalik sect worshipped Bhairav as Shiva's incarnation; followers ate meat, smeared cremation ashes and carried a Narmund in hand.
    • Mattamayura = a Shaiva sect of ancient India, found in inscriptions of the Chedi dynasty.
    • Basav is considered founder of the Lingayat sect of Shaivism.
    • Nathpanth was started by Matsyendra Nath at the end of the 10th century, taking Shiva as Adinath; Baba Gorakhnath promoted it.

    Shakta religion

    • People of the Shakta sect worshipped goddess Shakti; Shaiva Dharma is closely related to Shakta Dharma.
    • Shakta religion is also prehistoric: Mother Goddess worship was very popular in the Indus civilization; her statues were found in excavations.
    • Vedic literature tells of goddesses Saraswati, Aditi, Usha, Lakshmi.
    • Markandeya Purana has a detailed Goddess Mahatmya.
    • Kalika Purana (Kali Purana / Sati Purana) = a main upapurana of Shaktism.
    • Kalika Purana was likely composed in the Assam region; attributed to sage Markandeya.
    • Kalika Purana opens with legends of Devi bringing Shiva back from ascetic life to householder life by making him fall in love again.

    Chapter 7 · Ancient India

    Sixth century B.C.E - Political Condition

    136 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The list of 16 Mahajanapadas is in the Buddhist text Anguttara Nikaya and the Jain text Bhagavati Sutra.×3
    2. Kuru · Meerut, Delhi, Thaneshwar · Indraprastha×2
    3. Ajatashatru · Magadha×2
    4. Ajatashatru killed his father Bimbisara to take the throne, and was killed by his own son Udayin for the same reason.×2
    5. Hathigumpha inscription records a canal dug in Kalinga by Nanda king Mahapadmananda — evidence of King Nanda; first inscription to mention canals.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 25 UPPSC questions

    Sixteen Mahajanapadas: sources

    • Before Buddha's birth, ancient India was divided into 16 major states = 'Sixteen (Shodasha) Mahajanapadas'.
    • The list of 16 Mahajanapadas is in the Buddhist text Anguttara Nikaya and the Jain text Bhagavati Sutra.UPPSC ×3
    • Anguttara Nikaya list: Koshal, Kashi, Magadha, Anga, Vajji, Chedi, Malla, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchal, Matsya, Shurasena, Kamboja, Avanti, Assaka (Ashmaka), Gandhar.
    • Bhagavati Sutra list (some different names): Anga, Banga, Malay, Acha, Vacha (Vatsa), Magah (Magadha), Malav, Kochachha, Ladh, Moli (Malla), Koshala, Kashi, Padh, Sambhutar, Avaha, Vajji.
    • Panini's Ashtadhyayi mentions 22 Janapadas, and 3 most important: Magadha, Ashmak, Kamboj.
    • Panini, famous for Sanskrit grammar, was born at Salatura in Pushkalavati, Gandhara.
    • Ashtadhyayi = one of the earliest Sanskrit grammars: 4000 sutras (rules) in eight chapters, each divided into four sections (padas).
    • Four of the sixteen were very powerful: Koshal, Magadha, Vatsa, Avanti.
    • Eight of the 16 Mahajanapadas lay in present Uttar Pradesh: Kashi, Koshal, Vatsa, Malla, Kuru, Panchal, Shurasena, Chedi.UPPSC

    • Hastinapur and Indraprastha were Kuru capitals; Hastinapur city of the Mahabharata lay in Kuru.
    • Panchal at first had two parts; the famous city Kanyakubja lay in Panchala.
    • Panchal boundaries: Himalayan foothills (north), Chambal river (south), Koshala (east), Kuru (west).
    • Panchal was first a monarchy; it seems to have become a republic in the 6th–5th century BC.
    • Greek writers called Shurasena 'Sourasenoi' and its capital 'Mathora'; Shurasena was an ancient Yadava ruler of Mathura.
    • Anga's capital Champa: old name 'Malini' in the Mahabharata and Puranas; Bimbisara later annexed Anga to Magadha, which lay to its west.
    • Six great cities (metros) of Buddha's time, in the Mahaparinirvana-sutra: Champa, Rajgriha, Benaras, Saket, Kaushambi, Shravasti.
    • Ujjain (Malwa, Madhya Pradesh), one of Avanti's two capitals, was anciently called Avantika; capital of Avanti in Buddha's time.UPPSC
    • Uttarapatha (north-west ancient India) had two Janapadas: Gandhara and Kamboj.
    • Ramayana: Takshashila city was founded by Taksha, son of Bharat; Takshashila lay between the Indus and Jhelum.
    • Viratnagar (capital of Matsya) was founded by King Virat.
    • Cities named in both the Mahabharata and the Mahabhashya: Madhyamika (Nagari) and Viratnagar (Bairat).
    • Shravasti: Alexander Cunningham identified it with Sahet-Mahet (U.P.) in 1861; excavations show a crescent-shaped town plan.UPPSC
    • Kalpi town: Jalaun district (U.P.), on the bank of the Yamuna.UPPSC
    • Kalpi's ancient name = Kalpriya (Kalpriyanath / Kalpriya Nagari); built by King Vasudeva (printed as 4th century B.C. in one place, 4th century A.D. in another).

    Republics

    • Lichchhavis of Vaishali founded the world's first republic (6th century BC).
    • Vaishali is named after King Vishal of the Mahabharata era; a great Buddhist pilgrimage site and birthplace of Mahavira.
    • Vajji = largest and most powerful republic of Buddha's time; Vaishali was the capital of the Vajji confederacy; its rulers were Lichchhavis.
    • Chetak = head (king) of the Lichchhavi republic; Lichchhavi was one clan of the Vajji union.
    • Chetak's daughter Chelana was married to Magadha king Bimbisara.
    • Ten republics of Buddha's time: Shakya of Kapilavastu, Bhagga of Sumsumaragiri, Buli of Alakappa, Kalam of Kesaputta, Koliya of Ramgama, Malla of Kusinara, Malla of Pava, Moriya of Pipphalivan, Lichchhavi of Vaishali, Videha of Mithila.
    • Yaudheya was not among the early republics.UPPSC

    Magadha: capitals and Pataliputra

    • In ancient times the area along the river south of the Ganga was called Magadha (not Anarta, Takshashila or Chola).
    • Chola lay south of the Godavari river; Anarta was a Vedic-era kingdom.
    • Puranas: first dynasty of Magadha = Brihadratha; Brihadratha's son Jarasandha made Girivraj (Rajgriha) his capital.
    • Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata calls Rajgriha the capital of Jarasandha; Suttanipata calls Rajgriha 'Magadhham Puram'.
    • First (initial) capital of Magadha = Rajgriha (Girivraj, modern Rajgir).
    • At Rajgriha the first Buddhist Council was held and Mahavira gave his first sermon.
    • Pataliputra was founded by Ajatashatru of the Haryanka dynasty, successor of Bimbisara.
    • Udayin (Haryanka, son of Ajatashatru) first shifted the capital of Magadha from Rajgriha to Pataliputra.
    • Among Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka, Chandragupta Vikramaditya and Kanishka, the first to have Pataliputra as capital = Chandragupta Maurya.

    Note from the book One question on who first made Pataliputra his capital had no Udayin option; there Chandragupta Maurya is taken as the answer.

    • Capitals of the Magadhan empire in turn: Girivraja/Rajgriha, then Pataliputra; Kaushambi was never one — it belonged to Vatsa.
    • Pataliputra was also the capital of the Shishunaga, Nanda and Maurya dynasties.
    • Ancient Pataliputra (modern Patna) had the Ganga on the north and the Son on the west.
    • Ashoka held the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra (247 BC), presided by Moggaliputta Tissa; the first Jain council was also held there.
    • Megasthenes' 'Indica' describes the prosperity and rule of Chandragupta Maurya's time.
    • Pataliputra became the prime Buddhist centre in the Gupta period; its importance declined in the later Gupta period.

    Magadha: Haryanka dynasty

    • The first Magadhan empire rose in the 6th century BC; its real founder was Bimbisara (about 544–492 BC).
    • In the early 6th century BC Magadha was the most powerful city-state, among the richest Mahajanapadas; long rivalry with Koshala, Anga and Kashi.
    • The chapter note prints the same of Kashi: most powerful, richest in the early 6th century BC, rival of Koshala, Anga and Magadha.
    • Bimbisara = founder of the Haryanka dynasty, its first and most powerful emperor; Buddhist texts call him the first great ruler of Magadha.
    • Jivaka, famous physician and contemporary of Buddha, belonged to Bimbisara's court.UPPSC
    • Bimbisara sent Jivaka (Raj Vaidya) to Avanti king Chandapradyota to treat his jaundice.
    • Bimbisara got Kashi (Varanasi) as dowry on marrying Mahakoshala, sister of Koshala king Prasenjit.
    • Bimbisara died in 492 BC.
    • Ajatashatru 'Kunika' (about 492–460 BC), son of Bimbisara, of the Haryanka dynasty; an imperialist like his father.
    • Ajatashatru killed his father Bimbisara to take the throne, and was killed by his own son Udayin for the same reason.UPPSC ×2
    • Udayin of Magadha is different from King Udayan of Vatsa.
    • Magadha–Koshala struggle began early in Ajatashatru's reign; later a treaty: Prasenjit married his daughter Vajira to him and gave Kashi as dowry (bath money).
    • Magadha–Vajji estrangement began under Bimbisara and became open conflict under Ajatashatru.
    • Nirayavali Sutra: Lichchhavi chief Chetak formed a united front of 9 Lichchhavis, 9 Mallas and 18 Ganarajyas of Kashi-Koshala against Magadha.
    • Bhagavati Sutta: Ajatashatru won over them all, defeated the Lichchhavis and annexed the Vajjis to Magadha.

    • Matsya Purana: Shishunaga defeated Nandivardhan and annexed Avanti (Malwa) to Magadha.UPPSC
    • When Shishunaga made Vaishali his capital, he appointed his son as deputy-king of Varanasi.
    • In the 6th century BC Varanasi was the capital of Kashi Mahajanapada.

    Note from the book Who made Varanasi his second capital is not clear from the options given; U.P.P.S.C. accepted Shishunag.

    • The Nanda dynasty ruled Magadha after the Shishunaga dynasty ended.
    • Mahapadmananda (Ugrasen) = founder of the Nanda dynasty; Puranas: born of a Shudra woman; title 'Ekarat'.
    • Puranas also call Mahapadmananda Sarvakshatrantaka and Aparoparashurama.UPPSC
    • Nine Nanda kings: Ugrasen (Mahapadmananda), Panduk, Pandugati, Bhootpal, Rastrapal, Govishanak, Dashasiddhak, Kaivart, Dhanananda.
    • Last Nanda years: unrest due to extortion and heavy taxes on small items.
    • Chandragupta Maurya, helped by his preceptor Chanakya, killed the last Nanda Dhanananda and founded the Maurya empire — the dynasty after the Nandas.
    • Shunga dynasty: founded by Mauryan commander Pushyamitra Shunga after killing the last Maurya, Brihadratha, in 185 BC.
    • Kharavela = most important emperor of the Chedi dynasty of Kalinga; his Hathigumpha inscription is the main source on his reign.
    • Hathigumpha inscription records a canal dug in Kalinga by Nanda king Mahapadmananda — evidence of King Nanda; first inscription to mention canals.UPPSC ×2
    • It shows Mahapadmananda's Kalinga victory: King Nanda took away the statue of King Jinsen.
    • The inscription also records donation of villages to Jain monks and Kharavela's defeat of the Chola, Chera and Pandya states of the south.

    Coins, guilds, religious ferment, Karnata dynasty

    • Earliest extant coins of India = silver Aahat (Punch-marked) coins; marks were made by a stamp, hence the name.UPPSC
    • Punch-marked coins circulated from the 7th–6th centuries BC to the 1st century AD.
    • Shreni = organisation of traders and artisans; it controlled quality and price of goods and the conduct of members; prevalent in both North and South India.
    • 6th century BC: great religious upheaval across the world, and Vedic religion had become very complex.
    • Many sects arose in the middle Ganga valley; hermits of different faiths preached and refuted each other.
    • Elsewhere too: Confucius (China), Zarathustra (Iran), Pythagoras (Greece) challenged traditional assumptions.
    • Vedic religion stressed purity of Shlokas and Yajnas; priests' importance rose hugely; Yajnas cost much money and led to animal killing.
    • Nanyadev, a great warrior, founded the Karnata dynasty; capital Simraon.
    • Karnata period (1097–1324 AD) = golden period of Mithila.
    • Last Karnata ruler Harisimha Dev: great patron of art and literature; propounder of the Panji (genealogical) system.

    Chapter 8 · Ancient India

    Greek Invasion

    19 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Reasons for Alexander's success: no central power in India, his superior army, help from traitorous Indian rulers like Ambhi; not good administration.×3
    Quick quiz: 5 of 5 UPPSC questions

    Persian contact

    • Kurush / Cyrus II (558–529 BC) founded the Achaemenid Empire in central Iran in the 6th century BC.
    • Behistun, Persepolis and Naqsh-e-Rostam inscriptions belong to Darius I (522–486 BC) and later kings; they tell of India–Persia relations.
    • Behistun inscription names the 23 provinces of Darius I's empire.
    • Herodotus: India was the twentieth province of Darius's empire.
    • Ctesias was the state doctor (Rajya Vaidya) of Artaxerxes II.
    • Kharoshthi script grew out of the Iranian Aramaic script in north-western India, as a result of Persian contact.

    Nandas at the time of Alexander

    • Puranas and Buddhist texts give eight inheritors of Mahapadmananda.
    • Dhanananda, last ruler of the Nanda dynasty, was the contemporary of Alexander; Nandas ruled North India at his invasion.
    • Greek writers called Dhanananda Agrammese; Xenophon describes him as a wealthy person; Bhaddasala was his commander.

    Alexander's Indian campaign

    • After demolishing the Achaemenid Empire in 326 BC, Alexander began his Indian campaign with a huge army.
    • After nearly two years he went back towards Greece from Paatal in 325 BC; he was NOT defeated by Chandragupta Maurya.UPPSC
    • Ashvaka = frontier republic at the time of Alexander's invasion; capital Massaga.
    • Greek writers: the women of Massaga took up arms against Alexander after many men were killed; Alexander killed the women of the town.UPPSC
    • Puru (Porus)'s realm lay between the Jhelum and the Chenab; Alexander defeated him on the bank of the Jhelum.UPPSC
    • Impressed by Porus's courage, Alexander became his friend, returned his state and gifted him some more areas.
    • Reasons for Alexander's success: no central power in India, his superior army, help from traitorous Indian rulers like Ambhi; not good administration.UPPSC ×3
    • Dr. Hemachandra Rai Chaudhary lists 28 independent powers in India at that time.
    • Deimachus did not come to India with Alexander; Nearchus, Onesicritus and Aristobulus did.UPPSC
    • Strabo: Seleucid emperor Antiochus sent Deimachus as ambassador to the court of Bindusara.

    Maurya Empire

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. James Prinsep was the first to decipher the Brahmi script and read Ashoka's edicts.×4
    2. Sudarshan Lake (Girnar hills, Saurashtra) was built for irrigation on Chandragupta Maurya's order by Pushyagupta, governor of his western province; first lake in the Girnar area.×2
    3. Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman (150 AD) records this in Anarta and Saurashtra (Gujarat); it proves western India (Gujarat) was in Chandragupta's empire.×2
    4. Mauryan remains were found at Bulandibagh and Kumrahar near Patna = ancient Pataliputra.×2

    Quick quiz: 10 of 66 UPPSC questions

    Chandragupta Maurya: rise and sources

    • Chandragupta Maurya, one of India's greatest emperors, founded the Maurya Empire, the first Indian empire: he joined small fragmented kingdoms into one vast empire and first unified India politically.UPPSC
    • Maurya dynasty (321–185 BC) is older than the Kushana, Gupta (275–550 CE) and Vardhana dynasties.
    • Chandragupta extended his empire to the edge of present Iran; it ran from Iran (north-west) to present north Karnataka (south).
    • Chandragupta's early victories took his boundary from the Beas to the Indus river.
    • Unified Maurya empire: Bengal and Assam (east) to Afghanistan (west), Kashmir (north) to the Deccan plateau (south).
    • Chandragupta was the first king to conquer Malwa, Gujarat and Maharashtra.UPPSC
    • Chandragupta conquered the Deccan: Jain and Tamil sources and southern inscriptions show it; Ashoka conquered only Kalinga; Bindusara's victory is doubtful.
    • Mudrarakshasa of Vishakhadatta tells of Chandragupta Maurya's reign: its subject is the court intrigues of his time.
    • Mudrarakshasa calls Chandragupta 'a scion of the Nanda house', son of Nanda (Mahapadmanand), Maurya-putra, "Vrishal" and "Kulheen".
    • Dhundiraja wrote a commentary on Mudrarakshasa.
    • Dr. K.P. Jayaswal: Vishakhadatta and Chandragupta were contemporary; the play shows 'Durabhisandhi' (intrigue) in Chandragupta's court.
    • Other works of Vishakhadatta: Devichandraguptam and Abhisarika-vanchitaka (Abhisarika-bandhitakam; not found).
    • Greek writer Justin and others called Chandragupta Maurya 'Sandrokottos'.
    • William Jones was the first scholar to identify Sandrokottos with Chandragupta Maurya.
    • Justin described the meeting of Sandrokottos and Alexander the Great.UPPSC
    • Aerian and Plutarch called him Androkottus.
    PersonOther name
    ChandraguptaSandrocottus
    BindusaraAmitraghat (Amitrochates)
    AshokaPiyadasi
    ChanakyaVishnuguptaUPPSC
    • Chandragupta defeated the invading army of Seleucus, ruler (governor) of the eastern part of Alexander's (Macedonian) empire, in 305 BC.UPPSC
    • Seleucus = administrator of Sindh and Afghanistan appointed by Alexander.
    • Megasthenes, Greek historian, came to India in the 4th century BC and lived five years at the court of Chandragupta Maurya.UPPSC
    • Megasthenes was the ambassador of Seleucus Nicator.
    • Megasthenes wrote 'Indica' (in Greek) on contemporary India and Chandragupta's reign.
    • Greek texts call Pataliputra (modern Patna) 'Polibrotha' (Palibothra); a major political, commercial and cultural centre.
    • Order of visitors: Megasthenes (Chandragupta Maurya) → Fa-Hien (Chandragupta II Vikramaditya) → Hiuen-Tsang (Harshavardhana) → I-Tsing (Chinese traveller, 7th century AD).

    Chandragupta: Sudarshan lake and Pataliputra palace

    • Sudarshan Lake (Girnar hills, Saurashtra) was built for irrigation on Chandragupta Maurya's order by Pushyagupta, governor of his western province; first lake in the Girnar area.UPPSC ×2
    • Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman (150 AD) records this in Anarta and Saurashtra (Gujarat); it proves western India (Gujarat) was in Chandragupta's empire.UPPSC ×2
    • Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka both managed water resources in the Girnar region before the Christian era.UPPSC
    • Ashoka's governor Tushasp took out canals from the lake.
    • The Junagadh inscription of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman (Shaka ruler) mentions both Chandragupta and Ashoka.UPPSC
    • In the 2nd century AD Rudradaman's governor Suvisakh repaired the lake; later Skandagupta also repaired it.
    • Ashoka's edicts are also found at the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman; the rock also has edicts of Skandagupta.UPPSC
    • A large boulder within 2 km of Uparkot fort carries fourteen edicts of Ashoka.
    • Mauryan remains were found at Bulandibagh and Kumrahar near Patna = ancient Pataliputra.UPPSC ×2
    • Chandragupta's 80-pillared palace at Pataliputra was mainly of wood (wooden floors).
    • D.B. Spooner excavated: city wall remains from Bulandibagh, palace remains from Kumrahar.
    • Not linked with Chandragupta: Sanchi (stupa built by Ashoka); linked: Susima, Vishnugupta, Junagadh inscription.
    • Susima = eldest son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta Maurya.

    Kautilya and the Arthashastra

    • Kautilya greatly helped found the Maurya dynasty; he was prime minister, adviser and chief priest of Chandragupta Maurya.UPPSC ×2
    • Kautilya was also known as Vishnugupta and Chanakya; Vishnugupta is taken as his childhood name.UPPSC
    • Sage Chanak named his son Chanakya; Arthashastra names its author Kautilya, and Vishnugupta in one verse.
    • Researcher Trobman: Chanakya or Kautilya is probably the author's gotra (clan) name.
    • Kautilya = pioneer scholar of political science; his Arthashastra is a treatise on polity, principles of government and political policies; among the oldest books on India's political condition.UPPSC
    • Arthashastra gives a detailed account of Mauryan administration and the agrarian system.
    • Arthashastra introduced the Saptang theory of the state: King (Swami), Minister (Amatya), Territory (Janapada), Fort (Durg), Treasury (Kosa), Army (Danda), Allies (Mitra).
    • Mitra (Ally) = seventh part of the state, like its ear; allies help the king in peace and war.UPPSC
    • Kautilya separates ideal and fake allies: natural is better than artificial; a king with a greedy, lustful, cowardly friend is ruined.
    • Arthashastra is compared with Machiavelli's 'The Prince' (Il Principe).UPPSC
    • Dasa-Kalpa chapter of Arthashastra: a person could become a slave by judicial punishment; a female slave who bore her master a son became legally free.
    • But that son did not get the legal status of the master's son.
    • Arthashastra: the head of a convoy (caravan) of merchants was called Sarthwah.UPPSC
    • Arthashastra's two courts: Dharmasthiya (like civil courts) and Kantakshodhana (like criminal courts).
    • Arthashastra allows divorce and remarriage to a wife deserted by her husband.
    • Divorce existed in Mauryan times: wife could divorce for husband's long stay abroad or physical handicap; husband could leave a barren or adulterous wife.
    • Kautilya's rural tiers: Sthaniya (800 villages), Dronamukh (400), Karvatika (200), Samgrahan (10); ascending order = Samgrahana, Karvatika, Dronamukh, Sthaniya.

    Note from the book The question asking the ascending order of these units is itself incorrect: no option gives this order.

    Bindusara

    • Greek writers called Bindusara 'Amitrochates' = Sanskrit Amitraghat (killer of enemies); Jain texts call him 'Simhasena'.
    • Jain texts: Bindusara's mother was 'Durdhara'.
    • Divyavadana: a revolt broke out in Taxila in Bindusara's time; he sent his son Ashoka to suppress it.
    • Strabo: Syrian king Antiochus I Soter sent Deimachus as ambassador to Bindusara's court; he replaced Megasthenes.UPPSC
    • Pliny: Egypt's king Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent Dionysius as ambassador to the Mauryan court.
    • Bindusara asked the ruler of Syria for sweet wine, dry figs and a philosopher; Antiochus I sent all except the philosopher.
    • Buddhist evidence: Ashoka was viceroy of Avanti in his father's reign.
    • Samantapasadika of Buddhaghosha says Ashoka won Avanti Mahajanapada and merged it in the empire during Bindusara's rule.

    Ashoka: empire, Kalinga war, Dhamma

    • Ashoka's coronation on the throne of Magadha: 269 BC.
    • All India except Assam and the far south was in Ashoka's empire; his rock and pillar edicts show its extent (the map of his reign's close).
    • Sri Lanka was not part of Ashoka's empire; Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputta, Keralaputta and Tamraparni (Sri Lanka) lay outside it — called edge (border) states.
    • Kalinga victory = greatest event of Ashoka's reign; conquered eight years after coronation, i.e. 261 BC.
    • Ashoka annexed Kalinga because it controlled the land and sea routes to South India; reasons were political and economic.UPPSC
    • Kalinga was like a bridge between north and south; its people dominated the Indian Ocean and overseas trade and closed eastern sea routes to Magadhan merchants.
    • Kalinga also controlled the land routes from the Gangetic valley to the Deccan.
    • Ashoka announced a logical, practical 'Dhamma Niti'; his Dhamma rests on ethical principles for the welfare of humanity, not on any community.
    • Triple bases of Ashoka's Rajdharma: longanimity (tolerance), liberty and compassion.UPPSC
    • Jha and Shrimali (Prachin Bharat Ka Itihas): spirit of Ashoka's Dhamma comes from Lakkhana Sutta of Digha Nikaya, Rahulovada-Sutta and Dhammapada; he appointed Dhamma-Mahamatras in the 14th year of his reign.UPPSC
    • Ashoka's Dhamma was mainly a policy of peace, non-violence and religious toleration.
    • Ashoka built India's first hospital and herbal garden.UPPSC
    • He set up hospitals, public gardens, medicinal-herb gardens, dug wells, planted shade trees, and made a ministry for the care of aborigines and subject races.
    • Epithet 'Devanampriya' (beloved of the gods / handsome) shows Ashoka kept belief in Hinduism though Buddhist.
    • Third Buddhist Council: Pataliputra, in Ashoka's reign, president Moggaliputta Tissa; sources = Sinhalese Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa.UPPSC
    • Mauryan followers of Buddhism: Ashoka and his grandson Dasaratha; Dasaratha also took the title 'Devanampiya'.
    • After becoming Buddhist, Ashoka gave up hunting and began pilgrimages (dhamma-yatra); first he visited Bodhgaya.
    • Dhamma-yatras: Sambodhi (Bodhgaya) 10 years after coronation; Kanakamuni stupa enlarged 14 years after; Lumbini and Nigalisagar 20 years after.
    • Ashoka's pilgrimage route: Lumbini → Kapilavastu → Gaya → Sarnath → Kushinagar → Shravasti.UPPSC
    • Ashoka's relations with Syria and Egypt show the Mauryas had diplomatic ties with distant countries.UPPSC

    Ashoka's inscriptions: script, language, decipherment

    • Ashoka's inscriptions are of three classes: rock inscriptions, pillar (column) inscriptions, cave inscriptions; more than 40 edicts have been found.
    • The 14 Major Rock Edicts are found at: Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Kalsi, Girnar, Dhauli, Jaugada, Yerragudi, Sopara.
    • Most Ashokan inscriptions are in the Prakrit language — the language of the earliest stone inscriptions.UPPSC
    • Most are in the Brahmi script, as on Ashoka's pillars.
    • Only Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (near Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan) are in Kharosthi script, Prakrit language.
    • One ruined Aramaic inscription is from Taxila; another Aramaic one from Laghman.
    • Shar-i-Kuna (Kandahar) inscription is bilingual: Greek and Aramaic.
    • Kharosthi was written from right to left; a cursive script of north-west India (Gandhara culture, modern Afghanistan and Pakistan).
    • Kharosthi was deciphered by James Prinsep (1835 AD), Friedrich Grotefend (1836 AD), Lassen (1838 AD).
    • James Prinsep was the first to decipher the Brahmi script and read Ashoka's edicts.UPPSC ×4
    • Brahmi was first deciphered from letters inscribed on stone tablets.UPPSC
    • Prinsep first took King Devanampiya Piyadassi to be a Sri Lankan king; Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa showed the name was Ashoka's.
    • In 1915 the Maski inscription (Karnataka) settled the name 'Ashoka'.
    • Ashoka is generally called 'Priyadarshi' (Piyadasi), 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' (Beloved of the Gods) in his inscriptions.
    • Puranas call him 'Ashok Vardhan'.
    • Personal name 'Ashoka' occurs in the Gujarra, Maski, Nettur and Udagolam edicts.UPPSC
    • Gujarra minor rock edict: Datia district, Madhya Pradesh; on the main road from Ujjain to Bharuch.UPPSC
    • Kanganahalli relief inscription has 'Ranyo Ashoka' (King Ashoka) under a stone portrait of Ashoka with his queen.
    • Kanganahalli Buddhist stupa: bank of the Bhima river, Kalaburagi district, Karnataka.
    • Pre-Ashokan Brahmi script was found at Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka); also Piparaha, Sohgaura, Mahasthan.UPPSC
    • Bhabru (Bairat) inscription proves Ashoka a Buddhist; only here he calls himself 'Piyadasi Raja Magadha' (king of Magadha).
    • Kalsi (Dehradun district, Uttarakhand) is famous for Ashoka's rock edicts.UPPSC

    Ashoka's edicts: contents

    • Rock Edict I: no living being to be slaughtered or sacrificed here; earlier hundreds of thousands of animals were killed daily in the royal kitchen.
    • Rock Edict I: now only three are killed — two peacocks and a deer (deer not always); in future not even these.
    • Pillar Edict V bans killing of animals on certain days: 26 years after anointing, parrots, mainas, the arumna, ruddy geese and others were declared inviolable.
    • Pillar Edict V: fish not to be killed or sold on the three chaturmasis, the Tishya full moon (three days) and every fast day.
    • Major Rock Edict II names the South Indian kingdoms Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputta, Keralaputta and Tamraparni; Satavahana is not named.UPPSC ×2
    • Rock Edict II also names Yavana king Antiyoka and his neighbour kings, and medical treatment for men and animals.
    • Rock Edicts II and XIII tell of the Sangam kingdoms; XIII also names Chola, Pandya and Tamraparni.
    • Ashoka's 3rd edict names three officers: Yukta, Rajjuka, Pradeshika.
    • Rock Edict XI explains the policy of dhamma: respect to elders, not killing animals, generosity to friends.
    • Rock Edict XII = religious tolerance and synthesis, growth of the essence of all sects; one who praises his own sect and blames others harms his own sect.UPPSC ×2
    • Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war and victory and Ashoka's deep remorse.UPPSC
    • Rock Edict XIII: the way of conquest is dhamma, not war — the logical end of the process begun in Rock Edict I.
    • Rock Edict XIII names five Greek (Yavana) kings friendly with Ashoka: Antiyok (Antiochus II Theos, Seleucid ruler of Syria), Turmaya/Turamaya (Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Egypt), Antakini/Anikini (Antigonus Gonatas, Macedonia), Mag/Makmaas/Megaras (Cyrene), Alik Sundar/Aliero Sentro (Alexander of Epirus).UPPSC ×2
    • Ashoka's edicts state: "All our people should do good deeds, be free from all disasters, enjoy joy with minds unpolluted by jealousy."UPPSC

    Note from the book For this quotation UPPSC gave Harshavardhana in its answer key, but no proof is found in the sources; it is in Ashoka's edicts.

    • Rummindei pillar marks the birthplace of Buddha; Ashoka visited Lumbini 20 years after coronation.UPPSC
    • At Lumbini Ashoka remitted the Bali tax and cut land revenue from 1/6 to 1/8.
    • Sohgaura copper plate (Gorakhpur, U.P.) = earliest known copper plate; Mauryan record with the earliest royal order to store food-grains for famine.
    • Mahasthan inscription (Bogura district, Bangladesh) also describes famine relief measures.
    • Mauryan kings did not give land grants on religious basis; no peasant revolt against land grants is recorded.UPPSC
    • Earliest epigraphic record of religious land grants is in a Satavahana inscription; such grants are prominent in post-Mauryan records.

    Mauryan pillars, stupas, caves, art

    • Sarnath Pillar was built by Ashoka; four lions back to back on top = symbol of power; its replica is India's national emblem.UPPSC
    • Ashokan pillars are the best example of Mauryan architecture; all Mauryan columns are of Chunar sandstone.
    • Ashokan stone pillars are highly polished, monolithic, with tapering shafts; they are independent sculptures, not parts of architectural structures.
    • Lion Capital of Ashoka is at Sarnath, not Rajgir; Lothal = ancient dockyard; Sarnath = first sermon of Buddha; Nalanda = great seat of Buddhist learning.UPPSC
    • Sanchi Stupa (Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh) is considered the best stupa architecturally.UPPSC
    • Sanchi Stupa was built by Ashoka.UPPSC
    • Sanchi is world-famous for stupas, monasteries, temples and pillars dating from the 3rd century BC.
    • Ancient name of Sanchi = Kakanam: a 4th-century CE Gupta inscription calls it Kakanam Mahavihara.
    • Sanchi has 3 stupas on a hilltop: Stupa 1 is the main one; Stupa 2 holds remains of Ashoka's Dhamma Mahamatyas; Stupa 3 holds remains of Sariputra and Mudgalayan.
    • A gateway (torana) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi shows Ashoka's pilgrimage to the Bodhi tree with his two queens.
    • The Great Stupa at Sanchi is one of the oldest and best preserved Buddhist stupas; its toranas narrate Buddhist events in symbols.
    • Bharhut Stupa (near Satna, Madhya Pradesh) = fine example of Shunga architecture, built about 150 BC (also dated about 3rd century BC).
    • Bharhut stupa was discovered by Alexander Cunningham; it shows the people's movement in sculpture and architecture.
    • Amravati Stupa: right bank of the Krishna, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh; traced by Colin Mackenzie in 1797 AD.
    • Dhamekh Stupa (Sarnath, Varanasi) was first built in Ashoka's time; present form is of the Gupta period; built on a flat surface without a raised base.
    • Another place prints: Dhamekh Stupa was built in the 'Gupta period 500 BC' to replace an earlier structure built by Ashoka.

    • Barabar caves (Jahanabad district, Bihar): four caves; Ashoka's inscriptions on walls of three; dedicated to Ajivikas; Mauryan period (321–185 BC), not 6th century BC.UPPSC

    • Mauryan kings developed culture, art and literature, provincial division, and rule up to the Hindukush — not gold coins.UPPSC
    • Historian Smith: the Hindukush mountains were India's strategic frontier.
    • Regular gold coins in India are credited to the Indo-Greek kings.
    • Yukta = district officials who collected revenue; revenue officer for treasury and accounts, under the Pradeshika and Rajuka.
    • Rajjukas = Mauryan officers in rural areas: surveyors with judicial and assessment duties (land measurement, tax assessment).UPPSC
    • Pradeshika = top official of the division, like today's divisional commissioner; chief of district administration; also did judicial work.
    • Ashokan inscriptions show Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta were important officers of district-level administration.
    • Agraharika was not a Mauryan official; Yukta, Pradeshika, Rajjuka were.
    • Pradeshtha = officials who prevented crimes, linked to the Justice (Judicial) Department; Arthashastra's Pradeshtha was a divisional-level officer (administrator of commissionaries).
    • Samaharta regulated revenue collection in the Mauryan Mantriparishad.UPPSC
    • Antapal looked after the border forts.
    • 'Bhaga' and 'Bali' were sources of revenue; Arthashastra: king owned the land and his share of produce was Bhaga.UPPSC
    • Sitadhyaksha = head of agriculture and crown land; he collected land revenue, the chief income of the Mauryas.
    • 'Sita' = revenue from crown land.UPPSC
    • 'Vivit' (Vivita) = tax on pastures; officer of pasture land = Vivitadhyaksha.
    • 'Pranayam' (Pranay) = emergency tax in the Mauryan period.
    • Shulkadhyaksha collected trade and service taxes; Akradhyaksha controlled mines.
    • Pautavadhyaksha = in charge of weights and measures.UPPSC
    • Panyadhyaksha = head of the commerce department; Sunadhyaksha = chief of the slaughterhouse.
    • Agronomoi = district officers: collected revenue, watched irrigation, did legal administration and looked after road construction (UPPSC accepted road construction).UPPSC
    • 'Pankodakasannirodhe' = Mauryan penalty for throwing dirt or causing mud and water to collect on roads.
    • Town administration was by municipalities headed by a 'Nagarak' or 'Purmukhya'.
    • Village Assembly was free to decide any village matter in the Mauryan period.
    • Taxila (Punjab province, Pakistan) = most famous centre of learning in the Mauryan period, for Hindus and Buddhists from all over the world.
    • Vaishali: now a Bihar district, linked with Buddhism and Jainism; founded in the 6th century BC before Buddha's birth (563 BC); Mahavira was born at Kundgram there.
    • Nalanda = important Buddhist education centre; Buddha temples first built there in the Gupta period; Ujjain = conventional capital of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).
    OfficerDuty
    TalarOfficer of night guards
    PattakolaVillage tax collector
    SahsadhipatiOfficer of cases of dacoity
    BaladhipGuard of octroiUPPSC

    Megasthenes' Indica: city and society

    • Indica describes the municipal (city) administration of Pataliputra.UPPSC
    • Pataliputra had a 30-member council in six committees of five members each; town officials were called 'Astynomoi'.
    • Sixth board collected sales tax: one-tenth of earnings; tax evasion was punished with death.
    • Third committee kept the register of births and deaths — still a municipal function today.
    • Megasthenes' Indica divides Mauryan society into seven classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen and hunters, artisans and traders, soldiers, overseers or spies, councillors and assessors.UPPSC
    • Megasthenes' Indica states there was no slavery in India.UPPSC
    • Megasthenes: no one could marry outside his caste or take up an occupation other than his caste's.
    • Megasthenes said philosophers were of two types: Brahmins and Shramanas.
    • Brahmins: liberation through knowledge of Brahman; Shramanas: liberation through ascetic practice (shrama).

    Society, law and later texts

    • Memorising chronicles, dynastic histories and epic tales was the profession of the Maagadha.
    • Village rule through autonomous elected panchayats was evolved by the Dravids (Cholas); it was the base of their village administration.
    • Manusmriti (38th part) prohibits widow remarriage: a widower could remarry, a widow could not.UPPSC ×2
    • Manusmriti called foreign invaders who did not follow priestly customs (Shakas, Kushanas, Hunas, Pratihar) 'Fallen Kshatriyas'.UPPSC

    End of the Mauryas

    • Last Mauryan emperor = Brihadratha.
    • Brihadratha was killed by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BC (184 BC in one place), who founded the Shunga dynasty.
    • Pushyamitra Shunga was a fanatic Brahmin; he did two Ashwamedha Yajnas under the supervision of Patanjali, author of the Mahabhashya.
    • Last Shunga king Devabhuti was killed by a plot of his Brahmin Amatya Vasudeva Kanva, who took the throne.
    • Vayu Purana: last Kanva ruler Susharma was deposed by his Andhra servant Simuk (Sindhuk).

    Chapter 10 · Ancient India

    Post-Mauryan Period

    124 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Saka Samvat began in 78 AD; so December 2009 = Saka 1931 (2009 − 78).×3
    2. Kushanas circulated gold and copper coins on the widest scale; they issued gold coins regularly and the most copper coins.×2
    3. Vima Kadphises = first Kushana king to issue gold coins; he introduced gold coins for regular use, on a large scale.×2
    4. Ashvaghosha = poet laureate and contemporary of Kanishka; works: Saundaranand, Buddhacharita, Sariputraprakaran.×2
    5. Kharavela belonged to the Chedi dynasty, also called the Mahameghavahana dynasty; he was its best-known king.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 46 UPPSC questions

    Invaders and Indo-Greeks

    • Order of invaders in ancient India: Greeks (326 BC, Alexander) → Sakas (Scythians, 1st century BC) → Kushanas (1st century AD).UPPSC
    • Darius I (522–486 BC) = first Persian ruler to invade/capture some parts of India.
    • Herodotus: Darius conquered the lands around the Indus river, up to the desert of Rajputana, and parts of Punjab.
    • Strato II, Indo-Greek ruler (25 BC–10 AD), issued lead coins.UPPSC
    • Agathocles, Greco-Bactrian king (about 190–180 BC), issued silver coins showing both Sankarshana (Balram) and Vasudeva.UPPSC
    • Agathocles held Paropamisadae, a satrapy between Bactria and India; known mostly from his many coins.
    • Agathocles = first Greco-Bactrian ruler to put bilingual legends on coins, mainly Greek and Brahmi.
    • Milinda (Menander) = Indo-Greek ruler of north-western India; not a contemporary of Bimbisara, Buddha and Prasenjit.
    • Bimbisara (544–492 BC, Haryanka) = real founder of the Magadha empire; Prasenjit ruled Koshala; both were contemporaries of Buddha.
    • Sixteen coins of King Menander were found at Bairat.
