    Rudradaman and the Saka Kshatrapas

    • Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman (130–150 AD; dated about 150 AD) was found at Girnar hills, Gujarat; it tells Rudradaman I's achievements.
    • It is in Brahmi script; an early inscription in perfect Sanskrit; the earliest specimen of the 'Kavya' style.UPPSC
    • It credits Rudradaman I with supporting cultural arts and Sanskrit literature.
    • Rudradaman I repaired the embankments of Sudarshan Lake (artificial reservoir) without using forced labour.UPPSC
    • Sudarshan Lake was built under Chandragupta Maurya by his western province governor Pushyagupta, to check floods.
    • Karddamaka Kshatrapa coins: silver (frequent) and potin; Chastana issued silver and copper; copper coins were very rare.UPPSC
    • Gold : silver coin ratio in the Saka-Kshatrapa period = 1 : 35.

    Kushana coins

    • Indo-Greek kings introduced (and made popular) gold coins in northern and north-western India.
    • Kushanas circulated gold and copper coins on the widest scale; they issued gold coins regularly and the most copper coins.UPPSC ×2
    • Vima Kadphises = first Kushana king to issue gold coins; he introduced gold coins for regular use, on a large scale.UPPSC ×2
    • Kujula Kadphises circulated copper coins.
    • Vima Kadphises (Kadphises II), father of Kanishka I, took the title 'Sarvalokeshvara' (Lord of the Whole World).
    • Buddha is shown on the coins of Kushana ruler Kanishka.UPPSC
    • Yaudheya copper coins (several varieties) show standing six-headed god Kartikeya with a peacock on the right; found in the Kushana ruler's time.UPPSC
    • Evidence of the Yaudheyas' coins comes from the Puranas and the Ashtadhyayi.
    DynastyMetals of coins
    KushanasGold and copper
    GuptaGold and silver
    SatavahanasLead, copper, bronze, silver, potin (copper, silver and lead mixed); NOT goldUPPSC
    KalachurisGold, silver and copper
    • Satavahanas also issued punch-marked coins.

    Kanishka: dates and eras

    • Kanishka's Sarnath Buddha image inscription is dated 81 AD, three years after his coronation.UPPSC
    • Kanishka's coronation date is disputed; two international conventions in London (1913 and 1960); the second agreed on 78 AD.UPPSC
    • Saka Samvat began in 78 AD; so December 2009 = Saka 1931 (2009 − 78).UPPSC ×3
    • Jain texts: Sakas beat Vikramaditya's successor in 135 Vikrama Samvat and began Saka Samvat to mark it: 135 − 57 = 78 AD.
    • Most historians hold that Kushana ruler Kanishka started the Saka Samvat.
    • Vikrama Samvat began in 57 BC; its two other names are Krit and Malav.UPPSC
    • Jain texts put 470 years between Mahavira's salvation (527 BC) and Vikrama Samvat: 527 − 470 = 57 BC.
    • Gregorian calendar = internationally used civil calendar; Vikrama Samvat = Gregorian year + 57; Saka Samvat = Gregorian year − 78.
    • Difference between Vikrama Samvat and Saka Samvat = 135 years (e.g. 2019 → Vikrama 2076, Saka 1941).UPPSC
    • Saka Samvat is adopted as India's national calendar; Chaitra is its first month.
    • Chaitra 1 = 22 March normally, 21 March in a leap year; national calendar dates match the Gregorian calendar.

    Kanishka: court, empire, society

    • Ashvaghosha = poet laureate and contemporary of Kanishka; works: Saundaranand, Buddhacharita, Sariputraprakaran.UPPSC ×2
    • Vasumitra, renowned Buddhist scholar and Kanishka's contemporary, headed the Fourth Buddhist Council.
    • Kalidas belonged to the Gupta period; Kamban was not Kanishka's contemporary.
    • Scholars of Kanishka's court: Parsva, Vasumitra, Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna, Charaka, Mathara; Vishakhadatta was not among them.UPPSC
    • Charaka = court physician of Kanishka.
    • Patanjali belonged to the Shunga period (not Kanishka's court); author of the Mahabhashya.UPPSC
    • Rabatak inscription of Kanishka names four cities: Saket, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Sri Champa; Shravasti is not named.UPPSC
    • Rabatak inscription: found in 1993 at Rabatak near Surkh Kotal, Afghanistan; Greek script, Bactrian language.
    • Taxila University alumni: Kautilya, Chandragupta Maurya, Ayurvedacharya Charaka, King Prasenjit of Koshala, Ayurvedacharya Jivaka (of Bimbisara), Vasubandhu.UPPSC
    • Taxila University was a meeting point where students of different countries exchanged knowledge.
    • The Kushana empire spread outside India: northern Turpan (China) and Kashmir to the Vindhya hills (south); northern Afghanistan (west) to eastern U.P. and Bihar; the Maurya empire also went beyond India.
    • Maurya empire = first pan-India empire; at its height it covered parts of modern Iran and almost the whole subcontinent except the southern peninsula.
    • Chinese texts (73–94 AD): Kanishka (Yue-tche) asked to marry a Han princess and was refused; he marched in 86 AD with 70,000 men but Chinese general Pan Chao's smaller force defeated him.
    • Kushanas traded through the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, but no evidence describes a Kushana naval force.UPPSC
    • Proof of ports and trade centres: the travelogue 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' and the Arikamedu excavations.
    • 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' (Periplus Maris Erythraei): anonymous work of about mid-1st century CE by a Greek-speaking merchant — not by Ctesias, Pliny, Ptolemy or Strabo.
    • It was translated by Wilfred H. Scoff as 'The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea: Travel and Trade in the Indian Ocean by a Merchant of the First Century'.
    • Child marriage began in the Kushana period (1st century); age 8–10 years was thought best for a girl's marriage.
    • Ending of 'Upanayana' for females plus child marriage brought women to the lowest stage of society.

    Gandhara art

    • Gandhara School of Art developed in the Kushana period, with encouragement and protection from Kanishka.
    • Two major sculpture schools of the Kushana period with distinct styles: Gandhara and Mathura.
    • Gandhara style = synthesis of Indian and Greek art; also called Greco-Buddhist, Indo-Greek or Greco-Roman art; its subject was only Buddha.UPPSC
    • Gandhara Buddhist art grew from the merger of Greek, Syrian, Persian and Indian influences; flourished in the Saka and Kushan era.
    • Gandhara sculptures always used green schist as the medium; they were influenced by Greek sculpture.
    • Bamiyan (Afghanistan) was famous for Buddha statues cut into its hills; the Taliban destroyed them.UPPSC

    Shunga and Kanva dynasties

    • Order of rule: Maurya (about 321–185 BCE) → Shunga (about 185–73 BCE) → Kanva (about 73–28 BCE) → Kushan (1st–3rd century CE).
    • Pushyamitra Shunga, commander of the last Maurya Brihadratha, killed him in 185 BC and founded the Shunga dynasty.
    • The Ayodhya inscription records two Ashwamedha Yajnas performed by Pushyamitra Shunga.UPPSC
    • Ancestors of the Shungas belonged to Ujjain.
    • Last Shunga ruler Devabhuti was killed by his minister (Amatya) Vasudeva Kanva; the Kanvas then replaced the Shungas.
    • Kanvas were Brahmins, like the Shungas.

    Satavahanas

    • Satavahanas = most powerful dynasty in the South after the Mauryas.UPPSC
    • Puranas: Simuka (Sindhuk / Shiprak / Sisuk) founded the Satavahana dynasty after killing Kanva king Susharman.UPPSC
    • Satavahana is older than the Chalukyas, Pallavas and Rashtrakutas; founded by Simuka near the 2nd century BC (printed elsewhere as 1st century BC).UPPSC
    • Chronological order: Satavahanas (Simuka) → Vakatakas (Vindhyashakti, 3rd century AD) → Chalukyas of Gujarat (Mulraj I, 10th century AD).
    • Matsya Purana has the longest list of Andhra-Satavahana kings: 30 rulers.
    • Real capital of the Satavahanas = Paithan (Pratishthan).UPPSC
    • Initial capital of the Satavahanas is believed to be Amravati.UPPSC
    • Krishna, brother of Simuka, succeeded him.
    • Satakarni I, son and successor of Krishna, was first to hold the title 'Satakarni'; the Nanaghat inscriptions tell of his rule.
    • Gautamiputra Satakarni, patron of Brahmanism = protector of the Varna system: Nashik inscription says he allowed no inter-caste marriage among the four Varnas and stopped crossbreeding.
    • Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri calls her son Gautamiputra Satakarni 'Ekabrahmana' (unrivalled Brahmana), hinting at Brahmin origin.UPPSC
    • Satavahana period: Sanskrit, Prakrit and other folk languages developed, because the kings promoted them for literary writing.UPPSC
    • Satavahana kings nurtured Prakrit more than Sanskrit; the public aspect of the arts got more encouragement in their time.UPPSC
    • Political inscriptions show that Sanskrit was rarely used; Satavahana architecture and sculpture are associated with Buddhism.
    • Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh) has a platform with Ayaka (Aryak) pillars.UPPSC
    • After Satavahana power weakened, the Vakatakas rose in Dakshinapath; founder Vindhyashakti; Pravarasena was Vindhyashakti's son (not the reverse).
    • Puranas call the Ikshvaku rulers 'Shriparvatiya'.UPPSC
    • Ikshvakus were lords under the Satavahanas and became independent after their decline; founder Shrisantmula.

    Kharavela of Kalinga

    • Kharavela, king of Kalinga (present Odisha), is known chiefly from the Hathigumpha inscription, which he had inscribed.UPPSC
    • Hathigumpha inscription is undated and partly damaged; it records 13 years of Kharavela's reign; a few minor inscriptions are also in the Udayagiri caves.
    • Kharavela belonged to the Chedi dynasty, also called the Mahameghavahana dynasty; he was its best-known king.UPPSC ×2
    • Kharavela was a follower and patron of Jainism.UPPSC
    • Udayagiri and Khandagiri hills (Bhubaneswar, Odisha) have both natural and artificial rock-cut caves: Udayagiri 18, Khandagiri 15.
    • The Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri caves (near Bhubaneswar), not Khandagiri.

    Trade and other facts

    • Ancient India had many river ports and large entrepots (warehouses) of goods and traffic.UPPSC
    • Indus Valley: port Lothal and warehouses at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro show large trading hubs.
    • In historical times the Ganga, Indus and Kaveri were important trade and transport routes.
    • Ports Muziris and Sopara were famous for trade with Rome and Southeast Asia.
    • Eastern Roman ruler Justinian is known for Roman law: he fully revised it; the Corpus Juris Civilis is still the basis of civil law in many states.

    Chapter 11 · Ancient India

    Gupta and Post-Gupta Period

    320 facts · 13 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Maharshi Patanjali = founder of Yoga Darshan; he explained Yoga as a compact philosophical theory, so it is called 'Patanjali Darshan'.×4
    2. First Huna invasion of India came in the reign of Skandagupta (455-467 AD); he badly defeated the Hunas.×3
    3. Nyaya Darshan was propagated by Gautama, also called 'Akshapada'; its original text 'Nyayasutra' is Gautama's masterpiece.×3
    4. Chandragupta I was the first Gupta ruler to issue coins; no evidence of coins of the early rulers Srigupta and Ghatotkacha; Samudragupta's many coin types came after him.×2
    5. Historian V. A. Smith in 'The Early History of India' called Samudragupta the 'Napoleon of India' for his great military conquests.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 74 UPPSC questions

    Gupta dynasty: start and early rulers

    • Gupta dynasty ruled 275-550 AD; founded by King Srigupta around 275 AD; among exam options "319-500 AD" is the most accurate.
    • Chandragupta I (319-335 AD) = first powerful Gupta ruler; took the title 'Maharajadhiraja' (unlike his predecessors) to show his importance.
    • Gupta dynasty was founded by Srigupta, but the reign of Chandragupta I is taken as the beginning of the Gupta empire.
    • Chandragupta I was the first Gupta ruler to issue coins; no evidence of coins of the early rulers Srigupta and Ghatotkacha; Samudragupta's many coin types came after him.UPPSC ×2
    KingQueen
    Chandragupta (I)KumaradeviUPPSC
    SamudraguptaDuttadevi
    Chandragupta IIKubernaga
    Kumaragupta IAnantdevi
    • After Samudragupta his son Ramagupta became ruler but could not oppose the Saka invasion.
    • Chandragupta II killed his (elder) brother Ramagupta, married his wife Dhruvadevi and won against the Sakas.

    Samudragupta

    • Samudragupta ruled 335-375 AD; father = Chandragupta I; mother = Kumaradevi, a Lichchhavi princess.
    • Samudragupta is called 'Lichchhavi-Dauhitra' (son of the daughter / grandson of the Lichchhavis) because of his mother Kumaradevi.
    • Historian V. A. Smith in 'The Early History of India' called Samudragupta the 'Napoleon of India' for his great military conquests.UPPSC ×2
    • The Nalanda and Gaya copper plate inscriptions of Samudragupta give him the title 'Param Bhagavata' (first Gupta ruler with this title).UPPSC ×2

    Note from the book Param Bhagavata question: UPPSC gave Chandragupta II as the answer, while UGC accepted Samudragupta.

    • Tej Ram Sharma's book 'A Political History of the Imperial Guptas' describes the Ashvamedha Yajna done by Samudragupta.
    • After the Ashvamedha, Samudragupta took the title 'Prithivyama Pratiratha' = a man with no rival on earth (first brave man on Earth: 'Prithivyah Pratham Veer').UPPSC

    Note from the book UPPSC excluded the 'Prithivyah Pratham Veer' question (U.P.P.C.S. Pre 2016) from evaluation.

    • Meghavarman, Buddhist king of Sri Lanka (Ceylon), sent a missionary to Samudragupta; Samudragupta allowed him to build a monastery/Buddhist temple at Bodh Gaya (Chinese source).
    • Samudragupta is linked with the Eran inscription.
    • Samudragupta issued six types of gold coins: Garuda, Archer, Parashu (battle-axe), Ashvamedha, Vyaghra-Parakramah (tiger), Veena type.

    Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad pillar)

    • The Allahabad (Prayag) pillar inscription, engraved on an Ashoka pillar at Allahabad (Prayagraj), is associated with Samudragupta and tells of his reign and military campaigns.UPPSC ×2
    • It is also called 'Prayag Prashasti'; most important historical document of the classical Gupta age; written in excellent Sanskrit.
    • Harisena, court poet, minister and secretary of Samudragupta, wrote the Prayag Prashasti; he was not linked with Harsha.UPPSC
    • The Prashasti is a panegyric (eulogy/tribute) praising Samudragupta; lists his political and military achievements, including expeditions to the south.
    • The pillar was built by Ashoka, originally stood at Kaushambi; later shifted to Allahabad by Akbar.
    • Names of Jahangir and Birbal are also mentioned on the pillar.
    • The pillar has 4 inscriptions: (1) Ashokan inscription in Brahmi; (2) Queen's edict on the charity of Ashoka's wife Karuvaki; (3) Samudragupta's inscription by Harisena in Sanskrit language, Brahmi script; (4) Jahangir's inscription in Persian.UPPSC
    • Prayag Prashasti lists Koshala among the kingdoms and kings of 'Dakshinapath'; king of Koshala (Kosal) = Mahendra.

    Chandragupta II Vikramaditya

    • Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' ruled 375-415 AD.
    • Another name of Chandragupta II = Devagupta (evidence: Sanchi and Vakataka inscriptions); also called Devaraja (Sanchi inscription) and Devashri.UPPSC
    • Chandragupta II is called 'Saka Conqueror': he ended Saka power by defeating the last Saka king of western India, Rudrasimha III, in the first decade of the 5th century; then took the title 'Sakari' (destroyer of the Sakas).UPPSC
    • Victory over the mighty Sakas was his foremost success; annexing the Saka kingdom (Gujarat and part of Malwa) strengthened the empire and brought it in direct touch with western sea ports.
    • After the Saka victory Chandragupta II issued (dated) silver coins to mark his win over the Saka Kshatrapas; first Gupta ruler to issue silver coins.UPPSC
    • His silver coins are the strongest evidence of the Saka victory; they usually weigh about 30 to 33 grains.UPPSC
    • In the Gupta period Chandragupta II made Ujjain his second capital, so Ujjain's importance grew.
    • Chandragupta II is linked with the Udayagiri cave inscription; no record of Prabhavati Gupta is found there.UPPSC

    Mehrauli iron pillar

    • Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription (from Mehrauli, Delhi) now stands in the centre of the courtyard of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque near Qutub Minar; it describes king 'Chandra', taken to be Chandragupta II.UPPSC
    • By the Mehrauli inscription king Chandra was devoted to Vishnu and set up a Vishnu-dhvaja on a hill called Vishnupada.
    • The pillar is believed to have stood at Vishnugiri near Udaigiri Hills in Chandragupta II's time, around 410 AD.
    • Chandragupta II, a devotee of Vishnu, built the iron pillar in honour of Vishnu; Garuda, Vishnu's emblem-bearer, was engraved on its top.

    Fa-Hien

    • Fa-Hien (Faxian), Chinese Buddhist monk and pilgrim, came to India in the reign of Chandragupta II (not Harsha); he did not attend Kanishka's fourth Buddhist Council.
    • Fa-Hien travelled by the Silk Route through Central Asia to India and Sri Lanka, about 399-412 CE; stayed in India about ten years, early 5th century.
    • Fa-Hien was in India only for 10 years (402-412 AD); his whole trip from China was 399-414 AD.
    • Fa-Hien did not meet the emperor or the court; his account focuses on Buddhist life and monasteries.
    • Fa-Hien mentions a hospital at Pataliputra (the capital), endowed by benevolent citizens; poor and helpless patients got doctors, food and medicine there.
    • According to Fa-Hien, people used cowrie shells in routine trade; (another passage) people used Dinara for daily business.

    Vakatakas and Prabhavati Gupta

    • Vakataka dynasty ruled central and southern India from the 3rd century CE to the end of 5th / beginning of 6th century CE.
    • Founder of the Vakatakas = Vindhyashakti; his successor (son) Pravarasena I is called the real founder; in his time the kingdom reached from Bundelkhand (north) to the Deccan incl. modern Hyderabad (south); Puranas call him Pravira.
    • Pravarasena I (275-335 AD) was the first Vakataka ruler to call himself Samrat; he performed four Ashvamedha Yajnas and many Vedic sacrifices.UPPSC ×2
    • Pravarasena II of the same dynasty loved literature; he wrote 'Setubandha'.
    • Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, was married to Rudrasena II of the Vakataka dynasty (powerful in the Deccan); after his death she ruled the Vakataka kingdom as regent.

    Kumaragupta I and the Mandsaur (Dashpur) inscription

    • Kumaragupta I 'Mahendraditya' (415-455 AD) was the son of Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi.
    • Mandsaur Prashasti gives the achievements of Kumaragupta I; composed in Malwa by his contemporary Vatsabhatta (Vatsabhatti).UPPSC
    • The Dashpur (Mandsaur) inscription of Kumaragupta I's time is called the first advertisement of the world: it advertises the silk trade (silk fabrics).
    • The Dashpur inscription mentions the Tantuwayas (silk weavers' guild), from the Lata region (Gujarat), who built a Sun (Surya) temple at Dashpur; the same guild renovated it.
    • It also names Kumaragupta's governor Bandhuvarman, who repaired the Sun temple.
    • The inscription calls Dashpur Pashchimapur; it was composed by Vatsabhatti, not by Bhavabhuti.

    Skandagupta and the Hunas

    • First Huna invasion of India came in the reign of Skandagupta (455-467 AD); he badly defeated the Hunas.UPPSC ×3
    • This invasion was like a raid with no lasting impact, but it hastened the decline of the Gupta Empire (the dynasty most disturbed by Hunas).UPPSC
    • After Skandagupta's death the Hunas annexed many north-west regions in the 5th-6th century transition.
    • Bhitari Pillar inscription (Bhitari, Saidpur tehsil, Ghazipur district, U.P.) describes the war between Skandagupta and the Hunas.UPPSC
    • Toramana (a Huna) led the second Huna attack on India.
    • Mihirakula, of Central Asian Huna origin, was one of the most important Hephthalite emperors; the Gwalior inscription shows his territory included Gwalior.
    • Mihirakula was defeated by the Aulikara king Yashodharman of Malwa in 528 AD (other sources: 495 AD).UPPSC
    • Vasula Kavi composed Yashodharman's Sondani (Sondhni) inscription; an important historical and literary record of his reign; it tells of his victories and governance.
    • Causes of Gupta decline included Huna invasion, feudal set-up and later Guptas accepting Buddhism; Arab invasion was not a cause (Arabs came in the medieval era, much later).

    Gupta administration

    • Gupta rule was monarchical; Gupta rulers believed in their divine (supernatural) origin (more than the Mauryan rulers) and extended the tradition of land grants; administration was NOT highly centralised.
    • The Gupta king was king of many smaller kingdoms; feudal and provincial rulers had full independence in their areas (a federal-type system).
    • Administrative divisions in order: Bhukti → Vishaya → Vithi → Grama; the empire was divided into provinces called Bhukti.UPPSC
    UnitOfficer
    EmpireKing
    Bhukti (province)Uparika
    VishayaVishayapati
    VithiAayulan and Vithimahattar
    GramGramik / Ashtakuladhikari
    • Vishti = forced labour imposed by the state, provincial governor or local chief; counted as a source of state income, a kind of tax paid by the people.
    • Vishti is listed among taxes in Gupta copper inscriptions; the Junagadh inscription shows it was imposed in Gujarat and Malwa.
    • Vishti was not wage labour (wage labour existed but was not called Vishti); it could fall on anyone, not only the eldest son.

    Land, revenue and taxes

    • Gupta rulers donated the maximum number of villages to temples and Brahmins; income from village land went to the land's owner.
    • The Gupta Empire gave tax-free farm land to religious functionaries, i.e. Brahmins.
    • Gupta land revenue rate = one-sixth (1/6) of produce, paid by those who tilled the ruler's official land.
    • In every religious text (Hindu law) the land revenue rate is 1/6 of the produce.UPPSC
    • Land revenue is called 'Udranga' and 'Bhag' in Gupta inscriptions.
    • Irrigation tax in ancient India = 'Udakabhaga' (Udakabhog).UPPSC
    • Hiranya = cash tax in the Mauryan period.
    • Uparikara (Uparnika) = tax on farmers with no ownership rights in the soil / temporary tenants (farmers living on the land), or an additional cess.
    • 'Aprahat' = uncultivated forest land; a term of the Gupta revenue system.
    • Kulyavapa and Dronavapa = measures of land in the Gupta period.
    • Araghatta = water-lifting device: a large wheel with earthen pots tied to the ends of its spokes (Ar = spokes/wheel, Ghata = pot); used in ancient and early medieval India; known as the Persian wheel.

    Trade, ports, guilds and industry

    • When the Huna invasion ended the Roman Empire in the 3rd century AD, Indian merchants relied more and more on South-East Asian trade.
    • Tamralipti port in Bengal handled North Indian trade in the Gupta period; trade went to South-East Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra and northern India.UPPSC
    • Bhrigukachchha (Bharuch/Broach) = main west-coast port; North India's sea trade with western countries went from here.
    • Most Gupta trade was with South-East Asia, so Tamralipti was the most important port; Bharuch, Kalyan and Cambay were also used for North Indian trade.
    • India's early trade and cultural links with South-East Asia across the Bay of Bengal were helped by the monsoon winds, which made sea voyages easy.
    • Main centres of international trade in the Gupta period: Tamralipti, Bhrigukachchha, Arikamedu, Kaveripattanam, Muziris, Pratishthana, Sopara, Barberikam.
    • Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were ports handling foreign trade in the Gupta period (external and internal trade flourished).
    • Guilds (Shreni) were set up by merchants to regulate their trade; they fixed wages, rules of work, standards and prices and had judicial power over members.
    • Each guild had its own head, with no interference by the kingdom, but worked under royal recognition (not registered under the king's control); guilds also mattered in governing local bodies.
    • Head of a trade guild = Sarthavaha or Srenipramukh; the term Sarthavaha is linked with the Vaishya varna.
    • Rules of conduct for trade set by the guild head were called Samay and Srenidharma.
    • Gujarat, Bengal, Deccan and Tamil country were famous for textile (garment) manufacture; textiles were the chief industry of the Gupta period.
    • Warangal was famous for iron implements (3rd century AD); the 'Agaria' people lived there and iron-making was their traditional work.UPPSC
    • 'Kausheya' = word for silk in the Gupta and later Gupta periods.UPPSC

    Gupta coins

    • Gupta gold coins were called Dinara.UPPSC ×2
    • Gupta silver coins were called Rupaka.UPPSC
    • Gupta coins have been found in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Odisha; the most coins came from Bayana (Bharatpur, Rajasthan).
    • Gadhaiya (Gandhaiya) = a type of silver coin, issued on the lines of Sassanian coins.

    Society and culture in the Gupta age

    • Gupta period is called the Golden Age of ancient India for its excellent growth in art and culture.UPPSC
    • Towns declined gradually in the Gupta period; most prosperous towns of the valley declined.
    • Pataliputra was in ruins, a village with a small settlement, when Hiuen-Tsang came; Mathura, Sonpur, Hastinapur and Sravasti also show decline.
    • First inscriptional evidence of Sati = Eran inscription of 510 AD: wife of war commander Goparaja became sati.UPPSC
    • In Sanskrit plays of the Gupta period, women and Sudras speak Prakrit; upper varnas speak Sanskrit.
    • Except the Vedic age, women's condition was never good in ancient India; inferior status is seen in Gupta, Maurya and Chola ages; in no age were women equal to men.UPPSC
    • 'Mrichchhakatika' ('The Little Clay Cart') by Shudraka tells the love story of rich merchant Charudatta and Vasantasena, a courtesan's daughter.
    • Mrichchhakatika shows urban social life, politics and social change in the Gupta period; it also tells of some Shudra officers in Ujjayini.
    • Chess began in India in the Gupta period as 'Chaturanga'; it went from India to Iran and then Europe.UPPSC

    Science, mathematics and medicine

    • Dhanvantari, one of the Navratnas of Chandragupta II, was a master of Ayurveda.
    • Charaka and Sushruta were great Ayurveda scholars; Charaka was Kanishka's physician and wrote 'Charaka Samhita'.
    • Sushruta = father of surgery; resident of Kashi; period around 600 BC.
    • Shaunaka = a sage of the Rigveda; Shudraka = dramatist of the Gupta period; Saumilla = Gupta-period playwright remembered by Kalidasa.
    • None of Sushruta, Saumilla, Shudraka, Shaunaka worked on medicine in the Gupta period; Sushruta (600 BC) lived about 875 years before the Gupta start (275 AD).

    Note from the book BPSC's first answer key gave Sushruta for "medicine in the Gupta period"; the book says Sushruta cannot be a Gupta contemporary.

    • Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskara II), great astronomer and mathematician of the 12th century (not a Gupta contemporary, not linked with medicine), wrote 'Siddhanta Shiromani' and 'Lilavati'.UPPSC
    • Bhaskara I was a post-Gupta contemporary; he wrote Mahabhaskariya and Laghubhaskariya.
    • Aryabhatta, mathematician and astronomer, wrote 'Aryabhatiyam'; first to say day and night come from the earth's rotation on its axis.
    • Many special surgical instruments were in use by the 1st century AD; transplant of internal organs was not possible then; sine known in 5th century; cyclic quadrilateral known in 7th century.
    • Sine, cosine and inverse sine were known in the 5th century AD; they are in 'Surya Siddhanta' and 'Aryabhatiya'.
    • Brahmagupta described the cyclic quadrilateral (in 700 AD).

    Six systems of philosophy

    • Hindu philosophy = a group of darshans (philosophies, worldviews, teachings) that arose in ancient India.
    • Six mainstream systems (Saddarsana): Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta; Lokayata and Kapalika are not among them.
    PhilosophyPropagator
    NyayaGautam
    Purva MimamsaJaimini
    SankhyaKapil
    Vedanta / Uttar MimamsaBadarayana
    VaisheshikaUlook Kanad (Kanada Muni)
    YogaPatanjali
    PhilosophyMethod to achieve salvation
    Nyaya DarshanLogical thinkingUPPSC
    Mimamsa DarshanPerforming Vedic rituals
    Sankhya DarshanAcquisition of real knowledge
    Vedanta DarshanKnowledge of self
    • Bauddha (Buddhist) school is a Nastika school because it does not take the Vedas as a valid source of knowledge.
    • Indian philosophy grew through constant dialogue and debate between non-Vedic schools and other schools; Buddhism had a massive impact on Indian philosophy and culture.

    Sankhya

    • Sankhya is one of the oldest schools, one of six orthodox schools; Maharshi Kapila is its Acharya and earliest exponent.UPPSC ×2
    • Sankhya teaches that man's life is shaped by the forces of nature, not by any divine agency.
    • 'Sankhya Sutra' and Tattvasamasa (late 14th-15th century text of uncertain author) are traditionally attributed to Kapila.
    • Sankhya accepts rebirth (transmigration of the soul); it holds that self-knowledge, not any outside influence or agent, leads to liberation.
    • In Sankhya, nescience (ignorance) is the cause of sorrow; self-enlightenment through knowledge is the way out.
    • Satkaryavada (cause-effect doctrine) belongs to Sankhya: the effect pre-exists in the cause and is manifested from it.
    • This inseparable cause-effect link is called Avinabhava: no cause, no effect; example: without clay no pot can be made.

    Yoga

    • Maharshi Patanjali = founder of Yoga Darshan; he explained Yoga as a compact philosophical theory, so it is called 'Patanjali Darshan'.UPPSC ×4
    • Yoga's history is very old; it is described in the Upanishads, Mahabharata, Bhagavad Gita, Jain and Buddhist texts.
    • Ashtanga Yoga (eight-limbed yoga) of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras: Yama (social discipline), Niyama (personal discipline), Asana (postures), Pranayama (breath control), Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), Dharana (concentration), Dhyana (meditation), Samadhi (spiritual absorption); Anusmriti is not part of it.
    • Ashtanga Yoga is meant for physical, mental and spiritual development.
    • Antaranga Sadhana = the last three limbs, Dharana, Dhyana and Samadhi; internal aids to self-realization.
    • Patanjali, author of Mahabhashya, was a contemporary of Pushyamitra Shunga (184-148 BC).UPPSC

    Nyaya

    • Nyaya Darshan was propagated by Gautama, also called 'Akshapada'; its original text 'Nyayasutra' is Gautama's masterpiece.UPPSC ×3
    • 'Nyaya' means decision or logic; Nyaya recognizes 16 substances (logics).
    • In Nyaya, knowledge (Gyana) is a synonym of both Buddhi (cognition) and Upalabdhi (apprehension).
    • Gyana has two senses: restricted = unmanifested knowledge; broad = both manifested and unmanifested knowledge.
    • In Indian philosophy the means of gaining knowledge is called 'Pramana' (valid means of knowledge).
    • Navya-Nyaya school was founded by the work of Mithila scholar Udayana (Udayanacharya) and after him Gangesh.UPPSC

    Mimamsa

    • Jaimini started (Purva) Mimamsa.
    • The theory of Karma belongs to Mimamsa; it is also called Karma Mimamsa, Purva Mimamsa or Dharma Mimamsa.UPPSC
    • Mimamsa acharya Kumaril Bhatta is seen as the link between Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta.
    • Mimamsa holds that the Vedas contain the eternal truth.
    • Purva Mimamsa deals with 'Karmakanda'; Uttar Mimamsa with 'Gyankand'.
    • The doctrine of Apurva belongs to Mimamsa: an unseen force created by deeds, the mediator between Karma and its result (something not there before the deed).

    Vaisheshika

    • Maharshi Kanad founded the Vaisheshika school and gave the atom theory; he is called the founder of Indian Atomism.
    • Kanad was a scientist and philosopher; he gave the atomistic approach to physics and philosophy in Sanskrit.
    • Atom theory: material things are made of atoms; Vaisheshika marks the start of physics in India.
    • Kanad was first to prove the atom is the smallest unit of matter; it cannot be seen by the naked eye or divided further.
    • Vaisheshika stresses the study of substance (dravya); Earth, Water, Fire, Air and Sky combine to make new objects.

    Vedanta and Shankaracharya

    • Vedanta is one of the six darshans, often treated as the peak of Vedic thought; the word means 'the end of the Vedas' / climax of Vedic ideology.
    • Vedanta has three bases, the 'Prasthanatrayi': Upanishads, Brahmasutra and Bhagavad Gita.
    • Adi Shankaracharya was the main exponent (founder) of Advaita Vedanta; he systematized earlier philosophers' work.
    • Shankara's philosophy = non-dualism: Brahman is the one and only reality; everything else is mere illusion.
    • In Advaita Vedanta, Mukti (liberation) comes by knowledge (Gyana) of the identity of Atman (soul) and Brahman.
    • Shankara took many Buddhist ideas into his philosophy, so he is called 'Crypto-Buddhist'.
    • Visistadvaita = a main branch of Vedanta; means "non-dualism with differentiation"; Vaishnava saint Ramanujacharya (c. 1017-1137) spread it.
    • Great Vedanta scholars: Shankaracharya (8th century), Ramanuja (11th century), Madhava (13th century); Abhinav Gupta is not related to Vedanta.
    • Shankaracharya (also Shankar, Shree Shankaracharya) was born in Kaladi, a small village in Kerala, in the 8th century.UPPSC
    • Hinduism had declined with the rise of Jainism and Buddhism; it rose again with Shankaracharya.
    • Shankaracharya preached Vedanta, set up four religious centres and travelled all over India on foot to study and compile the Vedas; he countered the spread of Buddhism and Jainism; he did not name Prayag 'Teerthraj'.UPPSC
    • Four monasteries of Shankaracharya: Sringeri (Karnataka, south), Dwarka (Gujarat, west), Puri (Odisha, east), Jyotirmath / Joshimath (Uttarakhand, north).UPPSC
    • Shankaracharya's four centres are counted as the most important centres of Hinduism; his philosophy is called 'Advaita Vedanta'.
    • Vedanta philosophy has had an enormous impact on Hindu thought and culture; its great scholars gave varying interpretations of it.
    • Chardham = Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram; Mansarovar is not included.
    • Chota (lesser) Chardham in Uttarakhand = Gangotri, Yamunotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath.

    Charvaka (Lokayata)

    • Charvaka philosophy, originally called Lokayata, is the ancient school of Indian materialism; it values material things and pleasures.
    • Charvaka saying: "Live well as long as you live; live well even by borrowing, for once cremated there is no return."
    • Charvaka accepts direct perception, empiricism and conditional inference as sources of knowledge; it holds philosophical scepticism and rejects the Vedas, Vedic ritualism and supernaturalism.
    • Charvaka: "the conscious body is the soul"; body is the basis of consciousness, soul and body are the same; this view = 'Dehatmavada'.
    • Charvaka statement: "A body without consciousness is a corpse, and consciousness without a body is not a soul."
    • Ajita Kesakambali is credited as the forerunner of the Charvakas.
    • For Charvaka the highest value is Kama (pleasure): wisdom is to enjoy pleasure and avoid pain; it rejected austerities.
    • Sarvasiddhanta Samgraha on Charvaka: heaven's joy is good food, company of young women, fine clothes, perfumes, garlands, sandal paste; Moksha is death (end of life-breath).

    Eras (Samvat)

    EraStartsStarted by
    Vikram era57 or 58 BCVikramaditya, on his victory over the Sakas
    Saka era78 ADKanishka
    Gupta era (Gupta Samvat)319 AD (nearest option 320 AD)Chandragupta I
    Kali era3102 BCassumed start
    • Vikram Samvat is also called Krit Samvat and Malav Samvat.
    • Muslim rule in India began in 1192 AD after Ghori's victory in the battle of Tarain, though Muhammad Bin Qasim annexed Sindh in the early 8th century.UPPSC
    • Badami rock inscription of Pulakesin I is dated Saka 465 = Vikram Samvat 601 (465 + 78 + 58).
    • A Chalukya inscription of Saka year 556 = 634 AD (556 + 78).UPPSC

    Kingdoms after the Guptas

    • According to the Puranas, Chandravansh (Somvansha) was a prime dynasty of the Kshatriya varna; its rulers' prime place was Prayag.
    • After a natural calamity, the Dwapar Yug Chandravanshi king Samvaram set up his capital at Pratishthanpur (present Jhunsi, Prayagraj).UPPSC
    • From the Gupta decline to Harsha's rise, powers in North India were: the Guptas of Magadha, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, the Maukharis of Kanauj and the Maitrakas of Valabhi.
    • Later Guptas followed the Guptas as rulers of Magadha (present Bihar) and parts of North India, into the early 7th century.
    • Pushyabhutis of Thanesar (present Haryana) ruled parts of North India in the 6th and 7th centuries AD.
    • Maitrakas of Valabhi ruled western and northern parts of present Gujarat, late 5th to late 8th century AD.
    • Paramaras ruled western and central India incl. Malwa, 9th to 14th century AD, before the Delhi Sultanate took over.
    • Yadavas of Devagiri ruled western India from around 1187 to 1317 AD.
    • Maukharis were feudatories of the Guptas, originally from Gaya; they made Kannauj their capital.
    • Maukharis ruled parts of Uttar Pradesh and Magadha incl. Kannauj, till around 606 AD, when the Later Guptas reconquered it.
    • Main Maukhari rulers: Hari Varma, Aditya Varma, Ishvara Varma, Ishan Varma, Sharva-Varma (Sarva Verma), Graha-Varma.
    • A copper seal inscription of Maukhari king Sarvavarman (c. 6th century AD) was found at Asirgarh fort, north of Burhanpur, M.P. (not a Gaya copper plate); it gives the Maukhari genealogy from Harivarman.UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Ishwarverman – Jaunpur stone inscription; Ishanverman – Harha stone inscription; Jivit Gupta II – Deva Barnark inscription.

    Harshavardhana

    • By Banabhatta's Harshacharita, the Vardhana dynasty was founded by Pushyabhuti at Thaneshwar (Sthaneshwar); Harshavardhana was its greatest ruler.
    • Harshacharita was written by Banabhatta, Harsha's court poet; it is the main source for the Vardhana dynasty.
    • Harshacharita describes the author's contemporary ruler and the biographies of his ancestors.
    • Some information on Harsha also comes from Kalhana's Rajatarangini; Kalidasa's and Harisena's books say nothing of Harsha.UPPSC
    • Banabhatta was born at village Prithikuta on the Son river in Aurangabad district (present Bihar); others say Prithikuta village in Kannauj, U.P.
    • Banabhatta's father = Chitrabhanu; mother = Rajdevi.
    • Harsha shifted his capital from Thaneshwar to Kannauj to help his sister Rajyashri rule Kannauj; Chinese sources say Harsha and Rajyashri ruled Kannauj together.UPPSC ×2
    • Kannauj was a suitable place to rule Harsha's wide empire.
    • Harsha held two great religious assemblies: at Kannauj and at Prayag.UPPSC ×2
    • Kannauj council: for many religions and sects, to prove Mahayana's excellence; rulers of 20 countries came with Brahmins, shramanas and courtiers; Harsha presided.
    • 'Mahamoksha council' was held at the Sangam of Prayag every fifth year of Harsha's rule; Hiuen Tsang attended the 6th one, attended by 18 rulers.
    • Bhaskar Varman ruled Assam in Harsha's time; he was the last ruler of the Varman dynasty.
    • Harsha's southward march was stopped on the Narmada by Chalukya king Pulakesin II, who defeated him; recorded in Pulakesin II's Aihole inscription and by Hiuen Tsang.UPPSC
    • Pulakesin II also wanted to expand north, so war was certain; it was fought on the bank of the Narmada.
    • Pulakesin ruled much of modern Karnataka and Maharashtra; capital Badami in modern Bijapur district, Karnataka.
    • Harsha–Pulakesin battle is usually placed between 630 and 634 AD: after the battle of Vallabhi (not before 630); Pulakesin's Lohnara inscription (630 AD) omits Harsha, Aihole inscription (634 AD) mentions the battle.
    • In April 2016 Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute researchers fixed Pulakesin's victory over Harsha at 618 AD, from a newly found copper plate of Pulakesin II.

    Note from the book Pulakesin–Harsha battle year: the book finds 630-634 AD more correct (nearest option 634 AD); Jharkhand PSC accepted 618 AD.

    • Harsha leaned to Buddhism before meeting Hiuen-Tsang (not hostile to it); after meeting him Harsha gave royal patronage to Mahayana and became Buddhist.
    • After Harsha's death Kannauj became the centre of attraction for powers; it was called 'Mahodaya', 'Mahodayashri'.
    • Tripartite struggle for Kannauj among Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta (8th-9th century) = most important event of North India then; finally the Pratiharas won.

    Hiuen Tsang

    • Hiuen Tsang (Yuan Chwang) visited India in Harsha's reign; his coming was the most important event of Harsha's period.UPPSC ×2
    • He wished to see places linked with Buddha and study Buddhist texts; left for India in 629 AD from Changan, capital of the Tang ruler; he was a Buddhist.
    • Hiuen Tsang wrote 'Sei-Yu-Kei' (Si-Yu-Ki) on his India tour; he is remembered for it as it has much information on ancient India.UPPSC
    • Hiuen-Tsang was a contemporary of Taizong of the Tang dynasty, who had banned foreign travel to the West; still he came by the silk route in 629 AD (not sent as an emissary).UPPSC
    • He returned to China after 13 years; the emperor welcomed him, made him spiritual adviser; at the emperor's request he wrote "A Record of the Western Regions".
    • Hiuen Tsang went to Nalanda University in 637 AD and studied there; Acharya Sheelbhadra was its Vice-Chancellor.UPPSC
    • At Nalanda he learned Yogashastra for almost one and a half years; he gave a speech on his second visit.
    • Hiuen Tsang: roads and river-routes were not fully free from robbery (he was robbed many times); ordeals by fire, water and poison tested guilt; tradesmen paid duties at ferries and barrier stations.
    • He says punishment for crime was harsh; tax was levied on trade routes, river banks, products and goods, giving the state ample money.
    • Hiuen Tsang stayed in India and visited almost every province.
    • By Hiuen Tsang, Mathura was famous for cotton textiles and Varanasi for silk textiles.
    • By Hiuen Tsang, trade was the main reason for Thaneshwar's prosperity; Ujjayini and Kannauj were also prosperous.
    • Hiuen Tsang also visited Bhinmal.
    • The Sun temple of Multan is mentioned by Hiuen Tsang, Abuzaiyid, Al-Masudi and Alberuni; pilgrimage to Sambapur was linked with Sun worship.UPPSC

    Other travellers and Nalanda

    • Chinese traveller Sungyun travelled in India 518-521 AD (early 6th century); in three years he collected texts of Buddha's teachings.
    • I-tsing (Itsing) (671-695 AD) set out with 37 Buddhist companions in 671 or 672 AD to see Buddhist relics; companions left him, he went on alone from Canton; so not in 405, 635 or 637 AD.
    • I-tsing reached India by the southern sea route at Tamralipti (another passage: western sea route); returned to China in 693-94 AD via Sumatra.
    TravellerIndia visit
    Fa-Hien402–412 CEUPPSC
    Hiuen Tsang629–645 CE
    I-tsing671–695 CE
    Al-Masudi915-16 AD
    Al-Biruni1017–1030 CE
    • Chinese writers called India 'Yin-tu' and 'Thian-tu', a variation of Hindu or Sindhu.UPPSC
    • Nalanda University drew scholars and students from Tibet, China, Greece and Persia.
    • Nalanda was ransacked and destroyed by the army of Bakhtiyar Khalji (Muslims) at the end of the 12th century (around 1193 AD); the final blow (coup de grace) to Buddhism in India.
    • Nalanda is the most ancient monastery (among Nalanda, Udantpuri, Vikramshila, Bhaja); its history goes back to Buddha and Mahavira, 6th century BC.
    • Nalanda, the ancient university town, is in Bihar.
    • Excavations show no sign that the Nalanda site was occupied before the Gupta period (5th century AD).

    Post-Gupta economy and feudalism

    • In the post-Gupta period the main business centre shifted from Ujjain to Kannauj.
    • Kannauj lay on the banks of the Ganga and Jamuna, so it had business value and drew three powers: Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas.
    • Growth of feudalism was the main feature of post-Gupta agrarian structure, because a land-owning middle class and a dependent peasant class arose.UPPSC
    • Large land grants to officials, temples and nobles made landed intermediaries (landlords); cultivators became dependent peasants paying rent and services.
    • Essential elements of the feudal system: administrative structure based on control and possession of land; lord-vassal relationship between feudal lord and overlord.
    • Feudal system in India was laid in the Saka-Kushan period and peaked in the Rajput period; part of administration under Kushanas, Rajputs, Sultanate and Mughals.
    • Strong central authority divided the empire into parts run through feudals; feudals were weaker and followed the king's orders; they had rights to collect tax and to govern.
    • A master-slave relation between king and feudal is not found in India; Indian feudalism differed from Europe's.
    • 'Hundi' in post-Harsha sources = a bill of exchange; RBI: Hundis are financial instruments evolved on the Indian subcontinent for trade and credit.

    Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas

    • Pratihara dynasty was one of the most famous Agnikula clans; known as Gurjara-Pratihara from inscriptions.
    • First mention of the Gurjara caste = Aihole text of Pulakeshin II; Gurjars also appear in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.
    • Founder of the Gurjara-Pratiharas = Nagabhata I (730-756 AD); Gwalior inscription says he destroyed the large army of a Mlechcha king, probably the Arab ruler of Sindh.
    • Rashtrakuta dynasty was founded in 753 AD by Dantidurga; capital Manyakheta; he is said to have done a Hiranyagarbha (Mahadan) Yajna at Ujjaini.
    • Rashtrakuta Amoghavarsha I was born in 800 AD in the military camp of Sribhavan on the Narmada, when his father Govind III was returning from successful North India campaigns.

    Places

    • Bhilsa = archaeological site in Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh; Girinagar (Girnar) = group of mountains in Junagarh district, Gujarat.
    • Dwarasamudra = capital of the Hoysala dynasty, in modern Karnataka (not Maharashtra).
    • Sthanesvara (Thanesar) = historic town and Hindu pilgrimage centre on the Saraswati river in Haryana (not Uttar Pradesh).

    Chapter 12 · Ancient India

    Architecture in Ancient India

    149 facts · 12 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Kailasa temple was built by Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I in Dravidian style.×6
    2. Khajuraho temples show the excellence of Chandela architecture; built by the Chandela dynasty, mostly between 950-1050 AD; in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh.×4
    3. Ellora has 34 caves of different periods: caves 1-12 Buddhist (12), 13-29 Hindu (17), 30-34 Jain (5).×4
    4. Elephanta has two groups: a large group of five Hindu caves (Shaiva, dedicated to Shiva, with rock-cut sculptures) and a smaller group of two Buddhist caves.×3
    5. Konark Sun Temple (Odisha, 13th century) was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 53 UPPSC questions

    Khajuraho temples

    • Khajuraho temples show the excellence of Chandela architecture; built by the Chandela dynasty, mostly between 950-1050 AD; in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh.UPPSC ×4
    • Kandariya Mahadev Temple, attributed to (Chandela) king Vidyadhar (11th century), is the largest Khajuraho temple.UPPSC
    • Records describe the building of 85 temples at Khajuraho.
    • Khajuraho is a group of Hindu and Jain temples: dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, Shakta, Surya and Jaina patriarchs.UPPSC
    • Matangeshvara temple of Khajuraho is dedicated to Lord Shiva; built in King Dhanga's reign; Khajuraho temples are in Nagara style.UPPSC
    • Parshvanath temple is the famous Jain temple at Khajuraho; other temples: Chausath Yogini, Brahma, Lalguan Mahadev, Lakshmana, Vishvanath, Chitragupta.
    • Dashavatara Temple is not at Khajuraho: it is at Devgarh/Deogarh (Lalitpur), built in the Gupta period.
    • In Khajuraho temples all compartments of the temple are connected internally and externally.
    • Khajuraho group of monuments, Bhimbetka rock shelters and Sanchi Stupa are UNESCO World Heritage Sites; Mandu fort is not.
    • Khajuraho is known for Shaiva, Vaishnava and Jain temples.

    Chausath Yogini temple, Morena

    • Chausath Yogini temple is in Morena district (M.P.); an inscription of 1323 CE (Vikram Samvat 1383) says Kachchhapaghata king Devapala built it; its circular shape is popularly believed to have inspired the Indian Parliament building.
    • The circular shape likely stands for a Sri Yantra in which the Yoginis live, with the Supreme Yogini (Maha Sakti) in the centre (the circular central main shrine).
    • It is not the only circular temple in India, and it was not meant to promote the Vaishnava cult.

    Temple styles

    • Nagara, Dravida and Vesara are the three main styles of Indian temple architecture.
    • Nagara style developed and prevails across North India; temples of Odisha are purely of this style.
    • Dravida style developed in South India, especially between the Krishna River and Cape Comorin (Tamil Nadu).
    • Vesara style grew from a mix of Nagara and Dravida; also called Chalukya style because the last Chalukya rulers used it.
    • Free-standing (mortar and stone) temples began in the Gupta period; Ladkhan, one of the earliest temples, belongs to the Chalukyas of Badami; Kailashnath of Kanchi is NOT the earliest free-standing Dravida temple.
    • Kailashnath temple at Kanchi: built by the Pallavas; fine Dravida example; built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), completed by his son Mahendravarman II.
    • Kailasanathar Temple of Kanchipuram (Tamil Nadu) is in the Rajsimha style: intricate carvings, large Gopurams, finely detailed stone sculptures; main deity Shiva.
    • Teli Temple of Gwalior fuses Nagara and Dravida: its Shikhar (pinnacle) is Dravidian, its ornamentation Nagara.UPPSC
    • Hoysaleshwara temple ('Lord of the Hoysalas') at Halebidu, Karnataka, built in dark schist stone by the Hoysala king, is an example of Vesara style.
    • Hoysala temples are called hybrid or Vesara: neither fully Dravida nor Nagara; known by star-like ground-plans and profuse decorative carvings.
    • Panchayatana = a style of temple building: a central shrine surrounded by four subsidiary shrines; from Sanskrit Pancha (five) + ayatana (containing).
    • Panchayatana examples: Kandariya Mahadeo (Khajuraho); Brahmeshwar and Lingaraja (Bhubaneswar); Dashavatara (Deogarh, U.P.).
    • Gopuram = ornate monumental multi-storied tower over the gateway of a temple, mainly in South India; a key feature of Dravidian Hindu temples.UPPSC
    • Gopuram's origin goes back to early structures of the Pallavas; by the 12th century under the Pandyas these gateways dominated the temple's look, hiding the inner sanctuary by their huge size.
    • Under the Pandyas temples were built in Dravidian style: temples were small but had ramparts around; the gateways, 'Gopurams', were elegant, spacious and richly crafted.

    Gupta temples and art

    Gupta templeLocation
    Brick-built TempleBhitargaonUPPSC
    Dashavatara TempleDeogarh
    Shiva TempleBhumara
    Vishnu TempleEran
    • Dashavatara temple, Deogarh (Lalitpur) near Jhansi and the Garhwa temple sculptures near Allahabad are remains of Gupta art.
    • Dashavatara temple of Deogarh is the earliest known Panchayatan temple in North India.
    • Garhwa fort = a Gupta-period temple complex in Shankargarh, Prayagraj.
    • Bhitargaon temple (Kanpur, U.P.): built 5th-6th century AD in the Gupta period; one of the oldest brick temples of India.UPPSC
    • Bhitargaon temple: terraced brick building fronted with terracotta panel; square plan with double-recessed corners; faces east; tall pyramidal spire over the garbhagriha; Nagara style.
    ItemPlace
    StupaSanchi (M.P.)
    PaintingBagh (M.P.)
    Headless statue of KanishkaMathura (U.P.)
    Dashavatara TempleDeogarh (U.P.)UPPSC

    Ajanta and Bagh caves

    • Ajanta and Bagh caves are the two examples of Gupta-period cave painting; Bagh paintings show normal public life, while Ajanta paintings are Buddhist.
    • Ajanta and Ellora caves are in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar (formerly Aurangabad) district, Maharashtra.UPPSC ×2
    • An earlier group of Ajanta caves was made in the Satavahana period; the major part later in the Vakataka period (main patrons of Ajanta art).
    • Ajanta = Buddhist cave temples, carved out of the mountain rock, with figures of the Lord and others.
    • Ajanta murals and sculptures are masterpieces of (Buddhist) religious art, the finest surviving examples of Indian art; they show Buddha and the Jataka stories.
    • Ajanta paintings focus on Jatakas showing Buddha's previous life as a king; they also show flowers, trees and animals.
    • Ajanta caves lie in the gorge (valley) of the Waghora river.
    • Ajanta cave 16 has an important painted theme; cave 17 has a well-preserved Vakataka-age painting with a huge wheel, the "Wheel of Life".
    • Bodhisattva Padmapani painting in Cave 1 is among Ajanta's most famous murals; Padmapani = "one who holds the lotus".
    • Padmapani is shown among devotees, princesses and commoners, long dark hair under a jewelled crown, holding a blue lotus in his right hand.
    • Ajanta cave 26 has a grand image of Buddha's Mahaparinirvana.
    • Huge Varaha Avatar image of Vishnu is at the Udaygiri caves, Madhya Pradesh, not at Mount Abu.
    • 'Arjuna's Penance' (Descent of Ganga) is sculpted on huge boulders at Mamallapuram, Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu.
    • Ajanta has 30 rock-cut caves (a series of 29 Buddhist cave temples) built from 2nd century BC to 7th century AD.
    • Ajanta and Mahabalipuram are both rock-cut monuments, but not of the same period or the same religion.
    • Mural paintings are seen at Ajanta and Lepakshi temple, not at Sanchi Stupa.
    • Sanchi Stupa's core was a simple hemispherical brick structure over Buddha's relics, crowned by the Chhatra, a parasol-like structure of high rank to honour and shelter the relics.
    • Buddhist caves are not found at Sanchi and Bulsar; Bagh caves also have Buddhist art; Ajanta shows Buddha's life and teachings.
    • Sanchi stupa was built by Maurya emperor Ashoka; lies west of the Betwa river in Raisen district, M.P.
    • Pandu-lena cave shrines are in Nashik, Maharashtra, in the valley of the Godavari river.
    • Amravati Stupa = ruined Buddhist stupa at Amravati village, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh, on the banks of the Krishna river.
    • Lomas Rishi caves belong to the Mauryan period; in Barabar hills, Jahanabad district, Bihar; Nasik caves belong to the Satavahana period.

    Other rock-cut caves

    • Ancient rock-cut caves of western India are at Nasik, Ellora and Ajanta.
    • Nasik caves are also called 'Pandavleni' or Trirashmi caves; they show Buddhist devotional practices.
    • Kanheri caves (over 100 Buddhist caves): rock-cut monuments north of Borivali on Mumbai's western outskirts; show Buddhist influence; built from the 1st century BC.UPPSC
    • Bhimbetka rock shelters, not the Badami caves, are the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India; Ashoka (not Chandragupta Maurya) gave a Barabar cave to the Ajivikas; Ellora caves were made for different faiths.
    • Barabar Hill has four caves: Karan Chaupar, Lomas Rishi, Sudama, Vishva Zopari.
    • Bhaja caves (Bhaje village, Pune, Maharashtra) = Buddhist cave shrine; Sittanavasal cave temple = built by Pallava king Mahendravarman I for Jainism; Besnagar is not a Shaivite cave shrine.
    • Besnagar (M.P.) gives evidence of the Bhagwat religion; Greek ambassador Heliodorus set up the Garuda Pillar there.
    • Rock-cut elephant at Dhauli, made in Ashoka's reign (3rd century BC), is older than the Udayagiri Varaha image (5th century AD), Mahabalipuram rock-cut monuments (7th-8th century AD) and Lingaraja Temple (10th-11th century AD).

    Elephanta

    • Elephanta caves are believed to be built by the Rashtrakuta dynasty; Ellora and Elephanta belong to the Rashtrakuta period.UPPSC
    • Elephanta island lies on an arm of the Arabian Sea; caves date from the 5th to 6th century AD.
    • Elephanta has two groups: a large group of five Hindu caves (Shaiva, dedicated to Shiva, with rock-cut sculptures) and a smaller group of two Buddhist caves.UPPSC ×3
    • The famous Trimurti (Mahesa-murti) statue of Shiva is at Elephanta.UPPSC
    • The three-faced Shiva Trimurti is like the trinity of Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh, which was the royal insignia of the Rashtrakutas.

    Ellora and Kailasa temple

    • Ellora, locally 'Verul Leni', is 30 km from Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra; world-famous for rock-cut cave temples; the Rashtrakutas built most of the caves.UPPSC ×2
    • Ellora has 34 caves of different periods: caves 1-12 Buddhist (12), 13-29 Hindu (17), 30-34 Jain (5).UPPSC ×4
    • Ellora caves were made in various periods and are not linked with the Sakas.
    • Kailasa temple (cave 16) at Ellora is the finest example and a wonder of rock-cut architecture.UPPSC ×2
    • Kailasa temple was built by Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I in Dravidian style.UPPSC ×6
    • Kailasa is a remarkable Dravidian work for its proportion, workmanship and sculpture; designed to recall Mount Kailasa, home of Shiva.
    • Rashtrakuta kings supported Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta faiths but leaned towards Jainism; many court scholars writing in Sanskrit, Kannada, Apabhramsha and Prakrit were Jains.UPPSC
    • Amoghavarsha I was a disciple of Jain Acharya Jinasena, author of Adipurana.

    Jain temples

    • Dilwara Jain temples are at Mount Abu (Aravali), Rajasthan.UPPSC ×2
    • Vimal Vasahi, most famous Dilwara temple, was built by Vimal Shah, minister (feudatory) of Chalukya (Solanki) ruler of Gujarat Bheemdev I (Bhima I).
    • The Jain temple of Abu is famed for its extraordinary architecture and marvellous marble carvings.UPPSC
    • Palitana Jain temples stand on Shatrunjaya hill near Palitana city, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat; dedicated to the 1st Tirthankara Adinatha.
    • Sonagiri is 15 km from Datia (Madhya Pradesh); sacred to Digambar Jains for self-discipline, austerity and Nirvana.UPPSC ×2
    • Sonagiri has 103 Jain temples with sky-high spires; main one is Temple No. 57, of Lord Chandraprabhu.

    Temples of Odisha

    • Konark Sun Temple (Odisha, 13th century) was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.UPPSC ×3
    • Konark was designed as a huge solar chariot with twelve pairs of ornamental wheels pulled by seven rearing horses.
    • Konark is called the Black Pagoda (by European sailors); Jagannath Temple of Puri was called the White Pagoda.UPPSC
    • Lingaraj Temple at Bhubaneswar is one of Odisha's most popular and oldest temples; dedicated to Shiva (Lingaraj), also described as Harihara, a form of Shiva.UPPSC
    • Lingaraj temple is about 180 ft high (largest and tallest among Odisha temples in the options); enshrines a huge 'Swayambhu' (self-originated) Shivling; a finest example of Nagara style.UPPSC
    • Jagannath Temple is in Puri, Odisha (Orissa).
    • Temples of Bhubaneswar (Lingaraj) and Puri (Jagannath), and Konark Sun Temple (Puri), are in Nagara style.UPPSC
    • Idols of Jagannath, Subhadra and Balbhadra in the sanctum are made of neem wood; Bhavishya Purana calls it the most auspicious wood for Vishnu idols.
    • The wooden icon is repainted every year before the Ratha-yatra; replaced by a new image about every 12 or 19 years, when the month of Asadha comes twice in one year (luni-solar calendar).

    Other Sun temples

    • Sun Temple of Modhera is in Gujarat (Patan); built by King Bhimadeva I of the Solanki dynasty.
    • Arasavalli (village in Andhra Pradesh) has a prominent 7th-century Sun temple, believed built by King Devendra Verma of the Eastern Ganga (Kalinga) dynasty; Amarkantak and Omkareshwar are not Sun temples.
    • Omkareshwar temple: Khandwa district, M.P.; on Mandhata (Shivpuri) island in the Narmada; one of the 12 Jyotirlingas of Shiva.
    • Narmada, Son and Johila rivers rise at Amarkantak; Sri Jwaleshwar (Jaleswara) Mahadev temple, 8 km away on the Shahdol road, is dedicated to Shiva.

    Pallava and Chola temples

    • Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) rock-cut and Rath temples were built by the Pallavas; it was a famous centre of Pallava art and architecture.UPPSC ×3
    • Mahabalipuram is on the seashore about 55 km south of Chennai, on a hillock over the Coromandel coast (Bay of Bengal), Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
    • Its wonders: Shore Temple, Rathas (chariots) cut from a single rock, Arjuna's Penance, other cave temples; also called 'Mandapas' rock-cut caves.
    • Mahabalipuram was a pilgrimage place even before the Pallavas; built up in the 7th-10th century; its monuments are related to Shiva or Vishnu.
    • Pallava king Narasimha Varman built these temples, including the present Shore temple (as one passage says).
    • Narasimhavarman I (Mahamalla) (630-668 AD) built the Seven Ratha Temple, with seven rock-cut pagodas; the Mamalla style grew in his time.UPPSC
    • His title 'Mahamalla' = 'great wrestler'; the city Mamallapuram is named after him.
    • Draupadi Rath is the smallest of the monolithic raths of Mamalla style.UPPSC
    • Draupadi Rath: one passage says it has carvings (incl. Goddess Durga); another says no ornamentation and it rests on lion- and elephant-like sculptures.
    • The Panch Rathas have statues of an elephant, a lion and a Nandi bull beside them.
    • Order of building: Sapt Pagoda (Mamalla style, 640-674 AD) → Shore Temple (Rajsimha style, 674-800 AD) → Brihadeeswara (Rajaraja I) → Gangaikonda Cholapuram (Rajendra I).UPPSC
    • Korangnath Temple of Srinivasanallur was built under Chola ruler Parantaka I.
    • Rajarajeshwara / Brihadeeswara Temple, Thanjavur, was built in Rajaraja I's time, of granite stone.
    • Under Rajaraja's son Rajendra Chola the temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram was built.
    • Meenakshi Temple was built by the Pandyas.
    • Virupaksha temple is at Hampi, Karnataka; named after Shiva, called Virupaksha here.

    Temples abroad

    • Angkor Wat temple complex is in Kampuchea (now Cambodia); built by Khmer king Suryavarman II in the early 12th century in his capital Yashodharapura (present Angkor).UPPSC ×3
    • Angkor Wat is dedicated to Vishnu; world's largest religious structure; Khmer style architecture.
    • Borobudur stupa is on Java island, Indonesia; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.UPPSC

    • Takshashila lay between the Indus and Jhelum rivers; set up in 6th or 7th century BC; site in present Rawalpindi district, Punjab, Pakistan.UPPSC

    • At Naimisharanya Sage Dadhichi gladly gave his bones to the gods; from them the weapon Vajra was made, with which Indra beat the Asuras and regained kingship of Devloka.
    • Chitrakoot, Hindu pilgrimage site, falls in both Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh; Chitrakoot district is in U.P.; main holy place Kamadgiri (Lord Kamata Nath) lies partly in each state.

    Note from the book Chitrakoot temple state question (70th BPSC Re-Exam 2024): question does not say which temple; BPSC accepted Madhya Pradesh.

    Folk paintings

    • Pattachitra art belongs to Odisha; closely linked to Lord Jagannath and Vaishnav cults.
    • Manjusha art = folk art of Bhagalpur, Bihar; one of India's oldest painting arts.
    • Manjushas are temple-shaped boxes with eight pillars, made of bamboo, jute and paper; painted in only three colours: pink, green, yellow; used in Bishahari Puja.
    • Pithora painting = ritual painting of tribes in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.

    Note from the book Folk-painting question: one option speaks of 'all the four statements' though only three statements are given, so it cannot be correct.

    Chapter 13 · Ancient India

    South India (Chola, Chalukya, Pallava and Sangam Period)

    160 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Arikamedu (Pondicherry, south-eastern coast) excavations show brisk Indo-Roman trade in the early Christian centuries; a Roman settlement / trading station.×4
    2. Meenakshi temple is at Madurai, the Pandya capital, where the 1st and 3rd Sangams met under Agastya and Nakkirar.×3
    3. Tolkappiyam = treatise on (Tamil) grammar and poetry; the surviving (residual) text of the 2nd Sangam era and the oldest available text of Tamil literature.×2
    4. The Cholas were famous for naval power: strong standing army and navy; conquests of Ceylon and naval raids on Srivijaya, Sinhala and Maldives.×2
    5. The special feature of Chola rule was autonomy of village administration (local self-government, village assemblies); very systematic and well developed.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 48 UPPSC questions

    Sangam assemblies and Agastya

    • In Sangam texts the terms Kon, Ko and Mannan were used for the King.
    • Sangam = 'Conference of Poets' or 'Forum of Scholars'; the literature written there, the oldest in South India, made of several anthologies of poems, is 'Sangam Literature'.
    • Three Sangams were held under the patronage of the Pandya kings.
    SangamPlacePresident
    FirstMaduraiSaint Agastya (one table adds Tolkappiyar)
    SecondKapadapuramSaint Agastya
    ThirdMaduraiNakkirarUPPSC
    • Sage Agastya is credited with Aryanising South India; called "Father of Tamil Literature".
    • Agastya was born in Kashi; believed to have gone south from Kashi at the gods' request and settled there.

    Sangam literature and Tamil texts

    • Tolkappiyam = treatise on (Tamil) grammar and poetry; the surviving (residual) text of the 2nd Sangam era and the oldest available text of Tamil literature.UPPSC ×2
    • Its author Tolkappiyar was one of the 12 disciples of Saint Agastya; it is written in formula (sutra) style.
    • Tolkappiyam has three parts of nine sections, dealing with Ezhuttu (letter), Col (word) and Porul (subject matter).
    • Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal; it tells the tragic story of Kannagi and her husband Kovalan.UPPSC
    • Ilango Adigal: second son of Chera king Nedun-ceraladan (another passage: grandson of Chola king Karikal).
    Tamil textSubject
    ThirukuralPhilosophyUPPSC
    TolkappiyamGrammar
    SilapadikaramLove story
    ManimekalaiMerchant story
    • Kural, a Tamil text by poet Tiruvalluvar, is called the ethical Bible of Tamil and the Laghuveda of Tamil literature; also known as 'Muppal'.UPPSC
    • By hearsay, Thiruvalluvar was an incarnation (advent) of Brahma.
    • Ramavataram (Tamil Ramayanam) was written by Kamban.UPPSC
    • Thirumurai = collection of writings of Saivite saints, seen as a Fifth Veda: twelve-volume compendium of Tamil hymns to Shiva, 6th to 11th century CE, by various poets.
    • Thirumurai, with the Vedas and Saiva agamas, forms the base of Saiva Siddhantha philosophy in South India.
    • Alvars = 12 saint-poets devoted to Vishnu; Nayanars = 63 saint-poets devoted to Shiva; both of the South Indian (Tamil) Bhakti tradition.
    • Sangam literature is among the oldest Tamil literature; its poetry shows the social, economic and religious conditions of South India; the Varna classification was known to Sangam poets.
    • Sangam poems also show material culture, the warrior ethic and magical forces in nature.
    • 'Vattakirutal' = Tamil ritual of fasting unto death, common in the Sangam period: a king defeated in battle killed himself by starvation.
    • Siddhas (Sittars) of the Tamil region were monotheistic and condemned idolatry; Lingayats of the Kannada region questioned rebirth and rejected caste hierarchy.
    • Siddhas are traced to the Sangam period, but the word Siddha is not in Sangam literature; linked with Shaivism, Siddhanta philosophy, Tantra, science and technology in South India.
    • Lingayats challenged the caste idea of certain Brahmin groups, encouraged widow remarriage and disapproved of pre-puberty marriage.
    • Halbi = eastern Indo-Aryan (Aryan family) language of Bastar, Chhattisgarh; transitional between Oriya and Marathi; written in Oriya and Devanagari scripts.

    Sangam kingdoms: Chola, Chera, Pandya

    • Sangam literature describes the rise and growth of the Chola, Chera and Pandya rulers; the Kadamba or any other dynasty is not mentioned.
    • The three ruling dynasties of the Sangam Age were Chera, Chola and Pandya; the Pallavas were not rulers of this age.UPPSC
    • Chera state lay in present Kerala (south-west) and partly Tamil Nadu; capital Vanchi, also named Karur/Karuvur; some sources say Thondi; Puducherry was not its capital.
    • Udiyanjiral belongs to the Chera dynasty; first historical king of the Sangam period; legend says he fed all fighters of the Mahabharata war.
    • India's trade with the Roman empire began with the Chera kingdom in the Sangam period.
    • A Pandya king of South India sent an ambassador to Rome in 26 BC.
    • Pandya dynasty had the longest reign in South India (about 200 BC to 1378 AD); capitals: Korkai (early) and Madurai (later).
    • Vaigai (Vengi) river was the lifeline of the Pandya state; the Vengi river region was famous for fertility.UPPSC
    • The Vaigai rises in the Varushanadu hills near Madurai, Tamil Nadu (another passage: Kandan Manikanur near Madurai).
    • Pandya state lay south of the Cauvery: modern Madurai and Tirunelveli districts and some parts of Travancore (Kerala); capital Madura.
    • Uraiyur, on the Cauvery in Tiruchirappalli (Tamil Nadu), was a key Sangam town and the major centre of cotton trade.
    • Uraiyur was also called Koli and Varanam; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea calls it Argaru; it was the Chola capital in the Sangam era.

    Ports and Roman trade

    • 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea', the famous book of an unknown Greek sailor, lists the ports.
    • Main ports of the western coast: Naura, Tondi, Mushiri and Nelisanda.UPPSC
    • Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were ports.
    • Poompuhar (Tamil Nadu) = prosperous ancient port city, also called Kaveri Poompattinam / Kaveripattinam; capital of the early Chola kings.
    • Korkai = Pandya port city near the Bay of Bengal; shows developed trade with ancient Rome.
    • Muziris/Muchiri = port city in Kerala, one of the world's oldest ports; mentioned in Sangam literature.
    • Arikamedu (Pondicherry, south-eastern coast) excavations show brisk Indo-Roman trade in the early Christian centuries; a Roman settlement / trading station.UPPSC ×4
    • At Arikamedu an intaglio with a man's picture, identified as Augustus Caesar, was found, with beads and gems; many Roman objects came from here.
    • Dubreuil called Arikamedu "a true Roman city"; the Periplus calls it Poduke.UPPSC
    • Amphora jar = ancient tall jar with a long narrow neck and two handles; used in ancient Rome for wine or oil.UPPSC
    • 'Yavanapriya' (dear to Yavanas/Greeks) in Sanskrit = black pepper, a favourite of the costliest Roman cookery.
    • Pepper was the first spice used in Europe, with huge social and economic value; Greeks knew black pepper by the 4th century BC, as a rare, costly item.
    • South Indian merchant guilds: Manigramam, Nanadesi, Valanjiyar; their aim was to encourage trade and business.
    • Nanadesis and Manigrama = traders' guilds, among the biggest trading bodies of the early medieval period; they traded with foreign countries.UPPSC
    • Sreni = association of traders, merchants and artisans; Nagaram = local association of merchants.
    • Tagara was an important trade centre on the route between Kalyan and Vengi.
    • Motupalli was the famous trading seaport of the Kakatiyas; Marco Polo entered the Kakatiya kingdom here and wrote of Andhra Desh's prosperity and power.

    Chola rulers

    • The medieval Chola empire was founded by Vijayalaya (850-871 AD) in the 9th century, after the gap following the fall of the Sangam Cholas.
    • One passage says the Chola dynasty was set up in South India by Parantak I.
    • Parantaka I defeated the Madura/Pandya king Rajasimha and took the title "Madurai-Kond".
    • Battle of Takkolam (949 AD): Chola prince Rajaditya, son of Parantaka I, against western Gangas, Banas and Vaidunbas led by Rashtrakuta king Krishna III; Cholas lost and Rajaditya died on the field.UPPSC
    • Chola golden era began with the accession of Rajaraja I (985 AD); he was the first Chola king to create a navy.
    • Rajaraja I destroyed the Chera fleet at Trivandrum (Kandalur Salai) in the 10th century and captured the Pandya king.UPPSC
    • This feat is named in his inscriptions as "Kandalur salai kalam-arutta"; the Thanjavur inscription also records his defeat of the Chera navy at Kandalloor.
    • Larger Leiden Copper Plates and Tiruvalangadu inscription say he captured Pandya king Amarabhujanga (or his chief general) and overran Madurai.
    • After these wins Rajaraja took titles such as "Mummudi Cholan" (three-crowned Chola) and "Pandya-kula shani".
    • Rajaraja I invaded Sri Lanka, destroyed Anuradhapura and took only the northern part; the south stayed free.UPPSC
    • Rajendra I took the southern part too, so conquered all Sri Lanka (Ceylon), and brought king Mahinda V of Sinhaldweep to the Chola kingdom as prisoner.
    • Rajendra Chola I, son and successor of Rajaraja I, is counted among India's greatest rulers and generals.
    • Rajendra I defeated Pala ruler Mahipala, took the title Gangaikonda Chola and founded the new capital Gangaikonda Cholapuram.UPPSC
    • The Chola navy was the strongest in the area; under Rajendra I the Bay of Bengal became a 'Chola lake'.UPPSC
    • Chola Gangam (Ponneri) = artificial lake built by Rajendra Chola I to mark his victory over rulers of the Ganga basin, incl. Bengal kings and the Kalinga dynasty.UPPSC
    • Cholas beat Pandya and Chera rulers and dominated peninsular India; Rajendra I sent an expedition against the Sailendra empire of South-East Asia and took some areas, as trade with China was being hindered.
    • Tamil inscriptions: Rajendra I led a successful naval expedition in 1025 CE against Kadaram (Kedah) and Srivijaya, a maritime empire controlling the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and nearby islands.
    • The Cholas were famous for naval power: strong standing army and navy; conquests of Ceylon and naval raids on Srivijaya, Sinhala and Maldives.UPPSC ×2
    • In Kulottunga I's reign (1077 AD) a Chola goodwill (Buddhist) delegation of 72 merchants was sent to China.UPPSC
    • Ceylon king Vijayabahu declared Sinhala independent in Kulottunga I's time; Kulottunga showed no hostility and married his daughter to Sinhala prince Virapperumal.UPPSC
    • Chola emperors usually chose their 'Yuvraj' (heir) in their own lifetime; other empires also show emperors choosing the crown prince.
    • Around 1250 AD the Hoysala and Pandya kingdoms defeated Chola king Rajendra III; the Chola dynasty ended about 1279 AD.
    • Malik Kafur conquered South India about 1310 AD: Yadav, Hoysala, Kakatiya and Pandya.
    • Chola territory stretched from the Tungabhadra to the Krishna river banks; it covered the Coromandel coast and some parts of the Deccan: Uraiyur, Kaveripattinam, Thanjavur.UPPSC
    • Chola capital = Tanjore; later Gangaikondacholapuram too.UPPSC
    • We know far more about the Cholas than earlier dynasties because they had inscriptions on temple walls telling their victories.UPPSC
    • Rajaraja I began the practice of recording his ancestors' victories in inscriptions; Rajendra I and later kings followed.

    Chola administration

    • The special feature of Chola rule was autonomy of village administration (local self-government, village assemblies); very systematic and well developed.UPPSC ×2
    • Uttaramerur inscription details the working of the executive committee of the Gram Sabha; each village had its own committee, the 'Sabha', usually independent of central command.
    • Variyam = working committee supervising the activities of Chola villages.
    • Thotta Variyam = garden (horticulture) committee.UPPSC
    • Samvatsara Variyam = annual committee; Eri Variyam = tanks (lakes) and water supply; Pon Variyam = gold/finance committee.
    • Chola empire was divided into six provinces called 'Mandalam'.
    • A Mandalam was divided into 'Kottam' or 'Valanadu' (like commissionerates); each Kottam had many 'Nadu' (districts).
    • Assembly of a Nadu = 'Nattar'; village association = 'Kurram'; smallest unit = Gram Sabha.
    • Eripatti = land whose revenue was kept for upkeep of the village tank; Ghatikas = colleges generally attached to temples.
    • Taniyur = a very large village run as a single unit (not a village given to Brahmins).

    Chola art and temples

    • Brihadeeswara temple (Thanjavur), a fine Dravidian temple of Chola style, was built in Rajaraja I's reign; counted the largest and tallest temple in India.UPPSC
    • Its huge Nandi, cut from a single rock, outside the sanctum, is believed the tallest (biggest) Nandi idol in India; idols of 'Dwarpals' stand around the main shrine.UPPSC
    • Chola artists (Sthapati) were skilled carvers in stone and metal; they made more bronze than stone sculptures.
    • Bronze Nataraja (Shiva) idols of the Cholas, found in large numbers, are among the best sculptures of the world.UPPSC
    • Chola Nataraja images show Shiva with four arms.
    • Nataraja shows dancing Shiva as creator, preserver and destroyer; the dance is set in a halo.
    • Nataraja's hands: upper right holds the damru (first sound of creation); upper left holds agni (fire that destroys the universe); lower right makes abhayamudra; front left points to the raised left foot = refuge for the troubled soul.
    • Nataraja wears a man's earring in the right ear and a woman's in the left, a symbol of Ardhanarishwara.UPPSC
    • Dakshinamurti idol shows Shiva as a teacher (Guru) giving knowledge to devotees; it is installed facing south.UPPSC
    • Mighty gateways of South Indian temples are called Gopurams.
    • Dravidian style flourished under the Pandyas and Cholas; Pandya temples were small with many ramparts and grand, richly worked Gopurams; the special feature of Chola architecture is the Gopuram, not the temple.
    • Meenakshi temple is at Madurai, the Pandya capital, where the 1st and 3rd Sangams met under Agastya and Nakkirar.UPPSC ×3
    • Meenakshi temple was first built by Kulasekara Pandya; the lotus-shaped city surrounds it fully.

    Pallavas
