    • Simhavishnu took the title Avanisimha; he defeated the kings of Chola, Pandya, Singhal and Kalmra.
    • Mahendravarman I took the titles 'Mattavilasa', 'Vichitrachitta' and 'Gunabhara'; a great patron of art, literature and craft, and a scholar.
    • 'Vichitrachitta' and 'Gunabhara' occur in his inscription on the rock of the Mandagapattu rock-cut Trimurti temple.
    • Mahendravarman I wrote the Sanskrit farce (comic play) 'Mattavilasa Prahasana', which gave him the title 'Mattavilasa'.
    • Narasimhavarman I took the title 'Mahamalla' (great wrestler); the famous Panch Ratha temples were built in his reign.
    • Narasimhavarman I captured and destroyed the Chalukya capital Vatapi and took the title Vatapikonda; in 642 AD he sent two naval expeditions to Ceylon to help a Sri Lankan prince.UPPSC
    • Parmeshwaravarman I took the titles Lokaditya, Ekmalla, Ranajaya, Atyantakama, Ugradanda, Gunabhajana.

    Chalukyas and Kadambas

    • Vatapi, now Badami in Bagalkot district (Karnataka), was the Chalukya capital in the 6th-8th century (one passage: second capital, 6th-7th century).UPPSC
    DynastyCapital
    ChalukyasBadamiUPPSC
    PallavaKanchipuram

    PandyaMadurai
    CholaTanjore (Thanjavur)

    • Pulakesin I was the real founder of the Chalukya dynasty of Vatapi.
    • Pulakesin II (610-642 AD) was the most able and powerful (greatest) Chalukya ruler; the Aihole inscription tells his achievements.UPPSC
    • Aihole inscription, written by Ravikirti in Sanskrit language and southern Brahmi, names the poet Kalidasa: Ravikirti claims fame like Kalidasa and Bharavi.UPPSC
    • Chalukyas did not rule North India; their rule centred on the Deccan and South India, capital Badami (Vatapi).
    • Pulakesin II of Badami defeated Harshavardhana in 618 AD; among smaller Chalukya branches the Chalukyas of Kalyani were most prominent.
    • Chalukya administration gave women high posts.UPPSC
    • Vijaya Bhattarika, queen of Chandraditya (brother of Vikramaditya I), issued two copper plates in her name, was a fine poetess, and ran the administration after her husband's death.
    • Vijayaditya (another passage: Vikramaditya) granted a village to a Jain monastery on the advice of his younger sister Kumkumdevi.
    • Chinese traveller Ma-twa-lin (Matwalin) wrote on China-India relations in the Chalukya period.UPPSC
    • Chalukya king Kumarapala sent his minister to stop cruelty to animals in the Kashi region (Jain tradition).UPPSC
    • Kumarapala reigned 29 years; a Jain and disciple of Jain scholar Hemachandra; several medieval Jain scholars wrote chronicles of him.
    • Capital of the Kadamba rulers = Banavasi (Vanavasi), also called Vaijayanti.UPPSC
    • Kadamba dynasty was founded by Mayurasharman; Pulakesin II annexed the Kadamba state.

    Chapter 14 · Ancient India

    Ancient Literature and Litterateur

    148 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Ashtadhyayi – Panini; Mahabhashya – Patanjali; Nirukta – Yaska; Varttika – Katyayan.×3
    2. Daskumarcharitam was written by Dandin (Dandi); it describes the adventures of 10 princes.×2
    3. Milindapanha = Buddhist text in Pali; a dialogue between Indian monk Nagasena and Indo-Greek king Milinda (Menander).×2
    4. Sarvavarma · Katantra×2

    Quick quiz: 10 of 39 UPPSC questions

    Foreign writers

    • Greek author Herodotus = 'Father of History'; his book 'Historica/The Histories' describes Indo-Persian relations in the 5th century BCE.
    • 'The Natural History' was written by Pliny the Elder, a Roman author — not by Ptolemy.UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Life of Hiuen Tsang – Hui-li; Historial Philippical – Pompeius Trogus; The Histories – Herodotus.

    Grammar works

    • Ashtadhyayi – Panini; Mahabhashya – Patanjali; Nirukta – Yaska; Varttika – Katyayan.UPPSC ×3
    • Panini probably belonged to the 7th century B.C.
    • Patanjali (not Panini) was associated with Pushyamitra Shunga.

    Gupta period literature

    • Sanskrit literature reached its peak (apogee) in the Gupta period; the era is known for both prose and poetry.
    • Gupta-era classics: Amarakosha by Amarsimha, Kamasutra by Vatsyayana, Meghaduta by Kalidasa, Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta.UPPSC
    • Mudrarakshasa = Sanskrit historical drama by Vishakhadatta.UPPSC
    • Mudrarakshasa was written in the Gupta period but tells how Chandragupta Maurya, helped by Kautilya, overthrew the Nandas.
    • Mudrarakshasa also gives a picture of the socio-economic condition under the Mauryas.
    • Vishakhadatta = drama (playwright of Gupta dynasty); Varahamihira = astronomy/astrology; Charaka = medicine; Brahmagupta = mathematics.
    • Brahmagupta belonged to the Gupta dynasty; renowned astronomer and mathematician.
    • Chandragupta II loved art and culture; nine gems (Navratna) adorned his court.
    • Kalidasa was the most prominent Ratna of Chandragupta II; Amarsimha, a lexicographer, was also among the Navratna (not linked to Harshavardhana).
    • Amarkosha was written by Amarsimha, not Varahamihira; Varahamihira wrote Panchasiddhantika, Brihat Samhita and Brihat Jataka.
    • Panchasiddhantika of Varahamihira is based on Greek, Roman, Egyptian and Indian astronomy.UPPSC
    • Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira = encyclopedic work of the Gupta period.

    Kalidasa

    • Kalidasa = Sanskrit poet and dramatist; probably the greatest Indian writer of any epoch.
    • Seven genuine works of Kalidasa: Abhijnanashakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram, Raghuvamsham, Kumarasambhavam, Meghadutam, Ritusamharam.
    • Kumarasambhavam (epic poem) was composed by Kalidasa.
    • Meghaduta = a lyric poem; Raghuvansham = an epic poem (both by Kalidasa).
    • Janaki-haranam was written by Kumaradasa, not Kalidasa.
    • Shringara Shatakam is part of 'Shataka-traya', generally attributed to Bhartrihari, not Kalidasa.UPPSC
    • Uttararamacharitam = Sanskrit play in seven acts on the life of Lord Rama, written by Bhavabhuti, not Kalidasa.
    • Mrichchhakatikam was composed by Sudraka, not Kalidasa.
    • Malavikagnimitram = first play of Kalidasa; 5 acts; love story of King Agnimitra of Vidisha (Shunga dynasty, son of the dynasty's founder) and Malavika.UPPSC
    • It is often called 'Kalidasa Malavikagnimitram' in honour of Kalidasa; the Shungas are presumed to have ruled Magadha.

    Other Sanskrit poets and plays

    • Daskumarcharitam was written by Dandin (Dandi); it describes the adventures of 10 princes.UPPSC ×2
    • Kiratarjuniyam = epic poem by Bharavi, considered the most powerful poem in Sanskrit.UPPSC
    • Kiratarjuniyam describes the combat between Arjuna and Lord Shiva (in the guise of a kirata = mountain-dwelling hunter) at Indrakeeladri Hills.
    • Works with themes from the Mahabharata: Naishadhiyacharita, Kiratarjuniyam, Sisupalavadha (not Dasakumaracharita).
    • Naishadhiyacharita = story of Nala and Damayanti from the Mahabharata, written by Sriharsha.
    • Magha wrote Sisupalavadha: Sisupala insulted Lord Krishna, who beheaded him in the ensuing duel.
    • Svapnavasavadattam = Sanskrit play written by Bhasa.
    • The Sanskrit play Madhyama-vyayoga is attributed to Bhasa.
    • Kavyalankara was written by Bhamaha.
    • Natyashastra = the 'Bible' of North Indian classical music; a Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts.UPPSC
    • Natyashastra was written by Bharat Muni; it covers drama, dance and music, all aspects of classical Sanskrit theatre.
    • Kadambari was composed by Banabhatta, not Subandhu.UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Kalidasa – Raghuvansa; Bhasa – Svapna Vasavadattam; Harsha – Ratnavali; Harshacharita – Banabhatta.
    • Karpuramanjari was written by Rajshekhara, poet laureate of the Gurjar-Pratiharas — not by Harsha.UPPSC
    • Bhavabhuti, Hastimalla and Kshemeshvara were famous playwrights.
    • Bhavabhuti = major dramatist of the later Sanskrit dramatic period; court poet of King Yashovarman of Kannauj (8th century CE).
    • Bhavabhuti's works: Mahaviracharitam (early life of Rama), Malatimadhava (romance of Malati and Madhava), Uttararamacharitam.
    • Hastimalla = Kannada poet and playwright during the reign of the Hoysalas.
    • Kshemeshvara (990–c. 1070 CE) = 11th-century Sanskrit poet from Kashmir; an important work attributed to him: Dasavatar Charita.
    • Mattavilasa Prahasana was written by Pallava ruler and scholar Mahendravarman I; it describes social and religious life.UPPSC
    • The drama 'Lalit Vigraharaj' was authored by Somadeva.
    • Geet Govind = epic poem in Sanskrit by Jayadeva, 12th century; organized into twelve chapters.UPPSC
    • Jayadeva was the royal poet in the court of King Lakshman Sen of Bengal.UPPSC

    Harsha and Ashvaghosha

    • Harshavardhana is supposed to be the author of three plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda (Harshacharita is not his).UPPSC
    • Harsha was a great conqueror, religious-minded and generous king, and a great patron of education and learning.
    • Historian Rama Shankar Tripathi: "Harsha was a patron of letters. He appears to have wielded the pen with no less dexterity and effect than the sword".
    • The plays are said to be composed by a king named Harshadeva; he is identified with Harsha of Kannauj, as no other sovereign of this name fits.
    • Ashvaghosha, a noted poet, was instrumental in the propagation of Buddhism; he wrote the famous court poem Saundarananda Kavya.
    • Saundarananda was discovered and edited by Pandit Haraprasada Shastri.
    • Buddhacharita = poetic narrative of Buddha's life by Sanskrit poet Ashvaghosha, not Vasubandhu.
    • Correct pairs: Mrichchhakatikam – Sudraka; Mudrarakshasa – Vishakhadatta; Saundarananda – Asvaghosha.

    Kashmir chronicle: Rajatarangini

    • Kalhana, a Kashmiri Brahmin, wrote Rajatarangini ('River of Kings'), which gives the history of Kashmir.
    • Rajatarangini = metrical historical chronicle of Kashmir, particularly its kings; written in Sanskrit in the 12th century.
    • Jai Singh (Jaisimha, 1128–1149) of Kashmir was Kalhana's contemporary ruler; Kalhana completed Rajatarangini in his reign.UPPSC
    • Rajatarangini has 8 Tarangas and 7826 verses; the first three Tarangas narrate the conventional ancient history of Kashmir.UPPSC
    • Jonaraja continued the narration up to the reign of Sultan Zainul Abedin and also called it Rajatarangini (Rajavali); after his death his pupil Srivara continued it.UPPSC
    • Gaudavaho = Prakrit epic poem by Vakpati, poet in the court of Yasovarman, king of Kanauj; it describes the digvijaya of Yasovarman.

    Buddhist and Jain texts

    • Milindapanha = Buddhist text in Pali; a dialogue between Indian monk Nagasena and Indo-Greek king Milinda (Menander).UPPSC ×2
    • Milindapanha, written by Buddhist monk Nagasena, explains the eight different phases of agricultural works.
    • Jain texts: Parishishtaparvan (by Hemchandra) and Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana (by Chavund Rai/Chamund Rai).
    • Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist texts.

    • Sources on the Parmar dynasty: Navsahsank Charit of Padmagupta, Prabandha Chintamani of Merutunga, Harsola copper plate inscription of Siyaka-II, Bhoj's records of Banswara and Betma, Udaipur Prashasti of Udayaditya's period.
    • Navsahsank Charita describes Mount Abu as the origin place of the Parmaras.
    • Panchatantra = collection of Indian animal fables with wide circulation in India and the world; translated into 15 Indian and at least 50 foreign languages (question wording: 40 foreign).
    • Panchatantra was compiled in Sanskrit and is attributed to Pandit Vishnu Sharma.
    • In the Mughal era Abul Fazl translated Panchatantra into Persian as Ayar-e-danish.

    Epics, sayings and Puranas

    • "Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits" is stated in the Shrimad Bhagavad Geeta.UPPSC
    • "What is here is also found elsewhere, but if not here is found nowhere else" is said in the Mahabharata.UPPSC
    • Sangam Sahitya is silent about the trade routes of ancient India.
    • The ancient name 'Nilotpala' for the Mahanadi is stated in the Vayu Purana.

    Law texts

    • Manusmriti (Manav Dharmashastra) is mainly related to the social system; one of the 18 major Smritis.UPPSC
    • Manusmriti = earliest metrical work on Brahminical Dharma in Hinduism.
    • Its actual human author is presumed to have used the eponym 'Manu', linking the text with the first human being and first king of Indian tradition.
    • Manu is considered the originator of law in India (first/great law-giver).UPPSC ×2
    • Mitakshara = a vivarti (commentary) on the Yajnavalkya Smriti by Vijnanesvara; Dayabhaga = Hindu law treatise by Jimutavahana; both deal with laws of inheritance.
    • Mitakshara: sons can claim property during the father's lifetime; Dayabhaga: only after the father's death.
    • Mitakshara deals with property held by both male and female family members; Dayabhaga only with property held by male members.
    • Wrong statement: Mitakshara was civil law for upper castes and Dayabhaga for lower castes.

    Medicine, mathematics, astronomy and music

    • Charaka Samhita = comprehensive text on ancient Indian medicine (Ayurveda), by Acharya Charaka, the father of Indian medicine.
    • Charaka Samhita = oldest surviving Ayurveda text; divided into 120 chapters in eight sections.UPPSC
    • Charaka = famous court physician of Kanishka; believed to have lived in the 1st–2nd century CE (exact dates uncertain).
    • Ashtanga Samgraha – medical; Das rupaka – play; Lilavati – maths; Mahabhasya – grammar.UPPSC
    • Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskara II), 12th century, made significant contributions to mathematics and astronomy; he has six well-known works.
    • His book Siddhantasiromani has four parts: Lilavati, Bijaganita (Algebra), Ganitadhyay, Goladhyay; so he is specially known for Algebra.UPPSC ×2
    • Lilavati, a treatise on mathematics, was written by mathematician Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskar-II).
    • Aryabhatta = renowned mathematician and astronomer of ancient India; major work Aryabhatiya.
    • Aryabhatiya deals with astronomy, spherical trigonometry, arithmetic, algebra and plane trigonometry.
    • Aryabhatta was the pioneer to infer that the earth is spherical and rotates on its axis around the sun; also considered the father of Trigonometry.
    • Aryabhatta discovered the decimal place value.UPPSC
    • 'Zero' was discovered by an anonymous Indian in the second century B.C.; Arabs learned it from India and spread it to Europe.UPPSC
    • Arabs are found to have first used zero in 873 A.D.
    • Veena = most ancient instrument among veena, sitar, sarod and tabla; the other three were introduced in the medieval era.UPPSC

    Chapter 15 · Medieval India

    Early-Medieval Period

    124 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Vikramshila University (Mahavihara) was established by King Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty of Bengal.×9
    2. Jejakabhukti = ancient name of Bundelkhand (not Kaushambi); named after Jay Shakti or Jeja/Jejak, grandson of Nannuk.×2
    3. Lakshmanasena (1178–1206 A.D.) of the Sena dynasty reigned 28 years and started a new Samvat, the 'Lakshmana Samvat'.×2
    4. Nagabhatta I (730–760 A.D.) is considered the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty; the chapter also calls Vatsaraja the actual founder.×2
    5. Tripartite struggle for Kannauj (8th–9th century A.D.): Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta; Cholas were not part; Pratiharas finally won.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 37 UPPSC questions

    Chauhans and Tomars

    • Prithviraj III, ruler of Ajmer, is commonly known as Prithviraj Chauhan.UPPSC
    • Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad Ghori in the 1st battle of Tarain (1191 AD) but was defeated in the 2nd battle of Tarain (1192 AD).
    • Vigraharaj IV = most powerful Chauhan ruler; he defeated the Tomaras and took Eastern Punjab and Delhi; he also won over the Muslim ruler of Punjab.
    • Hammir Epic (Hammir Mahakavya) describes the Chauhans as Suryavanshi: scions of 'Chahman', the son of Sun.
    • Chauhans were one of the four fire clans; Vasudeva and Naradev are mentioned as the initial kings of the dynasty.
    • Jodhraj wrote Hammir Raso (not Abdur Rehman).UPPSC
    • Prithviraj Raso was written by Chand Bardai.
    • Visal Dev Raso was written by Narpati Nalh.
    • 'Prithviraja Vijaya' was written by Jayanak.
    • Anangpal Tomar (Tomar Rajput dynasty), originally feudatories of the Gurjar-Pratiharas, founded the city of Dhillika (modern Delhi) in 1052 AD.

    Chandelas of Jejakabhukti

    • Jejakabhukti = ancient name of Bundelkhand (not Kaushambi); named after Jay Shakti or Jeja/Jejak, grandson of Nannuk.UPPSC ×2
    • Nannuk (Nannuka) founded the Chandel dynasty; Jayashakti was also a Chandela ruler.
    • Dhangadev (Dhanga) was a king of the Chandel dynasty of Jejakabhukti.
    • Dhanga attained Moksha by abandoning his body in the waters of Ganga and Yamuna at the Sangam, Prayagraj.
    • Kandariya Mahadev temple was built by Vidyadhara (another passage: by Dhanga).
    • Chandela order: Yashovarman (925–950 AD) → Dhanga (950–1002 AD) → Vidyadhara (1017/19–1029 AD) → Keertivarman (1060–1100 AD).UPPSC
    • Alha and Udal were related to Mahoba; they were commandants of Chandel king Parmardidev (Parmal, 1165–1203 A.D.).
    • Parmardidev died after the battle with Prithviraj Chauhan.
    • The Chandel–Chauhan struggle is described in "Prithviraj Raso" by Chand Bardai and in "Alhakhand" of Parmal Raso by Jagnik.

    Pala dynasty and universities

    • Gopala founded the Pala dynasty; per Tibetan historian Lama Taranath he was born near 'Pundravardhana' and was elected king of Bengal.UPPSC
    • Kings chosen directly by the public: Pala founder Gopal and Pallava ruler Nandivarman Pallavamalla (not Harshavardhan or Yashovarman).UPPSC
    • Khalimpur inscription of Dharmapala describes the election of Gopala by the people to end Matsya Nyaya (Law of the Jungle).
    • After the unexpected death of Pallava ruler Permeshwar Varman, the people elected Nandivarman Pallavamalla as king.
    • Odantapuri (Udnapur) = prominent education centre in Bihar, established by Pala ruler Gopala.
    • Pundravardhana Bhukti was located in North Bengal; its territory expanded beyond northern Bihar under the Pala, Chandra and Sena dynasties.UPPSC
    • Dharmapala (770–810 A.D.), an enthusiastic Buddhist, was called "Paramsaugat" in his inscriptions.
    • Dharmapala built famous Buddhist monasteries at Vikramshila and Somapura (Paharpur).UPPSC
    • Renowned Buddhist commentator Haribhadra was part of Dharmapala's court.
    • Per Taranath, Dharmapala founded 50 religious schools but had no religious intolerance or bigotry.
    • Vikramshila University (Mahavihara) was established by King Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty of Bengal.UPPSC ×9
    • After the downfall of Nalanda, Vikramshila became the main centre of Buddhist studies.
    • Vikramshila was located at Bhagalpur in Bihar.
    • Vikramshila's curriculum: formalized Vedic learning, Vedic texts, rituals and the Vedangas — reasoning, medicine, law, astronomy and city planning.
    • Wrong statements on Vikramshila: located in Banka district; established by Gopala I.
    • Correct statements: the 'Vajrayana' sect of Buddhism flourished there; Astronomy, Logic, Law, Grammar and Philosophy were also taught.
    • Vikramshila University was demolished by Bakhtiyar Khalji.
    • Devapala (Pala king) was Buddhist, also known as "Param Saugat".
    • Devapala donated five villages at the request of Balaputradeva, Sailendra king of Java (ruler of Suvarnabhumi), who founded a Buddhist monastery at Nalanda; so Bihar's rulers had contact with Java-Sumatra.
    • The Nalanda copper-plate of Devapala records that Balaputradeva built the monastery with Devapala issuing the grant.
    • Taxila was not a centre of learning in the early medieval period; it was an early Buddhist centre of learning.
    • Taxila = capital of Gandhara State, in present-day Rawalpindi district of Pakistan.
    • Chanakya (Kautilya), Maurya emperor Chandragupta, Ayurvedic healer Charaka and Jivaka studied at Takshashila.
    • Taxila taught the Vedas and the eighteen arts, including archery and elephant lore.
    • Nalanda University was established in the 5th century A.D. by Kumar Gupta; Muslim invader Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked it at the beginning of the 12th century.
    • The university at Odantapuri was established during Pala rule.

    Gahadavalas and Senas

    • Kumaradevi, Buddhist queen of Govind Chandra Gahadavala, built the Dharmachakra Jain Vihar at Sarnath.UPPSC
    • Krityakalpataru was written by Lakshmidhar, minister of Govind Chandra.
    • Last powerful ruler of the Gahadavala dynasty = Jayachandra.
    • Lakshmanasena (1178–1206 A.D.) of the Sena dynasty reigned 28 years and started a new Samvat, the 'Lakshmana Samvat'.UPPSC ×2
    • Sena succession (father to son, fixed by inscriptions): Samantasena → Hemantasena → Vijayasena → Vallalasena (Ballal Sena) → Lakshmanasena → Visvarupasena.UPPSC

    Gurjara-Pratiharas

    • Pratiharas = most famous Rajput dynasty of the 'Agni' clan; also called Gurjara-Pratihara because of its link with the Gurjars.
    • Gurjars were first mentioned in the Aihole inscription of Pulakesin II and in Harshacharita of Banabhatta.
    • Nagabhatta I (730–760 A.D.) is considered the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty; the chapter also calls Vatsaraja the actual founder.UPPSC ×2
    • Nagabhatta I destroyed the army of the Maleksha ruler and saved western India from the Arab invasion — mentioned in the Gwalior inscription.
    • Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled much of northern India from the mid-8th to the 11th century; first at Ujjain, later at Kannauj.
    • Pratihara rulers: Nagabhatta I (730–760), Vatsaraja (775–800), Nagabhatta II (800–833), Mihir Bhoja I (836–885), Mahendrapala I (885–910), Devapala (948–949); Bharatrabhatta-I was not one.
    • Order: Vatsaraja (775–800 AD) → Nagabhatta II (800–833 AD) → Mahendrapala I (885–910 AD) → Mahipala (912–944 AD).UPPSC
    • Mihir Bhoj (836–885 A.D.) = greatest and most prominent Pratihara king.UPPSC
    • Mihir Bhoja I was a follower of Vaishnavism; titles 'Aadi Varaha' and 'Prabhas'.UPPSC
    • Mihir Bhoj was the son of Emperor Ramabhadra and queen Appa Devi, not of Nagabhatta-II.
    • Mihir Bhoj rebuilt the Pratihara empire, seized Kannauj around 836 AD and made it the capital.
    • Al-Masudi of Baghdad visited Gujarat in the 10th century A.D.; he testifies to the power, prestige and vast empire of the Pratiharas.
    • Al-Masudi calls the Gurjara-Pratihara kingdom Al-Juzr and the king Baura (probably a mispronunciation of Adivaraha), though Bhoja had died by then.
    • Arab traveller Suleman visited India in the reign of Mihir Bhoja (Bhoja I).
    • Tripartite struggle for Kannauj (8th–9th century A.D.): Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta; Cholas were not part; Pratiharas finally won.UPPSC ×2
    • After Harsha's death Kannauj attracted powerful dynasties; it was compared with Magadha of the Gupta period.
    • Kannauj = ancient city earlier called Mahodaya / Mahodaya Shri and Kanyakubja in the time of Mihir Bhoj.UPPSC ×2
    • Rajashekhara was court scholar of Gurjara-Pratihara king Mahendrapala I and his son Mahipala I.
    • Rajashekhara's works: Karpuramanjari, Kavyamimamsa, Viddhasalabhanjika, Bal Ramayana, Bhuvankosh (not Prabandhachintamani).
    • Dharmapala = prominent Pala king (770–810 A.D.); Harsha Vardhana = Pushyabhuti king (606–647 A.D.).

    Rashtrakutas

    • Danti Durga laid the foundation of the Rashtrakuta Empire in 753 AD; capital Manyakheta.
    • Danti Durga is said to have performed the Hiranyagarbha oblation at Ujjayini.UPPSC
    • Amoghavarsha I (Rashtrakuta) was born in 800 AD at Shribhavan near the Narmada in a military camp, when his father Govind III was returning from his North India campaigns.UPPSC
    • Govind III, successor of Rashtrakuta king Dhruva, attacked North India after consolidating the south and defeated Pratihara ruler Nagabhatta II.
    • Sanjan and Radhanpur copper plate inscriptions mention Govind III's victory.

    Dynasties, capitals and Solankis

    DynastyCapitalFounder

    CholaTanjore (Tanjavur)Vijayalaya, 9th century A.D.

    • Jain scholar Hemchandra gained fame under Solanki king Jaysimha Siddharaj (1093–1143 AD) but adorned the court of his successor Kumarapala (1143–1172 A.D.) as advisor.UPPSC
    • Chalukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja was religiously tolerant; Muhammad Aufi wrote that he gave 1 lakh Balom (currency) to restore a demolished mosque in Khambhat.UPPSC

    Paramaras and Kalachuris

    • Paramara dynasty was founded in the 9th century A.D. by Upendra or Krishnaraj; Dhara was the capital in the later phase.

    Note from the book Founder of Parmara dynasty: the commission accepted Kanakpala, whereas the correct answer is Upendra or Krishnaraj.

    • King Bhoj was a Paramara ruler who ruled over Dhara; the early capital of the Paramaras was Ujjain, later moved to Dhara.
    • After Bhoj's death scholars said: "Adya Dhara Nira Dhara, Niralamba Saraswati, Pandita Khandita sarve Bhoj Raje Divangate".
    • 'Samarangana Sutradhara' by Paramara king Bhoj is based on architecture and artificial scientific equipment.UPPSC

    Note from the book Book on artificial scientific equipment: the commission first took Bhoja as correct but changed the answer to Govindraja in its revised answer sheet.

    • Bhoj's other works: Saraswati Kanthabharan, Siddhanta Sangraha, Yoga Sutra Vritti, Rajamartand, Yukti Kalpataru, Charucharya.
    • Udaipur Prashasti praises Paramara King Bhoja: he obtained, accomplished and understood everything that no one else could.UPPSC
    • It says Bhoja, comparable to King Prithu, ruled the earth from Kailash to the Malaya mountains and from the rising to the setting mountains.
    • Samidheshwar temple of Chittor (also called Tribhuvan Narayan temple and Bhoj Jagti) was built by Paramara Raja Bhoj of Malwa.
    • It has a three-faced idol of Lord Shiva, very similar to the main Shiva idol of Elephanta cave, Mumbai.
    • Bhojshala temple, Dhar district (Madhya Pradesh), was set up by Paramara King Bhoj in 1035 A.D. as a Sanskrit school; presiding deity = Goddess Saraswati.UPPSC
    • Bhojshala is now in the premises of the Kamal Maula Mosque.
    • Gangeyadeva was a Kalachuri ruler, not a Parmar; Upendra, Munj and Udayaditya were Parmara rulers.
    • Gangeyadeva took the title Vikramaditya and restarted the issue of gold coins in early medieval north India after their extinction.
    • Arab writer Al-Biruni described Kalachuri ruler Gangeyadeva and his capital Tripuri.
    • Al-Biruni = Khwarazmian Iranian scholar and polymath of the Islamic Golden Age; wrote Tarikh al-Hind on Indian culture.

    Jurists, literature and economy

    • Famous jurists of early medieval India: Hemadri, Vigyaneshwara and Jimutavahana (not Rajashekhara).UPPSC
    • Vigyaneshwara wrote "Mitakshara"; Jimutavahana wrote "Dayabhaga".
    • "Gaudavaho" was written by Vakpati, court poet of Yashovarman, king of Kannauj.UPPSC
    • Araghatta = Persian wheel: a water-lifting device worked by bullocks, buffaloes or camels for irrigation; mentioned in Panchatantra and Rajatarangini.
    • Motupalli = very important seaport of the Kakatiya kingdom; now in Bapatla district, Andhra Pradesh; visited by Italian traveller Marco Polo.
    • Motupalli epigraph gives rates on sandal, camphor, rose-water, ivory, pearls, corals, copper, zinc, lead, silk, pepper and areca nuts — shows the port's exports and imports.

    Kashmir, Mithila and Bastar

    • Shahi Khan, brother of Ali Shah, took the throne of Kashmir in 1420 A.D. as Zain-ul-Abidin.UPPSC
    • Zain-ul-Abidin = greatest ruler of Kashmir, ruled nearly 50 years; called 'Akbar of Kashmir' for liberal religious policy, promotion of learning, and interest in art and architecture.
    • Nanyadev (1097–1147 AD) founded the Karnata dynasty; a great warrior; capital Simraungadh; ruled the Mithila region.
    • Harisimha (1295/1296–1324 AD) = last ruler of the Karnata dynasty; protector of art and literature; started the Panji system.
    • Kuruspal village is in Bastar district, Chhattisgarh; the Kuruspal inscription gives information about Someshwar I.
    • Kuruspal stone inscription of Someswardeva (much mutilated): records a village grant by king Someswardeva of the Nagavamsa.
    • Kuruspal Tank slab of Dharana Mahadevi: queen Dharna Mahadevi granted land near Kalamba village to god Kamesvara (Shiva) in Someshwardeva's reign.

    Chapter 16 · Medieval India

    Muslim Invasion of India

    80 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. First Muslim invaders of India were the Arabs; first successful Muslim invader = Muhammad-Bin-Qasim.×2
    2. Battle of Chandawar (1194 AD): Ghori defeated Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Kannauj.×2
    3. Turkish invasions succeeded because North India had no political unity: constant warfare among Indian rulers and many small kingdoms.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 22 UPPSC questions

    Islam and the names of India

    • Hazrat Muhammad, propounder of Islam (the "Holy Prophet"), was born about 570 A.D. in Mecca; he died in 632 A.D.UPPSC
    • Mecca is in Saudi Arabia; it is a religious pilgrimage place for followers of Islam.
    • Rigveda mentions the Bharatas as a tribe/people; the land name Bharat/Bharatavarsa comes in later Sanskrit texts (e.g. Vishnu Purana).
    • By tradition the country was named after Dushyanta's son 'Bharat'; some scholars say after Rishabhanath's eldest son 'Bharat'.
    • In the Rigveda, Bharata is defined as 'Sapta Sindhu'.
    • Most scholars feel the name "Hindu" came from invaders who could not pronounce the name of the Indus River.
    • Iranians called the country 'Hindustan'; Greeks called it 'India'.
    • The word 'Hindu' for the people of Hind was first used by Iranians/Persians (the exam answer given: the Arabs).

    Arab conquest of Sindh

    • First successful Muslim invasion of India: 712 AD, when Arabs under Muhammad-Bin-Qasim conquered Sindh.UPPSC
    • First Muslim invaders of India were the Arabs; first successful Muslim invader = Muhammad-Bin-Qasim.UPPSC ×2

    Note from the book Year of the first successful Muslim invasion is disputed among scholars: 711 A.D. per V.D. Mahajan, 712 A.D. per Harishchandra Verma.

    • Before 712 AD a campaign under Ubaidullah was sent to India, but he was defeated and killed.
    • Sindh was ruled by Dahir; Qasim defeated and killed him; Dahir ruled from his capital Arod (near modern Karachi).
    • Muhammad-Bin-Qasim was an Arab, born around 695 A.D.; nephew and son-in-law of Iraq's king Al Hajjaj.UPPSC
    • At the age of seventeen he was sent by Caliph al-Walid to lead an army to Sindh.
    • The Arab empire could not spread east of Sindh and Multan and gradually declined.
    • Dr. Stanley Lane-Poole: Arab conquest of Sindh "remained only an episode in history of India and Islam… an incomplete victory"; the Turks completed the task.
    • The Persian text 'Chachnama' tells about the Arab conquest of Sindh.
    • Chachnama ("Story of Chach") = main source for Sindh's history in the 7th–8th century A.D.; written in Arabic; author not clearly known.
    • It is named after Raja Chach of Sindh, whose son Dahir opposed Muhammad Bin Qasim.
    • Per Chachnama, Arod was the capital of the Indus country in the 6th and 7th century A.D.
    • Chachnama was translated into Persian by Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi.
    • Chachnama covers Sindh's history from 680 to 718 A.D.; Mirza Kalich Beg translated it fully from Persian to English in 1900 A.D.

    Mahmud of Ghazni

    • Towards the end of the 9th century, Trans-oxiana, Khurasan and parts of Iran were ruled by the Samanids (Iranian by descent).
    • Alptigin, a Turkish slave among the Samanid governors, set up an independent kingdom with capital Ghazni and founded the Ghaznavid dynasty.UPPSC
    • Ghaznavid dynasty is also called the Yamini dynasty; it soon took over the Samanid kingdom.
    • Turkish conqueror Mahmud succeeded his father and became ruler of Ghazni in 998 AD; built a huge Central Asian empire with capital Ghazni (Afghanistan).
    • Mahmud attacked India 17 times between 1000 and 1027 AD (17 times per Sir Henry Elliot); his aim was to plunder wealth, not to set up permanent Muslim rule.UPPSC
    • Baghdad's Caliph Al Qadir-Billah gave Mahmud the titles 'Yamin-ud-Daula' and 'Amin-ul-Millah'.
    • Mahmud first invaded the Chandelas in 1019–20 AD; Chandela king Vidyadhar, the most powerful ruler of the dynasty, repulsed his attacks.UPPSC
    • Chandelas ruled Central India from the 9th to the 13th century; first capital Khajuraho, later shifted to Mahoba.
    • Mahmud plundered the Somnath temple (1025/26 AD) during the reign of Bhimdev I (1022–63).
    • After Mahmud left with the loot, Bhimadeva I rebuilt the Somnath temple.
    • Somnath temple is in Gujarat on the shore of the Arabian Sea; one of the 12 Jyotirlingas; Al-Biruni described it in his travelogue.
    • India's first President Dr. Rajendra Prasad (not S. Radhakrishnan) was present at the Pran Pratishtha of the present Somnath temple.
    • Mahmud introduced silver coins with Arabic legend on the upper side and Sanskrit legend (Sharada script) on the other.UPPSC
    • In the middle of the coin was written in Sanskrit: "Avyaktmekam Muhammad Avatar Nripati Mahmud".

    Mahmud's court scholars

    • Mahmud patronised Persian learning and respected scholars and artists.
    • Utbi = court historian of Mahmud; wrote Kitab-ul-Yamini / 'Tarikh-i-Yamini'.UPPSC
    • Other court members: Albiruni, Baihaqi (writer of Tarikh-i-Subuktigin), Persian poets Uzari and Unsuri, Asjadi and Farrukhi.
    • Firdausi (not Firishta), scholar and court poet of Mahmud Ghaznavi, wrote Shahnama; titled 'Homer of the East'.
    • Firishta (1560–1620 A.D.), full name Muhammad Qasim Hindu Shah Astarabadi Firishta, wrote Tarikh-i-Firishta (Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi).
    • Firishta lived for some time in Murtza Nizam Shah's court at Ahmadnagar, then went to Bijapur; his book is dedicated to Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur.
    • Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni in the 11th century and stayed many years; called the father of Indian historical writing.UPPSC
    • Al-Biruni was the first Muslim to study the Puranas.UPPSC
    • Al-Biruni was born in 973 AD in Khwarizm (now Khiva), Central Asia.
    • His interests: history, astronomy, geography, logic, medicine, mathematics, religion and theology.
    • He studied Sanskrit and used the works of Brahmagupta, Balabhadra and Varahamihira.
    • Al-Biruni wrote 'Tahqiq-i-Hind' (Kitab-ul-Hind; 'Reality of Hindustan'), his most important work, in Arabic; it describes the social and cultural conditions of India.
    • Edward Sachau translated it from Arabic into English; Rajnikant Sharma translated it into Hindi.
    • Al-Biruni translated Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra into Arabic (Kitab Patanjal).
    • Al-Biruni was not a secular author: he gave no sympathetic reference to Mahmud's raid on Somnath in 1025/1026.UPPSC
    • True of Al-Biruni: writing influenced by India; a Sanskrit scholar; expert in trigonometry.

    Muhammad Ghori

    1. 1000Order: Mahmud Ghaznavi (1000–1027) → Muhammad Ghori (1175–1205) → Genghis Khan (1221) → Taimur (1398).UPPSC
    2. 1175Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori, Ghurid ruler of Ghor (present Afghanistan), first invaded India in 1175 AD (Multan); attacked Multan and Uch in 1175–76.
    3. 1178In 1178 AD Ghori invaded Gujarat; Mularaja II (or Bhimdev II), led by his widowed mother Naika Devi (the real regent), defeated him near Mount Abu — Ghori's first defeat in India.UPPSC
    4. 11911191 AD: first battle of Tarain — Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Ghori.
    5. 11921192 AD: second battle of Tarain — Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan and conquered North India.UPPSC
    6. 1192In 1192 AD Ghori (Muhammad Sam of Ghori) appointed Qutbuddin Aibak in charge of his Indian territories and made him administrator of Kuhram and Samana (first Iqta).
    7. 1194Battle of Chandawar (1194 AD): Ghori defeated Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Kannauj.UPPSC ×2
    8. 1206Aibak played a significant role in the second battle of Tarain; he ran northern India as Ghori's representative till 1206 AD and expanded Turkish power.
    9. 1221Genghis Khan threatened India in 1221 A.D. while chasing Jalaluddin Mingburni, son of the fugitive Khwarizm Shah.
    10. 1398Taimur attacked India in 1398 A.D.
    • Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori, Ghurid ruler of Ghor (present Afghanistan), first invaded India in 1175 AD (Multan); attacked Multan and Uch in 1175–76.
    • In 1178 AD Ghori invaded Gujarat; Mularaja II (or Bhimdev II), led by his widowed mother Naika Devi (the real regent), defeated him near Mount Abu — Ghori's first defeat in India.UPPSC
    • After this Ghori never tried to attack India from Gujarat's side.
    • 1191 AD: first battle of Tarain — Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Ghori.
    • 1192 AD: second battle of Tarain — Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan and conquered North India.UPPSC
    • The second battle of Tarain laid the foundation of Muslim power in India; a turning point and the most important battle in Indian history.UPPSC
    • Ghori's alertness and skilled battle techniques were the main factors in the Muslim victory.
    • Prithviraj, trying to escape, was caught near Sursati (modern Sirsa, Haryana).
    • Hasan Nizami's widely accepted view: Prithviraj's son was appointed to govern Ajmer; Prithviraj was given the death penalty when he tried to conspire for a revolt.
    • Battle of Chandawar (1194 AD): Ghori defeated Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Kannauj.UPPSC ×2
    • Chandawar is in present Firozabad district (U.P.), on the bank of the Yamuna near Agra.
    • Coins of Ghori bear the image of Goddess Lakshmi; on some others the Kalma is inscribed in Arabic.
    • Soon after Ghori's victories the Iqta system was introduced in northern India.
    • In 1192 AD Ghori (Muhammad Sam of Ghori) appointed Qutbuddin Aibak in charge of his Indian territories and made him administrator of Kuhram and Samana (first Iqta).
    • Aibak played a significant role in the second battle of Tarain; he ran northern India as Ghori's representative till 1206 AD and expanded Turkish power.
    • Order: Mahmud Ghaznavi (1000–1027) → Muhammad Ghori (1175–1205) → Genghis Khan (1221) → Taimur (1398).UPPSC
    • Genghis Khan threatened India in 1221 A.D. while chasing Jalaluddin Mingburni, son of the fugitive Khwarizm Shah.
    • Taimur attacked India in 1398 A.D.

    Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bihar and Bengal

    • Ghori and Aibak never thought of conquering Bihar and Bengal; their ordinary slave Ikhtiyar-ud-din Muhammad-Bin Bakhtiyar Khalji did it.UPPSC
    • He conquered Bihar (1193–1203 AD; another passage gives 1193 to 1206 A.D.), captured the capital Odantapuri and destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila.
    • He invaded Bengal between 1198 and 1204–05 AD; ruler Lakshmana Sena left without fighting.
    • The Turkish army entered and plundered the capital Nadia; the city surrendered in the king's absence.
    • Lakshmana Sena took refuge in East Bengal and ruled there for some time.
    • Bakhtiyar Khalji did not try to conquer the whole of Bengal; he made Lakhnauti his capital.

    Why the Turks succeeded

    • Turkish invasions succeeded because North India had no political unity: constant warfare among Indian rulers and many small kingdoms.UPPSC ×2
    • A strong kingdom in the north would have deterred the Turks; there was no unified resistance.
    • Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghori invaded northern India between the 11th and 12th centuries; Ghori's invasion led to the Delhi Sultanate.
    • Per Professor Habib, the Turkish victory of the North-Western province gave birth to an 'Urban Revolution' and a 'Rural Revolution'.

    Chapter 17 · Medieval India

    Delhi Sultanate: Slave Dynasty

    94 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Iltutmish (1211–36 AD) = real founder of the Delhi Sultanate; first Sultan to shift the capital from Lahore to Delhi and to introduce regular coins.×5
    2. Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign, chasing Jalaluddin Mengubirni of Khwarazm; Mongols were first seen on the Indus then.×3
    3. Raziyya Sultan (1236–40 AD) = first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.×2
    4. Balban made his government firm and centralized all authority; he also built strong forts on the north-west border against the Mongols — both true, but the second does not explain the first.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 19 UPPSC questions

    The Slave (Mamluk) dynasty

    • Delhi Sultans from 1206 AD to 1290 AD are popularly called the sultans of the Slave dynasty; founder Qutbuddin Aybak.UPPSC
    • Slave dynasty = first of five unrelated dynasties of the Sultanate period; Aibak and all his successors were slaves to their predecessors.
    • They were all Turks but of separate houses/lines, so 'Mamluk Sultans of Delhi' is the more appropriate name.

    Qutbuddin Aybak (1206–1210)

    • Qutbuddin Aybak (1206–1210 AD) was the first ruler of the Slave Dynasty.
    • He belonged to a Turk tribe called Aybak; born in Turkistan; ugly in appearance but intelligent and impressive in behaviour.
    • In childhood he was sold as a slave to the Qazi of Nishapur, Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi, who gave him education and military training.
    • He recited the Quran very melodiously, so he was famous as Quran Khwan (one who recites the Quran).
    • After the Qazi's death his sons sold Aybak; he was brought from Nishapur to Ghazni, where Muhammad Ghori bought him.
    • He was well-versed in Islamic theology, horse riding and swordsmanship; he won Ghori's confidence by talent, passion and honesty.
    • He was first made commander of a troop, then promoted to Amir-i-Akhur (master of the royal stable).
    • He came to India with Ghori and gave active support in battles; Ghori made him governor (viceroy) of his Indian empire.
    • Ghori died in 1206 A.D. on his way to Ghazni; having no son, his empire was inherited by his slaves.
    • Ghori's nephew Ghiyasuddin Mahmud took the throne of Ghor in 1206 A.D.; Taj-ud-Din Yalduz, Governor of Kirman, took the throne of Ghazni.
    • Aybak, Ghori's general in charge of Lahore and the north-Indian possessions, seems to have been Ghori's own choice to succeed him in India.
    • Aybak was invited by the Amirs of Lahore to assume power; his coronation was in June 1206 AD, three months after Ghori's death.
    • Aybak's capital was Lahore.UPPSC
    • He kept the capital at Lahore to frustrate Yalduz's ambition of annexing Punjab; he always stayed in Lahore and never got to move to Delhi.
    • Nasiruddin Qabacha of Multan refused to accept Aybak as ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
    • Aybak strengthened his position by matrimonial alliances with influential rival Turkish chiefs.
    • Aybak never took the title 'Sultan'; he was content with the titles 'Malik' and 'Sipahasalaar'.
    • In 1208 AD he got a letter of liberation from Ghori's successor Ghiyasuddin Mahmud, was freed from slavery and ruled as an independent sovereign.
    • For his generosity Aybak was called 'Lakh Bakhsh' (giver of lakhs).
    • Aybak = first Muslim ruler who settled and ruled in India, unlike earlier Muslims who only raided and plundered.
    • He patronized scholars Hasan Nizami and Fakhra-i-Mudabbir; both dedicated their works to him.
    • His four-year reign was mostly spent on revolts of nobles like Taj-ud-din Yalduz, Nasir-ud-din Qabacha and a few Hindu chiefs, yet he set up a firm administration.
    • Aibak built two mosques: 'Quwwat-ul-Islam' in Delhi and 'Adhai Din Ka Jhopra' in Ajmer (1192 AD).
    • Aybak started the Qutub Minar in Delhi; Iltutmish completed it.
    • Its fourth (topmost) storey was damaged by lightning; Firuz Shah Tughluq rebuilt the fourth floor and built the fifth; Ghiyasuddin Tughluq contributed nothing.UPPSC
    • Aybak died in 1210 AD after falling from his horse while playing Chaugan (a game like modern polo).
    • He was buried in Lahore near the Anarkali Bazaar.

    Iltutmish (1211–1236)

    • Iltutmish (1211–36 AD) = real founder of the Delhi Sultanate; first Sultan to shift the capital from Lahore to Delhi and to introduce regular coins.UPPSC ×5
    • He was the first to use pure Arabic coins: silver Tanka (175 grain; another passage: 175 gm) and copper Jital, the two basic coins of the Sultanate.
    • He started the tradition of inscribing the name of the Tankshal (mint) on coins.
    • Iltutmish was a Turk of the 'Ilbari' tribe (Eurasian Steppe of Turkestan).
    • Before becoming Sultan he was governor of Budaun, given for his services in the campaign against the Khokhars in 1205–06 AD.
    • He was with Ghori and Aybak in the Khokhar campaign; impressed by his courage and skill, Ghori freed him from slavery.
    • Iltutmish is called 'Slave of a slave': he was the slave of Aybak, himself a slave of Ghori; he later married Aybak's daughter.UPPSC
    • After Aybak's death, Amirali Ismail invited Iltutmish for coronation in Delhi with the approval of Turkish nobles; he declared himself Sultan in 1211 A.D.
    • He took control of the Delhi Sultanate as independent ruler after Aram Shah's death.
    • Rivals of Iltutmish: Tajuddin Yalduz in Ghazni, Nasiruddin Qabacha in Sindh, Ali Mardan in Lakhnauti; Malik Altunia was not a rival.
    • Iltutmish got approval as Sultan from the Khalifa, not from any Ghor ruler.
    • In 1229 AD the Caliph of Baghdad, Al-Muntasir Billah, gave him a 'Khilat' and the title 'Sultan-e-Azam' (Sultan the Great); he became the first legally independent Sultan of Delhi.UPPSC
    • The Khilat made Iltutmish a legitimate Sultan and the Delhi Sultanate an independent state; in theory it became part of Dar-ul-Islam under the Caliph.
    • Iltutmish then took the title 'Amir-ul-Mommini' (Commander of the Faithful) and had the Khalifa's name put on his coins.
    • He kept Delhi safe from the Mongols and from Yalduz and Qabacha; broke Rajput powers in the north; made his rule hereditary; issued coins in his name; made Delhi a beautiful capital.
    • Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign, chasing Jalaluddin Mengubirni of Khwarazm; Mongols were first seen on the Indus then.UPPSC ×3
    • Genghis Khan stayed near the Indus for 3 months but did not cross into India.
    • Mengubirni sought refuge; Iltutmish prudently refused asylum to avoid Genghis Khan's invasion.
    • Mengubirni stayed some time in the north-west; this led to Mongol attacks like the siege of Multan around 1224; his departure (~1223–24) did not end frontier troubles at once.
    • Original name of Genghis Khan = Temujin (Temuchin); a Mongolian ruler important in Mongol imperial expansion.UPPSC
    • Taimur began his conquests in 1370 A.D.; Muhammad bin Tughluq ruled 1325–1351 A.D., so Taimur did not cross the Indus in his reign.
    • Iranian ambassador Abdur Razzaq came to Vijayanagara in the reign of Deva Raya II.
    • Vasco da Gama reached the coast of Kerala in 1498 AD, when Narsa Nayaka's son Timma ruled Vijayanagara.
    • In 1225 A.D. Iltutmish defeated Hisamuddin Awaz (Sultan Ghiyas-ud-din Iwaz) in the Rajmahal hills near Teliyagarhi and annexed Bihar Sharif and Barh.
    • Awaz accepted subordination; Iltutmish appointed Malik-Jani as the new (first) Subedar of Bihar.
    • Per Ibn Battuta, Iltutmish set up two marble lion statues before his palace with bells round their necks that anyone could ring for justice.
    • Iltutmish appointed officials Qazi and Amir-i-dad in all cities.
    • Dr. R. P. Tripathi: the history of Muslim sovereignty in India begins with Iltutmish.
    • Dr. Ishwari Prasad: Iltutmish was undoubtedly the founder of the Slave Dynasty.

    Raziyya Sultan (1236–1240)

    • Raziyya Sultan (1236–40 AD) = first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.UPPSC ×2
    • Turkish nobles were reluctant to accept a woman as ruler, especially when she challenged their power.
    • She broke the prevailing gender norms of Islam for the first time in India.
    • She wanted power in the Sultan's hands, not divided among Chiefs (Sardars) or Iqtadars; this provoked the Turkish slave-nobles (Chahalgani).
    • Chahalgani (40 nobles) played an important role in overthrowing Raziyya.
    • Turkish nobles led by Malik Altunia, governor of Bhatinda, rebelled and removed her.UPPSC

    Balban (1266–1287)

    • Full name of Balban = Ghiyasuddin Balban; ninth Sultan of the Mamluk dynasty; ruled 1266–1287 AD.
    • His actual name was Baha-ud-din; also known as Ulugh Khan; an Ilbari Turk like Iltutmish; founded a new line, the Balban Dynasty.
    • Mongols caught Balban in childhood and sold him at Ghazni to Khwaja Jamaluddin of Basra.
    • He was brought to Delhi in 1232 AD; Iltutmish bought him in 1233 AD after the Gwalior victory and gave him the title Khasdaar.
    • Under Raziyya he rose to Amir-i-Shikar.
    • He joined the Turkish warlords' conspiracy against Raziyya; Bahramshah became Sultan and Balban got the title 'Amir-i-Akhur'.
    • By the grace of Badruddin Rumi he got the Jagir of Rewari.
    • He helped Alauddin Masudshah become Sultan and got the fief of Hansi.
    • In 1249 AD Balban married his daughter to Sultan Nasiruddin; he got the title 'Ulugh Khan' and the post 'Nayab-i-mamlikat'.
    • He was Wazir and heir of the last Shamsi Sultan, Nasiruddin Mahmud; he sat on Delhi's throne in 1266 AD.
    • He reduced the power of the treacherous nobility and raised the stature of the Sultan.
    • Despite few military achievements, he was the most powerful Sultan between Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji.
    • Balban adopted the policy of 'blood and iron'.UPPSC
    • Two features of his rule: divine right of the Sultan, and the Sultan must be autocratic.
    • His political ideology was inspired by the popular heroes of Persia; the king = God's representative on earth, 'Niyabat-i-Khudai'.
    • He said the Sultan's place comes after the Paigambar; the Sultan gets inspiration and strength from God, so public and Sardars cannot criticize him.
    • Balban took the title 'Zil-i-Ilahi' / 'Zille Allah' = Shadow of God; he was the first to use it.
    • Balban = first Sultan of Delhi to set out a theory of kingship, similar to the divine right of kings.
    • He told his son Bughra Khan: "The post of Sultan is a living symbol of autocracy."
    • Balban brought Iranian court traditions: 'Sijada' (prostration before the Sultan) and 'Paibos' (kissing the Sultan's feet).
    • Balban started celebrating the Persian festival 'Nawruz' in his court every year.
    • Balban made his government firm and centralized all authority; he also built strong forts on the north-west border against the Mongols — both true, but the second does not explain the first.UPPSC ×2
    • The Iqtadari system was introduced by Iltutmish, not Balban.
    • Balban abolished the 'Turkan-e-Chahalgani' set up by Iltutmish.
    • The only revolt of Balban's reign: Tughril Khan, Subedar of Bengal, in 1279 A.D.; Balban crushed it and hanged the rebels.
    • Tughril's rebellion was in protest against the appointment of Amin Khan in Bengal; Tughril fled fearing Balban's Bengal campaign.
    • Balban set up the military department 'Diwan-i-Arz'.
    • He made Imad ul-Mulk, a very honest and hardworking man, his military minister (Arz-i-Mamalik), free from the Wazir's financial control.
    • Balban called himself 'Helper of a Caliph' in his inscription on the walls of the mosque at Garhmukteshwar.UPPSC
    ← Muslim Invasion of IndiaKhalji Dynasty →

    Chapter 18 · Medieval India

    Khalji Dynasty

    79 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Alauddin Khalji introduced market control / price control (market reforms) in Delhi; it had nothing to do with paying lower wages to artisans.×5
    Quick quiz: 10 of 18 UPPSC questions

    Jalaluddin Khalji

    • Jalaluddin Khalji established the Khalji dynasty in 1290 AD.
    • He was crowned at the Palace of Kilokhari (Kilugarhi), built by Qaiqubad.
    • Dr. A. L. Srivastava: Jalaluddin was the first Turkish Sultan of Delhi who believed in the ideal of benevolent despotism.
    • Jalaluddin gave Alauddin the post of 'Amir-i-Tuzuk' and married his daughter to him.
    • Alauddin got the governorship of Kara-Manikpur for his role in suppressing the revolt of Malik Chhajju.

    Alauddin Khalji: titles and ambitions

    • Alauddin was the first Sultan of Delhi to establish state control over religion; he stayed free from the influence of the Ulema class.
    • He took the titles 'Yamin-ul-Khilafat' and 'Nasir-e-Amir-ul-Mominin'.UPPSC
    • Barani said of Alauddin: "When he attained Kingship, he was quite independent of rulers and orders of Shariat".
    • Alauddin took the title 'Sikandar-i-Sani' (second Alexander) and inscribed it on his coins.UPPSC
    • He wished to conquer the whole world and to start a new religion, but gave up the idea on the advice of his faithful friend, Kotwal Alla-ul-Mulk.
    • Alauddin set up a strong central government and raised a powerful, enormous army to protect the empire's boundaries.UPPSC
    • Alauddin kept a vast army at the centre and was the first Sultan of Delhi to pay soldiers in cash.

    Four ordinances against rebellion

    • Alauddin faced some rebellions early in his reign and issued four ordinances to suppress them.
    • First ordinance: gifts, pensions and donated land were banned; officials were ordered to collect more and more taxes.
    • Second ordinance: an intelligence (spy) department was set up.
    • Third ordinance: intoxicating drinks (alcohol, cannabis) and gambling were banned.
    • Fourth ordinance: marital relations and feasts among the nobles and Amirs were banned.

    Conquests in the north

    StateRuler at Alauddin's attack
    RanthamboreHamirdevaUPPSC
    ChittorRana Ratan Singh
    DevagiriRaja Rai Ramchandra
    GujaratKarnadeva
    • Order of conquests: Gujarat (1299 A.D.) → Ranthambor (1301 A.D.) → Chittor (1303 A.D.) → Warangal (1310 A.D.).UPPSC
    • Jaisalmer (1299 A.D.) → Ranthambor (1301) → Chittor (1303) → Warangal of the Kakatiyas (1309–1310).UPPSC
    • Per Jayasi, Padmini was the wife of Rana Ratan Singh.
    • Queen Padmini committed 'Jauhar' after Ratan Singh's death when Alauddin invaded Chittor, the capital of Mewar.
    • Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote 'Padmavat', based on the story of queen Padmini, in 1540 AD.
    • Amir Khusrau mentioned the love story of Suleman and Queen Shaiba, comparing Alauddin with Suleman and Padmini with Shaiba; Jayasi probably built Padmavat on this.

    Mongols

    • Zafar Khan, Alauddin's best and most courageous commander, died fighting the Mongols.
    • Mongols were so impressed by Zafar Khan's bravery and the Khalji army's persistence that they backed down by 30 miles.
    • Original name of Zafar Khan = Malik Hizabruddin.
    • After 1306 AD the Ravi river was the boundary between the Delhi Sultanate and the Mongols.UPPSC
    • In 1306 A.D. Mongols under Kabak attacked; Malik Kafur and Ghazi Malik stopped them on the bank of the Ravi.
    • In Alauddin's reign the Mongol Qutlugh Khwaja marched up to Delhi and besieged the city, while Alauddin was on the Chittor advance.
    • The first Mongol attack on India came in the reign of Iltutmish, not Jalal-ud-din Khalji.
    • In Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's reign Tarmashirin led a Mongol attack; the Sultan foiled it by occupying Kalanaur and Peshawar.
    • In Ghiyasuddin Tughluq's reign (1325 AD) a Mongol army under Shir Mughal crossed the Indus but was defeated by Malik Shadi, Subedar of Samana.

    Malik Kafur and the Deccan

    • Malik Kafur was called 'Hazar-Dinari'; Alauddin got him during the Gujarat conquest.
    • Nusrat Khan snatched Kafur in the Gujarat campaign from his master, who had bought him for a thousand dinars, and later presented him to Alauddin.
    • Malik Kafur rose as a skilled commander; he led the Sultanate's campaigns of conquest in the South (Deccan).
    • Alauddin's Deccan expeditions were for wealth and victory; he did not want to annex or interfere in the southern states.UPPSC
    • Dr. K.S. Lal: "the greed of wealth and lust of pride encouraged Alauddin Khalji to attack the states of South."
    • Ramchandra Dev was the ruler of Devgiri when Alauddin attacked.
    • Defeated in 1296 AD, Ramchandra Dev promised the province of Ellichpur's yearly income to Alauddin, but stopped sending it around 1305–1306 AD.
    • So Alauddin sent Malik Kafur against Devgiri in 1307 AD; Ramchandra Dev was defeated and surrendered.
    • Malik Kafur looted Devgiri and took Ramchandra Dev and his relatives to Delhi.
    • Alauddin treated him well, gave him the title 'Rai Rayan'; six months later sent him back with one lakh Tankas and Navsari district.
    • Malik Kafur also led a campaign against Ramchandra's son Shankar Dev (1313 AD; another passage: 1312 AD).
    • After Ramchandra Dev's death his son Shankar Dev ruled Devgiri; Ramchandra Dev was not ruler of Warangal.UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Devgiri – Shankar Dev; Hoysal – Veer Ballal; Madura – Veer Pandya.
    • In 1303 A.D. Alauddin's first attempt on Warangal failed: the Kakatiya army defeated his army.UPPSC
    • Kakatiya king Prataprudradev II raised a well-equipped army; Alauddin's army was led by Fakhruddin Juna and Malik Chhajju.

    Revenue system

    • Alauddin was the first Sultan to collect revenue by measuring the land; the department "Diwan-i-Mustakharaj" was set up for it.
    • His measurement-based system applied only to Delhi and nearby parts, not the whole empire; he also abolished powers of the old tax officers.UPPSC
    • He took tax collection away from the traditional officers (Khut, Muqaddam and Chaudhary) and abolished all their privileges.
    • Their lands were taxed too, so little difference remained between Khut (zamindar/landlord) and Balahar (ordinary farmer/agricultural labourer).
    • Main aim of his revenue and tax system: a powerful and autocratic state.
    • He took back land granted as 'Milq' (property, prize, idrarat pensions) and 'Waqf' (charitable land); so Khalisa land grew on a large scale.
    • Alauddin fixed 50% of the yield as land tax (Kharaj), based on measurement; Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq also charged 50%.
    • Alauddin = first Muslim ruler of India to fix revenue on the real income of the land.
    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq raised revenue to half the produce on Doab farmers (land between Ganga and Yamuna) to meet financial difficulties; his demand was based on estimated production.
    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughlaq (1325–51 C.E.) is considered an ill-fated idealist: his ambitious schemes and novel experiments failed as they were far ahead of their time.
    • Two new taxes of Alauddin: 'Ghari' (house) tax on houses and huts, and 'Charai' (grazing) tax on milch animals.UPPSC

    Market control

    • Alauddin Khalji introduced market control / price control (market reforms) in Delhi; it had nothing to do with paying lower wages to artisans.UPPSC ×5
    • He appointed Malik Kabool as Shehena (inspector of the market) with a large detachment of cavalry and infantry and wide authority.
    • The Shehena controlled all merchants and reported price changes and the market situation to the king.
    • Per Barani, the aim of market reforms was to support a huge army against the Mongols and to check rebellion among Hindus.
    • Barani: with normal wages the treasury would be finished within 5–6 years; so he cut soldiers' wages and fixed low prices so soldiers could live comfortably.
    • Alauddin's attempt to control market prices was highly successful.UPPSC
    • Separate markets in Delhi: grain market (Mandi); clothes and groceries (clothes, sugar, dry fruits, butter, oil); horses, slaves and cattle; miscellaneous commodities.
    • Each market was under a superintendent, Shahna-i-Mandi, helped by an intelligence officer.
    • Alauddin also got daily market reports from barids (intelligence officers) and munhiyans (secret spies).
    • Alauddin started state granaries and price-controlled sale of grain — the 'Public Distribution System' of the Sultanate period.UPPSC

    Later Khaljis

    • After Alauddin's death, Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Khalji was imprisoned by Malik Kafur; he later got out and took the throne.
    • Mubarak Khalji declared himself Khalifa; titles 'Al Imam', 'Ul-Imam', 'Khalifatullah' (which he was never fit for); the only Sultan to take the Caliph's title.UPPSC
    • Among Iltutmish, Alauddin Khalji, Muhammad-bin-Tughluq and Balban, none opposed the Khalifa's power, though the last three were practically independent rulers; only Mubarak Khalji did.
    • Iltutmish attacked Sultan Ghiyasuddin of Bengal, who also had the Khalifa's recognition — in a way opposing the Khalifa.
    • Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah (April–September 1320) was a convert to Islam from Hinduism.
    • He took the title 'Commander of the Prophet' (Paigamber-ka-Senapati).
    • His opponents called him 'enemy of Islam' and raised the slogan 'Islam is in danger'.
    ← Delhi Sultanate: Slave DynastyTughluq Dynasty →

    Chapter 19 · Medieval India

    Tughluq Dynasty

    79 facts · 8 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. He set up a new department, Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi (Diwan-i-Kohi), for the advancement of agriculture; crops were grown by rotation.×3
    2. Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was the first to introduce token currency in India.×3
    3. He came to India during 1333–42 AD in the reign of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq.×3
    4. He moved the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devgiri) — one of his most important experiments.×2
    5. Firuz Shah Tughluq opened an employment office: jobs were given after checking each person's qualifications and merit, to solve unemployment.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 27 UPPSC questions

    Ghiyasuddin Tughluq

    • Ghiyasuddin Tughluq (Ghazi Malik), a general of Alauddin Khalji, founded the Tughluq dynasty and was its first ruler.UPPSC
    • His mother was a Hindu Jat woman; his father was a Qaraunah Turk, a slave of Balban.
    • He led several important campaigns in Alauddin's reign and was governor of Multan and Dipalpur.
    • He earned the epithet 'Ghazi Malik' for repeated frontier fights against the Mongols: 20 routs per Barani, 29 victories per Ibn Battuta.
    • He took Delhi's throne by defeating (assassinating) Khusrau Shah and became Sultan in 1320 AD.
    • He was also called Ghazi Beg Tughluq or Ghazi Tughluq; so his successors were called 'Tughluq'.
    • Under him the land tax was fixed at 1/10 or 1/11 of the yield; in famine, tax was taken according to capacity to pay.
    • He took steps to improve the condition of farmers and restored the old rights of Khuts and Muqaddams.
    • Ghiyasuddin Tughluq is credited as the first ruler of the 14th century to dig canals for agriculture.UPPSC
    • Tax-free jagirs were given to government employees without any share in the revenue.
    • Harsh punishments of Alauddin's time were abolished, but tax defaulters, those dishonest with government money and thieves were severely punished.
    • Dynasty spans: Slave 1206–1290; Khalji 1290–1320; Tughluq 1320–1412; Lodi 1451–1526 — the Tughluqs ruled longest.UPPSC

    Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq: learning, agriculture, capital

    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq (1325–1351 A.D.) = most learned and educated Sultan of Delhi; versed in astronomy, mathematics and medicine.UPPSC
    • He set up a new department, Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi (Diwan-i-Kohi), for the advancement of agriculture; crops were grown by rotation.UPPSC ×3
    • Its work: give more support to farmers and bring more land under cultivation; a tract of about 30 karohs × 30 karohs was chosen.
    • He moved the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devgiri) — one of his most important experiments.UPPSC ×2
    • Reasons given: Devgiri was probably at the centre of the empire (Barani); to punish Delhi's people who wrote undeferential letters to the Sultan (Ibn Battuta).
    • He was the first Sultan of Delhi who tried to bring administrative and cultural unity of north and south India — probably the main reason.
    • Dr. K.A. Nizami: Qutbuddin Mubarak Khalji named Devgiri Qutbabad; Muhammad Tughluq named it Daulatabad.
    • Barani's five major policies of Muhammad Tughluq: tax increase in Doab; Devgiri (Daulatabad) as capital; token currency; planned Khurasan expedition; Qarachil expedition.

    Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq: coins and token currency

    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was the first to introduce token currency in India.UPPSC ×3
    • Per Barani, lack of silver in the treasury and the policy of expanding the empire forced the token currency.
    • Token currency was tried unsuccessfully in Iran under Gaykhatu and successfully under Kublai Khan; Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was inspired by them.
    • Modern historians note a worldwide shortage of silver, severe in India too.
    • His new gold coins were called 'Dinar' by Ibn Battuta; his token currency was in copper or bronze, to promote military power, not gold tokens for trade with West Asia and North Africa.
    • The token currency failed because the state had no control over minting; many fraud mints came up and Lagan was paid in forged coins.UPPSC
    • The token coin's value was equal to the silver coin.
    • His coins carried 'Al Sultan Zilli Allah' (Sultan is the shadow of God) and 'God is the supporter of Sultan'.

    Ibn Battuta

    • Ibn Battuta (1304–77 AD), African traveller of Moroccan origin, resident of the Tanzir region of Morocco.
    • He came to India during 1333–42 AD in the reign of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq.UPPSC ×3
    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq made him Qazi of Delhi; in 1342 AD he was sent to China as the Sultan's ambassador.
    • His travel book = Kitab-ul-Rihla.
    • A detailed description of the Sultanate postal system comes from Ibn Battuta's travelogue.UPPSC

    Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq: society and death

    • Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was the first Sultan of Delhi to join Hindu festivals, mainly Holi (Isami accuses him of this).UPPSC
    • He appointed non-Turks and Indian Muslims to government posts; Barani harshly criticized him for promoting low-born people like gardener, weaver, barber, cook.
    • While he was at Daulatabad, Taghi led a revolt in Gujarat; Taghi was defeated and fled to Sindh.
    • Chasing Taghi to Sindh, the Sultan fell sick on the way and died on March 20, 1351 near Thatta.
    • On Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq's death Badayuni wrote in "Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh": "The king was freed from his people, and the people from their king".UPPSC

    Firuz Shah Tughluq: welfare

    • Firuz Tughluq, cousin of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq, ruled after him (1351–1388 A.D.).
    • Firuz Shah Tughluq opened an employment office: jobs were given after checking each person's qualifications and merit, to solve unemployment.UPPSC ×2
    • He set up 'Diwan-i-Khairat': money help to poor Muslims, orphans, women and widows, and marriages of poor Muslim girls.
    • Firuz donated property to saints and religious people.
    • Firuz Tughluq = first Indian ruler to arrange Hajj at state expense.UPPSC
    • 'Dar-ul-Shafa/Shifa' = charitable (free) hospital set up by Firuz, with skilled Hakims.UPPSC
    • Firuz was very fond of slaves: about 1,80,000 slaves; he set up a separate department 'Diwan-i-Bandagan' for them.
    • He attended to slaves' education; each slave got 10 to 100 Tankas and sometimes estates; this hobby proved harmful to the state.
    • Balban set up 'Diwan-i-Arz' for a large standing army against the Mongol threat; his honest, hardworking commander Imad-ul-Mulk, freed from the Wazir's financial control, deserves credit for the army's good arrangement.
    • The branding system of horses was introduced by Alauddin, not Balban.
    • Firuz set up a 'Translation Department' so that Hindus and Muslims could exchange ideas better; some Sanskrit texts were put into Persian.UPPSC
    • In the Nagarkot expedition Firuz collected about 300 Sanskrit manuscripts from the Jawalamukhi temple library; Azizuddin Khan translated them into Persian.UPPSC
    • Firuz levied Jizya (religious tax on non-Muslims) on Brahmins, who had been exempt till then.UPPSC

    Firuz Shah Tughluq: public works

    • Firuz Shah Tughluq established the Public Works Department.UPPSC ×2
    • He is said to have built 200 new cities; prominent: Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad.
    • Per Firishta, Firuz built 40 mosques, 30 schools, 20 palaces, 100 inns, 200 towns, 100 hospitals, 5 tombs (Makabara), 100 public baths, 10 pillars and 150 bridges.
    • In his Bengal campaign he renamed Ikdala as Azadpur and Pandua as Firuzabad.
    • His chief architect = Malik Ghazi Shahana.
    • Each building's plan with cost estimate was put before the 'Diwan-i-Wajarat' before money was released.
    • Firuz Tughluq built the largest network of canals in India.
    • His five canals: Sutlej to Ghaggar (96 miles); Yamuna to Hisar (150 miles); Sirmor hill to Hansi; Ghaggar to Firozabad; Yamuna to Firozabad.
    • He dug 150 wells for irrigation and travellers; per Firishta he built 50 dams and 30 lakes.
    • Firuz = first Sultan of Delhi to levy the irrigation tax 'Haqq-i-Sharb', after taking the Ulema's opinion; 1/10 of produce from users of royal canals.UPPSC ×2
    • Firuz planted 1200 new gardens near Delhi, restored 30 old orchards of Alauddin's time and took steps to improve the quality of fruits.
    • Firuz focused on maintaining and rebuilding the buildings of his predecessors.
    • Firuz Shah Tughluq brought two Ashoka pillars to Delhi from Meerut and Topra (now in Yamuna Nagar district, Haryana).UPPSC ×2
    • The Topra pillar was re-set near the palace and mosque of Firozabad; the Meerut pillar near the present Bara Hindu Rao Hospital, Delhi, by the mound 'Kashke-Shikar'.

    End of the Tughluqs and Timur

    1. 1236Order: Rukn-ud-din (1236 A.D.) → Mubarak Khan (1316–1320) → Firuz Shah Tughluq (1351–1388) → Alam Shah (1445–1451).UPPSC
    2. 1236Rukn-ud-din became ruler in 1236 AD after Iltutmish, though Iltutmish had named Raziyya as successor.
    3. 1316Mubarak Khan became Sultan as Mubarak Khalji in 1316; Alam Shah was of the Sayyid dynasty.
    4. 1394Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah (1394–1412 AD) = last ruler of the Tughluq dynasty.
    5. 1398Timur, Turco-Mongol general of Central Asia, invaded India in 1398 AD, in the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah.
    6. 1412Timur's invasion destroyed Delhi and began the fall of the Tughluqs; the dynasty ended with Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah's death in 1412 AD.
    7. 1413Delhi's warlords elected Daulat Khan Sultan in 1413 AD; Khizr Khan defeated him.
    8. 1414In 1414 AD Khizr Khan took Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty, which ruled after Timur's invasion; he did not take the title Sultan.
    • Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah (1394–1412 AD) = last ruler of the Tughluq dynasty.
    • In his reign Khwaja Jahan founded the independent state of Jaunpur.
    • Nusrat Shah, another grandson (also called son) of Firuz, challenged Nasiruddin; the dynasty split: Nasiruddin in Delhi, Nusrat Shah in Firozabad.
    • Famous saying on Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah: 'The sultanate of Shahanshah extends from Delhi to Palam'.
    • Timur, Turco-Mongol general of Central Asia, invaded India in 1398 AD, in the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah.
    • Timur's stated aims: fight and destroy the Kafirs and plunder wealth.
    • Before leaving India, Timur appointed Khizr Khan Subedar of Multan, Dipalpur and Lahore.
    • Timur's invasion destroyed Delhi and began the fall of the Tughluqs; the dynasty ended with Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah's death in 1412 AD.
    • Delhi's warlords elected Daulat Khan Sultan in 1413 AD; Khizr Khan defeated him.
    • In 1414 AD Khizr Khan took Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty, which ruled after Timur's invasion; he did not take the title Sultan.
    • Order: Rukn-ud-din (1236 A.D.) → Mubarak Khan (1316–1320) → Firuz Shah Tughluq (1351–1388) → Alam Shah (1445–1451).UPPSC
    • Rukn-ud-din became ruler in 1236 AD after Iltutmish, though Iltutmish had named Raziyya as successor.
    • Mubarak Khan became Sultan as Mubarak Khalji in 1316; Alam Shah was of the Sayyid dynasty.

    Kashmir

    • Yousuf Shah Chak, last Muslim ruler of the Kashmir valley, was exiled to Bihar by Akbar; he died in Puri in 1592 AD and was buried in Nalanda.
