    Chapter 20 · Medieval India

    Lodi Dynasty

    32 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. In 1504 AD Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra on the Yamuna and made it his capital.×7
    Quick quiz: 7 of 7 UPPSC questions

    Lodi dynasty and order of Delhi dynasties

    • Lodi dynasty (1451–1526 A.D.) was of Afghan origin; it was the last ruling family of the Delhi Sultanate.UPPSC
    • Order of Afghan rulers: Bahlul Khan Lodi (1451–1489 A.D.) → Sikandar Shah (1489–1517 A.D.) → Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526 A.D.).
    • Order of Delhi dynasties: Slave/Ghulam/Mamluk (1206–1290 AD) → Khalji (1290–1320 AD) → Sayyid (1414–1451 AD) → Lodi (1451–1526 AD).UPPSC
    • Slave dynasty rulers (1206–90 AD): Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–10), Iltutmish (1211–36), Balban (1266–86); Ibrahim Lodi belonged to the Lodi dynasty.

    Bahlul Lodi

    • Bahlul Khan Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451 AD.
    • He took the throne of Delhi as 'Bahlul Shah Ghazi' and had the Khutba read in his name.
    • His most important victory was over Jaunpur; Jaunpur was known as Shiraz-i-Hind in this period.
    • Bahlul Lodi did not treat Hindus with religious fanaticism.
    • Reputed Hindu Sardars in his court: Rai Karan Singh, Rai Pratap Singh, Rai Nar Singh, Rai Trilokchandra and Rai Dadu.
    • He introduced the 'Bahlul coin', the main means of exchange before Akbar.
    • Before his death Bahlul named his third son, Nizam Khan, as successor; some chiefs opposed as his mother (Jaiband/Bibi Ambha) was a goldsmith's daughter.

    Sikandar Lodi

    • Backed by some powerful warlords, Nizam Khan took the throne as Sultan Sikandarshah (Sikandar Lodi) on 17 July 1489 AD.
    • Sikandar Lodi = greatest of the three Lodi rulers.
    • In 1504 AD Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra on the Yamuna and made it his capital.UPPSC ×7
    • Agra was founded to command eastern Rajasthan and the routes towards Malwa/Gujarat.
    • Sikandar Lodi was very hard-working, generous, kind to his subjects, but religiously orthodox.
    • His administration was noted for efficiency; roads were made safe and irrigation facilities given to peasants.
    • He worked to improve agriculture and trade and took keen interest in land revenue management.
    • He ordered nobles to present details of their expenditure; embezzlement was severely punished.
    • He started the land measure 'Gaj-i-Sikandari', later used by Sher Shah Suri and Akbar.
    • Sikandar Lodi abolished the octroi duty (several levies) on grain.UPPSC
    • He arranged free meals for the poor.
    • He banned 'Tazia' in Muharram and stopped Muslim women from visiting 'Peers' and 'Mazaars'.
    • A list of qualified and skilled persons was made and presented before him every six months.
    • He was educated and learned, with knowledge of Persian poetry.
    • He had an Ayurvedic treatise translated into Persian and named it 'Farhange Sikandari'.
    • 'Lajjat-i-Sikandarshahi', a masterpiece on singing, was composed in his reign.
    • Sikandar Lodi was very fond of hearing the Shehnai.
    • Sikandar Lodi wrote poems under the pen name 'Gulrukhi'.UPPSC

    Ibrahim Lodi

    • Battle of Khatoli (Khatauli), 1518 AD: Maharana Sanga badly defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
    • First battle of Panipat: Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi, 21 April 1526 A.D.; Ibrahim was defeated and killed on the battlefield; the Lodi dynasty ended.
    • Per Nayamatullah (Niyamatullah), no Sultan of India other than Ibrahim was killed on the battlefield.
    ← Tughluq DynastyVijayanagara Empire →

    Chapter 21 · Medieval India

    Vijayanagara Empire

    81 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Battle of Talikota, January 1565 AD: combined forces of Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar and Golconda defeated Vijayanagara; Barar was not included.×2
    2. The ruins of Hampi (Central Karnataka) represent the old capital of the Vijayanagara Empire.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 11 UPPSC questions

    Foundation

    • Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 AD by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka I, on the banks of the Tungabhadra.
    • Their line is called the Sangama dynasty after their father Sangama; they were also known as the Sangama brothers.
    • Harihara and Bukka were feudatories (warrior chieftains and loyal officials) of the Kakatiyas of Warangal.
    • After Warangal fell to the Delhi Sultans they shifted to Kampili and became ministers.
    • Muhammad Tughluq conquered Kampili and imprisoned them; it is believed they accepted (were forced to accept) Islam.
    • They were later sent south as Tughluq commanders to suppress the Kampili revolt (one passage: they suppressed it; another: they could not succeed).
    • Under the influence of Saint Vidyaranya they became Hindu again.
    • Their Guru Vidyaranya (Madhav Vidyaranya) and his brother Sayana, famous commentator of the Vedas, inspired the founding of Vijayanagara.
    • Sayana, commentator of the Vedic texts, was patronized by and flourished under the Vijayanagara rulers.UPPSC
    • The empire was founded on the south bank of the Tungabhadra near Anegundi Fort.
    • Harihara I founded a new city on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra (a tributary of the Krishna) and ruled as agent of a deity to whom all land south of the Krishna was supposed to belong.
    • Harihara I was the eldest son of Sangama; he built a fort on the west side of Karnataka; Bukka succeeded him.
    DynastyPeriod
    Sangama1336–1485 A.D.
    Saluva1485–1505 A.D.
    Tuluva1505–1570 A.D.
    Aravidu1570–1672 A.D.
    • These four dynasties ruled for over three hundred years.
    • Capitals of Vijayanagara in order: Anegundi, Vijayanagara, Penukonda, Chandragiri and later Vellore.

    Sangama rulers

    1. 1336Harihara I ruled 1336–1356 AD.
    2. 1356Bukka I (1356–77 AD) sent a mission to the Emperor of China in 1374 AD.
    3. 1365In 1365 the Vijayanagara army under Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka I, began and by about 1370 completed the conquest of the Pandyan country (Madurai region).
    4. 1365Telugu poet Srinath (1365–1441 AD) was in the court of Deva Raya II; also at the court of Pedakomati Vema Reddy, Reddy ruler of Kondavidu.
    5. 1377After Bukka's death in 1377 A.D. his son Harihara II took the throne with the title 'Maharajadhiraja'.
    6. 1410Devaraya I built a dam on the Tungabhadra around 1410 AD and a 24 km canal-cum-aqueduct from the river to his capital.
    7. 1422Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq came to Vijayanagara in the reign of Devaraya II (1422–46 AD), the most august ruler of the Sangama dynasty.UPPSC
    • Harihara I ruled 1336–1356 AD.
    • Bukka I (1356–77 AD) sent a mission to the Emperor of China in 1374 AD.
    • In 1365 the Vijayanagara army under Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka I, began and by about 1370 completed the conquest of the Pandyan country (Madurai region).
    • Kumara Kampana merged Madurai into the Vijayanagara Empire.
    • His wife Ganga Devi described his victories in her book 'Madhura Vijayam'.UPPSC
    • After Bukka's death in 1377 A.D. his son Harihara II took the throne with the title 'Maharajadhiraja'.
    • Harihara II won Kanara, Mysore, Trichinapalli and Kanchi; the ruler of Ceylon (Sri Lanka) sent ambassadors, rich yearly presents/tax.
    • Harihara II's biggest success: capturing Belgaum and Goa from the Bahamani state in the west.
    • Harihara II worshipped Virupaksha Shiva.
    • Devaraya I built a dam on the Tungabhadra around 1410 AD and a 24 km canal-cum-aqueduct from the river to his capital.
    • Devaraya I is credited with making the capital one of the largest cities of the 15th century.
    • Italian traveller Nicolo Conti (Niccolo de Conti) visited Vijayanagara in the time of Deva Raya I.
    • Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq came to Vijayanagara in the reign of Devaraya II (1422–46 AD), the most august ruler of the Sangama dynasty.UPPSC
    • Telugu poet Srinath (1365–1441 AD) was in the court of Deva Raya II; also at the court of Pedakomati Vema Reddy, Reddy ruler of Kondavidu.

    Note from the book Srinath's court question: CGPSC deleted this question in its revised answer key.

    Saluva and Tuluva dynasties

    • In 1485 A.D. Narasimha Saluva, feudal lord of Chandragiri, removed Praudha Deva Raya, last Sangama ruler, and founded the Saluva dynasty; ruled about five years.
    • Vira Narasimha dethroned Immadi Narasimha (son of Narasimha Saluva, last Saluva ruler) and founded the Tuluva dynasty.
    • After Vira Narasimha his younger brother Krishnadeva Raya (1509–1529 AD) ruled, followed by his half brother Achyuta Deva Raya.
    • Portuguese writer Farnao Nuniz (Nunes) visited in Achyuta Deva Raya's reign.
    • Nuniz: women were dancers, domestic servants and palanquin bearers; also wrestlers, astrologers, accountants and soothsayers.

    Krishnadeva Raya

    • Krishnadeva Raya (Tuluva dynasty) is considered the greatest ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire.

    Note from the book 'Who was enthroned 500 years ago' (2008): the question has an error, as Harihara-I and Kulottunga-I had also completed 500 years; nearest answer Krishnadeva Raya.

    • 2008 marked 500 years of Krishnadeva Raya's coronation.UPPSC
    • Kulottunga-I (1070–1120 AD) was the grandson of Chola emperor Rajendra-I.
    • Krishnadeva Raya fought the battle of Golconda with Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda; the Qutb Shahi army was defeated.
    • Sultan Quli Qutb Shah founded the Qutb Shahi dynasty in Golconda; he captured forts at Warangal and Kondaveedu while Krishnadeva Raya was fighting the rulers of Odisha.
    • Krishnadeva Raya kept friendly relations with the Portuguese and got guns and Arabian horses from Portuguese merchants.
    • On the request of Portuguese governor Afonso de Albuquerque, Krishnadeva Raya allowed a fort at Bhatkal (Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka).
    • His reign = classical era / golden age of Telugu literature.UPPSC
    • Ashtadiggajas = eight Telugu poets of Krishnadeva Raya's court, the eight pillars of his literary assembly.UPPSC
    • Krishnadeva Raya took the title 'Andhra Bhoj'.
    • He was himself an outstanding poet and writer; his 'Amuktamalyada' is one of the five epics of Telugu.
    • Allasani Peddana, greatest and foremost of the Ashtadiggajas, was given the title 'Andhra Kavita Pitamah'.
    • Peddana was a master of Telugu and Sanskrit, not Sanskrit and Tamil.
    • Poet Mallanarya in his court wrote Bhava Chinta Ratna and Veerasaivamrita in Kannada.
    • Bhava Chinta Ratna: on Shiva worship and philosophy, personal devotion; Veerasaivamrita: theories and religious aspects of the Veera Shaiva tradition.
    • Krishnadeva Raya founded the suburban town Nagalapuram near Vijayanagara in memory of his mother Nagala Devi.UPPSC
    • The Hazara Rama temple was built in Krishnadeva Raya's reign.
    • He also built the Vitthala (Shree Vijaya Vitthala) temple; work continued under Achyutaraya.
    • Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited Vijayanagara in his time.
    • Babur in his autobiography called Krishnadeva Raya the most powerful ruler of India.

    Telugu Kavitrayi

    • Telugu translation of the Mahabharata: started by Nannaya (11th century), continued by Tikkana (13th century) and Yerranna/Yerrapragada (14th century).UPPSC
    • These three are the 'Kavitrayi' (trinity of poets) of Telugu literature.

    Battle of Talikota and the Aravidu dynasty

    • Battle of Talikota, January 1565 AD: combined forces of Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar and Golconda defeated Vijayanagara; Barar was not included.UPPSC ×2
    • Per Firishta the battle was at Talikota, but the actual field lay between the villages Rakshasi and Tangadi.
    • Talikota is in Karnataka near Vijayapura district; the battle was a watershed that weakened one of the greatest south Indian empires before the Marathas.
    • Ruler at Talikota was Sadashiva Raya, but real power lay with his minister Rama Raya; Hussain Nizamashah killed Rama Raya in the battle.
    • Tirumala, brother of Rama Raya, dethroned Sadashiva at Penukonda in 1570 AD and founded the Aravidu dynasty (1570–1672 AD), the last Vijayanagara dynasty.
    • His successor was his eldest son Shri Ranga I; then Venkata II, one of the greatest Vijayanagara kings, who made Chandragiri his headquarters (capital).
    • Venkata II was a contemporary of Raja Wodeyar, who founded the kingdom of Mysore in 1612.

    Revenue and administration

    • Main source of state income was land revenue, fixed after the land was surveyed and categorized.
    • Land tax was normally one-third to one-sixth of the yield, depending on land category and crop quality.
    • The tax 'Shist' (Rai-rekha) was the main source of state income; the central revenue department was called 'Athavane' (Asthvan/Athvan).
    • Other income: wealth tax, trade tax, commercial tax, industry tax, social and community tax and fines on crime.
    • Land was assessed in four categories: wetland, dry land, orchards and woods; the rate varied with land quality, crop, soil and irrigation method; private workshop owners paid an industry tax.

    Hampi, temples and culture

    • The ruins of Hampi (Central Karnataka) represent the old capital of the Vijayanagara Empire.UPPSC ×2
    • Hampi stands on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra; its Group of Monuments (Vijayanagara district, Karnataka) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
    • The Virupaksha Temple at Hampi was built in the Vijayanagara period (one passage prints "7th century CE").
    • The Vijaya Vitthal Temple, with 56 carved pillars that give out musical notes, is at Hampi; built by Krishnadeva Raya (1509–29 AD) and continued under Achyutaraya of the Tuluva dynasty.
    • Kalyana Mandapas, for celebrating divine weddings, were a notable feature of Vijayanagara temples.
    • Yakshagaan dance tradition first developed in the Vijayanagara period; a traditional folk dance of coastal Karnataka based on mythological and religious stories.

    Hoysala sites

    • Dwarasamudra, the Hoysala capital, is now Halebidu in Hassan district, Karnataka; famed for heritage architecture.
    • Its ancient Hoysaleshwara temple (12th–13th century) is very famous.
    • In the reign of Hoysala ruler Narasimha I, architect Kedroz built it under Ketamal, Chief Officer of the Public Works Department.
    • The Chennakeshava temple at Belur was built by Hoysala ruler Vishnuvardhana.

    Chapter 22 · Medieval India

    Delhi Sultanate: Administration

    70 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi · Agriculture: direct aid to farmers to bring more land under cultivation · Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq×2
    2. Iltutmish was the first Turk ruler to introduce Arabic coins; he started the silver Tanka and the copper Jital.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 16 UPPSC questions

    Dynasties and nature of the state

    • Slave dynasty 1206–1290 AD; Khalji 1290–1320 AD; Tughluq 1320–1414 AD; Sayyid 1414–1451 AD; Lodi 1451–1526 AD.
    • Tughluq rule was the longest of the Sultanate period.
    • Most Sultans and Amirs of the Sultanate period were Turks.UPPSC
    • The Sultan was head of the central government and chief commander of the army.
    • Holders of influential posts were called Amirs; they had great effect when the Sultan was unfit, weak or under-age.
    • Barani did not consider the Delhi Sultans' state truly Islamic because the majority of the population did not follow Islam.
    • Medieval government was a composite structure: a fusion of Perso-Arabic, Turko-Mongol and Indian elements.
    • Zawabit = state laws in the Sultanate's administrative vocabulary.UPPSC
    • Hadis (Hadith) = Islamic law: collected reports of the sayings, customs and doings of Muhammad and his companions, and what he enjoined, tolerated or forbade.
    • Khareetadar = dispatcher of royal decrees.UPPSC

    Departments

    DepartmentWorkStarted by
    Diwan-i-MustakhrajRevenue; to deal with corruption and loot in the revenue systemAlauddin Khalji
    Diwan-i-RiyasatMarket controlAlauddin Khalji (not Balban)UPPSC
    Diwan-i-Amir-i-KohiAgriculture: direct aid to farmers to bring more land under cultivationMuhammad-Bin-TughluqUPPSC ×2
    Diwan-i-KhairatCharityFiruz Tughluq
    Diwan-i-BandaganSlavesFiruz Shah Tughluq
    Diwan-i-ArzMilitary (defence) departmentBalban
    Diwan-i-RisalatReligious matters and foreign affairs—
    Diwan-i-InshaGovernment (state) correspondence—
    Diwan-i-WizaratFinancial matters / revenue—
    • Balban (1266–1286 A.D.), a main architect of the Sultanate's government and institutions, separated the Diwan-i-Wizarat (Finance) and created the Diwan-i-Arz.
    • Balban reorganised the Diwan-i-Arz and deployed the army in different parts of the kingdom to put down rebellion.

    Wizarat

    • Wizarat = institution recognized by Islamic administration; the Abbasi Caliphs took the idea from Persia.
    • Non-Arabic institutions were being repealed; 'Wizarat' was the name used for the council of ministers under the emperor.
    • Abbas Fazal-Bin-Ahmad, skilled in administration, was the first Wazir, under Mahmud Ghazni (Ghaznavid administration).
    • Wazir = prime minister of the state and chief of the revenue/finance department (Diwan-i-Wizarat).
    • The Wazir looked after Lagaan, the tax system, donations and military expenditure; he supervised state income, expenditure and other departments.
    • The Tughluq period was the golden period (heyday) of Indian Muslim Wizarat; the Wazir's post peaked under Firuz Tughluq.UPPSC

    Army

    • Army organization and posts were based on the decimal system.
    • Head of a troop of horsemen = 'Sarkhel'.
    • 10 Sarkhels → one Sipahsalar; 10 Sipahsalars → one Amir; 10 Amirs → one Malik; 10 Maliks → one Khan.

    Taxes

    • Firuz Tughluq taxed according to Islamic (Quran) law: four taxes — Kharaj, Jizya, Khums and Zakat.
    • Khums = one-fifth share of war booty taken from non-believers, paid to the Caliph or Sultan.
    • Kharaj, Ushr and Muktai were taxes on land produce; Khums was not.
    • Normally 4/5 of the loot went to the soldiers and 1/5 to the treasury; Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq kept 4/5 in the treasury and gave 1/5 to soldiers.
    • 'Haqq-i-Sharb' = irrigation tax, levied by Firuz Tughluq at 10% of the crop yield on the advice of religious scholars.UPPSC
    • Firuz Tughluq abolished 21 grievous taxes.
    • Fawazil = excess amount paid to the exchequer by the Iqtadars.

    Iqta and land

    • Iltutmish first introduced the Iqta system in the Delhi Sultanate.UPPSC
    • In the Caliph's Islamic empire, land was granted to army officials for limited periods in lieu of regular wages.
    • The Iqta system began in the 9th century A.D. to relieve the treasury when low tax revenue and little war booty made salaries hard to pay.
    • The Iqta holder (Iqtadar/Muqti) collected revenue and taxes in his area.
    • Iqta revenue was not deposited directly in the Sultan's account; the Muqti used it for administrative and military expenses and kept troops for the Sultan.UPPSC
    • Siyasatnama by Abu Ali Hasan Ibn Ali Tusi (Nizam-ul-Mulk) is the source of information on the early Iqta system.
    • The Iqta system was not an indigenous Indian institution.
    • Sultanate territories were divided into Khalisa and Jagirs (Iqta); Khalisa = land under the state's direct control, Jagir = a revenue assignment given to a Mansabdar/Jagirdar, not under direct state control.UPPSC
    TermMeaning
    IqtaLand revenueUPPSC
    MahrousaProtected town
    KhalisaLand under state administration
    ShiqA portion of land

    Provincial and village administration

    • The province was divided into Parganas or Kasbas; the Pargana official Amil collected revenue.
    • At the Pargana level the Mushrif kept accounts and the Khazandar was in charge of the treasury.
    • Mir Bakshi headed the military department, nobility, information and intelligence agencies in Mughal administration, not under the Khaljis.
    • Ascending order of size: Pargana → Sarkar → Suba.
    • The empire was divided into Subas (head: Subedar); each Suba into Sarkars (head: Fauzdar); each Sarkar into Parganas or Mahals (head: Shiqdar).
    • Villages under a Pargana were called 'Mavada' or 'Deeha'; 'Nagla' were small colonies under a Mavada.
    • In Shahjahan's reign a unit called 'Chakla', holding a few Parganas, was formed between Pargana and Sarkar.
    • The village was the smallest unit of governance in the Sultanate.
    • Main village functionaries: Khut, Muqaddam and Patwari, working closely with the muqti for revenue collection.
    • 'Muqaddam or Chaudhari' = village headman, and as such the highest revenue authority in the village.
    • Chaudhary = highest (supreme) rural official of land revenue; main revenue collector for villages.
    • Traditional social structure: Sultan at the top, then his governors, then the village headman (Chaudhary).
    • At times of revolt the Sultanate reduced the influence of the Rais and took the Chaudhary's help to collect revenue.

    Coins

    • Two main currencies of the Sultanate period: Jital and Tanka.UPPSC
    • Iltutmish was the first Turk ruler to introduce Arabic coins; he started the silver Tanka and the copper Jital.UPPSC ×2
    • Tanka and Shashgani were silver coins; Jital was copper.
    • Ratio of Tanka to Jital = 1:48.
    • Iltutmish was the first to issue regular currency and to declare Delhi the capital.
    • The name of the last Khalifa of Baghdad first appeared on coins of Alauddin Masud Shah (1242–46 AD).UPPSC
    • Last Khalifa of Baghdad = Al-Mustasim (1242–58 AD).
    • The name of Khalifa al-Mustansir (served 1226–1242 A.D.) was on the coins of Iltutmish.

    Chapter 23 · Medieval India

    Delhi Sultanate: Art and Architecture

    48 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Kirti Stambha of Chittor was built by Rana Kumbha in memory of his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa; it is a unique monument of his achievements.×3
    2. Alauddin Khalji did NOT contribute to the building of Qutub Minar; Aybak, Iltutmish and Firuz Shah Tughluq did.×2
    Quick quiz: 5 of 5 UPPSC questions

    Use of paper

    • Use of paper in India is considered to have started around the 7th–8th century CE.
    • Written documents on paper are found from around the 11th century CE; in the 12th–13th century CE paper was also used in royal scriptures.

    Note from the book Start of paper use in India: BPSC gave "12th century CE" as the correct answer, though paper use is considered to have started around the 7th–8th century CE.

    Aybak and Iltutmish: early buildings and Qutub Minar

    • Qutbuddin Aybak built the Adhai Din Ka Jhopara mosque in Ajmer.
    • Aybak built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque near Raipithora Fort in Delhi (it is in Delhi, not Ajmer).UPPSC
    • Qutbuddin Aybak = first Muslim ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; he started Qutub Minar in Delhi but completed only its basement.
    • Qutub Minar was completed by Iltutmish.
    • In Firuz Shah Tughluq's time the fourth floor of Qutub Minar was damaged; he restored the fourth floor and built the fifth storey.UPPSC
    • Alauddin Khalji did NOT contribute to the building of Qutub Minar; Aybak, Iltutmish and Firuz Shah Tughluq did.UPPSC ×2
    • Qutub Minar is named after the famous Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki.
    • Qutub Minar: built in the 13th century, 238 feet (72.5 m) high (not 180 feet), tapering tower of five storeys.
    • Qutub Minar is a mix of polygonal and circular shapes; built largely of red and buff sandstone, with some marble in the upper storey.
    • Chand Minar: built in the 15th century, 210 feet high, tapering tower of four storeys.
    • Chand Minar is painted peach now; its facade once had chevron patterning on encaustic tile work and bold bands of Quranic verses.
    • Iltutmish built Sultangarhi, Hauz-e-Shamsi, Shamsi Eidgaah, Jama Masjid Shamsi (Badayun) and Atarkin-ka-Darwaza (Nagaur).

    Balban's tomb

    • Tomb of Sultan Ghiyasuddin Balban: in Mehrauli, New Delhi; built by himself in 1287 AD in rubble masonry.
    • Balban's tomb = first tomb in India built in a purely Indo-Islamic style; important in the development of Indo-Islamic architecture.UPPSC
    • The first true arches in India appeared in the Tomb of Balban.

    Khalji buildings

    • Alai Darwaza was built by Alauddin Khalji near the Qutub Minar.
    • Alai Darwaza: domed entrance of red sandstone adorned with white marble; completed in 1311 AD by Turkish craftsmen.
    • Alai Darwaza is one of the first buildings in India in the Indo-Islamic architectural style.
    • The horse-shoe arch was first introduced in the Alai Darwaza.
    • Alauddin Khalji built Hazar Sutun and Hauz-e-Alai in Delhi (Siri fort).
    • Ukha Mosque (Bayana, Rajasthan) was built by Malik Kafur Sultani in the reign of Sultan Mubarakshah Khalji.
    • Jamat Khana Masjid = oldest monument in the dargah complex of Hazrat Nizamuddin Aulia; built by Khizr Khan, son of Sultan Alauddin Khalji.

    Tughluq and Lodi buildings

    • Ghiyasuddin Tughluq (1320–25 AD), after founding the Tughluq dynasty, set up a city in Delhi named Tughluqabad.
    • The Moth Masjid was built in the reign of Sikandar Lodi.
    • Sikandar Lodi's tomb was built by Sultan Ibrahim Lodi.
    • Order of building: Qutub Minar (Aybak 1206–10 AD and Iltutmish 1211–36 AD) → Tughluqabad fort (Ghiyasuddin Tughluq 1320–1325 AD) → Lodi Garden (Lodi dynasty 1451–1526 AD) → Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar 1556–1605 AD).

    Kirti Stambha of Chittor

    • Kirti Stambha of Chittor was built by Rana Kumbha in memory of his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa; it is a unique monument of his achievements.UPPSC ×3
    • Kirti Stambha was built under the supervision of Jaita; its panegyrists were Atri and Mahesh.
    • Kirti-Stambha Prashasti was composed by Atri Kavi.

    Chapter 24 · Medieval India

    Delhi Sultanate: Literature

    91 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Amir Khusrau was born in 1253 AD at Patiyali in district Etah (now Kasganj district), Uttar Pradesh.×3
    2. He played a pioneering role in developing Khari Boli; known as the father (and promoter) of Hindi Khari Boli.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Al-Biruni

    • Kitab-ul-Hind (also Tahqiq-i-Hind, Tarikh-i-Hind) was written by Al-Biruni, a 10th–11th century AD Persian historian and scholar.
    • Al-Biruni's real name was Abu Rehan.
    • Al-Biruni studied India as a scientist; described its religious, literary and socio-political condition.
    • Tahqiq-i-Hind is one of his notable works; gives a detailed account of the history, geography and culture of India.

    Amir Khusrau: life and courts

    • Full (real) name: Abul Hassan Yaminuddin Khusrau, often called Amir Khusrau.
    • Amir Khusrau was born in 1253 AD at Patiyali in district Etah (now Kasganj district), Uttar Pradesh.UPPSC ×3
    • Khusrau was called, and called himself, Tuti-i-Hind (Parrot of India).UPPSC
    • He started composing poems at the early age of nine.
    • He referred to himself as a 'Turkish-Indian'.
    • Amir Khusrau was a poet, historian and musician; a great scholar and poet of his time.
    • Courts he was associated with: Nasiruddin Mahmud, Balban, Kaiqubad, Samsuddin Kayumars, Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Shihabuddin Umar, Mubarakshah, Ghiyasuddin Tughluq and Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq.
    • Amir Khusrau was the court poet of Alauddin Khalji.UPPSC
    • He was the disciple of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya.
    • Both Amir Khusrau and Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya witnessed the reign of more than seven Sultans of Delhi.
    • Khusrau was a prolific classical poet linked with the royal courts of more than seven rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.
    • He was the first Persian poet to depict the Indian environment in his poetry.UPPSC

    Amir Khusrau: language and works

    • Khusrau learned various Indian dialects, especially Hindavi, which he loved most.
    • Khusrau himself said he knew Sanskrit and other Indian languages, which are a part of Hindavi.
    • He played a pioneering role in developing Khari Boli; known as the father (and promoter) of Hindi Khari Boli.UPPSC ×3
    • Khusrau was a scholar of both Hindi (Hindavi) and Persian.UPPSC
    • He was the first author to use Hindi (Hindavi) phrases and words.
    • He started the new Persian poetry style Sabk-i-Hindi (Hindustani style); considered its father.
    • His saying: "Na Lafze Hindiwast aj Farsi Kam" = the words of Hindi are not less than those of Persian.
    • Works of Amir Khusrau: Qiran-us-Sadain, Miftah-ul-Futuh, Khazain-ul-Futuh (Tarikh-i-Alai), Ashika, Nuh Sipihr, Tughluq Namah.
    • Qiran-us-Sadain = his first Masnavi on a historical subject.
    • Tughluq Namah = the last historical Masnavi of Amir Khusrau.

    Amir Khusrau: music

    • Amir Khusrau was the originator in India of the early form of the musical style Qawwali.
    • Kitab-i-Nauras, a collection of songs praising Hindu deities and Muslim saints, was written by Ibrahim Adil Shah II, Sultan of Bijapur.
    • Ibrahim Adil Shah II founded the city of Nauraspur and made it his capital.
    • Indian music made Muslim society passionate about music; so Amir Khusrau emerged as a great musician of the Sultanate period.
    • Khusrau invented the Sitar by combining the Irani Tamboora and the Indian Veena; Sitar = finest example of Hindu-Muslim harmony in instruments.
    • He combined Indian and Persian melodies and introduced new melody styles like Iman, Zilf, Sajgari.
    • Tabla and Sitar were invented (made prevalent) by Amir Khusrau in the 13th/14th century.UPPSC

    Persian and Apabhramsa

    • Persian literature in India began to develop with the advent of Muslims; here it took a new, innovative form.
    • After the Delhi Sultanate was set up, Persian was given the status of official language; Sultans of Delhi patronised Persian.
    • Forms of Sanskrit spoken by the people were termed Apabhramsa.
    • In medieval Sanskrit texts 'Apabhramsa' denoted early forms of some of the modern Indian languages.
    • Scholars hold that the Hindi dialects of northern India and Kashmiri, Punjabi, Sindhi, Nepali, Shauryaseni, Marathi developed from Apabhramsa.

    Historical works of the Sultanate period

    • Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was written by Minhaj-us-Siraj (Minhaj-i-Siraj) and dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud.
    • Tabaqat-i-Nasiri: divided into 23 volumes; translated into English by H.G. Raverty; describes Muhammad Ghori's victory over India.
    • Tabaqat-i-Nasiri has the earliest description of Bakhtiyar Khalji's invasion of Bihar.
    • Tabaqat-i-Nasiri is an important source for the history of the foundation of Muslim rule in Bengal.
    • Literary evidence suggests Nalanda University was sacked in 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Turk.
    • Minhaj-i-Siraj, a Persian historian, reported thousands of monks burned alive and thousands beheaded as Khalji tried to uproot Buddhism.
    • Ziauddin Barani = Muslim political philosopher of the Delhi Sultanate; wrote two famous works, Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi and Fatwa-i-Jahandari.
    • Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi = a historical account of the Delhi Sultanate (history of the Tughlaq dynasty).
    • Fatwa-i-Jahandari guides Muslim rulers to follow political ideals based on Islamic principles.
    • Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi has two authors: Ziauddin Barani and Shams-i-Siraj Afif; Afif's is an account of the reign of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
    • Afif's book has the same title as Barani's but is very different in material and approach.
    • Order of texts: Kitab-ul-Hind (Al-Biruni) → Prithviraja-Raso (Chandarbardai) → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (Minhaj-i-Siraj) → Fatawa-i-Jahandari (Ziauddin Barani).UPPSC
    • Taj-ul-Masir was written by Sadruddin Muhammad Hassan Nizami.
    • Yahiya Bin Ahmad Sarhindi wrote Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi under the patronage of Sayyid Mubarakshah; it is the principal source for the history of Sayyid rulers.
    • Firuz Shah Tughluq wrote his memoirs, Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi; through it he wanted to prove himself an ideal Muslim ruler.UPPSC

    Quick quiz: 10 of 15 UPPSC questions

    Polo, rulers and their measures

    • The game of Polo was introduced in India by the Turks.UPPSC
    • Qutbuddin Aybak was fond of Polo (Chaugan); he died in 1210 AD while playing it.

    • Sher Shah Suri built a major road in the 16th century from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Lahore (Pakistan), also called Sadak-i-Azam.
    • Sadak-i-Azam served as an administrative link to the remote provinces of Sher Shah's vast empire.
    • In the reign of Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah, Hindu gods and goddesses were worshipped in the royal palaces of the Delhi Sultanate.UPPSC
    • Khusrau Shah took the throne of Delhi with the title 'Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah' after the assassination of Mubarak Shah.
    • Hamida Banu Begum = queen consort of Mughal emperor Humayun and mother of Akbar, the third Mughal emperor (not wife of Alauddin Khilji).UPPSC
    • Iltutmish = father of Raziyya; Gulbadan Begum = daughter of Babur; Shah Turkan = wife of Iltutmish.
    • Chand Bibi = Muslim woman warrior of medieval India; Regent of Bijapur and Regent of Ahmednagar (not Oudh).
    • Chand Bibi was the daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah-I of Ahmednagar.
    • Correct pairs: Bahadur Shah – Gujarat; Raziyya Sultan – Delhi; Baz Bahadur – Malwa.
    • Ain-ul-Mulk Multani served under Alauddin Khilji, Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Shah Tughlaq, not Iltutmish.
    • Alauddin Khalji sent Ain-ul-Mulk Multani to central India in 1305 AD, where he won Malwa.

    Travellers

    TravellerCountry
    Ibn BattutaMorocco
    Marco PoloVenice (Italy)
    Abdur RazzaqIran (not Turkey)UPPSC
    NunizPortugal
    • Marco Polo visited India during the rule of Pandya ruler Marvarman Kulshekhara (1268–1310 AD).
    • Iranian Ambassador Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara in the rule of Deva Raya II (1422–46 AD).
    • Nuniz, a Portuguese traveller, also visited Vijayanagara.
    • Order of arrival: Al-Biruni → Ibn Battuta → Tavernier → Manucci.UPPSC ×2
    • Al-Biruni = resident of Khiva (ancient Khwarizm); scholar and diplomat in the court of the last emperor of the Khiva dynasty before Mahmud Ghazni's victory over India.
    • Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud Ghazni during his invasion of India.
    • Ibn Battuta (1333–1342 AD) = Moroccan traveller; came to India in the reign of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq (1325–1351 AD).
    • Muhammad Tughluq appointed Ibn Battuta 'Qazi' of Delhi; later sent him to China as ambassador in 1342.
    • Ibn Battuta wrote his travel experiences in his book Rihla.
    • Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (17th century AD) = French gem merchant and traveller; began his voyage in the period of Shahjahan; made six voyages to the East.
    • Tavernier's travel account: "The Six Voyages of John Baptista Tavernier".
    • Niccolao Manucci (1653–1708 AD) = Italian traveller; reached India from his hometown Venice, travelling via Turkiye and Asia.
    • Manucci served Prince Dara Shukoh as a cannoneer; later took up the medical profession.
    • Manucci is famous for his work "Storia do Mogor or Mogul India, 1653–1708".
    • Ibn Battuta = world's greatest traveller of premodern times: about 44 countries and 73,000 miles (117,482 km) in 30 years.
    • Ibn Battuta crossed South Africa, Western Africa, Southern and Eastern Europe, Middle-East Asia, Indian Subcontinent, Middle Asia, South-Eastern Asia and China.
    • Marco Polo travelled approx. 24,000 miles over 24 years, starting in 1271; one of the pioneer nomads.
    • Marco Polo's travel account covers Middle East, Middle Asia, China and Mongolia; he was aided by Mongolian ruler Kublai Khan.

    Society: terms and customs

    • In the Sultanate period, high religious and judicial authorities (Ulema) were called Dastar-Bandan, as they wore an official turban.UPPSC
    • In Islam, Sayyids and Pirs are important groups of religious thinkers; those appointed as religious and legal officers were collectively called Dastar-Bandan, i.e. one who wears a cap or Kulah.
    • Among them, Sayyids wore pointed caps and were known as Kulah-Daran.
    • The earliest reference to the use of the magnetic compass in the Indian seas was given by Sadiduddin (Sadruddin) Muhammad Ibn Muhammad 'Aufi'.
    • Aufi's books: Lubab-ul-Albab and Jawami-ul-Hikayat; the compass reference is in Jawami-ul-Hikayat.
    • Jauhar practice started in the Rajput period; a distinct form of Sati done by Rajputs in the period of Hindu-Muslim conflict, as a response to Muslim invasions.
    • Rajput women committed Jauhar to protect their honour from Muslim invaders.
    • Hindu women feared becoming "booty for the captor"; committed Jauhar and Sati to avoid rape, torture and other ignominies.
    • Hemachandra Suri = great scholar and follower of Jainism.UPPSC
    • Hemachandra was introduced to Jai Singh Siddharaj and soon rose to prominence in the Solanki royal court.
    • Later Jai Singh built a Mandap on Abu Mountain and set up statues of Jain Tirthankaras.
    • In medieval India 'Panahi' and 'Upanah' were mentioned in the context of shoes.
    • Fanam = small gold coins issued from the medieval period to the 19th century in South India.
    • Indian peasants did not cultivate maize in the 13th–14th centuries; maize was brought by the Portuguese.UPPSC ×2
    • Ibn Battuta stated they usually cultivated rice, wheat, sugarcane and cotton thrice a year; various spices were sown in southern India then.
    • In medieval India 'Mahattara' and 'Pattakila' were designations of village headmen.
    • Article 'Village Administration in Ancient India' (Indian Political Science Association, January–March 2004, volume 65, No. 1): village was the centre of administration in 600–1200 AD.
    • Village government ran under the village headman, also known as Gramani.
    • Headman's names: Garmika or Grameyaka in northern India; Pattakila or Gramakuta in Maharashtra; Gavunda in Karnataka; Mahattaka in Uttar Pradesh.
    • Indian Epigraphical Glossary (writer Dinesh Chandra Sarkar) states Mahattaka = headman or a member of the Panchayat Board.

    Note from the book Dr. Harishchandra Verma's 'Madhyakalin Bharat Bhag-1' describes Mahattar differently: head of the categories of artisans found in inscriptions.

    Battle of Plassey1757 ADUPPSC ×2
    • Battle of Plassey, June 23, 1757: East India Company forces under Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the then Nawab of Bengal.
    • Mir Zafar, Rai Durlabh and Yar Latif Khan headed the Nawab's army; Mir Zafar was bribed by Clive and caused the Nawab's defeat.
    • Kalinga War: Ashoka led a vast army against Kalinga in 261 BC; freedom-loving Kalingans gave stiff resistance to the Mauryan army.
    • Ashoka's 13th Major Rock Edict throws light on the Kalinga war.
    • Kalinga war: at least 1 million Kalingans killed, another 50 thousand taken prisoner; almost an equal number of Magadha soldiers also killed.
    • Battle of Haldighati: fought at Haldighati, Rajasthan, in 1576 AD between Maharana Pratap and Akbar's forces.

    Chapter 26 · Medieval India

    Provincial Dynasty of North India and Deccan Province

    92 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Jaunpur was founded in the 14th century by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq in memory of his cousin Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq, whose real name was Jauna Khan.×4
    2. Under the Sharqis Jaunpur was a great centre of education and its cultural fame spread; it was called Shiraz-i-Hind (Shiraz of India / Shiraz of the East).×4
    3. Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu, 1347–1358 AD), a Sardar, took the title Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah and founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347 AD (14th century).×3
    4. Dwarasamudra was the capital of the Hoysalas (and Madurai of the Pandyas).×3
    5. Bijapur · Yusuf Adilshah (ruler of Bijapur, not Ahmadnagar) · Adilshahi×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Jaunpur and the Sharqi dynasty

    • Jaunpur was founded in the 14th century by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq in memory of his cousin Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq, whose real name was Jauna Khan.UPPSC ×4
    • Firuz Shah Tughluq built 300 new cities.
    • Firuz Shah Tughluq made Malik Sarwar governor of the region; he was a eunuch, notorious as the lover of Firuz Shah's daughter.
    • The Sultanate was in disarray from factional fighting for power, so Malik Sarwar declared independence.
    • Jaunpur became independent in 1394, in the reign of Sultan Mahmud Shah II; Khwaja Jahan Malik Sarwar founded the independent Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur (not Malwa).UPPSC
    • Malik Sarwar was a slave of Muhammad Shah II; the Sultan gave him the titles Malik-us-Sharq (Lord of the East) and Khwaja-i-Jahan.
    • Malik Sarwar and his adopted son Mubarak Shah founded the Sharqi Dynasty (dynasty of the East).
    • Jaunpur = independent Islamic kingdom in North India from 1394 AD to 1479 AD (about 85 years), ruled by the Sharqi Dynasty.
    • In 1479 AD Bahlul Lodi defeated the last ruler Hussain Shah Sharqi and made Jaunpur part of the Delhi Sultanate again.UPPSC
    • Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (1402–1440 AD, as per Gazetteer of Jaunpur) = greatest Sharqi ruler; a lover of knowledge and art; Jaunpur reached its greatest height under him.
    • In his reign a new style, the Sharqi style (Sharqi art/architecture), emerged; he built monuments in it.
    • In Sharqi style the simple type of minarets was removed and signs of Hindu influence began to appear.
    • Under the Sharqis Jaunpur was a great centre of education and its cultural fame spread; it was called Shiraz-i-Hind (Shiraz of India / Shiraz of the East).UPPSC ×4
    • Vidyapati beautifully described Jaunpur and Ibrahim Shah in 'Kirtilata Kavya'.

    Kashmir: Zain-ul-Abidin

    • Shahi Khan, brother of Ali Shah, took the throne of Kashmir as Zain-ul-Abidin in 1420 AD; greatest ruler of Kashmir.
    • Zain-ul-Abidin (1420–70 AD) is called Akbar of Kashmir for his religious tolerance and good deeds (public welfare).
    • He abolished Jizya on Hindus and banned cow slaughter; he was the first ruler to do so.UPPSC
    • Mahabharata, Dashavatara and Rajtarangini were translated into Persian in his period.
    • The scriptures 'Jain Prakash' and 'Jain-Vilas' were compiled during his rule.
    • He built the artificial island Zaina Lank in the middle of Wular Lake.
    • Sikandar Butshikan built the Jama Masjid in Kashmir in 1400 AD; Zain-ul-Abidin expanded (completed) it.
    • Features of the Kashmir Jama Masjid: turret, similarity with Buddhist pagodas, Persian style.

    Rajput and hill states

    • Scholars in the court of Kumbha: Muni Sunder Suri, Natha and Tilla Bhatt; Muni Jin Vijay Suri was in the court of Mughal emperor Akbar.
    • Correct ruler–state pairs: Rana Hamir – Mewar; Rana Chunda – Marwar; Malik Raja Farooqi – Khandesh.
    • Medieval states Champaka (Chamba) and Kuluta (Kullu) were in present Himachal Pradesh; Durgara was in Jammu and Kashmir.
    • Champaka, Durgara and Kuluta were related to Rajputs.
    • These three states rose after the downfall of the Tripartite-struggle states (Pal, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta).
    • Gujari Mahal was built by Raja Man Singh Tomar between 1486–1516 AD; a unique piece of architecture; now converted into a museum.

    Gujarat

    • Zafar Khan declared himself Sultan of Gujarat in 1407 AD with the name 'Sultan Muzaffar Shah'.
    • Muzaffar Shah defeated Hoshang Shah of Malwa and occupied Dhar, but later returned his kingdom.
    • Fateh Khan took the throne in 1458 AD with the title 'Abul Fateh Mahmood'; famous in history as Mahmud Begada.
    • Mahmud Begada's main victories: forts of Champaner and Girnar.
    • Bahadur Shah of Gujarat surrendered Diu to the Portuguese.
    • In 1535 AD Bahadur Shah made a treaty with Portuguese governor Nuno De Cunha for help against the Mughal danger.
    • In return the Portuguese were allowed to build a fortress in Diu and got a site in the harbour.
    • After the Mughal danger receded, the Shah of Gujarat realised his mistake in letting the Portuguese build the fort.

    Bahmani kingdom and its successor states

    • Bahmani kingdom arose in Muhammad-bin-Tughluq's reign from the rebellion of Amiran-e-Sadah in the Deccan.
    • Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu, 1347–1358 AD), a Sardar, took the title Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah and founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347 AD (14th century).UPPSC ×3
    • He made Gulbarga his (first) capital and named it Hasanabad.
    • He divided his empire into four provinces: Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar and Bidar; Gulbarga was the most significant.
    • He annexed southern Hindu rulers and started a new system of giving powers and Jagirs to his followers.
    • Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah abolished Jizya on the Hindus.

    • Correct pairs: Baz Bahadur – Malwa; Qutb Shah – Golconda; Sultan Muzaffar Shah – Gujarat.
    • Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur: skilful administrator, artist, poet, generous patron of arts; his people called him Jagatguru for his generous, tolerant approach.
    • He was also called 'Ablababa' or 'Friend of the poor' for helping the poor.
    • Under him the dynasty had its greatest period; he extended its frontier south up to Mysore.
    • He reverted to the Sunni sect of Islam but stayed tolerant of other religions.
    • Ibrahim Adil Shah II wrote the music collection Kitab-i-Nauras (Book of Nine Rasas) in the Deccani language.UPPSC
    • He founded a new capital/township, Nauraspur, to give shape to his idea of a musical city.
    • In the same era Firishta completed the famous history 'Tarikh-i-Firishta'.
    • Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur) = mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah; one of India's largest historic buildings and one of the world's largest domes.
    • Ahmad Nizam Shah founded the city/kingdom of Ahmadnagar.
    • Nizam Shahi dynasty ended when Shahjahan conquered and annexed Ahmadnagar (1632) and Hussain Nizam Shah-III was imprisoned for life in Gwalior Fort.
    • Shahjahan sent an army under Mahawat Khan to win Daulatabad fort; he bribed Fateh Khan with 10.5 lakhs to take over the fort.
    • Ruins of Golconda (capital of the Qutb Shahi dynasty) are scattered in Hyderabad.
    • Qutb Shahi kings ruled the region in the 16th–17th century; Aurangzeb later ended the dynasty and took Golconda; it was famous for diamonds.

    South Indian dynasties

    • Dwarasamudra was the capital of the Hoysalas (and Madurai of the Pandyas).UPPSC ×3

    • Hoysaleshvara temple at Halebidu is dedicated to Shiva; Chennakeshava temple at Belur is in Hoysala style.
    • None of Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya, Yadava set up their kingdoms in the early 8th century AD.
    • Hoysala Empire: powerful, ruled South India between the 10th and 14th centuries.
    • Gahadwal dynasty: Rajput dynasty; ruled parts of present Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in the 11th and 12th centuries.

    Chapter 27 · Medieval India

    Bhakti and Sufi Movement

    216 facts · 12 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Vaishnavism was popularised in Kamarupa, and introduced in Assam and Cooch Behar, by Shankaradeva, founder of the Ekasarana sect.×3
    2. Chronological order of saints: Namdev → Kabir → Guru Nanak → Chaitanya → Mirabai.×3
    3. Chishti order was established in India by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (first Chishti saint in India); he made Ajmer (Rajasthan) his abode.×3
    4. Naqshbandi order was against music (Sama); the most radical/orthodox Sufi order.×3
    5. Sufi saint Shah Muhammad Ghaus accepted Krishna as Wali/Auliya; most famous saint of the Shattari (Sattariyya) order.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 53 UPPSC questions

    Bhakti movement: origin and features

    • Devotional worship had a long history of almost a thousand years across the subcontinent.
    • Bhakti movement = Hindu religious movement whose main spiritual practice is loving devotion, among the Shaiva Nayanars and Vaishnava Alvars.
    • The earliest Bhakti movements (6th century) were led by the Vaishnava Alvars and the Shaiva Nayanars of the South; Alvar saints started the Bhakti movement.UPPSC
    • The early medieval Bhakti movement began in the Dravida region; spread north in the late medieval ages (13th–14th centuries onwards), when north India was under Islamic rule.
    • The movement spread with (elsewhere: was started by) the great philosopher Adi Shankaracharya in South India in the 8th century; he propounded pure monism 'Advaitavada' to remove the influence of Buddhism.
    • Bhakti movement was reborn in the 15th–16th century AD, encouraged by Kabir, Nanak, Tulsi, Sur and Mirabai.UPPSC
    • Buddha and Mirabai shared the belief that the world is full of sorrow; sorrow is the first of the Four Arya Truths of Buddhism.
    • Bhakti saints gave their verses in regional and local languages that followers could understand; this was the main reason local languages developed.
    • Bhakti saints' conduct was of a very high standard; many toured the country and met people of different views.
    • Bhakti saints helped the advance of Hindi, Kannada, Punjabi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil and other languages.

    Acharyas and their philosophies

    PhilosophyFounder
    AdvaitavadaShankaracharya
    VishishtadvaitavadaRamanujacharya
    Dvaitavada (Dvaita)MadhvacharyaUPPSC
    DvaitadvaitavadaNimbarkacharyaUPPSC
    Shuddhadvaita; PushtimargVallabhacharya
    • Ramanujacharya = earliest propagator of the Bhakti movement; his philosophy is called Vishishtadvaita in Sanskrit.UPPSC
    • Vishishtadvaita literally = "non-duality of reality as characterized by attributes".
    • Central idea of Vishishtadvaita: there is an ultimate principle, an absolute being, the source and substratum of all that exists.
    • The followers of Ramanuja are known as Vaishnava.UPPSC
    • Shuddha Advaitavada ("purely non-dual" philosophy) was propounded by Shri Vallabhacharya, founder and guru of the Vallabha sect.UPPSC
    • Vallabhacharya was the son of Telugu Brahmin Shri Lakshmana Bhatta of the Somyaji clan; said to have developed Vishnu Swami's views into Shuddha Advaita.
    • Mahaprabhu Vallabhacharya was born in the forest named Champaranya (Vikram Samvat 1535).
    • Vallabhacharya, a devotional philosopher, founded the Krishna-centred Pushti sect (Pushtimarg), a Vaishnava sect of Hinduism.UPPSC
    • Vallabhacharya was the second saint of the Krishnamargi branch.
    • Nimbarkacharya is related to the 'Sanaka' sect.
    • Nimbarka = Hindu philosopher and commentator; spread the Vaishnava doctrine of bhedabheda dvaitadvaita (duality in unity).
    • Nimbarka's dates are much disputed; generally believed to be 11th–12th century, so not a contemporary of Akbar.
    • Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (1564–1624 AD) was born after Kabir (1398–1518), so Kabir was not influenced by him.
    • Madhvacharya's Dvaitavada: the individual soul (atman), the material world and the Supreme Being (Paramatma) are distinct and fundamentally different.
    • Madhvacharya followed Saguna Bhakti, not Nirguna; held Lord Vishnu as the supreme deity and advocated his worship.
    • True statements: Vallabhacharya established Pushtimarg; Nimbarka propounded Dvaitadvaita; Ramananda advocated Rama Bhakti.
    • Order: Shankaracharya (8th century) → Ramanuja (1017–1137 AD) → Chaitanya (1486–1533 AD).
    • Nagarjuna was not a Bhakti proponent; he founded 'Nihilism' in the first/second centuries AD.
    • Tukaram, Tyagaraja and Vallabhacharya belonged to the medieval Bhakti movement.

    Shankaradeva

    • Kamarupa = ancient Indian state situated roughly in Assam.
    • Vaishnavism was popularised in Kamarupa, and introduced in Assam and Cooch Behar, by Shankaradeva, founder of the Ekasarana sect.UPPSC ×3
    • Ekasarana sect stressed devotion to one deity, Krishna (identified with Vishnu); opposed both rituals and idolatry.
    • Shankaradeva was known as the 'Chaitanya of Assam'.

    Ramananda

    • Ramananda = promoter of the Bhakti movement in northern India; great saint of North India.
    • Ramananda was born in 1299 AD at Prayag (Prayagraj) in an orthodox Kanyakubja Brahmin family; educated at Prayag and Varanasi.UPPSC
    • He believed in 'Saguna' God; spread the worship of Rama and Sita among the masses; changed the spiritual landscape of northern India.
    • Ramananda was the first Bhakti saint to use Hindi to spread his message.
    • Dictum 'Let no man ask a man's sect or caste' is Ramananda's; his pupils were from all castes, religions and sects.UPPSC

    RamanandaPrayagraj

    Kabir and other sants

    • Kabir (1398–1518 AD) was prominent among the 12 disciples of Ramananda.UPPSC
    • Kabir was born near Varanasi to a widowed Brahmin; brought up by the weaver couple Neeru and Neema.
    • Bijak = best-known compilation of Kabir's works (couplets); holy book of the Kabirpanthi sect (not of Dadu Dayal).
    • "Pothi Padh Padh Jag Mua, Pandit Bhaya Na Koye, Dhai Akhar Prem Ka, Padhe So Pandit Hoye" was written by Kabir Das.
    • Sabad, Sakhi and Ramaini are Kabir's compositions; his dialogues with Dharmadasa are in Amarmul (Anurag Sagar).UPPSC ×2
    • Saint Malukdas was born in the family of Lala Sundar Das Khatri in 1574 AD at Kada (now Kaushambi district, U.P.).UPPSC
    • Guru Ghasidas was born on 18 December 1756 AD at Giraudpuri village, Balodabazar-Bhatapara district, Chhattisgarh.
    • Guru Ghasidas's parents: Mahangudas and Amarautin.
    • Dadu Dayal lived 1544–1603 AD.
    • Tyagaraja lived 1767–1847 AD; devotee poet of the Bhakti path and a great musician of Carnatic music.

    Guru Nanak

    • Guru Nanak was born on April 15, 1469 AD in a Khatri family at Talwandi, Punjab, now called Nankana Sahib.UPPSC
    • Nankana Sahib = city and capital of Nankana Sahib district, western Punjab province (now in Pakistan).
    • Guru Nanak died in 1539 AD at Kartarpur (Derababa Nanak), now in Pakistan.
    • Guru Nanak (1469–1539 AD) founded the Sikh religion in the reign of Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517 AD).UPPSC
    • Nanak believed in monotheism; stressed worship of the one formless God (Ik Onkar), Nirakar Brahma; did not believe in anthropomorphism.
    • Guru Nanak's saying: "God does not ask about social class or birth; you must find your true home."
    • Guru Nanak started the free community kitchen Guru Ka Langar; followers ate together without caste distinction.
    • Guru Nanak was preaching when the Lodi dynasty fell and Babur took over (1526, first Battle of Panipat, Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi).

    Mirabai

    • Mirabai was the only daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore of Merta; born in a royal family in 1498 AD at village Kudaki, Merta, Rajasthan.
    • Mirabai was married to Prince Bhojraj, eldest son of Rana Sanga of Mewar.
    • Bhojraj died after a few years; then Mirabai spent her whole life worshipping Lord Krishna.
    • Mirabai was a contemporary of Tulsidas (1532–1623), Guru Nanak (1469–1539) and Chaitanya (1486–1533); not of Ramakrishna (1836–1886).
    • 'Rag-Govind' was written by Mirabai.

    Maharashtra saints: Namdev, Varkari sect, Tukaram

    • Namdev helped popularise the Bhakti movement in Maharashtra; born in 1270 AD at Narsi village (Maharashtra).
    • Namdev's teacher Visoba Khechar trained him for mystic life and showed him the omnipresent form of God.
    • Namdev belonged to the Varkari sect; had an important role in founding its ideology and glorious tradition.UPPSC ×2
    • Among Bhakti saints Namdev was much influenced by Islam; opposed idolatry, fasting, pilgrimage and harsh physical practices.UPPSC ×2
    • Namdev: "One stone is lovingly decorated (worshipped), another is walked upon; if one is a God, the other must also be a God."
    • Main seat (Peeth) of the Varkari sect = Pandharpur (Maharashtra), on the banks of River Chandrabhaga (Bhima) in Solapur district.
    • Varkari = religious movement within the Bhakti tradition of Vaishnavite Hinduism, linked with Maharashtra.
    • Varkaris worship Vitthal, presiding deity of Pandharpur, regarded as a form of Krishna.
    • Tukaram (born 1608, died 1650 AD) was a contemporary of Jahangir (1605–1627) and Shahjahan (1628–1658).

    Note from the book On Tukaram's contemporary, Shahjahan was not among the options, so Jahangir is taken as the correct answer.

    Chaitanya

    • Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534 AD in the chapter notes) was born in Nadia district of Bengal in a Brahmin family; one of the greatest Bhakti saints.
    • His father = Jagannatha Mishra; mother = Shachi Devi; childhood name = Nimai (Vishwambhar Mishra).
    • Chaitanya was a follower of Lord Krishna and preached his devotion (Vaishnava sect); also lived in Vrindavan for many days.UPPSC
    • Chaitanya Mahaprabhu founded the Madhyagauriya sect.

    Tulsidas and Hindi poets

    • Goswami Tulsidas was a contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir; Humayun, Akbar and Jahangir were emperors in his lifetime.UPPSC
    • Tulsidas had no relation with the court; spent most of his time in Banaras (Varanasi); mentioned in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari.
    • Ramcharitmanas was composed by Goswami Tulsidas (1532–1623 AD) in Awadhi.
    • Tulsidas wrote Gitavali, Kavitavali and Vinay Patrika; Ramcharitmanas and Vinay Patrika are his best works; 'Sahitya Ratna' is not his.
    • Sahitya Lahari was composed by Surdas, not Tulsidas.
    • Tulsidas was born at Rajapur village in Chitrakoot district (not Banda); his wife's name was Ratnawali (not Geetawali).UPPSC
    • U.P. Government will develop Rajapur village in Chitrakoot district, the birthplace of Tulsidas.
    • Rasik Priya is a famous work of Acharya Keshavdas (not Raskhan); his other famous works: Ramchandrika and Kavi Priya.UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Dhruvadas – Bhagat Namawali; Nabhadas – Bhaktamal; Usman – Chitrawali.
    • Premvatika was composed by Raskhan in Braj; it depicts the life of Krishna and the ideal of love/devotion.
    • Raskhan = poet and follower of Lord Krishna; real name Sayyid Ibrahim; 'Sujan Raskhan' is his other famous text; his language is pure Braj.
    • Rahim and Raskhan were poets of Hindi literature in the medieval Bhakti period, not Sufis.
    • Barahmasa was written by Malik Muhammad Jayasi; it is a part of Padmavat.
    • Jayasi's works: Padmavat (important place in Hindi literature), Barahmasa, Akharawat, Akhiri Kalam.
    AuthorWork
    Mulla DaudChandayanUPPSC
    Damodar KaviPadmavati Katha
    SomnathRag Vibodh
    Amir KhusrauAshiqa
    • Amir Khusrau (full name Abul Hasan Yaminuddin Khusrau), great poet and scholar, was not related to the Bhakti movement.
    • Khusrau's main texts: Qiran-us-Sadain, Miftah-ul-Futuh, Nuh Sipihr, Ashiqa, Tughluq Nama, Khazain-ul-Futuh.
    • Amir Hasan-i-Dehlavi is called the 'Sadi of India' (Sadi-i-Hind) for his great ghazals.UPPSC

    Sufism: basics and terms

    • In medieval India the emergence of Sufis helped promote (communal) harmony in society.
    • Sufi practices: meditation, remembrance, devotional practices like 'Sama', sometimes breath-focused remembrance (control of breath), severe ascetic exercises in a lonely place.
    • Sufis used holy songs and music to spread unity and harmony and to arouse spiritual ecstasy in their audience.
    • Sufism was born in a foreign land within early Islamic asceticism; later mainly influenced by Indian Vedanta philosophy.
    • Later some strands of Sufism developed theosophical systems, adopting traditions such as Neoplatonism.
    • Four philosophies some believe influenced Sufism: Advaitavada and Vishishta Dvaitavada of Aryans; New Aflatuni theory; liberal thinking; deep-rooted knowledge of Islam.
    • Khanqah = residence of Sufi saints; Sama = Sufi ceremony (music assembly); Shaikh = person authorised to teach and guide in Sufism.
    • Ulema = scholars of the religious laws of Islam; not related to Sufism.UPPSC
    • In the medieval period many Sanskrit works on music were translated into Persian, owing to the interest of rulers.UPPSC
    • Mahmud of Ghazni took many books to Ghazni; Firuz Tughluq and Sikandar Lodi had Sanskrit books translated into Persian; later Mughal emperors did so too.
    • Early Chishtis were fond of 'sama'; they supported music as a medium to reach God (true, but not the reason for the translations).
    • In India Hath Yog was practised by Nathpanthis; later Sufis also adopted Hath Yog practices.UPPSC
    • Nathpanth founder Guru Matsyendranath and his disciple started the practice of Hath Yog.

    Chishti order

    • Chishti order was founded at Chishti Sharif, Afghanistan, by Abu Ishaq Shami Chishti and his disciple Khwaja Abu Ahmad Abdal.UPPSC
    • Khwaja Abu Ishaq Shami of Syria migrated to Chist (Chishti Sharif, Afghanistan), hence called Chishti; 9th-generation descendant of Hazrat Ali.
    • Chishti order's name is from Chist in Afghanistan, not from a village in Ajmer; Muinuddin Chishti was its sponsor and most prominent figure in India.
    • Chishti order was established in India by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (first Chishti saint in India); he made Ajmer (Rajasthan) his abode.UPPSC ×3
    • Muinuddin Chishti came to India with Muhammad Ghori's army in 1192 AD (12th century); died in 1236 AD.
    • Muinuddin Chishti was born in Sijistan (Afghanistan and Iran) in 1138–39 AD; later moved with his parents to Khurasan province.
    • Muinuddin Chishti became a disciple of Khwaja Usman Chishti Haruni at Nishapur.UPPSC ×2
    • Muinuddin Chishti held that devotional music was one way to come closer to God.
    • Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was Muinuddin Chishti's main disciple; a Chishti saint from Delhi.
    • Raja Sahu, grandson of Shivaji, was the first Maratha chieftain to offer nazr (gift) at the Dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti, Ajmer.
    • Chishti order = a Sunni Sufi order within the mystic Sufi tradition of Islam.
    • Shaikh Abdul Jilani did not belong to the Chishti order; he founded the Qadiri order.
    • Baba Farid (Shaikh Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar) = Chishti saint; Chishti order gained more popularity in India by his efforts.
    • Some of Baba Farid's compositions were included by Guru Arjan in the Adi Granth (Guru Granth Sahib).UPPSC
    • Baba Farid was the son-in-law of Balban; born in Kothewal village, Multan district (Pakistan); Hansi and Ajodhan were his centres.
    • Baba Farid was the spiritual teacher of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, his most reputed disciple.UPPSC ×2
    • Baba Farid's two main disciples: Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya and Hazrat Alauddin Sabir Kaliyari.
    • Nizamuddin Auliya was born in Badayun, UP; first lived with Baba Farid at Ajodhan (Pakistan), later shifted to Delhi.
    • Nizamuddin Auliya's Dargah is in Delhi (not Multan); it is one of the most revered places in the Sufi order; he died in 1325 AD and was buried at Ghiyaspur, Delhi.UPPSC ×2
    • Correct pairs: Shaikh Moinuddin Chishti – Ajmer; Shaikh Burhanuddin Gharib – Daulatabad; Shaikh Mohammad Hussaini – Gulbarga.
    • Nizamuddin Auliya saw the reign of more than seven sultans but never went to anyone's court.
    • Sultan Jalaluddin tried to meet him through Amir Khusrau; on hearing the Sultan was coming, he moved to Ajodhan.
    • He refused to meet Alauddin Khalji: "There are two doors in my house; if the Sultan comes by one, I will go out by the other."
    • Nizamuddin Auliya was known as Mehboob-i-Ilahi (Favourite of God) and Sultan-ul-Mashaikh (King of Saints).UPPSC
    • Nizamuddin Auliya, like Baba Farid, gave peace to human hearts through his preaching.
    • He was called Mehboob-i-Ilahi for his generous, tolerant attitude; he adopted Yoga and was called 'Yogasiddha'.
    • Nizamuddin Auliya and Muinuddin Chishti were Sufi saints of the Chishti order.UPPSC
    • Shaikh Nasiruddin Mahmud, a chief disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, had the title Chirag-i-Dehlavi (Chirag-i-Delhi).UPPSC
    • Nasiruddin preached the teachings of his Pir but could not be as generous as him.
    • Shaikh Salim Chishti = notable among the last Chishti Sufis; son of Shaikh Bahauddin.
    • He lived in Arabia for several years and got the title Shaikh-ul-Hind.UPPSC ×2
    • On return he lived at Sikri, about 37 km from Agra, later developed by Akbar as Fatehpur Sikri.
    • Jahangir is said to have been born with the blessings of Shaikh Salim Chishti; Akbar (not Aurangzeb) was his contemporary.

    Other Sufi orders

    SufiOrder
    Khwaja Muinuddin ChishtiChishtiyaUPPSC
    Shaikh Ahmad SirhindiNaqshbandiya
    Dara ShukohQadiriya
    Shaikh ShahabuddinSuhrawardiya
    • Chishti influence: Delhi, Rajasthan and nearby areas (Delhi and Doab); Suhrawardi influence: Sindh and Punjab.
    • 'Auliya' is not an order but a title given to Nizamuddin, the famous saint of Delhi; his dominion was in Delhi (not Madhya Pradesh).
    • Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria started the Suhrawardi order in India.
    • Shaikh Sadr-ud-din Arif, Shaikh Rakh-ud-din Abul Fateh and Shaikh Jalaluddin Surkh were linked with the Suhrawardi sect.
    • Suhrawardi order entered India about the same time as the Chishtis; its activities stayed largely in Punjab, Multan and Sindh.
    • Firdausi (Firdausia) Silsila was established in Bihar; its most prominent Sufi and key propagator in Bihar = Sheikh Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri.
    • Firdausi order traces its origin to Najmuddin Kubra; treated as a collateral line of the Suhrawardiya; later close to the Chishtis in India (called a part of the Chishti order).
    • Qadiri order was founded by Shaikh Muhiuddin Abdul Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, counted among the great saints of Islam.
    • Abdul Qadir Jilani's titles: Mehboob-i-Sumani (God's lover), Piran-i-Pir (Chief of Pirs), Pir-i-Dastagir (Helpful Saint).
    • Qadiri order was preached in India in the 15th century by Shah Niamatullah (Deccan and Kashmir) and Makhdum Muhammad Jilani (Punjab), who first introduced it in India.
    • Makhdum Jilani made Uchha his education centre.
    • Naqshbandi order was founded by Khwaja Bahauddin Naqshband in the 14th century.
    • Khwaja Khawand Mahmud, a prominent Naqshbandi saint, came to India and made Kashmir his centre.
    • Naqshbandi order was mainly spread by Khwaja Baqi Billah (1563–1603), who came from Kabul on his master's orders.
    • Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, called 'Mujaddid' / Mujaddid Alif Sani (reformer of Islam), was Baqi Billah's main disciple; contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir (not Ibrahim Lodi).
    • Sirhindi propounded Wahdat-ul-Shuhud (positivist philosophy) over the mystic philosophy Wahdat-ul-Wajud.
    • Naqshbandi order was against music (Sama); the most radical/orthodox Sufi order.UPPSC ×3
    • The Sirhindi/Mujaddadi Naqshbandi branch opposed Sama, but the Ferozabadi (Delhi) branch practised Sama.
    • Naqshbandis opposed Akbar's liberal policies; Aurangzeb was influenced by this order.
    • Naqshbandi order was made popular in India by Babur; its essence = rigid adherence to Shariat and love for the Prophet.

    Note from the book Most orthodox Sufi order: answer given is Naqshbandi, but Jharkhand Public Service Commission's own answer was Suhrawardi.

    • Sufi saint Shah Muhammad Ghaus accepted Krishna as Wali/Auliya; most famous saint of the Shattari (Sattariyya) order.UPPSC ×3
    • Muhammad Ghaus had close relations with Mughal emperor Humayun and with Tansen.
    • His famous work 'Jawahir-i-Khamsa' expresses his spiritual quest and mystical practices.
    • He translated 'Amritkund' of Hatha Yoga into Persian as 'Bahar-al-Hayat'; it mentions Hath Yog practices.
    • Shattari saints tried to reconcile Muslims and Hindus by showing equality in religious ideas and practices.
    • Dewa Sharif (Barabanki, U.P.) = mazar of Sufi saint Haji Waris Ali Shah; a fair is held at the tomb every year.UPPSC

    Christianity and Islam: general facts

    • Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem (south of Jerusalem).
    • Easter = Christian festival of the resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day after his crucifixion.
    • Good Friday is observed in remembrance of the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ; by the Bible he was crucified on a Friday.UPPSC
    • Saint Francis of Assisi (1181 or 82–1226 AD) = Christian saint famous for his love of birds and animals.
    • Vatican City = sovereign state in Europe; area about 44 hectares; world's smallest independent country by both population and area.
    • Vatican City is governed by the Bishop of Rome (the Pope); also known as the capital of the Roman Catholic Church.
    • Medina = city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia; Islam's second holiest city after Mecca.
