    Chapter 28 · Medieval India

    Mughal Dynasty:Babur

    56 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. First Battle of Panipat: 21 April 1526 AD, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi; Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed.×3
    2. Battle of Khanwa: March 16, 1527 AD; Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar and took the title 'Ghazi'.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 15 UPPSC questions

    Origin and early life

    • Mughal dynasty was of Turkic-Mongol origin; Babur and the Mughal rulers belonged to the Chagatai branch of Turks.UPPSC
    • The name Chagatai came from the second son of Genghis Khan, ruler of central Asia and Turkistan.
    • Babur descended from the Turk-Mongol conqueror Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's side.
    • Full name: Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur; founder of the Mughal empire in India.
    • Babur was born on February 14, 1483 AD at Ferghana to Umar Shaikh Mirza and Qutlugh Nigar Khanum; he was the eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza.
    • After his father's death he took the throne of Ferghana (now in Uzbekistan) in June 1494 AD, aged 11 years and four months.
    • Babur's accession began the Timurid dynasty in the region; he set up the Mughal dynasty in India after Panipat, 1526.
    • Babur's life teaches success through patience and resolution; his father died in his childhood, yet he founded the Mughal Empire in India.
    • Babur captured Samarkand in 1501 AD; it lasted only eight months.
    • Shaybani Khan invaded Ferghana in 1501 AD, defeated Babur at the battle of Sar-e-Pul and occupied Samarqand.UPPSC
    • Shaybani Khan used the Uzbek 'Tulughuma' technique to defeat Babur at Sar-e-Pul.
    • Babur fled; for three years wandered the hills of Afghanistan and plains of Khurasan (central Asia).
    • Babur made several attempts to retake Samarkand but was beaten each time by Shaybani Khan.
    • After losing Samarkand and Ferghana, Babur moved to Kabul; after winning Kabul in 1504 he gave up the ancestral title 'Mirza' and took the title 'Padshah'.UPPSC

    Invitation to India

    • Alam Khan = uncle of Ibrahim Lodi; invited Babur to invade India, claiming his right to the Delhi throne.
    • In 1524 AD, during Babur's 4th campaign, there was a bitter feud between Sultan Ibrahim Lodi and Daulat Khan, governor of Punjab.
    • Ibrahim Lodi ordered Daulat Khan to his capital; Daulat Khan disobeyed and sent his son Dilawar Khan to Babur, asking help to dethrone Ibrahim and enthrone Alam Khan.UPPSC
    • Babur had already got the invitation of Rana Sanga, king of Mewar; he felt sure the chance to conquer India had come.

    First Battle of Panipat

    • First Battle of Panipat: 21 April 1526 AD, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi; Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed.UPPSC ×3
    • Ibrahim Lodi became Sultan of Delhi in 1517 AD after his father's death.
    • Ibrahim Lodi's army lost though larger in number; the whole area up to Delhi and Agra came under Babur.
    • Babur declared himself ruler on April 27, 1526 AD and founded the Mughal empire in India.
    • Babur used the Ottoman system of war at the first Battle of Panipat (1526).
    • Main reasons of victory: artillery (cannons, guns) led by Ali Quli, and the Tulughma and Araba tactics; gunners and horsemen also helped.
    • Babur's tactics in North India included gunpowder firearms and field artillery.
    • The main reason for Babur's victory at Panipat = his skilled warfare; his army was smaller than Ibrahim's.
    • Skilled commandants were the primary reason for Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi.UPPSC
    • Babur on Ibrahim: "an inexperienced young man careless in his movements, who marched without order, halted or retired without method and engaged without foresight."
    • Artillery (cannons) was used for the first time in India in the first Battle of Panipat.UPPSC
    • Babur himself first mentioned using artillery and guns in the Battle of Bajaur (Pakistan), 1519 AD.
    • Ustad Ali Quli led the artillery; Mustafa commanded the battalion of gunners.
    • Babur's generosity earned him the title 'Qalandar'.
    • Gunpowder entered India before Babur (used to demolish fort walls); credit for using it in cannons and guns goes to Babur.
    • Arch and dome were already introduced in the Sultanate period; Babur did not influence India's architecture.
    • In 'Babur Nama' Babur described local architecture as lacking shape and balance.
    • Babur ordered a garden built in Agra; also built a brick mosque in Panipat.
    • Sher Shah, who defeated Babur's son Humayun, built the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque.

    Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra

    • Babur declared 'Jehad' in the Battle of Khanwa.UPPSC
    • Battle of Khanwa: March 16, 1527 AD; Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar and took the title 'Ghazi'.UPPSC ×2
    • In 1528 AD Babur took Chanderi's fort; Medini Rai was killed in the war.
    • Battle of Ghaghra, 1529 AD: Babur beat Mahmud Lodi (Afghan rulers); the last battle Babur fought.
    • Babur's battles in order: First Panipat (1526) → Khanwa (1527) → Chanderi (1528, not 1530) → Ghaghra (1529).UPPSC

    Empire and administration

    • Babur's empire included Kabul, Punjab and the area of modern Uttar Pradesh; Rajasthan was not included, being under various Rajput rulers.
    • He governed by allotting fiefs/jagirs and paraganas, appointing nobles/princes to territorial charges.
    • Badakhshan (outside India) was given to Humayun; Kabul, Qandahar and Multan to Kamran.
    • Mir Yusuf Ali was made governor of Lahore; Bheera, Lahore, Dipalpur, Sialkot, Sirhind and Hisar-Firoza were given to different officers.
    • Babur brought innovative governance in the region from Ballia to Hisar, and Bayana and Gwalior; the empire stretched from Bihar up to Badakhshan.

    Babur's writings

    • Babur wrote his autobiography Tuzuk-i-Babri (Babur Nama) in Chagatai Turkish; Turki was not the official language of the Mughal court, Persian was.UPPSC
    • Babur Nama has an important place among autobiographies of the world.
    • In Babur Nama Babur mentioned two Hindu states: Vijayanagara and Mewar (Chittor).UPPSC
    • Babur wrote that when he was at Kabul, Rana Sanga had agreed: if the king reached Delhi from that side, Rana Sanga would invade Agra from his side.
    • Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan translated Babur Nama into Persian by Akbar's order.
    • Babur's verses are collected in the Turkish 'Diwan' (Diwan-i-Babur).
    • Babur wrote 'Mubaiyan', a book of Muslim law, in a new verse style, Masnavi.
    • Babur's 'Risal-i-Usaj' (Khat-i-Baburi) is considered the most innovative style.
    • Babri Masjid in Ayodhya was built by Mir Baqi, Babur's commandant (army chief).UPPSC
    ← Bhakti and Sufi MovementHumayun and Sher Shah →

    Chapter 29 · Medieval India

    Humayun and Sher Shah

    68 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Sher Shah introduced 'Patta' and 'Qabuliyat' to help peasants.×3
    2. Sher Shah died on 22 May 1545 AD at Kalinjar, during the siege of the Rajput fort; it was his last campaign.×2
    3. Sher Shah's tomb is at Sasaram (Rohtas district, Bihar); he was buried there.×2
    4. Purana Qila of Delhi, one of Delhi's oldest forts, was built in its present form by Sher Shah Suri (built by Sher Shah and Humayun).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 16 UPPSC questions

    Humayun: family and early campaigns

    • Humayun = eldest son of Babur; born in Kabul in 1508 AD; his mother Maham Begum was related to the Shia sect.
    • Kamran, Askari and Hindal were sons of Babur and half-brothers of Humayun; Usman was not his brother.UPPSC
    • Gulrukh Begum = mother of Kamran and Askari; Dildar Begam = mother of Hindal.
    • After Babur's death Humayun took the Mughal throne; he wanted firm control over northern India by subduing the Rajput states.
    • In the 1530s Humayun sent his brother Kamran Mirza against Rao Jaitsi (Rao Jait Singh), independent ruler of Bikaner.
    • By Beethu Souza's text Rao-Jaitsi-Ro-Chhanda, Rao Jaitsi defeated Kamran in battle.
    • Humayun invaded Kalinjar in 1531 AD and annexed Raisina Fort in 1535 AD.
    • Humayun first invaded Chunar Fort in 1532; besieged it for four months, then Sher Khan accepted his supremacy.
    • Sher Khan offered Humayun to surrender Bihar and pay 10 lakh dinars yearly tribute if allowed to keep Bengal; Humayun declined.
    • After the fall of the Delhi Sultanate, Humayun was the first ruler to issue a gold coin; after him Sher Shah also issued one.

    Note from the book First gold coin after the Sultanate: UKPSC accepted Akbar as the answer, which is wrong; Humayun is correct.

    Humayun's battles

    1. 1532Humayun's four major battles in order: Devara (Daurah) 1532 → Chausa 1539 → Kannauj 1540 → Sirhind 1555; Battle of Samugarh came later, in 1658.UPPSC
    2. 1532Daurah (Devara), 1532 AD: Humayun defeated Afghan rebels (Mahmud Lodi) on the banks of the Gomti.
    3. 1539Battle of Chausa, 26 June 1539 AD: Sher Shah defeated Humayun; a water fetcher named Nizam saved Humayun's life.
    4. 1540Battle of Kannauj, 17 May 1540 AD: Sher Shah again defeated Humayun; Humayun then fled from place to place.UPPSC
    5. 1555Humayun occupied Delhi after the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June 1555 AD.
    6. 1565Haji Begum built the tomb of her husband Humayun at Delhi (near Deen Panah) in 1565–1572 AD.
    7. 1658Battle of Samugarh (1658) was fought between Dara Shikoh and his two younger brothers Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh.
    • Humayun's four major battles in order: Devara (Daurah) 1532 → Chausa 1539 → Kannauj 1540 → Sirhind 1555; Battle of Samugarh came later, in 1658.UPPSC
    • Daurah (Devara), 1532 AD: Humayun defeated Afghan rebels (Mahmud Lodi) on the banks of the Gomti.
    • Battle of Chausa, 26 June 1539 AD: Sher Shah defeated Humayun; a water fetcher named Nizam saved Humayun's life.
    • The Chausa victory raised the prestige and power of Sher Shah (Sher Khan).
    • Battle of Kannauj, 17 May 1540 AD: Sher Shah again defeated Humayun; Humayun then fled from place to place.UPPSC
    • It is also called the Battle of Bilgram; Bilgram is an ancient town, now a municipal board in Hardoi district, U.P.
    • Humayun occupied Delhi after the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June 1555 AD.
    • Battle of Samugarh (1658) was fought between Dara Shikoh and his two younger brothers Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh.
    • Haji Begum built the tomb of her husband Humayun at Delhi (near Deen Panah) in 1565–1572 AD.
    • Humayun's Tomb = first double-dome mausoleum of Mughal architecture; a garden surrounds it.
    • Its architects: Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, a Persian, and his son Sayyid Muhammad.

    Sher Shah: rise

    • Sher Shah was the son of an Afghan Jagirdar of Sasaram, Bihar; original name Farid Khan; given the title 'Sher' after he killed a tiger.
    • Farid left home in 1494 AD and was educated at Jaunpur, then famous as 'Siraj-i-Hind' and a centre of education; Sher Shah was highly educated.UPPSC
    • Sher Khan took the title 'Hazrat-e-Ala' after defeating Nusrat Shah, ruler of Bengal.
    • After Chausa (June 26, 1539) he took the royal title 'Sher Shah', had the Khutba read and coins struck in his name.
    • Sher Shah = founder of the Sur Empire.

    Sher Shah: reforms

    • Sher Shah made revenue, administrative, military and currency reforms.
    • Sher Shah is considered the antecedent of Akbar as an administrative imperialist.
    • Sher Shah = brave warrior and architect of a brilliant administrative system; his qualities as a ruler were more remarkable than his battlefield victories.UPPSC
    • His brief reign of five years saw wise and salutary changes in every branch of administration.
    • Revenue: he held that satisfying the peasants was essential for the empire's stability.
    • His land revenue was based on Ryotwari, settled directly with cultivators; he used an improved, systematic method of measuring land and assessing revenue.
    • Sher Shah introduced 'Patta' and 'Qabuliyat' to help peasants.UPPSC ×3
    • Patta was given to the peasant by the central authority and stated the government's share; the peasant accepted it through Qabuliyat.
    • Administration: he learnt it managing his father's manor; knew the Mughals' military composition, administration and finance.
    • He headed the central government; administration was fully centralised before the victory over Bengal.
    • He divided the whole kingdom into 47 Sarkars (districts), as per Dr. Kanungo.
    • Bengal got a different system: divided into 19 Sarkars (as per Satish Chandra), each under a military official, the Shiqdar.
    • A non-military official 'Amir-i-Bangala' was appointed to assist, to end the threat of revolt; Qazi Fajilat held this post.
    • Military: inspired by Alauddin Khalji's reforms; recruited and paid soldiers directly.
    • Each soldier's chehra (face) was recorded and his horse branded with the imperial sign, to stop fraud.
    • Sher Shah built Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road), one of Asia's oldest and longest roads, from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Kabul (Afghanistan).

    Sher Shah: currency

    • Sher Shah's reign was an era of experiment in coin history; V.A. Smith: "It is the basis of the existing British currency".
    • His reformed currency circulated in the Mughal period and became the basis of British currency.
    • Sher Shah introduced pure gold, silver and copper coins and abolished mixed-metal (beaten) coins; he issued the pure silver 'Rupiya'.
    • Silver rupee weighed 178 grains, of which 173 grains were pure silver.
    • Copper 'Daam' weighed 308 grains (20 gm); one explanation prints 380 grains.
    • Exchange rate of Rupiya to Daam = 1:64.UPPSC
    • Coins carried Sher Shah's name, title and mint place in the Arabic language and Devanagari script.

    Sher Shah: Marwar, death and successors

    • Battle of Sammel: Maldeo Rathore lost to Sher Shah; his generals Jaita and Kumpa of Marwar fought hard with a few thousand men.UPPSC
    • Their valour caused heavy losses to Sher Shah's larger army.
    • Impressed by Rajput chivalry at Marwar, Sher Shah said: "I would have lost the empire just for a handful of millet" (bajra).UPPSC
    • Sher Shah died on 22 May 1545 AD at Kalinjar, during the siege of the Rajput fort; it was his last campaign.UPPSC ×2
    • Kirat Singh was king of Kalinjar then.
    • When all tactics failed he ordered the fort walls blown up with gunpowder and was seriously wounded by the explosion.
    • Islam Shah Suri, second son of Sher Shah, was his successor and the second ruler of the Sur Dynasty.
    • Islam Shah ruled all North India for 8 years; divided his troops into units of 200, 250 and 500; Sikandar Shah continued this practice.

    Sher Shah: buildings

    • Sher Shah's tomb is at Sasaram (Rohtas district, Bihar); he was buried there.UPPSC ×2
    • The tomb is an imposing brick structure partly veneered with stone, standing in the middle of a tank; one of the noblest specimens of Afghan architecture in India.
    • Sasaram tomb has an octagonal plan; begun in Sher Shah's reign (1540–45), completed August 16, 1545 in the reign of his son Islam Shah.
    • Sher Shah built the Sasaram tomb and the Qila-e-Kuhna Mosque (not the Tomb at Sikandra or Jama Masjid).
    • Akbar's tomb at Sikandra (Agra, U.P.) was begun in Akbar's reign and completed in 1612 AD under Jahangir.
    • Jama Masjid in Delhi was built under the patronage of Shah Jahan.
    • Sher Shah's short reign = a revolutionary era in Indian architecture.
    • Qila-i-Kuhna mosque, inside Purana Qila, Delhi, was built by Sher Shah in 1541 AD; famous for elegant architecture.UPPSC
    • Purana Qila of Delhi, one of Delhi's oldest forts, was built in its present form by Sher Shah Suri (built by Sher Shah and Humayun).UPPSC ×2
    • Purana Qila = inner citadel of Din-panah founded by Humayun (1533); Sher Shah renamed it Shergarh and added structures.
    • Sher Shah built the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and Sher Mandal in Purana Qila.

    Chapter 30 · Medieval India

    Akbar

    146 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Mahabharata was translated into Persian as Razmnama (book of wars) on Akbar's order, by Badauni, Naqib Khan and Faizi.×5
    2. Akbar's first matrimonial alliance with Rajputs was with the Kachhwaha house (of Amber/Amer).×2
    3. Hakim Khan Sur was the commander (commander-in-chief besides Maharana Pratap) of Rana Pratap's army at Haldighati.×2
    4. Order of events: abolition of Jizya (1564) → Ibadat Khana (1575) → Mahzar (1579) → Din-i-Ilahi (1582).×2
    5. Muzaffar Khan Turbati was made Diwan (Todar Mal as assistant) early in Akbar's reign; the Diwan's department grew from his appointment.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 39 UPPSC questions

    Birth, coronation and Bairam Khan

    • Akbar was born on 15 October 1542 AD at Amarkot, in the palace of Raja Veersaal.
    • Humayun died in a fatal accident, falling from the stairs of the Dinpanah library.
    • Akbar was crowned at Kalanaur (now in Gurdaspur district, Punjab) on 14 February 1556 AD, on news of Humayun's death; he was under 14 years old.
    • Shah Abdul Mali refused to join Akbar's coronation; Humayun used to call him 'Farjand' (son).
    • Bairam Khan was Akbar's guardian and regent; Akbar appointed him Wazir and gave him the title 'Khan-i-Khanan'.UPPSC
    • Akbar personally killed Adham Khan, son of Maham Anga, in 1562 AD, as he had murdered Akbar's prime minister Atgah Khan.UPPSC

    Rajput policy and conquests

    1. 1561Order: Mughal invasion of Malwa (1561) → Akbar marries princess of Amber (1562) → Karrani's conquest of Orissa (1568) → Battle of Tukaroi (1575).UPPSC
    2. 1562In 1562 Akbar went on pilgrimage to the Dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; his route lay through Amber.
    3. 1562Akbar married her in 1562 on his return from Ajmer; his first marriage with a Rajput girl.
    4. 1564Akbar sent about 50,000 cavalry with heavy artillery against Gondwana (1564 AD); Durgavati fought bravely but lost the battle between Garh and Mandla (modern Mandla district, M.P.).
    5. 1565Rao Chandrasena of Marwar fought the Mughal army at Bhadrajun (1565 AD in the chapter notes; 1571 AD in an answer explanation); surrounded, he fled to Siwana.
    6. 1569Salim (later Jahangir), heir to the throne, was born of this marriage on August 30, 1569 AD at Fatehpur Sikri.
    7. 1572Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1572–73 AD.
    8. 1572Daud Khan succeeded his father Sulaiman Karrani in 1572 AD; declared himself independent and invaded the Mughal fort of Patna.
    9. 1574Akbar ordered Munim Khan to crush the revolt; Munim Khan defeated Daud and annexed Bihar in 1574 AD; Daud fled to Bengal.
    10. 1576On 12 July 1576 Todarmal defeated Daud; thus Akbar merged Bengal and Bihar in his empire in 1576 AD.
    11. 1579Chandrasena annexed Sojat in 1579 AD; Akbar besieged him again, he fled to the hills and died in January 1581 AD.
    12. 1605Map of Akbar's empire at his death (1605): Gondwana = independent state; Lahore = part of the empire.
    • Akbar's first matrimonial alliance with Rajputs was with the Kachhwaha house (of Amber/Amer).UPPSC ×2
    • In 1562 Akbar went on pilgrimage to the Dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; his route lay through Amber.
    • Its ruler Raja Bihari Mal (Bharmal), to safeguard his position, submitted to Akbar at Sanganer and offered his daughter Princess Harkhabai (Jodha) in marriage.
    • Akbar married her in 1562 on his return from Ajmer; his first marriage with a Rajput girl.
    • Raja Bharmal = first Rajput king to accept Akbar's supremacy of his own accord.
    • Salim (later Jahangir), heir to the throne, was born of this marriage on August 30, 1569 AD at Fatehpur Sikri.
    • Order: Mughal invasion of Malwa (1561) → Akbar marries princess of Amber (1562) → Karrani's conquest of Orissa (1568) → Battle of Tukaroi (1575).UPPSC
    • Durgavati was custodian of the Hindu kingdom of Gondwana for her minor son Vir Narayan.
    • Akbar sent about 50,000 cavalry with heavy artillery against Gondwana (1564 AD); Durgavati fought bravely but lost the battle between Garh and Mandla (modern Mandla district, M.P.).
    • Surrounded by the enemy, Durgavati committed suicide.
    • Rao Chandrasena of Marwar fought the Mughal army at Bhadrajun (1565 AD in the chapter notes; 1571 AD in an answer explanation); surrounded, he fled to Siwana.
    • Chandrasena annexed Sojat in 1579 AD; Akbar besieged him again, he fled to the hills and died in January 1581 AD.
    • Like Maharana Pratap, Rao Chandrasena kept up his struggle for independence against the Mughals and did not surrender.
    • Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1572–73 AD.
    • Daud Khan succeeded his father Sulaiman Karrani in 1572 AD; declared himself independent and invaded the Mughal fort of Patna.
    • Akbar ordered Munim Khan to crush the revolt; Munim Khan defeated Daud and annexed Bihar in 1574 AD; Daud fled to Bengal.
    • On 12 July 1576 Todarmal defeated Daud; thus Akbar merged Bengal and Bihar in his empire in 1576 AD.
    • Map of Akbar's empire at his death (1605): Gondwana = independent state; Lahore = part of the empire.
    • Akbar's empire stretched from Bengal to Afghanistan in the north and from Kashmir to the Godavari in the south.

    Battle of Haldighati and Mewar

    • Akbar's main aim in the Battle of Haldighati was to subdue Rana Pratap and make him accept Mughal suzerainty.
    • In April 1576 AD Akbar deputed Man Singh with about 5000 soldiers against Maharana Pratap.
    • Man Singh went via Mandalgarh to Gogundagarh, fourteen miles from Haldighati; Rana Pratap came down from the hills to face him.
    • Battle of Haldighati was fought in June 1576 AD; Rana was defeated and took refuge in the Aravalli Hills.UPPSC
    • Hakim Khan Sur was the commander (commander-in-chief besides Maharana Pratap) of Rana Pratap's army at Haldighati.UPPSC ×2
    • Hakim Khan Sur = Pathan adventurer of the Sur Dynasty, a descendant of Sher Shah Suri; led about 5,000 Afghans in the battle.
    • Mewar did not accept Akbar's supremacy willingly; Rana Pratap kept up his struggle for a long time.UPPSC
    • After Rana Pratap's death his son Rana Amar Singh signed a treaty with Jahangir in 1615 AD.

    Salim's revolt and Abul Fazl's death

    • When Prince Salim began acting as an independent king at Allahabad (Prayagraj) and rebelled, Akbar called his friend Abul Fazl from the Deccan in 1602 AD.
    • Vir Singh Bundela killed Abul Fazl on his way back from the Deccan, in a plot by Prince Salim.

    Religious policy

    • Akbar patronised the Chishti sect, showing his faith in Sufism; he sought the company of saints and talked with zeal and humility.
    • He often visited the Mausoleum of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and the shrine of the contemporary Sufi Shaikh Salim Chishti at Sikri.UPPSC
    • Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax in 1563 AD and Jizya in 1564 AD under his liberal religious policy.
    • Akbar was the first Muslim ruler to see he could not consolidate Mughal rule without the confidence and active support of the Hindu majority.
    • He was the first medieval monarch to raise religious tolerance to the pinnacle of secularism; he tried to separate religion from politics.
    • Religion had been a divisive force in Indian society since the advent of Islam, which most people had refused to embrace.
    • His measures for religious harmony: freedom of worship, marriage alliances with Hindus, high civil and military posts to Hindus, translation of Hindu scriptures, Ibadat Khana, infallibility decree, freedom to build temples, land grants, regard for Hindu sentiments, reforms in Hindu society.
    • Akbar had not forsaken Islam; administrative unity, unity in law, cultural unity and religious policy make him a nationalist.
    • Akbar promulgated Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all, universal harmony) in place of the Islamic concept; it reflects political generosity, religious tolerance and a liberal cultural attitude.UPPSC
    • Through Sulh-i-Kul he tried to build Hindu and Muslim communities into national unity.
    • Akbar's reign is known for annexation of regions, provincial administrative system and judicial administration, not religious intolerance; he is world famous for religious liberalism.
    • Akbar built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 AD for philosophical and theological discussions with Ulemas, Sayyids and Shaikhs; a hall where he held discussions with scholars.
    • He opened the Ibadat Khana to all schools of religion in 1578 AD.
    • These discussions led to the Mahzarnama in 1579 AD, prepared by Shaikh Mubarak, father of Abul Fazl.
    • Mahzarnama ended the predominance of the bigoted orthodox and allowed the generous spirit Akbar wished to encourage.
    • Smith and Wolseley Haig called the Mahzarnama an infallibility decree; after it Akbar was titled Sultan-i-Adil or Imam-i-Adil.
    • In 1580 AD an Ulema, Mulla Muhammad Yazdi of Jaunpur, issued a 'Fatwa' against Akbar and asked all Muslims to rebel.UPPSC
    • Akbar launched Tauhid-i-Ilahi / Din-i-Ilahi in 1582 AD, for reconciliation between all religious schools.
    • Din-i-Ilahi = syncretic creed meant to merge the best elements of all religions; its 'prophet' was Abul Fazl.
    • Among Hindus only Birbal accepted Din-i-Ilahi; Raja Bhagawan Das and Man Singh bluntly refused.
    • Din-i-Ilahi was not a religion but an ideology based on Sufi pantheism.UPPSC
    • Jahangir's contemporary Mohsin Fani first described Din-i-Ilahi as an independent religion, in 'Dabistan-i-Mazahib'.
    • Smith: "Din-i-Ilahi is a monument of Akbar's foolishness, not of his wisdom".
    • Order of events: abolition of Jizya (1564) → Ibadat Khana (1575) → Mahzar (1579) → Din-i-Ilahi (1582).UPPSC ×2
    • Goa Church authorities sent priests to Akbar in 1595 AD to satisfy his curiosity about Christianity: the third mission; it met Akbar in Lahore.
    • First mission reached Fatehpur Sikri in 1580 AD; second reached Lahore in 1591 AD.
    • Third mission was led by Jerome Xavier, nephew of missionary saint Francis Xavier.
    • Antonio Monserrate was a member; Akbar hired him as tutor for his son Murad.
    • Akbar took part in festivals such as Basant, Holi, Diwali.
    • Stanley Lane-Poole: "This assimilation of the Hindu chiefs was the most conspicuous feature of Akbar's reign."
    • Dr. R.P. Tripathi: Akbar was both a child and a father of his era.

    Social and educational reforms

    • Akbar ordered that a man should marry only one wife, and another only if the first proved barren.UPPSC
    • He banned some social customs to improve society; encouraged widow remarriage and forcefully discouraged Sati.
    • Akbar tried to fix the marriage age at 14 for girls and at least 16 for boys; gave girls freedom to marry at their own will, not under parental pressure.UPPSC
    • Causes of Akbar's popularity: Mansabdari system, religious policy, land revenue system and social reforms.UPPSC
    • Akbar was the first Muslim ruler to practise religious harmony and treat Hindus and Muslims alike; child marriage and Sati were abolished in his reign.
    • Akbar is credited with establishing, consolidating and centralising Mughal administration.
    • His central administration, idea of kingship, provincial administration, revenue system, monetary policy and mansabdari became the foundation for his successors.
    • Akbar is called "an enlightened despot", like Queen Elizabeth I of England and Frederick the Great: liberal and tolerant, with complete authority of the empire vested in him; all subjects were equal before the law.UPPSC
    • Akbar introduced educational reforms in the curriculum, especially at primary level.
    • Subjects added at his command: arithmetic, logic, mensuration, geometry, astronomy, physiognomy, accountancy, public administration and agriculture.
    • Akbar had no formal education but patronised men of learning.

    Administration and Mansabdari

    • Under Akbar's central system Mir Bakshi headed the military department but was not chief commander of the army.
    • Bakshi recommended recruitment, proper rank and correct pay of soldiers; inspected mansabdars and troops and reported to the emperor.
    • Akbar revived Chehra (descriptive roll of each soldier) and Dagh (branding of horses) in 1573–74 AD.
    • Akbar's military system was based on Mansabdari; he organised soldiers by it in 1574–75 AD (19th year of reign, 1575 AD).UPPSC
    • Mansab = rank or position; Mansabdar = official holding a rank in the royal army or government office; based on the decimal system.
    • Three classes: Mansabdar (10 to below 500), Amir (500 to 2500), Amir-i-Azam (above 2500).
    • Mansabdari was introduced to ensure clean administration.
    • Mansabdari was borrowed from Mongolia (Central Asia): Genghis Khan's army used a decimal troop organisation; yet the system was largely new.
    • In Akbar's time mansabdars kept twenty horses for every ten cavalrymen, as horses needed rest on the march and replacement in war.
    • 'Diwan' is a Persian word adopted by Muslims in Caliph Umar's time for the treasury department.
    • Muzaffar Khan Turbati was made Diwan (Todar Mal as assistant) early in Akbar's reign; the Diwan's department grew from his appointment.UPPSC ×2
    • Todar Mal and Khwaja Shah Mansur later served in the finance ministry; Akbar sometimes appointed more than one diwan.
    • Diwan = supreme official of financial affairs and revenue.

    Land revenue: Zabti and Dahsala

    • Zabti system of land revenue was introduced in Akbar's reign: measurement-based assessment; revenue circles (dasturs) with per-bigha cash rates; Ain-i-Dahsala (ten-year average rates).
    • Zabti rested on schedules of Dastur-ul-Amal and Zabti Khasre for survey and revenue fixing; most of the area was under it.
    • Todarmal won fame in land revenue (land revenue reforms).UPPSC ×2
    • Ain-i-Dahsala was introduced by Akbar in the 24th year of his reign (1580 AD) and instituted by Todarmal; also called Todarmal Bandobast / Bandobast system / Todarmal settlement.
    • Todarmal was then finance minister; his main assistant was Khwaja Shah Mansoor; Muzaffar Khan Turbati also helped.
    • Akbar appointed Raja Todarmal and Muzaffar Khan Turbati as finance minister to re-assess land revenue; the Dahsala (Zabti) system of 1580 was meant to consolidate the Mughal empire.
    • Dahsala: average produce of crops and average prices of the last ten years (1571 to 1580 AD) were calculated.
    • One-third of the average was state share (Maal); two-thirds was left to cultivators (Kharaj).
    • Raja Todarmal, honoured for land revenue reforms, was the connecting link between Sher Shah and Akbar in land revenue measures.UPPSC
    • Abul Fazl wrote 'Ain-i-Akbari'.
    • Tansen's name was Ram Tanu Pandey; the title 'Tansen' was given by the king of Gwalior/Rewa, not Akbar.
    • Jahangir (not Akbar) married the sister of Raja Man Singh of Amber.
    • Raja Todarmal headed the revenue department; he was not commander-in-chief of Akbar's army.

    Fatehpur Sikri and other buildings

    • Sikri village, about 37 km from Agra, was the home of Sufi sage Shaikh Salim Chishti; Akbar often went there for his blessings.
    • Akbar founded Fatehpur Sikri (City of Victory), a fort-cum-palace town in Agra district, U.P.; Mughal capital from 1571 to 1585 AD.
    • Akbar's finest monuments are at Fatehpur Sikri.
    • Sikri buildings: Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Treasury, Panch Mahal, Khas Mahal, Kothi of Turki Sultana, Jodha Bai Mahal, Mariyam ki Kothi, Birbal ki Kothi, Swarn Mahal (Sunahala Makaan), Jama Masjid, Buland Darwaza, Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti.
    • Buildings in Gujarat and Bengal styles are found in the Sikri fort.
    • Percy Brown called the palace of Turkish Sultana a 'Pearl of Architecture' (one explanation says he called Sikri so).
    • Akbar built Buland Darwaza at Sikri as a victory tower for his conquest of Gujarat (not for Jahangir's birth), as one class of historians holds.UPPSC ×2
    • Percy Brown links Buland Darwaza with the southern victory (1601 AD).
    • Akbar built the Buland Darwaza and the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri.UPPSC
    • Jama Masjid of Fatehpur Sikri is called 'Shan-i-Fatehpur' (also 'Shah-i-Fatehpur' or 'Shan-i-Sikri').
    • Panch Mahal (Fatehpur Sikri): five-storey, pyramid-shaped, wholly columnar palace built like a Buddhist monastery; inspired by the multi-storey buildings of Nalanda.UPPSC
    • Panch Mahal is set asymmetrically on the pattern of a Persian badgir (wind-catcher tower); its ground floor has 84 pillars.
    • Akbari Mahal is in Agra Fort, not Fatehpur Sikri.
    • Agra Fort = earliest example of Akbari style; built by Akbar under his chief architect Kasim Khan.
    • Akbar built more than 500 buildings of red sandstone in Agra Fort.
    • Jahangir Mahal is inside Agra Fort; built by Akbar for Shahzada Salim.
    • Jahangir Mahal has intricate Hindu and Islamic motifs; inspired by the Palace of Man Singh of Gwalior.
    • Agra Fort, Allahabad Fort and Lahore Fort were built in Akbar's reign; the Red Fort of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan.UPPSC
    • Red Fort is of red sandstone; completed in 1648 AD.
    • Humayun's Tomb in Delhi is a synthesis of Persian and Indian architecture; built under Humayun's wife, designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas.
    • Akbar's tomb is at Sikandra, a small village founded by Sikandar Lodi, on the outskirts of Agra.UPPSC
    • Akbar named Sikandra 'Bahistabad'; he began the tomb, Jahangir completed it in 1613 AD.
    • Akbar's tomb has five storeys; its speciality is the domeless square apex.

    Babur1526–30 ADKabulUPPSC
    Humayun-Delhi
    Akbar1556–1605 ADSikandara
    Jahangir1605–1627 ADLahore
    Shah Jahan1628–1658 ADAgra

    Court: translations, scholars, artists

    • Akbar set up a translation department under his poet laureate Abul Fazl.
    • The Mahabharata was translated into Persian as Razmnama (book of wars) on Akbar's order, by Badauni, Naqib Khan and Faizi.UPPSC ×5
    • The Mahabharata translation was carried out under the direction of Faizi.
    • Abdul Qadir Badauni translated the Ramayana into Persian.UPPSC ×2
    • Faizi translated 'Leelavati'; Abul Fazl translated 'Kaliyadaman' into Persian.
    • Muhammad Husain of Kashmir, famous calligrapher of Akbar's court, was honoured with 'Zari Qalam'.UPPSC
    • Hari Vijay Suri, a Jain monk, stayed some years at Akbar's court and got the title Jagadguru.UPPSC ×2
    • Akbar invited Hari Vijay Suri to explain Jainism; moved by non-violence, Akbar turned vegetarian and banned slaughter of animals and birds.
    • Jain scholar Jin Chandra Suri got the title 'Yug Pradhan' from Akbar.
    • Daswant was Akbar's famous painter; son of a potter, became the first artist of his time; went insane and committed suicide at the height of his glory.
    • Painters listed in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari: Daswant, Basawan, Keshav Lal, Mukund, Miskin, Jagan, Mahesh, Khemkaran, Tara, Sanwal, Harivansh.
    • Abul Fazl = medieval writer who refers to the discovery of America.

    Akbar and the English

    • Akbar (1556–1605 AD) was a contemporary of Queen Elizabeth I of England (1558–1603 AD); he ruled India when the English East India Company was formed in 1600 AD.UPPSC
    • Ralph Fitch (1583–86 AD) = first English merchant to visit Agra and Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar's court).
    • Fitch travelled widely and left a valuable account of India's trade points and township centres of the 16th century.
    ← Humayun and Sher ShahJahangir →

    Chapter 31 · Medieval India

    Jahangir

    60 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Treaty of Chittor, 1615 AD: between Jahangir (who authorised Prince Khurram) and Rana Amar Singh of Mewar.×2
    2. Francisco Pelsaert = Dutch merchant who came to India in Jahangir's period.×2
    3. Jahangir, an outstanding author and critic, wrote his autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri in Persian.×2
    4. Jahangir died in 1627 AD; buried in a tomb garden at Shahdara, Lahore (Pakistan); Babur's tomb is at Kabul (Afghanistan); neither has a mausoleum in India.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 20 UPPSC questions

    Family and accession

    • Jahangir (Salim) was born on 30 August 1569 AD.
    • His first marriage (1584 AD) was with Man Bai, daughter of Bhagwandas, king of Amber, and sister of Man Singh.
    • Khusrau, son of Man Bai, was the eldest son of Jahangir.
    • Salim's second marriage was with Jagat Gosain, daughter of Uday Singh (the Mota Raja); Shahzada Khurram was her son.
    • Jahangir was crowned in Agra fort in November 1605 AD, a week after Akbar's death; took the title Nuruddin Muhammad Jahangir Badshah Ghazi.
    • Following Akbar's tradition, Jahangir began his rule generously and issued various populist (welfare) orders.
    • Jahangir gave high posts to his associates; he also rewarded Raja Vir Singh Bundela, the murderer of Abul Fazl.UPPSC

    Mansab change and Mewar

    • Do-aspa and Sih-aspa system was introduced by Jahangir.
    • Under it mansabdars kept extra soldiers without a rise in rank (zat).
    • Do-aspa: mansabdar kept double the horses needed for his 'Sawar' rank; Sih-aspa: three times.
    • Treaty of Chittor, 1615 AD: between Jahangir (who authorised Prince Khurram) and Rana Amar Singh of Mewar.UPPSC ×2
    • Rana accepted Mughal suzerainty; Jahangir returned Mewar and Chittor, which the Mughals had annexed in Akbar's reign.

    Nur Jahan and the Junta

    • Nur Jahan = cultured, educated, intelligent, dominating and ambitious wife of Jahangir.
    • Nur Jahan's Junta had five members: herself, her mother Asmat Begum, her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itmad-ud-Daula), her brother Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram; Jahangir and Mahabat Khan were not members.UPPSC
    • Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan) was son-in-law of her brother Asaf Khan; allied with Nur Jahan from 1611 to 1622.
    • When Nur Jahan swung her support to her son-in-law Shaharyar, Khurram left the junta and rebelled.
    • Jahangir's reign under Nur Jahan's influence has two parts: 1611–1622 AD (Khurram in the group) and 1622–1627 AD (Khurram out of it).

    Revolts

    • Those who rebelled against Jahangir: Khusrau, Khurram and Mahabat Khan (not Asif Khan).UPPSC
    • Khusrau, the eldest son, revolted just after the coronation; suppressed in 1606 AD.
    • Shahzada Khurram revolted in 1622 AD; defeated at Bilochpur in March 1623 under Mahabat Khan; conflict ended with submission by 1625 AD.
    • Mahabat Khan revolted against Jahangir in 1626 AD.

    English and other visitors

    • William Hawkins (1608–11 AD) was the first Englishman sent by the East India Company to Jahangir's court.UPPSC
    • Hawkins came to Surat in 1608 AD, reached Jahangir's court at Agra in 1609 AD; stayed at court 3 years; got a mansab of 400.
    • Jahangir gave Hawkins the title 'English Khan' and pressed him to marry a lady from Armenia.UPPSC
    • Sir Thomas Roe came to India as British ambassador in the reign of Jahangir; led the second delegation to his court.UPPSC
    • Roe was the first ambassador sent by British King James I to Jahangir's court.
    • Roe arrived at Surat on 18 September 1615 as ambassador of King James I.
    • Roe was received by Jahangir at Ajmer in January 1616 AD.UPPSC
    • Roe accompanied the emperor to Mandu, Ahmedabad and Ajmer; also went hunting with him; stayed one year in Agra.
    • Roe (1615–1619 AD) gave a clear picture of Jahangir's rule; he was sent to win favourable facilities for British trade with India.
    • Roe stayed in India till 1619 AD; returned to England with Jahangir's decree that the British would be welcomed at the Mughal court.
    • Order of arrival: Ralph Fitch (1583, first English traveller to India) → William Hawkins (1608) → Nicholas Dawnton (1614–15) → Sir Thomas Roe (court, January 1616).UPPSC
    • Francisco Pelsaert = Dutch merchant who came to India in Jahangir's period.UPPSC ×2
    • Pelsaert left a unique account of the Mughal empire: "Jahangir's India: The Remonstrantie of Francisco Pelsaert".
    • Peter Mundy = English East India Company factor and traveller; came in the reign of Shah Jahan.
    • Niccolo Manucci = Italian traveller who came to India at the time of the succession war.

    Painting and literature

    • Mughal painting reached its zenith under Jahangir.
    • Earlier, painting was tied to the contents of manuscripts; Jahangir freed it from this bondage.
    • Famous painters of the period: Farrukh Beg, Daulat, Mansur, Abul Hasan.
    • Jahangir gave Abul Hasan the title Nadir-ul-Zaman; he was a portrait artist.UPPSC
    • Jahangir gave Ustad Mansur the title Nadir-ul-Asra.UPPSC
    • Ustad Mansur specialised in painting plants and animals (greatest painter of birds).UPPSC
    • Famous painters of Jahangir's court: Manohar, Bishandas, Mansur; Basawan was Akbar's court painter.
    • Jahangir, an outstanding author and critic, wrote his autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri in Persian.UPPSC ×2
    • In it Jahangir recorded both his merits and demerits.
    • The memoir has three parts: preface by Muhammad Hadi (written after Jahangir's death, on his early life); the original text by Jahangir; a third part by Muhammad Hadi.
    • Babur wrote his autobiography 'Tuzuk-i-Babri' in Turkish.

    Tombs and buildings

    • Jahangir died in 1627 AD; buried in a tomb garden at Shahdara, Lahore (Pakistan); Babur's tomb is at Kabul (Afghanistan); neither has a mausoleum in India.UPPSC ×2
    • Tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula at Agra was built by Nur Jahan between 1622–1628 AD after her father's death.
    • It stands on the left bank of the Yamuna; first tomb in India made entirely of white marble.
    • Pietra dura = decorating walls with floral designs of semi-precious stones; first used in India in the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula.

    • Govind Palace (Bir Singh Palace) = seven-storey building at Datia, Madhya Pradesh.UPPSC
    • It was built by Raja Bir Singh Deo in 1614 AD with bricks and stones; excellent specimen of Bundela architecture; its wall paintings attract travellers.
    • Tomb of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya is in Delhi, not Ajmer; he died in 1325 AD and was buried at Ghiyaspur (Delhi).UPPSC
    • Correct pairs: Akbar's Tomb – Sikandara; Jahangir's Tomb – Shahdara; Tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti – Fatehpur Sikri.
    • Amir Khusrau and Hasan Muhammad Dehlavi were eminent disciples of Nizamuddin Auliya.

    Chapter 32 · Medieval India

    Shah Jahan

    59 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Upanishads were translated into Persian in Shah Jahan's reign by Dara Shikoh as Sirr-i-Akbar; about 52 Upanishads.×6
    2. Shah Jahan abolished the Persian (Iranian) court custom of 'Sijda', started by Balban.×2
    3. Kavindracharya (Kavindra Acharya Saraswati of Banaras, scholar of Sanskrit and Hindi) was a dependent poet of Shah Jahan, who patronised him; led a delegation of Banaras pandits and got the pilgrim tax on Banaras (Kashi) and Allahabad abolished.×2
    4. Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi, was built by Shah Jahan; the main building of Shahjahanabad.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 16 UPPSC questions

    Family and accession

    • Shahzada Khurram (Shah Jahan) was born in 1592 AD in Lahore; son of Jahangir.
    • His mother = Jagat Gosain, daughter of Mota Raja Uday Singh, ruler of Marwar.
    • In 1612 AD Khurram married Arjumand Banu Begum, daughter of Asaf Khan; she is famous as Mumtaz Mahal.
    • Shah Jahan took the throne with the title 'Abul Muzaffer Shihabuddin Muhammad Sahib Kiran-i-Sani'; crowned in Agra.
    • Shah Jahan shifted the capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi).UPPSC
    • Shah Jahan abolished the Persian (Iranian) court custom of 'Sijda', started by Balban.UPPSC ×2

    Deccan, Qandahar and Balkh

    • Ahmadnagar was included in the Mughal Empire in 1600 AD.
    • Hussain Nizam Shah III, ruler of Ahmadnagar, was imprisoned in Gwalior fort.
    • Nizam Shahi sardar Shahaji Bhonsle continued the struggle in the name of a child, Murtaza Nizamshah III.
    • In 1636 AD Shahaji was surrounded by the Mughals in Chunar Fort; he handed over several forts and Murtaza Nizamshah III.
    • Murtaza Nizamshah III was imprisoned in Gwalior fort; Shahaji took service under Bijapur State.
    • Aurangzeb was governor of the Deccan twice under Shah Jahan: 1636–44 AD and 1653–1658 AD.UPPSC
    • He held the post till he won the war of succession and became emperor.
    • Map of Shah Jahan's empire: Golconda was not part of it; Aurangzeb captured Golconda in 1687.
    • Qandahar was the root of dispute between the Shah of Iran and the Mughals: strategic and economic grounds, and a prestige issue.
    • The expansion of both dynasties depended mostly on suzerainty over Qandahar.
    • Loss of Qandahar was a big strategic blow; it exposed the Mughal kingdom to outside attacks.
    • Qandahar finally slipped from Mughal hands in Shah Jahan's period, weakening them on the North-West frontier.
    • Motive of Shah Jahan's Balkh and Badakhshan campaign: remove the Persian representative and secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakhshan, which border Kabul.
    • It was not to conquer Samarqand and Ferghana, the Mughal homelands.
    • This would help control the rebel Afghan tribes near Ghazni and Khyber; it became a buffer state between Mughals and Persians.
    • Kohinoor diamond was found in the mines of Golconda; Mir Jumla presented it to Shah Jahan.UPPSC
    • Mir Jumla = Persian noble, reputed diamond dealer, minister of Abdullah Qutub Shah, Sultan of Golconda (1626–1672 AD).
    • The Sultan, angry at Mir Jumla for accepting Shah Jahan's mansab, seized all his property.
    • Shah Jahan sent Aurangzeb to attack Golconda; the matter was settled by a treaty.
    • Mir Jumla was later called to Agra and given the title 'Muazzam Khan'.

    Literature and the golden age

    • Shah Jahan's period is called the Golden Age of the Mughals for growth in art, literature and education.
    • Dr. A.L. Srivastava, in 'Mughalkaleen Bharat' (1526–1803 AD), called Shah Jahan's regime the golden period of medieval Indian history.
    • This is true only on the basis of art and especially architecture; J.N. Sarkar and V.A. Smith do not accept it, but R.S. Sharma does.
    • Elphinstone wrote that Shah Jahan's period was the most prosperous in Indian history.
    • Two Persian styles prevailed: Indo-Persian (Indian style dominant) and Iranian-Persian (native Persian).
    • Abul Fazl (Akbar's courtier) was the best promoter of the Indo-Persian style.
    • Indo-Persian scholars: Abdul Hamid Lahori, Muhammad Waris and Chandrabhan Brahmin.
    • Iranian-Persian scholars: Ameeni Qazwini and Jalaluddin Tabatabai; the Iranian poetry style was dominant then.
    • Shah Jahan appointed the Persian-style poet Kaleem (Abu Jalih) as court poet (poet laureate).UPPSC
    • Other Persian poets: Qudsi, Mir Muhammad Yahya (Kashi), Salim, Masih, Rafi, Farrukh, Munir, Shoda, Chandrabhan Brahmin, Hajiq, Dileri.
    • Kavindracharya (Kavindra Acharya Saraswati of Banaras, scholar of Sanskrit and Hindi) was a dependent poet of Shah Jahan, who patronised him; led a delegation of Banaras pandits and got the pilgrim tax on Banaras (Kashi) and Allahabad abolished.UPPSC ×2
    • His language was a perfect mix of Awadhi and Braj; 'Kavindra Kalplata' was written in praise of Shah Jahan.

    Dara Shikoh

    • Dara Shikoh, eldest of Shah Jahan's four sons, was the most educated scholar and writer.
    • Among the given choices, Dara Shikoh was the first Muslim to study Hindu scriptures.UPPSC
    • He translated Hindu texts like the Upanishads, Yoga Vashisht and Bhagwat Gita into Persian.
    • Upanishads were translated into Persian in Shah Jahan's reign by Dara Shikoh as Sirr-i-Akbar; about 52 Upanishads.UPPSC ×6
    • Majma-ul-Bahrain is Dara Shikoh's original work and masterpiece.
    • Shah Jahan gave Dara the title 'Shah Buland Iqbal'.UPPSC
    • Lane-Poole compared Dara with Akbar for his tolerance and generosity.
    • Dara was handed to Aurangzeb by a Baluchi chieftain, Malik Jeevan.
    • A special judicial committee named by Aurangzeb declared Dara a heretic and ordered death; he was killed in 1659 AD.
    • Dara's head was buried in the Taj Mahal complex, Agra; his body in the Tomb of Humayun complex, Delhi.UPPSC

    Note from the book Many history books do not mention Dara's burial details; Delhi is the appropriate answer, as Dara's tomb is in the Tomb of Humayun complex.

    Buildings

    • Shah Jahan gathered designers, engineers and architects from India, Persia and Central Asia to build the Taj Mahal.
    • Taj Mahal = best example of Mughal architecture, blending Indian (Hindu), Persian (Iranian) and Islamic styles.
    • Jama Masjid of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan.UPPSC
    • Shah Jahan's buildings: Diwan-e-Aam, Diwan-e-Khas, Sheesh Mahal, Moti Masjid (Agra), Khas Mahal, Musamman Burj, Nagina Masjid, Jama Masjid (Delhi), Taj Mahal, Red Fort.
    • Like Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri, Shah Jahan founded the city of Shahjahanabad in Delhi and filled it with magnificent buildings.
    • Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi, was built by Shah Jahan; the main building of Shahjahanabad.UPPSC ×2
    • Red Fort = irregular octagon with two long sides on west and east; western gate = Lahori Darwaza, southern gate = Delhi Darwaza.

    Buland Darwaza, Fatehpur SikriAkbar

    Chapter 33 · Medieval India

    Aurangzeb

    52 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Despite Mughal victory at Purandar fort and the siege of Raigarh, Jai Singh made the Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji in June 1665 AD.×5
    2. As emperor, Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).×3
    3. The Mughal army had the largest number of Hindu generals under Aurangzeb: 31.6% (Athar Ali's nobility data), over half of them Marathas.×3
    4. Aurangzeb was crowned twice: first on July 21, 1658 in Delhi; second on June 5, 1659 in Delhi after success at Khajwa and Deorai.×2
    5. Tomb of Rabia-ud-Daurani, modelled on the Taj Mahal, is called the 'Second Taj Mahal', 'Dakkhani Taj' (Taj of the Deccan) or 'Mini Taj'.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 18 UPPSC questions

    War of succession and coronation

    1. 1540Order of battles: Bilgram (1540) → Sarnal (1572) → Dharmat (1658) → Jajau (1707).UPPSC
    2. 1540Battle of Bilgram, 1540: Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun.
    3. 1572Battle of Sarnal (Gujarat), 1572: Mughal army under Akbar defeated Ibrahim Mirza.
    4. 1658Dara was the eldest and Aurangzeb the third son of Shah Jahan; Aurangzeb ruled India from 1658 to 1707 AD, as the sixth Mughal emperor.
    5. 1658Battle of Dharmat (near Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh), April 15, 1658: Aurangzeb defeated Dara Shikoh's forces led by Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Jodhpur and Qasim Khan.
    6. 1658Battle of Samugarh, May 29, 1658: joint forces of Aurangzeb and Murad defeated Dara Shikoh.
    7. 1658Order: defeat of Shuja near Banaras (February 1658) → Dharmat (15 April 1658) → Samugarh (29 May 1658) → Deorai (1659).UPPSC
    8. 1658Aurangzeb was crowned twice: first on July 21, 1658 in Delhi; second on June 5, 1659 in Delhi after success at Khajwa and Deorai.UPPSC ×2
    9. 1707Battle of Jajau, 1707: Bahadur Shah I vs Muhammad Azam Shah, for succession after Aurangzeb's death.
    • Aurangzeb succeeded Shah Jahan not by the rule of primogeniture but by force of the sword; there were no clear rules of succession.UPPSC
    • The sword was the symbol of power in the Mughal period; succession was settled only by its strength.
    • Dara was the eldest and Aurangzeb the third son of Shah Jahan; Aurangzeb ruled India from 1658 to 1707 AD, as the sixth Mughal emperor.
    • Battle of Dharmat (near Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh), April 15, 1658: Aurangzeb defeated Dara Shikoh's forces led by Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Jodhpur and Qasim Khan.
    • At Dharmat Dara was supported by Raja Jaswant Singh; Aurangzeb by Prince Murad.
    • Battle of Samugarh, May 29, 1658: joint forces of Aurangzeb and Murad defeated Dara Shikoh.
    • Order: defeat of Shuja near Banaras (February 1658) → Dharmat (15 April 1658) → Samugarh (29 May 1658) → Deorai (1659).UPPSC
    • Order of battles: Bilgram (1540) → Sarnal (1572) → Dharmat (1658) → Jajau (1707).UPPSC
    • Battle of Sarnal (Gujarat), 1572: Mughal army under Akbar defeated Ibrahim Mirza.
    • Battle of Bilgram, 1540: Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun.
    • Battle of Jajau, 1707: Bahadur Shah I vs Muhammad Azam Shah, for succession after Aurangzeb's death.
    • Aurangzeb was crowned twice: first on July 21, 1658 in Delhi; second on June 5, 1659 in Delhi after success at Khajwa and Deorai.UPPSC ×2
    • His title: 'Abul Muzaffar Muhiuddin Muhammad Aurangzeb Bahadur Alamgir Padshah Ghazi'.
    • Shahzada Sulaiman Shikoh, son of Dara, defeated in the war of succession, took refuge with Prithvi Shah, ruler of Srinagar Garhwal.
    • Prithvi Shah's successor Medini Shah handed him to Aurangzeb; he was jailed in Gwalior Fort and died there, killed by an excessive dose of opium.

    Shivaji, Rajputs and Prince Akbar

    • At the start of 1665 AD Aurangzeb sent a large army under Raja Jai Singh of Amber to suppress Shivaji.
    • Jai Singh = Kachhwaha ruler, expert in arts of peace and war; clever diplomat who saw that friendship with Shivaji was needed to win Bijapur.
    • Jai Singh besieged Purandar Fort, where Shivaji had lodged his family and treasure; Shivaji opened talks.
    • Despite Mughal victory at Purandar fort and the siege of Raigarh, Jai Singh made the Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji in June 1665 AD.UPPSC ×5
    • Aurangzeb's rebellious son Muhammad Akbar revolted in 1681 AD, weakening Aurangzeb's position against the Rajputs.UPPSC
    • Akbar was disappointed with the Rajput war; liberal in ideas, he did not believe in his father's fanatic policy.
    • Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar and Durgadas, Rathore leader of Marwar, offered him the forces of Mewar and Marwar if he declared himself king of India.

    Deccan conquests and the British

    • As Subedar of the Deccan for the second time, Aurangzeb took an aggressive policy against Golconda and Bijapur.
    • Shah Jahan's peremptory orders stopped the operations; treaties were made with Golconda (1656 AD) and Bijapur (1657 AD).
    • As emperor, Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).UPPSC ×3
    • Abul Hasan Qutb Shah was king of Golconda when Aurangzeb seized it in 1687.UPPSC
    • Aurangzeb is said to have opened Golconda fort with 'keys of gold', as Akbar opened Asirgarh fort.
    • Map of Aurangzeb's kingdom at his death in 1707 includes Bijapur and Golconda.
    • First Mughal–British conflict was in 1686 AD, in Aurangzeb's reign; Mughal governor Shaista Khan drove the British, including Job Charnock, out of Hooghly.
    • None of these came in Aurangzeb's reign: Peter Mundy (Shah Jahan's reign), William Hawkins and Thomas Roe (Jahangir's), Antonio Monserrate (Akbar's).

    Personality, nobility and religious policy

    • Aurangzeb had extraordinary personal qualities among the Mughals; high moral standards; far from vices, pleasures and extravagance.
    • Some contemporaries called him 'Shahi Darvesh'; Muslims considered him 'Zinda Peer'.UPPSC
    • The Mughal army had the largest number of Hindu generals under Aurangzeb: 31.6% (Athar Ali's nobility data), over half of them Marathas.UPPSC ×3
    • The share was 22.5% in Akbar's reign and 22.4% in Shah Jahan's.
    • Akbar had abolished Jizya; Aurangzeb re-imposed Jizya on non-Muslims in 1679 AD.UPPSC
    • Jizya classes: income below 200 Dirham a year paid 12 Dirham; 200 to 10,000 Dirham paid 24; above 10,000 Dirham paid 48.
    • Exempt from Jizya: women, slaves, children under 14, beggars and unemployed persons; subordinate Hindu kings and Brahmins had to pay.
    • A European traveller wrote his motive in reviving Jizya was to increase his treasure; this seems only partly true.
    • Aurangzeb was a Sunni Muslim; his religious policy was not moved by any idea of worldly profit.
    • He tried to enforce Quranic law: Jihad (holy wars) against non-Muslim lands (Dar-ul-Harb) till they become Dar-ul-Islam.
    • He stopped putting tilak by hand on the forehead of Hindu kings, a practice started by Akbar.
    • Prostitutes were to marry or leave the country; Basant, Holi, Diwali were banned in the court.

    Family and buildings

    • Bibi Ka Maqbara (Aurangabad, now Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra) was built in Aurangzeb's reign by his son Azam Shah for his mother Rabia-ud-Daurani.
    • Tomb of Rabia-ud-Daurani, modelled on the Taj Mahal, is called the 'Second Taj Mahal', 'Dakkhani Taj' (Taj of the Deccan) or 'Mini Taj'.UPPSC ×2
    • It has intricate designs, carved motifs, imposing structures and a landscaped Mughal-style garden.
    • Moti Masjid inside the Red Fort, Delhi, was built by Aurangzeb.UPPSC ×2
    • Mehrunnisa was a daughter of Aurangzeb; Jahan Ara, Roshan Ara and Gauhar Ara were daughters of Shah Jahan.UPPSC
    • Aurangzeb's other daughters: Jebunissa, Zinat-un-Nissa, Badrunnisa and Jubadtunnisa.
    • Aurangzeb gave the title 'Sahibat-uz-Zamani' to Jahan Ara.UPPSC
    • Jahan Ara = eldest daughter of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal; elder sister of Aurangzeb.
    • Samarth Ramdas, great saint of Maharashtra (born 1608, died 1681 AD), was a contemporary of Aurangzeb.UPPSC
    • Guru Ramdas, the fourth Sikh guru, was a contemporary of Akbar.

    Chapter 34 · Medieval India

    Mughal Administration

    93 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Quick quiz: 10 of 20 UPPSC questions

    Administrative units

    • Akbar divided the empire into units for easy administration.
    • Mughal district = Sarkar; each Suba (province) was divided into several Sarkars.UPPSC
    • Sarkar was further divided into Pargana (sub-district) or Mahal; several villages made one Pargana.
    • Chief officers of each Sarkar: Faujdar, Amalguzar, Qazi, Kotwal, Bitikchi and Khajandar.
    • Chakla = territorial unit between Subah and Pargana, but not identical to Sarkar; used especially in Shah Jahan's rule.UPPSC

    Central officers

    • Mir Bakshi = head of the military department (army) in the Mughal period.UPPSC
    • Mir Bakshi was appointed by the leading nobles of the court.
    • Mir Bakshi fixed monthly salary of soldiers by a signed certificate called Sarkhat.
    • Provincial Bakshis worked under the control of Mir Bakshi.
    • Mir Bakshi was in charge of intelligence gathering and recommended military appointments and promotions to the emperor.
    • Mir Bakshi's duty: supervising land revenue officials, besides salaries of the military department.UPPSC
    • Head of land revenue administration = Diwan/Wazir.
    • Sir Jadunath Sarkar called Mir Bakshi Vetanadhikari (Pay Master); the Pay Master's duty was of Diwan-i-Tan.
    • Mughal Empire was originally a military state; growth of its central government system depended on military power.UPPSC
    • It is debated whether the Mughal Empire was a military state, but most historians accept Mansabdars had military duties.
    • The Mughals had a large army which helped expand and strengthen the empire.
    • Muhtasib = officer in charge (censor) of public morals; acted as police-cum-judge for canon law among Muslims.
    • Prostitutes were expelled from the city and settled at a place named Shaitanpura.
    • Mint officer in the Mughal period was called Daroga.
    OfficerDuty
    Diwan-i-TanLooked after jagirs and salariesUPPSC
    Mustaufi (Mustarfi)Examined income and expenditure of the state
    MushrifLooked after the office
    VakianavisKept a proper list of main events and firmans

    Diwans of the emperors

    EmperorDiwan
    AkbarMuzaffar KhanUPPSC
    JahangirGhiyas Beg Itmad-ud-Daulah
    Shah JahanSadullah Khan
    AurangzebAsad Khan

    Manucci

    • Niccolao Manucci, an Italian traveller, was appointed physician (doctor) in the Mughal army.UPPSC
    • Manucci first joined Dara Shikoh's army as an artilleryman; took up medicine after Dara Shikoh's death in 1659.

    Ahadi and Dakhili troopers

    • Besides soldiers of Mansabdars, there were two other types of cavalry: Ahadi and Dakhili.
    • Ahadis = gentlemen-troopers: served singly, attached to no chief, recruited directly by the emperor as their immediate colonel; did not attach themselves to Mirzas.
    • Ahadis had their own muster-master.
    • Ahadis were part of Akbar's standing army of a few thousand, had several horses and were known as excellent archers.
    • Ahadis were single men with no following of mounted retainers.
    • Dakhili soldiers were also recruited by the Emperor but kept in the service of Mansabdars.

    Mansabdari system

    • Akbar introduced the Mansabdari system; it became the main basis of Mughal military and civil administration (official nobility of the state).UPPSC
    • Mansabdari was introduced mainly to give clean and better administration.
    • 'Mansab' is an Arabic word meaning rank, position or status.
    • Mansabdari ranked government officials and fixed their civil and military duties and remuneration.
    • Mir Bakshi was responsible for smooth working of the Mansabdari system; most Mansabdars were recruited on his recommendation.
    • The Emperor himself appointed and promoted Mansabdars; he could raise, lower or remove a mansab and dismiss them at will.
    • Mansabdari existed in the Mughal period; Mansabdars were selected on qualification (true, but not the reason for its existence).
    • Not all Mansabdars were military officers; high civil officers were also Mansabdars and graded accordingly; system was common to military and civil departments.
    • A Mansabdar could be asked to do any civil or military service.
    • Abul Fazl mentioned 66 grades of Mansabdars, but only 33 categories were in practice.
    • Lowest Mansabdar commanded 10 soldiers; the highest 10,000 soldiers.
    • Mansabdars were paid in cash according to their grades.
    • Salary due to the soldiers was added to the Mansabdar's personal salary.
    • Mansabdari system was not hereditary.
    • 'Zat' and 'Mansab' designations were granted and there were three classes of Mansabdars; Mansabdars were not hereditary officials and their salary was not paid by the Diwan office.UPPSC
    • From his salary a Mansabdar met personal expenses and kept a fixed quota of horses, elephants, camels, mules and carts.
    • Akbar introduced the dual system of Zat and Sawar in the 40th year (1591-95).
    • Sawar rank could not exceed Zat rank (the normal rule).UPPSC
    • Exception: for a Mansabdar serving in difficult terrain amid rebels, the state raised Sawar rank without changing Zat rank.
    • Mashrut (conditional rank) = increase of Sawar rank for a temporary period.

    Jagirdars and Zamindars

    • Under Akbar all territory was divided into two: Khalisa and Jagir.
    • Khalisa revenue went to the imperial treasury; Jagir revenue was assigned to Jagirdars in lieu of cash salary according to rank.
    • Jagirdars used the revenue for their salary and to meet their military obligation.
    • Judicial and police functions were performed locally by Zamindars, not by Jagirdars; Jagirs were not hereditary while Zamindari was hereditary.
    • Jagir-holders were shifted from one jagir to another; transfers stopped them from developing local roots.
    • Jagirs were transferable and could be seized too.
    • Zamindars were present in practically every part of the empire and held the most significant position in the agrarian structure.
    • Zamindar comes from two Persian words: Zamin (land) and dar (holder).

    Land revenue and grants

    • Land revenue was the principal source of state income in Mughal India.UPPSC
    • Central feature of the Mughal agrarian system: taking the peasant's surplus produce (above subsistence level) as land revenue.
    • Maal in Mughal administrative vocabulary = land revenue.UPPSC
    • Madad-i-Maash = revenue-free land grant to scholars (learned persons) and religious persons; also called Suyurghal.
    • Madad-i-Maash was given as charity to pious or worthy persons.
    • Nobles gave Madad-i-Maash to support saints, religious institutions, religious places and upkeep of Mashaikhs; it showed composite culture and harmony.
    • Sadr (Sadr-us-Sudur) inspected all donated lands and watched that donations were not misused.
    • Donated lands were not transferable; the grantee had a right of inheritance over them.
    • Batai (Bantai) = system of calculating revenue by crop sharing; real produce was divided between state and peasants.
    • Sher Shah Suri used 3 systems for calculating revenue: Nasq/Muktai/Kankut; Nakadi or Jabti; Galla Bakshi or Bantai.
    • Bantai was of 3 types: Khet Bantai, Lank Bantai, Raasi Bantai.
    • In Akbar's reign, land revenue in the Deccan was paid on the number of ploughs (per plough).UPPSC
    • In North India under Akbar, Diwan Todarmal set up a systematic land revenue method; none such existed in the Deccan.
    • The Deccan plough fact is given in J.N. Sarkar's book 'History of Aurangzeb', page 190.

    Tobacco

    • The Portuguese brought tobacco to India; it soon became very popular among common people.
    • Jahangir saw its harmful effects and banned tobacco by an order in 1617 A.D.UPPSC

    Coins

    • Babur introduced silver and copper coins; his silver coin was called Shahrukh.UPPSC
    • Akbar, like Sher Shah, tried to regulate the state currency; chief copper coin of Akbar's time was the Dam (true, but not the reason).UPPSC
    • Under Akbar and his successors, gold coins, silver rupees and copper Dams circulated widely for trade.
    • Three basic Mughal coins: Mohur of gold, Rupee (Rupiya) of silver, Dam of copper.UPPSC
    • Dam was a copper coin largely created by Sher Shah (part of his tri-metallic system) and continued under the Mughals.
    • Akbar issued coins with figures of Ram and Sita and the Devanagari legend 'Ram Siya'.UPPSC
    • Jahangir put his own figure on his coins and Nur Jahan's name with his own on some coins.
    • Some Jahangir coins showed him holding a cup of alcohol in hand.
    • Taza sikka = coin newly minted in the current or previous year.
    • Chalani (current) = coins issued and circulating in the reigning emperor's time.
    • Khazana = coins minted in earlier reigns.

    Canals

    • Shahab (Shihab) Nahr was built by restoring Firuz Shah's canal Rajabwah.UPPSC
    • In Akbar's time first Shihabuddin Khan and later Nuruddin Muhammad Tar reconstructed the canal.
    • Shihabuddin Khan, Akbar's Governor of Delhi, repaired it for irrigation and renamed it Shahab Canal.

    Chapter 35 · Medieval India

    Music and Paintings of Mughal Period

    72 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Humayun laid the foundation of Mughal painting during his exile in Persia and Afghanistan.×3
    2. Aurangzeb was a skilled instrumentalist who played the Veena.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 13 UPPSC questions

    Beginning of Mughal painting

    • Mughal paintings showed battle (war) scenes, animals, birds, natural scenery and courtiers.UPPSC
    • Mughal paintings were a unique blend of Indian, Persian and Islamic painting.
    • Humayun laid the foundation of Mughal painting during his exile in Persia and Afghanistan.UPPSC ×3
    • In exile Humayun met two noted painters: Khwaja Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali.
    • Humayun and his son Akbar learned drawing and painting from these two artists.
    • An advanced atelier was set up in the palace.

    Painting under Akbar

    • Akbar set up Karkhanas for painting; the imperial painting establishment was called Tasvir Khana.
    • Akbar's painting Karkhanas: Agra 1558-1572 A.D., Fatehpur Sikri 1572-1585 A.D., Lahore 1585-1601 A.D., again Agra 1603-1605 A.D.
    • Akbar got many texts painted; the first major project was Dastan-i-Amir Hamza.
    • Dastan-i-Amir Hamza was illustrated first under Mir Sayyid Ali and later under Abdus Samad.
    • Dastan-i-Amir Hamza: earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript, begun in Humayun's period; took 15 years; about 100 painters; about 1400 paintings.
    • It tells the heroic deeds of the Persian hero Amir Hamza, uncle of Prophet Muhammad.
    • Daswant and Basawan were famous painters of Akbar's court.
    • Akbar was so impressed by Daswant that he supported him to become the leading painter of his time.
    • Akbar-era painters named in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari: Daswant, Basawan, Keshav Lal, Mukund, Mishkin, Farrukh, Jagan, Mahesh, Khemkaran, Tara, Sanwal, Harivansh, Rai.
    • European paintings were introduced in Akbar's court through the Portuguese.
    • Mughal painters got two things from Europeans: portrait of a person; making far objects small in size.
    • Painting began to develop in Humayun's period; European influence on Mughal painting began under Akbar.
    • Mishkin was a European painter in Akbar's court.

    Painting under Jahangir

    • Mughal painting reached its zenith under Jahangir (1605-27); his period = 'Golden Age of Mughal Paintings'.
    • Jahangir mainly patronised painting; he was a highly skilled connoisseur and had his own atelier.UPPSC
    • Jahangir shifted emphasis from illustrated manuscripts to albums and individual portraits.
    • Jahangir encouraged paintings of events of his own life, individual portraits, and studies of birds, flowers and animals, rather than fiction illustrations.
    • Jahangir's interest in portraiture led to much growth of this art form.
    • Jahangir was fascinated with art, science and architecture from a young age; painting also served his scientific interest in nature.
    • Jahangir kept a huge aviary, recorded every specimen and organised experiments.
    • Jahangir patronised European and Persian arts.
    • Jahangir's court painters: Abul Hasan, Ustad Mansur, Farrukh Beg, Bishan Das, Aqa Reza, Muhammad Nadir, Muhammad Murad, Manohar, Madhav, Govardhan.UPPSC
    • Abul Hasan had the title Nadir-uz-Zaman; Ustad Mansur had the title Nadir-ul-Asr.
    • Abul Hasan painted Jahangir's coronation; it is the frontispiece of Jahangir's autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
    • Ustad Mansur, a 17th-century Mughal court artist, excelled in painting nature, plants, birds and animals.
    • Mansur documented animals and plants that Jahangir met on military expeditions or received as donations.
    • Khwaja Abdus Samad was a painter of Humayun's and Akbar's reigns, not of Jahangir's period.

    Schools of painting

    • Pahari School, Rajput School, Mughal School and Kangra School are different styles of painting (medieval).UPPSC
    • Hill (Pahari) paintings = paintings of the hill states of the north-western Himalayan region.
    • Pahari area: Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Tehri Garhwal and Pauri Garhwal of Uttarakhand.
    • Mughal school spread from the court to regional centres and gave rise to Pahari and Rajasthani schools.
    • Kalighat school was indigenous and not affected by Mughal painting.
    • Kishangarh school (Rajasthan) is famous for painting, known across India for courtesan paintings.
    • Raja Sawant Singh, scholar and art patron who became king in 1748 A.D., inspired the Kishangarh school of Radha-Krishna theme.
    • Main Kishangarh artists: Amirchand, Chhotu, Bhawanidas, Nihalchand, Sitaram.
    • The famous Kishangarh portrait of the courtesan Bani-Thani was made by Nihalchand.

    Music: Aurangzeb and ragas

    • Aurangzeb banned music as anti-Islamic.
    • Yet most books on Indian classical music in Persian were written in Aurangzeb's period.
    • Aurangzeb was a skilled instrumentalist who played the Veena.UPPSC ×2
    • Todi Raga is sung early in the morning.
    • Todi, a Hindustani classical raga, gives its name to the Todi thaat, one of the ten modes of Hindustani music.
    • Todi was sung by Bhats and Charans (minstrels) in the emperor's court.

    Tansen and Swami Haridas

    • Tansen and Swami Haridas were the leading Dhrupad singers of Akbar's reign.UPPSC
    • Swami Haridas: spiritual poet and classical musician with many devotional compositions, especially in Dhrupad style.
    • Tansen, Baiju Bawra and Gopal Nayak were trained by Swami Haridas.
    • Swami Haridas founded the Haridasi school of mysticism, still found in North India.
    • His followers built 5 worship centres (ashrams): Sri Banke Bihariji, Nidhivan, Temple of Gorelal, Sri Rasik Bihari, Thatti Khana.UPPSC
    • Tansen's original name was Ramtanu Pandey.
    • Tansen was one of Akbar's Navratnas (nine jewels) and a famous musician of his court.
    • The title 'Tansen' was given by Raja Vikramjit Singh of Gwalior, not by Akbar; Akbar gave the title 'Mian'.
    • Akbar also gave Tansen the title Kanthabharanvanivilas.
    • Tansen composed Dhrupads on Hindu gods and goddesses, composed songs on his patrons and invented many Ragas.
    • Tansen was born in a Hindu family and was a Vaishnava musician.
    • Before Akbar, Tansen was patronised by Raja Ramchandra Singh of Rewa (Bhata region); Akbar called him from there and gave a high post.UPPSC
    • Tansen's tomb is in Gwalior, near the tomb of Saint Hazrat Ghaus.UPPSC
    • Hazrat Ghaus's teachings influenced Tansen to convert to Islam.

    Other musicians and styles

    • Akbar was a learned musician; he studied Hindu music under Lala Kalawant.UPPSC
    • Vilas Khan was the main singer of Jahangir's court.
    • Singers of Shah Jahan's court: Jagannath, Ramdas, Sukhsen, Sursen, Lal Khan, Durrang Khan.
    • Raja Mansingh Tomar, Tansen and Sadarang-Adarang were greats of Hindustani music; Mal Gurjari is a Raga invented by Raja Mansingh Tomar.UPPSC
    • Khyal singing became popular in the time of Muhammad Shah 'Rangila'.
    • Tappa style was refined and encouraged at the court of Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah (18th century).UPPSC
    • Sadaranga and Adaranga were two great composers of Khayal gayaki at Muhammad Shah's court.
    • New forms of music of this time: Tarana, Dadra and Ghazal.
    • Folk forms such as Thumri and Tappa were also taken into the country's music.
    • Tappa is based on folk music sung by the camel drivers of Punjab.

    • Futuhat-i-Alamgiri: Ishwardas Nagar was a Mughal officer; the work has some significant events of Aurangzeb's reign.
    • Masir-i-Alamgiri chronicles the history of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.

    Baburnama

    • Tuzuk-i-Baburi, Babur's autobiography, is also called Baburnama; written in the Turkish language.
    • Baburnama was translated (from Persian) into English by John Leyden and William Erskine.UPPSC

    Gulbadan Begum and Maham Anaga

    • Gulbadan Begum was the daughter of Babur; born 1523 A.D., died 1603 A.D.UPPSC ×2
    • Gulbadan Begum wrote historical records in the Mughal period: her book Humayun Nama records many historical events.UPPSC
    • She wrote that she penned the history of Babur and Humayun on Akbar's orders; Akbar greatly respected her.
    • Humayun Nama describes the battle between Humayun and Kamran.
    • Maham Anaga built the Khair-ul-Manzil mosque (Mughal architecture), opposite the Purana Qila, Delhi.UPPSC
    • Khair-ul-Manzil later served as a Madarsa; today it is also known as Madarsa-e-Begum.UPPSC

    Translations

    • Hitopadesha = collection of Sanskrit fables in prose and verse.
    • Hitopadesha was translated into Persian by Taj-ul-Din Mufti al-Maliki (Tajul Mali) as 'Mufarrih-al-Qubal'.UPPSC
    • Panchatantra translations: Nasrullah Munshi Shirazi → 'Kalila-wa-Dimnah'; Mulla Husain Waiz Kashifi → Anwar-i-Suhaili.UPPSC
    • Abul Fazl translated the Sanskrit Panchatantra into Persian as Ayar-i-Danish.
    • Akbar set up a translation department under the supervision of poet laureate Faizi.
    • Akbar's translation department translated works of Sanskrit, Arabic, Turkish, Greek and many other languages.
    • Yogavasistha was translated into Persian by Nizamuddin Panipati in the reign of Akbar.

    Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari

    • Akbarnama was written by Abul Fazl, one of Akbar's nine gems, from 1590 to 1596 A.D. (seven years).UPPSC

    Note from the book Some books say Akbarnama took more than 7 years (12 or 13 years); so UPPSC did not evaluate this question.

    • Akbarnama has three volumes: first = ancestors of Akbar; second = Akbar's own reign; third = Ain-i-Akbari.UPPSC
    • Ain-i-Akbari, in Persian by court historian Abul Fazl, gives Akbar's administration, court, army, revenue and geography.

    Shah Jahan's historians

    • Abdul Hamid Lahori was an official historian of Shah Jahan's reign.
    • Lahori wrote Padshahnama (Badshahnama), the history of Shah Jahan; he joined Shah Jahan's court as a traveller.
    • Shahjahannama (Chronicles of Shah Jahan) was written by Inayat Khan in the 17th century.
    • Shahjahannama was translated into English by A.R. Fuller in the 19th century A.D.

    Language and script

    • Persian was the court, official and administrative language of the Mughals.UPPSC
    • Urdu was the language of princely courts such as Delhi and Lucknow.
    • Akbar was a protector of many languages.
    • Nastaliq was a Persian script used in medieval India in the Mughal period.
    • Aurangzeb was an expert in writing the Nastaliq script.

    Hindi literature

    • Akbar's tolerance and balanced attitude let Hindi grow; his reign is called the golden era of Hindi poetry.
    • Both Hindus and Muslims had equal rights on Hindi.
    • Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana was the Muslim scholar with the most significant contribution to Hindi literature.
    • Rahim was a master of Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Sanskrit, Hindi and Rajasthani; 'Rahim Satsai' is his famous collection of couplets.
    • Nagri Das (Servant of Radha) was the pen-name of Raja Sawant Singh (17th-18th century) of Kishangarh state, Ajmer.UPPSC ×2
    • Sawant Singh wrote many verses in praise of Lord Krishna; Kishangarh rulers patronised the Nimbarka sect.
    • Keshavdas (1555-1617 A.D.) wrote 'Ramachandrika' and 'Rasik-Priya'.UPPSC
    • Keshavdas was a Sanskrit scholar and Hindi poet; Rasik Priya is a pioneering work of the Ritikaal of Hindi literature.
    • Works of Keshavdas: Ramachandrika, Rasik Priya, Ratan Bavani, Kavipriya, Chhandamala.
    • Ram Rasayan, Ganga Lahari and Prabodh Pachasa are works of Padmakar, not Keshavdas.

    Hemu and Prithviraj

    • Hemu = Hem Chandra Vikramaditya.
    • Hemu rose to be army chief and Prime Minister of Adil Shah Suri of the Sur dynasty.
    • Hemu fought Afghan rebels from Punjab to Bengal and the Mughal forces of Akbar and Humayun in Agra and Delhi; won 22 battles in a row.
    • Hemu defeated Tardi Beg (Targi Begh) and took the title Vikramaditya, used earlier by many Hindu kings since Vedic times.
    • Hemu lost the Second Battle of Panipat and was beheaded by Bairam Khan, commander of Akbar's army.
    • Historian B.N. Luniya called Prithviraj Chauhan 'the last sun of Indian glory'.UPPSC

    Tansen's name

    • Tansen's real name was Ramtanu Pandey; after conversion to Islam he was named Ata Ali Khan.

    • Dam = copper coin issued by Sher Shah Suri; in the Mughal period one Rupiyah (silver) = 40 dam.
    • Desai = revenue collector at district level in the Maratha period.
