    • Jarib = land measurement unit in the Mughal period, not a tax.UPPSC

    Surat, Nauroz, education

    • Surat was called Babul Mecca (Gate of Mecca), 'Meccai dwar' and 'Meccabari'; Haj pilgrims left for Mecca from Surat.
    • Mughals adopted the Nauroz festival from Persia (Iran), i.e. from the Zoroastrians.UPPSC
    • Nauroz was a national festival celebrated for nineteen days; preparations began long before.
    • Abdul Qadir Badauni called Nauroz 'Nauroz-i-Jalali'.
    • The Madarsa specialising in Muslim Jurisprudence in the Mughal period was at Lucknow.UPPSC
    • Mulla Nizamuddin, born in Sihali (Lucknow), originated the new curriculum 'Dars-e-Nizami'.
    • Dars-e-Nizami included Tafsir (exegesis of Quran), Hadith (tradition of Prophet Muhammad) and Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence).

    Famous queens in order

    • Order of queens: Padmini → Durgawati → Tara Bai → Ahilya Bai.UPPSC ×2
    • Padmini: queen of Chittor, wife of Rana Ratan Singh; Khalji defeated and killed Ratan Singh at Chittor and wanted her by force; she committed Jauhar (similar to Sati).
    • Rani Durgavati: Hindu warrior queen of Gondwana, regent for her son; defeated by Akbar, she stabbed herself to death.
    • Tara Bai Bhonsle: queen of Chhatrapati Rajaram; kept alive resistance to Mughal occupation of Maratha lands after her husband's death.
    • Ahilya Bai: Holkar queen of the Maratha-ruled Malwa kingdom; Indore was held by the Holkar dynasty.

    Trade and travel terms

    • Muallim = navigator, an employee on Indian merchant ships (a worker, not a ship).
    • Muallim held a spherical device to read positions of stars and the sun and find the ship's correct position.
    • Banjaras in medieval India were generally traders.
    • Banjaras moved place to place, sometimes with thousands of oxen laden with food grain, salt, ghee and daily goods.
    • Banjaras specialised in caravan trading and also in textile embroidery.
    • Sarais = places giving temporary accommodation to Indian and foreign travellers, pilgrims, merchants and traders.
    • Sarais ringed cities and dotted the sub-continent; mostly built on a simple square or rectangular plan.
    • Sarais were public places full of people of varied cultures; this led to cross-cultural interaction and syncretic tendencies.

    Chapter 38 · Medieval India

    Sikh Sect

    42 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Nanak appointed Bhai Lehna as his successor; he was later known as Guru Angad.×2
    Quick quiz: 9 of 9 UPPSC questions

    The ten Gurus

    • Guru Nanak was the founder of Sikhism and the first Guru of the Sikhs.
    • Sikhism has 10 Gurus: Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ramdas, Arjan Dev, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, Gobind Singh.
    • Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539 at the age of 70.
    • Nanak appointed Bhai Lehna as his successor; he was later known as Guru Angad.UPPSC ×2

    Guru Angad and Guru Amardas

    • Guru Angad, the second Guru, started (is the progenitor of) the Gurumukhi script.UPPSC
    • 'Gurumukhi' comes from the Punjabi word 'Gurumukha' = from the mouth of the Guru.
    • Guru Amardas divided the religious empire into 22 parts (branches) called Manji.
    • Each Manji was under a Sikh; a local Sikh preacher was appointed at each place.

    Guru Ramdas and Amritsar

    • Fourth Guru Ramdas established the city of Amritsar.UPPSC
    • Amritsar district Gazetteer: Ramdas got from Akbar a land grant of about 500 bighas where Amritsar now stands.
    • Ramdas dug the holy tank and began building a temple in its midst.
    • Some sources say Akbar gifted the land to Bibi Bhani, wife of Guru Ramdas.
    • Some other sources say Ramdas bought the land from the zamindars of the villages.
    • Ramdas died in 1581 A.D.; his son and successor Guru Arjan completed the temple.
    • Guru Ram Das organised a network of Sikhs to collect offerings, called Masand.
    • Dasvandh = practice by which Sikhs pay one-tenth of their income to the Guru.

    Guru Arjan Dev and Adi Granth

    • Guru Arjan Dev, fifth Guru (1581-1606 A.D.), compiled the Adi Granth or Guru Granth Sahib in 1604 A.D.
    • Adi Granth has preachings of six Sikh Gurus and many Hindu/Muslim saints like Kabir, Baba Farid, Namdev and Raidas.
    • Among the earliest compositions in the Adi Granth is that of Vaishnav poet Jaydev; the last added were of Guru Tegh Bahadur.
    • Arjan Dev built Sri Harmandir Sahib in the middle of the Amritsar pond (lake).
    • Arjan Dev founded two cities: Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (in Jalandhar Doab).
    • Prince Khusrau revolted against Jahangir in 1606 A.D. and fled from Agra towards Punjab/Afghanistan.
    • Khusrau met Guru Arjan Dev at Tarn Taran; the Guru gave blessings, shelter and some financial help.UPPSC
    • Jahangir was angry, fined Arjan Dev and accused him of conspiracy.
    • After he refused the fine, Arjan Dev was imprisoned and put to death by torture in 1606 AD: the first great martyrdom.
    • Wrong pairs: Guru Amar Das – Miri and Piri; Guru Ramdas – Dal Khalsa; Guru Gobind Singh – Manji. Dal Khalsa was established by Kapur Singh.

    Guru Tegh Bahadur

    • Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur were sentenced to death by Jahangir and Aurangzeb respectively.UPPSC
    • Guru Tegh Bahadur (1664-1675 A.D.) was the ninth of ten Gurus, revered as the ninth Nanak.
    • By his son Guru Gobind Singh's records, he resisted persecution and promised to protect Kashmiri Hindus.
    • Aurangzeb called him to Delhi and offered him to abandon his faith and convert to Islam; he refused.
    • Tegh Bahadur and his associates were arrested; Aurangzeb had him executed in public at Chandni Chowk, Delhi, in November 1675.

    Guru Gobind Singh and Khalsa

    • Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth and last Guru (last prophet) of the Sikhs.
    • Guru Gobind Singh was born in 1666 A.D. in Patna (Bihar).
    • His greatness: he formed the military order of the Sikhs, turning them into the military sect 'Khalsa Panth'.
    • Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa Panth and called the whole Sikh community 'Khalsa'.UPPSC
    • Khalsa Panth was set up on 13 April 1699, Baisakhi day, at Anandpur Sahib: more than 300 years ago.
    • He ordered each Sikh to take the surname Singh (male) or Kaur (female).
    • He ordered the 5 K's: Kesh, Kangha, Kachha, Kripan and Kada.
    • Guru Gobind Singh was assassinated at Nanded, Maharashtra, by an Afghan noble in 1708 A.D.
    • Nanded Gurudwara (Huzur Sahib, 'Takhat Sachkhand Sri Hazur Abchalnagar Sahib') stands at his cremation site.UPPSC

    Banda Bahadur and Hem Kund

    • Banda Bahadur's other (original) name was Lachman Dev or Lakshan Dev; this name was given to him by Guru Gobind Singh.UPPSC
    • A famous Sikh Gurudwara is at Hem Kund (Chamoli, Uttarakhand).

    Maratha State and Confederacy

    71 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Balaji Vishwanath · 1713-1720×4
    2. Ashtapradhan = Council of Eight Ministers under Shivaji in the Maratha administration (reached 8 by 1674).×3

    Quick quiz: 10 of 27 UPPSC questions

    Rise of Maratha power

    • Reasons of Maratha rise: religious consciousness, geographical security, political awakening and high quality of leadership (all).UPPSC
    • Maratha rise was neither specific nor the result of unstable circumstances of one specific period.
    • The main reason for the rise was its residents (people).
    • Unity on regional/collective consciousness, religious toleration and integration of social groups grew a feeling of nationalism.
    • Geographical conditions of Maharashtra helped Maratha power to flourish.
    • High leadership quality of Shivaji and other Maratha leaders contributed to the rise.
    • Map question: the shaded area shows the extent of territories ruled by the Marathas.

    Shivaji: life and events

    1. 1627Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort in 1627 or 1630 A.D.; took the title Chhatrapati in 1674 A.D.UPPSC
    2. 1648Order of events: victory on Fort of Chakan 1648 A.D. → start of clash with Mughals 1657 A.D. → Afzal Khan episode 1659 A.D. → attack and sack of Surat 1664 A.D.UPPSC
    3. 1659In 1659 A.D. Bijapur Sultan Adil Shah II sent trusted commander Afzal Khan to suppress Shivaji; Shivaji killed him.UPPSC
    4. 1665Treaty of Purandar, 1665 A.D.: between Shivaji and the Mughals under Jai Singh.
    5. 1666In 1666 A.D. Aurangzeb put Shivaji under house arrest in Jaipur Bhawan at Agra; Shivaji escaped from there.
    6. 1672Shivaji defeated the Mughals in the battle of Salher in 1672 A.D.UPPSC
    7. 1674Shivaji (Shivaji Bhonsle) was formally crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 A.D. at Raigarh.UPPSC
    8. 1680Shivaji died in 1680 A.D. at the age of 53 or 50 years.
    • Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort in 1627 or 1630 A.D.; took the title Chhatrapati in 1674 A.D.UPPSC
    • Shivaji (Shivaji Bhonsle) was formally crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 A.D. at Raigarh.UPPSC
    • Shivaji made Raigarh his capital.UPPSC
    • Pandit Vishweshwar alias Gaga Bhatta, great scholar of Benares (Varanasi), performed the coronation and declared Shivaji a Kshatriya.
    • Shivaji died in 1680 A.D. at the age of 53 or 50 years.
    • Samarth Ramdas was Shivaji's guru.
    • Ramdas is remembered for the Advaita Vedantic text 'Daasbodh'; he also wrote the poem 'Shivastuti' in praise of Shivaji.
    • Order of events: victory on Fort of Chakan 1648 A.D. → start of clash with Mughals 1657 A.D. → Afzal Khan episode 1659 A.D. → attack and sack of Surat 1664 A.D.UPPSC
    • In 1659 A.D. Bijapur Sultan Adil Shah II sent trusted commander Afzal Khan to suppress Shivaji; Shivaji killed him.UPPSC
    • Treaty of Purandar, 1665 A.D.: between Shivaji and the Mughals under Jai Singh.
    • In 1666 A.D. Aurangzeb put Shivaji under house arrest in Jaipur Bhawan at Agra; Shivaji escaped from there.
    • Shivaji defeated the Mughals in the battle of Salher in 1672 A.D.UPPSC
    • Shivaji faced opposition from big Deshmukhs (powerful landlords) who wanted to keep their power and influence.UPPSC
    • Deshmukhs did not favour an independent Maratha state; they wanted to stay feudal subordinates of Bijapur for autonomy and special privileges.
    • Silver coins of Shivaji's kingdom: Lari, Rupaya and Taka; Ruka was a coin of the Kakatiya dynasty.UPPSC

    Ashtapradhan

    • Ashtapradhan = Council of Eight Ministers under Shivaji in the Maratha administration (reached 8 by 1674).UPPSC ×3
    MinisterOther nameWork
    Peshwa—Prime Minister of the King
    AmatyaMazumdarFinance and Revenue Minister
    MantriWaqianavis (Waknis)Interior Minister: internal affairs, especially intelligence and espionage
    SachivSurnavis (Surnis)In charge of all correspondence
    SumantDabirForeign Minister
    SenapatiSar-i-Naubat (Sarnobat)Military: appointments, organisation and food supply of the armyUPPSC

    • Mazumdar, Dabir, Waknis and Surnis were all officers of Shivaji's Ashtapradhan.
    • Shivaji was advised by a Council of Ministers, but ministers did not hold independent charge.UPPSC
    • Ashtapradhan did not work as a cabinet; each minister was head of his department.
    • Shivaji could accept or reject their advice; the Ashtapradhan acted as Shivaji's secretaries.
    • Ministers' main work: follow Shivaji's orders and look after the state.

    Successors of Shivaji

    RulerReignRelation
    Sambhaji1680-1689 A.D.Elder son of ShivajiUPPSC
    Rajaram1689-1700 A.D.Second son of Shivaji
    Shivaji II1700-1708 A.D.Son of Rajaram
    Chhatrapati Shahuji1708-1749 A.D.Son of Sambhaji
    • Rajaram led the Marathas as representative of Shahu from 1689 to 1700 A.D.
    • After Rajaram's death, widow Tarabai put his four-year-old son Shivaji II on the throne and became regent.
    • Tarabai led the struggle against the Mughals from 1700 A.D. and took the forts of Singhgarh, Raigarh and Satara.UPPSC
    • At Aurangzeb's death the Maratha leadership was in the hands of Tarabai.UPPSC ×2

    Peshwas

    PeshwaTenure
    Balaji Vishwanath1713-1720UPPSC ×4
    Bajirao I (elder son of Balaji Vishwanath; appointed by Shahu)1720-1740
    Balaji Bajirao (appointed by Shahu after Bajirao's death)1740-1761
    Madhavrao I1761-1772

    • After Sambhaji, power came to Balaji Vishwanath, who made the administration easy and convenient (under Shahu).
    • Chhatrapati Shahu appointed Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa; November 1713 marked the shift of power from Chhatrapati to Peshwa.
    • Balaji Vishwanath's main achievement: a temporary Mughal-Maratha agreement that properly defined authority and region.
    • By the time of Balaji Bajirao the post of Peshwa became hereditary; the king became a non-entity and Peshwa the virtual ruler.UPPSC
    • By the Treaty of Sangola, 1750 A.D., the Peshwa became the real and effective head of the Maratha confederacy; Shahu's successors depended on the Peshwa's will.UPPSC
    • After Madhavrao's death in 1772 A.D., his brother Narayanrao fell victim to a conspiracy of uncle Raghunathrao, who wanted to be Peshwa.
    • After Mughal decline the Marathas became the strongest native power, able to take the Mughals' place.UPPSC
    • Maratha power rested on the people of Maharashtra, united on Maratha identity; they failed to develop a concept of unified India (a major criticism).

    Maratha revenue terms and script

    • Saranzami system = feudal-military land grant (land revenue) system of the Marathas.
    • Saranzami land was given for livelihood of Maratha Jagirdars, for upkeep of forts and troops for public service.
    • Chauth = Maratha claim of revenue for protection; collected from provinces known as Mughalai.UPPSC
    • Modi script was used in Maratha documents, especially revenue and administrative records.

    Abdali and Third Battle of Panipat

    • In January 1757 A.D. Ahmad Shah Abdali entered Delhi and looted up to Agra and Mathura.
    • Before returning he confirmed Alamgir II as Emperor and Imad-ul-Mulk as Prime Minister.
    • Abdali made Rohilla chief Najib-ud-Daulah (Najib Khan) his chief agent and Mir Bakshi of the empire.UPPSC
    • Third Battle of Panipat: 14 January 1761, Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau vs Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali.UPPSC
    • The Marathas were badly defeated by the Afghans.UPPSC ×2
    • Immediate reason: Abdali wanted revenge as the Marathas had expelled his Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore.
    • Kashiraj Pandit, eyewitness historian, said the Third Battle of Panipat proved catastrophic for the Marathas.
    • A merchant's message to Balaji Bajirao: "Two pearls have been dissolved, 22 gold coins have been lost and of the silver and copper the total cannot be cast up."

    Ahilyabai

    • Ahilyabai was a Maratha ruler of the Holkar dynasty; Holkars belong to Indore; under her the capital moved to Maheshwar.

    Bahadur Shah I and Jahandar Shah

    • After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 A.D. his 63-year-old son Muazzam (Shah Alam) took the throne as Bahadur Shah I.UPPSC
    • Khafi Khan gave Bahadur Shah I the title Shah-e-Bekhabar.
    • Jahandar Shah was the first Mughal emperor who proved weak and unfit for governance.
    • Jahandar Shah got the throne with the help of the powerful Amir Zulfiqar Khan.
    • Jahandar Shah was defeated in battle by his nephew Farrukh Siyar and killed in February 1713.
    • People called Jahandar Shah 'lewd Moron'.

    Farrukh Siyar and Sayyid brothers

    • Farrukh Siyar by a farman of 1717 A.D. granted duty-free trading facilities to the English in Bengal.UPPSC
    • Under it the East India Company could trade without duty on paying an annual tax of Rs. 3000.
    • In the later Mughal period, nobles who came to power were called king-makers.
    • Sayyid brothers Hussain Ali and Abdullah were the 'King Makers'; most powerful from 1713 to 1720 AD.UPPSC
    • Sayyid brothers were leaders of the Hindustani group.
    • They made Farrukh Siyar king in 1713 AD and dethroned him in 1719 AD.
    • Then puppet kings Rafi-ud-Darjat, Rafi-ud-Daula and Muhammad Shah sat on the throne with their help.
    • Sayyid brothers lost power during Muhammad Shah's reign.

    Muhammad Shah and Nadir Shah

    • Muhammad Shah (1719-1748 A.D.) was the last Mughal emperor to sit on the Peacock Throne (Mayur Singhasan / Takht-i-Taus), built by Shah Jahan.
    • Nadir Shah attacked India in 1739 A.D. and defeated the Mughals in the battle of Karnal.
    • Muhammad Shah was the Mughal emperor at the time of Nadir Shah's attack.UPPSC
    • The invasion ended in the sack of Delhi: wide destruction, looting and loss of many lives.
    • It hastened Mughal decline and the rise of regional powers.
    • Contemporary historian Anand Ram Mukhlis: Nadir Shah took to Iran sixty thousand rupees, many thousand gold coins, gold of one crore rupees, jewels of fifty crores, the Kohinoor and the Peacock Throne.
    • Mukhlis remarked: "the accumulated wealth of 348 years changed owners in a moment."
    • Muhammad Shah spent most of his time watching animal fights.
    • People called Muhammad Shah Rangeela for his obsession with wine and beauty and apathy to administration.
    • A group of eunuchs and ladies dominated the Mughal Darbar (government) under Muhammad Shah (1719-48).UPPSC

    Shah Alam II

    • Shah Alam II (1759-1806 A.D.): real name Ali Gauhar.
    • Shah Alam II was not allowed to enter Delhi by Wazir Ghaziuddin; he was a victim of court conspiracies.
    • Shah Alam II reached Delhi with Maratha help in 1772 A.D.
    • The English captured Delhi in 1803 A.D. during his rule.

    Bahadur Shah Zafar

    • The last Mughal emperor was Bahadur Shah Zafar / Bahadur Shah II (1837-1857 A.D.).
    • His father was Akbar II (Akbar Shah II, 1806-1837 A.D.).UPPSC
    • Zafar was called the 'Emperor without Empire'.
    • Zafar was a pensioner of the British and head of the royal court of the Red Fort, Delhi; he died in 1862 A.D.
    • Ibrahim Zauq and Asad Ullah Khan Ghalib taught poetry to Zafar.
    • Hasan Askari, a Sufi saint, was Zafar's Pir (spiritual guide).
    • Zafar got Rs 1 lakh per month pension from the East India Company (not less than one lakh).UPPSC
    • Pension: Rs 99,000 given in Delhi and Rs 1,000 for regular family expenses in Lucknow.
    • "The rule of the Lord of the world extends from Delhi to Palam" was said about the last Tughlaq ruler Nasiruddin Mahmud, not Zafar.

    Note from the book BPSC removed the question on the extent of Bahadur Shah Zafar's empire from evaluation.

    Awadh

    • Saadat Khan was the first Nawab of Oudh (Awadh).UPPSC
    • Turanis established Hyderabad and Iranis established Oudh.
    • Saadat Khan was appointed governor of Oudh in 1722 A.D.; he governed through his heir, nephew Safdarjung, and played high politics at court.
    • After Saadat Khan's death, Safdarjung refused even nominal loyalty to the Mughal Emperor.
    • Independent Awadh state was formed in Muhammad Shah's reign; Saadat Khan was its founder and had joined the conspiracy against the Sayyid brothers.UPPSC
    • Saadat Khan sided with Muhammad Shah against the Sayyid brothers; pleased, Muhammad Shah gave him the title Burhan-ul-Mulk.

    Hyderabad and other states

    • Chin Qilich Khan alias Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the independent Kingdom of Hyderabad in 1724 A.D.UPPSC
    • Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated and killed Mughal governor Mubariz Khan in the Battle of Sakhar-Kheda (Deccan), 1724 A.D., and became the real king.
    • Qilich Khan was called Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah (he was not Mubariz Khan).
    • Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah gave Nizam-ul-Mulk the title Asaf-Jah (not Zulfiqar Khan).
    • Nizamat of Arcot was set up by Aurangzeb; it was a legal dependency of the Nizam of Hyderabad, not an offshoot of Hyderabad state.
    • Mysore Kingdom emerged out of the Vijayanagara Empire: powerful under the Wodeyar dynasty, first a vassal of Vijayanagar.
    • Ali Muhammad Khan set up the petty kingdom of Rohilkhand, using the collapse of authority in north India after Nadir Shah's invasion (1739 A.D.).
    • Ahmad Shah Durrani began invading India in 1748 A.D.; Rohilkhand was not formed from his territories.

    Sawai Jai Singh

    • Sawai Jai Singh (Jai Singh II) (1688-1743 A.D.) of Amber (Kachhwaha) was a great Rajput king of the 18th century.
    • He founded Jaipur city and made it a centre of science and art.
    • Jai Singh II, a renowned astronomer, built the Jantar Mantar observatory in Delhi.UPPSC
    • He built well-equipped observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi.UPPSC
    • He did not build an observatory at Allahabad.UPPSC
    • He prepared a set of astronomical charts named Jiz Muhammad Shahi.
    • He patronised the translation of Euclid's 'Geometry' into Sanskrit.
    • He performed two Ashvamedh sacrifices during his reign.

    Quick quiz: 10 of 29 UPPSC questions

    Vasco da Gama

    • Vasco da Gama reached the port of Calicut on the western coast on 20 May 1498 A.D.UPPSC
    • He discovered a new and alternative sea route from Europe to India.
    • Zamorin (Samuthiri; ancestral title of Calicut's rulers), then ruler of Calicut, welcomed Vasco da Gama.UPPSC
    • One theory: Arab navigator Ahmad Ibn Majid helped him; authentic historical evidence says a Gujarati sailor (route guide) helped him reach Calicut.
    • On his first trip he stayed in India about three months (not one year) and returned to Portugal with ships of Indian goods.
    • Vasco da Gama revisited India in 1502 A.D. and 1524 A.D. (not 1501).

    Note from the book Chhattisgarh PSC's model answer key accepted both "Zamorin ruled Calicut in 1498" and "Vasco da Gama revisited India in 1501" as correct.

    • His cargo of black pepper gave 60 times more profit than the expedition's cost; this lured other merchants to India.
    • His arrival began a new era of trade between the Portuguese and Indians.

    Portuguese in India

    • The Portuguese were the first Europeans to come to India for trade (1498).UPPSC ×5
    • The Portuguese came first in 1498 A.D. and left last in 1961 (longest stay); de jure transfer in August 1962.
    • Portuguese Governor-General of Goa in 1961: Manuel Antonio Vassalo e Silva (1958-61 A.D.).
    • Governor-General of Goa when India became independent in 1947: Jose Ferreira Bossa.
    • The Portuguese were the first Europeans to set up sea (maritime) trade centres in India.
    • The Portuguese set up their first factory at Calicut in 1500 A.D.
    • Portuguese merchants set up commercial firms at the ports of Calicut, Goa, Daman, Diu and Hooghly.
    • Francisco de Almeida came in 1505 A.D. as the first Portuguese Viceroy in India.
    • Almeida gave the Blue Water Policy to protect Portuguese trade and establish authority in the Indian Ocean.
    • Blue Water Policy: "The Portuguese should be the sole trade power in the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean."
    • Almeida annexed Diu in 1509 A.D.; the victory made the Portuguese most powerful in the Indian Ocean.
    • Battle of Diu, 1509 A.D.: Portuguese defeated the combined forces of the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt, Gujarat sultanate and Zamorin of Calicut.
    • The Portuguese set up a monopoly over the Indian Ocean and taxed ships passing through their area.
    • Afonso de Albuquerque came in 1509 A.D. after Almeida as Governor (Viceroy), 1509-15 A.D.
    • Albuquerque is the real founder of Portuguese power in India; he made the Portuguese State a strong regional power.UPPSC
    • Albuquerque captured Goa from the Adil Shahi Sultanate of Bijapur in November 1510 A.D. (not 1499).
    • Goa's capture was his first big achievement; it fixed Portuguese monopoly on the south-western naval coast.
    • The Portuguese kept Goa as the epicentre of their culture and entity.
    • Albuquerque encouraged Portuguese men to marry Indian women, to increase Portuguese presence and form permanent colonies.
    • Albuquerque captured Malacca, an important South-East Asian market, in 1511 A.D. and Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, in 1515.
    • First Portuguese fort (first European fort in India) was built at Cochin in 1503 by Albuquerque on his first visit; named 'Emmanuel Fort'.UPPSC
    • Almeida built Portuguese fortresses at Cannanore and Anjediva in 1505.
    • Nuno da Cunha became Governor in 1529 A.D. after Lopo Vaz de Sampaio and stayed till the end of 1538 A.D.

    Portuguese in Bengal

    • In 1535 A.D. Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah, ruler of Bengal, promised the Portuguese forts at Chittagong and Satgaon for their help against Sher Shah Suri's invasion.
    • After that Portuguese colonies were set up through Bengal; Chittagong was known as their great port.
    • In the 16th century Satgaon declined and was replaced by Hooghly.
    • In 1579 A.D., with Akbar's permission, the Portuguese founded their settlement at Hooghly; built forts and warehouses along the river.
    • Hooghly town, near Chuchura (Chinsurah), became a major European trading centre.
    • In 1599 A.D. the Portuguese reached Bandel (Hooghly district, West Bengal) and built 'Bandel Church' (Basilica of the Holy Rosary).
    • Portuguese factories in Bengal: Hooghly and Bandel.UPPSC
    • The Portuguese used Hooghly as a base for piracy (plunder) in the Bay of Bengal.
    • In 1632 A.D. Shah Jahan ordered Bengal Subedar Qasim Khan to destroy Portuguese establishments at Hooghly; thousands of Portuguese were imprisoned.

    The Dutch

    • In 1602 A.D. the Dutch States General (parliament) chartered a United East India Company with capital of 6,500,000 Guilders.
    • The Dutch were the first, among the given options, to start a joint stock company to trade with India.
    • The first joint stock company for India trade was actually the English East India Company (London, 1600 A.D.); the Dutch one came in 1602 A.D.
    • The Dutch company had a monopoly to trade and to attack and win territories in India and eastern countries.
    • Its eastern centre was Batavia (now Jakarta); it ran the Dutch eastern empire; its partners worked as a private group.
    • The Dutch set up their first factory at Masulipatnam on the east coast (Andhra Pradesh) in 1605 A.D.
    • Dutch east-coast factories were not on land granted by Gajapati rulers; Gajapati rule had declined by the 16th century.
    • First Dutch factory in Bengal: Pipali (1627 A.D.); about 1676 A.D. they left Pipali and set up a new factory at Balasore.
    • Dutch trade with Bengal began properly in 1653 A.D. with their establishment at Chinsurah; factory properly set up around 1656-57 A.D.
    • Dutch factories in Bengal: Chinsurah and Hooghly; severe floods of 1600 A.D. had ruined earlier Hooghly factories.UPPSC
    • The Dutch fort at Chinsurah was called Fort Gustavus.
    • By the end of the 17th century Dutch factories were at Qasim Bazar, Patna, Dhaka, Malda and Balasore.

    English East India Company: founding

    • A group called Merchant Adventurers formed the English East India Company in 1600 A.D.
    • Its name: 'The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies'.
    • Queen Elizabeth I granted its royal charter in December 1600 to trade with the East Indies.
    • Akbar (1556-1605 A.D.) was Emperor of India when the Company was formed in London.UPPSC ×2
    • The Levant Company (1592) got the first charter: monopoly of trade with the Ottoman Empire (the Levant) and its eastern areas including India.UPPSC
    • The Levant Company traded in silk and spices.
    • Elizabeth I's Royal Charter gave the East India Company an exclusive 15-year monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, including India.
    • Secret of the Company's success: no nationalism in India; Company army had western training and modern arms; Indian soldiers lacked fidelity and served whoever paid enough.UPPSC

    English factories

    1. 1590Aurangzeb made John Child's expulsion from India a condition; Child died (printed as 1590 A.D.) before it was carried out.
    2. 1608Captain William Hawkins sailed on the Company's ship Hector and reached Surat in 1608 A.D.
    3. 1608Hawkins was sent by the Company with the King's credentials; he came in 1608, not in 1611.
    4. 1609After Portuguese resistance, Hawkins reached Jahangir's court at Agra in April 1609 A.D. but got no permission for a factory.
    5. 1611Captain Middleton landed at Swally near Surat and got trade permission from the Mughal Governor in 1611 A.D.
    6. 1611The English set up their first temporary factory at Masulipatnam in 1611 A.D., in the reign of Jahangir.
    7. 1611If only European presence is counted, the first factory at Surat was Portuguese in 1611 A.D.; officially and permanently, English in 1613 A.D.
    8. 1612Captain Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese in 1612 A.D. in the naval battle of Swally, near modern Surat; it broke Portuguese monopoly.
    9. 1613The English set up their first permanent factory at Surat in 1613 A.D., with Jahangir's permission.UPPSC ×2
    10. 1613English factories in the first quarter of the 17th century: Surat 1613; Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda and Broach by 1619; Masulipatnam 1611.
    11. 1616The English were the first European company to set up a factory at Surat; Dutch followed in 1616 A.D., French in 1668 A.D.UPPSC
    12. 1628Later English factories: Armagaon 1628; Hariharpur and Balasore (Odisha) 1633.
    13. 1633The English opened their first factory in South India at Masulipatnam, and their first in Eastern India in Orissa in 1633.
    14. 1662Bombay came to the English from the Portuguese as dowry: Charles II married Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza in 1662 A.D. under the marriage treaty of 1661.

    16. 1688India's first Municipal Corporation was set up at Madras (former Presidency city) on 29 September 1688 as 'Madras Nagar Nigam (Madras Municipal Corporation)'; at present called Greater Chennai Municipal Corporation.UPPSC
    17. 1688John Child, British Governor of Bombay, blockaded Bombay and other Mughal ports on the western coast in 1688 and tried to seize Mecca (Hajj) pilgrims.
    18. 1798Nawab Saadat Ali Khan II of Awadh handed the Fort of Prayagraj (Allahabad) to the British in 1798 AD.
    • Captain William Hawkins sailed on the Company's ship Hector and reached Surat in 1608 A.D.
    • After Portuguese resistance, Hawkins reached Jahangir's court at Agra in April 1609 A.D. but got no permission for a factory.
    • Hawkins carried a letter signed by King James I asking favourable treatment for British traders; his mission was both royal embassy and commercial venture.
    • Hawkins was sent by the Company with the King's credentials; he came in 1608, not in 1611.
    • Hawkins spoke Turkish well; impressed, Jahangir gave him the title 'English Khan' and a mansab of 400.UPPSC
    • Captain Middleton landed at Swally near Surat and got trade permission from the Mughal Governor in 1611 A.D.
    • Captain Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese in 1612 A.D. in the naval battle of Swally, near modern Surat; it broke Portuguese monopoly.
    • The English set up their first temporary factory at Masulipatnam in 1611 A.D., in the reign of Jahangir.
    • The English set up their first permanent factory at Surat in 1613 A.D., with Jahangir's permission.UPPSC ×2
    • The English were the first European company to set up a factory at Surat; Dutch followed in 1616 A.D., French in 1668 A.D.UPPSC
    • If only European presence is counted, the first factory at Surat was Portuguese in 1611 A.D.; officially and permanently, English in 1613 A.D.
    • The English later set up factories at Ahmedabad, Burhanpur, Ajmer and Agra.
    • English factories in the first quarter of the 17th century: Surat 1613; Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda and Broach by 1619; Masulipatnam 1611.
    • Later English factories: Armagaon 1628; Hariharpur and Balasore (Odisha) 1633.
    • The English opened their first factory in South India at Masulipatnam, and their first in Eastern India in Orissa in 1633.
    • The English Company set up a factory at Madras on land leased from a representative of the Vijayanagara empire.
    • The Company first made Surat its Western Presidency; later it was shifted to Bombay.
    • Bombay came to the English from the Portuguese as dowry: Charles II married Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza in 1662 A.D. under the marriage treaty of 1661.
    • Charles II gave Bombay to the East India Company in 1668 at 10 pounds annual rent.
    • Job Charnock, chief of Qasim Bazar factory, chose Sutanuti instead of Hooghly for the English trade centre and so founded Calcutta.UPPSC
    • India's first Municipal Corporation was set up at Madras (former Presidency city) on 29 September 1688 as 'Madras Nagar Nigam (Madras Municipal Corporation)'; at present called Greater Chennai Municipal Corporation.UPPSC
    • John Child, British Governor of Bombay, blockaded Bombay and other Mughal ports on the western coast in 1688 and tried to seize Mecca (Hajj) pilgrims.
    • Aurangzeb ordered Sidi Yakub to besiege Bombay; the British surrendered and sought peace.
    • Aurangzeb made John Child's expulsion from India a condition; Child died (printed as 1590 A.D.) before it was carried out.
    • Nawab Saadat Ali Khan II of Awadh handed the Fort of Prayagraj (Allahabad) to the British in 1798 AD.
    • None of these was introduced by the English: soil-and-crop based land revenue assessment, mobile cannons, tobacco and red chilli cultivation.
    • Land revenue assessment by nature of soil and quality of crops began under Sher Shah Suri and Akbar.
    • Mobile cannons in warfare came in the Mughal era; Akbar's ordnance factory made various types of cannons.

    The French

    • Colbert, finance minister of Louis XIV, founded the French East India Company in 1664 A.D.; he is considered its founder.UPPSC
    • The French East India Company was formed in the reign of Louis XIV.UPPSC ×2
    • Its name: Compagnie Francaise Pour le Commerce des Indes Orientales (Compagnie francaise des Indes orientales).
    • The French state was the largest shareholder and bore most of the company's expenses.
    • In 1667 A.D. Francois Caron led an expedition to India and set up the first French factory at Surat in 1668.
    • Marcara, a Persian who came with Caron, founded another French factory at Masulipatnam in 1669 A.D. with permission of the Sultan of Golconda.
    • Under Dupleix the French occupied Madras in 1746.
    • Dupleix was the first European to take part in quarrels of Indian princes to gain territory.
    • Dupleix first placed European forces in Indian courts at Indian expense; his tactics were later used by the English to conquer India; he sowed the seeds of European rule in India.

    Carnatic Wars

    • The Carnatic Wars were fought between the English and the French.UPPSC
    WarYearsResult
    First Carnatic War1746-48Ended by Treaty of Aix-la-ChapelleUPPSC
    Second Carnatic War1749-54 (not 1750-52)Inconclusive warUPPSC
    Third Carnatic War1758-63Ended by Treaty of Paris
    First Mysore War—The British lost
    • First Carnatic War was an extension of the Austrian War of Succession, which began in Europe in 1740.
    • In 1746 the English and French began war in India without the consent of their home nations.
    • Immediate cause: English navy under Commodore Barnett seized French ships.
    • Carnatic Nawab Anwaruddin sent 10,000 men under Mahfooz Khan against the French (to besiege them in Madras).
    • French under Captain Paradise defeated the Nawab's force at St. Thome on the Adyar river; the war is memorable for this battle.
    • Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (18 October 1748) ended the Austrian Succession War and the First Carnatic War; Madras went back to the English.UPPSC ×2
    • Battle of Ambur, 1749 A.D. (not 1752): first major battle of the Second Carnatic War.
    • Ambur was started by Muzaffar Jang, supported by Joseph Francois Dupleix and led by Chanda Sahib, against Carnatic Nawab Anwar-ud-din Khan.
    • They fought Anwar-ud-din because he backed Nasir Jang's claim to be Nizam of Hyderabad.
    • Anwar-ud-din was defeated and killed at Ambur; Chanda Sahib took control of the Carnatic.
    • The French failed in the Deccan mainly due to weak naval strength, while the English had a strong force.UPPSC
    • Voltaire: in the Austrian Succession War French naval strength fell so much that hardly any battleship was left for the Seven Years War.
    • Causes of British success over the French: naval superiority, huge wealth and manpower from the conquest of Bengal, better coordination in the British army.UPPSC

    Opium and saltpetre

    • Europeans got the best saltpetre (shora) and opium from Bihar; Bihar was famous for opium production in British rule.
    • Opium was the chief economic base of the triangular trade between India, China and England (18th-19th centuries).
    • The East India Company held a monopoly of opium cultivation in Bengal and Bihar and forced farmers to grow it.
    • Opium was exported to China, where demand was high despite government bans.
    • Opium profits bought Chinese tea, silk and porcelain for England; English manufactured goods went to India.
    • This exploitative system led to the Opium Wars between Britain and China.
    • Silk and black pepper were also traded, but opium was the chief base.

    East India Company and Nawabs of Bengal

    87 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Buxar was the most decisive battle for establishing British supremacy in India.×5
    2. Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, by a farman of 12 August 1765, granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company.×3
    3. Murshid Quli Khan was the last Governor (Subedar) of Bengal appointed independently by the Mughal Emperor.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 15 UPPSC questions

    Murshid Quli Khan and Alivardi Khan

    • Murshid Quli Khan was the last Governor (Subedar) of Bengal appointed independently by the Mughal Emperor.UPPSC ×2
    • Mughal Emperor Farrukh Siyar promoted Murshid Quli Khan as Governor of Bengal in 1717 A.D.
    • After his death his son-in-law Shujauddin became Governor; Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' only ratified it.
    • Murshid Quli Khan shifted his capital from Dhaka to Maksudabad and named it Murshidabad.
    • Murshid Quli Khan started the Izara system in land settlement.
    • Alivardi Khan (1740-1756 A.D.) compared Europeans with honeybees: left undisturbed they give honey; if disturbed they bite you to death.

    Siraj-ud-Daula and Black Hole

    • After Alivardi Khan's death his grandson Siraj-ud-Daula became Nawab of Bengal.
    • Black Hole tragedy took place in his reign on 20 June 1756 A.D.
    • J.Z. Holwell, one of the 23 survivors: 146 English prisoners were put in a cell 18 feet long and 14 feet 10 inches wide.
    • 123 of them died of suffocation; only 23 survived.
    • Contemporary Muslim historian Ghulam Hussain does not mention this incident in his book 'Siyar-ul-Mutakherin'.

    Battle of Plassey

    • Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757 A.D.: Robert Clive's Company troops defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula of Bengal.UPPSC
    • Plassey (now Palasi) battlefield is on the banks of the Bhagirathi river in Nadia district, West Bengal.
    • Part of the Nawab's army was under three traitors: Mir Jafar, Yar Latif Khan and Rai Durlabh.
    • Siraj fled from the battlefield to Murshidabad; this led to his defeat.
    • Plassey began British supremacy in India and founded the British empire: the Company's first decisive military success.
    • Plassey gave instant military and commercial gains to the British.
    • Plassey founded the British empire in India, but Buxar (1764 AD) actually established British superiority.
    • Plassey set the ground for British political rule over Bihar, Bengal and Orissa, leading states of agriculture and handicrafts.
    • After Plassey, Bengal was in British control; Clive placed Mir Jafar on the throne.
    • In exchange Mir Jafar ceded the 24 Parganas, south of Calcutta, to the British and gave 2,34,000 pounds to Clive as personal gift.

    Robert Clive

    • Robert Clive is known as the founder of the British (English) Empire in India; he sowed the seeds of British rule.
    • Clive was Governor (of Bengal) twice: 1758-60 A.D. and 1765-67 A.D.
    • Clive signed (forced) the Treaty of Allahabad with Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.
    • The White Mutiny broke out among English soldiers during Clive's governorship.
    • Plunder of Bengal's resources by the Company began in Clive's governorship; he set up a 'Predatory State' in Bengal.
    • Clive was a statesman in the mask of a soldier; William Pitt called him "Heaven-Born General".UPPSC
    • K.M. Panikkar: from 1757 to 1773 AD the Company made Bengal a 'State of Robbers'.

    Mir Qasim

    • Mir Qasim (1760-63 A.D.) was the ablest of Alivardi Khan's successors.
    • He had proved his ability as Faujdar of Poornia and Rangpur.
    • Mir Qasim shifted his capital from Murshidabad to Munger.UPPSC
    • Reason: to stay away from Calcutta's constant interference and the intrigues of Murshidabad.
    • He organised his army on the European model.
    • He set up an arms factory at Munger to make tanks and matchlock guns.
    • To improve Bengal's finances he fined embezzling officers heavily and introduced some new taxes.

    Battle of Buxar

    • Battle of Buxar, 22/23 October 1764 AD: British defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.
    • The English army at Buxar was led by Major Hector Munro; Henry Vansittart was then Governor of Bengal.
    • Buxar was the most decisive battle for establishing British supremacy in India.UPPSC ×5
    • During Buxar the Nawab of Bengal was Mir Jafar.UPPSC
    • During Buxar Delhi was ruled by Shah Alam II.
    • Buxar made the English a great power in northern India and contenders for supremacy over the whole country.
    • The area up to Allahabad came under the British and the door of Delhi was opened; Buxar changed the course of Indian history.
    • Buxar confirmed the result of Plassey and set British supremacy over Banaras and Allahabad (Prayagraj) across the Ganges.
    • Buxar completed what Plassey had begun and proved the British had no strong competitor.
    • Sir James Stephen: "The battle of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as the origin of British power in India."
    • Plassey was won by treachery; Buxar showed the superiority of English arms and military skill.
    • Plassey made the English the sole controllers of Bengal; Buxar raised the Company's political prestige all over India.
    • Also printed: Buxar is regarded as the first decisive military success of the English Company in India.

    Treaty of Allahabad and Diwani

    • The Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765 A.D.) was signed after the Battle of Buxar (1764 A.D.).
    • By it Shah Alam II agreed to live at Allahabad under the Company's protection.
    • Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula surrendered Allahabad and Kora to Emperor Shah Alam II.
    • Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, by a farman of 12 August 1765, granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company.UPPSC ×3
    • Diwani = fiscal revenue collection authority.
    • Robert Clive was Governor of Bengal when Diwani was granted.UPPSC
    • In return the Company paid the emperor Rs 26 lakh a year as pension.
    • Najm-ud-Daula, son of Mir Jafar, was accepted as Nawab of Bengal.
    • The farman legalised the Company's political authority in Bengal; British rule then expanded all over India including Delhi.
    • Clive started the Dual Government system in Bengal.
    • The Company was neither willing nor able to collect revenue itself, so it appointed two deputy Diwans.
    • Deputy Diwans: Mohammad Raza Khan for Bengal (Murshidabad) and Raja Shitab Rai for Bihar.
    • So all Diwani and Nizamat work was done by Indians but authorised by the Company.

    Shah Alam II and after

    • Rohilla Sardar Ghulam Qadir took Delhi in July 1788; in August 1788 he ousted Shah Alam II and blinded him.
    • In 1803, in Shah Alam II's time, Delhi fell completely to the East India Company.
    • Shah Alam II and his successors Akbar II (1806-37 AD) and Bahadur Shah II (1837-57 AD) were mere pensioners of the Company.

    Khasi tribe

    • The British came to Sylhet (then in Bengal Presidency) in 1765 AD after getting the Diwani of Bengal.
    • The first hill tribe the British met after the Diwani grant of 1765 was the Khasi.
    • After the Burma War, David Scott tried to link Assam (Brahmaputra Valley) with Sylhet by roads through Jaintia and Garo hill areas.
    • The Khasis of these areas resisted strongly (revolted) under Tirot Sing.

    Hindu officers of Oudh

    • Raja Tikait Rai was 'Artha Mantri' (Diwan) of Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula of Oudh; certain Hindu castes usually held high posts under the Nawabs of Oudh.UPPSC
    • Examples: Raja Tikait Rai and Raja Jhaulal under Asaf-ud-Daula.
    • Nawab Safdar Jung appointed Raja Naval Rai as 'Bakshi' and 'Deputy Governor of Bengal' (as printed).

    Battles of the 18th-19th century

    • Order of battles: Ambur (1749) → Plassey (1757) → Wandiwash (1760) → Buxar (1764).
    • Battle of Ambur (August 1749 A.D.), near Vellore: armies of Muzaffar Jung, Chanda Sahib and the French defeated and killed Anwar-ud-din.
    • After Ambur, Muzaffar Jung became Subedar of the Deccan; Dupleix became Governor of all Mughal territories south of the river Krishna.
    • The Nizam gave some districts of the Northern Circars to the French; a French army under Bussy was stationed in Hyderabad.
    • Battle of Wandiwash (January 1760 A.D.): the British (East India Company) defeated the French.UPPSC
    • At Wandiwash Sir Eyre Coote led the British; the defeated French commander was Count de Lally.
    • With Wandiwash the power of the French in India came to an end.
    • Battle of Chillianwala, 13 January 1849 A.D.: Lord Gough led the British, Sher Singh the Sikh army; it ended undecided.
    • Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General at the time of Chillianwala.
    • Battle of Khurda/Kharda (1795 A.D.): Marathas defeated the Nizam.

    Maratha resistance

    • The Marathas opposed the British most vigorously in India.UPPSC
    • Marathas built their power on the ruins of the Mughal Empire; the British also used these conditions.
    • Marathas were suppressed after three Anglo-Maratha Wars.
    • The British lost the first Anglo-Maratha war badly; it ended with the Treaty of Salbai.
    • Lord Wellesley trapped the Peshwa in the Subsidiary Alliance in 1802.
    • Lord Hastings set up British supremacy after destroying the remaining Maratha strength in 1818.

    Regional States : Punjab and Mysore

    94 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Maharaja Duleep Singh was the last ruler of the Sikh Empire; he ruled 1843-1849 AD.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 18 UPPSC questions

    Ranjit Singh: rise

    1. 1772Punjab was part of Ahmad Shah Abdali's territory; after his death in 1772 A.D. Sikh misls took most of it, except Multan, Kashmir and some smaller regions.
    2. 1780Ranjit Singh was born on 13 November 1780 A.D. at Gujranwala to Maha Singh, chief of the Sukerchakia Misl.UPPSC
    3. 1792A council of regency ran the administration from 1792 to 1797 A.D.: his mother, mother-in-law and Diwan Lakhpat Rai.
    4. 1797Ranjit Singh took power directly in 1797.
    5. 1798In 1798 AD Zaman Shah attacked Punjab; while returning, his cannons fell into the Jhelum river.
    6. 1799In 1799 A.D. Ranjit Singh took Lahore and made it his capital.UPPSC
    7. 1802He captured Amritsar from the Bhangi Misl in 1802.
    • Ranjit Singh was born on 13 November 1780 A.D. at Gujranwala to Maha Singh, chief of the Sukerchakia Misl.UPPSC
    • His father Maha Singh died when he was 12 years old.
    • A council of regency ran the administration from 1792 to 1797 A.D.: his mother, mother-in-law and Diwan Lakhpat Rai.
    • Ranjit Singh took power directly in 1797.
    • Punjab was part of Ahmad Shah Abdali's territory; after his death in 1772 A.D. Sikh misls took most of it, except Multan, Kashmir and some smaller regions.
    • Ranjit Singh could consolidate his empire as the Afghans were busy in internal fights.
    • In 1798 AD Zaman Shah attacked Punjab; while returning, his cannons fell into the Jhelum river.
    • Some sources say Chenab river, but Jhelum is accepted by many historians.
    • Ranjit Singh sent the cannons back; pleased, Zaman Shah allowed him to rule Lahore.
    • In 1799 A.D. Ranjit Singh took Lahore and made it his capital.UPPSC
    • Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (for his service and for providing tanks and artillery) and made him Subedar of Lahore.
    • He captured Amritsar from the Bhangi Misl in 1802.
    • Thus political capital Lahore and religious capital Amritsar were both under Ranjit Singh.

    Ranjit Singh: treaty, conquests, rule

    • Treaty of Amritsar, 25 April 1809: between Ranjit Singh and the British; signed by Charles Metcalfe on behalf of Governor-General Lord Minto I.
    • Treaty terms: Ranjit Singh to accept river Sutlej as boundary and British suzerainty over his vassals across the river.
    • The English recognised the Maharaja as sole sovereign on his side of the Sutlej.
    • The treaty stopped expansion south of the Sutlej; as Cunningham said, he was free to spread his kingdom in the west.
    • Ranjit Singh annexed Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819; so Srinagar was in his kingdom) and Peshawar/North-West Frontier, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (1834).UPPSC
    • Ranjit Singh set up the Adalat-i-Ala at Lahore; it heard appeals from district and provincial courts.UPPSC
    • Ranjit Singh set up modern foundries (factories) at Lahore and Amritsar to make cannons.
    • Ranjit Singh said: "God intended me to look upon all religions with one eye, that is why he took away the light from the other."UPPSC
    • Shah Shuja, grandson (descendant) of Ahmad Shah Abdali, gave the Kohinoor diamond to Ranjit Singh.
    • Shah Shuja sat on the throne of Kabul in 1803 AD.
    • His brother Shah Mahmud, with Barakzai chief Fateh Khan and Dost Muhammad, dethroned him and took Kashmir and Peshawar.
    • Shah Shuja then asked Ranjit Singh for help and presented the Kohinoor.

    Successors of Ranjit Singh

    • Ranjit Singh died in 1839; his son Kharak Singh (Khadag Singh) succeeded him.
    • Kharak Singh was an opium addict.
    • Two rival groups caused growing chaos in Punjab during his reign.
    • Dogra brothers: Dhyan Singh, Gulab Singh and Suchet Singh.
    • Sandhawalia Sardars (aides of Chait Singh): Atar Singh, Lahna Singh and his nephew Ajit Singh.
    • Treaty of Lahore, March 1846: the British army occupied Lahore and forced the Sikhs to sign.
    • Lahore terms: Maharaja ceded all territories beyond the Sutlej forever, and gave up all forts between Sutlej and Beas to the Company.UPPSC
    • Other Lahore terms: promise not to interfere in the administration; Sikhs to pay one and a half crore rupees as war indemnity.
    • Battle of Chillianwala, 13 January 1849 A.D.: English under Lord Gough vs Sikhs under Sher Singh; ended undecided.
    • Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General during Chillianwala.

    Duleep Singh and annexation

    1. 1843Maharaja Duleep Singh was the last ruler of the Sikh Empire; he ruled 1843-1849 AD.UPPSC ×2
    2. 1849By Lord Dalhousie's proclamation of 29 March 1849 Punjab was merged into the British Empire after the Anglo-Sikh war.
    3. 1849After annexation in 1849 Dalhousie made a three-member Board to administer Punjab.
    4. 1853Duleep Singh accepted Christianity in 1853 A.D., visited Russia, and re-accepted Sikhism in 1886 A.D.
    5. 1854Duleep Singh was sent (exiled) to England in 1854 on a pension, for study.
    6. 1893Duleep Singh died in Paris (France) on 22 or 23 October 1893; his funeral (cremation) was in England.UPPSC
    • Maharaja Duleep Singh was the last ruler of the Sikh Empire; he ruled 1843-1849 AD.UPPSC ×2
    • By Lord Dalhousie's proclamation of 29 March 1849 Punjab was merged into the British Empire after the Anglo-Sikh war.
    • All territories of Duleep Singh became part of the Indian British Empire.
    • Duleep Singh was sent (exiled) to England in 1854 on a pension, for study.
    • His pension: not less than 4 lakh and not more than 5 lakh rupees a year (£40,000 to £50,000), not Rs 2,50,000.UPPSC
    • The pension was for him, his relatives and maintenance of the state's employees.
    • Duleep Singh accepted Christianity in 1853 A.D., visited Russia, and re-accepted Sikhism in 1886 A.D.
    • Duleep Singh died in Paris (France) on 22 or 23 October 1893; his funeral (cremation) was in England.UPPSC
    • After annexation in 1849 Dalhousie made a three-member Board to administer Punjab.
    • Board of Three: Sir Henry Lawrence (President), John Lawrence and Charles Grenville Mansel; H.M. Elliot and Robert Montgomery were not members.UPPSC

    Haidar Ali

    • In 1742 A.D. the Mysore army under Venkata Raya conquered Dindigul.
    • There were eighteen Palayams (Palayakkars) under Dindigul Semai, with Dindigul as capital.
    • These Palayams wanted independence and refused to pay taxes to Venkata Raya.
    • In 1755 A.D. the Mysore king sent Haidar Ali to Dindigul; he controlled it, became de facto ruler and set up a modern armoury (sepoy post) in the fort.UPPSC
    • Later Haidar Ali became ruler of Mysore.
    • In 1777 Haidar Ali appointed Purshana Mir Saheb as governor of Dindigul.

    Anglo-Mysore Wars

    WarYearsEnded byBritish head
    First Anglo-Mysore War1767-69 A.D.Treaty of Madras, 4 April 1769Harry Verelst, Governor of Bengal
    Second Anglo-Mysore War1780-84 A.D.Treaty of MangaloreWarren Hastings, Governor-General
    Third Anglo-Mysore War1790-92 A.D.Treaty of Srirangapatna, March 1792Lord Cornwallis (in command)
    Fourth Anglo-Mysore War1799 A.D.Tipu killed; Srirangapatna takenLord Wellesley, Governor-General
    • Haidar Ali won the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69).UPPSC
    • Haidar captured Mangalore in 1768 and reached Madras in 1769; the helpless English signed the Treaty of Madras on his terms.
    • Harry Verelst's dates are printed as 1734-85.
    • Second war: Haidar Ali allied with the Nizam and Marathas against the British.
    • Haidar besieged Arcot in 1780; in July 1780 he attacked the Carnatic.
    • On 10 September 1780 Colonel William Baillie's British army was defeated by Haidar Ali and Tipu at Pollilur (Perambakam).UPPSC
    • The British separated the Nizam and the Marathas from Haidar.
    • Sir Eyre Coote defeated Haidar Ali at Porto Novo (1 July 1781).
    • Eyre Coote also fought Haidar at Pollilur and Sholingur in 1781; at Pollilur (as printed) Haidar was outrightly defeated and his army faced heavy loss.
    • Treaty of Srirangapatna (March 1792) was signed between Tipu Sultan and Lord Cornwallis for the Company.
    • It also included representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maratha Empire.
    • Tipu had to cede half his kingdom; it was divided among the Marathas, British and Nizam.
    • Tipu had to pay Rs 330 lakh as war indemnity; his two sons were kept hostage until 3 crore rupees were paid.
    • In the third war Tipu sought help from Kustuntunia and France through ambassadors, in vain.
    • Tipu Sultan was defeated and killed fighting in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, 1799.UPPSC
    • On 4 May 1799 the British took Srirangapatna Fort; Tipu died in its defence; this ended Mysore's glorious history.
    • All members of Tipu's family were imprisoned in Vellore.
    • British commanders of the fourth war: Arthur Wellesley (brother of Governor-General Lord Wellesley), Stuart and General Harris.
    • For this victory the Lord Society of Ireland gave Wellesley the title of Marquess.
    • After the war the minor Krishnaraja Wodeyar III (Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar) of the Wodeyar dynasty was placed on the Mysore throne.
    • The British took Kanara, Coimbatore and Srirangapatna.

    Tipu Sultan

    • Tipu Sultan made Srirangapatna his capital.
    • Tipu set up a Jacobin Club there and became its member; it was founded by French officials as a branch of the Jacobin Club of France.
    • Tipu planted the 'tree of liberty' at Srirangapatna as a symbol of Mysore-France friendship.
    • Tipu Sultan set up embassies abroad on modern lines: Iran, Istanbul, Afghanistan, France.UPPSC
    • He sent ambassadors to keep friendly relations and get help against the British.
    • Tipu gave money for making the idol of Goddess Sharda in the Sringeri temple.

    Begum Samru and other facts

    • Begum Samru (1750-1836 A.D.; some sources give birth year 1753) built a famous church at Sardhana near Meerut.UPPSC
    • Her husband was the European Walter Reinhardt Sombre (Walter Joseph Reinhardt), who gave military service to many states.
    • Sombre got the Jagir of Sardhana for helping Mughal emperor Shah Alam II defeat Zabita Khan (at the instance of Najaf Khan).
    • Begum Samru became ruler of Sardhana after her husband's death.
    • Revenue farming in Bengal was introduced by Murshid Quli Khan, not Ali Mardan Khan.
    • Sawai Jai Singh of Amber had Euclid's 'Elements of Geometry' translated into Sanskrit; observatories at Mathura, Ujjain, Jaipur, Delhi and Varanasi.
    • Mir Jafar conspired with the English against Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah in the Battle of Plassey (1757 A.D.).
    • In the Third Battle of Panipat (1761 A.D.) Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas, not Ibrahim Lodi.
