    Governor/Governor General/ Viceroy

    309 facts · 21 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Awadh was annexed in February 1856 by Dalhousie on the charge of maladministration against Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.×6
    2. Ripon's resolution of 18 May 1882 strengthened local self-government; he is 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India.×5
    3. Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793.×3
    4. Subsidiary Alliance system was introduced (given final shape, codified in 1798) by Lord Wellesley.×3
    5. Slavery abolished by Act V of 1843 under Governor-General Lord Ellenborough (tenure 1842–44).×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 69 UPPSC questions

    Robert Clive

    1. 1000Clive's gift ban was conditional: gifts above Rs. 1000 needed the Governor's prior permission.
    2. 1744Clive arrived in Madras in 1744 as a clerk of the East India Company.
    3. 17571757: Company troops defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey → creation of British Raj in India.
    4. 1764Battle of Buxar: 22/23 October 1764; fought under the leadership of Hector Munro.
    5. 1765Clive's re-arrival in India: 3 May 1765; Treaty of Allahabad: August 1765.
    6. 1765Clive enforced the Dual Government system in Bengal in 1765; administration divided into Diwani and Nizamat.
    7. 1766From 1 January 1766 double batta was given only to soldiers serving outside Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad).
    • Robert Clive is widely considered the founder of British India (British Empire in India).
    • Clive arrived in Madras in 1744 as a clerk of the East India Company.
    • Clive's leadership consolidated the Company's commercial and territorial position in India.
    • 1757: Company troops defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey → creation of British Raj in India.
    • Battle of Buxar: 22/23 October 1764; fought under the leadership of Hector Munro.
    • Clive's re-arrival in India: 3 May 1765; Treaty of Allahabad: August 1765.
    • Clive enforced the Dual Government system in Bengal in 1765; administration divided into Diwani and Nizamat.
    • Clive made both civil and military reforms of the Company's services.
    • Clive's civil reforms: banned gifts to officials, controlled (banned) private trade, made internal tax compulsory.
    • Clive's gift ban was conditional: gifts above Rs. 1000 needed the Governor's prior permission.
    • Clive's military reform: ended double batta (dual allowance) for European officers.
    • From 1 January 1766 double batta was given only to soldiers serving outside Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad).
    • Clive was not the first Governor-General of Bengal.

    Warren Hastings

    • Warren Hastings became Governor of Bengal in 1772 and Governor-General of Bengal in 1774.

    Note from the book One exam question wrongly called Warren Hastings "Governor of India"; he was Governor of Bengal (1772) and Governor-General of Bengal (1774).

    • Order of events: Battle of Buxar (1764) → Clive's re-arrival (May 1765) → Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765) → Warren Hastings Governor of Bengal (1772).
    • Regulating Act 1773: British Parliament set up government in Bengal = Governor-General + four councillors ("Council of four"), total five.
    • Regulating Act 1773 was passed after acquiring Bengal, to regulate Company administration; the Company's Governor became Governor-General of Bengal.
    • The Governor-General was head of government and chairman of the Executive Council; had a casting vote if votes were equal.
    • The council was established to look after the affairs of Bengal.
    • Warren Hastings = first Governor-General of Bengal (1774, under Regulating Act 1773).
    • Warren Hastings ended the dual government of Bengal in 1772 by order of the Court of Directors.
    • Court of Directors (1772) ordered the Calcutta council and its chiefs to act as Diwan and administer Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
    • Warren Hastings dismissed both deputy Diwans: Muhammad Raza Khan and Raja Shitab Roy.
    • Warren Hastings shifted the State treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta.
    • Warren Hastings believed the whole land belonged to the ruler.
    • In revenue reform Warren Hastings used the trial and error method.
    • Warren Hastings firmly laid the foundation of civil administration; Cornwallis raised the superstructure on it.
    • Banaras Rebellion (1781) was led by Raja Chet Singh.UPPSC
    • In the Banaras Rebellion Warren Hastings ran away with his soldiers and took refuge in Chunar Fort.
    • Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in Calcutta on 15 January 1784 by Sir William Jones, when Warren Hastings was Governor-General.UPPSC
    • Ring Fence policy (also called 'Security Cell' / policy of siege / buffer state) is related to Warren Hastings and Wellesley.UPPSC
    • Warren Hastings fought Mysore and the Marathas to gain status equal to other Indian states.
    • Ring Fence aim: create buffer states to protect Company territory from Afghans and Marathas.
    • Under Ring Fence the Company agreed to protect Oudh if the Nawab of Oudh bore the expenses.
    • Wellesley's main aim was to make Indian states rely on his army power.
    • Warren Hastings faced impeachment proceedings (1788–1795) for injustices, atrocities and arbitrary acts.UPPSC ×2
    • British Parliament dropped all charges in view of his service; he was acquitted in April 1795.
    • It was said that Warren Hastings had done all this for the benefit of the empire.
    • Pitt's India Act is matched with Warren Hastings.

    British policy towards Indian states

    PolicyPeriod
    Company's struggle for equality with Indian provinces1740–1765
    Ring Fence ('Security Cell' / policy of siege)1765–1813
    Subordinate Isolation (subordinate separation)1813–1857
    Subordinate Union1858–1935
    Equal Federation (equal union)1935–1947

    Cornwallis

    • Lord Cornwallis was Governor-General of Bengal 1786–1793 and again 30 July 1805 – 5 October 1805.
    • Cornwallis died at Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) on 5 October 1805; his grave/tomb is at Ghazipur.UPPSC
    • Cornwallis is known for Istamarari (Permanent Settlement), the judicial code and as promoter of Indian administrative services.
    • Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793.UPPSC ×3
    • Cornwallis's rule is remembered for two events: Permanent Settlement in Bengal and the Third Mysore War.
    • Major events of Cornwallis's tenure: ban on slave trade, start of civil services, police services, Permanent Settlement.
    • Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–1792) is associated with Cornwallis; he himself took charge of the army.UPPSC
    • Treaty of Srirangapatna (1792): Tipu Sultan gave up almost half of his state.
    • Reforms in police, judiciary, taxation and Faujdari-related Acts took place under Cornwallis.
    • British built a hierarchical justice system of Diwani and Faujdari courts; started by Warren Hastings, made more rigid by Cornwallis.
    • Cornwallis first concentrated all powers in the Collector.
    • 1787: District Collector made Diwani Judge of Diwani courts and given some Faujdari powers.
    • Cornwallis gave limited judicial powers to the Company's revenue collectors, who already served as civil magistrates.
    • Cornwallis established the judicial organisation in India; his criminal and judicial regulations still underpin the Indian judicial system.UPPSC
    • 1790: Company took over administration of justice from the Nawab.
    • Cornwallis introduced circuit courts with a superior court at Calcutta having power of review over circuit court decisions.
    • 1790–92: District Faujdari courts with Indian judges abolished; four Circuit Courts set up (three for Bengal, one for Bihar).
    • Circuit Courts were headed by European officials; justice delivered with help of Indian Kazis and Muftis.
    • Cornwallis started rule by specification of law: regulations codifying administrative, revenue and judicial reforms of the Company in Bengal.
    • Cornwallis Code (1793) = collection of his judicial reforms, based on 'Separation of Powers'.
    • Cornwallis Code separated revenue and judicial administration; Collector lost judicial and faujdari powers, kept only taxation powers.
    • A new hierarchy of officers was created for District Diwani Courts; District Judges were also given Faujdari and police work.
    • Cornwallis reorganised and professionalised the civil service (1793): created the Covenanted Civil Service, later the Indian Civil Service.UPPSC
    • Cornwallis forbade private trade and gifts, raised salaries, separated functions, gave legal form to civil service rules; called reformer of civil service.
    • Cornwallis restructured administration, abolished the revenue boards and laid down new laws for them.
    • 1793: Cornwallis removed police duties from landlords (zamindars); set up a police station in every 20–30 square miles.
    • The police officer of the station was the Daroga, appointed and supervised by the Magistrate.
    • Farmers saw the Daroga as local representative of the "aura and authority (pride) of Company Bahadur".UPPSC

    George Barlow and Vellore

    • Vellore Mutiny (1806) took place under Governor-General Sir George Barlow.
    • Vellore Mutiny was a protest against interference in social and religious practices of sepoys.
    • Vellore sepoys unfurled the flag of the ruler of Mysore.

    Wellesley and Subsidiary Alliance

    • Lord Wellesley was Governor-General 1798–1805.
    • Wellesley came to India in 1798 (one explanation prints 1797), the darkest period of British history.
    • Britain was then in a life-and-death struggle with France; the European front against France had been disbanded.
    • Napoleon had conquered Egypt and Syria and was seriously thinking of attacking India.
    • Wellesley used Subsidiary Alliance to establish British sovereignty and avert the fear of Napoleon; he kept the British flag flying.
    • Subsidiary Alliance system was introduced (given final shape, codified in 1798) by Lord Wellesley.UPPSC ×3
    • Wellesley first followed non-intervention in princely states, later adopted Subsidiary Alliance.
    • Wellesley did not invent the method; it existed earlier, evolved gradually and got final shape from him.
    • Dupleix was the first European to lend his army to an Indian ruler for a fixed payment.
    • First such British instance: 1765 treaty with Awadh (Oudh), precursor of subsidiary alliance; Company to guard Awadh's borders for fixed payment.

    Note from the book Nawab of Oudh is the first ruler to join a subsidiary alliance (1765); Hyderabad is the answer if asked the first state in Wellesley's subsidiary alliance.

    • Nizam of Hyderabad was the first to enter Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798 and 1800).
    • Order of Wellesley's alliances: Hyderabad (1798, 1800) → Mysore (1799) → Tanjore (October 1799) → Awadh (November 1801) → Peshwa (December 1802) → Bhonsle of Nagpur/Berar (December 1803) → Sindhia (February 1804).UPPSC
    • Bharatpur (1803–05) is also listed with Sindhia.
    • Other states listed: Holkar (1818), Jodhpur (1818), Udaipur/Mewar (1818), Bundi (February 1818), Bikaner (March 1818), Jaipur (April 1818), Machheri, Bharatpur.
    • Peshwa Bajirao II was the first Maratha chief to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance.
    • Treaty of Bassein (now Vasai): 31 December 1802, between English East India Company and Peshwa Bajirao II, after the Battle of Poona.UPPSC
    • Bassein terms: about 6,000 British troops to reinstate and protect the Peshwa at Poona; Peshwa to give land with revenue of 26 lakh a year.
    • Subsidiary Alliance aims: keep a large army at others' expense, guard India from Napoleonic danger, establish British paramountcy over Indian states.
    • Securing a fixed income for the Company was not an aim of Subsidiary Alliance.
    • Aim of subsidiary alliances with Rajput states: establish British sovereignty; brought Indian states within British political power.
    • Wellesley used the alliance to make Indian provinces puppets of the British.
    • Term 1: ruler accepts permanent British force in his territory and pays a subsidy for its maintenance.
    • Term 2: ruler accepts a British Resident in his state.
    • Term 3: ruler will not enter any further alliance with any other power.
    • Term 4: ruler will not employ Europeans other than the British.
    • Term 5: in conflict with another state, ruler accepts the resolution decided by the British.
    • Term 6: ruler acknowledges East India Company as paramount power in India.
    • Term 7: in return Company protects the state from external dangers and disorders.
    • Term 8: if payments fail, part of the ruler's territory is taken as penalty.
    • Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) took place under Lord Wellesley.UPPSC
    • Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) was fought under Lord Wellesley, not Lord Hastings.UPPSC
    • Major events of Wellesley's tenure: Subsidiary Alliance, Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Second Anglo-Maratha War, Fort William College at Calcutta.
    • Battle of Buxar 1764; trade in India opened for British citizens and companies 1813; Company's monopoly in India 1833.

    Lord Hastings

    1. 1813Lord Hastings was Governor-General 1813–23.
    2. 1814Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16) took place under Lord Hastings (not Sir John Shore); ended by Treaty of Sugauli.UPPSC ×2
    3. 1814First Anglo-Nepal war (1814) ended without result; second took place in 1815.
    4. 1815Treaty of Sugauli signed 2 December 1815, ratified 4 March 1816.
    5. 18151815: Almora in Kumaon was won; Major-General Ochterlony forced Gorkha sardar Amar Singh to hand over the Fort of Malwa.
    6. 1817Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) took place under Lord Hastings, not Cornwallis.UPPSC ×2
    7. 1817Charles Metcalf negotiated the subordinate alliances of 1817–18 with Rajputana states.
    8. 1818After the war Lord Hastings abolished the title of Peshwa (1818) and merged Peshwa's regions in Bombay Presidency.UPPSC
    9. 1820Sir Thomas Munro was Governor of Madras 1820–1827.UPPSC
    10. 1830British got control of the hill tract of Shimla; land for Shimla station/town was actually transferred in 1830 from Keonthal/Patiala.
    • Lord Hastings was Governor-General 1813–23.
    • Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16) took place under Lord Hastings (not Sir John Shore); ended by Treaty of Sugauli.UPPSC ×2
    • Treaty of Sugauli signed 2 December 1815, ratified 4 March 1816.
    • First Anglo-Nepal war (1814) ended without result; second took place in 1815.
    • 1815: Almora in Kumaon was won; Major-General Ochterlony forced Gorkha sardar Amar Singh to hand over the Fort of Malwa.
    • British army then stood only 30 miles from Kathmandu.
    • By Sugauli Nepal ceded Kumaon, eastern Garhwal and some parts of the Terai (also printed: Kumaon, Garhwal and Shimla districts).
    • Ranikhet and Nainital lie in Kumaon (present Uttarakhand), so they came under the Company by Sugauli.UPPSC
    • Kathmandu stayed Nepal's capital; the treaty only provided for a British Resident there.
    • British got control of the hill tract of Shimla; land for Shimla station/town was actually transferred in 1830 from Keonthal/Patiala.
    • Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) took place under Lord Hastings, not Cornwallis.UPPSC ×2
    • After the war Lord Hastings abolished the title of Peshwa (1818) and merged Peshwa's regions in Bombay Presidency.UPPSC
    • Company also took political authority over Bundelkhand, Malwa and other Peshwa-dominated regions.
    • Lord Hastings wanted British paramountcy; this needed suppression of Marathas and Pindaris.
    • He saw Rajputana states as natural allies against Marathas and Pindaris.
    • Charles Metcalf negotiated the subordinate alliances of 1817–18 with Rajputana states.
    • Sir Thomas Munro was Governor of Madras 1820–1827.UPPSC
    • Munro = father of the Ryotwari System: land tax collected directly from ryots (owners of land).

    William Bentinck

    • Lord William Bentinck became Governor-General of Bengal in July 1828; ruled seven years (1828–35); returned to England in 1835.
    • Charter Act 1833 tried to fully centralise administration; Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India.
    • Bentinck = first Governor-General of India (Charter Act 1833).
    • Charter Act 1833 was passed in Bentinck's time.
    • Under Bentinck the old policies of war and annexation were abandoned or reduced; he is remembered for administrative and social reforms, not for consolidating the empire.UPPSC
    • Bentinck's social reforms: abolition of Sati, abolition of slavery (Charter Act 1833), suppression of Thugs; also acted against female infanticide.
    • Bentinck is matched with social reforms; he also worked on education and freedom of the press.
    • Removal of disabilities due to change of religion came in 1850, not under Bentinck.
    • On the Court of Directors' wish Bentinck followed neutrality towards Indian states.
    • Jaipur misrule led to an attack on the British Resident, yet Bentinck did not interfere.
    • He also did not interfere in Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota and Bhopal.
    • Exceptions for extreme misrule: Bentinck took over Mysore (1831), Kachhar (1832), Kurg (1834) and Jayantia (1835).UPPSC ×2
    • Bentinck abolished Sati in 1829 by Bengal Sati Regulation = Regulation XVII (17) of 1829 of the Bengal Code; declared it a crime.UPPSC ×2
    • In 1830 the Sati regulation was extended to Madras and Bombay Presidencies.
    • Sati means 'holy and virtuous woman'; Hindu marriage is a Sanskar meaning 'relation of spirits'.
    • 18th-century Brahmins believed a Sati sent seven generations of her husband to heaven.
    • Sati was common among high Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Rajputs.
    • Akbar tried to abolish Sati; Marathas abolished it entirely in their state.
    • Portuguese tried to stop Sati in Goa; French in Chandranagar.
    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy started the campaign against Sati.
    • Bentinck appointed Captain Sleeman to suppress the Thugs.
    • Sleeman arrested 1562 thugs between 1826 and 1835; many hanged, the rest exiled for life.
    • Organised thuggee ended by 1839 (also printed: 1837).
    • Thugs included Hindus and Muslims; worshipped Kali, Durga or Bhavani; offered the cut head at the goddess's feet.
    • Macaulay laid the foundation of modern (English) education during Bentinck's tenure.
    • Macaulay's aim: 'a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in tastes, opinions, morals and intellect'.
    • Macaulay's proposal approved on 7 March 1835; English to be the language of high-level administration.
    • Charles Metcalfe removed restrictions on the press; called 'liberator of the Indian press (newspapers)'.UPPSC
    • Cleveland set up the 'Hill Assembly Plan' for development of Adivasis (Scheduled Tribes).
    • Cleveland put the whole hill range of the Pahariyas under one Hill Assembly of hereditary hill chiefs called sardars.
    • Hill Assembly met twice a year; could inflict or rescind capital punishment.
    • Sardars had to report all crimes and law-and-order problems of their villages to the authorities.

    Slavery

    1. 1789Export of slaves from Bengal was stopped by the declaration of 1789.
    2. 1811Laws on slaves were made in 1811 and 1823.
    3. 1833Charter Act 1833 asked the Governor to make a law ending slavery as early as possible.
    4. 1843Slavery abolished by Act V of 1843 under Governor-General Lord Ellenborough (tenure 1842–44).UPPSC ×3
    5. 1843Act of 1843 removed legal enforceability of slave property in civil courts; slavery illegal in most parts (also printed: all parts) of British India.
    6. 18601860: Indian Penal Code made slavery a crime.
    • Export of slaves from Bengal was stopped by the declaration of 1789.
    • Laws on slaves were made in 1811 and 1823.
    • Charter Act 1833 asked the Governor to make a law ending slavery as early as possible.
    • Slavery abolished by Act V of 1843 under Governor-General Lord Ellenborough (tenure 1842–44).UPPSC ×3
    • Act of 1843 removed legal enforceability of slave property in civil courts; slavery illegal in most parts (also printed: all parts) of British India.
    • 1860: Indian Penal Code made slavery a crime.
    • IPC was repealed and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita came into force in 2024.

    Auckland, Ellenborough and Afghan policy

    • First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–1842): Company vs Afghanistan, under Governor-General Lord Auckland, not Lytton.UPPSC
    • Sindh was fully merged into the British Empire in March 1843 under Lord Ellenborough (1842–44), by Charles Napier.UPPSC ×2
    • Also printed: the merger of Sindh was the main reason for the First Anglo-Afghan War.
    • Masterly Inactivity policy in Anglo-Afghan relations: began under Ellenborough, continued till Lord Northbrook.
    • Masterly Inactivity is linked with John Lawrence; the policy evolved and was fully followed in his time.UPPSC ×2
    • Term 'Masterly Inactivity' came from an article by J.W.S. Wiley in the Edinburgh Review.

    Dalhousie

    1. 1832Earlier railway proposals: early plan of 1832, Lord Hardinge's plan of 1844.
    2. 1835Part of Sikkim including Darjeeling was ceded in 1835; more Sikkim territory taken in 1850; Sikkim never fully merged with British India.
    3. 1848Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General 1848–56; came in 1848; also called 'The Earl of Dalhousie'.
    4. 1849Punjab was merged in 1849.
    5. 1853Dalhousie made the first comprehensive railway policy in 1853 and strongly promoted railways.
    6. 1853First railway line: Bombay to Thane, 1853, in Dalhousie's time.UPPSC ×2
    7. 1853Great Indian Peninsula Railway Company started the first rail service (Boribandar, Bombay to Thane, 1853).
    8. 18541854: James Outram became British Resident of Awadh in place of W.H. Sleeman; he was Resident at annexation.UPPSC
    9. 1854Dalhousie set up a separate Public Works Department (first in 1854); before him public works were under the army board.
    10. 1856Awadh was annexed in February 1856 by Dalhousie on the charge of maladministration against Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.UPPSC ×6
    11. 1857Henry Lawrence was British Resident at Lucknow in the 1857 revolt; killed by the revolutionaries.
    12. 1880Railway expansion sped up between 1880 and 1900; Curzon's role was administrative: Railway Board, 1905.
    • Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General 1848–56; came in 1848; also called 'The Earl of Dalhousie'.
    • Dalhousie's real name: James Andrew Broun Ramsay.
    • Dalhousie formulated and implemented the Doctrine of Lapse.UPPSC ×2
    • Doctrine of Lapse: annex a state if its ruler died childless or was manifestly incompetent.
    • Order of lapse annexations: Satara → Jaitpur, Sambalpur → Baghat → Udaipur → Jhansi → Nagpur; Karnataka and Jaipur are not in the list.UPPSC ×3
    State annexed by Doctrine of LapseYear
    Satara (first state annexed)1848UPPSC
    Jaitpur1849
    Sambalpur (in Orissa)1849
    Baghat1850
    Udaipur1852
    Jhansi1853 (also printed 1854)
    Nagpur1854
    • Punjab was merged in 1849.
    • Awadh was annexed in February 1856 by Dalhousie on the charge of maladministration against Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.UPPSC ×6
    • 1854: James Outram became British Resident of Awadh in place of W.H. Sleeman; he was Resident at annexation.UPPSC
    • Outram reported Awadh's administration corrupt (polluted) and people's condition miserable; this report was the basis of annexation.
    • Dalhousie sent the report to London to get permission to merge Awadh.
    • Henry Lawrence was British Resident at Lucknow in the 1857 revolt; killed by the revolutionaries.
    • Of Sind, Gwalior, Awadh and Satara, only Gwalior was not annexed by the British.
    • Dalhousie annexed part of Sikkim (Darjeeling and other far areas) on the pretext that its king misbehaved with two English doctors.UPPSC
    • Sikkim was a small state between Nepal and Bhutan.
    • Part of Sikkim including Darjeeling was ceded in 1835; more Sikkim territory taken in 1850; Sikkim never fully merged with British India.
    • Dalhousie made the first comprehensive railway policy in 1853 and strongly promoted railways.
    • Earlier railway proposals: early plan of 1832, Lord Hardinge's plan of 1844.
    • First railway line: Bombay to Thane, 1853, in Dalhousie's time.UPPSC ×2
    • Great Indian Peninsula Railway Company started the first rail service (Boribandar, Bombay to Thane, 1853).
    • Railway aim 1: carry raw materials from the interior to ports and open Indian markets to British goods.
    • Railway aim 2: move the army quickly to remote areas to crush revolts.
    • Railway expansion sped up between 1880 and 1900; Curzon's role was administrative: Railway Board, 1905.
    • Dalhousie set up a separate Public Works Department (first in 1854); before him public works were under the army board.
    • A large amount was spent on public works through the PWD.

    Canning and the Crown

    1. 1856Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was passed under Lord Canning by the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.UPPSC ×2
    2. 1857Queen's Proclamation was the most important result of the 1857 revolt.
    3. 1857Titles 'Rai Bahadur' and 'Khan Bahadur' were given to loyal native rulers and zamindars for suppressing the 1857 revolt; evidence of conferral in 1859 and 1860, so not under Ripon, Lytton, Mayo or Dufferin.
    4. 1858Government of India Act 1858 passed by British Parliament on 2 August 1858; power moved from Company to the Crown.
    5. 1858The 1858 Act legally abolished the Company and created the Secretary of State; it led to the Queen's Proclamation.
    6. 1858Queen's Proclamation was read by Lord Canning on 1 November 1858 at a Durbar in Allahabad (Prayagraj).UPPSC ×2
    7. 1858Queen Victoria became ruler of India in 1858.
    8. 1858Queen's Proclamation of 1858 restored the right of native rulers to adopt an heir; policy of conquest and annexation was abolished.UPPSC
    9. 18611861: Lord Canning appointed Alexander Cunningham as Archaeological Surveyor.
    10. 1896Dhondo Keshav Karve founded a widow ashram in Poona in 1896.
    • Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was passed under Lord Canning by the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.UPPSC ×2
    • The Act legalised widow remarriage and children born of it.
    • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was an important figure of the Bengal Renaissance.
    • Dhondo Keshav Karve and Vishnu Shastri were propagators of widow remarriage.
    • Dhondo Keshav Karve founded a widow ashram in Poona in 1896.
    • Government of India Act 1858 passed by British Parliament on 2 August 1858; power moved from Company to the Crown.
    • The 1858 Act legally abolished the Company and created the Secretary of State; it led to the Queen's Proclamation.
    • Queen's Proclamation was read by Lord Canning on 1 November 1858 at a Durbar in Allahabad (Prayagraj).UPPSC ×2
    • Queen's Proclamation was the most important result of the 1857 revolt.
    • Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.UPPSC
    • Queen Victoria became ruler of India in 1858.
    • Queen's Proclamation of 1858 restored the right of native rulers to adopt an heir; policy of conquest and annexation was abolished.UPPSC
    • The Proclamation changed policy towards native states so they could be used for rescue in a crisis.
    • Titles 'Rai Bahadur' and 'Khan Bahadur' were given to loyal native rulers and zamindars for suppressing the 1857 revolt; evidence of conferral in 1859 and 1860, so not under Ripon, Lytton, Mayo or Dufferin.
    • 1861: Lord Canning appointed Alexander Cunningham as Archaeological Surveyor.

    Mayo

    1. 1861Indian Councils Act 1861 began legislative devolution; Mayo's Resolution was its probable outcome.
    2. 1869Lord Mayo was Viceroy 1869–72.
    3. 1870Lord Mayo started financial decentralisation in 1870 (Mayo's Resolution of 1870).
    4. 1871Department of Archaeological Survey was set up in 1871 on recommendation of the Duke of Argyll, George John Douglas Campbell, Secretary of State.
    5. 1871The Earl of Mayo was Governor-General in 1871; Cunningham became Director General of the separate Archaeological Survey.
    6. 1872First census in British India: 1872, under Lord Mayo; regular (proper) census began in 1881 under Lord Ripon.UPPSC ×2
    • Lord Mayo was Viceroy 1869–72.
    • First census in British India: 1872, under Lord Mayo; regular (proper) census began in 1881 under Lord Ripon.UPPSC ×2
    • Lord Mayo was killed by a convict, Sher Ali Afridi, in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; first Viceroy killed in office.UPPSC ×2
    • Lord Mayo started financial decentralisation in 1870 (Mayo's Resolution of 1870).
    • Indian Councils Act 1861 began legislative devolution; Mayo's Resolution was its probable outcome.
    • Mayo's Resolution: first step to separate Central and Provincial finances; tried to rectify existing imparity; focused on actual needs of provinces.
    • Control of some departments (education, medical services, roads) passed to provincial governments, for efficiency and financial constraints.
    • This began local financial management; provinces could use local taxation to balance their budgets.
    • Resolution said local interest, supervision and care are needed for funds of education, sanitation, medical relief and local public works.
    • It hoped to develop self-government, strengthen municipal institutions and associate Natives and Europeans more in administration.
    • Department of Archaeological Survey was set up in 1871 on recommendation of the Duke of Argyll, George John Douglas Campbell, Secretary of State.
    • The Earl of Mayo was Governor-General in 1871; Cunningham became Director General of the separate Archaeological Survey.

    Note from the book A Chhattisgarh question on who set up the Archaeological Survey Department was cancelled, as neither Mayo nor Argyll was an option.

    Lytton

    • Lord Lytton became Viceroy in 1876 (served 1876–1880), appointed by Conservative Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli.
    • Lytton changed Afghan policy: followed the aggressive 'Forward Policy' in place of 'Masterly Inactivity'.
    • Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–1880) took place under Lytton.
    • Royal Titles Act was passed by British Parliament in 1876.
    • Grand Delhi Durbar held by Lytton in January 1877; Queen Victoria proclaimed Empress (Sovereign) of India on 1 January 1877.
    • Queen Victoria received the title Kaiser-i-Hind (Qaiser-i-Hind).
    • Vernacular Press Act (Native Press Act) 1878 was passed under Lord Lytton, not Curzon; also called the 'Gagging Act'.
    • Some historians call it the silencing act for its strict censorship.
    • The Act let government censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press and stop criticism of British policies.
    • Its purpose: control printing and circulation of seditious material causing disaffection against British Government.
    • Under the Act Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, Sahachar and many others were charged.
    • Sir Erskine Perry called it a dangerous step against India's right to expression.
    • S.N. Banerjee called it 'lightning from the sky'.
    • Indian Arms Act 1878: criminal offence for Indians to carry arms without a licence.
    • Arms Act did not apply to British, Anglo-Indians, Europeans and certain government personnel.
    • Famine Commission set up in 1878 under Sir Richard Strachey (Strachey Commission) in Lytton's time; it gave the Famine Codes.
    • The Famine Codes were criticised for handling of the 1876–1878 famine, which caused heavy loss of life.

    Ripon

    1. 18801880: Liberal Party came to power in England under Gladstone, a supporter of freedom; Lord Ripon was appointed Viceroy.
    2. 1881First Factory Act 1881 was made under Lord Ripon, for factories employing 100 or more.
    3. 1881Act of 1881: no employment of children below 7; children of 7–12 to work at most 9 hours a day; four holidays a month.
    4. 1881Act of 1881 also required dangerous machinery to be fenced; it focused on safety of child labour.

    6. 1882Ripon's resolution of 18 May 1882 strengthened local self-government; he is 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India.UPPSC ×5

    9. 1883Sir C.P. Ilbert, law member of the Viceroy's executive council, presented the Bill in the Legislative Council on 2 February 1883.
    10. 1891Second Factory Act 1891 gave a weekly holiday.
    • 1880: Liberal Party came to power in England under Gladstone, a supporter of freedom; Lord Ripon was appointed Viceroy.
    • Lord Ripon is seen as the most pro-Indian, most liberal Viceroy.
    • Ripon's resolution of 18 May 1882 strengthened local self-government; he is 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India.UPPSC ×5
    • The 1882 resolution is seen as the beginning of modern self-government in India.
    • Ripon wanted to develop municipalities; he said political education of the country begins there.
    • Local boards set up in rural areas; district sub-division, Tehsil or Taluka boards in every district; municipalities in cities.
    • These bodies were given several tasks and sources of income.
    • Ripon asked provinces to examine their finances and fix which expenses could pass to local administration.
    • First Factory Act 1881 was made under Lord Ripon, for factories employing 100 or more.
    • Act of 1881: no employment of children below 7; children of 7–12 to work at most 9 hours a day; four holidays a month.
    • Act of 1881 also required dangerous machinery to be fenced; it focused on safety of child labour.
    • Factory Act 1881 did not fix wages or allow trade unions.
    • Second Factory Act 1891 gave a weekly holiday.
    • N.M. Lokhande was a pioneer of the labour movement in India.
    • Lokhande improved working conditions of textile mill-hands in the 19th century; took bold initiatives on caste and communal issues.
    • Ilbert Bill (1883), under Ripon not Lytton: allow Indian judges and magistrates to try British offenders in criminal cases at district level.
    • Sir C.P. Ilbert, law member of the Viceroy's executive council, presented the Bill in the Legislative Council on 2 February 1883.
    • The Bill aimed to end judicial disqualification based on race and equalise European and Indian judges.
    • The Bill met intense opposition in Britain and from British settlers in India, who saw it as an attack on their privileges.

    Dufferin

    • Lord Dufferin was Viceroy 1884–88.
    • Third Anglo-Burma War: 1885; Burma added to British India on 1 January 1886 = last major extension of British territory, under Dufferin.
    • A.O. Hume founded the Indian National Congress during Dufferin's tenure.

    7. 1901Imperial Cadet Corps was formed under Curzon; approved by the Secretary of State in November 1901.

    Match of offices and persons

    • Offices by Act: Governor-General of Fort William in Bengal (Regulating Act 1773), Governor-General of India (Charter Act 1833), Governor-General and Viceroy (1858), Governor-General and Crown Representative (Government of India Act 1935).
    • Match given: Regulating Act 1773 → Cornwallis; Act of 1833 → Dalhousie; Act of 1858 → Minto; Act of 1935 → Wavell.

    Note from the book Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General under the 1773 Act; Cornwallis is matched only because Hastings was not among the choices.

    Chapter 45 · British rule, revolts and reform

    Economic Impact of British Rule on India

    102 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Permanent Settlement of land revenue was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793.×5
    2. Ryotwari System was devised by Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read; Cornwallis was not linked with it.×3
    3. 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' was written by Dadabhai Naoroji and published in 1901; it set out the drain theory.×3
    4. Dadabhai Naoroji (1825–1917), 'Grand Old Man of India', propounded the Drain of Wealth theory.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 19 UPPSC questions

    Home charges and trade policy

    • Indian administration was in British hands and run to serve the interests of England.
    • Home Charges = expenditure incurred in England by the Secretary of State for India on behalf of India (Indian Government).
    • Home Charges included: India Office establishment, pensions and gratuities paid in England to retired civil servants, purchase of military stores, interest on debts, interest on railway capital, non-effective army charges; funds for wars outside India were not included.
    • Home Charges also covered dividends to East India Company shareholders, interest on public debt raised abroad, civil and military charges, store purchases in England.
    • Interest and profit on private foreign capital was another important leakage from national income.
    • India made huge payments for banking, insurance and shipping services.
    • Imperial Preference = special privileges (concessions) on British imports in India; an empire-wide preferential tariff arrangement.
    • Under it Britain pledged free entry for most colonial goods while imposing tariffs on foreign imports.
    • Result: almost no (nominal) duty on British imports in India, but heavy duty on Indian exports in Britain.
    • The rich preferred to invest in land; so industries lacked capital and had no independent development under British rule.
    • Mid-18th century: Bengal emerged as an essential supply source for the Company's sales in Europe.
    • Company's staple exports from Bengal in mid-18th century: cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium (also cloth and sugar).
    • 40% of Central revenue was spent on the military force in British India.UPPSC

    Permanent Settlement

    • Permanent Settlement of land revenue was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793.UPPSC ×5
    • Other names: Istimrari, Malgujari (Maalguzari), Bishwedari.
    • It was launched in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Varanasi of U.P.; covered about 19% of British India.
    • Permanent Settlement was made with the Zamindars (landlords), recognised as proprietors (owners) of the land.
    • Zamindars gave 10/11 of total revenue to the Company and kept 1/11 for their duties.
    • In the Permanent Settlement Zamindars were small capitalists.
    • It recognised the rights of hereditary or lawful successors of the landlords.
    • Government believed these landlords would stay faithful to the British.
    • Landlords got the right to transfer or sell their land.
    • Revenue payable by each landlord for his Zamindari was fixed once and for all; tax rate would not rise in future.
    • All rights of landlords depended on paying the fixed revenue on the fixed date at the government treasury; rights ended on failure.
    • Sunset clause: if the Zamindar did not pay by sunset of the fixed date, his Zamindari was taken over, auctioned and passed to a new owner.
    • Reasons for increased litigation after 1793: loss of all rights on non-payment, and more intermediaries between farmers and landlords.
    • Many Zamindars did not issue pattas to farmers because there was no official check on them; they only had to pay 10/11 of collection.
    • In Bihar the Permanent Settlement ensured a fixed amount of revenue for the Company.
    • By the 19th century demand for land rose; landlords raised rents; peasants revolted.
    • Bengal (and Bihar) Tenancy Act 1885 defined the rights of landlords and tenants in Bengal and Bihar.

    Ryotwari System

    • Ryotwari System was devised by Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read; Cornwallis was not linked with it.UPPSC ×3
    • Ryotwari was the second land revenue system after Permanent Settlement.
    • Alexander Read first applied it in Baramahal district (Tamil Nadu), acquired by the Company in 1792; first settlement of Madras Presidency.UPPSC
    • Read, assisted by Munro, fixed the state demand at 50% of the estimated produce of the fields.
    • Munro as Governor of Madras (1820–27) extended Ryotwari to all parts of the province except permanently settled areas.
    • Also printed: Munro and Read introduced the Ryotwari system in 1820.
    • Ryotwari spread to Madras, some parts of Bombay, Assam and Coorg (part of modern Karnataka); one list adds Eastern Bengal.UPPSC
    • Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal and Ryotwari in Madras.
    • Ryotwari prevailed in most of South India; it was the standard system of Madras Presidency.
    • In Ryotwari the ryot (peasant) owns and occupies the land and pays revenue directly to the government.
    • Every registered holder of land is recognised as proprietor and is responsible for direct payment to the state.
    • Ryotwari features: rent paid directly by peasants, government gave pattas to ryots, lands surveyed and assessed before being taxed.
    • Ryotwari covered about 51% of British India.
    • Land tax rate was very high and collection very strict; this became a major cause of struggle between moneylenders and peasants.
    • Ryots were not exempted from revenue for bad harvests or natural calamities; only a few remissions or reduced rents sometimes.
    • Thomas Munro said: "The Ryotwari is a system which has always prevailed in India."
    • Mirasidars = village elites of South India, often high caste, who claimed ownership of the whole village land; farmers worked under them.
    • Banian = Indian agent of the East India Company doing commercial work; Mirasidar = designated revenue payer to the state in Ryotwari.
    • Aurang = Persian term for a warehouse where goods are collected before sale (not in-charge of treasury).

    Mahalwari and other systems

    • Mahalwari System: unit of revenue settlement is the village or mahal; village land belongs to the village community.
    • The community was jointly responsible for paying the land revenue.
    • Mahalwari covered about 30% of British India: United Provinces, Central Provinces and Punjab (with some changes).
    • Mahalwari was devised by Holt Mackenzie, territorial secretary of the Board of Revenue, in 1822 in Bengal Presidency.
    • Under Mahalwari the whole village was one unit called 'Mahal'; revenue was not fixed but revised periodically.
    • British used different land revenue systems (Permanent, Ryotwari, Mahalwari) in different parts; this created different classes in the peasantry.UPPSC
    • Mahalwari is matched with the North-West Provinces.
    • Bombay Presidency mainly had Ryotwari; Taluqdari system was chiefly in Awadh (Oudh), not Bombay.UPPSC
    • Punjab Land Alienation Act passed in 1900; it stopped land transfer from farmers to non-farmers.
    SystemRegion
    JajmaniNorth IndiaUPPSC
    Bara BaluteMaharashtra
    MirasiTamil Nadu
    AdadeKarnataka

    Drain of wealth

    • Drain of wealth = constant flow of wealth from India to England without adequate economic, commercial or material return.
    • Drain Theory: part of India's national wealth or annual product was exported to Britain for which India got no material return.
    • Before 1813 the Company's recurring surplus came from oppressive land revenue, monopoly trade profits and exactions by Company officials.
    • The Company used this surplus as 'investment' to buy exportable goods in India and elsewhere; India got nothing in return.
    • This system was ended by the Charter Act of 1813.
    • From 1813 the drain took the form of 'unrequited' exports; so India generally had a favourable balance of trade till World War II.UPPSC
    • Dadabhai Naoroji called the drain the "evil of all evils" and the main cause of Indian poverty.
    • Dadabhai Naoroji (1825–1917), 'Grand Old Man of India', propounded the Drain of Wealth theory.UPPSC ×2
    • Naoroji's works: 'England's Duties to India' (paper), 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India', 'The Wants and Means of India', 'On the Commerce of India'.
    • 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' was written by Dadabhai Naoroji and published in 1901; it set out the drain theory.UPPSC ×3
    • The theory is attributed to Naoroji partly because he decided to estimate India's national net profit.
    • Naoroji's causes of drain: external rule and administration; India paid Britain's civil and army expenses; wealth sent to England without return.
    • Naoroji: India bore the burden of territory building inside and outside India.
    • Naoroji's most effective contribution: he exposed the economic exploitation of India by the British.
    • He was the first Indian nationalist to prove by research that a definite amount was sent to England every year.
    • Naoroji with W.C. Bonnerjee founded the London Indian Society in 1865 to expose the plight and exploitation of Indians.
    • Naoroji was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, on the Liberal Party ticket, in 1892.
    • Romesh Chunder Dutt also stressed the drain; in 'The Economic History of India' he said half of India's net revenue flowed out every year.
    • Indian National Congress accepted the Drain Theory at its Calcutta session, 1896.
    • Congress (1896) declared the drain the real cause of frequent famines and poverty of Indians.
    • Economic critics of colonialism (1870–1905): Dadabhai Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer, R.C. Dutt, Govind Ranade, G.V. Joshi, Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
    • R.C. Dutt was an ICS officer; these critics wrote India's economic history and held colonialism the main hurdle to economic growth.
    • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan did not believe in the drain theory; he was loyal to the British and felt Muslims could develop only under British rule.
    • Karl Marx called British economic policy in India disgusting.
    • Under British rule a vast number of Indian cultivators lived in dejection and unmitigated impoverishment.

    Deindustrialisation and commercial agriculture

    • Deindustrialisation in India started in 1813; ending the Company's trade monopoly aggravated it.UPPSC
    • 1813: Company's commercial monopoly ended, except tea and opium trade and trade with China.
    • Saint Helena Act 1833 (Government of India Act 1833) ended the Company as a trading body; it became purely administrative.
    • By the 1833 Act the Company lost its monopoly of trade with China and other parts of the Far East.
    • First half of 19th century: Industrial Revolution ruined Indian handicrafts.
    • British policy turned India into an exporter of raw materials and a consumer of finished goods.
    • Machine-made British goods were cheap and good; demand for Indian handicrafts fell even at home.
    • Indian goods could not sell in Britain because of high tariffs.
    • Commercialisation of Indian agriculture was an economic result of British rule in the 19th century.
    • Farmers were forced to grow indigo and other cash crops as raw material for British factories.
    • Result: urban population declined and domestic industries were destroyed.
    • 19th-century agriculture also became commercial through use of modern agricultural equipment; Indians began growing crops for commercial use on a large scale.
    • Assam Company, the first tea company in Assam, was formed in England in 1839 with a capital of Rs. 5 lakh.UPPSC
    • Assam Company's headquarters is at Nazira, Assam; oldest tea company in Assam still working.
    • Sir Arthur Cotton, a British irrigation engineer, is the pioneer of irrigation works in South India.

    Chapter 46 · British rule, revolts and reform

    Revolt of 1857

    210 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Lord Canning (1856–62) was Governor-General during the revolt of 1857.×3
    2. The revolt began on 10 May 1857 at Meerut.×2
    3. Tatya Tope's real name: Ramchandra Pandurang Tope.×2
    4. Khan Bahadur Khan of Rohilkhand led the revolt at Bareilly.×2
    5. Maulvi Liyaqat Ali led the 1857 uprising at Allahabad (Prayagraj), not Lucknow.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 36 UPPSC questions

    Causes and the cartridge issue

    • December 1856: Company decided to replace the old iron Brown Bess (standardised musket) with the new Enfield Rifle.
    • Training and trials of the new rifle were fixed at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot.
    • The upper cover of the cartridge had to be bitten off by mouth while loading it into the muzzle.
    • January 1857: rumour spread that cartridges were deliberately greased with cow and pig fat.
    • Sepoys believed the rifle was a British attempt to destroy their religion; this suspicion of interference in religion was the immediate cause of the revolt.
    • The cartridge issue insulted both Hindu and Muslim religious practices.
    • Anglo-Indian historians held sepoy discontent and greased cartridges to be the main cause.
    • Modern historians: cartridges were only a spark that set off explosives piled up by political, social, religious and economic discontent.
    • Main cause of the revolt was the (exploitative) policy of the British Empire; grievances burst out like a volcano.UPPSC
    • The revolt had diverse political, economic, military, religious and social causes.
    • Sepoys = generic term for native Indian soldiers of the Bengal Army; they had their own grievances against the Company.
    • Underlying grievances included taxation and land annexations by the Company.
    • Within weeks dozens of army units joined the peasant army in widespread rebellion.
    • The old aristocracy, Hindu and Muslim, whose power the Company was eroding, also rebelled.
    • Sepoy grievances: officers' efforts to spread Christianity, order to travel on ships, stoppage of Bhatta; inefficiency of officers was not a cause.
    • Hindus believed sea travel could cost them their religious status.
    • A more immediate grievance: no foreign service allowance (Bhatta/Batta) for serving in Sindh or Punjab.
    • Sir William Howard Russell, correspondent of 'The Times' (London), wrote: "Nobody in North India looks at the white man's car with a friendly view."
    • Russell was an Irish reporter sent to India by The Times to report on the 1857 mutiny.

    Barrackpore and Mangal Pandey

    • First sepoys to refuse cartridge practice were at Berhampore in late February 1857; refusal then spread.
    • 29 March 1857: soldiers at Barrackpore (West Bengal) refused the greased cartridges; Mangal Pandey attacked and wounded two officers.UPPSC
    • The two officers: Sergeant Major James Thornton Hewson and Lieutenant and Adjutant Henry Baugh.
    • Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry.
    • The British disbanded the 34th Bengal Native Infantry Regiment and punished the culprits.
    • Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857, not on 29 March 1857.
    • Lieutenant General Sir John Bennet Hearsey was commanding officer at Barrackpore when the revolt broke out.UPPSC

    Meerut and Delhi

    • The revolt began on 10 May 1857 at Meerut.UPPSC ×2
    • At Meerut the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry (85 of 90 troopers) refused the new cartridges and rebelled openly.
    • Also printed: the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry and the twentieth regiment of the British Indian Army at Meerut revolted on 10 May 1857.
    • Meerut sepoys fired on (murdered) their officers, broke the jail, freed imprisoned comrades and marched to Delhi.
    • Major General William Hewitt had 2200 European soldiers but did not try to stop them.
    • The march of sepoys to Delhi's Red Fort was the first event of the 1857 war.UPPSC
    • Lieutenant General George Dobson Percival Willoughby resisted at Delhi but was defeated.
    • Delhi sepoys joined the rebels; rebels captured Delhi on 12 May 1857.
    • On 11 May the sepoys proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar Emperor of Hindustan (India).
    • Bahadur Shah was old and could not give able leadership.
    • Success at Delhi spread the revolt to Oudh, Rohilkhand, Western Bihar and other areas.
    • Bahadur Shah gave Bakht Khan real authority and the title 'Saheb-e-Alam Bahadur'; Bakht Khan's area was Delhi.UPPSC
    • Nawab Hamid Ali Khan is matched with Delhi.UPPSC
    • May 1857: Battle of Shamli between forces of Hazi Imdadullah and the British.
    • Occupation of Delhi was short-lived; the English recaptured Delhi on 20 September 1857 (also printed 20–21 September).UPPSC
    • Sikhs and Pathans of Punjab and North West Frontier Province helped the British recapture Delhi.
    • Chapatis (bread) and lotus flowers carried the message; they are the symbol of the revolt.
    • Some historians call the mutiny a wide, well-planned conspiracy.
    • They cite chapatis and lotus reaching remote North Indian villages, and prophets, hermits and plays of Madaris.
    • The 1857 revolt was the first expression of organised resistance; began as a sepoy revolt, later joined by the masses.

    Jhansi

    • Rani Lakshmi Bai (Manikarnika) was born at Kashi/Benaras (now Varanasi).UPPSC
    • Her birth date is printed as c. 19 November 1828 in one place and 19 November 1835 in another.
    • Her father Moropant went to the court of King Gangadhar Rao.
    • At 14 she married Maharaja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi, a Maratha king; she was his widow.
    • 1853: Gangadhar Rao died without a biological heir; adopted son Damodar Rao was left as heir.
    • Dalhousie did not recognise the adopted son and annexed Jhansi by Doctrine of Lapse in 1854.
    • Doctrine of Lapse: kingdom of a ruler dying without a biological heir is annexed by the Company.
    • Revolt in Jhansi began in June 1857 (4 June 1857), not 11 May; sepoys started it and Lakshmi Bai later took control.UPPSC
    • Rani left for Gwalior after the fall of Jhansi; her revolt ended with her martyrdom after a long battle.
    • Lakshmi Bai died on 17/18 June 1858 at Gwalior; her samadhi (mausoleum) is in Gwalior.
    • Her last battle was against General Hugh Henry Rose.
    • Hugh Rose: "Among the Indian revolutionaries the woman lying here is the only man."
    • Another wording of Hugh Rose: "Sleeping Beauty is the only man among all Indian rebel leaders."

    Lucknow and Oudh

    • Revolt at Lucknow (Oudh) began on 30 May 1857 under Begum Hazrat Mahal.UPPSC
    • She declared her minor son Birjis Qadr Nawab and took charge of all affairs.

    Note from the book Many reference books and official websites give 4 June 1857 as the start of the Lucknow revolt, while the NCERT class 12 book gives 30 May 1857.

    • Hazrat Mahal was the wife of Wajid Ali Shah.
    • 21 March 1858: Colin Campbell regained Lucknow with the help of the Gurkha Regiment.
    • Nana Saheb and Begum Hazrat Mahal both escaped to Nepal.
    • Nana Saheb fled to Nepal in 1859 after the British retook Kanpur; his later fate is unclear (died there, or lived in disguise).
    • Hazrat Mahal fled to Nepal in 1858 after Lucknow was retaken; she died there in 1879.
    • The largest number of sepoys in the revolt came from Oudh: more than 75,000; one member of each family joined.UPPSC
    • During the revolt 60% of Bengal Army soldiers were from Oudh and the North West Province.
    • Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah led the revolt from Faizabad (now Ayodhya); also matched with Awadh and Lucknow.
    • Ahmadullah Shah was the bitterest enemy of the British.
    • He was native of Chinapattan (Madras) and migrated to Faizabad.
    • He asked people of all religions to unite and wipe the English out of India.
    • British view: 'a man of great abilities, of undaunted courage, of stern determination and by far the best soldier among the rebels'.
    • A reward of Rs. 50,000 was placed on his arrest (dead or alive).

    Kanpur

    • 5 June 1857: rebel sepoys halted at Kalyanpur; 6 June they returned to Kanpur and Nana Saheb (Nana Dhondhu Pant) took their lead.
    • Nana Saheb was proclaimed Peshwa at Kanpur (30 June 1857 as per R.C. Majumdar; also printed: Nana Saheb revolted and was accepted as Peshwa on 5 June 1857).
    • Tatya Tope was Nana Saheb's commander-in-chief (general military advisor).UPPSC
    • Tatya Tope's real name: Ramchandra Pandurang Tope.UPPSC ×2
    • Tatya Tope was betrayed by his friend Man Singh, captured in the forest of Paron and put to death by the British.
    • Captured 7 April 1859; military court verdict 15 April 1859; hanged 18 April 1859 at Sipri/Shivpuri.
    • Tatya Tope was born in 1814 at Yeola, Maharashtra; only child of Pandurang and Rukhmabai.
    • He grew up at Bithoor, where he met Nana Saheb Peshwa; a personal adherent and great admirer of Nana Saheb.
    • After British reoccupation of Kanpur he led the Gwalior contingent and forced Lieutenant General Charles Ash Windham to retreat from Kanpur.
    • He later came to the rescue of Rani Lakshmibai; was defeated by General Napier's troops.
    • Tatya Tope was the only person who saw the rebellion from the Kanpur revolt to his end on 18 April 1859.
    • Azimullah Khan was advisor and secretary of Nana Saheb; called 'Krantidoot'.
    • Azimullah Khan is matched with the revolt at Kanpur and Fatehpur.UPPSC

    Bareilly and Allahabad

    • Khan Bahadur Khan of Rohilkhand led the revolt at Bareilly.UPPSC ×2
    • Bahadur Shah II appointed him Viceroy in Rohilkhand.
    • He raised an army of 40 thousand and fought hard; treated Hindus and Muslims equally.
    • Maulvi Liyaqat Ali led the 1857 uprising at Allahabad (Prayagraj), not Lucknow.UPPSC ×2
    • Liyaqat Ali belonged to village Mahgaon, Chail Pargana, District Allahabad; a religious teacher.
    • He captured Khusro Bagh and declared India's independence; Khusro Bagh became sepoy headquarters.
    • He took charge as Governor of liberated Allahabad; the mutiny there was suppressed by General Neil.
    • Sambhalpur – Surender Sahi; Ganjam – Radhakrishna Dandsena; Kashmir – Gulab Singh.

    Bihar and Kunwar Singh

    • Kunwar Singh led the 1857 revolt in Bihar.
    • Kunwar Singh was zamindar (king) of Jagdishpur (now Bhojpur district) in Shahabad region of Bihar; born there.UPPSC
    • Jagdishpur was the centre of the Bihar revolt; Kunwar Singh deposed British rule and set up his own government.
    • He lost his zamindari due to British policies, so he joined the revolt.
    • The mutiny at Patna (Danapur) was led by Kunwar Singh, a dynamic old Rajput.
    • Babu Kunwar Singh was nearly eighty years old in 1857.
    • 25 July 1857: he took command of soldiers who revolted at Danapur; two days later he occupied Arrah, the district headquarters.

    Note from the book BPSC's own key gave Patna as the place where Kunwar Singh joined the rebellion; this is called wrong, and Arrah is correct.

    • August 1857: Major Vincent Eyre relieved Arrah, defeated Kunwar Singh and destroyed Jagdishpur.
    • Kunwar Singh reached Lucknow in December 1857; occupied Azamgarh in March 1858 but soon left.
    • Pursued by Brigadier Douglas, he retreated to Bihar.
    • 23 April 1858: victory near Jagdishpur over Captain Le Grand; 26 April 1858: he died in his village.
    • His brother Amar Singh continued the struggle and ran a parallel government in Shahabad district for long.
    • October 1859: Amar Singh joined the rebel leaders in the Nepal Terai.
    • Bihar revolt was suppressed by William Taylor, Commissioner of Patna division, and Major Vincent Eyre.
    • Bihar centres of revolt: Arrah, Danapur, Gaya, Patna, Muzaffarpur, Shahabad; Munger was unaffected.

    Other centres and leaders

    1. 1797Ghalib was born on 27 December 1797 in Agra and died in Delhi on 15 February 1869.UPPSC
    2. 1857Maniram Dutt Dewan, an Assamese nobleman, led the 1857 plot in Assam.UPPSC
    3. 1857Saadat Ali Khan fought the British in 1857 at Indore.
    4. 1857Nawab Fazil Mohammad Khan of Bhopal led the main movement there and gave his life in 1857.
    5. 1857Leaders active in 1857: Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Tatya Tope, Nana Saheb (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Maulavi Ahmadullah (Faizabad), Begum Zeenat Mahal (Delhi).
    6. 1857Bhagat Singh was not linked with 1857; Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar and Tatya Tope were rebel leaders.
    7. 1857Uddham Singh was not linked with 1857; he was a revolutionary of Punjab.UPPSC
    8. 1857Col. St. Legar, Lt. Col. Gibbs and Col. Wallace are not associated with the Revolt of 1857.UPPSC
    9. 1857Mirza Ghalib saw the revolt of 1857 with his own eyes.
    • Maniram Dutt Dewan, an Assamese nobleman, led the 1857 plot in Assam.UPPSC
    • He declared Kandarpeswar Singha, grandson of the last king, as king and planned an armed insurrection; was caught and hanged.
    • Thakur Kushal Singh of Auwa defeated the joint army of the English and Jodhpur.
    • Ajmer, Neemuch and Auwa were centres of the revolt; Jaipur was not.
    • Saadat Ali Khan fought the British in 1857 at Indore.
    • Nawab Fazil Mohammad Khan of Bhopal led the main movement there and gave his life in 1857.
    • Leaders active in 1857: Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Tatya Tope, Nana Saheb (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Maulavi Ahmadullah (Faizabad), Begum Zeenat Mahal (Delhi).
    • Bhagat Singh was not linked with 1857; Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar and Tatya Tope were rebel leaders.
    • Uddham Singh was not linked with 1857; he was a revolutionary of Punjab.UPPSC
    • Col. St. Legar, Lt. Col. Gibbs and Col. Wallace are not associated with the Revolt of 1857.UPPSC
    • Chittor was not affected by the revolt; Jhansi, Jagdishpur and Lucknow were prominent centres.
    • Mirza Ghalib saw the revolt of 1857 with his own eyes.
    • Ghalib was born on 27 December 1797 in Agra and died in Delhi on 15 February 1869.UPPSC

    Who helped the British

    • Scindias of Gwalior gave the most help to the British in suppressing the revolt.
    • Canning said: "If Scindia joins the rebels, I will pack off tomorrow."
    • Sir Dinkar Rao, minister of Gwalior, and Salar Jung, minister of Hyderabad, were praised by European historians for loyalty.
    • Rulers who actively helped the British: Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore, Nizam of Hyderabad, King of Jodhpur, Nawab of Bhopal.
    • Also: Sikh rulers of Patiala, Nabha and Jind, other Sikh sardars of Punjab, Maharaja of Kashmir.
    • Canning said these rulers acted as barriers against the high, fast-moving wave of the sea, without which the British would have been washed out.
    • Nizam of Hyderabad did not rebel against the Company; Raja of Vijayanagaram, Polygar of Tamil Nadu and Dewan Velu Thampi of Travancore did.
    • The British suppressed the revolt in Rajput states because local Rajput rulers did not support the rebels.
    • The educated middle class remained neutral (or sided with the British).
    • They saw the rebellion as regressive, reactionary and anti-modern; believed the British would bring progress.
    • Later they came to know the cruel strategy of the British behind this.
    • Moneylenders (sahukars) and landlords did not take part; moneylenders and merchants opposed it for economic reasons.

    Spread and reasons for failure

    • The revolt spread over a wide area with public support, yet did not become an all-India revolt.
    • South India stayed largely quiet; Bengal and Punjab were only marginally affected; parts of eastern and western India were involved.
    • Another list of areas outside the revolt: entire South India, Punjab and land to its north and west, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh.
    • Main cause of failure: lack of common strategy and central organisation (leadership).
    • The revolt was poorly organised, with little coordination and nominal central leadership.
    • Rebels lacked a clear understanding of colonial rule, a forward-looking programme, coherent ideology, political perspective or social alternative.
    • Official sources record much Hindu-Muslim and inter-regional unity among rebels, but central leaders lacked unity.
    • Modern nationalism was unknown; each fought for own interest, sharing only hatred of alien rule.
    • Failure causes: limited area, no unity or planning, no unified leadership and discipline, better British resources, traitors, British troops back from Crimea.UPPSC
    • Also: least support of native rulers; non-cooperation of Sikhs, Punjabis and the educated middle class.
    • Bahadur Shah Zafar's leadership lacked popular support and rulers of important states stayed away; so the revolt failed to win freedom.
    • Most important reason for failure: native kings of major territories supported the British.

    British officers and government

    1. 1855Viscount Palmerston (Henry John Temple, 3rd Viscount) was British Prime Minister during the revolt; tenure 1855–1858 and 1859–1865.UPPSC
    2. 1856Lord Canning (1856–62) was Governor-General during the revolt of 1857.UPPSC ×3
    3. 1856Canning passed the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856.
    4. 1857Canning made Allahabad (Prayagraj) the emergency headquarters in 1857.UPPSC
    5. 1857Brigadier General John Nicholson was wounded leading the capture of Delhi; died nine days later on 23 September 1857.
    6. 1857Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence, Chief Commissioner of Oudh ('Lawrence of Lucknow'), was wounded on 2 July and died on 4 July 1857 defending the Residency.
    7. 1857Brigadier General James George Smith Neill died in September 1857 trying to reach the Residency during the siege.
    8. 1857Major-General Sir Henry Havelock died of dysentery in November 1857, a few days after the siege was lifted.
    9. 1861Indian High Courts Act 1861 set up High Courts at Bombay, Calcutta and Madras; formally established by Letters Patent of 1862 under Canning.
    • Lord Canning (1856–62) was Governor-General during the revolt of 1857.UPPSC ×3
    • Canning was the last Governor-General appointed by the Company and the first Viceroy appointed by the Crown.
    • Canning made Allahabad (Prayagraj) the emergency headquarters in 1857.UPPSC
    • Indian High Courts Act 1861 set up High Courts at Bombay, Calcutta and Madras; formally established by Letters Patent of 1862 under Canning.
    • Canning passed the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856.
    • Viscount Palmerston (Henry John Temple, 3rd Viscount) was British Prime Minister during the revolt; tenure 1855–1858 and 1859–1865.UPPSC
    • Sir Henry Lawrence, Major General Henry Havelock and Brigadier General Neil died at Lucknow.UPPSC
    • Brigadier General John Nicholson was wounded leading the capture of Delhi; died nine days later on 23 September 1857.
    • Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence, Chief Commissioner of Oudh ('Lawrence of Lucknow'), was wounded on 2 July and died on 4 July 1857 defending the Residency.
    • Brigadier General James George Smith Neill died in September 1857 trying to reach the Residency during the siege.
    • Major-General Sir Henry Havelock died of dysentery in November 1857, a few days after the siege was lifted.

    Views and books on 1857

    • The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 is called the First War of Independence in India and the Indian Mutiny in England.
    • Sir James Outram and W. Taylor called the revolt a result of a Hindu-Muslim conspiracy.
    • Outram: a Muslim conspiracy that made use of Hindu grievances.
    • John Lawrence and Seeley: only a Sepoy Mutiny.
    • T.R. Holmes: a war between barbarism and civilisation.
    • V.D. Savarkar, in 'The Indian War of Independence 1857', called it a planned, organised struggle and the First War of Independence.UPPSC
    • R.C. Majumdar: "the so-called First National War of Independence of 1857 is neither First, nor National, nor a war of Independence".UPPSC ×2
    • Majumdar's reason: a large part of the country was unaffected and many sections took no part.
    • Government of India appointed Majumdar to write on 1857; after differences he published 'The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857' on his own in 1957.
    • Majumdar's first proposal was turned down; later he joined the Board of Editors for the freedom movement history, then left and wrote independently.
    • Surendra Nath Sen = official historian; his 'Eighteen Fifty-Seven' was published in 1957, commissioned by the Indian government.UPPSC
    • S.N. Sen was the first Director of the National Archives of India.
    • R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen held that Indian nationalism in the mid-19th century was in an embryonic stage.
    • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wrote 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (Urdu): first Indian to write in an Indian language on the causes of 1857.UPPSC
    • It was written/submitted in 1858 and published in 1859; later translated as 'The Causes of the Indian Revolt'.

    Results of the revolt

    • The revolt gave a death blow to East India Company rule; rule passed to Queen Victoria.UPPSC
    • Queen's Proclamation was declared on 1 November 1858 at a Durbar in Allahabad by Lord Canning.
    • The Proclamation was the most important outcome of 1857; it put British India under direct control of the Crown.
    • Proclamation promises: no extension of territory, no interference in religion, equal protection of law for all.
    • Also: secularism and religious neutrality; no more annexation of native states; kings allowed to adopt.
    • Of all assurances only the abandonment of conquest and annexation was fulfilled.UPPSC
    • Objects of the Proclamation: disclaim annexation of Indian states and place Indian administration under the Crown; not to regulate Company trade.
    • The Act of 1858 is called the 'Act of Administrative Reforms in India'.
    • 1858 Act: Company territories to be governed by and in the name of the Queen; Company lost its powers.
    • Secretary of State for India got the powers of the Court of Directors; a Council of fifteen members assisted him as an advisory body.
    • Secretary of State became the real channel of communication between Britain and India.
    • The Crown could appoint the Governor-General and Governors of Presidencies.
    • An Indian Civil Service was to be created under the Secretary of State.
    • All Company property and assets passed to the Crown, along with its treaties and contracts.
    • Peel Commission was set up after the revolt to reorganise the Indian Army.
    • The Commission divided the army on caste, religion, race and community lines.
    • European soldiers rose from 45,000 (1857) to 65,000 (1863); Indian troops cut from 2,38,000 to 1,40,000.
    • Ratio of European to Indian soldiers: 1:2 in Bengal; 1:3 in Madras and Bombay.
    • After the revolt the British recruited Gurkhas, Sikhs and Punjabis from the north.
    • Soldiers of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar had played a big role in the revolt, so the British distrusted them.
    • 1 November 1858: Queen Victoria declared reorganisation of the army on a policy of separation and conflict.

    Other Civil Uprisings

    Quick quiz: 10 of 26 UPPSC questions

    Indigo Revolt

    • The revolt of 1857 gave confidence to fight the British and led to other civil uprisings.
    • Indigo Revolt (1859–60) took place in Bengal immediately after the revolt of 1857.
    • Indigo Revolt began in Govindpur village, Nadia district, West Bengal.
    • Leaders: Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas, former employees of an indigo planter; peasants refused to sow indigo.
    • Cause: British planters forced peasants to take advances and sign fraudulent contracts, to grow indigo on least profitable (unacceptable) terms.
    • September 1859: all cultivators revolted; all indigo factories shut down due to the strike.
    • By 1860 it spread to Nadia, Pabna, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur.
    • Bengal's intelligentsia supported it through public meetings, rallies, journals and newspaper articles.
    • Harishchandra Mukherjee, editor of 'Hindu Patriot', played a major role.
    • Dinabandhu Mitra wrote the play 'Neel Darpan' (1858–1859) on the atrocities of indigo planters on farmers.UPPSC
    • Indigo cultivation declined by the early 20th century: artificial dyes made it unprofitable in the world market.

    Sanyasi Revolt and Bankim Chandra

    • Sanyasi Rebellion (Bengal): 1763–1800.
    • Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel 'Anandamath' is based on the Sanyasi Revolt; he made it famous.UPPSC ×3
    • 'Vande Mataram', the national song, is taken from Anandamath; composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee.
    • 'Vande Mataram' was first sung at the Calcutta session of Congress, 1896, by Rabindranath Tagore.
    • Causes of Sanyasi revolt: peasants, landlords and artisans ruined by British rule and its new economic policy.
    • A terrible famine came in 1770; sanyasis were humiliated by the ban on pilgrimage.
    • Warren Hastings suppressed the Sanyasi uprising after a long campaign.
    • Bankim Chandra and Joddu Nath Bose were the first graduates of Calcutta University; 'Sitaram' was Bankim's last novel.UPPSC

    Wahabi, Kuka, Pagal Panthi and Faraizi movements

    • Wahabi Movement ran from the 4th to the 7th decade of the 19th century; gave organised, stiff resistance to the British.
    • Syed Ahmad Barelvi of Rae Bareli was its proponent (leader).
    • He was inspired by Abdul Wahab of Arabia; in India the movement drew mainly on Shah Waliullah of Delhi.
    • It was a revivalist movement: return to true Islam as the way out of socio-political oppression.
    • Wahabi ideas spread to North-West Frontier Province, Bengal, Bihar, Kabul and Central Provinces.
    • Syed Ahmad captured Peshawar for a time in 1830 and issued coins in his name there.
    • He was killed in the Battle of Balakot (1831).
    • After his death Patna became the centre of the Wahabi Movement.UPPSC
    • Later Wahabi leaders: Maulvi Qasim, Vilayat Ali, Inayat Ali, Ahmadullah.
    • After Patna, branches opened in Hyderabad, Madras, Bengal, U.P. and Bombay.
    • Kuka and Wahabi movements began as religious revolts and became political movements to remove British rule.
    • Kuka (Namdhari) Movement = socio-religious reform movement among Sikhs of Punjab, mid-19th century.UPPSC
    • It was started by Bhagat Jawahar Mal (Sian/Sai Sahib) in the 1840s and Baba Balak Singh.
    • They stressed devotion to one God, spiritual purity and revival of Sikh values; aim was to purge Sikhism of superstition.
    • Baba (Guru) Ram Singh (1816–1885) organised the Namdhari sect and made it a powerful movement.
    • Called 'Kuka' because followers shouted ecstatic cries called 'Kuk' in devotion.
    • Ram Singh preached monotheism, prayer, meditation (Naam Simran) and strict moral discipline.
    • He opposed caste, female infanticide, early marriage and exchange of daughters in marriage.
    • He popularised simple, cheap Anand marriages.
    • The movement took political overtones against British rule; the British grew suspicious.
    • 1872 Kuka uprising against cow slaughter and British authority was severely suppressed; peak clashes 1871–72.
    • Ram Singh was exiled in 1872 (Rangoon; state prisoner at Mergui, Burma) and died there in 1885.
    • Kuka revolt is dated 1840–72; its main centres were in Punjab.
    • Pagal Panth was a semi-religious sect founded by Karim/Karam Shah of North Bengal.
    • The Pagalpanthi rebellion was a rebellion of the Garo tribe.UPPSC
    • Tribal peasants organised under Karam Shah's son Tipu Shah to fight zamindars' oppression.
    • Tipu Shah (printed with the year 1852) became leader after his father Karim Shah's death in 1813.
    • Under him the sect became a peasant rebellion against zamindars and indirectly against the Company.
    • Main cause: heavy oppression and extra taxes on raiyats.
    • After division of Sherpur zamindari in 1820, litigation and Company financial pressure raised tax burdens further.
    • Tipu Shah said land belongs equally to all as God's creation; an oppressive ruler has no moral right to rule.
    • Tipu Shah and his mother Chandi Bibi (Pir-Mata) ran an independent administration in Sherpur for over two years.
    • Gar-jaripa, a mud fort north of Sherpur, was his capital.
    • He captured Sherpur in 1825, became king, and appointed a judge, a magistrate and a collector.
    • Tipu Shah had religious and political aims: to uphold the religion and rights of the peasants of Bengal.
    • Tipu Shah was arrested several times between December 1824 and January 1825, tried and imprisoned.
    • Janku Pathor and Dubraj Pathor continued the movement for some time.
    • Faraizis = followers of the Muslim sect founded by Haji Shariatullah of Faridpur, Eastern Bengal.
    • Faraizis advocated radical religious, social and political changes.
    • Shariatullah's son Dudu (Dadu) Miyan led the Faraizi rebellion; organised peasants against landlords and indigo planters.UPPSC
    • Faraizi revolt ran from 1818 to 1862; after Dudu Miyan's death it merged into the Wahabi Movement.

    • Pabna peasant uprising (Bengal): 1873–76, against zamindari oppression, illegal abwabs/forced levies and rent enhancement.
    • Order: Sanyasi (1763–1800) → Indigo (1859–60) → Kuka (1871–72) → Pabna (1873–76).UPPSC
    • Pabna rebellion is also dated 1873–85; intense in 1873–76, after that only a legal dispute.UPPSC
    • Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 clarified farmers' land rights, the main demand of the Pabna movement.
    • Deccan (Kisan) Riots: 1875.
    • Immediate cause of the Deccan Riots of 1875: shadow of famine and high interest rates charged by Mahajans.
    • Order: Santhal Rebellion (1855–56) → Sepoy Mutiny (1857) → Indigo Revolt (1859–60) → Deccan Riot (1875).
    • Movements after 1857: Indigo Revolt, Deccan Agriculturists Riots, Birsa Munda Uprising; Santhal Rebellion was before.
    • Barhiyataal resistance in Munger demanded restoration of Bakasht land.
    • Eka Movement (1921–22) was started by farmers of Hardoi, Behraich, Sitapur (Barabanki) and other districts of Uttar Pradesh (Oudh).UPPSC
    • Eka issue: collection of 50% more tax than the accepted tax; leader Madari Pasi.
    • Eka Movement is also dated 1922 in one match list.
    • Moplah Revolt took place in 1921 in Malabar (Tirurangadi), Kerala.UPPSC ×2
    • Moplah tenants (sharecroppers) were Muslims; landlords (zamindars) were Hindus.
    • Moplah causes: landlord exploitation, resistance to British Raj, Khilafat movement.
    • Moplah grievances: no security of tenure, renewal fees, high rent and other landlord oppression.
    • Moplah (Malabar) Rebellion was an extended version of the Khilafat movement in Kerala.
    • Tebhaga Movement (1946–47), Bengal, started under Bangiya Pradeshik Kisan Sabha.
    • Tebhaga demand: cut rent rate to 1/3 as recommended by the Floud Commission.
    • Tebhaga is printed as a movement 'against the sharecroppers and Jotedars'; most prominent leaders Kampram Singh and Bhuvan Singh.
    • N.M. Lokhande (Narayanji Meghaji Lokhande, 1848–1897) was the first to organise the labour movement in India.
    • Lokhande worked for cotton mill workers in the 19th century and on social and communal issues.

    Revolts of South and West India

    1. 1767Chuar Revolt (1767–1802) broke out in Bankura and Midnapore, Bengal, not Madhya Pradesh.UPPSC
    2. 1800Ganjam rebellion: 1800–1805 (its leader is given as Dhananjay); Gumsur rebellion: 1808–1837.
