    5. 1818Bhil uprising (1818–31) centred in Khandesh (present Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh).UPPSC
    6. 1818British occupation of Khandesh in 1818 angered the Bhils, who feared outsiders.
    7. 18191819: general Bhil insurrection; small groups ravaged the plains.
    8. 1820Gaekwad of Baroda, backed by the British, forced the Waghera chief to take up arms; peace treaty in 1820.
    9. 18221822: Ramoshis revolted under Chittar (Chittur) Singh and plundered around Satara.
    10. 1825Ramoshis revolted again in 1825–26; the area stayed disturbed till 1831–32.
    11. 18251825: Bhils revolted again under Sevaram; British suppressed it ruthlessly.
    12. 1844Gadakaris revolted at Kolhapur in 1844–45.UPPSC
    13. 1845Vasudev Balwant Phadke (1845–83) founded Ramosi Krishak Jatha (Ramoshi farmers group) in Maharashtra.

    16. 1879Rampa Rebellion 1879–80; Pabna 1873–76; Bengal Indigo 1859–60; Jaintia Rebellion 1860–63.UPPSC

    18. 1883Phadke got a life sentence; died in 1883 from a hunger strike in Kala Pani.
    19. 1883Govind Giri launched the Lasodia Movement among Bhils and founded 'Samp Sabha' in 1883 to organise Bhils.
    • 1805: Wellesley forced the Maharaja of Travancore (Kerala) into Subsidiary Alliance.
    • The Maharaja was unhappy and would not pay the subsidy; the British Resident was rude.
    • Diwan Velu Thampi revolted in Travancore (Kerala), backed by the Nair battalion.UPPSC
    • Ganjam rebellion: 1800–1805 (its leader is given as Dhananjay); Gumsur rebellion: 1808–1837.
    • Gumsur revolt was led first by Shrikar Bhanja, later by his son Dhananjay Bhanja II.
    • Vasudev Balwant Phadke (1845–83) founded Ramosi Krishak Jatha (Ramoshi farmers group) in Maharashtra.
    • Phadke, among the earliest revolutionaries, organised the Ramoshi tribes into a fighting force.
    • Phadke got a life sentence; died in 1883 from a hunger strike in Kala Pani.
    • Ramoshi hill tribes lived in the Western Ghats; resented British rule and administration.
    • 1822: Ramoshis revolted under Chittar (Chittur) Singh and plundered around Satara.
    • Ramoshis revolted again in 1825–26; the area stayed disturbed till 1831–32.
    • Gadakaris = hereditary fort-servants/garrison men of Maratha forts, mainly in Kolhapur region.
    • Gadakaris revolted at Kolhapur in 1844–45.UPPSC
    • Causes: disbanded from fort service; their lands put under the Mamlatdar; harsh land revenue and acquisition policies.
    • British army struggled hard to suppress the Gadakari rebellion.
    • Waghera Revolt in Okha Mandal, Gujarat, was against the British: 1818–1819.
    • Gaekwad of Baroda, backed by the British, forced the Waghera chief to take up arms; peace treaty in 1820.
    • Another Waghera revolt episode took place in Okhamandal in 1858–59.
    • Bhil uprising (1818–31) centred in Khandesh (present Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh).UPPSC
    • Bhils lived in the hill ranges of Khandesh, upland basin of the Deccan tableland.
    • British occupation of Khandesh in 1818 angered the Bhils, who feared outsiders.
    • Officials blamed Peshwa Bajirao II and his minister Trimbakji Dengle for inciting the Bhils.
    • Real causes: agricultural hardship and fear of the new English government.
    • 1819: general Bhil insurrection; small groups ravaged the plains.
    • 1825: Bhils revolted again under Sevaram; British suppressed it ruthlessly.
    • British used force and conciliation, yet failed to win over the Bhils.
    • Some Bhil agitation also took place in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh in the 19th–20th century.
    • Koli tribes rose in the Taranga hills of Mehsana district, Gujarat.
    • Chuar Revolt (1767–1802) broke out in Bankura and Midnapore, Bengal, not Madhya Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Rampa hill area lies north of the Godavari in Andhra Pradesh.
    • Rampa tribal revolt was against moneylenders and the Forest Acts; dated 1879 (1879–80).
    • Madras Forest Act 1882 curbed tribal movement in forests and stopped 'Podu' (shifting cultivation).
    • Rampa Rebellion 1879–80; Pabna 1873–76; Bengal Indigo 1859–60; Jaintia Rebellion 1860–63.UPPSC
    • Surji Bhagat and Govind Guru (Govind Giri) reformed tribals in the second half of the 19th century.
    • Their area: Mewar, Dungarpur, Banswada, Pratapgarh, Sirohi, Pali (Bagar).
    • Govind Giri launched the Lasodia Movement among Bhils and founded 'Samp Sabha' in 1883 to organise Bhils.
    • Govind Guru is also called Lasodhiya.
    RevoltLeaderDetails
    Paika Rebellion, 1817, Khordha (Odisha)Bakshi JagabandhuFull name Jagabandhu Vidyadhar Mahapatra Bhramarbar Ray; born at Rorunga near PuriUPPSC
    Bareilly Rebellion, 1816Mufti Muhammad AiwazOpposed the police tax
    Malabar (Wayanad) revolt, 1802Edachana Kungan NairCommander of Nair army of Kerala Varma Pazhassiraja; backbone of attack on British military camp
    Sylhet (Pratapgarh) RebellionRadharamLocal landlord who opposed British rule in Sylhet

    Sepoy mutinies before 1857

    • Order before 1857: Bengal Sepoy Mutiny (1764) → Vellore Mutiny (1806) → Kutch Rebellion (1816–32) → Kol Revolt (1831–32) → Santhal Revolt (1855–56).
    • Bengal Sepoy Mutiny 1764: sepoys (a battalion) of Hector Munro's army joined Mir Qasim at Buxar.
    • Vellore Mutiny (July 1806) took place under Governor-General Sir George Barlow (1805–1807).
    • Vellore sepoys rose against interference in social and religious customs; raised the flag of the Raja of Mysore.
    • Barrackpur Mutiny: November 1824; Berhampur Revolt: February 1857.UPPSC

    Tribal revolts of East and North-East

    • Key common factor of 19th-century tribal revolts: complete disruption of the old agrarian order of tribal communities.
    • Other reasons: new land revenue and tax on tribal products; foreign missionaries; moneylenders, traders and revenue farmers as middlemen.
    • Khonds lived in the hills of Orissa and nearby districts, almost independent; also described as stretching from Bengal to Tamil Nadu, covering the central provinces.
    • Khonds rebelled from 1846 to 1855 under Chakra Bisoi, a young king.
    • Khonds rose against the ban on human sacrifice (Mariah), new taxes and entry of zamindars.
    • Ghumsar, Kalahandi and other tribals joined; Khonds opposed the Mariah Agency.
    • Kol Revolt (1831–32) in Chhotanagpur was led by Buddho Bhagat (also Ganga Narayan).
    • Kols live in Chhotanagpur: Ranchi, Singhbhum, Hazaribagh, Palamu, Manbhum.
    • 1831: new land laws brought outsiders (Hindu, Sikh, Muslim farmers, moneylenders) who exploited the tribes.
    • Kol rebels killed about a thousand outsiders; order returned only after large military operations.
    • Kols of Singhbhum had independent power under chiefs; resisted the Rajas of Chota Nagpur and Mayurbhanj.
    • Kol rebels burnt houses and looted property of settlers; the revolt continued off and on and was finally crushed.
    • Ho (Hoz) Revolt: 1820–21, in then Santhal subdivision of Bihar (now Singhbhum, Jharkhand).
    • Munda and Ho tribes of Chhotanagpur (then Bihar) challenged the British army in 1831; unrest lasted till 1837.

    Note from the book There was no revolt named 'Chhotanagpur Tribal Revolt'; if the Ho revolt (1820–21) is meant, the year is 1820.

    • Chhotanagpur revolts: Chero (1800), Kol (1831–32), Santhal (1855–56), Munda (1899–1900).
    • Bhumij Revolt (1832–33) was led by Ganga Narain in Jungle Mahal region.
    • Bhumij = 'one born from the soil'; it began as an inheritance dispute in Barabhum zamindari (West Bengal).
    • Bhumij cause: persecution by the king and exploitative British policies.
    • Ahom Revolt (1828) was led by Gomdhar Kunwar; so 'Ahom – 1815' is wrong.UPPSC ×2
    • Khasi Rebellion (1829–33) was led by Teerat Singh.
    • Khairwar tribal movement (1874) was led by Bhagirath Manjhi.
    • Surendra Sai, claimant to the throne of Sambalpur, led revolts against the British; surrendered in 1862.
    • Kuki revolt (1917–19) took place in Manipur and Tripura.UPPSC

    Note from the book 'Kuki Rebellion 1860–90' and 'Kuka Revolt 1832–34' are both wrong matches in one question; it should be cancelled or both accepted.

    • Kuki revolt began in 1917 against the order to join the Labour Corps for World War I.
    • Tana Bhagat Movement began in 1914 in Chhotanagpur among the Oraon tribe.
    • Tana Bhagat leaders: Oraon saints Jatra Bhagat, Balram Bhagat and Devmenia Bhagat; so it is not linked to 'Nayak'.UPPSC
    • Tana Bhagats opposed taxes imposed by the British.
    • Haipou Jadonang, Naga leader of Manipur, was the first tribal leader inspired by Mahatma Gandhi.
    • Jadonang with Rani Gaidinliu started social and religious reforms and freedom struggle.
    • Thakkar Bapa (Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar) first used the word 'Adivasi' for tribal people.
    • Thakkar Bapa was a member of the Servants of India Society; worked for untouchables and tribals.
    • He toured with Gandhi (Harijan tour, 1933–34); General Secretary of Harijan Sevak Sangh set up by Gandhi.

    Santhal Rebellion

    • Santhal Rebellion (Hool) took place in 1855–56.
    • Leaders: four brothers Sidhu (Sido), Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav; Sidhu was the chief leader.
    • Area: Damin-e-Koh, between Bhagalpur and the Rajmahal hills.
    • Moneylenders and the British exploited Santhals together; interest of 50 to 500% was charged.
    • Santhals rose against the British revenue system and the zamindari system.
    • Their main enemy was the 'Dikus' (corrupt government officers), not the 'Whites'/'Sahibs'.
    • 30 June 1855: over ten thousand Santhals met at Bhognadih (near Barhait, Sahibganj) and resolved to fight.
    • Santhals said the Dikus had betrayed them, forced them into slavery and abused their women; they pledged to fight till independence.
    • The win over Major Burrough fuelled the rebellion, which spread like wildfire.
    • The Santhal revolt is described as held in Bihar, Jharkhand and Odisha.
    • Sidhu said: "God said to me that this country is not of bosses. God will fight from our side."
    • Santhals defeated the British force of Major Burrough at Pirpainati (near Bhagalpur).
    • Gokko, an old headman, was an important leader of Godda; Mahajan Deen Dayal Rai is also a key name; Santhals never held sovereignty over the Ganga valley near Muzaffarpur.UPPSC
    • Brown, Commissioner of Bhagalpur, and Major General Lloyd ruthlessly crushed the revolt.
    • Sidhu was arrested and hanged; Kanhu was killed in action; revolt ended in 1856.
    • After the revolt a separate district 'Santhal Pargana' was created; transfer of Santhal land to non-Santhals was made illegal.
    • This came through the Santhal Pargana Tenancy Act.
    • Santhal Pargana was called 'Narikhand' in ancient times.
    • Buddhist literature calls it 'Kajangala'; in Mahabharata times it was part of Anga Mahajanapada.

    Birsa Munda

    • Birsa Munda led the Munda Rebellion or Ulgulan ('Great Tumult') of 1899–1900 (also printed 1895–1900).UPPSC
    • Mundas had collective farming; zamindars, contractors and moneylenders attacked it.
    • Munda leaders fought about 30 years to save their farming; the earlier agitation was Sardari Larai (also printed: Birsa's movement itself was popularly known as Sardari ladai).
    • Khuntkatti (Mundari) = customary common land tenure of Mundas as original clearers of the forest; it gave them a preferential rent rate.
    • Khuntkatti was eroded by jagirdars and thikedars coming as merchants and moneylenders.
    • Revolt began against replacing collective farming with zamindari or individual ownership.
    • 1895: Birsa claimed a vision of God; declared himself prophet (Messenger of God) with healing powers.
    • Birsa turned the revolt into a religious and political movement.
    • Thousands flocked to hear Birsa's 'new word' with its prophecy of an imminent deluge.
    • Birsa's main aims: social reform in tribal areas and keeping away from British rule.
    • Ulgulan sought the right of indigenous people over resources taken by landlords, moneylenders and colonial rulers.
    • The Munda revolt was the most famous revolt of its time; it took place south of Ranchi.
    • Birsa is called 'Dharti Aaba' (Father of Earth) or 'Jagat Pita'; born in 1875.
    • He said they would fight non-tribals and colour the land red with their blood like a red flag.
    • He called for worship of one god, 'Sing Bonga'.
    • Birsa asked Mundas to fight superstition, give up animal sacrifice and intoxicants, wear the sacred thread, worship in the Sarna (sacred grove).
    • It was a revivalist movement to purge Munda society of foreign elements; used Hindu and Christian idioms.
    • Two reasons for the movement: agrarian discontent and the coming of Christianity; it aimed to rebuild tribal society breaking up under colonial rule.
    • Ulgulan aimed at an independent Munda Raj, but Birsa did not favour a separate state.
    • Birsa's working area was Ranchi (Ranchi/Khunti to Singhbhum, Chakradharpur; one line says Ranchi to Bhagalpur).
    • Christmas Eve 1899: Mundas shot arrows and tried to burn churches across six police stations in Ranchi and Singhbhum.
    • January 1900: police stations targeted; rumour of attack on Ranchi on 8 January; rebels defeated on 9 January.
    • Birsa was captured asleep in Jamkopai forest, Chakradharpur, on 3 February 1900.
    • Birsa died in prison on 9 June 1900.
    • Nearly 350 Mundas were tried; three hanged and 44 transported for life.
    • Birsa Munda's revolt took place in Bihar (now Jharkhand).

    Chapter 48 · British rule, revolts and reform

    Development of Education in Modern India

    115 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Indian Women's University · 1916 · Bombay (explanation paragraph says Pune) · D.K. Karve×3
    2. Asiatic Society of Bengal = founded at Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, who became its first President.×2
    3. Hunter Commission stressed reform and development of primary education.×2
    4. Deccan Education Society (formerly New English School): main founders Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahadeo Ballal Namjoshi, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Vaman Shivram Apte.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 22 UPPSC questions

    Early British attitude and oriental learning

    • In the early phase of their rule, the British showed no interest in the advancement of learning in India.
    • Some Britishers took interest in spreading education through personal effort and for political gain.
    • Warren Hastings = Governor-General of Bengal 1774–85; a prolific scholar and staunch supporter of oriental learning.
    • Warren Hastings encouraged the study of Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic.
    • Calcutta Madarsa = first Madarsa set up by the British in India; founded by Warren Hastings in 1780 for Muslim law and related subjects.UPPSC
    • Mulla Majduddin = first principal (Najin) of the Calcutta Madarsa.
    • Calcutta Madarsa taught Farsi, Arabic and Muslim law; its graduates worked as interpreters in the British Raj.
    • Sanskrit College, Benaras (Varanasi) = founded 1791 by Jonathan Duncan, the Resident at Benaras, for Hindu law, philosophy and literature.
    • Sanskrit College at Benaras was not founded by William Jones.
    • Charles Wilkins, Nathaniel Halhed and Jonathan Duncan contributed to oriental studies under Warren Hastings' patronage and support.
    • Oriental education got a foothold by the efforts of Wilkins, Jones, Colebrook and William Carey.
    • Halhed published a Bengali grammar, 'A Grammar of the Bengal Language', in 1778.
    • Sir Charles Wilkins = first Englishman to translate the Bhagavad Gita into English; Warren Hastings wrote its preface.

    Asiatic Society

    1. 1784Asiatic Society of Bengal = founded at Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, who became its first President.UPPSC ×2
    2. 1789Sir William Jones was the first to translate Kalidasa's Abhigyan Shakuntalam into English, in 1789.UPPSC
    3. 1822Raja Rammohan Roy was offered membership of La Societe Asiatique (Asiatic Society of Paris), which was established in 1822.UPPSC
    4. 1828Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha movement in 1828, which gave rise to Brahmo Samaj, a Bengali socio-religious reform movement.
    5. 1892Dadabhai Naoroji = Liberal Party MP in the UK House of Commons 1892–1895; first Asian to be a British MP.
    6. 1893Swami Vivekananda represented India at the Parliament of the World's Religions, United States, 1893; founded Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
    • Sir William Jones was appointed Judge of the Supreme Court at Calcutta during Warren Hastings' tenure (also called Justice of Calcutta High Court).
    • Asiatic Society of Bengal = founded at Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, who became its first President.UPPSC ×2
    • The Society was set up with Warren Hastings' cooperation; Hastings declined its Presidentship in favour of Sir William Jones, as he was himself a scholar and Orientalist.UPPSC

    Note from the book On Hastings declining the Presidentship, the Commission's answer held that the reason does not explain the assertion; the book holds that the reason (Hastings was a scholar and Orientalist) correctly explains it.

    • The Society tried to throw light on India's past through its publication Asiatick Researches.
    • At the Society, research on oriental education and culture began; British civilians were taught Indian languages, laws, customs, religion and geography.
    • Sir William Jones was the first to translate Kalidasa's Abhigyan Shakuntalam into English, in 1789.UPPSC
    • Raja Rammohan Roy was offered membership of La Societe Asiatique (Asiatic Society of Paris), which was established in 1822.UPPSC
    • Dadabhai Naoroji = Liberal Party MP in the UK House of Commons 1892–1895; first Asian to be a British MP.
    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha movement in 1828, which gave rise to Brahmo Samaj, a Bengali socio-religious reform movement.
    • Swami Vivekananda represented India at the Parliament of the World's Religions, United States, 1893; founded Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

    Fort William College

    • Fort William College, Calcutta (Kolkata) = founded on 10 July 1800 (not 10 June) by Governor-General Lord (Richard) Wellesley; not by Arthur Wellesley.
    • Its purpose = to train and teach British civilians (civil servants) for administration in India, in Indian languages: Persian and Hindustani.UPPSC

    Reason for modern education and Charter Act 1813

    • Main reason the British spread modern education = need for educated Indians in minor administrative posts, to reduce expenditure on administration.
    • Charter Act 1813 = first to allot not less than Rs. 1 lakh per year for education of Indians.UPPSC
    • Charter Act 1813 = Act of the UK Parliament that renewed the East India Company's charter and continued Company rule in India.
    • Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's commercial monopoly except the tea trade and trade with China.

    Orientalist–Anglicist controversy and Macaulay

    • In 1823 the Governor-General in Council appointed the General Committee of Public Instruction, responsible for granting the one lakh rupees for education.
    • English education was introduced by three things: Charter Act 1813, General Committee of Public Instruction 1823, and the Orientalist–Anglicist controversy.
    • The Committee had 10 members with Lord Macaulay as President.
    • Attitudes shifted towards English education mainly due to the missionaries and the political influence of the English language.
    • The controversy over the medium of instruction went on for 12 years.
    • Committee was split: 5 members were Anglicists (English medium) and 5 were Orientalists (classical languages), so no decision by vote.
    • William Bentinck appointed Macaulay, Law Member of the Governor-General's Executive Council, as head of the Committee of Public Instruction to report on the medium dispute.
    • Macaulay advocated English education: European literature and science through English medium.UPPSC
    • Macaulay's Minute (issued 2 February 1835) laid the foundation of the modern education system in India.
    • Macaulay held Indian learning inferior to European: "A single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia."
    • Macaulay suggested English as the language of higher education with Western literature as the subject of study.
    • Macaulay's view: the Indian public mind might expand under the English system and be educated into a capacity for better government.
    • English education was introduced under Lord William Bentinck, who accepted Macaulay's proposal on 7 March 1835; English became the medium of Indian education.UPPSC
    • Resolution of 7 March 1835: the great object of the British Government = promotion of European literature and science; all education funds best spent on English education alone.
    • The Government Resolution of 1835 made English the official and literary language of India.
    • Bentinck's Resolution opened a new chapter in Indian education; Western education then began to spread rapidly.
    • Downward Filtration Theory was related to education in colonial India.
    • Filtration theory: education is first given to the higher class and slowly percolates down to the lower classes and general public.
    • Macaulay propounded the Filtration Theory: the Company should educate only an elite group, which would later educate the masses.UPPSC
    • Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay = British politician and historian; Law Member in the Supreme Council of India; head of the Law Commission 1834–1838.
    • Macaulay prepared the manuscript of the Indian Penal Code.
    • Macaulay had an important role in making English the official language and medium of education, and European literature, philosophy and science the goal of Indian education.
    • Macaulay on the East India Company: "The Company is an anomaly, but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly."UPPSC

    Wood's Despatch 1854

    • At the 1853 renewal of the Charter Act, a systematic pattern of education was felt necessary for India.
    • Wood's Despatch was issued on 19 July 1854 by Sir Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control; it was related to education.
    • Wood's Despatch = "Magna Carta of English Education in India"; first comprehensive plan for the spread of education in India.
    • It introduced the grants-in-aid system and recommended universities; it did not recommend English at all levels.
    • It recommended English as medium for higher studies and stressed government support for female education and vocational training.
    • Recommendation: an education department in every province.
    • Recommendation: universities on the model of London University in big cities: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.
    • Recommendation: at least one Government school in every district.
    • Recommendation: affiliated private schools to be given grants.
    • Recommendation: Indian natives should also be trained in their mother tongue.
    • Recommendation: a systematic method of education from primary level to university level.
    • First three universities (Calcutta, Madras, Bombay) were set up in 1857 on the model of London University.

    Education commissions and plans

    Commission / PlanYearAppointed by / HeadMain points
    Hunter Commission (first Indian Education Commission)1882Lord Ripon; headed by W.W. HunterReviewed educational development after 1854
    University Commission1902Lord Curzon; chairman Sir Thomas RaleyIndian members: Syed Hussain Bilgrami and Justice Gurudas Banerjee; led to University Act 1904
    Sadler Commission1917British Government; chairman Dr. M.E. Sadler, Vice-Chancellor of Leeds UniversityStudied problems of Calcutta University
    Sargent Plan1944Report on educational reformsMake Indian education more vocational and scientific
    • Hunter Commission stressed reform and development of primary education.UPPSC ×2
    • Hunter Commission recommended vocational training in secondary education and pointed out inadequate facilities for female education.
    • Hunter Commission's recommendations were only partially implemented.
    • Hunter Commission on Education is dated 1882–83; Hartog Committee is dated 1929.
    • Sadler Commission was related to education.UPPSC
    • Sadler Commission's two Indian members: Dr. (Sir) Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin Ahmad.
    • Sadler Commission was to inquire into Calcutta University and make wider recommendations on secondary, intermediate and university education.
    • Sadler Commission: improving secondary education is a necessary condition for improving university education.
    • Sadler Commission strongly criticised the University Act 1904 and found no proper coordination between colleges and universities.
    • Sargent Plan: universal, compulsory and free primary (basic) education for all children aged 6–14.
    • Sargent Plan stages: junior basic (6–11) and senior basic (11–14).

    National education movement

    • Rangpur National School = set up on 8 November 1905; first milestone in national education.
    • Rangpur National School aimed to give indigenous education, general and technical, to Indians.
    • Citizens of Rangpur held a conference on 16 November 1905.
    • On 16 November 1905 a session in Calcutta decided to set up the National Council of Education, Bengal, for science, national literature and technology.
    • National Council of Education (NCE), Bengal was formed on 15 August 1906.
    • Also printed: Satish Chandra Mukherjee and others constituted the NCE, Bengal on 11 March 1906; Bengal National College was inaugurated later on 14 August 1906.

    Colleges and societies

    InstitutionYearPlaceFounder
    Hindu College1817CalcuttaRaja Ram Mohan Roy with David Hare (one question adds Alexander Duff)UPPSC
    Delhi College1824Delhi–
    Mayo College1875Ajmer–

    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy was among the earliest propagators of modern education in India.
    • Hindu College, Calcutta (1817) is older than Delhi College, Mayo College and M.A.O. College.UPPSC
    • Deccan Education Society (formerly New English School): main founders Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahadeo Ballal Namjoshi, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Vaman Shivram Apte.UPPSC ×2
    • Justice Ranade was not a founder of the Deccan Education Society; he was one of its five patrons.
    • Dhondo Keshav Karve = social worker and reformer of Maharashtra; supported widow remarriage and women's education; founded the widow remarriage association.
    • Karve's Home for Widows (now Maharshi Karve Stree Shikshan Samstha) aimed to make high-caste widows self-supporting through jobs.
    • Karve himself married a Brahmin widow; he was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1958.

    Aligarh

    • M.A.O. College began in 1875 as Madarsatul Uloom Musalmanan-i-Hind; renamed Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1877; became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.
    • Theodore Beck, Principal of M.A.O. College, encouraged Muslim separatist tendencies in the last decades of the 19th century.
    • Aligarh Movement, led by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in the late 19th century, aimed to promote Western scientific (modern) education among Indian Muslims.
    • Aligarh Movement stressed scientific and Western learning while preserving Islamic values.
    • Aligarh Movement sought socio-political upliftment and a progressive Muslim identity; it influenced the later demand for separate representation.

    Banaras Hindu University

    • Madan Mohan Malaviya vigorously advocated religious education in Indian universities.UPPSC
    • Malaviya = educationist and politician; founded BHU in 1916; Vice-Chancellor of BHU 1919–1939.
    • Malaviya published magazines and newspapers in English and Hindi: Hindustan, Indian Union (also printed India Union), Abhyudaya, Maryada and The Leader.
    • Central Hindu School later became the centre from which BHU developed.
    • BHU was established in 1916 with the cooperation of Annie Besant and the efforts of Madan Mohan Malaviya.
    • Central Hindu School was included in the new university in 1917; at present it is a constituent institute of BHU.
    • Lord Hardinge II, the Viceroy, laid the foundation stone of BHU on 4 February 1916, Basant Panchami day.UPPSC
    • Among AMU, Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar University Lucknow, BHU and Allahabad University, BHU was the first Central University.UPPSC

    Chapter 49 · British rule, revolts and reform

    Development of Press in Modern India

    138 facts · 10 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Commonweal · Annie Besant (editor) · English paper from Madras×5
    2. Bengal Gazette = first newspaper in India; English paper started at Calcutta in 1780 by James Augustus Hicky.×2
    3. Harish Chandra Mukherjee, editor of Hindoo Patriot, boldly exposed exploitation of indigo farmers and helped them in every way.×2
    4. Tilak started Kesari and Mahratta in 1881 at Poona, now Pune (also printed: Mumbai); Kesari served the freedom struggle.×2
    5. B.R. Ambedkar started the Marathi fortnightly Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 44 UPPSC questions

    Beginning of press

    • Portuguese set up the first printing press in Asia at Goa in 1556.
    • Bengal Gazette = first newspaper in India; English paper started at Calcutta in 1780 by James Augustus Hicky.UPPSC ×2
    • Many newspapers were published between 1766 and 1789.
    • Udant Martand = first Hindi newspaper; published from Calcutta (Kolkata) on 30 May 1826.UPPSC
    • Udant Martand came out every Tuesday; published by Pt. Jugal Kishore Shukla.

    Press laws

    1. 1799Lord Wellesley first imposed press censorship: Censorship of Press Regulations (Act), 1799.UPPSC
    2. 1799The 1799 regulations imposed almost wartime press restrictions including pre-censorship.
    3. 1807In 1807 the 1799 Act was extended to pamphlets, books and magazines.
    4. 1818Lord Hastings abolished strict pre-censorship in 1818; papers no longer had to be submitted to a government officer before publication.
    5. 1823John Adams, acting Governor-General, banned the Indian press in 1823: Rs. 400 fine and imprisonment for publishing without licence.
    6. 1823Under the 1823 rule the District Magistrate could seize the publication house; so Raja Ram Mohan Roy had to stop Mirat-ul-Akhbar.
    7. 1835The Press Act was enacted in August 1835 under acting Governor-General Charles Metcalfe, known as the Liberator of the Indian Press.
    8. 1878Vernacular Press Act, 1878 was passed by Lord Lytton (1876–1880); it gagged the native-language press and was called the 'Gagging Act'.UPPSC
    9. 1882There was popular protest against the Act; Lord Ripon repealed it in 1882.UPPSC
    • Lord Wellesley first imposed press censorship: Censorship of Press Regulations (Act), 1799.UPPSC
    • The 1799 regulations imposed almost wartime press restrictions including pre-censorship.
    • In 1807 the 1799 Act was extended to pamphlets, books and magazines.
    • Lord Hastings abolished strict pre-censorship in 1818; papers no longer had to be submitted to a government officer before publication.
    • John Adams, acting Governor-General, banned the Indian press in 1823: Rs. 400 fine and imprisonment for publishing without licence.
    • Under the 1823 rule the District Magistrate could seize the publication house; so Raja Ram Mohan Roy had to stop Mirat-ul-Akhbar.
    • Lord William Bentinck was positive towards the press; a bill for press freedom was introduced in his tenure.

    Note from the book No year option was accepted for Bentinck giving press freedom: the bill came in his tenure, but the Act was passed under Metcalfe.

    • The Press Act was enacted in August 1835 under acting Governor-General Charles Metcalfe, known as the Liberator of the Indian Press.
    • Vernacular Press Act, 1878 was passed by Lord Lytton (1876–1880); it gagged the native-language press and was called the 'Gagging Act'.UPPSC
    • The Act let the District Magistrate, without prior Government permission, make the printer and publisher of a vernacular paper sign a bond.
    • Bond = not to cause disaffection against the government or antipathy between persons of different religion, caste and race.
    • Security could be demanded and forfeited on violation; on repeat offence press equipment could be seized.
    • Under the Act, proceedings were started against Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.
    • There was popular protest against the Act; Lord Ripon repealed it in 1882.UPPSC

    Journalists punished

    • Surendra Nath Banerjee = first Indian jailed for doing his duty as a journalist; jailed on 2 April 1883 for his article in The Bengalee.UPPSC
    • Also printed: B.G. Tilak was imprisoned for anti-British journalism in 1882; first Indian punished for doing his duty in this field.
    • Tilak was arrested after the murder of W.C. Rand and officer Charles Ayerst.
    • Grounds: the poem "Shivaji's utterances" in Kesari and his Shivaji festival speech justifying Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan.
    • The prosecution portrayed Tilak's defence of Afzal Khan's killing as incitement to kill British officials.
    • In 1897 Tilak got 18 months' imprisonment for sedition: charged with inciting the Chapekar brothers through Kesari articles.
    • Abul Kalam Azad's Al-Hilal was banned in 1914 by the Press Act.

    Raja Ram Mohan Roy and early Bengal papers

    1. 1821He published the Bengali weekly Sambad Kaumudi in 1821.
    2. 1822He published the Persian weekly Mirat-ul-Akhbar in 1822.UPPSC
    3. 1858Som Prakash, Bengali weekly, was started in 1858 by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
    4. 1861Indian Mirror was published from Calcutta; founded 1861 by Debendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh; Gandhiji was not associated with it.UPPSC
    5. 1862Girish Chandra Ghosh started The Bengalee in 1862; it passed to S.N. Banerjee in 1879.
    6. 1868It was launched on 20 February 1868 as a Bengali weekly at village Palua Magura, Jessore district (present Bangladesh); later published from Kolkata.
    7. 1878Amrita Bazar Patrika turned into an English paper overnight in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
    8. 1886The Indian Mirror (January 1886) called the Indian National Congress "the nucleus of a future Parliament of our country".
    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy used the press to spread his views; he knew English, Bengali, Persian, Arabic, Greek and Latin.
    • He published the Bengali weekly Sambad Kaumudi in 1821.
    • He published the Persian weekly Mirat-ul-Akhbar in 1822.UPPSC
    • Samachar Darpan is linked with J.C. Marshman.UPPSC
    • Som Prakash, Bengali weekly, was started in 1858 by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
    • Vidyasagar mooted the idea of Som Prakash; Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan was its first editor.
    • Som Prakash supported the farmers during the Indigo movement.
    • Indian Mirror was published from Calcutta; founded 1861 by Debendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh; Gandhiji was not associated with it.UPPSC
    • Indian Mirror was a daily; Keshav Chandra Sen and Narendra Nath Sen were in its editorial department.
    • The Indian Mirror (January 1886) called the Indian National Congress "the nucleus of a future Parliament of our country".
    • Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by Shishir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh.
    • It was launched on 20 February 1868 as a Bengali weekly at village Palua Magura, Jessore district (present Bangladesh); later published from Kolkata.
    • Amrita Bazar Patrika turned into an English paper overnight in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
    • Girish Chandra Ghosh started The Bengalee in 1862; it passed to S.N. Banerjee in 1879.

    Hindoo Patriot and Indigo Revolt

    • Hindoo Patriot (1853) = first newspaper published by Indians in English; started by Girish Chandra Ghosh.UPPSC
    • Hindoo Patriot editors: Girish Chandra Ghosh (1853–55), Harish Chandra Mukherjee (1855–61), Kristo Das Pal (1861–1884).
    • Later editors were helped by Madan Mohan Ghosh and Dwarka Nath Tagore.
    • Surendra Nath Banerjee was editor of Hindoo Patriot during 1874–75 in London and 1878 in Delhi.
    • Indigo Revolt = peasant uprising of indigo farmers against indigo planters in Bengal; a direct fight against exploitation of farmers.
    • Special feature of the Indigo Movement: intellectuals actively campaigned in support of the struggling farmers.
    • Harish Chandra Mukherjee, editor of Hindoo Patriot, boldly exposed exploitation of indigo farmers and helped them in every way.UPPSC ×2
    • Girish Chandra Ghosh also worked for the Indigo Movement.
    • Kristo Das Pal admired British governance and British liberalism; under him Hindoo Patriot represented high-class Bengali landowners.

    Tilak and revolutionary papers

    • Tilak started Kesari and Mahratta in 1881 at Poona, now Pune (also printed: Mumbai); Kesari served the freedom struggle.UPPSC ×2
    • Kesari was in Marathi and was Tilak's main paper of the Home Rule Movement; Mahratta was in English.
    • Gopal Ganesh Agarkar was the first editor of Kesari; Tilak was the first editor of Mahratta; later Tilak published both.
    • Bangawasi, Kaal and Kesari supported revolutionary movements and criticised Congress for its moderate (liberal) policies.UPPSC
    • Sandhya, Yugantar and Kaal advocated revolutionary extremism.UPPSC
    • Sandhya and Yugantar were in Bengal; Kaal was in Maharashtra.
    • Yugantar was published by Bhupendra Nath Dutt and Barindra Kumar Ghosh; Gandhi was not associated with it.UPPSC
    • Aurobindo Ghosh was editor of the English weekly Bande Mataram (Vande Mataram).UPPSC
    • Vande Mataram, English paper, was founded in 1906 by Bipin Chandra Pal.
    • Bipin Chandra Pal edited it from 6 August 1906 to 15 October 1906.
    • Sri Aurobindo edited it from 24 October 1906 to 27 May 1907.
    • It was a daily; from 2 June 1907 it became a weekly.
    • From 10 September 1909 Vande Mataram was published from Paris with Hardayal as editor; Madame Bhikaji Cama handled publication and distribution.

    Papers abroad and Ghadar

    • The Free Hindustan was started by Tarak Nath Das in North America (Vancouver).
    • Hindustan Ghadar Party was formed in 1913 at San Francisco by Indian migrants in USA and Canada.
    • Ghadar Party aimed to organise an army to overthrow British rule in India; headquarters at San Francisco.
    • Founders: Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna and Kartar Singh Sarabha.
    • Ghadar was a weekly and the manifesto of the party.UPPSC
    • First issue of Ghadar came out on 1 November 1913 at San Francisco in Urdu.UPPSC
    • From 9 December 1913 Ghadar was also printed in Gurmukhi script.
    • Ghadar was later published in Marathi, Hindi, English and Gujarati; one edition in Pashto.

    Gandhiji's papers

    • Indian Opinion was started by Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa in 1903.
    • Mansukh Lal Hiralal Nazar was the first editor of Indian Opinion; he was Secretary of the Natal Congress.UPPSC
    • Indian Opinion was published in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil and English; not in Urdu.UPPSC
    • Young India began as a bi-weekly from Bombay on 7 May 1919 under Gandhiji's supervision.
    • Young India was started by Home Rule members Jamnadas Dwarkadas and Shankarlal Banker (publisher), of Annie Besant's Home Rule League.UPPSC
    • Jamnadas Dwarkadas and Shankarlal Banker were its founding members and editors of its early version.
    • On 8 October 1919 Gandhi became editor of Young India; it became a weekly from Ahmedabad.
    • Young India = English weekly edited by Gandhi during 1919–1931; an influential platform of the freedom struggle.

    Note from the book The question on who started 'The Young India' was removed by Bihar PSC because it wrongly wrote "The Young India" instead of "Young India".

    • Young India was not linked with revolutionary activities; Gandhi used it to spread his ideas of non-violence.
    • Gandhi started the weeklies Harijan (English), Harijan Bandhu (Gujarati) and Harijan Sevak (Hindi).
    • First issue of Harijan came out on 11 February 1933 from Pune, Maharashtra.UPPSC
    • Papers started by Gandhi: Indian Opinion, Harijan, Young India and Navjeevan.

    Ambedkar, Azad, Lajpat Rai, Nehru

    1. 1905Lala Lajpat Rai started the Urdu daily Vande Mataram from Lahore (printed dates: 1905-06; also 1920).UPPSC
    2. 1912Abul Kalam Azad started the Urdu weekly Al-Hilal in 1912.

    • On 20 July 1924 B.R. Ambedkar founded Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in Bombay for the moral and material uplift of untouchables.
    • B.R. Ambedkar started the Marathi fortnightly Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).UPPSC ×2
    • Mook Nayak is linked with B.R. Ambedkar.
    • Abul Kalam Azad started the Urdu weekly Al-Hilal in 1912.
    • Al-Hilal criticised oppressive British policies; it was shut down in 1914.
    • Azad published Al-Balagh in 1915.
    • Lala Lajpat Rai started the Urdu daily Vande Mataram from Lahore (printed dates: 1905-06; also 1920).UPPSC
    • Lajpat Rai started The People, an English weekly, from Lahore in 1925.
    • Lajpat Rai earlier published Young India in America in 1916.
    • Qaumi Awaz, Urdu paper, was started by Jawaharlal Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai in 1945 from Lucknow; not by Abul Kalam Azad.UPPSC ×2
    • Qaumi Awaz stopped publication in 2008.
    • Motilal Nehru started the English paper The Independent in February 1919 at Allahabad, demanding Home Rule; it was not Ambedkar's.UPPSC ×2

    Chapter 50 · British rule, revolts and reform

    Socio-Religious Movements

    260 facts · 12 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Servants of India Society was founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale on 12 June 1905 at Fergusson Hill, Pune.×6
    2. Raja Ram Mohan Roy = Father of Indian Renaissance, Father (Prophet) of Indian Nationalism, Father/Maker of Modern India, First Modern Man, Yugdoot, 'Bridge between past and future'.×4
    3. Keshab Chandra Sen founded Bharatiya Brahmo Samaj (Brahmo Samaj of India, Neo/Navin Brahmo Samaj) on 11 November 1866.×3
    4. Vivekananda represented India at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893.×3
    5. Satya Shodhak Samaj · 1873 · Pune · Jyotiba Phule · Phule was its first president×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 71 UPPSC questions

    Nature of 19th century reform

    • Early 19th century: a new modern vision arose among enlightened sections of Indian society; it shaped events for decades.
    • This reawakening is sometimes, not with full justification, called 'Renaissance'; it also gave rise to some undesirable by-products.
    • 19th century religious reform movements mainly attracted intellectuals, urban upper castes and liberal princes; the poor ordinary class stayed almost outside.
    • The movements mostly affected intellectuals and middle-class people.
    • Socio-religious movements led to the modernisation of India because rationalism and scientific temper were at their core.
    • All reforms (Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Parsi) aimed to spread modern education and fight social evils.
    • Reformers stressed a rational understanding of social and religious ideas and a scientific, humanitarian outlook.
    • The educated Hindu middle class was the first to be influenced by Western civilisation.
    • The new Western-educated class was deeply affected by rationalism, scientism and humanism.
    • Reformers, inspired by the Enlightenment, rejected superstition, pilgrimage and idolatry.
    • Brahmo Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission and Arya Samaj had no political mission but helped develop the spirit of patriotism.
    • All three helped social reform and the development of education.
    • Dayanand Saraswati, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and Raja Ram Mohan Roy were all proficient in Sanskrit.UPPSC
    • Chronology: Tulsidas (16th century) → Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833) → Dayanand Saraswati (1824–1883) → Vivekananda (1863–1902).

    Raja Ram Mohan Roy

    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy = Father of Indian Renaissance, Father (Prophet) of Indian Nationalism, Father/Maker of Modern India, First Modern Man, Yugdoot, 'Bridge between past and future'.UPPSC ×4
    • He was the first Indian to start a movement against the evils of Indian society.
    • Atmiya Sabha (1815, Calcutta) = first society founded by Roy; to spread monotheistic ideals of Hinduism; not founded by Debendranath Tagore.UPPSC ×2
    • Atmiya Sabha's followers were mostly rich and influential youth.
    • Calcutta Unitarian Committee was set up by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Dwarkanath Tagore and William Adam.
    • Mughal Emperor Akbar II gave Ram Mohan Roy the title 'Raja' in 1830.UPPSC
    • Akbar II sent him as ambassador to the court of British King William IV in 1830 to plead for a rise in his pension and allowances.
    • Roy died of meningitis on 27 September 1833 at Stapleton near Bristol, England; his Samadhi (mausoleum) is at Bristol.
    • Roy was an ardent advocate of Western education through English; he did not protest against it.UPPSC
    • Roy's view: moderate Western education is needed to pull Indians out of darkness and give them partnership in administration.
    • Roy's letter of 11 December 1823 to Lord Amherst opposed a Sanskrit school under Hindu pandits.
    • In the letter he said the Sanskrit system would keep the country in darkness.
    • He asked for instruction in mathematics, natural philosophy, chemistry, anatomy and other useful sciences, taught by Europe-educated men in a well-equipped college.
    • Roy opposed idol worship, child marriage and Sati.
    • Roy loved and respected the traditional philosophical systems of the East, and wanted Indians to accept rationalism, science, human dignity and equality of men and women.
    • Roy held that the purest form of Hinduism is contained in the Upanishads.UPPSC
    • Roy launched the Bengali weekly Samvad Kaumudi on 4 December 1821; its official editor was Bhavanicharan Bandopadhyay, not Roy.UPPSC
    • Samvad Kaumudi led the campaign against Sati (widow burning) and backed other progressive values.
    • Samachar Chandrika (1822) was started by Bhavani Charan Bandyopadhyay to oppose Roy's religious and social ideas.UPPSC
    • Roy strongly opposed the Jury Act of 1826.UPPSC
    • Jury Act 1826 brought religious distinction into the judicial system, reflecting British religious superiority.
    • Under it only Christians could be jurors in trials of Christians (Indian or European); Christians could also judge Hindus and Muslims.
    • Hindus and Muslims could be jurors only in trials of Hindus and Muslims, not of Christians.

    Brahmo Samaj

    • Brahmo Sabha, later called Brahmo Samaj, was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy on 20 August 1828 at Calcutta.UPPSC
    • Roy formed it in a house rented from Feringhee Kamal Bose; Tarachand Chakroborty was its first secretary.
    • Brahmo Samaj = first Hindu reform movement influenced by modern Western liberal ideas and a new reading of ancient Indian texts.
    • Brahmo Samaj was based on monotheism: one omnipresent, omniscient God; universal worship.UPPSC ×2
    • It opposed idolatry and denied the need for a priestly class; it did not teach that the Vedas are infallible.
    • It denied anthropomorphism and sacerdotalism; it had no place for social customs and rituals.
    • It stressed humanity without regard to colour and character, and aimed to improve the condition of women.
    • Debendranath Tagore founded Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839 at Kolkata to spread Roy's ideas.
    • Tattvabodhini Sabha promoted rational thinking, study of ancient texts and the essence of the Upanishads; it merged into Brahmo Samaj in 1859.
    • Debendranath Tagore = Hindu philosopher and religious reformer.
    • Maharishi Debendranath Tagore (1817–1905) joined Brahmo Samaj in 1843 and carried it forward as a theist movement.
    • Debendranath Tagore appointed Keshab Chandra Sen as Acharya of Brahmo Samaj.
    • Keshab Chandra Sen joined Brahmo Samaj in 1857, made it popular and opened branches in Uttar Pradesh and Madras.
    • Debendranath stripped Keshab of the title 'Acharya' in 1865 over differences of opinion.
    • Keshab Chandra Sen founded Bharatiya Brahmo Samaj (Brahmo Samaj of India, Neo/Navin Brahmo Samaj) on 11 November 1866.UPPSC ×3
    • Adi Brahmo Samaj = the original Samaj under Debendranath Tagore after the 1866 split; Roy did not found it.UPPSC

    Note from the book Historians B.L. Grover and R.L. Shukla, other books and exam bodies wrongly called Keshab Chandra Sen the founder of 'Adi Brahmo Samaj'; the book says the fact is the opposite.

    • Sources cited for this: thebrahmosamaj.net, Gazetteer of India vol. II, and Macmillan's history by Puri, Das and Chopra.
    • In 1878 Keshab married his daughter, under 14, to the king of Cooch Behar; the Samaj split again.
    • Anand Mohan Bose and Shivnath Shastri then formed Sadharan Brahmo Samaj.
    • Keshab Chandra Sen founded the 'Tabernacle of New Dispensation' temple and the Indian Reform Association.
    • Indian Reform Association was formed on 29 October 1870 with Keshab Chandra Sen as president.
    • Keshab Chandra Sen said Brahmovad should be made the religion of the world.
    • Young India was published by Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.
    • Keshab's reform programme: against child marriage and polygamy; for widow remarriage and inter-caste marriage.
    • Under Keshab Chandra Sen, Brahmo Samaj campaigned for women's education; Vinoba Bhave founded Sarvodaya Samaj to work among refugees.
    • Sarvodaya Samaj also aimed to raise Indians' living standard and promote Gandhi's principles.

    Ramakrishna and Vivekananda

    • Ramakrishna Paramahamsa: Hari, Ram, Allah and Christ are names of the same God; there are many ways to God and salvation.
    • Sharadamani Mukhopadhyaya (Sharada Devi) = wife of Ramakrishna Paramhansa; married at age five in 1859.
    • Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902) spread Ramakrishna's message in simple language and emerged as the preacher of Neo-Hinduism.
    • Vivekananda represented India at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893.UPPSC ×3

    Note from the book On the question asking the year of the Chicago speech (options 1863, 1892, 1881, 1894), all options were wrong and M.P.P.S.C. gave bonus marks to all.

    • Vivekananda tried to fit Ramakrishna's message to the needs of contemporary Indian society.
    • At Chicago he gave a short introduction to Hinduism and spoke on "The meaning of the Hindu religion".
    • After Chicago he visited the United States and England and promoted Hinduism.
    • Vivekananda said the Hindu religion had become restricted to food only.
    • He was displeased at religion's silence on the exploitation of the poor by the wealthy.
    • He gave no political messages but raised self-dignity in the new generation; he was a staunch patriot.
    • Subhas Chandra Bose: "So far as Bengal is concerned, Vivekananda may be regarded as the spiritual father of the modern nationalist movement."
    • Vivekananda propagated Practical Vedanta: Vedanta should be practical in every sphere of life.
    • His first speech on Practical Vedanta was on 10 November 1896 in London.
    • Vivekananda wrote Raja Yoga, Karma Yoga, Bhakti Yoga and Jnana Yoga.UPPSC
    • Vivekananda = 'Patron saint' of India; quote: "Truth can be stated in a thousand different ways, yet each one can be true."
    • Vivekananda was a leading thinker of the Indian Renaissance.
    • Ramakrishna Mission was founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897 (May 1897), not by Ramakrishna Paramhansa.UPPSC ×2
    • He founded it with his sanyasi associates and lay disciples of Sri Ramakrishna.
    • The Mission was officially registered in 1909 under the Societies Registration Act 1860.
    • Headquarters: Belur, Howrah (West Bengal).
    • Twin ideals: "For one's liberation and the welfare of the world at large".
    • The Mission = non-political, non-sectarian spiritual movement doing humanitarian, social and cultural service; inspired by ancient Indian culture.
    • Its ideal is Pure Vedanta; main aim = highest spiritual upliftment of the inner self.
    • It accepted traditional Hindu practices such as idol worship, rituals and symbols in their original form.
    • Second feature: belief in the truth of all religions; all faiths are different ways to the one God.
    • It works in education, health, welfare of the poor, relief and rehabilitation, arts and culture, morality, ethics and spirituality, regardless of caste, creed and religion.
    • It was the last famous religious movement of the 19th century; aimed at harmony of religions, of East and West, of ancient and modern.
    • Sister Nivedita: "The British Empire is rotten to the core, corrupt in every direction and tyrannical and mean."

    Dayanand Saraswati and Arya Samaj

    • Dayanand Saraswati (original name Mulshankar / Mool Shankar Tiwari) was born in 1824 in a rich Brahmin family in Morvi princely state, Kathiawar, Gujarat.
    • He wandered for fifteen years (1845–60) in search of knowledge.
    • In 1860 he came under Swami Virajananda Saraswati at Mathura; he began preaching in 1864.
    • In 1867 he hoisted the Pakhand Khandini Pataka on the bank of the Ganga against superstition and bad rituals.
    • In November 1869 he held a great Shastrartha with leaders of Hindu orthodoxy at Kashi.
    • Arya Samaj was founded by Dayanand Saraswati in April 1875 at Bombay.UPPSC
    • Arya Samaj headquarters shifted to Lahore in 1877, which speeded up the movement.
    • Arya Samaj spread rapidly as a reaction against Western influences.
    • Aims: re-establish Vedic religion in pure form; integrate India socially, politically and religiously; promote noble ideas true for all mankind.
    • Arya Samaj advocated peaceful and progressive human living; Dayanand used it as a platform against the social evils of Hindu society.
    • Dayanand gave the slogan "Go back to the Vedas": a call to revive Vedic learning and purity of religion.UPPSC
    • He called all beliefs added after the Vedic period false religion; he denied the authenticity of the Puranas, blaming them for idolatry.
    • He rejected idol worship, incarnations and tantra-mantra; he worked against child marriage and casteism.
    • He popularised the doctrine that the Vedas are infallible; he identified Hinduism with the religion instituted in the Vedas.
    • His aim was the oneness of all religions, of society and of the nation.
    • He made a logical, scientific and critical analysis of faith.
    • Dayanand is called the "(Martin) Luther of India" for his religious reforms.UPPSC
    • Satyarth Prakash (The Light of Truth), 1875, is Dayanand's masterpiece (magnum opus) and the sacred book of Arya Samaj.UPPSC ×2
    • Other works: Rigvedadibhashya Bhumika, Rigveda Bhashya, Advaitmat Khandan, Panch Mahayajya Vidhi and Ved-Viruddh-mat-Khandanam.
    • Dayanand was the first to use the word 'Swaraj' and accepted Hindi as the national language.
    • He was the first to urge giving up foreign goods and adopting Swadeshi goods; these ideas were later used in the national movement.
    • Dayananda said "India for the Indians"; per Annie Besant he was the first to say India is only for Indians; this was his political message.
    • He felt Western civilisation's stranglehold was a colonial design to submerge Indian national identity in the British Empire.
    • Shuddhi Movement was started by Arya Samaj to bring back to Hinduism those who had converted to other religions.UPPSC
    • Arya Samaj gave Hindus self-confidence and self-reliance, and it accepted the superiority of Hindus and rejected White Race superiority; the second does not explain the first.UPPSC
    • Arya Samaj followers played an important role in the growth of knowledge and education.
    • Arya Samaj split into two groups over Western education.
    • Swami Shraddhanand (Mahatma Munshi Ram Vij) and Lekhraj opposed Western education; they set up 'Gurukul' in 1902.
    • Lala Lajpat Rai and Hansraj supported Western education; they set up Dayanand Anglo Vedic College.
    • Lala Lajpat Rai was an Arya Samaj member; he did not oppose its appeal to the authority of the Vedas.

    Prarthana Samaj and Ranade

    • Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 at Bombay by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen.UPPSC
    • It was a religious and social reform movement of Maharashtra, much like Brahmo Samaj.
    • M.G. Ranade joined in 1869 and was its chief guide; R.G. Bhandarkar also joined two years after its founding.UPPSC
    • Aims: oppose the caste system, raise the marriage age of males and females, promote widow remarriage and women's education.
    • Ranade = "Father (Precursor) of cultural renaissance in Western India"; his reform movement continued till the end of the 19th century.
    • Dhondo Keshav Karve and Vishnu Shastri were Ranade's followers in social reform.
    • Ranade and Karve started a widow remarriage movement and founded the 'Hindu Widows Home' to educate widows.
    • Indian National Social Conference was founded in 1887 by M.G. Ranade and Raghunath Rao.
    • Its aims: abolish polygamy, child marriage and patriarchy (also printed: oligarchy); it met yearly alongside the Congress for many years.
    • Ranade relied on legislation against social ills and worked against child marriage and the Purdah system.
    • It was formed because the Congress did not want social reforms in its deliberations, keeping its platform for political affairs only.
    • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was launched on 2 April 1870 at Pune by G.V. Joshi, S.H. Sathe and S.H. Chiplonkar; Ranade joined in November 1871.
    • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was one of the strongest political organisations of 19th century India.
    • Paramahansa Mandali = secret socio-religious group founded in Bombay, Maharashtra, by Dadoba Pandurang Tarkhadkar.
    • Paramahansa Mandali began religious reform in Bombay; it promoted monotheism and reform in Hindu society.

    Jyotiba Phule and anti-caste movements

    • Jyotiba Phule was born in 1827 in a gardener's family; he ran a powerful non-Brahmin movement.
    • Phule wrote Gulamgiri.UPPSC
    • He also wrote 'Sarvjanik Satyadharm Pustak'; his books criticised the Brahmans' scriptures.
    • Main aim of Satya Shodhak Samaj = uplift of backward classes: welfare of Dalits and lower castes.
    • It sought to free Shudras from Brahmanical scriptures, make them aware of human rights and end mental and religious slavery.
    • Satya Shodhak Samaj was an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra, to free Shudras and Ati Shudras from Arya-Brahmin exploitation.UPPSC
    • Savitribai headed its women's section and worked for lower-caste girls.
    • 'Deenbandhu' helped spread the movement to the remotest parts of Maharashtra.
    • The women's movement in India began largely under the inspiration of Jyotiba Phule.

    Note from the book On the women's movement question, the Bihar PSC considered no option correct and starred it; the book says Ramabai would have been correct if listed.

    • Phule believed social evils could end only by uplifting women and Dalits; he opened the first girls' school in India in 1848.
    • Ramabai Ranade, wife of M.G. Ranade, also inspired the women's movement; she founded 'Seva Sadan'.
    • Justice Party (1916, Madras Presidency) called the Congress Brahmin-dominated and claimed communal representation for non-Brahmins like that given to Muslims.UPPSC
    • Justice Party = non-Brahmin body for lower castes and backward classes; demanded social justice and educational opportunities.
    • Self-Respect Movement was started by E.V. Ramaswami Naicker (Periyar) for equal rights of so-called lower castes in Tamil Nadu.
    • All India Anti-Untouchability League (later Harijan Sevak Sangh) was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in 1932.
    • All India Kisan Sabha was founded by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati in 1936 at Lucknow; Sahajanand President, N.G. Ranga General Secretary.
    • Bahishkrit Hitkarini Sabha was formed by B.R. Ambedkar, not by Jyotiba Phule.UPPSC
    • Young Bengal Movement: Henry Vivian Derozio; United Indian Patriotic Association: Syed Ahmad Khan.
    • Neo-Buddhism = Dalit Bauddha Movement started by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; it redefined Buddhism and founded the new sect 'Navayan'.
    • Nadars demanded the right to enter temples in 1899, causing a terrible riot in Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu.
    • Tilak: "If God were to tolerate untouchability, I would not recognise him as God at all."UPPSC
    • Tilak said this at a conference on abolition of untouchability; he held all Indians are children of the same motherland.
    • Tilak is called Lokmanya or Betaj Badshah.
    • Hali System concerned bonded labour.UPPSC
    • Tarkeswar Movement (1924, Bengal) was against corrupt priests (Mahant) of the Tarkeswar Shiva temple.UPPSC
    • The Tarkeswar priests were accused of misbehaviour, harassment and unjust money demands on pilgrims.

    Maharashtra reformers and widow remarriage

    • Gopal Hari Deshmukh (1823–92), reformer of Maharashtra born in Pune, was known as 'Lokahitvadi'.UPPSC
    • At 25 he began writing reform articles in the weekly 'Prabhakar' under the pen name Lokahitvadi.
    • He wrote 108 articles in the first two years, known as 'Lokahitawadinchi Shatapatre'.
    • He became a member of the Governor-General's Council in 1880.
    • He appeared at the Delhi court in hand-woven Khadi as a supporter of national self-reliance.
    • Vishnu Parashuram (Shastri) Pandit led the widow remarriage campaign in Maharashtra.UPPSC
    • He founded the Widow Remarriage Association (Punarvivahottejak Mandali / Vidhwa Vivah Samaj) in the 1850s (also printed 1850) and launched the widow remarriage movement.
    • Vishnu Shastri published a Marathi translation of Vidyasagar's book in Indu Prakash in 1868.
    • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Principal of Sanskrit College, Calcutta, fought for widow remarriage using sanction of the Hindu Dharmashastras.
    • Hindu Widows Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was passed on 25 July 1856 through Vidyasagar's campaign.UPPSC
    • The Act gave legal safeguards against loss of certain forms of inheritance for a remarrying Hindu widow.
    • Vidyasagar was the first secretary of Bethune College (Hindu Female School, later Bethune Female School).
    • J.E.D. Bethune established a girls' school in Calcutta.
    • Vidyasagar, asked if God exists: "I have no time to think about God because a lot of work has to be done on this earth."UPPSC
    • D.K. Karve of Western India is linked with women's education and widow remarriage.UPPSC
    • Karve was Secretary of the Widow Remarriage Association.UPPSC
    • Karve founded the Hindu Widows Home in 1896 at Pune and the first Women's University in 1916 at Bombay.
    • Vishnushastri and D.K. Karve were leaders connected with widow welfare.
    • Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu founded the Rajahmundry Social Reform Association (printed dates: 1871 and 1878), to encourage widow remarriage.
    • Veeresalingam = reformer of Madras Presidency; father of the Telugu Renaissance movement.
    • Through the Association he fought the hiring of nautch girls and led a campaign for widow remarriage.

    • Malabari campaigned against child marriage and for widow remarriage through editorials; he is famous for legally eliminating child marriage.

    • K.M. Panikkar called Gokhale 'the first diplomat of modern India'.
    • Panikkar praised Gokhale's peaceful methods and efforts to win international support for India's cause.

    Theosophical Society

    • Founders: Russian (now Ukrainian) noblewoman Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, American army officer Colonel Henry Steel Olcott, William Quan Judge and others.
    • Blavatsky and Olcott moved to India in 1879, where the Society spread rapidly.
    • In 1882 they set up the international headquarters at Adyar, a suburb of Madras (Chennai).
    • Annie Besant was the main reason for the Society's success in India.UPPSC
    • Annie Besant came in contact with the Society in 1882, became a member in 1889 and came to India in 1893.
    • She became chairman of the Society after Colonel Olcott's death in 1907.
    • She held Hinduism to be the most spiritual and esoteric religion and believed in rebirth.
    • Theosophical Society is linked with Annie Besant, not with Mahadev Govind Ranade.UPPSC
    • Mahatma Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, not Gandhinagar.

    • Deoband Movement began in 1866 at Deoband, Saharanpur district, U.P., to overthrow British rule and restore Islamic rule.UPPSC
    • Darul Uloom Deoband's foundation was laid on 31 May 1866.

    • Nadwah-ul-Ulama played an important role in Muslim social reform.
    • Faraizi Movement was started by Haji Shariatullah.
    • Faraizi Movement opposed British rule for denying Muslims religious freedom and confiscating their rights.

    Political Organisations Established Before Congress

    58 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Asiatic Society of Bengal · 15 January 1784 · Calcutta · Sir William Jones×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 16 UPPSC questions

    Raja Ram Mohan Roy and the first bodies

    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the first Indian to struggle for political reforms; guide of social reform and political movements in modern India.
    • Roy wrote about human rights and the growth of democratic values.
    • Bipin Chandra Pal called Ram Mohan Roy the first Indian political reformer; some historians give this credit to Surendra Nath Banerjee.
    • Zamindari Association (Landholders Society), Calcutta, 1838 = first political organisation in India.
    • It began organised political activity and constitutional agitation for redress of grievances.
    • Its aim was to safeguard the rights and interests of zamindars (landlords); founded by Dwarkanath Tagore and fellow zamindars.
    • Bengal British India Society was founded in 1843 by the efforts of George Thompson, whom Dwarkanath Tagore brought from England to organise the political movement.UPPSC
    • George Thompson was president of the Bengal British India Society.
    • British Indian Association was started in October 1851 at Calcutta; Radhakant Deb was its first president.
    • British Indian Association founder members: Rajendralal Mitra, Radhakant Deb (President), Debendranath Tagore (General Secretary) and Harish Chandra Mukherjee.
    • Hindu Mela was founded in 1867 by Nabagopal Mitra, inspired by Rajnarayan Basu.
    • Hindu Mela aimed to promote nationalist feeling and the use of indigenous goods among the masses.

    Poona Sarvajanik Sabha

    • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was one of the strongest political organisations of 19th century India.
    • M.G. Ranade joined in November 1871 and gave it fresh vigour and fine leadership.
    • In 1875 the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha sent a petition to the House of Commons demanding India's direct representation in the British Parliament.

    Indian Association and Surendranath Banerjee

    • Indian Association of Calcutta was the most important pre-Congress nationalist organisation, with an all-India character.
    • Indian Association preferred the middle class over landlords; its purpose was to include everyone, not only middle-class people.
    • Surendranath Banerjee passed the Civil Services exam in 1869 but was disqualified over a dispute about his exact age.
    • He was reappointed after a court judgment, but was dismissed from the Indian Civil Service in 1874 for a minor judicial error.
    • He was a founding member of the Indian Association and the Indian National Conference.
    • He published 'The Bengalee' to promote mass consciousness; he was Congress President twice.
    • Indian National Conference, organised by Surendranath Banerjee, merged with the Indian National Congress in 1886.UPPSC
    • The two merged because their objective, ideology and methods were alike; this helped Indian integration and the Congress.
    • Indian National Liberal Federation is linked with Surendranath Banerjee; it held a liberal, pro-British view in politics.
    • India League's purpose: promote nationalism and political education in India.

    Associations in England

    • Dadabhai Naoroji founded the East India Association in 1866 in London to discuss Indian questions and influence British public opinion.UPPSC
    • Bristol Indian Association was set up in September 1870; renamed 'The Indian Association' in October 1870; renamed National Indian Association in 1871.
    • It was founded in England by Mary Carpenter, Keshav Chandra Sen and Elizabeth Adelaide Manning.
    • This 'Indian Association' worked for women's education, so it was not a political organisation.UPPSC

    Bombay and other bodies

    • Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji are known as the Trimurti of Bombay.
    • Pherozeshah Mehta became president of the Bombay Presidency Association; he urged Indians to take Western education and culture to uplift India.
    • Also printed in one matching list: Bombay Presidency Association against Dadabhai Naoroji, and Poona Sarvajanik Sabha against Mahadev Govind Ranade.
    • United Indian Patriotic Association = political body to build close relations between the Muslim community and the British Government.
    • Servants of India Society was established by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1905.

    Chapter 52 · Freedom struggle

    Indian National Congress

    129 facts · 11 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Congress was established during the viceroyalty of Lord Dufferin (1884–88).×5
    2. Badruddin Tyabji = first Muslim President of the Congress; presided over the 3rd session at Madras, 27–30 December 1887.×5
    3. W.C. Bonnerjee (Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee) presided over the first session = first President of the Congress.×4
    4. Annie Besant = first woman President of the Congress (32nd session, Calcutta, 26–29 December 1917).×4
    5. Bal Gangadhar Tilak was never elected President of the Congress.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 45 UPPSC questions

    Founding of the Congress

    • Indian National Congress was founded by A.O. Hume (Allan Octavian Hume), a retired British officer of the Indian Civil Service.
    • In 1884 Hume set up the Indian National Union, the precursor of the Congress.
    • Hume visited Kolkata, Mumbai and Madras, then took the initiative to call the first meeting of the Union at Poona.
    • Its objective: a share in government for educated Indians, and a platform for civil and political dialogue with the British Raj.
    • The Congress was set up in 1885.UPPSC
    • First session: 28–30 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay.UPPSC ×2
    • It was first fixed for Poona but shifted to Bombay due to an outbreak of cholera.
    • At this session, on Dadabhai Naoroji's advice, the name Indian National Union was changed to Indian National Congress.
    • 72 delegates took part in the first session.
    • W.C. Bonnerjee (Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee) presided over the first session = first President of the Congress.UPPSC ×4
    • A.O. Hume was the first General Secretary of the Congress (1885).UPPSC
    • Hume was never President of the Congress.
    • Surendranath Banerjee was not present at the founding session of the Congress.UPPSC
    • Reason: he was presiding over the second Indian National Conference at Calcutta in December 1885; the first Conference was held in December 1883.
    • Indian Association was founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan in Bengal in 1876 to promote youth nationalism.
    • The Congress was established during the viceroyalty of Lord Dufferin (1884–88).UPPSC ×5
    • Dufferin ridiculed the Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority' (short-sighted minority) of the Indian people.UPPSC ×2

    Early objectives and demands

    • W.C. Bonnerjee's 1885 objectives did not include expressing views on social issues with the consent of the educated class.
    • Objective 1: promote contact and friendship among Indians defending the country's interests.
    • Objective 2: build national unity by removing feelings of caste, sect and regional bias.
    • Objective 3: unite all classes and communities of India and create a sense of one nation.
    • Objective 4: formulate and present public demands.
    • Initially there was an arrangement not to raise social issues from the Congress platform.
    • In the first stage the Congress demanded separation of judiciary from executive; it never demanded their unification.
    • Early demands: greater voice for Indians in government and administration; Indians in high posts.
    • Early demands: legislative councils to be more representative, with more power, and set up in provinces that had none.
    • Early demands: repeal of the Arms Act; freedom of speech and expression.

    Early sessions

    2. 1887Muslim delegates: 2 in the first session, 33 in the second, 81 in the third (1887), 221 in the fourth (1888).
    3. 1887Badruddin Tyabji = first Muslim President of the Congress; presided over the 3rd session at Madras, 27–30 December 1887.UPPSC ×5
    4. 1887607 delegates took part in the 1887 Madras session.
    5. 1887At Madras 1887 the working of the Congress was first handed to a committee of delegates; a Subjects Committee was appointed for the first time.
    6. 1889British Committee of the Indian National Congress was set up in London in July 1889 under the presidency of Sir W. Wedderburn to gain support for the Congress.
    • Second session: Calcutta, 27–30 December 1886, President Dadabhai Naoroji; 436 registered delegates took part.
    • Muslim delegates: 2 in the first session, 33 in the second, 81 in the third (1887), 221 in the fourth (1888).
    • Badruddin Tyabji = first Muslim President of the Congress; presided over the 3rd session at Madras, 27–30 December 1887.UPPSC ×5
    • 607 delegates took part in the 1887 Madras session.
    • At Madras 1887 the working of the Congress was first handed to a committee of delegates; a Subjects Committee was appointed for the first time.
    • British Committee of the Indian National Congress was set up in London in July 1889 under the presidency of Sir W. Wedderburn to gain support for the Congress.
    • It was a committee of the Indian National Congress.
    • It brought out the journal 'India' to tell the British about Indian matters (a monthly that later became weekly; also printed simply as a weekly).

    Critics of the Congress

    • Sir Syed Ahmed Khan was never connected with the Indian National Congress.
    • Sir Syed was in judicial service during the revolt of 1857 and was loyal to the British.
    • He became an opponent of the Congress due to misinterpretations by the British.
    • He published the magazine "Rajbhakt Muslim" to show loyalty to the British; he spread his ideas through "Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq".
    • In 1888 Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Raja Shiv Prasad Singh "Sitar-i-Hind" of Banaras founded the United Indian Patriotic Association.
    • Its aim was to stop the Congress spreading its ideals to the masses and to keep people away from the Congress.
    • Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh, teaching Western subjects, science and Muslim religion.
    • Lala Lajpat Rai wrote that the "Congress movement was neither inspired by the people nor devised or planned by them."
    • Lala Lajpat Rai first used the safety valve theory, in 'Young India', to attack the Moderates.
    • Lajpat Rai considered the Congress the brainchild of Dufferin, meant to protect the British Government from threats.
    • Lord Curzon declared in 1900: "The Congress is tottering to its fall, and one of my greatest ambitions while in India is to assist it to a peaceful demise."UPPSC ×2
    • The British assumed the Congress under the Moderates was weak, lacked Indians' trust and would collapse easily.

    Women presidents

    • Annie Besant = first woman President of the Congress (32nd session, Calcutta, 26–29 December 1917).UPPSC ×4
    • Annie Besant was of Anglo-Irish origin, one of the few foreigners with a major role in the freedom movement.
    • She was President of the Theosophical Society 1907–1933 and founded the Home Rule League in 1916.
    • Sarojini Naidu (1879–1949) = first Indian woman President of the Congress (40th session, Kanpur, 1925).
    • Sarojini Naidu was a famous poet, a trusted colleague of Gandhiji and went to jail many times.
    • She was Governor of U.P. during 1947–49, the first Indian woman to hold that post.

    • A.O. Hume was called the Father of the Congress at the 1912 Bankipore session.
    • Lord Wellingdon took part in the Bombay session of 1915.UPPSC
