    Chapter 53 · Freedom struggle

    Moderates and Extremists in Congress

    80 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Tilak accused the Congress of practising the politics of prayer, petition and protest.×4
    2. Sir Valentine Chirol called Tilak the "Father of Indian Unrest".×4
    3. Four main Extremist leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh; they were not Moderates.×3
    4. Tilak started the Ganpati festival and Shivaji Mahotsav in Maharashtra to rouse nationalist feeling among the masses.×3
    5. Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a Moderate, not an Extremist.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Moderate era

    • The first two decades of the Congress (1885–1905) are called the moderate (liberal) era.
    • Prominent Moderates: Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendra Nath Banerjee, Mahadev Govind Ranade, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Anand Mohan Bose.
    • Moderates trusted British justice and generosity; they never aimed at aggressive nationalism for independence.
    • Moderate leaders supported Europe's rich democratic and scientific culture and strongly criticised the economic aspects of British imperialism.
    • Moderates advocated constitutional reforms, political participation and expansion of modern education.
    • They supported English education, believing it would build a modern outlook and social progress.
    • Dadabhai Naoroji's book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" highlighted the economic drain, heavy taxation and decline of Indian industries.
    • Moderates tried to address such concerns by constitutional means, not direct confrontation.
    • Moderates' method of protest = constitutional agitation.
    • Moderate methods: annual conferences, speeches, elaborate resolutions, petitions to the British Parliament, deputations to England, appeal to the British sense of justice and fair play.
    • Most Moderate leaders came from urban areas.
    • Urban Moderates named: Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee and Surendra Nath Banerjee.
    • The Moderate-phase Congress was dominated by prosperous and middle-class advocates (barristers), doctors, engineers, journalists and literary people.
    • Titles and high posts charmed them; they came from metropolitan cities and had no link with the common masses.
    • Pherozeshah Mehta: the Congress voice is not the voice of the masses, but citizens in touch with it must understand and spread these feelings.
    • Dadabhai Naoroji first demanded 'Swaraj' (self-rule) for India in 1904 at the International Socialist Congress and kept stressing it.UPPSC
    • Naoroji demanded Swaraj in his presidential address at the 1906 Congress session.

    Gokhale

    • Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a Moderate, not an Extremist.UPPSC ×2
    • Gokhale believed in the purity of means and ends; he was the political guru of Mahatma Gandhi.
    • Gokhale first took part in politics in 1889.
    • In 1897 Gokhale and Dinshaw Wacha were asked to give evidence on Indian expenditure before the Welby Commission.
    • Gokhale was elected to the Bombay Legislative Council in 1899 and to the Imperial Council of the Governor-General in 1901.
    • Gokhale led the moderate nationalists; he advocated moderate, constitutional agitation and gradual reform.
    • Gokhale was a social reformer, senior Congress leader and founder of the Servants of India Society, which worked for the underprivileged.

    Rise of the Extremists

    • International events that influenced the national movement before Gandhi: Italian-Abyssinian War (1898), Boxer Movement in China, revolutionary movement in Ireland, Japan's victory over Russia.
    • In the Italian-Abyssinian War the Italian colonial power was defeated; the Boxer movement against imperialists in China ran 1899–1901.
    • Japan's defeat of Czarist Russia in 1905 had the most impact; it broke the illusion that the white race was invincible.
    • Extremist leaders emerged in the early 1900s; after 1906 extremism came to dominate the national movement.
    • Four main Extremist leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh; they were not Moderates.UPPSC ×3
    • The neo-nationalist group of Lal, Bal, Pal was disillusioned with the early moderate policies; Tilak pioneered the new ideology.
    • Extremist ideology = getting self-government by aggressive means instead of petitions and constitutional ways.
    • Extremists' main aim was 'Swaraj'; they believed in self-sacrifice, mass movement, aggressive resistance, strong determination and passive resistance.
    • Extremists had no faith in the goodwill of the British public or Parliament, nor in merely holding conferences.
    • Swaraj as defined in the Congress presidential address, Calcutta, 1906 = self-government like that of the United Kingdom or the Colonies.
    • For Extremists independence meant complete freedom from foreign control; for Moderates, self-rule under the colonial empire.
    • Tilak accused the Congress of practising the politics of prayer, petition and protest.UPPSC ×4
    • The Congress policy of prayer and petition ended, or shrank to a minimum, under Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
    • Tilak was one of the strongest opponents of the British Empire and strongly recommended agitation.
    • Many intellectual Congressmen became Tilak's followers; Lala Lajpat Rai of Punjab and Bipin Chandra Pal of Calcutta became his staunch followers and opposed the moderate policies.
    • First Congress session: Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, 28–30 December 1885; Extremists commented negatively on the Congress.
    • Bipin Chandra Pal called the Congress a "Begging Institute".UPPSC
    • Bipin Chandra Pal was a Brahmo Samaj leader and social reformer; he published the weekly 'New India' in 1901.UPPSC
    • Lala Lajpat Rai called the Congress conference the "Annual National Festival of Educated Indians".
    • Indian Muslims in general stayed away from the Extremist movement because of the Extremists' policy of harping on the Hindu past.
    • Aurobindo Ghosh: "Independence is the purpose of our lives and only Hindu religion will fulfil this objective. Nationality is a religion, a gift of God."

    Swadeshi Movement and Surat split

    • The Swadeshi Movement led to the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists.
    • Surat split: the Congress divided at the Surat session in December 1907, when revolutionary terrorism was gaining momentum.
    • Moderates opposed the resolutions on Swaraj, Swadeshi, national education and boycott of foreign goods; this difference led to the split.
    • Moderates believed in settling issues with the Government by deliberation.
    • Aurobindo Ghosh was the main leader of the Swadeshi Movement (begun 1905 against the partition of Bengal).UPPSC
    • Other Swadeshi leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra) and Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal).
    • Aurobindo was one of the four pillars of the Extremists (Lal, Bal, Pal, Ghose).
    • Aurobindo was arrested in 1908 in the Maniktalla garden raid; given one year's imprisonment but released for lack of evidence.
    • He later became a sage, withdrew from revolutionary activity and moved to Pondicherry (Puducherry).

    Lala Lajpat Rai

    • Lala Lajpat Rai is known as 'Sher-e-Punjab' and 'Punjab Kesari'; Extremist representative of Punjab.
    • Lajpat Rai, Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal together are called Lal-Bal-Pal.
    • Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi charge during a protest against the Simon Commission and died on 17 November 1928.
    • After reading his biography, Lajpat Rai accepted the Italian revolutionary Mazzini as his political guru.UPPSC
    • He translated Mazzini's 'The Duties of Man' into Urdu.
    • Lajpat Rai wrote short biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji, Shri Krishna and Swami Dayanand Saraswati; he stayed in America and was elected to the Central Assembly.
    • He lived in America during his exile from 1907 and returned during the First World War.
    • His other works: 'Unhappy India' and 'The Story of My Deportation'.

    Bal Gangadhar Tilak

    • Tilak believed in service and sacrifice and dared to challenge the British Empire; staunch supporter of Swadeshi.
    • Through his efforts the Congress began to criticise British policies instead of praising British rule.
    • Sir Valentine Chirol called Tilak the "Father of Indian Unrest".UPPSC ×4
    • Tilak went to England to file a defamation suit against Chirol but lost.
    • Tilak founded the English weekly 'The Mahratta' and the Marathi weekly 'Kesari'; both were extreme nationalist papers, which brought him within reach of criminal law; his speeches and writings were judged radical and he was sentenced.
    • The Government accused Tilak in the murder case of Rand (Plague Commissioner of Pune) and Ayerst; he got 18 months' rigorous imprisonment.
    • He came out of jail a national hero; several events together made him 'Lokmanya' Tilak.
    • After his 1897 sedition conviction and the rejection of his Privy Council appeal, Max Muller and Sir William Hunter led a petition to the Queen.
    • Max Muller pleaded for mercy for Tilak: "My interest in Tilak is that of a Sanskrit scholar."UPPSC
    • In 1908 Tilak was sentenced to 6 years for sedition and kept in Mandalay Jail, Burma (Myanmar).
    • The 1908 charge was for printing an anti-British article in 'Kesari'.
    • Tilak wrote 'Gita Rahasya' in Mandalay prison.
    • Tilak declared: "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it."
    • Tilak started the Ganpati festival and Shivaji Mahotsav in Maharashtra to rouse nationalist feeling among the masses.UPPSC ×3
    • Tilak was not a communalist but a staunch nationalist; he used religion as a political weapon, not for communal ends.UPPSC
    • Tilak's approach of close contact with the people is seen as a forerunner of M.K. Gandhi's.
    • Tilak died on 1 August 1920; his bier was lifted by Mahatma Gandhi, Maulana Shaukat Ali and Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew.UPPSC
    • Maulana Hasrat Mohani read the elegy after Tilak's death.

    Chapter 54 · Freedom struggle

    Revolutionary Movements in India

    173 facts · 11 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. In 1904 Mitra Mela was turned into the secret society Abhinav Bharat Society, founded by V.D. Savarkar.×4
    2. Chandra Shekhar Azad, key member of HRA, escaped and was never arrested by the British.×3
    3. Ram Prasad Bismil · Gorakhpur Jail, 19 December 1927×3
    4. The slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad' ('Long Live Revolution') was written by Maulavi Hasrat Mohani; Bhagat Singh used it first and made it popular.×3
    5. Barindra Ghosh, with Bhupendra Nath Dutt, spread revolutionary ideas in Bengal; their activities led to the formation of Anushilan Samiti.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 50 UPPSC questions

    Savarkar, Mitra Mela and Abhinav Bharat

    • Mitra Mela was founded by Vinayak Damodar (V.D.) Savarkar in 1899.UPPSC
    • In 1904 Mitra Mela was turned into the secret society Abhinav Bharat Society, founded by V.D. Savarkar.UPPSC ×4
    • Abhinav Bharat was set up at Nasik in Maharashtra; branches also opened in Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka.UPPSC
    • Savarkar founded the Abhinav Bharat Society during his college education in Pune.
    • Savarkar set up a branch of Abhinav Bharat Society in 1906 at India House, London.
    • Savarkar wrote the book 'The Indian War of Independence 1857', giving a nationalist view of the 1857 revolt; it carried his views.
    • In the book he analysed the circumstances of the 1857 uprising and attacked British rule as unjust and oppressive.
    • Through this book Savarkar became one of the first writers to call 1857 India's 'First War for Independence'.
    • Savarkar wrote the biography of Mazzini to inspire Indian nationalists.
    • Savarkar was arrested in London and sent to India by ship; he jumped into the sea from the sailing ship to escape, but was re-arrested as the alarm was raised.
    • He had planned the escape and told his friend to keep track of the ship.
    • Savarkar was brought to India with others charged in the Nasik conspiracy case and sentenced to life imprisonment.
    • In one matching, Abhinav Bharat → G.D. Savarkar, Mitra Mela → V.D. Savarkar, Indian Republican Army → S. Sen, Hindustan Republican Association → S.N. Sanyal.UPPSC
    • Organisation → leader: Abhinav Bharat Society → V.D. Savarkar; Anushilan Samiti → Sri Aurobindo Ghosh; Ghadar Party → Lala Hardayal; Swaraj Party → C.R. Das.
    • Abhinav Bharat Society and Anushilan Samiti were revolutionary organisations.UPPSC
    • United Indian Patriotic Association: founded by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Raja Shiv Prasad in 1888 to oppose the Congress.
    • Kuka Movement is linked with Guru Ram Singh.

    Nasik Conspiracy Case

    • Anant Laxman Kanhere, of the Karve Group and a member of Abhinav Bharat, shot dead Jackson, District Collector of Nasik, on 21 December 1909; this is the Nasik Conspiracy Case.UPPSC
    • Kanhere, Krishnaji Gopal Karve and Vinayak Deshpande were hanged in the Jackson murder case.
    • 27 members of the Abhinav Bharat Society were convicted and punished in the Nasik case.
    • Rash Behari Bose was associated with the Delhi Conspiracy Case, not the Nasik case.

    RSS

    • Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh was founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar on 27 September 1925 at Nagpur.
    • RSS was founded as a social organisation to give training and unite the Hindu community; headquarters at Nagpur, Maharashtra.

    Chapekar brothers and Tilak

    • Vyayam Mandal was founded at Poona in 1896-97 by the Chapekar brothers: Damodar Hari, Bal Krishna Hari and Vasudeo Hari Chapekar.
    • Vyayam Mandal was founded with clear political intentions.
    • In June 1897 the Chapekar brothers killed Rand, President of the Poona Plague Committee, and Lieutenant Ayerst.
    • Damodar Hari Chapekar and his brothers were hanged; they were arrested on information given by the Dravid brothers.
    • It was alleged that the Brahmins of Poona under Tilak had conspired in the murder of Rand and Ayerst.
    • The British charged Tilak with inciting the murders through his writings but got no evidence to prove it.
    • In July 1897 Tilak was arrested for sedition under Section 124-A of the IPC and sentenced to 18 months; this caused huge protests across the country.
    • This made Tilak an all-India leader and the public gave him the title Lokmanya (during the revolutionary movement).UPPSC
    • Tilak started the Lathi Club, Hindu Akhada, Ganapati Mahotsava and Shivaji Mahotsava.UPPSC

    Anushilan Samiti and Yugantar

    • Anushilan Samiti was a revolutionary organisation that believed in the path of violence.
    • Anushilan Samiti was founded at Midnapur in 1902 by Gyanendra Nath Basu.
    • Calcutta: first branch in March 1902 by Satish Chandra Basu; second branch in 1902 by Pramath Nath (P.) Mitra, Jatindra Nath Mukherjee (Bagha Jatin) and Barindra Nath Ghosh.UPPSC
    • Another Anushilan Samiti was founded at Dhaka in October 1906 by Pulin Bihari Das.
    • Founders of Anushilan Samiti are also given as P. Mitra and Pulin Das.
    • Hemchandra Kanoongo was assistant and bomb expert of the Calcutta Anushilan Samiti.
    • Sachindra Nath Sanyal set up a branch of Anushilan Samiti at Patna in 1913.
    • Barindra Ghosh was the younger brother of Sri Aurobindo Ghosh; influenced by Aurobindo, he joined the revolutionary movement.
    • In 1905 Aurobindo Ghosh wrote the pamphlet 'Bhawani Mandir', describing in detail a centre for organising revolutionary work.
    • Barindra Ghosh, with Bhupendra Nath Dutt, spread revolutionary ideas in Bengal; their activities led to the formation of Anushilan Samiti.UPPSC ×2
    • Yugantar (weekly newspaper) was published in 1906 under Barindra Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Dutta.
    • Jatindranath Mukherjee (1879-1915), a Bengali revolutionary called Bagha Jatin, led the reorganised Yugantar Party.UPPSC
    • Jatindranath Mukherjee was a follower of Vivekananda and Aurobindo Ghosh.
    • He was an active member of Yugantar, Anushilan Samiti and the Gadar Party.
    • Howrah Conspiracy Case (1910) is linked with Jatindranath Mukherjee.
    • Aurobindo Ghosh gave the theory of Passive Resistance in his newspaper Bande Mataram.
    • Aurobindo held that the British must leave India at once and Indians must keep protesting until they leave.

    Barrah Dacoity

    • Barrah Dacoity (1908) = first major venture of the revolutionary terrorists in East Bengal; at the Barrah zamindar's residence in Dhaka district.
    • It was planned and led by Pulin Behari Das, who founded the National School in Dhaka to develop a revolutionary army.

    Muzaffarpur bombing and Alipore case

    • Kingsford was Chief Presidency Magistrate of Calcutta; Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki went to Muzaffarpur (Bihar) to kill him.
    • On the evening of 30 April 1908 they waited at the gate of the European Club and threw bombs at a carriage.
    • Kingsford was not in the carriage; Mrs. and Miss Kennedy, wife and daughter of barrister Pringle Kennedy, were killed.
    • Mr. Kennedy was a sympathiser of the national movement.
    • Prafulla Chaki committed suicide; Khudiram Bose was caught and hanged.
    • Alipore Conspiracy Case (1908): 49 persons, including Aurobindo Ghosh and his brother Barindra Kumar Ghosh, were accused of waging war, conspiracy and possessing illegal arms and bombs.
    • 19 persons were sentenced; Aurobindo Ghosh was released, successfully defended by Chittaranjan Das.UPPSC ×2
    • Kanhai Lal Dutt and Satyendra Bose shot dead Narendra Gosain, a government witness in the Alipore case, inside the prison; they were sentenced to death.

    Hindustan Republican Association

    • Revolutionaries of northern India were disillusioned by the sudden suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
    • A conference of young revolutionaries at Kanpur in October 1924 founded the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA).UPPSC
    • HRA founding members: Sachindra Nath Sanyal (President), Ram Prasad Bismil, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Chandra Shekhar Azad.
    • Shiv Verma was not a member of HRA; he joined its renewed form, HSRA.UPPSC
    • Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad and Ram Prasad Bismil were earlier members of HRA; Bhagat Singh joined HRA in 1925.
    • Shiv Verma was sentenced to life imprisonment in the Lahore Conspiracy.

    Kakori Train Action

    • On 9 August 1925 HRA looted the government treasury from a train at Kakori, near Lucknow (Kakori Conspiracy / Kakori Train Action).UPPSC ×2
    • The train was the "Eight Down Saharanpur-Lucknow passenger train" of Northern Railway's Lucknow-Saharanpur section.
    • The robbery was led by Ram Prasad Bismil; others involved: Chandra Shekhar Azad, Sachindra Sanyal, Manmath Nath Gupta, Rajendra Lahiri.
    • About 40 (also given as 43) revolutionaries were arrested.
    • Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Roshan Singh (also printed Roshan Lal) and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged.
    • Chandra Shekhar Azad, key member of HRA, escaped and was never arrested by the British.UPPSC ×3
    • Keshab Chakravarthy and Murari Lal Gupta also escaped earlier.
    • Surya Sen was not associated with the Kakori incident.
    • Bhagat Singh was not associated with the Kakori conspiracy.UPPSC
    • The court appointed Jagat Narayan Mulla as public prosecutor in the Kakori case.UPPSC
    • Jogesh (Yogesh) Chandra Chatterjee, a founder member of HRA, got life imprisonment in the Kakori case; he wrote the book 'In Search of Freedom'.
    • His book says Pandit Motilal Nehru formed the Kakori Case Defence Committee under the leadership of Govind Ballabh Pant.UPPSC

    Note from the book An article by Shankar Narayan Rao on the PIB website names Pandit Motilal Nehru as president of the Kakori defence committee; UPPSC first keyed Motilal Nehru, then revised to Govind Ballabh Pant.

    Kakori martyrPlace of hanging
    Ram Prasad BismilGorakhpur Jail, 19 December 1927UPPSC ×3
    Rajendra LahiriGonda
    Roshan SinghAllahabad (now Prayagraj)
    Ashfaqullah KhanFaizabad (now Ayodhya) Jail, 19 December 1927
    • Ashfaqullah Khan was the first recorded Muslim hanged for India's freedom; hanged at the age of 27.UPPSC
    • Ashfaqullah Khan was born on 22 October 1900 at Shahjahanpur, Uttar Pradesh.

    Note from the book If the 1857 revolt is counted, the answer becomes Azizuddin: after suppressing the Delhi revolt in 1857 the British hanged Mughal prince Azizuddin and 6 other Mughal princes at the Delhi Gate.

    • Ram Prasad Bismil refused milk offered two days before (on the eve of) his hanging, saying "I will drink only my mother's milk".UPPSC

    Note from the book UPPSC first accepted Ram Prasad Bismil for the milk question, but later removed the question from the answer sheet.

    • Bismil, an excellent poet, recited a sher just before the gallows: "Malik teri raza rahe, aur tu hi tu rahe; baki na main rahun, na meri aarzu rahe; jab tak tan mein saans, ragon mein lahu rahe; tera hi zikr-e-yaar aur teri hi justju rahe".
    • "Sarfaroshi ki tamanna ab hamare dil mein hai, dekhna hai zor kitna baju-e-qatil mein hai" was written by Bismil Azimabadi, not Ram Prasad Bismil.
    • Bismil Azimabadi's original name was Saiyad Shah Muhammad Hasan; born 1901 in Binaha village, Patna.
    • The ghazal was published in 1922 in the magazine "Sabah" of Qazi Abdul Gaffar.
    • "Daro-deewar pe hasrat ki nazar karte hain, khush raho ahle-vatan ham to safar karte hain" was said by Wazid Ali Shah, last Nawab of Awadh.UPPSC ×2
    • Indian revolutionaries used to sing this poem during imprisonment and before capital punishment.

    Kanpur Conspiracy Case

    • Kanpur Conspiracy Case (1924): some communist leaders were tried at Kanpur to repress the growing power of communists in India.
    • 13 originally accused: M.N. Roy, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shaukat Usmani, Ghulam Hussain, S.A. Dange, M. Singaravelu, R.L. Sharma, Nalini Gupta, Shamuddin Hassan, M.R.S. Velayndhun, Doctor Manilal, Sampurnananda, Satyabhakta.UPPSC
    • M.A. Ansari was not associated with the Kanpur Conspiracy Case.
    • Socialist ideology spread in India in the third decade of the 20th century; the government jailed socialist leaders to suppress it.
    • Shripad Amrit Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, Shaukat Usmani and Nalini Gupta were jailed on false charges in the Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case; each got four years' imprisonment.

    HSRA

    • Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was set up in September 1928 at Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi.UPPSC
    • HSRA was founded under the leadership of Chandra Shekhar Azad, who changed the name of HRA to HSRA.UPPSC ×2
    • Those who reorganised HRA under Azad: Vijay Kumar Singh, Shiv Verma, Jai Dev Kapoor, Bhagat Singh, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Sukhdev.
    • Bhagat Singh was one of the founder members of HSRA.
    • HSRA operated more dangerously from 1928 to 1931.
    • In December 1928 Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad and Rajguru killed Assistant Superintendent of Police John (J.P.) Saunders.
    • Saunders was killed to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death: he had ordered the lathi charge on the procession against the Simon Commission.
    • Association → founder: Revolt Group → Surya Sen; HRA → Ram Prasad Bismil; HSRA → Chandra Shekhar Azad; Punjab Naujawan Bharat Sabha → Bhagat Singh.UPPSC
    • Ram Prasad Bismil was a founder member of HRA and had a special role in the Kakori conspiracy.
    • No organisation named 'Hindustan Socialist Democratic Union' existed in history.
    • Srikrishan Saral's book 'Indian Revolutionaries 1757-1961', Vol-3, gives that name for the 1928 body of Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad and Sachindra Sanyal; contemporary documents and authentic histories call it HSRA.
    • Yatindranath was martyred in 1915 itself.
    • Gopen Chakravarti and Dharani Goswami were members of the Calcutta Anushilan Samiti, linked with the communist movement and accused in the Meerut conspiracy; they were not members of HSRA.
    • Womesh Chandra Banerjee was a moderate leader and the first president of the Indian National Congress.

    Note from the book On the 'Hindustan Socialist Democratic Union' founder question no option is correct; UPPSC took "Yatindranath, Ajay Ghosh, Phanindranath Ghosh" as correct in its initial key.

    Assembly bomb and Lahore Conspiracy Case

    • On 8 April 1929 HSRA members Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw a harmless bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly, "to make the deaf British Government hear".UPPSC ×2
    • The bomb was thrown while proceedings on the Trade Disputes and Public Safety Bills were going on.
    • It was a low-intensity bomb used to protest against an Act, and they ensured there were no deaths.
    • Right after the bombing Bhagat Singh and his friends surrendered voluntarily and were put on trial.
    • Bhagat Singh was born in September 1907, so he was a little more than 21 years old at the Assembly bombing.
    • Lahore Conspiracy Case (1929-1930): Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru and others of HSRA were tried for killing ASP J.P. Saunders.UPPSC ×2
    • 18 members of HSRA were arrested and charged in the Lahore conspiracy.
    • A special tribunal was constituted by the Governor-General; in October 1930 it gave capital punishment to Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev.
    • Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were hanged on 23 March 1931.
    • Batukeshwar Dutt was not hanged; he was sent to Cellular Jail (Andaman) for Kala-Pani punishment.
    • The three were secretly cremated on the bank of the Sutlej at Hussainiwala in Firozpur district; Shaheed Bhagat Singh's memorial stands there.UPPSC
    • Every year on 23 March thousands of people come to the memorial to pay homage.
    • Their hanging was a major turning point in India's freedom struggle.
    • The slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad' ('Long Live Revolution') was written by Maulavi Hasrat Mohani; Bhagat Singh used it first and made it popular.UPPSC ×3
    • Bhagat Singh said: "Criticism and independent thinking are the two indispensable qualities of a revolutionary".UPPSC
    • Bhagat Singh's words were not rigid or ideologically regimented; he insisted on a scientific and critical attitude towards all things.
    • Chandra Shekhar Azad carried on his activities even after Bhagat Singh's arrest; he had dodged police since Kakori and also escaped in the Lahore Conspiracy matter.
    • Azad was the only HSRA member never arrested by police.
    • On 27 February 1931 police surrounded Azad in Alfred Park (Chandra Shekhar Azad Park), Allahabad (Prayagraj); he was martyred in the gunfight.UPPSC

    Jatin Das

    • Jatindra (Jatin) Das took part in Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement in 1921.
    • Later he joined the revolutionaries and made bombs to help Bhagat Singh and comrades.
    • Jatin Das was arrested on 14 June 1929 under the supplementary Lahore Conspiracy Case.UPPSC
    • He began a hunger strike for jail reforms and died on 13 September 1929 after 63 days of fasting.UPPSC

    Naujawan Bharat Sabha

    • Naujawan Bharat Sabha was founded by Bhagat Singh in March 1926.
    • Early members with Bhagat Singh: Chhabil Das, Yaspal, Ramchandra, Bhagvati Charan Vohra.
    • It was a left-wing association that sought revolution against the British Raj by gathering worker and peasant youths and spreading Marxist ideas.
    • It was part of the Hindustan Republican Association.
    • Ambika Chakravarti was not an early member; he joined the Naujawan Bharat Sabha at a later stage.UPPSC
    • Ambika Chakravarti was a member of the Chittagong Jugantar Party and took part in the Chittagong Armoury Raid led by Surya Sen.

    Chittagong Armoury Raid

    • Chittagong Armoury Raid: an attempt to raid the armoury of the police and auxiliary forces at Chittagong in Bengal.
    • It was organised by Surya Sen, also famous as "Master Da".
    • Surya Sen set up the Indian Republican Army (IRA) in Bengal; he also established the Revolt Group at Chittagong.
    • IRA members with Surya Sen: Ganesh Ghosh, Loknath, Nirmal Sen, Ambika Chakraborty, Naresh Roy, Kalpana Dutt, Ananda Gupta, Tegra (Tegrabal).
    • The armoury was raided on 18 April 1930.
    • On 22 April 1930 government forces and the IRA fought; 80 soldiers and 12 revolutionaries were killed.
    • Surya Sen was arrested on 16 February 1933 and hanged on 12 January 1934.
    • Kalpana Dutt was arrested with Surya Sen and got life imprisonment.

    Chapter 55 · Freedom struggle

    Revolutionary Activities Outside India

    65 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Shyamji Krishna Verma founded the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) in London in February 1905.×4
    2. Raja Mahendra Pratap, with Barakatullah Khan, set up the first provisional Government of India at Kabul (Afghanistan) on 1 December 1915, during World War I.×3
    3. Rash Behari Bose founded the Indian Independence League there and was unanimously elected its President.×3
    4. It was founded in the United States of America by Indians living in the USA and Canada.×2
    5. She is famous as the 'Mother of the Indian Revolution'.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 20 UPPSC questions

    Indian Home Rule Society and India House

    • Shyamji Krishna Verma founded the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) in London in February 1905.UPPSC ×4
    • IHRS set up a nationalist student hostel, 'India House' (1905-10), in London to foster radical Indian nationalist thought.UPPSC
    • Aim of the society: self-rule, by spreading nationalist ideas among Indians in Britain and by intimidating the British Government.
    • A monthly journal, 'The Indian Sociologist', was started from here in January 1905.
    • Shyamji left London for Paris because of the over-activeness of the government machinery, and later went to Geneva.
    • Abhinav Bharat Society was extended to England in 1906 after revolutionary activities were banned in India; V.D. Savarkar set it up when he went to London to study law.

    Ghadar Party

    • The Ghadar Party was founded on 21 April 1913 (at Oregon) to free India from British rule.
    • It was founded in the United States of America by Indians living in the USA and Canada.UPPSC ×2
    • It was a revolutionary association of expatriate Indians with headquarters at San Francisco.UPPSC
    • In 1913 Sohan Singh Bhakna founded the 'Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast' at San Francisco.UPPSC
    • The society published a newspaper named 'Ghadar', so it became famous as the Ghadar Party.
    • Sohan Singh Bhakna was the first Chairman (President) of the Ghadar Party.UPPSC
    • Lala Hardayal was a founder member and the torchbearer of the Ghadar Party.UPPSC
    • The 'Ghadar' newspaper was published in Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati and Hindi.
    • Prominent members: Ramchandra, Barakatullah, Rash Behari Bose, Raja Mahendra Pratap, Abdul Rahman, Madam Bhikaji Cama, Bhai Parmanand, Kartar Singh Sarabha and Pt. Kashiram (Kanshiram).
    • Rash Behari Bose was actively associated with the Ghadar Party.
    • Barindra Kumar Ghosh was linked with the Alipore Bomb case; Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee with the Kakori Conspiracy (Kakori Train Action).
    • Khudiram Bose was not associated with the Ghadar Party.UPPSC
    • Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb at Kingsford on 30 April 1908 at Muzaffarpur, Bihar; the wife and daughter of Mr. Kennedy, an Indian sympathiser, died.
    • Prafulla Chaki committed suicide; Khudiram Bose was hanged on 11 August 1908 aged 18 years, 8 months, 8 days.
    • Lala Har Dayal, revolutionary and scholar, was appointed to teach Indian philosophy and Sanskrit at Stanford University in California (USA); this chance to be Professor of Indian Philosophy came in 1911.
    • During World War I, San Francisco was the centre of the Ghadar revolutionaries; it lies in the western part of the USA (West America).

    Note from the book If America is divided only into North and South America continents, the answer for the Ghadar base becomes North America.

    • After the decline of the Swadeshi movement, the torchbearers of nationalism had become inactive.
    • The outbreak of World War I in 1914 was the cause of the Ghadar revolution; nationalists took it as an opportunity.
    • The popular idea then: "Any distress on England is an advantage for Indians and it should be taken as a chance."
    • Ghadar revolutionaries in North America, and Lokmanya Tilak and Annie Besant with their Swadeshi organisations in India, used this opportunity.
    • Ghadar revolutionaries tried to overthrow British rule through armed struggle.
    • The Ghadar Movement was an early 20th century international political movement of expatriate Indians; its official birth is the meeting of 21 April 1913.

    Provisional Government at Kabul

    • Raja Mahendra Pratap, with Barakatullah Khan, set up the first provisional Government of India at Kabul (Afghanistan) on 1 December 1915, during World War I.UPPSC ×3
    • Raja Mahendra Pratap was President and Maulavi Barakatullah Khan was Prime Minister.
    • Germany and Russia recognised this government.

    Madam Bhikaji Cama

    • Madam Bhikaiji Rustom Cama was born on 24 September 1861 to Parsi parents, in an extremely wealthy Parsi business family; her father was Sorabji Patel.
    • She was married to Rustomji, an advocate and social worker.
    • She served as personal secretary of Dadabhai Naoroji.
    • She joined the freedom movement after coming into contact with European scholars and students.
    • She supported revolutionary nationalism and ran revolutionary activities from Europe and America.
    • At the International Socialist Congress at Stuttgart (Germany) on 22 August 1907 she became the first person to hoist the Indian flag on foreign land.UPPSC
    • The statement that she unfurled the flag at Paris in 1907 is wrong.
    • The flag was designed jointly by V.D. Savarkar, Shyamji Krishna Verma and Bhikaiji Cama.
    • She is famous as the 'Mother of the Indian Revolution'.UPPSC ×2
    • She worked for Indian freedom while living in Paris; returned to Mumbai in 1935 and died in August 1936.
    • Madam Bhikaji Cama, M. Barkatullah, V.V.S. Iyer and M.N. Roy were prominent revolutionaries working for India's freedom from different foreign countries.

    Madan Lal Dhingra and Udham Singh

    • Madan Lal Dhingra and Udham Singh were hanged for killing British officials in England.UPPSC
    • On 1 July 1909 Madan Lal Dhingra shot dead Curzon Wyllie and Cowasji Lalkaka at a meeting of the National Indian Association.
    • Curzon Wyllie was political aide-de-camp to the Secretary of State for India.
    • Udham Singh killed Michael O'Dwyer, former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab, in London in March 1940.
    • O'Dwyer was responsible for endorsing and upholding the actions taken during the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.

    Komagata Maru

    • Kamagata Maru was a Japanese steamliner (ship) chartered by Gurdit Singh, a rich Punjabi businessman, to take Indian immigrants to Canada.UPPSC
    • The 'Kamagata Maru episode' is linked with Baba Gurdit Singh (printed "Gurdip Singh" in the option by error).UPPSC
    • The ship left in 1914 with 376 Indians for Vancouver port, but the Canadian authorities refused them entry.
    • A Shore Committee was formed under Hussain Rahim, Balwant Singh and Sohan Lal Pathak to protect the rights of the Indian travellers.
    • Bhagwan Singh, Barkatullah, Ramchand and Sohan Singh also ran a movement in favour of the Indian emigrants.
    • When the ship reached Budge Budge port at Calcutta, angry passengers clashed with British police.
    • In police firing 20 passengers were killed, one drowned and 202 were sent to jail.

    Chronology and headquarters

    • Order: Ghadar Party founded (21 April 1913) → Indian Independence Committee at Berlin (after 1915) → Central Assembly Bomb Case (8 April 1929) → Chittagong Armoury Raid (18 April 1930).UPPSC
    • During World War I (1914-1918) the Berlin Committee was founded in Germany; after 1915 it was renamed the Indian Independence Committee.
    • Chittagong Armoury Raid (Chittagong uprising): 18 April 1930, led by Surya Sen, in Bengal Presidency (now in Bangladesh).
    • On 8 April 1929 Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt hurled two bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly chamber while it was in session.

    Indian Independence League

    • Rash Behari Bose was an Indian living in Japan; he held a conference in Tokyo on 28-30 March 1942 to discuss India's political problems.
    • It was given organised form at the Bangkok Convention in June 1942, to which Subhas Chandra Bose was invited.
    • Rash Behari Bose founded the Indian Independence League there and was unanimously elected its President.UPPSC ×3

    Chapter 56 · Freedom struggle

    Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi Movement

    75 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Vande Mataram became overnight the national song of Bengal and later the theme song (rally cry, anthem) of the national movement during the Swadeshi Movement.×3
    2. Krishna Kumar Mitra, editor of 'Sanjivani', in a special edition of 13 July 1905 first suggested the boycott of British goods.×2
    3. On 7 August 1905 a historic meeting at the Town Hall, Calcutta began the anti-partition movement, one of the first mass protests.×2
    4. At the Delhi Durbar on 12 December 1911 King George V annulled the partition of Bengal.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 17 UPPSC questions

    Partition of Bengal: dates and people

    1. 1793Permanent Settlement of Bengal: Lord Cornwallis, 1793; Subsidiary Alliance: Lord Wellesley.
    2. 1848Doctrine of Lapse (annexation policy): Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-56.
    3. 1899Bengal was partitioned in the tenure of Viceroy Lord Curzon (1899-1905).UPPSC
    4. 1903Sir Andrew Henderson Leith Fraser, an ICS officer, was Lieutenant Governor of Bengal from 1903 to 1908; he played an important role in planning the partition.UPPSC
    5. 1905The resolution on the partition of Bengal was signed on 19 July 1905; BPSC took 19 July as the declaration date.
    6. 1905The British Government (Lord Curzon) announced the partition on 20 July 1905.
    7. 1905The partition formally came into force on 16 October 1905.
    8. 1905Among Permanent Settlement, Subsidiary Alliance, annexation policy and Partition of Bengal, the partition (July 1905) came last.UPPSC
    • The resolution on the partition of Bengal was signed on 19 July 1905; BPSC took 19 July as the declaration date.
    • The British Government (Lord Curzon) announced the partition on 20 July 1905.
    • Bengal was partitioned in the tenure of Viceroy Lord Curzon (1899-1905).UPPSC
    • The partition formally came into force on 16 October 1905.
    • Sir Andrew Henderson Leith Fraser, an ICS officer, was Lieutenant Governor of Bengal from 1903 to 1908; he played an important role in planning the partition.UPPSC
    • Bengal was split into East and West: East Bengal merged with Assam to form a new province, 'Eastern Bengal and Assam'.
    • Eastern Bengal and Assam included Rajshahi, Chittagong and Dhaka; Dacca (now Dhaka) was its capital.
    • The second part included the Bengal province, Orissa and Bihar.
    • Curzon drew the line so that the western part was a Hindu-majority area and the eastern part a Muslim-majority area.
    • Among Permanent Settlement, Subsidiary Alliance, annexation policy and Partition of Bengal, the partition (July 1905) came last.UPPSC
    • Permanent Settlement of Bengal: Lord Cornwallis, 1793; Subsidiary Alliance: Lord Wellesley.
    • Doctrine of Lapse (annexation policy): Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-56.

    Reason for partition

    • The British called the partition an administrative necessity; Curzon called it "a mere readjustment of administrative boundaries".
    • The real reason was to weaken the growth of nationalism in Bengal.UPPSC
    • Bengal was then considered "the nerve-centre" of Indian nationalism; Curzon decided to divide the politically advanced communities into separate provinces.
    • One main objective was to divide the unity of the people of Bengal.
    • Curzon: "Calcutta is the centre from which the Congress Party is manipulated throughout the whole of Bengal and indeed the whole of India ..... The whole of their activity is directed to creating an agency so powerful that they may one day be able to force a weak government to give them what they desire."

    Start of the anti-partition and Swadeshi movement

    • Surendranath Banerjee led the agitation against the partition of Bengal (1905).UPPSC
    • Surendranath Banerjee said the partition announcement "fell on us like a bomb (shell)".
    • Krishna Kumar Mitra, editor of 'Sanjivani', in a special edition of 13 July 1905 first suggested the boycott of British goods.UPPSC ×2
    • In his opinion the manufacturing of British goods should be abolished.
    • He asked people to boycott British goods, mourn the partition and break all links with British officers and offices.
    • Krishna Kumar Mitra was a freedom fighter, journalist and Brahmo Samaj leader; 'Sanjibani' was his nationalist Bengali weekly, in which he advocated freedom of the press.
    • A public gathering at Bagerhat (then in Khulna district, Bengal Presidency) on 16 July 1905 supported his suggestion.
    • On 7 August 1905 a historic meeting at the Town Hall, Calcutta began the anti-partition movement, one of the first mass protests.UPPSC ×2
    • The Swadeshi Movement was formally proclaimed at this meeting and the historic Boycott resolution was passed; boycott of British goods became national policy.UPPSC
    • The announcement of the partition of Bengal was the immediate cause of the Swadeshi Movement, which began as a reaction to it.
    • Swadeshi and Boycott were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during the anti-partition agitation.
    • It was an economic strategy aimed at the British Empire.
    • 7 August is celebrated as National Handloom Day every year in memory of the Swadeshi Movement launched on 7 August 1905.
    • 16 October 1905 was observed as a day of mourning in the whole of Bengal; hearths in the houses were kept unlit.
    • On Rabindranath Tagore's suggestion the day was celebrated as 'Rakhi Diwas'; people tied rakhis on each other's wrists as a symbol of brotherhood.
    • In Calcutta most offices were closed and a strike was observed in some jute mills and railway workshops.
    • Vande Mataram became overnight the national song of Bengal and later the theme song (rally cry, anthem) of the national movement during the Swadeshi Movement.UPPSC ×3

    Leaders and spread

    • Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai were the prominent leaders of the Swadeshi idea.
    • They wanted a country-wide Swadeshi movement; the Moderates wanted it limited to Bengal and preferred constitutional methods.
    • The Swadeshi Movement was not limited to Bengal; it spread across the country.UPPSC
    RegionLeader of Swadeshi Movement
    Maharashtra (Bombay and Pune)Bal Gangadhar Tilak
    Punjab and Uttar PradeshAjit Singh and Lala Lajpat Rai
    DelhiSyed Haider RazaUPPSC
    Madras PresidencyV.O. Chidambaram PillaiUPPSC
    • Ashwini Kumar Dutt founded the Swadesh Bandhav Samiti to organise the masses for the movement.
    • Ashwini Kumar Dutta, not Liyakat Hussain, led the Muslim peasants of Barisal in their agitation.
    • In 1889 the scheme of national education was formulated by Satish Chandra Mukherjee.
    • The Bengal National College was founded in 1906 with Aurobindo as Principal.
    • Tagore preached the cult of Atmasakti; its main plank was social and economic regeneration of the villages.

    Participation

    • Women took an active part for the first time in any movement: they came out of their houses, joined rallies and sat in protest.
    • Farmers and Muslims showed limited participation and stayed apart from the Swadeshi and Boycott movements.
    • Only some specific Muslims were influenced; the movement did not influence the farmers of Bengal, Barisal being an exception.
    • The movement affected only the high and middle classes of society.
    • It is also said to have spread to all classes and groups, including women, children, school and college students; this made the British reverse the partition order.
    • People opposed British offices and institutes and boycotted foreign goods.

    Programme and results

    • Programmes against the partition: Boycott, Swadeshi and National education (not Non-cooperation).
    • Swadeshi was complementary to Boycott: with the boycott of foreign goods, the use of indigenous goods grew.
    • The movement helped set up Swadeshi industries: textile mills, banks, chemical works and insurance companies; Swadeshi stores were opened.
    • National education and Indian languages were encouraged.
    • The movement revived indigenous artisan crafts and industries; the National Council of Education was set up as part of it.

    Annulment of partition

    • At the Delhi Durbar on 12 December 1911 King George V annulled the partition of Bengal.UPPSC ×2
    • King George V and Queen Mary were presented to Indian dignitaries and princes as Emperor and Empress of India at the Durbar.
    • The King also declared the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
    • Bengal was reorganised as a new province; Orissa and Bihar were separated from Bengal.

    Tagore, Nevinson and art

    • Rabindranath Tagore criticised parts of the Swadeshi movement (aggressive and exclusive nationalism, sole reliance on boycott) and pleaded for better relations between East and West.UPPSC
    • He believed the West had made some mistake in understanding the East, but the East need not do the same with the West.
    • Tagore denounced European imperialism and at times fully supported Indian nationalists, yet shunned the Swadeshi movement.
    • He denounced it in his September 1925 essay "The Cult of the Chakra" (an allusion to elements of Gandhism and the Non-cooperation Movement).
    • He called British control of India a "political symptom of our social disease" and urged steady and purposeful education instead of blind revolution.
    • British journalist Henry Woodd (H.W.) Nevinson was associated with the Swadeshi Movement.UPPSC
    • His brief: to "discover the causes of the present discontent and to report, without prejudice, the opinions of leading Indians as well as officials".
    • He travelled across India for four months, reporting for the Manchester Guardian, Glasgow Herald and Daily Chronicle; he compiled the reports into the book 'The New Spirit in India'.
    • Abanindranath Tagore painted the famous image of Bharat Mata in 1905 during the Swadeshi Movement.
    • Bharat Mata is shown as a goddess with four hands in a saffron sari; the image became a symbol of nationalism and unity.
    • Abanindranath Tagore and his brother Gaganendranath Tagore founded the Indian Society of Oriental Art in 1907, initiated by E.B. Havell.UPPSC
    • Its aim: to revive precious Indian art and culture and build new consciousness among the masses.
    • Abanindranath was the first Indian artist to gain international recognition and the principal artist of the society; his elder brother Gaganendranath was also an artist.
    • He was a major exponent of Swadeshi values in Indian art and gave new life to the Indian School of Art.

    Chapter 57 · Freedom struggle

    Congress: Benaras, Calcutta, and Surat Session

    44 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Gopal Krishna Gokhale presided over the 1905 Benaras session of the Congress.×3
    2. The Congress split into Moderates (Naram Dal) and Extremists (Garam Dal) at the Surat session, December 1907, its 23rd session; this was the first split of the Congress.×3
    3. Dadabhai Naoroji is known as the 'Grand Old Man of India'; he was a Parsi intellectual, educationist and early political and social leader.×2
    4. Rash Behari Ghosh became President of the Surat session.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 13 UPPSC questions

    Gokhale and the Benaras session (1905)

    • Gopal Krishna Gokhale presided over the 1905 Benaras session of the Congress.UPPSC ×3
    • Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in the same year, 1905.
    • The Congress took up the Swaraj call at the Benaras session, 1905; it was fully passed at the Calcutta session, 1906.
    • Purpose of the Swaraj resolution: to secure self-rule, boycott British products, revive domestic products and Indian industrial production, and get a better education policy for India.
    • Gokhale was born on 9 May 1866 in Ratnagiri (Maharashtra).
    • He graduated from Elphinstone College in 1884 and became professor of Political Economy and History at Fergusson College, Poona.
    • He was a protege of social reformer Mahadev Govind Ranade and a member of the Deccan Education Society.
    • He first joined the Congress in 1889 at the Bombay session.
    • He became a member of the Bombay Legislative Council and then of the Imperial Legislative Council.
    • He fought for decades for greater political representation and power over public affairs for common Indians.
    • Gokhale was the political mentor of Gandhiji, who often called him 'Mahatma'.
    • A biographer on Gokhale: graduate at 18; professor and associate editor of the Sudharak at 20; Secretary of the Sarvajanik Sabha and of the Provincial Conference at 25; Secretary of the National Congress at 29; leading witness before an important Royal Commission at 31; provincial legislator at 34; Imperial legislator at 36; Congress President at 39; a patriot whom Mahatma Gandhi regarded as his master.

    Calcutta session (1906)

    • In 1906 the Congress was close to splitting over the presidentship of the Calcutta session; the split was avoided by agreeing on Dadabhai Naoroji, who presided.
    • The extremists were more popular than the moderates and could have taken over the Congress had they elected a leader from among them, but this was not done.
    • The moderates chose Naoroji; he was respected by moderates and extremists alike.
    • Four resolutions were passed at Calcutta in 1906: Swaraj (self-government), Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education; annulment of the partition of Bengal was not one of them.
    • 'Swaraj' was first uttered as the goal of the Indian people at the Calcutta session, December 1906, in Naoroji's presidential address.UPPSC
    • Naoroji declared that the Congress goal, 'Self-Government or Swaraj', was the same as that of the United Kingdom.
    • The moderates toned the resolution down to self-government as in the self-governing British colonies.
    • At the Calcutta session of 1906 the flag of Swaraj for India was unfurled by the session president, Dadabhai Naoroji.
    • Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920) said "Swaraj is my birthright, I shall have it"; he is taken as the first leader to use the word 'Swaraj'.UPPSC

    Note from the book The word 'Swaraj' was first used by Dayanand Saraswati; Tilak is only the closest answer.

    Dadabhai Naoroji

    • Dadabhai Naoroji is known as the 'Grand Old Man of India'; he was a Parsi intellectual, educationist and early political and social leader.UPPSC ×2
    • He was the first Indian elected to the British Parliament (House of Commons), in 1892, from Central Finsbury.UPPSC
    • He was elected on the ticket of the Liberal Party, not the Conservative Party.UPPSC
    • He presided over the Congress three times (not four): 1886, 1893 and 1906.UPPSC
    • He was the first Indian appointed professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy (Physics) at Elphinstone College, Bombay.
    • In 1851 he started the Gujarati newspaper 'Rast Goftar'.
    • He wrote the book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'.
    • He worked as Professor of Gujarati at University College, London, and laid the foundation of women's education in Bombay.
    • C.Y. Chintamani (editor, journalist, liberal politician): many intelligent and selfless leaders served the people of India, but in his era no one was like Dadabhai Naoroji.
    • Gokhale said: "If there is the divine in man, it is in Dadabhai Naoroji" (also given as "if there is a God somewhere, he is Dadabhai Naoroji").

    Surat split (1907)

    • The Congress split into Moderates (Naram Dal) and Extremists (Garam Dal) at the Surat session, December 1907, its 23rd session; this was the first split of the Congress.UPPSC ×3
    • The dispute was over the presidentship: Moderates wanted Rash Behari Ghosh, Extremists wanted Lala Lajpat Rai.
    • Rash Behari Ghosh became President of the Surat session.UPPSC ×2
    • The Extremists wanted a guarantee that all four Calcutta resolutions would be accepted; the Moderates (liberals) were not in favour of continuing them.
    • To pressure the Moderates the Extremists decided to oppose even the duly elected president Rash Behari Ghosh.
    • Both sides came prepared for conflict; members fought with each other at the session and the Congress split.
    • The Surat split was led by Tilak.
    • In 1907 the Extremists (Garam Dal) were led by Lala Lajpat Rai and the Moderates (Naram Dal) by Rash Behari Ghosh.
    • Main reason for the split: the Extremists' lack of faith in the capacity of the Moderates to negotiate with the British Government.
    • The Extremists wanted to extend the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement; the Moderates did not.
    • The process of the split began over the strategies of the Congress movement, the objectives of the Congress and people's participation in the movement.
    • The Indian National Congress was formed in 1885.
    • Moderates and Extremists reunited at the Congress session of 1916, presided over by Ambika Charan Mazumdar, not S.P. Sinha.

    Chapter 58 · Freedom struggle

    Formation of Muslim League (1906)

    26 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dhaka, President of the Welcome Committee and organiser of the political meetings, proposed the League and hosted the founding meeting; he is taken as its founder.×2
    2. The League refused to accept the Muslims attached to the Congress, posing as the only institution representing Indian Muslims; the claim that only the League had this right is wrong.×2
    Quick quiz: 5 of 5 UPPSC questions

    Shimla Deputation

    • On 1 October 1906 a Muslim delegation (Simla Deputation, 35 prominent Muslim leaders) led by Aga Khan III met Viceroy Lord Minto at Shimla.
    • It demanded a separate electorate for Muslims in elections at all levels of governance.
    • The deputation aimed to win the sympathy of British rule on matters of Muslim interest.
    • In October 1906 the Muslim representatives at Shimla under Aga Khan III decided to form a separate Muslim representation to protect Muslim interests.
    • The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) accepted the separate electorate for Muslims.

    Founding of the League

    • The All India Mohammadan Educational Conference met at Dhaka in December 1906; the Muslim League was founded there.
    • The All India Muslim League was founded in 1906 at Dhaka (Bangladesh) to safeguard the rights of Indian Muslims.
    • Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dhaka, President of the Welcome Committee and organiser of the political meetings, proposed the League and hosted the founding meeting; he is taken as its founder.UPPSC ×2
    • Founder members: Salimullah Khan, Aga Khan III and Mohsin-ul-Mulk.
    • A 60-member temporary committee was formed with Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Waqar-ul-Mulk as joint secretaries (also given as jointly appointed secretary of the Muhammadan Educational Conference).
    • Aga Khan III was the first President of the Muslim League.UPPSC
    • Aga Khan's goal was the advancement of the Muslim agenda and protection of Muslim rights in India.
    • The League's headquarters was at Lucknow.

    Objectives

    • Objective 1: to promote feelings of loyalty to the British government among Indian Muslims and remove any misconception about the government's intentions in its measures.
    • Objective 2: to protect and advance the political rights and interests of Indian Muslims and respectfully represent their needs and aspirations to the government.
    • Objective 3: to prevent any feeling of hostility among Indian Muslims towards other communities, without prejudice to the other objects.

    Sessions and stand

    • The first annual session of the Muslim League was held at Karachi in 1907; the next at Amritsar in 1908.UPPSC
    • After these, League sessions were held erratically in different parts of the country.

    Note from the book On the year from which the League held regular annual conventions, BPSC accepted 1925, which the book calls incorrect.

    • At the Amritsar session (30-31 December 1908) the League made its clear and formal demand for separate electorates, denouncing joint electorates.
    • The Muslim League formed in 1906 supported the partition of Bengal and demanded separate electorates under Aga Khan III.
    • Hakim Ajmal Khan was one of the leaders who started the nationalist and militant Ahrar movement.
    • Sayyed Ahmad Khan opposed the Indian National Congress when it was formed.
    • Maulana Barkat Ullah and Maulana Obeidullah Sindhi were among those who formed a Provisional Government of India in Kabul.
    • The League refused to accept the Muslims attached to the Congress, posing as the only institution representing Indian Muslims; the claim that only the League had this right is wrong.UPPSC ×2
    • A London branch of the Muslim League was set up in 1908 under the presidency of Syed Ameer Ali, to press the British Government for the Muslim cause.
    • W.W. Hunter, in his book 'The Indian Musalmans', wrote: "The Muslims, if contented and satisfied, would become the greatest bulwark of British power in India."

    Chapter 59 · Freedom struggle

    Morley-Minto Reforms

    16 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Reservation of seats and separate electorates for Muslims sowed the seeds of discord that later divided the country.×2
    Quick quiz: 4 of 4 UPPSC questions

    The Act of 1909

    • In 1905 Lord Minto replaced Lord Curzon as Viceroy of India; John Morley was then Secretary of State for India.
    • The reforms begun by these two are the Morley-Minto Reforms, passed by the British Parliament as the Indian Councils Act, 1909.UPPSC
    • The Act brought a limited increase in the involvement of Indians in the governance of British India.

    Separate electorate

    • The biggest fault of the Act was communal representation: a separate electorate for Muslims.UPPSC
    • Muslim members of the councils were elected only by Muslim voters, not by the general electorate.
    • Separate constituencies were marked for Muslims.
    • For the first time Muslims were recognised as a completely separate community in India; India's unity was demolished in one stroke.
    • Reservation of seats and separate electorates for Muslims sowed the seeds of discord that later divided the country.UPPSC ×2
    • It set off the "cancer" of "Hindu-Muslim disharmony", which ended in the partition into India and Pakistan.
    • The principle of communal representation was retained and pushed further by the Government of India Act, 1919.
    • Gandhiji said: "The Morley-Minto Reforms have been our undoing. Had it not been for the separate electorates then established then we should have settled our differences by now."
    • Rajendra Prasad considered Lord Minto the father of Pakistan, as the 1909 reforms introduced communal electorates.

    Events of 1911

    • The annulment of the 1905 Partition of Bengal and the shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi were both announced at the Delhi Durbar on 12 December 1911.UPPSC
    • Administrative reorganisation (formation of 'Bihar and Orissa') became effective in 1912.
    • The formal and gradual transfer of offices to Delhi was completed in 1912.
    • The Lucknow Pact between the Congress and the Muslim League took place in 1916, not 1911.
    ← Formation of Muslim League (1906)Delhi Durbar and Change of Capital →

    Chapter 60 · Freedom struggle

    Delhi Durbar and Change of Capital

    21 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The capital shifted to Delhi during the tenure of Lord Hardinge II.×2
    Quick quiz: 4 of 4 UPPSC questions

    Delhi Durbar, 1911

    • In December 1911 a grand Delhi Durbar was held to welcome British King George V and Queen Mary.
    • On 12 December 1911 George V annulled the Partition of Bengal and announced the reunification of East and West Bengal.
    • Calcutta (now Kolkata) was the capital of India under the British until 1911.
    • George V announced the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi on 12 December 1911.UPPSC
    • The transfer was completed in 1912; if both 1911 and 1912 are options, 1912 is preferred.
    • The capital shifted to Delhi during the tenure of Lord Hardinge II.UPPSC ×2

    Bihar and Orissa

    • It was announced that Bengal would be reconstituted as a new province; Bengal got this identity in 1912 after East and West Bengal reunited.
    • The carving out of Bihar from Bengal was announced at the Delhi Durbar on 12 December 1911.
    • The province of 'Bihar and Orissa' was proclaimed on 22 March 1912 and came into existence on 1 April 1912; Bihar was thus first separated from Bengal in 1912.
    • In 1936 Bihar became a separate province.
    • The Calcutta High Court still exercised jurisdiction over the new province of Bihar and Orissa.
    • Assam was restored to its previous position of 1874.

    Hardinge Bomb Case

    • A bomb was thrown at Viceroy Lord Hardinge II on his state entry into Delhi.UPPSC
    • The Delhi Conspiracy Case (Delhi-Lahore Conspiracy, Hardinge Bomb Case) was a 1912 plot to kill Hardinge on the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
    • It was hatched by the revolutionary underground of Bengal and Punjab, headed by Rash Behari Bose.
    • On 23 December 1912 a homemade bomb was thrown into the Viceroy's howdah as the ceremonial procession passed through Chandni Chowk, Delhi.
    • Anushilan Samiti was responsible for throwing the bomb at Hardinge.UPPSC
    • Fourteen persons were accused; Awadh Bihari, Master Amir Chand, Bhai Balmukund and Basant Kumar Biswas were given death sentences.
    • Balraj and Harvansh Sahay got life imprisonment; Dinanath turned approver.
    • Bhagwati Charan Vohra was not involved in the Hardinge bomb incident.
    • Rash Behari Bose, who played the main role, fled to Japan and escaped the trial.

    Chapter 61 · Freedom struggle

    Lucknow Session of Congress (The Lucknow Pact)

    21 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Ambika Charan Majumdar presided over the Lucknow Congress session of 1916.×5
    2. Both passed separate resolutions on constitutional reforms and agreed to work together on a common programme: the Lucknow Pact or Congress-League Scheme, signed in 1916.×2
    Quick quiz: 8 of 8 UPPSC questions

    Lucknow Pact, 1916

    • In December 1916 both the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League held their sessions at Lucknow.UPPSC
    • Both passed separate resolutions on constitutional reforms and agreed to work together on a common programme: the Lucknow Pact or Congress-League Scheme, signed in 1916.UPPSC ×2
    • The agreement was confirmed by the annual sessions of the Congress on 29 December and of the League on 31 December 1916.
    • It settled the composition of the legislatures and the quantum of representation for the two communities.
    • Ambika Charan Majumdar presided over the Lucknow Congress session of 1916.UPPSC ×5
    • Congress and League together released 19 bulletins to give a positive direction to the political scene.
    • Anti-British feeling among Muslims after the war between Britain and Turkey opened the way for Congress-League unity.
    • The Lucknow Pact was an important step towards Hindu-Muslim unity; this unity weakened the British attitude.
    • Under the pact the Congress for the first time accepted separate electorates for Muslims, a great gain for the League.
    • Some Congress leaders still opposed this demand.
    • Both organisations jointly demanded dominion status for the country.
    • In 1916 the British Government announced a policy to increase Indian involvement in government and gradually develop local self-government institutions.

    Reunion and architects

    • The session was significant for two reasons: Extremists, separated for nine years (since 1907), rejoined the Congress; and the Congress-League pact was made.
    • Annie Besant and Tilak played the main role in bringing the Extremists back into the Congress.UPPSC
    • Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah were the main architects of the Congress-League (Lucknow) Pact.UPPSC
    • Sarojini Naidu called Jinnah, chief architect of the Lucknow Pact, the 'Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity'.
    • At the Lucknow session of 1916 Raj Kumar Shukla told Mahatma Gandhi of the problems of the Champaran peasants.UPPSC

    Congress-League consensus

    • 1916 to 1922 was the period of consensus between the Congress and the League.UPPSC
    • The rupture began in 1920, when Jinnah resigned from the Congress over disagreement with Mahatma Gandhi's approach.
    • The Lucknow Pact was only a temporary arrangement; the League kept its own identity and pressed separate political rights for Muslims.
    • Both acted jointly till 1922; the pact dissolved with the Non-Cooperation Movement and the League went back to its old ideology.
    ← Delhi Durbar and Change of CapitalHome Rule League Movement →

    Chapter 62 · Freedom struggle

    Home Rule League Movement

    38 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Annie Besant first spoke of the movement in her weekly newspaper The Commonweal on 2 January 1914; so she is taken as launching the first Home Rule League Movement.×2
    Quick quiz: 5 of 5 UPPSC questions

    Two Home Rule Leagues

    • During World War I Annie Besant and Tilak decided to put new life into the national movement; two Home Rule Leagues were started under them.UPPSC
    • Tilak started his Home Rule League in April 1916 with headquarters at Poona; he used the term 'Home Rule' in place of Swaraj.
    • Annie Besant started her Home Rule League in September 1916 with headquarters at Adyar near Madras.
    • Annie Besant first spoke of the movement in her weekly newspaper The Commonweal on 2 January 1914; so she is taken as launching the first Home Rule League Movement.UPPSC ×2
    • Her programme covered religious freedom, national education, and social and political reforms, with self-government under the British Commonwealth as the objective.
    • Joseph Baptista was the first president of Tilak's Home Rule League and N.C. Kelkar its secretary.
    • George Arundale was the organising secretary of Annie Besant's Home Rule League.
    • S. Subramania Iyer was associated with Annie Besant's Home Rule League; he founded it with her at Adyar.
    • H.S. Olcott was not associated with the Home Rule League; he was related to the Theosophical Society.
    • C.R. Das was not associated with the Home Rule Movement.UPPSC
    • Tilak's area: Karnataka, Maharashtra (except Bombay), Central Provinces and Berar; the rest of India was Annie Besant's area.
    • Tilak's League was the most organised League.
    • The two Leagues never merged; Besant: "Some of Tilak's supporters dislike me and some of mine dislike him. We however, had no quarrel with each other".
    • The two Leagues were complementary; there was no dispute between Tilak and Besant and both continued to exist.
    • Besant promoted her League through The Commonweal (weekly) and New India; Tilak through Mahratta and Kesari.

    Aim and nature

    • For both, 'Swaraj' meant responsible government at central and provincial levels under the British Empire, with treatment like the white-ruled dominions Canada and Australia.
    • The object was Home Rule or self-governance within the British Empire by all constitutional means, and to educate and organise public opinion for it.
    • The movement aimed at self-government being granted to India within the British dominions during the war; it stayed within constitutional limits.
    • The Home Rule Movement began a new phase of the freedom movement because it put a perfect picture of self-government before the nation.
    • Tilak and Besant toured the whole country carrying the message of Home Rule to the masses.
    • The Home Rule Movement became popular and powerful in India during the First World War.UPPSC
    • Tilak linked Swaraj with the demand for linguistic states and education in the vernacular languages.
    • Tilak gave the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it".

    Lucknow session, 1916

    • The Lucknow session of the Congress in December 1916 gave Home Rule supporters the chance to show their strength.
    • A train was reserved to carry Tilak's supporters to Lucknow; some called it 'Congress Special', others 'Home Rule Special'.
    • George Arundale asked Besant's League supporters to be present at Lucknow in huge numbers.
    • Tilak's Home Rule League established a tradition to which the Congress was pinned for many years.

    Annie Besant

    1. 1847Annie Besant (1847-1933), a theosophist, settled in India and worked for its liberation; she is mostly associated with the Home Rule Movement.UPPSC
    2. 1875The Theosophical Society was founded in 1875 by Colonel Henry Steel Olcott, Madame Helena Petrovna Blavatsky and William Quan Judge; Annie Besant joined it in 1889.
    3. 1916Annie Besant's league was the All India Home Rule League (founded September 1916); Tilak's was the Indian Home Rule League.
    4. 1917Annie Besant started the Home Rule Movement and was the first woman President of the Congress (Calcutta session, 1917), but did not found the Theosophical Society.
    5. 1918Annie Besant visited Bihar (Patna) twice in 1918: on 18 April to strengthen the Home Rule League's activities and on 25 July to understand the views of the Home Rulers.
    6. 1920In 1920 the All India Home Rule League elected Mahatma Gandhi as President; he changed its name to 'Swarajya Sabha'.
    • Annie Besant (1847-1933), a theosophist, settled in India and worked for its liberation; she is mostly associated with the Home Rule Movement.UPPSC
    • She was inspired by the Irish Home Rule Movement and launched her League on the lines of the Irish Home Rule Leagues.
    • She started the movement to demand self-governance at all levels of administration; her League became active throughout India.
    • She was arrested with her co-workers and released after widespread agitation against the government's action.
    • Annie Besant was a proponent of the Fabian movement.
    • The Theosophical Society was founded in 1875 by Colonel Henry Steel Olcott, Madame Helena Petrovna Blavatsky and William Quan Judge; Annie Besant joined it in 1889.
    • Annie Besant started the Home Rule Movement and was the first woman President of the Congress (Calcutta session, 1917), but did not found the Theosophical Society.
    • Annie Besant visited Bihar (Patna) twice in 1918: on 18 April to strengthen the Home Rule League's activities and on 25 July to understand the views of the Home Rulers.
    • On these visits she held meetings, increased contact with local workers and strengthened the League's organisational base.
    • Annie Besant's league was the All India Home Rule League (founded September 1916); Tilak's was the Indian Home Rule League.
    • In 1920 the All India Home Rule League elected Mahatma Gandhi as President; he changed its name to 'Swarajya Sabha'.
