    Chapter 63 · Freedom struggle

    Gandhi and His Early Movements

    183 facts · 8 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. From the early 19th century European planters bound the farmers by agreement to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land: the Tinkathia (Teen Kathiya) system.×4
    2. Champaran Satyagraha (Bihar, 1917) was Gandhi's first Satyagraha, first civil disobedience and first successful Satyagraha in India; it was a farmers' movement.×3
    3. Rabindranath Tagore gave Gandhi the title 'Mahatma' during the Champaran Satyagraha.×3
    4. Gandhi first attended a Congress session at Calcutta in 1901.×2
    5. Gandhi promised Gokhale to spend his first year in India studying the country "with his ears open but his mouth shut".×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 58 UPPSC questions

    Early life

    • Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, Gujarat.
    • His education began in a pathshala in Porbandar; at seven he moved to Rajkot on his father's transfer and studied there till high school.UPPSC
    • He was married to Kasturba at the age of 13.
    • He studied in Samaldas Arts College, Bhavnagar, in 1885.
    • He trained as a barrister (studied law) at the Inner Temple, London.
    • His father Karamchand Gandhi, better known as 'Kaba Gandhi', was Diwan of Porbandar, Wankaner and Rajkot.UPPSC

    South Africa

    1. 1893On 24 May 1893, aged 23 (also given as 24), Gandhi went to Durban, South Africa, as legal counsel in a case of Gujarati trader Dada Abdullah.
    2. 1893In June 1893 Dada Abdullah sent him to Pretoria in the Transvaal; the journey first took him to Pietermaritzburg, where he was thrown out of the train.UPPSC
    3. 1894In 1894 Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in South Africa; he was imprisoned several times during the long movement there.
    4. 1901During his South Africa years Gandhi came to India in 1901 and opened his law office at Bombay in 1902.
    5. 1901Gandhi first attended a Congress session at Calcutta in 1901.UPPSC ×2
    6. 1903He started the newspaper Indian Opinion in South Africa (in English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil); first issue June 1903.UPPSC
    7. 1903In 1903 he founded a law firm in Johannesburg and lived there till 1910 (before moving to Tolstoy Farm); he applied the principle of Trusteeship (South Africa, 1903).UPPSC
    8. 1904He set up the Phoenix Ashram (Phoenix Farm) in 1904 near Phoenix station, Durban, on land he bought.
    9. 1910In 1910 he and his colleagues set up a new colony, Tolstoy Farm, and began living there.
    • On 24 May 1893, aged 23 (also given as 24), Gandhi went to Durban, South Africa, as legal counsel in a case of Gujarati trader Dada Abdullah.
    • He lived in South Africa for about 21 years.
    • In June 1893 Dada Abdullah sent him to Pretoria in the Transvaal; the journey first took him to Pietermaritzburg, where he was thrown out of the train.UPPSC
    • He had a first-class ticket and sat in the first-class compartment; a European called railway officials, who ordered him to the van compartment, as 'coolies' and non-whites were not allowed in first class.
    • Gandhi protested and showed his ticket; on refusing to leave he was pushed out and his luggage tossed on to the platform.
    • In 1894 Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in South Africa; he was imprisoned several times during the long movement there.
    • He started the newspaper Indian Opinion in South Africa (in English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil); first issue June 1903.UPPSC
    • In 1903 he founded a law firm in Johannesburg and lived there till 1910 (before moving to Tolstoy Farm); he applied the principle of Trusteeship (South Africa, 1903).UPPSC
    • He set up the Phoenix Ashram (Phoenix Farm) in 1904 near Phoenix station, Durban, on land he bought.
    • Phoenix Ashram was Gandhi's first (oldest) ashram; it was reopened on 27 February 2000.
    • In 1910 he and his colleagues set up a new colony, Tolstoy Farm, and began living there.
    • Gandhi adopted 'Seva Dharma' in South Africa: he served helpless poor patients as an attendant in Rustomji's charity hospitals.UPPSC
    • He gave voluntary service there as a compounder and also served the wounded soldiers of the Boer War.
    • In South Africa Gandhi discovered himself: from a shy, timid youth he became a successful organiser and leader.
    • The struggles in South Africa prepared Gandhi to lead the national movement; but that struggle was fully non-violent and based on Satyagraha, not militancy.UPPSC
    • During his South Africa years Gandhi came to India in 1901 and opened his law office at Bombay in 1902.
    • Gandhi first attended a Congress session at Calcutta in 1901.UPPSC ×2
    • That session, chaired by Dinshaw Wacha, passed Gandhi's resolution on Africa.

    Return to India and Gokhale

    • Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915; people welcomed him warmly.
    • His struggles and victories in South Africa had made him popular in India too.
    • Gopal Krishna Gokhale was Gandhi's political guru (mentor); under his influence Gandhi joined India's active politics.UPPSC
    • Gokhale visited South Africa in 1912 at Gandhi's invitation.
    • Gokhale gave Gandhi personal guidance, including knowledge of India and the issues facing common Indians; in his autobiography Gandhi calls Gokhale his mentor and guide.
    • By 1920 Gandhi had emerged as the leader of the Indian independence movement.
    • Gandhi promised Gokhale to spend his first year in India studying the country "with his ears open but his mouth shut".UPPSC ×2
    • Gandhi's first major public speech in India was at the opening of Banaras Hindu University (BHU), Varanasi, in February 1916.UPPSC

    Ashrams at Ahmedabad

    • In 1915 Gandhi set up the Satyagraha Ashram at Ahmedabad, first at the Kocharab Bungalow of Jivanlal Desai, a barrister and friend.
    • Gandhi wanted farming, animal husbandry and other activities needing much more land.
    • On 17 June 1917 the Ashram moved to a 36-acre site on the banks of the Sabarmati at Ahmedabad; it came to be known as Sabarmati Ashram.

    Gandhi's thought: state, socialism and politics

    • Gandhi stressed practical idealism rather than idealism.
    • Like Marx he believed in the removal of the State and did not mind being called a Philosophical Anarchist.UPPSC
    • His thought has also been linked to Utopian socialism and compared with strands of Marxist and western liberal thought.
    • In his ideal non-violent state every citizen would feel self-governing, so the state would not be needed to enforce the law.
    • Yet in present circumstances he did not favour abolishing the state: humans cannot yet manage collective affairs alone, so state and law are needed, with minimum jurisdiction.
    • Truth and Non-Violence were the twin principles of Gandhi's Ram Rajya and the base of the modern society of his dreams.UPPSC
    • Some believe his policy of truth came from Hindu religion and non-violence from Buddhist, Jain and Christian ideology.
    • For Gandhi 'Truth' stands for 'reality'; he described Truth as existence, consciousness and bliss.
    • Gandhi: Ahimsa is the means, Truth is the end; non-violence is the way to attain truth.UPPSC
    • Gandhi: Ahimsa and Truth are so intertwined that they cannot be separated, like two sides of a coin or of a smooth unstamped metallic disc.
    • Gandhi: means must always be within our reach, so Ahimsa is our supreme duty; if we take care of the means we reach the end sooner or later.
    • Gandhi: whatever the difficulties or reverses, we may not give up the quest for Truth, which alone is, being God Himself.
    • Gandhi said "Wrong means never take us to right ends"; means and ends are two sides of a coin, and immoral means vitiate the end.UPPSC
    • Gandhi was convinced that if we take care of our means, the end will take care of itself.
    • Gandhi strongly supported the principle "Which is morally wrong can never be politically right".UPPSC
    • Gandhi was a true socialist who cared for both private and social interests and wanted to make social justice work in practice.
    • Gandhi to Louis Fischer: "I am a true socialist and the aim of my socialism is progress of all" (Sarvodaya).
    • Gandhi's socialism has glimpses of Marxism; he gave extraordinary importance to labour.
    • He wanted work for everyone according to capacity and pay according to need.
    • Gandhi: "I am engaged in solving the same problem that faces scientific socialists. It is true, however, that my approach is always and only through unadulterated non-violence".
    • Gandhi is called an Individualist among Socialists and a Marxist among Socialists.UPPSC
    • Gandhi and Marx both aimed at a stateless and classless society; Gandhi's means were non-violent, Marx's violent.
    • For Gandhi politics meant activity for social uplift and public welfare.UPPSC
    • His most important political suggestion was decentralisation of power: power to Gram Panchayats to manage and administer their villages.
    • Gandhi's model of politics joined morality (ethics), religion and humanity; it had no place for authority (State power), as he wanted a stateless society.UPPSC
    • According to Gandhi the cruelest form of violence is the persistence of poverty.UPPSC
    • Gandhi called self-control the best means of family planning.

    Satyagraha

    • Gandhi first called the struggle in South Africa 'passive resistance' and later replaced the term with Satyagraha; he is best known for using passive resistance to win Indian independence.UPPSC
    • For Gandhi the two differed: passive resistance is a political weapon, Satyagraha is moral power; he compared them to the north and south poles.
    • Gandhi's nephew Magan Lal Gandhi first used the term 'Sadagraha' in a competition and was rewarded; Gandhi improved it to 'Satyagraha', so Gandhi coined the word.UPPSC
    • Satyagraha = Satya (truth) + Agraha (insistence): 'insistence on truth'.
    • Gandhi was the first to start Satyagraha during India's freedom struggle.
    • Fasting was the first weapon and strike the last step in the Gandhian strategy of Satyagraha.UPPSC
    • He termed fasting 'Fire Arrow'; Satyagraha is also said to be 'Agni-Baan' for him.
    • The aim of Satyagraha was not to defeat the enemy but to change his heart, through the suffering the Satyagrahi takes on himself.UPPSC
    • Satyagraha means non-violence as a force greater than violence; the weapon is Ahimsa, the Satyagrahi must be firm in belief and bear no ill feeling to enemies.

    Western influences

    • Gandhi read 'Unto This Last' by John Ruskin in South Africa; his autobiography says the book changed his life and most influenced him.
    • Its message for Gandhi: "The good of the individual is contained in the good of all"; on this he built his idea of the welfare of all.
    • Thoreau, Ruskin and Tolstoy strongly influenced Gandhian ideology.UPPSC
    • From Henry David Thoreau (essay on Civil Disobedience) he learnt civil disobedience and the benefit of refusing to pay taxes.
    • Ruskin taught him to respect physical labour.
    • Tolstoy's "The Kingdom of God is within you" became the base of his non-violence and non-cooperation.

    Champaran Satyagraha (1917)

    • Champaran Satyagraha (Bihar, 1917) was Gandhi's first Satyagraha, first civil disobedience and first successful Satyagraha in India; it was a farmers' movement.UPPSC ×3
    • Mahatma Gandhi led the Champaran Satyagraha and was the national leader of the Champaran indigo movement.
    • From the early 19th century European planters bound the farmers by agreement to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land: the Tinkathia (Teen Kathiya) system.UPPSC ×4
    • Tinkathia, the most prevalent system in Champaran = three kathas per bigha; factory owners got the tenant to grow indigo on a set part of his holding at a fixed price.
    • Planters imposed Tawan (a lump-sum compensation or illegal levy) and other cesses to exploit farmers and make leaving the contract impossible.
    • Towards the end of the 19th century German synthetic dyes pushed indigo out of the market; planters then demanded higher rents and illegal dues as the price of release.
    • Resistance had surfaced in 1908.
    • In 1917 Champaran farmers were protesting against having to grow indigo with barely any payment.
    • The Champaran movement was to solve the problems of indigo workers.UPPSC
    • The Champaran movement was basically against cash crops.
    • Pt. Raj Kumar Shukla, a local indigo cultivator, persuaded and invited Gandhi to Champaran to look into the exploitation of farmers.UPPSC ×2
    • Raj Kumar Shukla made the request on meeting Gandhi at Lucknow.
    • Gandhi reached Patna on his way to Champaran with Rajkumar Shukla and began his mission of freeing bonded labour with the Champaran Satyagraha.
    • Gandhi arrived in Champaran on 10 April 1917 with eminent lawyers Brajkishore, Rajendra Prasad, Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Acharya Kripalani and others.
    • Acharya J.B. Kripalani was one of Gandhi's colleagues in the Champaran investigation; Rajendra Prasad did not persuade Gandhi to come.
    • Gandhi's Champaran colleagues: J.B. Kripalani, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Mahadev Desai, C.F. Andrews, Dr. Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Braj Kishor Prasad, H.S. Polak.UPPSC
    • Jai Prakash Narayan was not connected with the Champaran movement.
    • Ram Manohar Lohia was not related to the Champaran Satyagraha.
    • J.B. Kripalani was a teacher by profession; Rajendra Prasad taught for some time but was basically a lawyer.
    • The government instituted the Champaran Agrarian Committee to look into the peasants' grievances.
    • The committee was appointed in agreement between the Indian Government and Gandhiji; Gandhi was a member.
    • Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee: president F.G. Slay; members D.J. Reid, Mahatma Gandhi, L.C. Adami, Raja Harihar Prasad, Narayan Singh, G. Rainny and M.E.L. Tainer; Anugrah Narayan was not a member.UPPSC
    • The planters agreed to return 25% of the illegally collected money; so the first Satyagraha succeeded.
    • A very significant aspect of Champaran: drastic decrease in the cultivation of plantation and commercial crops.
    • Champaran Satyagraha was limited to Champaran; Gandhi's first all-India movement was the Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919).UPPSC
    • Champaran proved that Satyagraha in South Africa was not a fluke but a powerful way of conflict resolution.
    • N.G. Ranga opposed Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha.UPPSC
    • Rabindranath Tagore gave Gandhi the title 'Mahatma' during the Champaran Satyagraha.UPPSC ×3
    • Batak Mian, cook of a British indigo plantation manager in Bihar (known as Erwin), saved Gandhi from poisoning in 1917.
    • Erwin invited Gandhi to dinner during the Champaran Satyagraha and coerced Batak Mian to poison him through milk; Batak Mian broke down and told Gandhi.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad confirmed the story in a 1950s speech at Motihari, cited in Delhi University Professor Dr. Girish Mishra's article "Gandhi's Champaran Struggle".

    Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918)

    • After Champaran, Gandhi took up the dispute between cotton mill owners and workers of Ahmedabad over the plague bonus (February-March 1918).
    • The Ahmedabad Satyagraha was for industrial (cotton mill) workers.UPPSC ×2
    • When Champaran is not a choice, Gandhi's first Satyagraha is taken as the one against payment of low wages to workers (Ahmedabad).UPPSC
    • Gandhi advised the workers to strike and demand a higher plague bonus.
    • Gandhi went on a "fast unto death" to strengthen the workers; this was his first use of the hunger strike as a weapon.UPPSC
    • The mill owners gave in after 21 days of strike and agreed to submit the issue to a tribunal.
    • The tribunal later awarded the 35% increase (bonus / dearness allowance) the workers had demanded.
    • Anasuya Behn, sister of Ambalal Sarabhai, was a main lieutenant of Gandhi in this struggle; her brother, Gandhi's friend, was one of the main advisers.

    Kheda Satyagraha (1918)

    • Kheda, like Champaran, was a farmers' movement.
    • In Kheda (Gujarat) crops failed in 1918; the government gave no revenue concession and did not stop collecting land revenue, so Gandhi organised a Satyagraha for the farmers.
    • Kheda peasants suffered poverty, famine and British discrimination; famine had destroyed the region's agrarian economy.
    • The revolt was against taxes and rents; the government threatened to seize property if taxes were unpaid.
    • Kheda was against high taxes people could not pay due to crop failure and plague epidemic.
    • No Permanent Settlement was proposed for Gujarat.

    Order of Gandhi's movements

    EventYear
    Champaran Satyagraha1917UPPSC
    Ahmedabad Mill StrikeFebruary-March 1918
    Kheda SatyagrahaMarch-June 1918
    Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act1919
    Non-Cooperation Movement1920-1922
    Civil Disobedience Movement1930
    • The Rowlatt Act was passed to curb revolutionary activities in India.
    • Gandhi led the Kheda Satyagraha (1918), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930) and Quit India Movement (1942); Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.UPPSC
    • Gandhi was not related to the Swadeshi Movement (1905-1911, against the partition of Bengal); he was then in South Africa.UPPSC
    • Khilafat Movement, Individual Satyagraha and Quit India Movement were led by Gandhi.
    • Gandhi did not take part directly in the Vaikom Satyagraha.
    • Vaikom Satyagraha: a movement in Travancore (modern Kerala) for temple entry of the depressed classes, against untouchability and caste discrimination; Gandhi took part indirectly in 1925.UPPSC
    • Gandhi led the Rajkot Satyagraha, Kheda Satyagraha and Non-Cooperation Movement.
    • In the Rajkot Satyagraha, after a 4-day hunger strike, Gandhi agreed to settle with the ruler of Rajkot through the Viceroy's mediation.

    Boycott, economy and Harijan service

    • Gandhi said "destruction is the best method of dealing with foreign clothes"; he linked it with the nation's self-respect.UPPSC
    • His boycott of British goods was effective because the British saw India as a major market for manufactured goods.UPPSC
    • The boycott promoted the production and sale of Indian goods such as crafts and homemade items.
    • Gandhi: each country's economy should be decided by its climate, land and the nature of its people; so he never opposed mechanisation in the USA.UPPSC
    • He stressed an economy based on non-violence, held that centralisation leads to exploitation and inequality, and did not favour mechanisation in India.
    • His economics opposed all exploitation, whether of one group by another or of one country by another.
    • He wanted a system where a person can freely choose work and labour, and the revival of Indian goods industries so that no one goes hungry.
    • He stressed cottage industries: making jaggery, thrashing grass, extracting oil, paper making, leather work.
    • He stressed rural industries such as khadi, handlooms, sericulture and handicrafts, since India lives in its villages.
    • Rural industries use family labour, little capital, local raw materials and local markets; they reduce the burden on agriculture and check migration to cities.
    • According to Gandhi, socio-economic improvement of untouchables can come by setting up cottage industry for them.UPPSC
    • Gandhi opposed planned development in India; he was opposed to industrialisation and mechanisation.UPPSC
    • He backed cottage and village industries and labour-intensive enterprises; under Gram Swaraj the village was a self-sufficient economic unit.
    • 'Gandhian Innovation', a term coined by Prof. Prahlad and R.A. Mashelkar, means to produce more from less input for more people: "serving people with fewer resources and at a lower cost".UPPSC
    • Gandhi fought hard to improve the status of untouchables, and launched the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience Movements.UPPSC
    • 'Service to Harijans' was his prime constructive programme; in his weekly Harijan he called it a spiritual act of soul acting upon soul.
    • Gandhi: "Service of Harijan is the breath of my life without which I won't survive one single minute"; Stanley Wolpert quotes it as "the breath of life, more precious than the daily bread".

    Titles and tributes

    • Subhash Chandra Bose was the first to call Gandhi 'Father of the Nation', in July 1944 on Azad Hind Radio from Rangoon.UPPSC ×2
    • Bose said: "India's last war of independence has begun… Father of our Nation, in this holy war of India's liberation, we ask for your blessings and good wishes."
    • Lord Mountbatten called Gandhi the 'One Man Boundary Force'.UPPSC
    • Mountbatten's wire: Punjab had 50,000 soldiers and large-scale rioting; Bengal's force was one man and there was no rioting.
    • Gandhi named Yerawada Central Jail (Pune, Maharashtra) 'Mandir'; he spent several years there.UPPSC
    • Gandhi resigned from the Congress in 1934 and never again became a formal member; at Independence he was not a member of the Congress.
    • On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse, a Hindu extremist, shot Gandhi.
    • Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru said: "The light has gone out of our lives and there is darkness everywhere. I do not know what to tell you and how to say it. Our beloved leader, Bapu as we called him, the Father of the Nation, is no more."

    Associates

    1. 1915He met Gandhi in 1915 and stayed his follower for life; Gandhi called him his 'fifth son'.
    2. 1921He joined the Non-Cooperation Movement and gave up his title 'Rai Bahadur' in 1921.
    3. 1921In 1921 he brought Vinoba Bhave to Wardha to start a branch of the Satyagraha Ashram.
    4. 1923Bajaj served as AICC treasurer for many years and went to jail in 1923 and 1930; unique among capitalists as a full-time Congress activist.
    5. 1923In 1923 a tricolour flag procession at Nagpur in memory of Jallianwala Bagh was banned; Bajaj led the Nagpur Flag Satyagraha and got 18 months' jail and a Rs. 3,000 fine.
    6. 1925Andrews was president of the All India Trade Union Congress in 1925 and 1927 (also given as from 1925 to 1927); he went with Gandhi to the Round Table Conference in London.
    7. 1930He was jailed again in 1930 during the Civil Disobedience Movement.
    8. 1930Balchand Hirachand, in an April 1930 letter to FICCI, urged businessmen to stop sitting on the fence and join those fighting for Swaraj.
    9. 1930In May 1930 FICCI decided to boycott the Round Table Conference while Gandhi stayed away and until the Viceroy promised dominion status.
    10. 1942Pyarelal Nayyar was Gandhi's secretary (since 1942) during the Noakhali communal riots.
    • Pyarelal Nayyar was Gandhi's secretary (since 1942) during the Noakhali communal riots.
    • His sister Dr. Sushila Nayyar was Gandhi's personal doctor; Pyarelal also played an important role in the Dandi March.
    • Jamnalal Bajaj: cotton (cloth) merchant, banker, Congressman, social worker and close associate of Gandhi.
    • Bajaj was an industrialist, philanthropist and freedom fighter; his leadership as commander of the Flag Satyagraha made him a national leader.
    • Bajaj was born in Sikar district (Rajasthan) and adopted by a rich businessman of Wardha.
    • He met Gandhi in 1915 and stayed his follower for life; Gandhi called him his 'fifth son'.
    • He took part in the Congress at the age of 30; he was treasurer of the Congress and founder of Gandhi Seva Sangh.
    • Bajaj served as AICC treasurer for many years and went to jail in 1923 and 1930; unique among capitalists as a full-time Congress activist.
    • He joined the Non-Cooperation Movement and gave up his title 'Rai Bahadur' in 1921.
    • In 1921 he brought Vinoba Bhave to Wardha to start a branch of the Satyagraha Ashram.
    • He worked for abolishing untouchability, Harijans' entry into Hindu temples and promotion of khadi; he took deep interest in village industry and handloom cloth.
    • In 1923 a tricolour flag procession at Nagpur in memory of Jallianwala Bagh was banned; Bajaj led the Nagpur Flag Satyagraha and got 18 months' jail and a Rs. 3,000 fine.
    • He was jailed again in 1930 during the Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • Balchand Hirachand, in an April 1930 letter to FICCI, urged businessmen to stop sitting on the fence and join those fighting for Swaraj.
    • In May 1930 FICCI decided to boycott the Round Table Conference while Gandhi stayed away and until the Viceroy promised dominion status.
    • Charles Andrews (Deenbandhu Andrews), Gandhi's close English associate, taught at St. Stephen's College, Delhi.
    • He loved Indians and wanted to be an Indian; he was close to Rabindranath Tagore, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Mahatma Gandhi.
    • He lived with Gandhi at Phoenix; Gandhi gave him the title 'Deenbandhu' for his devotion to the poor.
    • Andrews was president of the All India Trade Union Congress in 1925 and 1927 (also given as from 1925 to 1927); he went with Gandhi to the Round Table Conference in London.

    Chhattisgarh visits

    • Gandhi first came to Chhattisgarh on 20 December 1920, at Dhamtari; he came again on 24 November 1933.
    • Maulana Shaukat Ali accompanied Gandhi on the 1920 tour, which was on the invitation of Sundarlal Sharma.
    • Shaukat Ali was part of the Khilafat movement and attended the first and second Round Table Conferences.

    Chapter 64 · Freedom struggle

    Peasant Movement and Kisan Sabha

    66 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Bardoli Satyagraha (1928): peasant movement in Bardoli taluka, Surat district, led by Vallabhbhai Patel.×3
    2. Baba Ramchandra emerged in mid-1920 as peasant leader of Oudh (Awadh); made the movement strong and combative; had extraordinary organisational capability.×2
    3. All India Kisan Congress was formed at Lucknow on 11 April 1936.×2
    4. Pochampalli was in Andhra Pradesh, now Telangana (Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, carved out of Nalgonda).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 11 UPPSC questions

    Bijolia Movement

    • Bijolia Movement = first peasant movement of India; in Mewar state (modern Rajasthan).
    • Cause: feudal exploitation of peasants was common in Mewar in the latter half of the 19th century.
    • Bijolia Movement began in 1897, led by local farmers; lasted about 44 years, one of India's longest peasant movements.
    • First phase leader: Sadhu Sitaram Das (led in 1913); second phase leader: Vijay Singh Pathik (from 1915).
    • Vijay Singh Pathik: renowned freedom fighter and peasant leader; organised Mewar farmers against excessive taxes imposed by the rulers.
    • Prayag's Abhyudaya and Calcutta's Bharat Mitra newspapers regularly published Bijolia news; Pathik did not go to Gandhi to inform him about it.

    Kisan Sabhas in U.P. and Awadh

    • Home Rule League workers were very active in Awadh (Oudh); they organised peasants into 'Kisan Sabha'.
    • U.P. Kisan Sabha formed February 1918 by Indra Narayan Dwivedi and Gauri Shankar Mishra, supported by Madan Mohan Malaviya; Jawaharlal Nehru was not associated.UPPSC
    • These sabhas spread so much awareness that a huge number of U.P. farmers joined the 1918 Delhi Session of Congress.
    • 'Nai-Dhobi Bandh' = social boycott against exploiting landlords, started by farmers in an estate of Pratapgarh district (Oudh), end of 1919; first sign of grass-roots peasant activity.
    • Summer 1920: Kisan meetings called by village panchayats became frequent in villages of Taluqdari Oudh.
    • Jhinguri Singh and Durgapal Singh played an important role in this movement at first.
    • Baba Ramchandra emerged in mid-1920 as peasant leader of Oudh (Awadh); made the movement strong and combative; had extraordinary organisational capability.UPPSC ×2
    • Oudh Kisan Sabha was established in 1920 by Baba Ramchandra's efforts.
    • Baba Ramchandra: a sanyasi, earlier an indentured labourer in Fiji (island nation in the Pacific); carried Tulsidas' Ramayana on his back and recited verses to rural audiences.
    • Baba Ramchandra took active part in the Non-Cooperation Movement in Oudh and organised peasants against landlords.

    Eka Movement

    • Eka (Unity) Movement (1921–22): grass-roots leaders were Madari Pasi (of a lower class family), other low-caste leaders and many small zamindars.
    • Eka Movement was started by peasants of Hardoi, Barabanki, Bahraich and Sitapur (U.P.); discontent resurfaced towards end of 1921.UPPSC
    • Eka issues: rents 50% higher than recorded rates; oppression by thikedars in charge of revenue collection; practice of share-rents (rent collected in produce).
    • Eka aim: change of rent into cash; peasants did not refuse rent but insisted on cash payment because of high inflation.
    • Eka meetings had a symbolic religious ritual with vows: pay only recorded rent but on time; not leave when evicted; refuse forced labour; no help to criminals; abide by Panchayat decisions.
    • Severe repression by the authorities ended the Eka Movement by March 1922.

    Swami Sahajanand and Bihar Kisan Sabha

    • Swami Sahajanand Saraswati founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) in 1929.
    • Swami Sahajanand led the peasant (farmers') movement in Bihar; closely linked with the Kisan Sabha Movement of the 1930s.
    • His agricultural reform programme aimed to end the Zamindari system and give ownership rights to farmers; he is called 'Kisan-Pran'.
    • Karyanand Sharma, Rahul Sankrityayan, Panchanan Sharma, Yadunandan Sharma and many other communist leaders helped him take the Bihar Kisan Sabha movement to village level.
    • Sahajanand published the newspaper 'Lok Sangraha' to highlight peasants' hardships.
    • Sahajanand (1889–1950), sanyasi, farmers' rights activist and freedom fighter, ran the Hindi weekly 'Hunkar' from Patna.
    • Just before his death (1950) he formed the All India United Kisan Sabha (AIUKS); basic demand: nationalisation of land, waterways and all sources of energy and wealth.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad was associated with the Kisan Movement in Bihar; he was President of the Constituent Assembly and first President of India.
    • Bakashat agitation of Bihar is linked to Swami Shraddhanand Saraswati.

    All India Kisan Sabha

    • All India Kisan Congress was formed at Lucknow on 11 April 1936.UPPSC ×2
    • Swami Sahajanand Saraswati presided over the first session and became its first (founder) President.UPPSC
    • N.G. Ranga became the first General Secretary.UPPSC
    • Jawaharlal Nehru also addressed the first meeting of the All India Kisan Sabha (Lucknow, April 1936).UPPSC
    • Kisan Congress was later renamed All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS).
    • A Kisan manifesto was issued and a periodical was started under Indulal Yagnik.
    • AIKS held its second session along with the Congress session at Faizpur in 1936; chaired by N.G. Ranga.
    • Congress manifesto (especially agrarian policy) for the 1937 provincial elections was strongly influenced by the AIKS agenda.
    • N.G. Ranga founded the Bhartiya Kisan Vidyalaya.
    • Fazlul Haq founded the Bengal Praja Party (Krishak Praja Party) in 1929.

    Peasant leaders of the 1930s

    Leader / organisationArea of influence
    Sahajanand SaraswatiBiharUPPSC
    Khudai KhidmatgarsNWFP
    Swami RamanandHyderabad
    Abdul Hamid KhanSouthern Assam
    • Khudai Khidmatgar or Lalkurti organisation, led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, was active in the Civil Disobedience Movement in NWFP.

    Bardoli Satyagraha

    • Bardoli Satyagraha (1928): peasant movement in Bardoli taluka, Surat district, led by Vallabhbhai Patel.UPPSC ×3
    • Bardoli taluka saw intense politicisation after Gandhi joined national politics; Gandhi's followers like the Mehta brothers ran a sustained campaign there since 1922.
    • On its success, Mahatma Gandhi, on behalf of the women of Bardoli, gave Patel the title 'Sardar'.

    Tebhaga Movement

    • Tebhaga Movement (Bengal, 1946) was started under the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha.
    • Bengal Provincial Kisan Council decided in September 1946 to launch it in the harvesting season of November 1946; Bargadars (share-croppers) were eager for struggle.
    • Tebhaga demand ("sharing by third"): landlord's share reduced from one-half of the crop to one-third; two-thirds to the share-cropper.
    • The movement sought to implement the Flood Commission's recommendation of one-third share to the landowner.
    • In response the Bargadari Act was passed: share-croppers pay only one-third of harvest to landlords.
    • Districts of North Bengal were most affected by the Tebhaga Movement.

    Bhoodan Movement

    • Acharya Vinoba Bhave started the Bhoodan Movement on 18 April 1951; aim: give land to landless farmers.
    • Bhoodan began at Pochampalli village, then in Nalgonda district.
    • Pochampalli was in Andhra Pradesh, now Telangana (Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, carved out of Nalgonda).UPPSC ×2
    • Vinoba visited Nalgonda district for the Sarvodaya conference; the district was then a centre of communist activities; he stayed at Bhudan Pochampalli village.
    • First donation: landlord (zamindar) Ramchandra Reddy gave 100 acres to 40 Harijan families.
    • Vinoba organised the Sarvodaya Samaj for non-violent social change through land reforms with landlords' willing cooperation.
    • Large landlords were persuaded to gift at least one-sixth of their land; Bhoodan was most successful in Orissa.
    • Bhoodan was an attempt at land reform and institutional change in agriculture.
    • October 1951: Vinoba set a target of 50 million acres by 1957; the movement continued beyond 1957 but later waned.
    • Jaya Prakash Narayan left active politics and joined the Bhoodan Movement in 1954.
    • Vinoba Bhave: great spiritual leader and reformer; first person chosen for Individual Satyagraha in 1940.

    Chapter 65 · Freedom struggle

    Trade Union and Communist Party

    31 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Lala Lajpat Rai = first President of AITUC; presided over its first (inaugural) session at Bombay, 1920.×5
    2. Kanpur Conspiracy Case (1924) was against leaders of the Communist movement, to stop growing communist influence.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 10 UPPSC questions

    Early trade unions

    • Madras Labour Union (1918), formed by B.P. Wadia and V. Kalyanasundaram = first modern trade union of India.UPPSC
    • It mainly had textile workers of the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills.
    • Soon after, two unions were formed in Bombay, one in Calcutta (the Indian Seamen's Union) and four in Madras.
    • Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association set up 25 February 1920 by Anasuya Sarabhai (its president) and Mahatma Gandhi, after the 1918 Ahmedabad mill strike.

    All India Trade Union Congress

    1. 1919Motive for forming AITUC: establishment of the International Labour Organization in 1919; Indian workers decided to organise as unions.
    2. 1920All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) founded by N.M. Joshi on 31 October 1920 at Bombay.
    3. 1920Lala Lajpat Rai = first President of AITUC; presided over its first (inaugural) session at Bombay, 1920.UPPSC ×5
    4. 1926Revolutionary (militant) phase of the trade union movement = 1926–1939.
    5. 1929AITUC split for the first time in 1929 at Nagpur; Jawaharlal Nehru presided over that session.UPPSC
    6. 1929Nagpur 1929 session showed a trial of strength between leftists and rightists (moderates or reformists).
    7. 1929Moderates under N.M. Joshi, V.V. Giri and B. Shiva Rao set up a separate Indian (All India) Trade Union Federation in 1929; it was not founded by S.A. Dange.
    • All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) founded by N.M. Joshi on 31 October 1920 at Bombay.
    • Lala Lajpat Rai = first President of AITUC; presided over its first (inaugural) session at Bombay, 1920.UPPSC ×5
    • Joseph Baptista = Vice President; Dewan Chaman Lal (Bajaj) = General Secretary; all were founding members.
    • Motive for forming AITUC: establishment of the International Labour Organization in 1919; Indian workers decided to organise as unions.
    • AITUC split for the first time in 1929 at Nagpur; Jawaharlal Nehru presided over that session.UPPSC
    • Nagpur 1929 session showed a trial of strength between leftists and rightists (moderates or reformists).
    • Moderates under N.M. Joshi, V.V. Giri and B. Shiva Rao set up a separate Indian (All India) Trade Union Federation in 1929; it was not founded by S.A. Dange.
    • Revolutionary (militant) phase of the trade union movement = 1926–1939.
    • Main leaders of this phase: M.N. Roy, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shripad Amrit Dange, Shaukat Usmani.

    Communist movement

    • Communist International founded in March 1919 by Vladimir Lenin and the Bolshevik Party of Russia.
    • M.N. Roy went to Russia (Moscow) on Lenin's invitation and became the first Indian member of the Communist International.
    • 17 October 1920: M.N. Roy headed the group that founded the Indian Communist Party at Tashkent.
    • Other Tashkent founders: Abani Mukherjee, Mohd. Ali, Mohd. Shafique, Evelyn Roy Trent, Rosa Fitingov and M.P.T. Acharya.
    • Kanpur Conspiracy Case (1924) was against leaders of the Communist movement, to stop growing communist influence.UPPSC ×2
    • Kanpur accused: M.N. Roy, Shripad Amrit Dange, Ghulam Hussain, Ramcharan Lal Sharma, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shaukat Usmani, Singaravelu Chettiar, Nalini Gupta, Shamuddin Hassan, M.R.S. Velayndhun, Dr. Manilal, Sampurnanand and Satyabhakta.
    • Kanpur charge: conspiracy to set up a revolutionary organisation; "to deprive the Emperor of his sovereignty over British India" by complete separation through violent revolution.
    • Meerut and Peshawar conspiracy cases were also against Communist leaders.
    • Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929–33) drew world-wide publicity; Einstein, H.G. Wells, Harold Laski and Roosevelt criticised it and sympathised with the convicts.UPPSC
    • In the Meerut case 32 labour leaders were charged; 31 were arrested, including two Britishers.

    Parties

    1. 1925Labour Swaraj Party formed in Bengal in 1925 under Congress; became Workers and Peasants Party of Bengal in 1926.
    2. 1927Workers and Peasants Party of Bombay Province formed in 1927 from the Congress Labour Party (which arose within Congress in Bombay Province in 1926).
    3. 1928Workers and Peasants Party formed in United Province in 1928; in Punjab it was named Kirti Kisan Party.
    4. 1928All India Workers and Peasants Party was formed at the Calcutta conference of these provincial parties in December 1928 (not 1927).
    5. 1934Saumyendranath Tagore founded the Revolutionary Communist Party of India (RCPI) in 1934, breaking away from the CPI.UPPSC
    6. 1940M.N. Roy founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.UPPSC
    • Labour Swaraj Party formed in Bengal in 1925 under Congress; became Workers and Peasants Party of Bengal in 1926.
    • Workers and Peasants Party of Bombay Province formed in 1927 from the Congress Labour Party (which arose within Congress in Bombay Province in 1926).
    • Workers and Peasants Party formed in United Province in 1928; in Punjab it was named Kirti Kisan Party.
    • All India Workers and Peasants Party was formed at the Calcutta conference of these provincial parties in December 1928 (not 1927).
    • Aim of the Workers and Peasants Party: work within Congress to make it more revolutionary and an organisation of common people.UPPSC
    • M.N. Roy founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.UPPSC
    • 'Bandi Jeevan' is a masterpiece written by Shachindranath Sanyal.
    • Saumyendranath Tagore founded the Revolutionary Communist Party of India (RCPI) in 1934, breaking away from the CPI.UPPSC

    Chapter 66 · Freedom struggle

    Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)

    51 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Rabindranath Tagore returned his 'Knighthood' (title 'Sir') to the Government in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 31 May 1919 (also given as 30 May 1919).×6
    2. (Chettur) Shankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council in protest against the massacre.×4
    3. Sequence: Dr. Satyapal's arrest (9 April 1919) → Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) → Amritsar Congress Session (December 1919).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 19 UPPSC questions

    Rowlatt Act

    • 1917: Government set up a (Sedition) committee under Justice Sidney Rowlatt to report on criminal conspiracies linked to revolutionary movements and suggest legal changes.
    • Rowlatt Act was based on the recommendations of the 'Sedition Committee'; in the Rowlatt Satyagraha Gandhiji tried to use the Home Rule League.
    • Rowlatt Act was passed in March 1919 by the Imperial Legislative Council.UPPSC
    • Its purpose: to curb national and revolutionary (sedition) activities.
    • It let the Government arrest and imprison suspects without trial or warrant, search any place without warrant, and try some cases without jury (summary procedures).
    • The Act was called "No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal" (no plea, no lawyer, no appeal); Gandhiji, the Press and the Congress called it the 'Black Act' (Black Law).
    • Official name: Anarchical and Revolutionary Crime Act (1919), popularly known as the Rowlatt Act.
    • Rowlatt Act was passed during the viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921).UPPSC
    • Congress and the Indian public opposed the Act because it aimed to limit individual liberty.
    • The Act curbed fundamental rights such as freedom of expression, put severe restrictions on the press and strengthened police powers.
    • Swami Shraddhanand suggested starting the protest against the Act with non-payment of lagaan (no-tax campaign).UPPSC

    Rowlatt Satyagraha

    • Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) = Gandhiji's first bold step (first venture) in all-India politics.
    • It was the first all-India struggle against the British government, though largely restricted to cities.
    • Against the Rowlatt Act Gandhiji used stages: Rowlatt Satyagraha with hartals/civil disobedience (1919), then non-cooperation and Khilafat movement (began January 1921).
    • Champaran Peasant Movement (1917), Ahmedabad Mill Workers Movement (1918) and Kheda Peasant Movement (1918) were limited to specific issues of one section and a small area.
    • Rowlatt Satyagraha opposed curbs on press freedom and detention without trial; all sections, religions, castes, age groups and both genders joined.
    • National newspapers and political journals made Gandhi a popular figure.
    • Gandhi organised a country-wide strike on 6 April 1919 against the Act.
    • Demonstrations against the Simon Commission did not coincide with it: the Commission reached India on 3 February 1928, met with strikes and the slogan 'Simon! Go Back'.

    Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

    • Enactment of the Rowlatt Act immediately preceded the massacre; its wave of popular indignation led to Jallianwala Bagh.UPPSC
    • The massacre happened in the context of the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
    • Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal, popular Punjab leaders, were arrested by the Deputy Commissioner of Amritsar on 9 April 1919.
    • Sequence: Dr. Satyapal's arrest (9 April 1919) → Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) → Amritsar Congress Session (December 1919).UPPSC ×2
    • At Amritsar the arrest of Gandhiji and of Kitchlew and Satyapal aroused a wave of protests.
    • Jallianwala Bagh (Amritsar) massacre took place on 13 April 1919, Baisakhi day.
    • The unarmed crowd had gathered to protest against the arrest of Kitchlew and Satyapal and the Government's repressive measures.UPPSC
    • Others had come for the annual Baisakhi fair; many villagers from outside the city did not know martial law had been imposed.
    • Brigadier General Reginald Edward Harry Dyer entered with troops, blocked the exits and fired without warning on the peaceful crowd.
    • The park was an enclosed ground with a small exit gate, which was closed; firing lasted about ten minutes and stopped only when ammunition ran out.
    • Deaths: about 379 killed and hundreds wounded (estimate cited by UK Parliament); also given as about a thousand killed and many thousands wounded in ten minutes, and as thousands killed.
    • Lord Chelmsford was Viceroy at the time of the massacre.UPPSC
    • Other events of Chelmsford's tenure: Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, dyarchy in provinces), Rowlatt Act 1919, start of Non-Cooperation Movement.
    • Montagu called the Jallianwala Bagh massacre 'Preventive Murder' (Preventive Killing).UPPSC
    • Non-Cooperation Movement started in 1920; Communal Award came in 1932; Simon Commission came in 1928.

    Reactions

    • Rabindranath Tagore returned his 'Knighthood' (title 'Sir') to the Government in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 31 May 1919 (also given as 30 May 1919).UPPSC ×6
    • Tagore gave up the Knighthood because of the massacre, not to join the Non-Cooperation Movement.UPPSC
    • Tagore wrote to the Governor-General: "The time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring in their incongruous context of humiliation..."
    • (Chettur) Shankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council in protest against the massacre.UPPSC ×4
    • Gandhiji was given the task of drafting the Congress Inquiry Committee report on the massacre.UPPSC

    Note from the book UPPSC first keyed Mahatma Gandhi for the drafting question, but removed the question in its revised answer key.

    Hunter Committee

    • Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee) was appointed to inquire into the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
    • Head: Lord William Hunter, a Senator of the College of Justice of Scotland; 7 members: 4 British and 3 Indians.
    • Indian members: C.H. Sitalwad, Pt. Jagat Narayan and Sultan Ahmad Khan.
    • Before the Hunter report, Congress gave its view: Dyer's act was inhuman and martial law in Punjab had no justification.
    • Hunter report (1920) did not find the Government guilty: said disorder can become revolt, so martial law was needed and firing justified; called it Dyer's error of judgement.
    • The report condemned most of Dyer's decisions but agreed with martial law in Punjab.
    • It criticised Gandhi's method of Satyagraha and held him partly responsible for the "deteriorated" law and order.
    • Dyer was told to resign as Brigade Commander and sent to England, relieved of his command.
    • British newspapers showed Dyer as protector of the Empire; the Lords praised him as 'Lion of British Empire'; he was given the 'Sword of Honour'.

    Udham Singh

    • Udham Singh, a Punjab revolutionary, shot dead Sir Michael O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall, London, on 13 March 1940 to avenge the massacre.UPPSC
    • O'Dwyer was Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab at the time of the massacre; he had approved Dyer's action and was believed to be its main planner.
    • Udham Singh had witnessed the Amritsar events and was himself wounded.
    ← Trade Union and Communist PartyKhilafat Movement →

    Chapter 67 · Freedom struggle

    Khilafat Movement

    31 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Khilafat Movement was mainly started by the Ali Brothers: Maulana Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali; Abul Kalam Azad also joined.×2
    2. According to K.M. Munshi, Jinnah warned Gandhiji not to encourage the fanaticism of Muslim religious leaders and their followers; Jinnah saw Gandhi's support of Khilafat as an endorsement of religious zealotry.×2
    3. Madan Mohan Malviya did not support the Khilafat Movement; he opposed Gandhi's endorsement of it.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 10 UPPSC questions

    Background and aims

    • Indian Muslims considered the Sultan of Turkey the Khalifa (Caliph) of the Islamic empire.
    • In the First World War Turkey fought against the Allied countries.
    • British statesmen promised Indian Muslims fair treatment of Turkey and not to break up its empire, to win their support.
    • After the war the Turkish Empire was dismembered by the Treaty of Sevres; the Khalifa was stripped of his post.
    • It ended in 1922 (after Treaty of Lausanne, 1922): the last Ottoman Sultan was deposed and left Constantinople in a British warship.
    • Main objectives of the Khilafat Movement: rouse anti-British feelings among Indian Muslims; save the Ottoman Empire and preserve the Khilafat.

    Leaders and committee

    • Khilafat Movement was mainly started by the Ali Brothers: Maulana Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali; Abul Kalam Azad also joined.UPPSC ×2
    • Khilafat Committee members: Shaukat Ali, Muhammad Ali, Abul Kalam Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani and Dr. Ansari.
    • The All India Khilafat Committee was created at Lucknow.
    • The Ali brothers, Hasrat Mohani and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad organised a Khilafat Party.
    • Haji Shariatullah = Islamic reformer of British India who founded the Faraizi Movement (not linked to Khilafat).
    • Hakim Ajmal Khan gave up the title Haziq-ul-Mulk during the Khilafat agitation; the British had given it in 1908.UPPSC

    Gandhi and the Congress

    • Mahatma Gandhi was elected President of the All India Khilafat Conference at Delhi (23–24 November 1919) on 24 November; it was chaired by Fazlul Haq.UPPSC
    • Gandhiji supported Khilafat to win Indian Muslims' support against the British.
    • Gandhi saw Khilafat as a golden opportunity for Hindu-Muslim unity that would not come again in a hundred years.
    • Congress supported the Khilafat Movement mainly for reinstatement of the Caliph and getting the sympathy of Muslims.UPPSC
    • The movement gained popularity and an aggressive pace when Gandhiji joined it.
    • The Amritsar Congress session of December 1919 gave a great fillip to the Khilafat agitation.
    • Result of Khilafat: Hindu-Muslim differences narrowed; unity arose from anger against the British over Turkey.UPPSC
    • Gandhi suggested non-violent non-cooperation to the Khilafat Committee in 1920; in June 1920 the Committee at Allahabad (now Prayagraj) accepted it unanimously and asked Gandhi to lead.
    • September 1920: special Calcutta session under Lala Lajpat Rai adopted the Non-Cooperation resolution.

    Opponents and other facts

    • M.A. Jinnah (then a Nationalist) opposed linking Khilafat with Swaraj and denounced Gandhi's participation; told him not to bring religion into politics.UPPSC
    • According to K.M. Munshi, Jinnah warned Gandhiji not to encourage the fanaticism of Muslim religious leaders and their followers; Jinnah saw Gandhi's support of Khilafat as an endorsement of religious zealotry.UPPSC ×2
    • Madan Mohan Malviya did not support the Khilafat Movement; he opposed Gandhi's endorsement of it.UPPSC ×2
    • Malviya was the foremost educationalist, legal luminary, scholar and editor of pre-Independent India.
    • Swami Shraddhanand spoke on Hindu-Muslim unity from the pulpit of Jama Masjid, Delhi, on 4 April 1919 before 30,000 Muslims.UPPSC
    • Aitchison's remark "In this instance, we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus" relates to the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement (1919–22).
    • In 1919–22 Muslims joined the nationalist stream with unprecedented Hindu-Muslim unity; at this time Jinnah said "we are first Muslims then Indians".

    Moplah Rebellion

    • Moplah Rebellion (1921) was an offshoot of the Khilafat Movement.
    • Moplah peasants revolted against oppressive Hindu landlords allied with the British; a pitched battle with a British regiment killed several Europeans.
    • Khilafat meetings and Moplah peasant meetings became hard to tell apart, so the two movements merged.
    ← Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)Non-Cooperation Movement →

    Chapter 68 · Freedom struggle

    Non-Cooperation Movement

    93 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Rabindranath Tagore opposed burning of foreign clothes; he wrote to Gandhi calling it 'a ruthless waste' (indiscriminate or callous waste).×5
    2. Gandhiji withdrew (suspended) the Non-Cooperation Movement because of the violence at Chauri Chaura.×3
    3. Gandhiji promised (at the AICC) 'Swaraj within one year' if the movement was effectively carried out.×2
    4. Chauri Chaura incident: 4 February 1922.×2
    5. Chauri Chaura is in Gorakhpur district, United Provinces (Uttar Pradesh).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 28 UPPSC questions

    Launch and resolutions

    1. 1857Non-Cooperation was the major event of the freedom struggle after the First War of Independence of 1857; it marked the start of the Gandhian movement against colonialism.
    2. 1917Champaran Movement (1917) for indigo cultivators in Bihar was the first movement started by Gandhi.
    3. 1919After the 1919 reforms failed Indian aspirations, Congress sought Swaraj (self-government) under Mahatma Gandhi.UPPSC
    4. 1920Gandhiji launched the Non-Cooperation Movement on 1 August 1920.UPPSC
    5. 1920It lasted from 1920 to February 1922; it is counted as the first mass movement led by Gandhiji.UPPSC
    6. 1920Special Congress session at Calcutta, September 1920, presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai, passed Gandhi's Non-Cooperation resolution.
    7. 1920At the Nagpur session (December 1920) the resolution was ratified; C.R. Das himself moved it.UPPSC
    8. 1920At Nagpur 1920 Congress changed its objective: attainment of 'Swaraj' by all legitimate and peaceful means.
    9. 1930Salt March (Dandi March) lasted from 12 March 1930 to 6 April 1930.
    • Gandhiji launched the Non-Cooperation Movement on 1 August 1920.UPPSC
    • It lasted from 1920 to February 1922; it is counted as the first mass movement led by Gandhiji.UPPSC
    • Champaran Movement (1917) for indigo cultivators in Bihar was the first movement started by Gandhi.
    • Non-Cooperation was the major event of the freedom struggle after the First War of Independence of 1857; it marked the start of the Gandhian movement against colonialism.
    • Causes: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre (Punjab atrocities) and the Khilafat question; Salt Law was not a cause.UPPSC
    • Salt March (Dandi March) lasted from 12 March 1930 to 6 April 1930.
    • Special Congress session at Calcutta, September 1920, presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai, passed Gandhi's Non-Cooperation resolution.
    • Calcutta session discussed the Khilafat question and the Government's failure to protect innocent people of Punjab and punish British officers.
    • Leaders decided the only way to vindicate national honour was Swaraj through Non-Cooperation.
    • The session was attended by most national leaders and almost 300 delegates from Bihar; the resolution passed with a great majority.
    • At Calcutta the resolution was opposed by senior leaders like C.R. Das and Madan Mohan Malviya.
    • At the Nagpur session (December 1920) the resolution was ratified; C.R. Das himself moved it.UPPSC
    • At Nagpur 1920 Congress changed its objective: attainment of 'Swaraj' by all legitimate and peaceful means.
    • Plan in stages: first non-cooperation and boycott; if Swaraj did not come within a year or the Government used repression, then civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes.
    • Gandhiji promised (at the AICC) 'Swaraj within one year' if the movement was effectively carried out.UPPSC ×2
    • After the 1919 reforms failed Indian aspirations, Congress sought Swaraj (self-government) under Mahatma Gandhi.UPPSC

    Programme

    • Resolution's advice: resign from administrative bodies, give up honorary titles, withdraw children from Government schools and colleges, refuse official events, boycott British courts and foreign goods, adopt Swadeshi goods and garments.
    • Nagpur programme: renunciation of titles and honours; boycott of law courts and foreign cloth; panchayats to settle disputes; strict non-violence.
    • Titles were to be fully renounced; keeping them without public use was not part of the programme.
    • Gandhiji called for boycott of the Prince of Wales' visit to India in 1921, seen as a symbol of British power.
    • The movement urged people to give up alcohol, causing a big fall in government revenue.
    • Government of Bihar and Odisha circulated a list of famous drinkers (Alexander, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Shakespeare) to publicise alcohol's benefits.

    Participation

    • The movement got wide success in western India, Bengal and northern India.
    • C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Rajendra Prasad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vithalbhai Patel, Vallabhbhai Patel and Lala Lajpat Rai gave up legal practice and boycotted courts.UPPSC
    • Rajendra Prasad, a pleader of Bihar, left his lucrative practice for the movement; he wrote the book 'India Divided'.
    • M.A. Jinnah did not support the Non-Cooperation Movement.UPPSC
    • Gandhiji got the 'Kaiser-i-Hind' title in 1915 from Lord Hardinge II for humanitarian work in South Africa; he returned it in 1920 during Non-Cooperation.UPPSC
    • Kaisar-i-Hind Medal: given by the British monarch to civilians of any nationality for distinguished service advancing the interests of the British Raj.
    • When Gandhiji arrived in India, Britain was in World War I; he supported Britain in the war.
    • Jamnalal Bajaj returned the title of 'Rai Bahadur'.
    • Bal Gangadhar Tilak supported Non-Cooperation but died on its first day (1 August 1920), so could not see its result.UPPSC
    • Tilak agreed with non-cooperation (June 1920) but opposed boycott of legislative council elections set up by the 1919 Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
    • Swami Vidyanand, a peasant leader, led cultivators in Bihar and linked peasant issues with Non-Cooperation.
    • Rahul Sankrityayan (original name Kedar Nath Pandey) was active in Chhapra, Bihar; he and Nagnarayan spread the message there.
    • Rahul Sankrityayan (1893–1963), born in Azamgarh, U.P.; 'Mahapandit', Father of Hindi travel literature; spent forty-five years on travels.
    • Jayaprakash Narayan (born Sitab Diyara, Saran, Bihar) left Patna College with 20 days left for his exams; then joined Congress-run Bihar Vidyapeeth.
    • E.V. Ramaswami Nayakar (Erode Venkatappa Ramasamy, 'Periyar') took part in Non-Cooperation; he left Congress in 1925.UPPSC

    Non-Cooperation in the towns

    • Not true that only upper castes and the rich took part; the Justice Party of Madras did not boycott council elections.
    • 1919–1922 saw two mass movements: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation.
    • Students left government schools and colleges in large numbers; headmasters and teachers resigned; lawyers gave up practice.
    • Indian business groups, gaining from Swadeshi, supported the economic boycott.
    • Peasants took part actively, but it led to confrontations between lower and upper castes.
    • The movement was first led by the middle classes; later many had reservations about Gandhi's approach.
    • Oppressed masses got a chance to voice grievances against the British and their Indian oppressors.
    • Women joined in large numbers, gave up purdah and gave ornaments to the Tilak Fund.
    • Police reprisals were violent and many lives were lost.
    • Justice Party (Madras Presidency) did not support the movement; preferred British presence and working within the system; disliked Gandhi's praise of Brahminism.

    Institutions and Tagore

    • Founded during Non-Cooperation (1920–22): Kashi Vidyapith (Varanasi, 1921), Gujarat Vidyapith (Ahmedabad, 1920), Jamia Millia Islamia (Aligarh, 1920; later shifted to Delhi).UPPSC
    • Madan Mohan Malviya founded Banaras Hindu University at Varanasi in 1916; he was its Vice-Chancellor from 1919 to 1939.
    • Rabindranath Tagore opposed burning of foreign clothes; he wrote to Gandhi calling it 'a ruthless waste' (indiscriminate or callous waste).UPPSC ×5
    • Tagore stressed constructive (creative) programmes over mass agitation; called cloth-burning unwise and said he could not obey it.

    Chauri Chaura

    • Chauri Chaura incident: 4 February 1922.UPPSC ×2
    • Chauri Chaura is in Gorakhpur district, United Provinces (Uttar Pradesh).UPPSC ×2
    • Villagers had gathered at the police station to protest the arrest of their leader during a campaign against liquor sale.
    • Police fired on the protesters; the angry mob burnt the police station, killing 23 policemen; 3 civilians also died.
    • 225 persons were arrested; the Sessions Judge of Gorakhpur sentenced 170 to death.
    • No local lawyer came forward; Madan Mohan Malaviya, aided by Krishna Kant, defended them before the Chief Justice of Allahabad High Court.
    • Malaviya had been away from law for nearly a decade; 151 accused were saved from the gallows, 19 were executed.
    • Source cited: Sitaram Chaturvedi's biography "Madan Mohan Malaviya (Builders of Modern India)", Publications Division.
    • PM Narendra Modi inaugurated the Chauri Chaura centenary celebration at Chauri Chaura, Gorakhpur, on 4 February 2021 by video conferencing.

    Withdrawal

    • Gandhiji withdrew (suspended) the Non-Cooperation Movement because of the violence at Chauri Chaura.UPPSC ×3
    • The movement ended in 1922 (12 February 1922).UPPSC
    • At the time of Chauri Chaura Gandhiji was at Bardoli (Gujarat), about to start mass civil disobedience, which was also suspended.UPPSC
    • Congress Working Committee met at Bardoli on 11–12 February 1922 and suspended the movement: the Bardoli resolution.
    • Sequence: Chauri Chaura incident (4 February 1922) → Bardoli Resolutions (12 February 1922) → suspension of Non-Cooperation.UPPSC
    • Bardoli resolution: suspend mass civil disobedience; advise cultivators to pay revenue and dues; stop all offensive preparatory activity.
    • Suspension was to last until the atmosphere was non-violent enough to prevent atrocities as at Gorakhpur or hooliganism as at Bombay and Madras.
    • Workers were urged to take up constructive work: popularise khadi, set up national schools, work for Hindu-Muslim unity.
    • 24 February 1922: AICC met at Delhi and limited all activities amounting to violation of law; individual law-breaking could continue with permission.
    • At that Delhi meeting Dr. Moonje tabled a vote of censure against Gandhiji for calling off the movement.UPPSC
    • The sudden suspension shocked Gandhi's followers; C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru strongly opposed it.UPPSC
    • Gandhi was arrested on 10 March 1922 (not 1921) and sentenced for six years.
    • Sequence: police firing at Chauri Chaura → crowd burns police station → Gandhi postpones movement → Gandhi arrested.
    • Gandhiji gave his first major public speech at Banaras Hindu University.
    • Gandhi called the Satyagraha at Nadiad on 14 April, during martial law after Jallianwala Bagh, his "Himalayan Blunder".

    Results

    • Results: Congress became a mass movement for the first time, Hindu-Muslim unity grew, fear of British might left people's minds.
    • Main outcome of the 1921–22 movement: Hindu-Muslim unity; communal unity and massive Muslim participation gave it a mass character.UPPSC
    • It showed Congress had the support of vast sections; people became conscious of political rights, lost trust in the British and gained self-reliance.
    • It introduced people to modern techniques of politics and made them hungry for freedom; showed readiness to sacrifice and face repression.
    • Revival of revolutionary activities in 1923–28 was due to Gandhiji's postponement of Non-Cooperation.
    • Disappointed nationalists, unhappy with Gandhi's leadership and non-violence, were inspired by violent revolutions in Russia, China, Ireland and Turkey.
    • Anti-Non-Cooperation Association was started by big businessmen in 1920 against the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat Movement.
    • Its founders: Jamnadas Dwarkadas, Purshottamdas Thakurdas, Cowasji Jehangir, Pheroze Sethna and M.C. Setalvad.
    • Bombay businessmen feared the movement would encourage labour strikes, which had earlier turned violent in Bombay Presidency.
    • Gandhi lacked acceptance in the Maharashtra region, which still remembered Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

    Note from the book CGPSC deleted the question on who set up the anti-non-cooperation assembly in its final answer key.

    Chapter 69 · Freedom struggle

    Formation of Swaraj Party (1923)

    36 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. C. Rajagopalachari and Rajendra Prasad were not members of the Swaraj Party.×3
    2. Founders: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, in January 1923, as a party within the Congress.×3
    3. Vithalbhai Patel became the first Indian Speaker (President) of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925 (President in August 1925); biggest achievement of the Swaraj Party.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 12 UPPSC questions

    Background

    • Government of India Act 1919 set up the Central Legislature (Council of States and Legislative Assembly) and Provincial Legislative Councils.
    • Congress boycotted them on Gandhiji's direction and did not contest the 1920 elections.
    • Withdrawal of Non-Cooperation and Gandhiji's arrest created an atmosphere of hopelessness.
    • After Non-Cooperation, Congress split into pro-changers (enter legislatures) and no-changers (boycott legislatures).
    • Pro-changer leaders: C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru and Vithalbhai Patel; no-changer leaders: Vallabhbhai Patel, C. Rajagopalachari and Rajendra Prasad.
    • C. Rajagopalachari and Rajendra Prasad were not members of the Swaraj Party.UPPSC ×3
    • C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru proposed that Congress fight elections, enter the councils and continue the struggle from within; most Congressmen rejected it.
    • The split came at the Gaya session of Congress, December 1922.

    Swaraj Party

    • Swaraj Party was formed after the failure (withdrawal) of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
    • Founders: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, in January 1923, as a party within the Congress.UPPSC ×3
    • C.R. Das, then Congress President, resigned the presidency to form the Swaraj Party.UPPSC
    • Reasons for founding: withdrawal of Non-Cooperation by Gandhi; entering councils to wreck the Government of India Act 1919 from within by obstruction.UPPSC
    • C.R. Das = President of the party; Motilal Nehru = General Secretary.
    • Other main leaders: S. Srinivasa Iyengar (founder of the Swaraj Party at Madras) and N.C. Kelkar.
    • Sri Krishna Singh led the Swaraj Dal branch formed in Bihar.
    • Legislative Council elections were held in November 1923; Swarajists won 42 of 104 elected seats and a clear majority in the Central Provinces assembly.
    • In the Central Legislative Assembly Swarajists joined hands with liberals and independents like Jinnah and Malviya.UPPSC
    • The party demanded responsible Government in India with necessary changes in the Government of India Act 1919.
    • Vithalbhai Patel became the first Indian Speaker (President) of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925 (President in August 1925); biggest achievement of the Swaraj Party.UPPSC ×2
    • Vithalbhai Patel was also a co-founder of the Swaraj Party.

    C.R. Das

    • Chittaranjan Das was called 'Deshbandhu' = 'Friend of the Country'.UPPSC
    • He studied law in London and became an advocate in India; a lawyer and revolutionary freedom fighter.
    • He defended Aurobindo Ghose and won his acquittal in the Alipore Bomb Conspiracy Case.
    • After Non-Cooperation failed he proposed a strategy to end dyarchy; Congress did not accept it.
    • C.R. Das gave the slogan "Swaraj should be for common people, not only for classes" ("Swaraj for the masses, not for the classes").
    • To him, "Swaraj is government by the people and for the people."

    Other parties

    1. 1916Madan Mohan Malviya was a founder member of the Hindu Mahasabha; he founded Banaras Hindu University in 1916.
    2. 1918Surendranath Banerjee and other Liberal leaders welcomed the reforms; when Congress condemned the report in 1918, moderates left and formed the Indian (National) Liberal Federation (also called All India Liberal Federation).
    3. 1918In 1918 the moderates accepted the Montford Reforms report and the extremists opposed it; the old moderate remnants who broke away included Sapru, Jayakar and Chintamani.
    4. 1918It was founded in 1918 by Surendra Nath Banerjee; T.B. Sapru, V.S. Srinivas Sastri and M.R. Jayakar were prominent leaders.
    5. 1919Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were framed at the end of World War I and embodied in the Government of India Act 1919.
    6. 1922Madan Mohan Malviya and Motilal Nehru decided to launch the Independent Party on 16 December 1922.UPPSC
    • Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were framed at the end of World War I and embodied in the Government of India Act 1919.
    • Surendranath Banerjee and other Liberal leaders welcomed the reforms; when Congress condemned the report in 1918, moderates left and formed the Indian (National) Liberal Federation (also called All India Liberal Federation).
    • In 1918 the moderates accepted the Montford Reforms report and the extremists opposed it; the old moderate remnants who broke away included Sapru, Jayakar and Chintamani.
    • It was founded in 1918 by Surendra Nath Banerjee; T.B. Sapru, V.S. Srinivas Sastri and M.R. Jayakar were prominent leaders.
    • Madan Mohan Malviya and Motilal Nehru decided to launch the Independent Party on 16 December 1922.UPPSC
    • Madan Mohan Malviya was a founder member of the Hindu Mahasabha; he founded Banaras Hindu University in 1916.

    Chapter 70 · Freedom struggle

    Simon Commission (1927)

    35 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. It was boycotted because it had no Indian member; this angered all political groups; Indians called it the 'White Commission'.×5
    2. He was severely injured in the police lathi charge during this protest and died on 17 November 1928.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 12 UPPSC questions

    Appointment

    • Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford reform) provided for a commission after ten years to review its working and suggest new steps.
    • The 1919 Act was passed on the recommendations of Lord Chelmsford and Samuel Montagu to introduce self-governing institutions gradually; it introduced diarchy in the provinces.
    • Simon Commission (Indian Statutory Commission) was appointed in November 1927 by the British Conservative Government of PM Stanley Baldwin.
    • Its task: report on the working of the 1919 Act and whether India was ready for further constitutional (administrative) reforms.UPPSC
    • Chairman: Sir John Simon; 7 members, all white, no Indian.
    • Sir John Simon belonged to the Liberal Party.UPPSC
    • Clement Attlee (Labour Party), UK Prime Minister at India's independence, was also a member.
    • Indians were kept out of the Commission on the suggestion of Lord Irwin.UPPSC

    Boycott and visit

    • It was boycotted because it had no Indian member; this angered all political groups; Indians called it the 'White Commission'.UPPSC ×5
    • Boycotters: Indian National Congress and a section of the Muslim League headed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
    • Congress decided to boycott it at its Madras session, December 1927.
    • Simon Commission reached Bombay (India) on 3 February 1928; a countrywide strike was held that day.UPPSC
    • Places it visited saw complete strikes and the slogan "Simon! Go Back".
    • The Commission visited India twice: 3 February to 31 March 1928, and 11 October 1928 to 13 April 1929.UPPSC

    Recommendations

    • True of the Commission: set up to inquire into the 1919 Act, headed by Sir John Simon, recommended a federal form of government, opposed by Indian leaders.UPPSC
    • It advised a Central legislature of federal (not unitary) character, with members elected indirectly from provincial legislatures.
    • It recommended replacing diarchy with responsible Government in the provinces.

    Lala Lajpat Rai

    • Lala Lajpat Rai led a non-violent protest against the Simon Commission at Lahore in 1928; the reason was that it had no Indian member.
    • He was severely injured in the police lathi charge during this protest and died on 17 November 1928.UPPSC ×2
    • Lala Lajpat Rai, a major political leader of Punjab, is known as 'Punjab Kesari'.

    Nehru Report

    • All Parties Conference was held at Delhi in February 1928; President: Dr. M.A. Ansari.
    • 29 organisations attended, in response to the Simon Commission and the challenge of Lord Birkenhead, Secretary of State for India.
    • The conference proposed drafting a constitution for responsible government; parties present besides Congress: Hindu Mahasabha, Muslim League, Khilafat Committee.
    • Nehru Report (1928) was prepared by an all-party committee headed by Motilal Nehru, as an answer to the Simon Commission.
    • Its subject was constitutional arrangements in India.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru was the committee's secretary; it had 10 members including two Muslims.
    • Tej Bahadur Sapru and Jayakar were members of the Nehru Report committee; they are taken as the first to demand dominion status.UPPSC
    • Motilal Nehru in March 1926 demanded a representative conference to frame a Constitution for Dominion Status; Govind Ballabh Pant was not linked to it.
    • Nehru Report asked for Dominion Status, not complete independence.
    • It recommended joint electorates with seats reserved for minorities, and fundamental rights; no separate electorates or weightage for minorities.
    • Fundamental rights named: free expression of opinion (speech); peaceful assembly without arms; forming associations or unions.

    Reactions to Nehru Report

    • Radical youth nationalists led by Jawaharlal Nehru opposed the Nehru Report and wanted complete independence as the immediate goal.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose founded the Independence for India League in 1928 to demand complete independence, not Dominion Status.UPPSC
    • The League helped unite progressive forces against British rule.
    • Jinnah put forth his Fourteen Points in March 1929 (Muslim League) against the Nehru Report, to safeguard Muslim political rights in a self-governing India.UPPSC

    Lahore Session of Congress, Proposal of Complete Independence (1929)

    21 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Lahore Session (December 1929) passed the Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution for the first time.×7
    2. Jawaharlal Nehru was President of the Lahore Session, 1929.×4
    3. At midnight of 31 December 1929 Nehru hoisted the tricolour flag of independence on the bank of the Ravi river at Lahore.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 10 UPPSC questions

    Earlier sessions

    1. 1916The rift between extremists and moderates was resolved at the 1916 Lucknow session.
    2. 1921Ahmedabad Session (1921): Maulana Hasrat Mohani proposed defining Swaraj as complete independence free from all foreign control, as the goal of Congress.
    3. 1921C.R. Das was elected President of the 1921 Ahmedabad session but was in jail; Hakim Ajmal Khan presided as acting President.
    4. 1921Congress session of 1921 first resolved that India must have a foreign policy.
    5. 1927Madras annual session (1927) was chaired by Dr. M.A. Ansari; it demanded a constitution for Swaraj, rejected the Simon Commission and passed a Hindu-Muslim unity proposal.
    6. 1927Madras 1927 objected to sending Indian troops to China, Mesopotamia and Persia (not China and Japan); Purna Swaraj was adopted in 1929, not 1927.
    7. 1928Calcutta Session (1928): Congress gave the British an ultimatum to accept the Nehru Report within the year or face a mass movement.
    • Ahmedabad Session (1921): Maulana Hasrat Mohani proposed defining Swaraj as complete independence free from all foreign control, as the goal of Congress.
    • C.R. Das was elected President of the 1921 Ahmedabad session but was in jail; Hakim Ajmal Khan presided as acting President.
    • Congress session of 1921 first resolved that India must have a foreign policy.
    • Madras annual session (1927) was chaired by Dr. M.A. Ansari; it demanded a constitution for Swaraj, rejected the Simon Commission and passed a Hindu-Muslim unity proposal.
    • Madras 1927 objected to sending Indian troops to China, Mesopotamia and Persia (not China and Japan); Purna Swaraj was adopted in 1929, not 1927.

    Note from the book Chhattisgarh PSC keyed "only (ii)" as not true for the 1927 session question; the book holds (ii) and (iii) are both not true.

    • Calcutta Session (1928): Congress gave the British an ultimatum to accept the Nehru Report within the year or face a mass movement.
    • The rift between extremists and moderates was resolved at the 1916 Lucknow session.

    Lahore Session 1929

    • Government inaction on the Nehru Report led Congress to declare 'Purna Swaraj' as its goal.
    • Lahore Session (December 1929) passed the Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution for the first time.UPPSC ×7
    • Jawaharlal Nehru was President of the Lahore Session, 1929.UPPSC ×4
    • It was the first Congress session presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    • Nehru prepared and moved the Purna Swaraj resolution and declared Purna Swaraj the aim of Congress.UPPSC
    • In his presidential address Nehru said: "we have but one goal today that of independence".
    • The Nehru Report, which sought only Dominion Status, was rejected at this session.
    • At midnight of 31 December 1929 Nehru hoisted the tricolour flag of independence on the bank of the Ravi river at Lahore.UPPSC ×2
    • The two-nation theory was not rejected at Lahore by any resolution, though Congress as a party opposed it.

    Lahore resolutions

    • Lahore resolutions (31 December 1929): no benefit from the Round Table Conference; Dominion Status plan of the Nehru Report given up; 'Swaraj' means Complete Independence; AICC may start Civil Disobedience when it thinks fit.
    • Abolition of untouchability was not among the Lahore resolutions.UPPSC
    • The Round Table Conference point can be taken as India's foreign policy, as only the British Government could make India's foreign policy.

    Purna Swaraj Day

    • Congress Working Committee on 2 January 1930 fixed 26 January 1930 as 'Purna Swaraj Day' (Complete Independence Day).
    • 26 January was to be kept every year as 'Purna Swadhinta Divas'; till 1947 it was called Purna Swaraj Day.
