    Chapter 72 · Freedom struggle

    Civil Disobedience Movement

    75 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Webb Miller, American journalist, stayed with Gandhi at Sabarmati Ashram during the Dandi March and reported the Dharsana Satyagraha.×4
    2. Abbas Tayabji led the movement after Gandhi's arrest (also given: Gandhi was arrested at Sholapur).×3
    3. Gandhi launched the salt agitation in 1930; his object was not to make salt free for the poor.×2
    4. On 6 April 1930 Gandhi broke the Salt Law at Dandi by picking up a lump (handful) of salt; also given as making salt by boiling seawater.×2
    5. Dandi March was started to break the Salt Law.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 23 UPPSC questions

    Start of the movement

    • Lahore Session (1929) authorised the Congress Working Committee to launch Civil Disobedience.
    • February 1930: CWC's second meeting at Sabarmati Ashram gave the leadership of the movement to Mahatma Gandhi.
    • Before the movement Gandhi put 11 demands before Viceroy Irwin, including abolition of the Salt Tax and of government monopoly on salt.
    • Britain's Salt Act of 1882 barred Indians from collecting or selling salt; they could only buy it.
    • The Government had banned sale of salt and taxed it, which hit the poor hard.
    • Gandhi launched the salt agitation in 1930; his object was not to make salt free for the poor.UPPSC ×2
    • Aims of the Salt Satyagraha: break (repeal) the salt laws and curtail the government's power; Purna Swaraj was not its aim.

    Dandi March

    • Dandi March began on 12 March 1930.
    • It started from Sabarmati Ashram.UPPSC
    • Gandhi walked with 80 chosen volunteers, 241 miles, to Dandi, a coastal village in Navsari district, Gujarat.
    • The march lasted 24 days; it reached Dandi on 5 April 1930.
    • On 6 April 1930 Gandhi broke the Salt Law at Dandi by picking up a lump (handful) of salt; also given as making salt by boiling seawater.UPPSC ×2
    • Dandi March was started to break the Salt Law.UPPSC ×2
    • The Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi March.UPPSC ×2
    • Gandhi started the Civil Disobedience Movement from Dandi in 1930.

    Note from the book BPSC's final answer key gave Sabarmati for where Gandhi started Civil Disobedience in 1930; the book calls that incorrect and keys Dandi.

    • Not correct about the march: that Gandhi prepared salt at the seashore; it was an all-pedestrian march from Sabarmati ending at Dandi village by the sea.UPPSC ×2
    • Not correct: that the march started on 15 March 1930; it started on 12 March and took 24 days.UPPSC
    • Gujarat sent the highest number of satyagrahis in the Dandi March.UPPSC
    • "I want world sympathy in this battle of Right against Might": Gandhi at Dandi, 5 April 1930, to Indian and foreign journalists.UPPSC
    • "Sedition has become my religion": Gandhi during the Salt Satyagraha–Dandi March (speech of 18 March 1930).
    • Gandhi said the British Empire deserved sedition, not loyalty, so he made sedition "My Dharma".
    • Subhas Chandra Bose compared the Dandi March with Napoleon's march from Elba to Paris.
    • English editor Brailsford mocked: "Can an Emperor be unseated by boiling sea water in a kettle?"
    • The Statesman replied: "Mr. Gandhi can boil the seawater till they got the Dominion Status".

    Arrests and Dharsana

    • Convicted for breaking the salt law: Madan Mohan Malviya, Devadas Gandhi, K.M. Munshi, B.G. Kher, Mahadev Desai, C. Rajagopalachari, Vithalbhai Patel; Gandhi too was arrested.UPPSC
    • Gandhi was arrested on 5 May 1930, before the planned raid on Dharsana salt works, and sent to Yerwada Jail.UPPSC
    • Abbas Tayabji led the movement after Gandhi's arrest (also given: Gandhi was arrested at Sholapur).UPPSC ×3
    • Sarojini Naidu led the movement after Abbas Tayabji's arrest and led the Dharsana salt depot raid on 21 May 1930.
    • Webb Miller, American journalist, stayed with Gandhi at Sabarmati Ashram during the Dandi March and reported the Dharsana Satyagraha.UPPSC ×4
    • Webb Miller wrote that in 18 years of reporting riots and revolts he had never seen such a horrible event as Dharsana.
    • Gandhi asked the Dharsana marchers not to resist, not even raise a hand against blows.
    • Acharya Vinoba Bhave, a close ally of Gandhi, was first arrested in 1930 for joining the Civil Disobedience Movement.UPPSC

    Women

    • Sarojini Naidu, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur and Kamladevi Chattopadhyaya all took part in Gandhi's Salt Satyagraha.
    • Women's participation is considered maximum in the Salt Satyagraha (Civil Disobedience Movement).UPPSC
    • Gandhi saw a supportive role for women, but they demanded a more active one; he chose them for picketing liquor and foreign cloth shops for their capacity for non-violence.
    • Dr. Radhabai was arrested on 13 June 1932 while leading a procession in the Second Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • Dr. Radhabai was at the forefront of all of Gandhi's movements.

    Spread in the regions

    • C. Rajagopalachari led the Vedaranyam March (April 1930) from Trichinopoly (Tiruchirappalli) to Vedaranyam on the Tanjore coast to break the Salt Law.
    • Vedaranyam is now on the Vedaranyam beach of Nagapattinam district; the march was the second of its kind after Dandi; marchers collected salt from the sea.
    • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts), a volunteer body in NWFP (organised in 1929), and led it.UPPSC
    • Khudai Khidmatgars called for Pathan regional nationalist unity and a struggle against colonialism.
    • The Red Shirt organisation was founded to throw out the British.UPPSC
    • They also sought better conditions for wage-earners (labourers).
    • NWFP Muslims played an important role in Civil Disobedience under Ghaffar Khan; Muslims of other provinces stayed away.
    • Peshawar Incident (1930): Garhwal Rifles soldiers under Chandra Singh Garhwali refused to fire on an unarmed crowd during Civil Disobedience.UPPSC
    • Jiatrang Movement arose in Manipur, led by Naga tribal woman Rani Gaidinliu during Civil Disobedience (1930s).UPPSC
    • Agitation against Chaukidari Tax in Begusarai was part of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • In Bihar, besides making salt, people opposed the Chowkidari tax; farmers refused to pay it in 1930.
    • Chowkidari tax was collected from farmers to pay village watchmen (chowkidars), a kind of police.
    • Salt Satyagraha at Bihpur, Bhagalpur was led by Mahadev Lal Sarraf, Deep Narayan Singh, Rameshwar Narayan Agrawal, Kailash Bihari Lal and Zeharul Hasan Hashmi.
    • Prabhavati Devi was a freedom fighter from Patna.
    • Bihar women in the freedom movement: Prabhavati Devi, Rajvanshi Devi, Suniti Devi and Radhika Devi.

    After the movement

    • After the failure of Civil Disobedience, Gandhiji gave importance to constructive programmes.
    • 17 September 1934: Gandhi announced his resignation from Congress by public statement; October 1934: he formally retired from active politics for Harijan uplift.
    • September 1932: Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League; 1933: he started the weekly 'Harijan'.

    Chapter 73 · Freedom struggle

    Gandhi-Irwin Pact

    16 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Quick quiz: 4 of 4 UPPSC questions

    Signing of the pact

    • Viceroy Lord Irwin released Gandhiji from jail on 26 January 1931, seeing the growing Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • Gandhi–Irwin talks began in (mid) February 1931 through the efforts of Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar, who acted as mediators.
    • Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931, before the Second Round Table Conference in London.
    • The Second Round Table Conference in London was held in the backdrop of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
    • Main purpose of the pact: make Congress participation in the Round Table Conference easier.UPPSC
    • Sarojini Naidu called Irwin and Gandhi 'The Two Mahatmas'.UPPSC

    Terms

    • Congress, under Gandhiji, agreed to withdraw (discontinue) the Civil Disobedience Movement.UPPSC
    • Congress agreed to take part in the Second Round Table Conference; Gandhi also agreed to stop boycotting British goods.
    • The pact included: invitation to Congress to the Round Table Conference, withdrawal of ordinances against Civil Disobedience, release of only those prisoners not charged with violence.
    • Gandhiji's suggestion for an enquiry into police excesses was not accepted in the pact.
    • Withdrawal of all ordinances curbing Congress activities and of all prosecutions except those involving violence.
    • Right to peaceful picketing at foreign cloth shops and liquor shops.
    • Permission to make salt in coastal areas without Salt Tax.

    Reactions

    • People were disappointed: the pact did not commute the death sentences of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru.
    • Alan Campbell Johnson, Irwin's biographer, called Gandhi's gains in the pact "Consolation Prizes".UPPSC
    • He said Irwin's only surrender was agreeing to negotiate.

    Note from the book UPPSC first keyed S.C. Bose for the "Consolation Prizes" question; its revised key gave Alan Campbell Johnson.

    Karachi Session

    • Karachi Session of Congress was held on 29–31 March 1931 with Vallabhbhai Patel as President.UPPSC
    • It was held to ratify (endorse) the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, also called the Delhi Pact.
    • Resolutions on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Policy (programme) were passed for the first time at Karachi.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru, with the help of M.N. Roy, drafted the resolutions on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme.
    • Karachi was the first session where Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence) was defined.
    • Facing black-flag demonstrations, Gandhiji said: "They might kill me but they cannot kill Gandhism".
    • Subhas Chandra Bose called the Karachi Session the 'pinnacle of Mahatma Gandhi's popularity and prestige'.UPPSC

    Chapter 75 · Freedom struggle

    Round Table Conference

    29 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Gandhi attended only the Second Round Table Conference.×2
    2. Congress took part for the first time, and only, in the Second Conference.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 13 UPPSC questions

    First Round Table Conference

    • Simon Commission's two-volume report was published on 10 June and 24 June 1930; political organisations rejected it.
    • First Round Table Conference was held in London from November 1930 to January 1931 (summoned 1930), at St. James Palace.UPPSC
    • It was held in an atmosphere of frustration; the main Congress leaders were in jail.
    • 89 Indian delegates took part; Congress did not attend the First Conference.UPPSC
    • Main objective of the Round Table Conference: discuss the Simon Commission Report and improve the political situation.
    • Participants: Tej Bahadur Sapru, Srinivas Shastri, Maulana Muhammad Ali (Jauhar), Muhammad Shafi, Aga Khan III, Fazlul Haq, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Homi Mody, M.R. Jayakar, Dr. B.S. Moonje, B.R. Ambedkar and Sundar Singh Majithia.
    • K.T. Paul represented Indian Christians at the First Conference.UPPSC
    • It was inaugurated by the King Emperor (George V) and chaired by British PM Ramsay MacDonald.
    • At the First Conference Dr. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes; Poona Pact gave them representation in local bodies and civil services; Congress skipped the Third.

    Second Round Table Conference

    • Second Round Table Conference: 7 September 1931 to 1 December 1931, London.
    • Mahatma Gandhi was the sole official representative of Congress at it, after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
    • Gandhi attended only the Second Round Table Conference.UPPSC ×2
    • Congress took part for the first time, and only, in the Second Conference.UPPSC ×2
    • Sarojini Naidu, Madan Mohan Malviya and Annie Besant also took part with Gandhi.UPPSC
    • Others present: Mahadev Desai, B.R. Ambedkar; Pyarelal Nayyar came as Gandhi's private secretary; Jawaharlal Nehru did not attend.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad did not take part in the Second Conference.UPPSC
    • False: that Nehru represented Congress at the Second Conference; true: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) implied Congress would attend it.UPPSC
    • Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) terms: stop Civil Disobedience, Congress to join the Round Table Conference, withdraw ordinances curbing Congress, withdraw prosecutions.
    • Gandhi sailed from Bombay to London on the ship S.S. Rajputana.UPPSC
    • In London Gandhi stayed at Kingsley Hall.UPPSC
    • The Second Conference failed completely over communal issues (communal delegations).
    • Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits (depressed classes); Gandhi refused.
    • The conference ended on 1 December 1931; Gandhi returned to India from London empty-handed in December 1931.
    • Gandhi said: "It is true that I returned barehanded but I am content that the Flag I had been handed was never let down by me and I never compromised with the honour of that flag".

    Third Conference and overall

    • Third Round Table Conference: 17 November 1932 to 24 December 1932.
    • Congress did not send representatives to the First and Third Conferences.
    • B.R. Ambedkar took part in all three Round Table Conferences.UPPSC
    • Ambedkar is given as the only Indian to take part in all three; it is also given that both Dr. Ambedkar and Tej Bahadur Sapru attended all three.
    • The three were not separate conferences but three sessions of a single Conference, so calling them First, Second, Third Conferences is incorrect.

    Chapter 76 · Freedom struggle

    Communal Award and Poona Pact (1932)

    40 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Poona Pact concerned the depressed classes; its purpose was to give representation to the untouchables.×4
    2. Ghanshyam Das (G.D.) Birla was its first President.×4
    Quick quiz: 10 of 15 UPPSC questions

    Communal Award

    • The Second Round Table Conference reached no consensus on separate electorates for depressed classes and other communities.
    • His Majesty's Government had declared (endorsed by Parliament) that if communities failed to agree, it would devise and apply a scheme.
    • British PM Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award on 16 August 1932.UPPSC
    • The Award gave each minority some reserved seats in the legislatures, to be filled through separate electorates.UPPSC
    • For the first time (August 1932) a separate electorate was made for the untouchables (depressed classes), now treated as a minority.
    • Depressed-class voters would also vote in the general constituency.
    • Earlier Muslims and Sikhs were treated as minorities; Europeans, Anglo-Indians and Indian Christians had got separate electorates in 1919.
    • Award gave separate electorates to Muslims, Indian Christians, Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, depressed classes and others; only for provincial legislatures.
    • Buddhists were not given separate electorates or reserved seats by the Award.UPPSC

    Gandhi's fast

    • Gandhiji began his first fast unto death on 20 September 1932 against the Communal Award.
    • He fasted in Yerwada Jail.
    • The fast ended on 26 September 1932 after the Poona Pact was approved.
    • 14 August 1931: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar told Gandhi in Mumbai, "History tells that Mahatmas, like fleeting phantoms, raise dust, but raise no level."UPPSC
    • Gandhi and Ambedkar were in conflict over the situation of the depressed classes.

    Poona Pact

    • Poona Pact came after the Communal Award; it is called the pact of Dr. Ambedkar and Gandhiji.UPPSC
    • It was signed on 24 September 1932 at 5 o'clock in the evening.
    • Poona Pact concerned the depressed classes; its purpose was to give representation to the untouchables.UPPSC ×4
    • M.K. Gandhi did not sign the Poona Pact.UPPSC
    • Signed by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar for the depressed classes and Pt. Madan Mohan Malaviya for the Hindu community; it was between Gandhi's followers and Ambedkar.
    • Other signatories: M.R. Jayakar, Devdas Gandhi, Vishwas, Raja Bhoj, P. Baloo, Gavai, Thakkar, Solanki, Tej Bahadur Sapru, G.D. Birla, Rajagopalachari, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Rao Bahadur Srinivasan, M.C. Rajah, C.V. Mehta, Bakhale and Kamath.
    • Many people signed the document in Bombay; Rajagopalachari exchanged his pen with Dr. Ambedkar after signing.
    • Reserved seats for depressed classes in provincial legislatures: 71 under Communal Award, raised to 148 by Poona Pact (147 in some books).
    • Poona Pact accepted joint electorates; 18% of general seats in the Central Legislature were reserved for depressed classes.
    • Poona Pact defeated the purpose of the Communal Award; it paved the way for reserved seats for SC and ST in Parliament and State Assemblies.UPPSC

    Harijan work and organisations

    • After the Poona Pact Gandhiji lost interest in Civil Disobedience and took up Harijan uplift as an all-India political and social programme.
    • Mahatma Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League (All India Harijan Sevak Sangh) on 30 September 1932, to remove untouchability.UPPSC
    • All India Anti-Untouchability League was the former name of the Harijan Sevak Sangh.UPPSC
    • Ghanshyam Das (G.D.) Birla was its first President.UPPSC ×4
    • Gandhi started the weekly 'Harijan' in 1933; Harijan tours also followed.
    • Babu Jagjivan Ram founded the All India Depressed Classes League.UPPSC
    • B.R. Ambedkar founded the All India Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942.
    • M.C. Rajah founded the All India Depressed Classes Association in 1926.

    Chapter 77 · Freedom struggle

    Congress Socialist Party (1934)

    27 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Founders: Jayaprakash Narayan and Acharya Narendra Dev; J.P. was associated with this party.×2
    Quick quiz: 4 of 4 UPPSC questions

    Formation

    • May 1934: AICC met at Patna to set up a Congress Parliamentary Board to fight elections.
    • Some AICC members met separately and founded the All India Congress Socialist Party; its first meeting was at Patna.
    • Congress Socialist Party's first session was in 1934.
    • The party was officially inaugurated in October 1934 at Bombay, where its policies and working methods were decided.
    • Founders: Jayaprakash Narayan and Acharya Narendra Dev; J.P. was associated with this party.UPPSC ×2
    • Jaya Prakash Narayan was convener of the All India Congress Socialist Party at Patna, 1934.UPPSC
    • J.P. Narayan = General Secretary; Acharya Narendra Dev = President; Ashok Mehta was among the founder members.
    • Not formed in January 1934; Jawaharlal Nehru never formally joined it.UPPSC
    • Members: Ashok Mehta, Achyut Patwardhan, Minoo Masani, Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia, Purushottam Trikam Das, Yusuf Meherally, Ganga Sharan Sinha and Kamla Devi Chattopadhyay.

    Ideology

    • Aim: push Congress towards a clear socialist agenda: full independence, abolition of landlordism, nationalisation of key industries.
    • CSP was a socialist caucus within the INC; it rejected Gandhi's "anti-rational mysticism" and the CPI's sectarian attitude to Congress.
    • Influenced by Fabianism and Marxism, CSP advocated armed struggle as well as non-violent resistance.
    • CSP promoted decentralised socialism: cooperatives, trade unions, independent farmers and local authorities to hold much economic power.
    • As secularists they hoped to overcome communal divisions through class solidarity.
    • CSP did not advocate boycott of British goods and tax evasion, dictatorship of the proletariat, or separate electorates for minorities.

    Bihar Socialist Party

    • Phulan Prasad Varma formed the Bihar Socialist Party in 1931 at a meeting in his home; J.P. Narayan is also named as its founder.
    • It was formed from within the Indian National Congress; influenced by Marx, Lenin and the Fabian Society.
    • Bihar Socialist Party is also given as founded by Ganga Sharan Sinha, Rambriksha Benipuri and Ramanand Mishra (in 1991).
    • J.P. Narayan belonged to the Bihar Socialist Party; Ganga Sharan Sinha, Rambriksha Benipuri and Ramanand Mishra were also associated with it.
    • Sri Narsingh Narayan Azad, a socialist, was an important member of the Bihar Socialist Party.

    Jayaprakash Narayan

    • Jayaprakash Narayan is known as 'Loknayak'.
    • In the Quit India Movement (1942) he secretly organised the masses with Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali.
    • 5 June 1974: he called for 'Sampoorna Kranti' (total revolution) from Gandhi Maidan, Patna.
    • He was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1999.
    • 'Jaya Prakash Day' was celebrated in April 1946 for his release from prison.
    • A rally at Bankipur Maidan, Patna demanded his release and criticised the policy of arresting political persons.

    Bombay Manifesto

    • Bombay Manifesto (May 1936), signed by 21 Bombay businessmen, openly opposed Nehru's preaching of socialist ideas at the Lucknow Session; the business community largely supported it.

    Chapter 79 · Freedom struggle

    Tripuri Crisis of Congress (1939)

    15 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Bose became Congress President for the second time at the Tripuri Session, held in 1939.×3
    2. After Bose resigned in 1939, Dr. Rajendra Prasad became Congress President.×2
    Quick quiz: 6 of 6 UPPSC questions

    Haripura Session 1938

    • Subhas Chandra Bose became Congress President in 1938, elected unopposed at the Haripura Session (February 1938); his first time as President.UPPSC
    • Haripura is in Gujarat.UPPSC

    Tripuri Session 1939

    • Tripuri is in Jabalpur (Madhya Pradesh).
    • Bose became Congress President for the second time at the Tripuri Session, held in 1939.UPPSC ×3
    • At Tripuri, Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya, the candidate supported by Gandhiji.UPPSC
    • Vote count at Tripuri: Bose 1580 votes, Pattabhi Sitaramayya 1377 votes.

    The dispute and resignation

    • Dispute between Bose and Gandhi (right wing) after Tripuri centred on formation of the Congress Working Committee; Bose resigned over it.
    • Gandhi was against Bose's point of view on modernization and his working conduct.
    • After Bose resigned in 1939, Dr. Rajendra Prasad became Congress President.UPPSC ×2
    • After the Tripuri crisis (1939), Bose resigned as Congress President and founded the Forward Bloc.
    • Forward Bloc was based on leftist ideology: a left-wing nationalist political party.

    Bose and the Second World War

    • Bose saw a war between Germany and Britain as a godsend opportunity for Indians to exploit to their advantage.
    • When Second World War clouds were over Europe, Bose wanted freedom for India through a military blow to the British Government in India.
    • Bose believed the old Irish saying: "England's difficulty is Ireland's opportunity" (also put as "Need of England is an opportunity for Ireland").
    • So Bose tried to persuade Congress and Gandhiji to take the help of Britain's enemy to free India.

    Chapter 80 · Freedom struggle

    Indian Princely States

    31 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Butler Committee 1927

    • The Indian States Committee was appointed in 1927 under chairman Sir Harcourt Butler; popularly called the Butler Committee.
    • Purpose: to investigate and clarify the relationship between the paramount power (Crown) and the princes of the Princely States; improve their relations.
    • The princes chose Sir Leslie Scott as their representative (retained as counsel) to put their view before the Butler Committee.
    • Recommendation: relationship of the paramount power with the states was not merely contractual but a living, growing relationship shaped by circumstances and policy.
    • Recommendation: British paramountcy preserved the princely states.
    • Recommendation: states should not be transferred, without their agreement, to a new government in British India responsible to an Indian legislature.

    States People's Movement

    • In the 1920s, people's movements were launched in the princely states; they were called State Peoples Conference or Praja Mandals.
    • Praja Mandal movements ran parallel to the freedom struggle in Indian-ruled states such as Kashmir, Nizam's Hyderabad and Travancore.
    • They were led by people of the princely states, who were under local aristocrats and not the British Raj directly.
    • They campaigned against the feudatory rulers, and sometimes British administrators, to improve their civil rights.
    • All India States People's Conference was set up in December 1927.
    • More than 1500 political workers from various states took part in it.
    • Balwant Rai Mehta, Manilal Kothari and G.R. Abhayankar played an important role in organizing it.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru was elected President of the All India States People's Conference in 1939.
    • Nehru was elected to represent the common national interest of political struggles of the Princely States and British India.

    Integration of the states

    • British Government set up two independent Dominions; suzerainty over Indian States lapsed, so the princely states had to decide their accession.
    • This complicated the merger of states into one Union.
    • Most princely states acceded to the Indian Dominion in 1947; territorial mergers/integration continued later.UPPSC
    • By 15 August 1947 all princely states had joined except Junagarh, Jammu & Kashmir and Hyderabad.UPPSC
    • These three states were made to join the Union of India by the end of 1948.
    • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel led the integration of states; political integration of India was largely achieved under him.
    • Patel took charge of the States Department in 1947 and handled the situation with great statesmanship.
    • Patel appealed to the patriotic and nationalist feelings of the Princes.
    • Patel asked the states to hand over External Affairs, Defence and Communications to the Indian Dominion.

    Kashmir, Hyderabad and Punjab

    • On 26 October 1947, Maharaja Hari Singh of Kashmir signed the Instrument of Accession and handed it to Jawaharlal Nehru.
    • Indian Army entered Jammu and Kashmir on 27 October 1947 to repel the invaders.
    • Nehru appointed Sheikh Abdullah as Prime Minister of Jammu and Kashmir on 5 March 1948.
    • Standstill Agreement was signed between the State of Hyderabad and the Dominion of India on 29 November 1947.UPPSC
    • It was signed by the Nizam of Hyderabad, Mir Osman Ali Khan, and Lord Mountbatten, Governor-General and Viceroy of India.
    • At Partition, Punjab province came forward with a plan for a united and independent existence.
    • Due to Sardar Patel's effort, PEPSU was formed from Eastern Punjab, Patiala and the hilly states; the idea of an independent state was rejected.

    Chapter 81 · Freedom struggle

    Second World War

    14 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    The war: dates and British Prime Ministers

    • Second World War began on 1 September 1939 when Germany attacked Poland.
    • It ended after six years, in September 1945.
    • British Prime Ministers during the war (1939-45): Neville Chamberlain (1937-40) and Winston Churchill (1940-45).
    • Churchill's tenures as Prime Minister: 1940-45 and 1951-55.

    India dragged into the war

    • On 3 September 1939, Viceroy Lord Linlithgow announced that India stood against Germany in the war.
    • Linlithgow put India into the war without consulting Indian people, leaders or elected councils, and declared an Emergency in the country; this angered Indian officials.

    Congress policy on the war

    • Congress policy: cooperate with Britain only on assurance of complete independence; no support for the war until independence was granted.UPPSC
    • Congress Working Committee asked Britain to announce its war objectives and demanded India's independence after the war.
    • Congress resolution condemned the Nazi attack on Poland and criticized the ideology of Nazism and Fascism.
    • The resolution said India could not join a war fought to protect democratic liberty while India itself was denied liberty under British colonial rule.
    • So it is false that Congress assisted the British in the war, and false that it did so expecting complete independence.UPPSC

    Resignation of Congress ministries 1939

    • Congress ministries in all provinces resigned in 1939 because the Viceroy declared war against Germany without the consent of the Congress ministries (Indians).
    • The ministries resigned after 28 months in office.
    • Not the causes of resignation: failure to form cabinets in the other four provinces, rise of the Congress left wing, or communal turbulence in provinces.

    Chapter 82 · Freedom struggle

    Demand for Pakistan

    30 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Muhammad Iqbal (poet and political philosopher) first gave the idea of a separate Muslim nation/state (an autonomous Muslim-majority homeland); it first found definite expression in his presidential address at the Allahabad Session of Muslim League, 1930.×3
    2. The Pakistan (Lahore) Resolution was passed on 23 March 1940.×2
    3. Sarojini Naidu called Jinnah the "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity".×2
    4. Iqbal remarked to Nehru in a meeting: "You are a patriot, while Jinnah is a politician."×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 12 UPPSC questions

    Iqbal and the idea of a separate Muslim state

    • Muhammad Iqbal (poet and political philosopher) first gave the idea of a separate Muslim nation/state (an autonomous Muslim-majority homeland); it first found definite expression in his presidential address at the Allahabad Session of Muslim League, 1930.UPPSC ×3
    • Source cited for this: R.C. Majumdar, "The History and Culture of the Indian People: Struggle for Freedom", page 613.
    • Iqbal was inspired by the spirit of Pan-Islam.
    • In that address Iqbal declared Hindus and Muslims two separate nations in the religious, social, cultural and historical context.
    • Iqbal said: "I would like to see Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan amalgamated into a single state."
    • Iqbal said: self-government within or without the British Empire, a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim state, is the final destiny of Muslims, at least of North-West India.

    The word Pakistan

    • The word PAKSTAN (later Pakistan) was first used/coined in 1933 by Chaudhary Rahmat Ali, a Cambridge University student and Pakistani nationalist.
    • He used it in his pamphlet (letter) "Now or Never; Are we to Live or Perish for Ever?"
    • The name came from five northern units of British India: Punjab, Afghan Province (North-West Frontier Province), Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan.
    • The idea of Pakistan gained momentum and led to the independent state of Pakistan in 1947.

    Lahore Session and Pakistan Resolution 1940

    • Muslim League session was held at Lahore from 22 to 24 March 1940; there the League formally demanded Pakistan as an independent, sovereign state (division of India).
    • Mohammad Ali Jinnah presided over the Lahore Session, 1940.UPPSC
    • The Pakistan (Lahore) Resolution was passed on 23 March 1940.UPPSC ×2
    • The session demanded separate independent Muslim states in the North-Western and Eastern zones of India.
    • Jinnah's Two Nation theory was accepted at the Lahore Session.UPPSC
    • Jinnah led the movement for a separate Pakistan; at Lahore he said he would accept nothing less than a separate Muslim country.
    • The Pakistan Resolution was drafted by Sikandar Hayat Khan.
    • The resolution was presented by Fazlul Haq on 23 March 1940 and approved by Khaliquzzaman.UPPSC
    • Sir Sikandar Hayat Khan, Fazlul Haq and Khaliquzzaman played an important role in preparing the outline of the Pakistan proposal.
    • Resolution text: no constitutional plan is workable or acceptable to Muslims unless contiguous geographical units are demarcated into regions, with necessary territorial readjustments.
    • First Pakistan Day was observed on 23 March 1941; the League also celebrated Pakistan Day on 23 March 1943.UPPSC

    Jinnah

    • Sarojini Naidu called Jinnah the "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity".UPPSC ×2
    • She said so for his nationalist views and for bringing a compromise between Muslim League and Congress.
    • In 1919 Jinnah gave testimony before the Parliament Select Committee and said he spoke as an Indian Nationalist.
    • Asked by Major Oksbergi if he wanted to end Hindu-Muslim discrimination at the earliest, Jinnah said he would be the happiest person when that day came.
    • Iqbal remarked to Nehru in a meeting: "You are a patriot, while Jinnah is a politician."UPPSC ×2
    • Nehru recorded this remark on page 352 of his book "The Discovery of India".
    • Jinnah supported the two-nation theory, presided over the Lahore Session 1940, and did not take part in the Non-Cooperation Movement (he did not support it); "he always had dairy" is not true.UPPSC
    • Jinnah raised the slogan "Divide and Quit" during the Second World War.
    • Meaning: the British should first divide India into Hindustan and Pakistan and then leave India.

    Chapter 83 · Freedom struggle

    Individual Satyagraha (1940)

    14 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Acharya Vinoba Bhave was chosen by Gandhi as the first Satyagrahi; he started the Individual Civil Disobedience.×3

    Start and aims

    • After completely rejecting the August Offer, Congress started Individual Satyagraha under Gandhiji's leadership.
    • It was a symbolic moral protest against the British Government's policy towards India.
    • Individual Satyagraha started on 17 October 1940.
    • In October 1940 Gandhiji called for a limited Satyagraha by a few selected individuals; it was kept limited so as not to disrupt Britain's war efforts.UPPSC
    • Two aims: show Indian people's displeasure at British India's participation in the war, and give the British another chance to accept Indian demands.
    • Gandhiji and Congress did not want a mass movement to disrupt the British war effort because of their anti-Nazi stand.

    The Satyagrahis

    • Acharya Vinoba Bhave was chosen by Gandhi as the first Satyagrahi; he started the Individual Civil Disobedience.UPPSC ×3
    • Jawaharlal Nehru was the second Satyagrahi.
    • Brahma Dutt was the third Satyagrahi.
    • Vinoba Bhave started his Individual Satyagraha from Pavnar, Maharashtra.

    Sarvodaya

    • Sarvodaya means "Universal Uplift" or "Progress of all".
    • The term was first coined by Mahatma Gandhi as the title of his 1908 translation of John Ruskin's tract on political economy, "Unto This Last".
    • Gandhi later used the term for the ideal of his own political philosophy.
    • Vinoba Bhave founded the "Sarvodaya Samaj" in 1948 to spread Gandhiji's ideals.
    ← Demand for PakistanCripps Mission (1942) →

    Chapter 84 · Freedom struggle

    Cripps Mission (1942)

    14 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Background and arrival

    • With Japan's power rising, the international community, especially USA, China and Australia, pressed Britain for a political settlement with India (to grant freedom).
    • Sir Stafford Cripps arrived in India in March 1942 to negotiate with Indian politicians.
    • British Prime Minister Winston Churchill sent the Cripps Mission, to get India's help and participation in the Second World War.

    Cripps proposals

    • After the Second World War India would get Dominion Status (an Indian Union with Dominion status), not full independence.
    • Dominion status meant: linked by common allegiance to the Crown, but not subordinate in domestic or external affairs to any external authority.
    • Indians would get the right to frame their own Constitution; an elected constitution-making body would be set up after the war.
    • Any province not agreeing to the new Constitution could stay out of the proposed Union and retain its present constitutional position.
    • Cripps's draft declaration included all four: Dominion status; all provinces and States merged into an Indian Union; any province or State may stay outside the Union; Constitution made by the people of India.UPPSC
    • Not part of the Cripps proposals: a new executive council with equal representation for Hindus and Muslims.UPPSC

    Reactions and negotiators

    • Mahatma Gandhi called the proposal a "post-dated cheque on a falling (crashing) bank".
    • Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Azad were the official Congress negotiators with the Cripps Mission.

    Lord Linlithgow

    • Lord Linlithgow called Gandhi's movements "Political Blackmail".UPPSC
    • Linlithgow was the longest-serving Viceroy and Governor-General of India: 1936 to 1943.
    • The Quit India Movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi during Linlithgow's tenure.

    Chapter 85 · Freedom struggle

    Quit India Movement

    100 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Louis Fischer, American journalist and biographer of Gandhi, was with Gandhiji at the time of the Quit India Movement.×5
    2. Aruna Asaf Ali was a major woman organiser of underground activities in the Quit India Movement.×4
    3. Gandhiji gave the mantra "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro) in the Quit India Movement: "We shall either free India or die in the attempt."×3
    4. Ballia (Uttar Pradesh) · Parallel government · August 1942 · Led by Chittu Pandey×3
    5. Azad was Congress President for six consecutive years, the most years before independence; India's political situation was very fragile in his tenure.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 31 UPPSC questions

    Background

    • Quit India Movement was launched in response to the failure of the Cripps Mission/Proposals (March 1942).
    • After Cripps failed, it was clear Britain wanted India as a partner in the Second World War without Indian consent but was not ready for any real agreement.
    • By spring 1942 the struggle seemed inevitable.
    • Causes of the movement: Indian disappointment with the Cripps Mission, threat of Japanese attack on India, and the AICC resolution of August 1942.
    • Gandhiji never provoked people to adopt violent means in his articles.
    • The slogan "Quit India" was coined by Yusuf Meher Ali.

    Wardha resolution, July 1942

    • Congress Working Committee met at Wardha during 5-14 July 1942 and passed the Quit India resolution on 14 July 1942.
    • On 6 July 1942 Gandhi first discussed his "Quit India Policy" at the Working Committee.
    • Leaders present at Wardha: Jawaharlal Nehru, Abul Kalam Azad, Vallabhbhai Patel, Mahatma Gandhi, Aruna Asaf Ali, Achyut Patwardhan, Dr. Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
    • Maulana Abul Kalam Azad chaired the meeting and was Congress President when the Quit India resolution was passed.UPPSC
    • Azad was elected Congress President at the Ramgarh Session, 1940; no Congress session was held for five years (1941-45), so he stayed President.
    • Azad was Congress President for six consecutive years, the most years before independence; India's political situation was very fragile in his tenure.UPPSC ×2

    Bombay session, August 1942

    • All India Congress Committee met on 7-8 August 1942 at Gowalia Tank Maidan (now August Kranti Ground), Bombay; the movement was launched from here.UPPSC ×2
    • The Wardha Resolution was confirmed here; after a few changes the Quit India Resolution was adopted by the AICC on 8 August 1942.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru moved (presented) the Quit India resolution in the AICC on 8 August 1942.UPPSC
    • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel supported the resolution.UPPSC
    • Mahatma Gandhi himself prepared the draft of the resolution, with the help of Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
    • The Committee asserted India's right to freedom and decided on a non-violent mass struggle on the widest possible scale.
    • Quit India Movement began on 9 August 1942.UPPSC
    • The movement was led by Mahatma Gandhi, who launched it in August 1942.

    Gandhiji's statement and Do or Die

    • Gandhi on the eve of the movement: government servants should not leave work but openly declare their allegiance to Congress.
    • Soldiers should refuse to fire on their countrymen (not leave their posts).
    • Students should leave studies only if they could stay firm on that decision until independence.
    • Princes should accept the sovereignty of their people; states to be declared part of the Indian nation; people to accept a king's leadership only if he links his future with theirs.
    • Gandhiji gave the mantra "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro) in the Quit India Movement: "We shall either free India or die in the attempt."UPPSC ×3
    • Gandhi said: "I am not going to be satisfied with anything short of complete freedom."
    • Gandhi said the British might offer abolition of salt tax or the drink evil, but he would say "nothing less than freedom".
    • Gandhi said of the mantra: "You may imprint it on your hearts and let every breath of yours give expression to it."
    • In the Do or Die speech Gandhi said: "I do not want to make the instrument either of Russia's defeat or of China's."
    • Gandhi asked all Congressmen and Indians to keep discipline through non-violence.
    • Pattabhi Sitaramayya on Gandhi's speech: that day Gandhiji spoke as if moved by the power of an Avatar and Paigambar.
    • Quit India Movement awakened and encouraged people because they absorbed the slogan "Do or Die".

    Arrests: Operation Zero Hour

    • In the early hours of 9 August 1942, Gandhiji and other top Congress leaders were arrested under Operation Zero Hour, before the movement could start.
    • Gandhiji was arrested in Bombay.UPPSC
    • Gandhiji and Sarojini Naidu were kept in the Aga Khan Palace, Poona (Pune).
    • Congress Working Committee members kept in Ahmednagar Fort: Jawaharlal Nehru, Abul Kalam Azad, Govind Ballabh Pant, Dr. Prafulla Chandra Ghosh, Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Dr. Syed Mahmud, Acharya Kripalani.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad could not come to Bombay; arrested at Patna on 9 August 1942 under Bharat Security Rules and sent to Bankipur (Patna) Jail.
    • Shivkumar and Ram-nandan Mishra were arrested in Hazaribagh; Ram-nandan Mishra was first arrested in Cuttack and later moved to Hazaribagh.
    • After the movement was announced, Congress was declared an illegal body.
    • Baldev Sahai resigned as Advocate General in 1942 in protest against the arrests and other oppressive acts of government.

    Nature and spread of the movement

    • The 1942 movement had maximum impact in Bombay, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and Madras; the whole country took part.
    • The movement was not so non-violent: official figures say in the first week 250 railway stations were damaged or destroyed, over 500 post offices and 150 police stations attacked.
    • The rulers used heavy violence to suppress it; Gandhi in 1942 refused to condemn the people's violence, calling it an answer to the rulers' huge violence.
    • Arrest of main leaders before the start (also printed as arrest of all major leaders on 8 August 1942) made the movement more aggressive and spontaneous.
    • Since Gandhiji was in jail, he did not actually get to lead the movement.
    • The movement did not attract the labour class in general (monetary constraints, fear of repression, effect of trade unions), unlike students and farmers.

    Note from the book The book marks two questions on "not true about Quit India Movement" as having no clear key: both "non-violent" and "led by Gandhi" are not correct; UPPSC accepted "Congress was declared an illegal body" as the answer.

    • After Gandhi's arrest, rioting broke out at once across the country with many violent demonstrations; thousands of freedom fighters were arrested.
    • Quit India (Bharat Chhodo Andolan; Gandhi gave the call on 8 August 1942) became the most powerful movement in the freedom struggle.
    • Riots from the movement were widest in Bihar and United Provinces, where it became a revolt.
    • Self-instilled centres of mass revolt: Azamgarh, Ballia, Gorakhpur (Eastern United Provinces); Gaya, Champaran, Saran, Purnia, Shahabad, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur (Bihar).
    • Police repression angered the public, who attacked police stations, railway stations and post offices; rail lines were uprooted and rail services totally disrupted.
    • Centres of public anger: Medinipur district (Bengal), Ballia district (Uttar Pradesh) and Munger district (Bihar).
    • Uprooting of railway tracks happened mostly in Bihar; Munger was the most affected district, cut off from the outside world for 2 weeks.
    • The movement spread among farmers; some groups farmed by day and rioted at night, showing glimpses of the Revolt of 1857.
    • Viceroy Linlithgow, in a telegram to PM Churchill, called it by far the most serious rebellion since the Revolt of 1857, because of the massive peasant upsurge.

    Officials of the time

    • Lord Wavell was Commander-in-Chief of the Indian Army during the Quit India Movement; later Viceroy and Governor-General, 1943-1947.UPPSC
    • Winston Churchill (1940-1945) was Prime Minister of England during the Quit India Movement.

    Who stayed away

    • Hindu Mahasabha, Communist Party of India, Unionist Party (Punjab) and Muslim League did not support the Quit India Movement.UPPSC
    • RSS kept away from the Quit India Movement; from 1940 to the end of foreign rule in 1947 it joined no national movement. It is false that RSS thought the movement would delay freedom.
    • Muslim League under Jinnah condemned the movement; Jinnah said lawlessness would capture India if the British left.
    • Jinnah acted as a staunch ally of the British and asked Muslims to stay away; so the British and Muslims came closer through shared hatred of Congress.UPPSC

    Underground leadership and Congress Radio

    • Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta, J.P. Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia gave alternate underground leadership when other leaders were arrested.
    • Leaders who escaped arrest organised the public secretly; main ones: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali.
    • A secret Congress Radio was broadcast from different parts of Bombay (also printed: different parts of India); it could be heard up to Madras.
    • Usha Mehta ran the secret Congress Radio; she was a key member of the small underground group that managed it.UPPSC
    • Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia broadcast regularly on Congress Radio; he directed the movement from underground and set up an underground radio station.UPPSC
    • Aruna Asaf Ali was a major woman organiser of underground activities in the Quit India Movement.UPPSC ×4
    • Aruna Asaf Ali is remembered for hoisting the tricolour (Congress flag) at Gowalia Tank ground, Bombay, in 1942; she was also an educator, political activist and publisher.
    • Jayaprakash Narayan gained recognition as a national leader during the Quit India Movement.
    • Jayaprakash Narayan escaped from the high-security Hazaribagh jail and organised underground activities.UPPSC
    • He escaped with his comrades on Diwali, 9 November 1942.
    • Yogendra Shukla escaped with J.P. Narayan on 9 November 1942, was later arrested at Muzaffarpur and sent to Patna (brought there on 7 December 1942).
    • All India Azad Dasta was formed by Jayaprakash Narayan at Bakri Ka Tapu in the Terai region of Nepal for guerrilla war against the British.

    Other participants and martyrs

    • Shri Krishna Singh, known as "Bihar Kesari", took active part in the movement; later first Chief Minister of Bihar.
    • Rampyari Devi, wife of Jagat Narayan Lal, addressed an assembly in Bankipur and called on people to quit government jobs.
    • Brothers Gangaram and Kheemdev were martyred in police firing at Almora in 1942 during the Quit India Movement.
    • In the Dictionary of Martyrs Vol. 2 they are named Gangadutt and Kheemananda.
    • Matangini Hazra, aged 73, fell to British bullets leading a protest march at Tamluk, Bengal, in 1942.
    • Kanaklata Barua was shot dead while leading a procession to hoist the national flag at the police station of Gohpur subdivision, Sonitpur district, Assam.
    • Kanaklata Barua: AISF leader; joined the Mrityu Bahini ("Death Army") of Gohpur youth; shot in September 1942 at about age 17 at Borangabari, Gohpur.
    • Shanti Ghosh was not linked to the Quit India Movement; she was a member of the revolutionary group Yugantar.UPPSC
    • On 14 December 1931 Shanti Ghosh and Suniti entered a District Magistrate's bungalow and shot him dead at point-blank range.

    Louis Fischer

    • Louis Fischer, American journalist and biographer of Gandhi, was with Gandhiji at the time of the Quit India Movement.UPPSC ×5
    • Fischer came to India in May 1942 and spent one week with Gandhiji at Sevagram Ashram, Wardha.
    • Fischer with American intellectuals Pearl Buck, Edgar Snow, Fredrick L. Schuman and Norman Thomas demanded India's independence.

    Parallel governments

    • Setting up of parallel governments at several places was an important feature of the movement.
    PlaceNamePeriodLeaders / work
    Ballia (Uttar Pradesh)Parallel governmentAugust 1942Led by Chittu PandeyUPPSC ×3
    Tamluk (Midnapore), BengalTamralipta Jatiya SarkarDecember 1942 to August 1944Ran relief programmes for storm victimsUPPSC
    Satara (Maharashtra)Prati SarkarAugust 1943 to May 1946; longest-runningY.B. Chavan and Nana Patil
    Talcher (Orissa)Praja MandalFor some timeNot named
    • "Raiyati Sarkar — Kheda (Gujarat)" is not a correct match for a parallel government.

    Gandhi in jail and release

    • "Operation Rubicon" was the secret British code word to be used if Gandhiji died during his fast unto death in Aga Khan Palace.UPPSC
    • Gandhiji was released on 6 May 1944 because of bad health.
    • Churchill on Gandhi's release: "When we are winning around the globe, how can we be defeated by this old man who is our enemy for a long time."

    Significance and after

    • The movement, though short-lived and badly crushed, showed British rule was not wanted; it was the culmination of the national movement.UPPSC
    • People's firm determination hastened the British decision to quit; a mechanism for transfer of power now had to be found.
    • C. Rajagopalachari's pamphlet "The Way Out" (1944) proposed a solution to the constitutional deadlock between Congress and Muslim League.
    • The Rajagopalachari formula: Congress to offer the League a Muslim Pakistan based on plebiscite.
    • Plebiscite = direct vote of all members of an electorate on an important public question, such as a change in the Constitution.
    • The formula was opposed even by Congress; Jinnah rejected it and the talks failed.

    Chapter 86 · Freedom struggle

    Subhas Chandra Bose and Azad Hind Fauj

    80 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Advocates on the Committee: Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Kailash Nath Katju, Asaf Ali and Jawaharlal Nehru.×3
    2. After the Tripuri crisis he resigned as Congress President and founded the Forward Bloc in 1939.×2
    3. Rabindranath Tagore gave Bose the title "Desh Nayak" (National Leader) in 1938 at Shantiniketan, after Bose became Congress President.×2
    4. Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, the women's regiment of the INA, in 1943.×2
    5. INA officers were court-martialled at the Red Fort, Delhi, in November 1945.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 23 UPPSC questions

    Life of Subhas Chandra Bose

    • Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was born on 23 January 1897 at Cuttack, Orissa (Odisha) division of Bengal province.UPPSC
    • He graduated from Scottish Church College (affiliated to University of Calcutta) in 1919 and passed the Indian Civil Services exam in 1920.
    • C.R. Das was the political guru of Subhas Chandra Bose.UPPSC
    • Bose presided over the 51st Congress session at Haripura (Gujarat) in 1938 and the 52nd at Tripuri (Madhya Pradesh) in 1939; he later resigned.
    • After the Tripuri crisis he resigned as Congress President and founded the Forward Bloc in 1939.UPPSC ×2
    • Sheel Bhadra Yajee, freedom fighter from Bihar linked with Gandhi and Bose, joined Bose to found the All India Forward Bloc and was active in the INA movement.
    • Rabindranath Tagore gave Bose the title "Desh Nayak" (National Leader) in 1938 at Shantiniketan, after Bose became Congress President.UPPSC ×2
    • Mahatma Gandhi called Bose "Patriot of Patriots".

    Bose in Germany

    • Bose escaped at night from house arrest in January 1941 in disguise and left Calcutta; the 1938 session he presided was Haripura, not Tripuri.

    Note from the book The book notes that in the English version of that question "Provincial" was printed for "Provisional", so the Bihar Public Service Commission removed it from evaluation.

    • Bose reached Germany on 3 April 1941.
    • The honorific "Netaji" was given to Bose in Germany.
    • Six months later, with German government help, he founded the "Free India Centre"; there he printed pamphlets for India's independence and gave many speeches.
    • Adolf Hitler approved it and in late 1941 allowed Bose to organise an army for the independence war.
    • Bose raised "The Free Indian Legion" from 10,000 Indian prisoners of war of General Erwin Rommel's North Africa battles.

    Origin of the Indian National Army

    • In December 1941, in the Malay forests, the Punjab battalion led by Captain Mohan Singh was defeated by the Japanese army.
    • Lt. Colonel L.V. Fitz Patrick (English origin) was a prisoner of war; Bangkok-resident Indian Giani Pritam Singh took their responsibility.
    • Giani Pritam Singh built friendship between the Japanese and Mohan Singh with other Indian soldiers.
    • Giani Pritam Singh Dhillon was active in the Indian Independence Movement and the Gadar Party.
    • He and Iwaichi Fujiwara reached an agreement of collaboration at Bangkok in December 1941, even before Japan declared war.
    • The plans began long before the war among a group of revolutionaries based in Bangkok.
    • It was Giani Pritam Singh's idea, with Fujiwara, to release Indian soldiers and ask them to join an Indian National Army.
    • The INA was the brainchild of Giani Pritam Singh and Japanese Major Iwaichi Fujiwara (along with Mohan Singh).UPPSC
    • Where Giani Pritam Singh and Fujiwara are not named, the idea and founding of the INA is credited to Captain Mohan Singh.UPPSC
    • Mohan Singh was a British Indian Army officer; when the British Army retreated before Japan he joined hands with the Japanese.
    • The Japanese handed Indian soldiers to Mohan Singh and he recruited them into the Azad Hind Fauj.
    • Mohan Singh agreed in December 1941 to lead the army, at the insistence of Giani Pritam Singh and Fujiwara.
    • The Indian National Army was founded in 1942 (February 1942) under Mohan Singh, from defeated Indian soldiers of the British Army's Malay expedition.UPPSC
    • Another date given for the INA's formation under Mohan Singh: 15 July 1942.
    • Azad Hind Fauj (INA) was officially constituted in September 1942.
    • Captain Mohan Singh was the first Commander of the INA.UPPSC
    • One explanation says Mohan Singh was not the founder but only the first operational Commander of the INA.
    • The first INA was dissolved in December 1942 after doubts about Japanese motives caused distrust between Mohan Singh and the League leadership, notably Rash Behari Bose.
    • Many of the first INA's volunteers later joined the second INA under Subhas Chandra Bose.
    • The INA was first formed in the Second World War with Japan's support; Captain Mohan Singh and Rash Behari Bose had key roles in its early organisation.

    Bose takes over the INA

    1. 1942Singapore was under Japanese occupation 1942-1945; it became part of Malaysia in 1963.
    2. 1943Bose gained control of the Azad Hind Fauj in 1943; he is remembered as Netaji.
    3. 1943Subhas Chandra Bose reached Tokyo in June 1943 and arrived in Singapore on 2 July 1943.
    4. 1943Rash Behari Bose offered to resign as President and gave command of the INA to Subhas Bose on 4 July 1943; Subhas Bose became Supreme Commander.UPPSC
    5. 1943In October 1943 in Singapore, Bose named the Indian Independence League as Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj).
    6. 1943Singapore island was then part of British Malaya, so the Azad Hind Fauj of 1943 was set up in Malaya.
    7. 1965On 9 August 1965 the Malaysian Parliament separated Singapore from Malaysia by an agreement; Singapore became a free country that day.
    • Bose gained control of the Azad Hind Fauj in 1943; he is remembered as Netaji.
    • Subhas Chandra Bose reached Tokyo in June 1943 and arrived in Singapore on 2 July 1943.
    • Rash Behari Bose offered to resign as President and gave command of the INA to Subhas Bose on 4 July 1943; Subhas Bose became Supreme Commander.UPPSC
    • On 26 August 1943 Bose officially took charge of the INA and renamed it Azad Hind Fauj.
    • Bose took command of the INA, reorganised it and gave the battle cry "Chalo Delhi / Delhi Chalo".
    • In October 1943 in Singapore, Bose named the Indian Independence League as Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj).
    • Singapore island was then part of British Malaya, so the Azad Hind Fauj of 1943 was set up in Malaya.
    • Singapore was under Japanese occupation 1942-1945; it became part of Malaysia in 1963.
    • On 9 August 1965 the Malaysian Parliament separated Singapore from Malaysia by an agreement; Singapore became a free country that day.
    • Head office of the Azad Hind Fauj was at Rangoon (Yangon).

    Provisional Government of Free India

    • On 21 October 1943 Bose proclaimed the Provisional Government of Free India (Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind, Azad Hind Sarkar) at Singapore.UPPSC
    • It was recognised by 9 countries including Japan.
    • The nine: Japan, Germany, Italy, Thailand, Burma (Japanese controlled), Philippines (Japanese-sponsored Second Philippine Republic), Manchukuo (Japanese puppet state in Manchuria), Independent State of Croatia, Japanese-controlled government in China.
    • Indonesia did not recognise the Azad Hind Government.UPPSC
    • After freeing the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from the British, Bose hoisted his flag there and named Andaman "Shaheed" and Nicobar "Swaraj" Island.

    Regiments and slogans

    • Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, the women's regiment of the INA, in 1943.UPPSC ×2
    • It was named after Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi; it aimed to overthrow British rule with help from Imperial Japan.
    • Other INA units: Subhash Brigade, Nehru Brigade, Azad Brigade and Gandhi Brigade.
    • In Burma (Myanmar) Bose told his soldiers: "Give me blood and I promise you freedom" (Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga).
    • From the same speech: "It is blood alone that can avenge the blood that the enemy has spilt. It is blood alone that can pay the price of freedom."
    • Bose also said the ultimate sacrifice of life remained and that priests ready to give their lives to the Goddess of freedom were needed.
    • The slogan "Jai Hind" was given by S.C. Bose; it was the greeting/salute of the Azad Hind Fauj and is now the nation's slogan.UPPSC
    • "Jai Hind" was suggested by Abid Hasan, Bose's secretary, and formally adopted as the greeting in the Azad Hind Fauj.

    People linked and not linked with the INA

    • Associated with Azad Hind Fauj: Major General Shahnawaz Khan, Colonel Prem Kumar Sahgal, Colonel Shaukat Ali Malik; Major Kartar Singh was not.UPPSC
    • S.A. Dange (Shripad Amrut Dange) was not linked with the INA; he belonged to the Communist Movement in India.
    • B.C. Dutta was not related to the INA.UPPSC
    • Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were officers of the Indian National Army tried in the Red Fort trial of 1945.

    INA trials at Red Fort

    • INA officers were court-martialled at the Red Fort, Delhi, in November 1945.UPPSC ×2
    • Azad Hind Fauj week was observed 5-11 November 1945 and Azad Hind Fauj Day on 12 November 1945.UPPSC
    • Colonel Prem Sahgal, Colonel Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon and Major General Shahnawaz Khan, prisoners of war in Singapore, faced a joint court-martial.
    • Charges: waging war against the King (treason), torture, murder, attempt to murder and abetment to murder during World War II.
    • Prem Sahgal, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon and Shah Nawaz were sentenced to transportation for life.
    • Abdul Rashid (Rashid Ali) was sentenced to 7 years imprisonment.UPPSC
    • Mohan Singh did not face the Red Fort trials.
    • Congress formed the INA Defence Committee; Bhulabhai Desai was its leader and the leading defence counsel.UPPSC
    • Advocates on the Committee: Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Kailash Nath Katju, Asaf Ali and Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC ×3
    • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel did not advocate in the INA Red Fort trial.UPPSC
    • Muslim League also joined the all-India agitation over the trials.
    • Countrywide protests and party pressure forced Commander-in-Chief Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck to commute the three life sentences and free the other INA soldiers.

    Dates of 1945-46 events

    • Main events of 1945: Wavell Plan, Shimla Conference and INA Trial; the Naval Mutiny was in 1946.
    EventDate
    Wavell Plan14 June 1945
    Shimla Conference25 June to 14 July 1945
    INA TrialNovember 1945
    Naval Mutiny18-23 February 1946

    Nehru and guerrilla war plan

    • At the Congress Working Committee meeting at Allahabad (Prayagraj; printed date April-May 1947), Jawaharlal Nehru got a majority for his plan of guerrilla war against the Japanese.
    • This rested on India's clear stand against Nazism, Fascism and imperialism, which Nehru opposed.

    Chapter 87 · Freedom struggle

    Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)

    37 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Its three members (cabinet ministers): Lord Pethick Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade) and A.V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty).×4
    2. The Mission was led (presided over) by Lord Pethick Lawrence, Secretary of State for India.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 10 UPPSC questions

    Sending and members of the Mission

    • After World War II the Labour Party under Attlee won elections in Britain; Attlee was sympathetic to India's demand for freedom.
    • Clement Attlee became British Prime Minister on 26 July 1945.
    • On 19 February 1946 Attlee announced the dispatch of the Cabinet Mission for constitutional reforms.
    • The Cabinet Mission arrived in Delhi on 24 March 1946, after the Second World War.UPPSC
    • The Mission was led (presided over) by Lord Pethick Lawrence, Secretary of State for India.UPPSC ×2
    • Its three members (cabinet ministers): Lord Pethick Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade) and A.V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty).UPPSC ×4
    • Not members: Wavell, Ramsay MacDonald, J. Andrew, Lord Emery, John Simon, William Wood.
    • Viceroy Lord Wavell did not take part in every step but was present.
    • John Simon's Simon Commission was set up to report on the Government of India Act, 1919.
    • The Mission was sent to work out a constitutional arrangement for the transfer of power; not to set up a national government, nor to work out Jinnah's Pakistan demand.
    • Its aim was to preserve India's unity and grant it independence.
    • It held extensive discussions in April with almost all major leaders of the country.

    Proposals of 16 May 1946

    • The Mission announced its recommendations on 16 May 1946; the plan for a united Dominion of India came to be known by this date.
    • It proposed a three-tier polity for India.UPPSC
    • It recommended a federal government: all India, including the Princely States, to form a Federation (Union of India). It did not enlarge powers of Indian courts or provide for more Indians in the ICS.
    • The Union (Centre) would handle only foreign affairs, defence and communications.
    • Provinces and states would enjoy all other powers.
    • The Muslim League's demand for Pakistan was rejected.
    • Parts of the plan: provincial grouping, interim cabinet of Indians, right to frame the Constitution.
    • The Union would have an Executive and Legislature made of representatives of British Indian Provinces and Princely States.
    • A Constituent Assembly would be formed from representatives of Provincial Legislative Assemblies, Chief Commissioners' Provinces and Princely States, to frame a Constitution for the Indian Union.
    • A province would have the right to leave the Union in future, after elections under its new Constitution.
    • It suggested reconstitution of the Viceroy's Executive Council and an interim government with all portfolios, including War Member, held by Indian leaders.

    Grouping of provinces

    • The major recommendation was to divide the provinces into three sections/groups: A, B and C.
    GroupProvinces
    AMadras, Central Provinces and Berar, United Provinces, Bihar, Bombay, Orissa; also Chief Commissioners' Provinces Delhi, Ajmer-Marwar and Coorg
    BPunjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh; also Baluchistan
    CBengal and Assam

    Reactions

    • Mahatma Gandhi was totally in favour of the Cabinet Mission Plan.UPPSC
    • Gandhi said: "It is the best document the British Government could have produced in the circumstances"; he cautioned that their best may possibly be harmful.
    • Congress accepted the proposals related to the Constituent Assembly.
    • Congress rejected the idea of the interim government because the Muslim League had been given disproportionate representation.
    • Muslim League first approved the Plan, then rejected it when Congress said it could change the scheme by majority in the Constituent Assembly.
    • Muslim League withdrew its acceptance in 1946 and also joined the Interim Government in 1946; both true, but the second does not explain the first.UPPSC
    • Muslim League joined the Interim Government on 13 October 1946 on repeated request of Lord Wavell.

    Maulana Azad

    • Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was Congress President when the Cabinet Mission came.UPPSC
    • Congress Working Committee authorised him to hold talks; he negotiated with the Mission members on 6 April 1946.
    • Azad, as Congress President (1940 to 1946), negotiated with both the Cripps Mission and Lord Wavell.
    ← Subhas Chandra Bose and Azad Hind FaujConstituent Assembly (1946) →

    Chapter 88 · Freedom struggle

    Constituent Assembly (1946)

    34 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Constituent Assembly that framed India's Constitution was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan.×3
    2. Each province got seats roughly at one seat per ten lakh (10 lakh) population, on a communal basis.×2
    Quick quiz: 7 of 7 UPPSC questions

    Growth of the idea

    • The earliest non-official draft of the Constituent Assembly idea was in the Swaraj Bill of 1895, shaped by Bal Gangadhar Tilak's directions.
    • In the 20th century Gandhiji first pointed to this idea in 1922, saying the Indian Constitution should be made as per India's need.
    • On 8 February 1924 Motilal Nehru moved the "National Demand" resolution in the Central Legislative Assembly.
    • It called for a round table conference to set up a constitution-making body; a pivotal early demand for a Constituent Assembly.
    • After this M.N. Roy proposed the demand; Jawaharlal Nehru restated its basic concepts.
    • The Swaraj Party demanded a Constituent Assembly at Ranchi in 1934.
    • Congress officially stated the idea at its Faizpur Session (December 1936), explaining it at length and stressing its importance.UPPSC

    Formation under the Cabinet Mission Plan

    • The Constituent Assembly that framed India's Constitution was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan.UPPSC ×3
    • The Cabinet Mission arrived at Delhi on 24 March 1946.
    • Secretary of State Pethick Lawrence said its aim was a plan to form a Constituent Assembly for free India's constitution and to arrange an interim government.
    • The Assembly was to be made of representatives of provincial legislative assemblies, Chief Commissioners' provinces and princely states.
    • Each province got seats roughly at one seat per ten lakh (10 lakh) population, on a communal basis.UPPSC ×2
    • Three voter groups: General, Muslims and Sikhs (Sikhs only in Punjab).
    • The Constituent Assembly was elected by the Provincial Assemblies in 1946; first-ever elections for it, for 296 British Indian province seats, completed by July 1946.
    • Results: Congress 208, Muslim League 73, others/independents 15.
    • Mohammad Ali Jinnah was not a member of the Constituent Assembly of India.
    • The National Executive of the Socialist Party (1946) called for dissolving the Constituent Assembly and re-electing it by universal adult suffrage.
    • Socialist leaders Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia argued that an Assembly indirectly elected by Provincial Legislatures did not properly represent common Indians.

    Meetings and chairmen

    • The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946.UPPSC
    • Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was its first provisional (temporary) Chairman.
    • Sachchidananda Sinha was associated with the Quit India Movement.
    • On 11 December 1946, at Delhi, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent Chairman (President) of the Constituent Assembly.UPPSC
    • At its formation the Constituent Assembly was not a sovereign body.
    • At midnight of 14 August 1947 (15 August 1947) it was declared sovereign for the Dominion of India, with Rajendra Prasad as its President.UPPSC
    • The Constituent Assembly was the first Parliament of independent India.
    • Rajendra Prasad later became the first President of India.
    • The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949.

    Committee heads

    PersonCommittee headed
    Dr. B.R. AmbedkarDrafting Committee
    Jawaharlal NehruUnion Powers Committee, Union Constitution Committee
    Vallabhbhai PatelAdvisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Tribal and Excluded Areas

    G.V. Mavalankar

    • G.V. Mavalankar was Speaker of both the Central Legislative Assembly (British era) and the Lok Sabha of free India.
    • Speaker of Central Legislative Assembly: 24 January 1946 to 14 August 1947.
    • First Speaker of Lok Sabha after independence: 1952 to 1956.
    • Speaker (President) of Bombay Legislative Assembly: 1937 to 1946.

    Chapter 89 · Freedom struggle

    Formation of Interim Government (1946)

    31 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Muslim League observed Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946.×3
    2. The first Interim Government was announced on 24 August 1946 and formed (took office) on 2 September 1946.×2
    Quick quiz: 7 of 7 UPPSC questions

    Formation

    • On 12 August 1946 Lord Wavell invited Congress President Jawaharlal Nehru to form the Interim Government.
    • Jawaharlal Nehru headed the Interim Government (Cabinet) formed in 1946.
    • The first Interim Government was announced on 24 August 1946 and formed (took office) on 2 September 1946.UPPSC ×2
    • It was formed from the newly elected Constituent Assembly as per the Cabinet Mission Plan.
    • Muslim League did not join at first; it boycotted the government set up on 2 September 1946.

    Ministers and portfolios

    • The Interim Government had twelve ministers (out of a planned 14).
    • The twelve: Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Asaf Ali, C. Rajagopalachari, Sarat Chandra Bose, Dr. John Mathai, Sardar Baldev Singh, Sir Shafat Ahmed Khan, Jagjivan Ram, Syed Ali Zaheer, C.H. Bhabha.
    MinisterPortfolio

    Sardar Vallabhbhai PatelHome, Information and Broadcasting, princely states portfolio
    Dr. Rajendra PrasadFood and Agriculture
    Baldev SinghDefence
    Asaf AliCommunication: Railways and TransportUPPSC
    Jagjivan RamLabour
    Liaquat Ali KhanFinanceUPPSC
    Joginder Nath MandalLaw
    • B.R. Ambedkar was not a member of the Interim Cabinet.UPPSC
    • Abul Kalam Azad was not a member of this Interim Government; Liaquat Ali Khan too was not a minister on 2 September 1946.UPPSC

    Muslim League joins

    • After a series of meetings between Jinnah and Lord Wavell, and Wavell's repeated requests, the League decided to join on 13 October 1946.
    • Five League members joined the Interim Government in October 1946; the League nominees joined on 26 October 1946.
    • Three earlier ministers resigned to make room for them: Syed Ali Zaheer, Sarat Chandra Bose and Sir Shafat Ahmed Khan.
    • Members after the League joined: Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Ibrahim Ismail Chundrigar, C. Rajagopalachari, Baldev Singh, Liaquat Ali Khan, Ghazanfar Ali Khan, Jagjivan Ram, Abdur Rab Nishtar, Asaf Ali, C.H. Bhabha.
    • As Finance Minister, Liaquat Ali Khan in his budget imposed several high taxes on traders, businessmen and industrialists.

    Bengal ministry

    • After the 1946 elections the Muslim League formed its government in Bengal.
    • The Krishak Praja Party under A.K. Fazlul Haq joined hands with the League in a coalition; later a Muslim League cabinet was formed, which ruled till 14 August 1947.
    • H.S. Suhrawardy was the League leader in Bengal and Prime Minister of the province.

    Direct Action Day

    • Muslim League observed Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946.UPPSC ×3
    • The League rejected the Viceroy's interim cabinet decision and demanded a separate Pakistan.
    • By riots that day it wanted to show that Hindus and Muslims could not live together in one country.
    • Calcutta was the main centre of these riots; the Noakhali riots began later, in October 1946.
    • One explanation names Noakhali as the centre of riots during the action.
    • The League had formally demanded a separate Muslim state in the Pakistan (Lahore) Resolution on 23 March 1940 at its Lahore general session.
