    Chapter 90 · Freedom struggle

    Partition of India and Independence

    88 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Britain freed India in 1947 because Britain had become weak during the Second World War.×3
    2. It was the formula/basis for the transfer of power (sovereignty) and partition of the country; the platform of Indian independence.×3
    3. J.B. Kripalani was Congress President then, at partition and at the transfer of power on 15 August 1947.×3
    4. The Bill received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947, the date the Act came into force.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 26 UPPSC questions

    Attlee's declaration

    • Clement Richard Attlee was Prime Minister of Britain when India became independent; he was PM from 1945 to 1951.
    • Attlee belonged to the Labour Party, which was in power in the U.K. at India's independence.UPPSC
    • George VI was the British monarch at Indian independence; king of the United Kingdom from 1936 until his death in 1952.
    • On 20 February 1947 Attlee declared in the House of Commons that the British would leave India by a date before (30) June 1948, after transferring power.
    • Attlee also said that if a constitutional decision was not reached in time, the British could transfer the government to any of them.
    • Britain freed India in 1947 because Britain had become weak during the Second World War.UPPSC ×3
    • People of various castes, religions, organisations and parties contributed to independence.

    Mountbatten as Viceroy

    • Attlee made Lord Mountbatten Viceroy in place of Wavell; he took charge on 24 March 1947 with vast powers and a mandate to oversee the British withdrawal, and began the transfer of power.
    • Mountbatten was the last British Viceroy and Governor-General of India (1947-48).
    • His specific instruction was to keep India united if possible.
    • He was to transfer power in the way best for India's future happiness and prosperity, decide by Indian conditions, and let Britain leave with honour and least damage.
    • From 133 recorded talks with Indian politicians between 24 March and 6 May 1947 he concluded that the Cabinet Mission Plan was impractical.
    • He then prepared a substitute plan called "Plan Balkan"; the Balkan Plan was Mountbatten's brainchild.
    • Plan Balkan: separate dominions for Pakistan, the Princely States and the rest of British India, with certain key areas run by a Central Government.
    • He saw that power could not be passed to one central assembly, as Congress and Muslim League could not agree on terms.
    • Mountbatten concluded a united India was unachievable and that partition and the formation of Pakistan were a must.

    Gandhi and partition

    • Gandhi first met Mountbatten on 31 March 1947.
    • As an alternative to partition, Gandhi suggested inviting Jinnah to form the government (hand over the Interim Government to him as Prime Minister), so that communal riots would stop.
    • Congress leaders and the Congress Working Committee did not accept this suggestion.
    • Gandhi said: "If Congress wishes to accept partition it will be over my dead body"; he would never support partition till his last breath.
    • Gandhi told his attendants: "Today I find myself all alone"; even Sardar and Jawaharlal thought he was wrong and that peace would return if partition was agreed.
    • Gandhi said the future of independence gained at this price was going to be dark.
    • Gandhi said: "Let it not be said that Gandhi was party to Indian vivisection."
    • Though opposed in principle, Gandhi accepted the partition resolution at the AICC meeting of 14-15 June 1947 and urged Congress to accept it to avoid more communal bloodshed.

    Mountbatten Plan, 3 June 1947

    • The Mountbatten Plan for partition was officially declared on 3 June 1947.
    • It was the formula/basis for the transfer of power (sovereignty) and partition of the country; the platform of Indian independence.UPPSC ×3
    • Mountbatten prepared it keeping Attlee's instructions in mind; the prevailing communal violence led him to announce it.
    • He fixed 15 August 1947 as the date for transfer of power.
    • The plan provided for immediate transfer of power on the basis of Dominion Status.
    • Punjab and Bengal Legislative Assemblies would meet in two groups, Hindus and Muslims, to vote on partition; a simple majority of either group meant partition.
    • Sindh would take its own decision.
    • Referendum in NWFP, Sindh, Baluchistan and Sylhet district of Assam would decide the fate of these areas.
    • Since Congress had conceded a unified India, its other points were met: no independence for princely states (they must join India or Pakistan).
    • Also ruled out: independence for Bengal, and accession of Hyderabad to Pakistan (Mountbatten backed Congress on this).
    • Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Patel represented Congress in the Partition Council headed by Lord Mountbatten.UPPSC
    • The last chance to avoid partition was lost with the rejection of the Cabinet Mission plan.
    • The Cabinet Mission plan of 16 May 1946 meant a united India with autonomous Muslim and Hindu majority provinces, rejecting Pakistan.
    • Muslim League approved that plan on 6 June 1946, rejected it on 29 July, and called Muslims to "Direct Action" for Pakistan; 16 August 1946 was fixed as Direct Action Day.

    Congress accepts partition

    • Congress agreed to partition in 1947 mainly to avoid large-scale communal riots; it accepted the Mountbatten Plan but never accepted the Two-Nation Theory.UPPSC
    • The AICC at Delhi accepted the partition proposal on 14-15 June 1947 (both dates are found).
    • J.B. Kripalani was Congress President then, at partition and at the transfer of power on 15 August 1947.UPPSC ×3
    • Kripalani became Congress President at the Meerut Session, 1946; he held the post from 23 November 1946 to November 1947.UPPSC
    • The partition resolution was moved by Govind Ballabh Pant and seconded by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad; also supported by Sardar Patel and Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Frontier Gandhi) voted against partition at this meeting.UPPSC
    • Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew called the resolution a "surrender of nationalism in favour of communalism".UPPSC
    • Kitchlew was President of the Punjab Provincial Congress Committee and strongly opposed partition; after independence he left Congress and joined the Communist Party of India.

    Congress Presidents after Kripalani

    YearSessionCongress President
    November 1947Kripalani resignedDr. Rajendra Prasad (interim)
    1948JaipurPattabhi Sitaramayya
    1950NasikPurushottam Das Tandon

    Indian Independence Act 1947

    • The Indian Independence Act, 1947 provided for partition into two new dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947.
    • It implemented the Mountbatten Plan; the British Government gave the plan formal approval through this Act.
    • The British Parliament passed the Act in July 1947.UPPSC
    • Attlee presented the Bill in the House of Commons on 4 July 1947; Commons passed it on 15 July 1947 and the Lords the next day.
    • The Bill received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947, the date the Act came into force.UPPSC ×2
    • Under the Act the British Government kept no control over either dominion from 15 August 1947.
    • British sovereignty did not continue in free India; but the British sovereign did appoint the last Governor-General of free India.

    Boundary Commissions

    • Mountbatten formed the Punjab Boundary Commission and Bengal Boundary Commission on 30 June 1947.
    • British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe was chairman of both; their task was to demarcate the boundaries between India and Pakistan.UPPSC
    • They were to mark boundaries in Punjab and Bengal on the basis of contiguous Muslim and non-Muslim majority areas, also weighing other factors.
    • Each commission had four members (judges): two from Congress and two from the Muslim League.
    • The Radcliffe Line became the India-Pakistan border when the Award was published on 17 August 1947, two days after partition.

    Midnight of 14-15 August 1947

    • At midnight of 14/15 August 1947 the Constituent Assembly, as Provisional Parliament, assumed sovereign power to govern the country.
    • Under the Act the existing Central Legislature ceased; the Constituent Assembly, mainly a constitution-making body, also became the Dominion Legislature.
    • To avoid confusion the two functions were separated; the Constituent Assembly (Legislative) began work from 17 November 1947.
    • A special session of the Constituent Assembly was held in New Delhi at midnight; Nehru, as first Prime Minister, gave a historic, inspiring speech.
    • Sucheta Kripalani sang "Vande Mataram", "Jan-Gan-Man" and Iqbal's "Sare Jahan Se Achha Hindustan Hamara" there.UPPSC
    • Mahatma Gandhi took no part in Independence Day celebrations on 15 August 1947; saddened by partition, he spent the day fasting and in prayer.UPPSC

    First office-holders

    • The Governor-General, Lord Mountbatten, appointed Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister of India.UPPSC
    • Lord Mountbatten (1947-48) was the first Governor-General of independent India.UPPSC
    • C. Rajagopalachari (1948-50) was the first and last Indian Governor-General, and the last Governor-General of independent India.UPPSC
    • Rajagopalachari held the post until 26 January 1950; he was Chief Minister of Madras 1952-54.
    • In 1959 he left Congress over differences and formed the Swatantra Party.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the first Law Minister of free India, on Mahatma Gandhi's recommendation; he chaired the Drafting Committee.UPPSC
    OrderPresident of IndiaTerm
    FirstDr. Rajendra Prasad1950-1962UPPSC
    SecondSarvapalli Radhakrishnan1962-1967
    ThirdZakir Hussain1967-1969
    FourthV.V. Giri1969-1974

    Constitution and Republic Day

    • The Constitution was ready on 26 November 1949; provisions like Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60 and 324 came into force from that date.
    • It was enforced on 26 January 1950 because Congress had celebrated 26 January 1930 as the first Independence Day.
    • 26 January was declared Republic Day.
    • At the 1929 Lahore session Congress adopted Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) as its goal.
    • At midnight of 31 December 1929 the tricolour was unfurled on the banks of the river Ravi.
    • 26 January 1930 was marked as the first Independence Day, to be celebrated every year.

    Sayings on British rule and Saurashtra Sangh

    • R. Coupland said: "Indian nationalism was the child of the British Raj, and the British authorities blessed its cradle."UPPSC
    • But Coupland forgot that Indian nationalism was an unwanted (involuntary) child, denied milk in childhood and then choked (throttled).
    • K.M. Panikkar said the greatest achievement of British rule was the unity (unification) of India.UPPSC
    • Saurashtra Sangh was formed on 15 February 1948 by merging 222 principalities: 217 of Kathiawar Agency and 5 others.

    Chapter 91 · Freedom struggle

    Constitutional Development of India

    132 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly of India trade, except trade in tea and trade with China.×2
    2. The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the Government of India from the East India Company to the Crown, which now ruled India directly.×2
    3. The Indian Councils Act, 1861 empowered the Governor-General to issue ordinances in an emergency; valid for at most 6 months.×2
    4. High Courts at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were set up under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (established in 1862).×2
    5. Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 31 UPPSC questions

    Regulating Act 1773

    • The British Parliament passed the Regulating Act in 1773 to curb rampant corruption and misgovernance.
    • Its aim: put the East India Company's activities in India (territories mainly in Bengal) under the supervision of the British Government.
    • Madras and Bombay Presidencies came under the Calcutta Presidency; the Governor-General of Fort William got supervisory powers over them.
    • The Act first provided for the post of Governor-General of Bengal (the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General).UPPSC
    • Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor-General of Bengal.
    • The Governor-General had a Council of four, who could vote but had no veto.
    • The Act required the Company's directors to present to the British Government all correspondence and documents on the Company's administration.
    • The Regulating Act set up India's first Supreme Court, at Fort William, Calcutta, with a Chief Justice and three other (puisne) judges.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court came into being in 1774; Sir Elijah Impey was its first Chief Justice.
    • Its other judges: Robert Chambers, Le Maistre and John Hyde.
    • It was the supreme judiciary over all British subjects, including in the provinces of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

    Pitt's India Act 1784 and Act of 1786

    • Pitt's India Act, 1784 set up the Board of Control in Britain to fully regulate the affairs of the East India Company.UPPSC
    • The Act of 1786 gave the Governor-General (Cornwallis) power to overrule his Council in special cases.UPPSC
    • The special cases: matters of peace, defence or well-being of the Indian empire; he could override the Council's majority.
    • The 1786 bill was brought to persuade Cornwallis to accept the Governor-Generalship of Bengal; he wanted the powers of both Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief.

    Cornwallis Code 1793

    • Cornwallis's judicial reforms took final shape in 1793 in the Cornwallis Code, based on the principle of Separation of Powers.
    • Influenced by 18th-century French philosophers, he separated revenue administration from the administration of justice.
    • The Collector was head of the district revenue department and also had wide judicial and magisterial powers.
    • By the 1793 Regulation the Collector lost judicial and magisterial powers because Cornwallis was alarmed at such absolute power in one person.
    • Cornwallis's reasoning: a Collector sitting as judge of the Diwani Adalat could not fairly redress wrongs he did as collector or assessor of revenue.
    • So neither landlords nor cultivators could see the Collector as an impartial judge in revenue cases.
    • A new officer, the District Judge, was created to preside over the District Civil Court, with magisterial and police functions.

    Charter Act 1813

    • The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly of India trade, except trade in tea and trade with China.UPPSC ×2
    • For the next 20 years the Company kept control of the revenue of British territorial acquisitions in India.
    • The Act asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories in India.
    • It allowed Christian missionaries to come to India.UPPSC
    • It made the Company responsible for Indians' education, with an annual grant of 1 lakh rupees for promoting education.UPPSC

    Charter Act 1833

    • The Charter Act of 1833 ended all the Company's commercial privileges, including the tea trade and China trade monopoly.UPPSC
    • The Company ceased to be a mercantile body and kept only political/administrative work on behalf of the Crown.
    • The charter was renewed on condition that the Company give up trade entirely and let Europeans settle freely in India.
    • The Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India by this Act.
    • All financial, administrative and law-making powers were centralised in the Governor-General-in-Council.
    • A Law Member was added as the 4th member of the Governor-General's executive council.
    • The Law Member was to be British (not an Indian) and not from the Company; he could act only for legislative purposes, without sitting or voting in executive meetings.
    • Lord Macaulay was the first Law Member.
    • In 1834 almost all of present Uttar Pradesh was separated from Bengal Presidency to form the North-Western Provinces under Agra Presidency.UPPSC
    • The Company had acquired this area gradually from the last quarter of the 18th century to the mid-19th century.

    Note from the book The question on abolition of the monopoly on trading of "tea and sugar" was treated as wrong by MPPSC, with bonus marks; had it said "sugar and China" in place of "sugar and tea", Charter Act 1833 would be the answer.

    Charter Act 1853

    • The Charter Act of 1853 opened civil service recruitment to competitive examination, without discrimination (as in the 1833 Act's clause).
    • The Court of Directors lost its right of patronage.
    • A Committee with Macaulay was formed in 1854 to give effect to recruitment by competition.
    • Salaries of Board of Control members, its Secretary and officers were to be fixed by the Crown but paid from Company funds.
    • Directors were reduced from 24 to 18, of whom 6 were to be nominated by the Crown.
    • The 1853 Act for the first time created a functioning Legislative Council in India, with 12 members.UPPSC
    • It was a decisive step in separating the Executive and the Legislature.

    Government of India Act 1858

    • The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the Government of India from the East India Company to the Crown, which now ruled India directly.UPPSC ×2
    • Powers of the Board of Control and Court of Directors passed to the Secretary of State for India.
    • The Secretary of State was a member of the British Parliament, responsible to it, and assisted by the Council of India.
    • The Council of India had 15 members: 8 appointed by the Crown and 7 elected by the Court of Directors.

    Indian Councils Act 1861

    • The Indian Councils Act, 1861 empowered the Governor-General to issue ordinances in an emergency; valid for at most 6 months.UPPSC ×2
    • The Act strengthened the Viceroy's authority by replacing corporate functioning with the portfolio (departmental) system.
    • Lord Canning started the portfolio system: each department was given to one council member; this laid the base of ministerial government in India.
    • The Viceroy's council was expanded for law-making with additional members: minimum 6, maximum 12.
    • They were nominated by the Viceroy for two years; at least half had to be non-officials.
    • By the 1861 Act the Viceroy's executive council was given law-making powers.
    • Madras and Bombay Presidencies got back their law-making power and could amend existing law, but their laws needed the Governor-General's assent.
    • High Courts at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were set up under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (established in 1862).UPPSC ×2

    Indian Councils Act 1892

    • The Indian Councils Act, 1892 let council members discuss the budget, without the right to vote on it or move amendments.UPPSC
    • Members could ask questions on matters of public interest after six days' notice; no supplementary questions.
    • The principle of representation and indirect election was first brought in by the 1892 Act.UPPSC

    Press Acts

    • Acts to control the press were passed in 1835, 1867, 1878 and 1908.
    YearActDetail
    1835Press ActFor censorship of media
    1867Press and Registration of Books ActNot given
    1878Vernacular Press ActBy Lord Lytton; to control printing and circulation of seditious material
    1908Press Act of Lord MintoGovernment could seize any anti-government publication

    Indian Councils Act 1909

    • The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced communal representation: separate electorates for Muslims.
    • Lord Minto is known as the Father of Communal Electorate in India.
    • The 1909 Act was the most short-lived of Britain's constitutional experiments in India.
    • Ramsay MacDonald called it an incomplete and short-term deal between democracy and bureaucracy.

    Montagu Declaration and the 1919 Act

    1. 1917The reforms declaration of 20 August 1917 is called the Montagu Declaration, after Secretary of State Edwin Montagu.
    2. 1918The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), by Secretary of State Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford, became the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919.
    3. 1919David Lloyd George was Prime Minister of England when the 1919 Act (Montagu-Chelmsford Act, also printed as Indian Councils Act, 1919) was passed; his tenure was 1916 to 1922.
    4. 1919The 1919 Act is not called the Morley-Minto Reforms Act; it is the Montagu-Chelmsford (Mont-ford) Reforms.
    5. 1919The Government of India Act 1919 came into force in 1921.
    6. 1919The 1919 Act classified central and provincial subjects, clearly defining the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial Governments.
    7. 1919Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919.UPPSC ×2
    8. 1919Under the 1919 Act much authority went to the provinces; governance was generally federal in structure, not unitary, though the Governor-General had major executive powers.UPPSC
    9. 1919The post of Indian High Commissioner was created by the Government of India Act, 1919.
    10. 1919Part V of the 1919 Act provided for a statutory Commission after 10 years to review the system; the Simon Commission of 1927 came from this.
    11. 1919Central Legislative Assembly elections under the 1919 Act were held in 1923, 1926, 1930, 1934 and 1945 (the last).
    12. 1937The provincial assembly elections of 1937 were held under the Government of India Act 1935.
    • The reforms declaration of 20 August 1917 is called the Montagu Declaration, after Secretary of State Edwin Montagu.
    • The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), by Secretary of State Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford, became the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919.
    • The Montagu-Chelmsford proposals concerned constitutional reforms, to bring in self-governing institutions gradually.
    • David Lloyd George was Prime Minister of England when the 1919 Act (Montagu-Chelmsford Act, also printed as Indian Councils Act, 1919) was passed; his tenure was 1916 to 1922.
    • The 1919 Act is not called the Morley-Minto Reforms Act; it is the Montagu-Chelmsford (Mont-ford) Reforms.
    • The Government of India Act 1919 came into force in 1921.
    • The 1919 Act classified central and provincial subjects, clearly defining the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial Governments.
    • Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919.UPPSC ×2
    • Dyarchy = provincial subjects divided into two categories, Reserved and Transferred; a dual government brought in for responsible government in provinces.UPPSC
    • Reserved subjects (Finance, Law and order, Army, Police) stayed with the Governor and his executive council.
    • Transferred subjects (Public health, education, agriculture, Local Self-Government) went to ministers responsible to the Provincial Legislature.
    • Sir Lionel Curtis is known as the father of Dyarchy.
    • Under the 1919 Act much authority went to the provinces; governance was generally federal in structure, not unitary, though the Governor-General had major executive powers.UPPSC
    • 50 subjects were given to Provinces: Education, Local Self-Government, Medical Relief, Public Health and Sanitation, Agriculture, Cooperative Societies, Public Works, Excise, Justice, Police, Irrigation and Waterways, Labour, Welfare and Industrial Disputes and others.
    • The Central Legislature had 47 subjects, such as Defence, Foreign Affairs, Money and Communication.
    • The post of Indian High Commissioner was created by the Government of India Act, 1919.
    • Part V of the 1919 Act provided for a statutory Commission after 10 years to review the system; the Simon Commission of 1927 came from this.
    • Central Legislative Assembly elections under the 1919 Act were held in 1923, 1926, 1930, 1934 and 1945 (the last).
    • The provincial assembly elections of 1937 were held under the Government of India Act 1935.

    Civil Services

    1. 1887The Aitchison Commission report (1887) opposed holding the Indian Civil Service exam in India and England together.
    2. 1919The Government of India Act 1919 was the basis for the separate ICS exam in India from 1922; on 1 January 1941 Indians (617) outnumbered Europeans (585) in the ICS.UPPSC
    3. 1922The ICS exam was held simultaneously in India and England from 1922.UPPSC
    4. 1924The Lee Commission (1924) recommended an independent, impartial Public Service Commission; it was set up in 1926.
    5. 1935The 1935 Act set up separate Public Service Commissions for central and provincial services; the central one became the Federal Public Service Commission (set up 1 April 1937).
    6. 1937From 1937 the Federal Public Service Commission and the Civil Service Commission (UK) held their exams separately.
    7. 1950In 1950, after the Constitution, the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed Union Public Service Commission.
    • The Aitchison Commission report (1887) opposed holding the Indian Civil Service exam in India and England together.
    • The Montagu-Chelmsford Report recommended more Indians in administration and a simultaneous ICS exam in India and England.UPPSC
    • It also proposed that at least one-third of posts be held by Indians.
    • The ICS exam was held simultaneously in India and England from 1922.UPPSC
    • The Government of India Act 1919 was the basis for the separate ICS exam in India from 1922; on 1 January 1941 Indians (617) outnumbered Europeans (585) in the ICS.UPPSC
    • The Lee Commission (1924) recommended an independent, impartial Public Service Commission; it was set up in 1926.
    • The 1935 Act set up separate Public Service Commissions for central and provincial services; the central one became the Federal Public Service Commission (set up 1 April 1937).
    • From 1937 the Federal Public Service Commission and the Civil Service Commission (UK) held their exams separately.
    • In 1950, after the Constitution, the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed Union Public Service Commission.

    Government of India Act 1935

    • The Simon Commission Report was the baseline of the Government of India Act, 1935.UPPSC
    • Chain: Nehru Report of the All-Party Conference; Simon Commission Report; three Round Table Conferences (1930-1932); White Paper of 1933; Joint Select Committee of British Parliament; then the Act.
    • The Act was passed in August 1935 and received Royal Assent on 2 August 1935.
    • It was the longest and most elaborate, most complex British enactment for India: 14 parts, 321 sections and 10 schedules.
    • It provided for an All-India Federation of British India and princely states and a Federal Legislature.UPPSC
    • It introduced Provincial Autonomy: provinces got more independence in certain administrative areas, though the Governor still held significant powers.
    • It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced dyarchy at the Centre; the reserved/transferred distinction in provinces ended.
    • Governors could veto legislative action and legislate on their own; communal representation was not abolished.
    • It established a Federal Court, with provincial autonomy and an All-India Federation at the Centre.
    • Other provisions: bicameral central legislature, system of provincial government, Provincial Legislative Assemblies, division of powers between Centre and provinces, direct elections.
    • Provincial assembly membership was altered to include more elected Indian representatives.
    • The Governor-General's Executive Council was restructured with more Indian members, but he kept ultimate authority; the Act had no provision for its own appraisal.
    • Reserved seats under joint electorate were expanded to include Scheduled Castes, Muslims, Sikhs, Europeans, Anglo-Indians and Indian Christians.
    • Residuary powers in the Federation were given to the Governor-General.
    • The India Council was abolished by the Government of India Act 1935.UPPSC
    • With dyarchy started at the central level, subjects were divided into Reserved and Transferred; provinces got more autonomy.
    • The 1935 Act introduced the "Principle of Constitutional Autocracy".
    • The 1935 Act is a main source of the Indian Constitution; the present Constitution is very similar to it.UPPSC
    • Its "Instrument of Instructions" became the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution in 1950; critics called that part holy phrases.

    Federal scheme and the princes

    • The real British aim in including Princely States in the Federation was to use the princes to counter-balance the anti-imperialist doctrines of nationalist leaders.
    • Princely States had about 25% of India's population.
    • Upper House: 260 members, 156 for provinces and 104 for Princely States.
    • Lower House: 375 members, 250 for provinces and 125 for Princely States.
    • State members were not to be elected.
    • The princely states refused to join, alarmed by the rapid spread of the National Movement; the federation was never fully implemented.
    • The British failed to overcome the opposition of Congress, Muslim League and the princes to the Federal Scheme.
    • The Federal Scheme was withheld except for the Federal Court; the provincial scheme began on 1 April 1937.

    Reactions to the 1935 Act

    • Jawaharlal Nehru called the 1935 Act "a machine (car) with strong brakes but no engine".UPPSC
    • Congress rejected the 1935 Act at the Lucknow Session, 1936, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    • Nehru called the Act (the Governor-General's safeguards and special powers) a "Charter of Slavery".UPPSC
    • Nehru was Prime Minister of India 1947-1964, architect of Panchsheel (Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence) and creator of the Non-Alignment policy.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said, in the debates on Constitution-making, that he need not beg pardon for the charge that the draft Constitution reproduced a major part of the 1935 Act.UPPSC
    • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel said in the Constituent Assembly: "Can you show me one free country where there are separate electorates? The British element is gone, but they have left mischief behind."UPPSC

    Protection of Civil Rights Act

    • The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 is not a landmark of constitutional development under British rule.
    • It was enacted and notified on 8 May 1955 as the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955; amended and renamed in 1976.
    • It extends to the whole of India and punishes the practice of untouchability.

    Anglo-Afghan relations

    • 19th century: fear of Russian expansion towards India was the basis of Anglo-Afghan relations.UPPSC
    • Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) between Russia and Iran raised British fear of Russian influence; experts in England called it "The Crisis in India".
    • British feared a Russian invasion of India through the Khyber and Bolan Passes; North-Western passes were the key to entering India.
    • British view: Afghanistan should be under a friendly government in line with the British.
    • British Forward Policy in Afghanistan: aggressive plan to make a buffer state against Russia; advocated by Lord Auckland, during the First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42).

    Famines

    • Orissa (Odisha) famine of 1866-67 was called the "Sea of Calamity".UPPSC
    • Orissa famine deaths: about one million; another figure: at least 1.3 million (13 lakh), one-third of the population, died in 1866 from starvation and disease.
    • Odisha was then quite isolated from the rest of India, so the famine hit it hardest.
    • Campbell Commission (George Campbell, 1866): formed after the Orissa famine to study causes and suggest prevention and relief.
    • Strachey Commission (appointed 1878, after the Great Famine of 1876-78) prepared the Indian Famine Code, 1883.UPPSC
    • Lyall Commission: famine inquiry after the 1896-97 famine; suggested relief measures.
    • Famine commissions = Campbell, Lyall, Strachey; Hunter Commission was not one, it dealt mainly with education.

    Pindaris, Thugs and social reformers

    • Lord Hastings (Governor-General from 1813) suppressed the Pindaris.UPPSC
    • Pindaris first mentioned in 1689, at the time of the Mughal attack on Maharashtra.
    • Early 19th century Pindari leaders: Chittu, Wasil Muhammad, Karim Khan.
    • Hastings surrounded the Pindaris: from Bengal in north and east, Gujarat in west, Deccan in south.
    • Army of 113,000 men and 300 cannons: northern part under Hastings, southern under Thomas Hislop.
    • End of 1817: Pindaris driven out of Malwa and across the Chambal; January 1818: practically exterminated.
    • Major General Sir William Henry Sleeman suppressed Thuggee.
    • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: pillar of Bengal Renaissance; carried on Raja Rammohan Roy's reform; started widow remarriage.
    • Vidyasagar opened colleges to lower-caste students (earlier only for Brahmins); people called him "Daya Sagar" (ocean of kindness).
    • Justice M.G. Ranade: judge, politician, writer, reformer; set up the Social Conference Movement against child marriage and heavy spending on marriages; backed widow remarriage and female education.

    Revolt of 1857 and Ghadar Party

    • 1857: Kunwar Singh led in Bihar; Khan Bahadur Khan led in Ruhelkhand.
    • 1857: Tatya Tope led the armies at Kanpur for Nana Saheb.
    • 1857: Faizabad leader was Maulavi Ahmed Ullah, not Zeenat Mahal; Zeenat Mahal was Bahadur Shah Zafar's queen.
    • Ghadar Party (first called Pacific Coast Hindustan Association) formed in 1913 at San Francisco, USA by Sohan Singh Bhakna, Lala Har Dayal and others (not Lala Lajpat Rai).
    • Har Dayal's paper "Ghadar": first issue 1 November 1913; in 1914 he went to Switzerland and brought out anti-British paper "Vande Matram".

    Early nationalists and growth of nationalism

    • Most early nationalists saw British rule as an act of Providence meant to bring modernisation; they complained only against "Un-British rule".UPPSC

    Note from the book The explanation says the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, though the printed answer marks it as not the correct explanation.

    • They believed British rule brought industrialisation, education, administrative facilities and other reforms.
    • Study of history built nationalism in late 19th century in three ways: urging struggle against miserable conditions, refuting the British picture of Indians as backward and unfit to rule, and writing of India's glorious past.
    • Tripura joined the freedom movement early in the 20th century because Bengal revolutionaries took shelter there under British pressure.
    • The King of Tripura employed educated Bengalis in his administration.
    • Practice of indirect election in India began in 1892.UPPSC
    • Dominant castes of pre-independence Bihar: Bhumihar, Rajput, Kayastha; Kurmi was not dominant.

    Pacts and national movement details

    1. 1784Warren Hastings (not Lord Minto) was Governor-General of Bengal when Pitt's India Act, 1784 was passed.UPPSC
    2. 1899Rama Devi: called "Maa" in Odisha; born 3 December 1899 at Satyabhamapur (Cuttack); met Gandhi and Kasturba on 23 March 1921.
    3. 1905Swadeshi Movement began in protest against the Partition of Bengal (1905).
    4. 1905Partition of Bengal was declared on 20 July 1905; Swadeshi Movement formally declared on 7 August 1905 at Town Hall, Calcutta.
    5. 1907Order: decision to partition Bengal → Swadeshi declaration → Swaraj accepted as Congress goal (Calcutta session) → Surat Split (1907).UPPSC
    6. 1907Surat session, 1907: Congress split on the Swadeshi issue.
    7. 1909Indian Councils Act, 1909: passed by Secretary of State John Morley and Viceroy Lord Minto; so called Morley-Minto Reforms.UPPSC
    8. 1916Tilak announced his Home Rule League at the provincial conference at Belgaum, April 1916.
    9. 1916Lucknow Pact (Congress-League Pact), 1916: reached at the joint session of Congress and Muslim League at Lucknow, December 1916, by efforts of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Tilak.
    10. 1917Champaran Satyagraha (1917): Gandhi's first Satyagraha and first peasant Satyagraha in India; for indigo farmers of Champaran, Bihar.
    11. 1919Khilafat Movement (1919-24): movement of Indian Muslims led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, supported by Gandhi.
    12. 1919Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) began Dyarchy in the provinces; Government of India Act, 1935 gave Provincial Autonomy.
    13. 1921Moplah Revolt (1921): peak of a series of riots by Mappila Muslims of Malabar, Kerala against the British and Hindu landlords in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
    14. 1927Simon Commission: appointed 1927, came to India 1928 to study constitutional reform.
    15. 1927Correct pairs: Indian Navy Act 1927; Civil Disobedience Movement 1930; Second Round Table Conference 1931.
    16. 1927Butler Committee (Indian States Committee, 1927; chairman Sir Harcourt Butler): to examine relations between the Paramount Power and native rulers.
    17. 1928First All India Socialist Youth Congress: Calcutta, 27 December 1928; presided by Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    18. 1929Deepavali Declaration: by Viceroy Lord Irwin, 31 October 1929, on dominion status for India.UPPSC
    19. 1929Trade Disputes Act, 1929: provided a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes.UPPSC
    20. 1929Butler Committee visited 16 states, reported in 1929, and advised on financial and economic relations of the two.
    21. 1930Dandi March (Salt March), began 12 March 1930: from Sabarmati Ashram, to make salt at coastal village Dandi and break the salt tax law; started Civil Disobedience.
    22. 1930Rama Devi Choudhary: took part in the 1930 Salt Satyagraha and Civil Disobedience; arrested more than once; the question also credits her with the Bijoliya Peasant Movement and the 1932 Civil Disobedience Movement.
    23. 1931Gandhi-Irwin Pact opened the way for Congress/Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference, London, September-December 1931.
    24. 1931Civil Disobedience was discontinued after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931).
    25. 1932Poona Pact, 24 September 1932: between Ambedkar and Gandhi; 148 seats reserved for untouchables under a joint electorate, instead of a separate electorate for Dalits.
    26. 1932Communal Award: announced from Whitehall by British PM Ramsay MacDonald on 16 August 1932, under "divide and rule".
    27. 19341 August 1934: Gandhi began Individual Civil Disobedience; it failed, being short and disappointing; this was the final withdrawal of the movement.UPPSC
    28. 1939Congress ministers resigned in October 1939 because Britain put India into the Second World War without Indian consent.
    29. 194053rd Congress session: March 1940, Ramgarh (now Jharkhand), president Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
    30. 1942Cripps Mission, 1942: offered limited self-government to gain Indian cooperation in the war.
    31. 1945Wavell Plan: set out by Viceroy Lord Wavell on 14 June 1945 to end the political deadlock; discussed at the Shimla Conference.
    32. 1945Shimla Conference (also printed as "Shimla Pact", 1945): Viceroy invited Indian leaders on 25 June 1945 to discuss the Wavell offer.
    33. 19451945: a rumour spread of a Congress-League alliance through the Bhulabhai Desai - Liaquat Ali Pact.
    34. 1946Interim National Government under Nehru was announced on 24 August 1946 and formed on 2 September 1946.

    • Gandhi-Irwin Pact opened the way for Congress/Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference, London, September-December 1931.
    • Poona Pact, 24 September 1932: between Ambedkar and Gandhi; 148 seats reserved for untouchables under a joint electorate, instead of a separate electorate for Dalits.
    • Poona Pact was signed by Pt. Madan Mohan Malviya (for Gandhi) and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, after senior leaders stepped in: efforts of Malviya, C. Rajagopalachari, Rajendra Prasad and Purushottamdas.
    • Congress ministers resigned in October 1939 because Britain put India into the Second World War without Indian consent.
    • 53rd Congress session: March 1940, Ramgarh (now Jharkhand), president Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
    • Cripps Mission, 1942: offered limited self-government to gain Indian cooperation in the war.
    • Champaran Satyagraha (1917): Gandhi's first Satyagraha and first peasant Satyagraha in India; for indigo farmers of Champaran, Bihar.
    • In Champaran, Europeans forced cultivators to grow indigo (a blue dye); they could not grow food and were paid poorly.
    • Jallianwala Bagh: British troops fired on a large unarmed crowd in an open space at Amritsar on Baisakhi day; about a thousand (or thousands) killed, many more wounded.
    • Swadeshi Movement began in protest against the Partition of Bengal (1905).
    • Women's participation was a major gain of the Swadeshi Movement; urban middle-class women joined processions.
    • After Swadeshi, women took part in every movement: Home Rule, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience; all four drew women out of the home.UPPSC
    • Tilak announced his Home Rule League at the provincial conference at Belgaum, April 1916.
    • Civil Disobedience was discontinued after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931).

    • Lucknow Pact (Congress-League Pact), 1916: reached at the joint session of Congress and Muslim League at Lucknow, December 1916, by efforts of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Tilak.

    • Wavell Plan: set out by Viceroy Lord Wavell on 14 June 1945 to end the political deadlock; discussed at the Shimla Conference.
    • Wavell's proposals: Interim Government before constitution-making; balanced representation of communities; all council members except Viceroy and military chief to be Indian leaders; defence to stay with the Viceroy.
    • Trade Disputes Act, 1929: provided a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes.UPPSC
    • The Act ran on trial for five years; set up Boards of Conciliation and Courts of Inquiry for trade disputes.
    • It banned strikes or lock-outs without notice in public utility services: railways, post, telegraph, telephone.
    • Partition of Bengal was declared on 20 July 1905; Swadeshi Movement formally declared on 7 August 1905 at Town Hall, Calcutta.
    • Order: decision to partition Bengal → Swadeshi declaration → Swaraj accepted as Congress goal (Calcutta session) → Surat Split (1907).UPPSC
    • At the Calcutta session, president Dadabhai Naoroji said the Congress aim was self-government like Britain and its dominions.
    • Surat session, 1907: Congress split on the Swadeshi issue.
    • Gandhi-Irwin Pact is also called the Delhi Pact; Gandhi stood for Congress, Irwin for the British Government.
    • 1 August 1934: Gandhi began Individual Civil Disobedience; it failed, being short and disappointing; this was the final withdrawal of the movement.UPPSC
    • Shimla Conference (also printed as "Shimla Pact", 1945): Viceroy invited Indian leaders on 25 June 1945 to discuss the Wavell offer.
    • Cabinet Mission reached India on 24 March 1946, met parties and officials, and published its proposal on 16 May 1946.
    • With the Cabinet Mission, Jinnah first realised Britain was ready to transfer power without his consent.
    • 1945: a rumour spread of a Congress-League alliance through the Bhulabhai Desai - Liaquat Ali Pact.

    Congress and national movement facts

    1. 1923Banaras session of All India Hindu Mahasabha, August 1923: presided by Madan Mohan Malviya; about 1500 delegates (Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, Parsis).
    2. 1928Bardoli (Surat district, Gujarat): Mehta brothers (Kalyanji and Kunwarji) and Dayalji Desai began the farmers' movement in 1928; Patel led it later.
    3. 1928Aga Khan (Maulana Sultan Mohammed Shah) presided over the All Parties Muslim Conference, Delhi, 31 December 1928 - 1 January 1929.UPPSC
    4. 1931Gandhi and Lord Irwin met on 19 February 1931; after fifteen days of talks signed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931.
    5. 1931Karachi Congress session, 1931 approved (did not oppose) the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
    6. 1931First Round Table Conference failed mainly because Congress was absent; Government then drew Congress to the Second (1931).
    7. 1946Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha interim president; Dr. Rajendra Prasad elected permanent president on 11 December 1946.
    8. 1946Royal Indian Navy Revolt, 1946: Indian sailors at Bombay and Karachi rose against the Government.
    9. 1946Naval revolt began 18 February 1946: sailors of HMIS Talwar at Bombay harbour struck against bad food and conditions; surrendered after Sardar Patel's assurance on 24 February 1946.
    10. 1947Congress president in 1947 was J.B. Kripalani, not Nehru.
    • Gandhi and Lord Irwin met on 19 February 1931; after fifteen days of talks signed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931.
    • Karachi Congress session, 1931 approved (did not oppose) the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
    • First Round Table Conference failed mainly because Congress was absent; Government then drew Congress to the Second (1931).
    • Rowlatt Act roused popular anger and led to Jallianwala Bagh; Subhash Chandra Bose formed the Forward Bloc; Bhagat Singh was a founder of Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.
    • Congress president in 1947 was J.B. Kripalani, not Nehru.
    • Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha interim president; Dr. Rajendra Prasad elected permanent president on 11 December 1946.
    • Nehru was not in the first Congress Ministry of the United Provinces.
    • Sarabandi (no-tax) Campaign of Bardoli was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

    Gandhi: statements and incidents

    • Karachi session, March 1931: Gandhi said "Gandhi may die, but Gandhism will remain forever".UPPSC ×2
    • His words: "They might kill me, but they cannot kill Gandhism. If truth can be killed, Gandhism can be killed."
    • Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S) strategy of Gandhi: active resistance, then truce or talks, then struggle again if aims unmet.

    Note from the book BPSC deleted the S-T-S question from its final key; it accepted the strategy was most used in the Civil Disobedience Movement.

    Industry, labour and social cases

    1. 1818First Indian cotton cloth mill: 1818 at Fort Gloaster (Kolkata); it failed.
    2. 1854First successful modern cloth mill (first cotton textile mill of Bombay): 1854, by Parsi cotton merchant Cowaszee Nanabhoy Davar.
    3. 1880Word "Boycott" comes from Captain Charles C. Boycott, an Irish land agent; first used as a political weapon in 1880.
    4. 1884Rakhmabai case (1884-1888) was about age of consent and restitution of conjugal rights; she was a child bride.
    5. 1891Rakhmabai: one of the first practising women doctors of colonial India; her case led to the Age of Consent Act, 1891.
    6. 1894Gandhi helped end indentured labour: raised it in South Africa in 1894; talked with Viceroy Chelmsford; system banned in July 1917.
    7. 1896First advertisement of Indian cinema: The Times of India (Bombay), 7 July 1896, "The Marvel of the Century".
    8. 1896Same day (7 July 1896) the Lumiere brothers (France) gave the first cinematography show at Watson's Hotel, Bombay.
    9. 19071 August 1907: Robert Baden-Powell camped with 20 boys on Brownsea Island, Dorsetshire for a fortnight; start of the movement in the UK.
    10. 19081908: scouting spread worldwide with first instalment of his "Scouting for Boys"; in India scouting began 1909, guiding 1911.
    11. 1914Gandhi-Smuts Agreement (1914) ended the 3-pound tax on indentured labourers.
    12. 1919International Labour Organisation (ILO) came into being in 1919.
    13. 1919N.M. Joshi went as labour representative to the first ILO summit at Washington, 1919; B.P. Wadia went as his adviser.UPPSC
    14. 1929Whitley Commission (Royal Commission on Labour, 1929, chairman J.H. Whitley): to report on existing conditions of labour and make recommendations.
    15. 1930Gandhi broke the salt law on 6 April 1930; Nehru, Mahadev Desai and others jailed; Congress declared illegal.
    16. 1943Bengal Famine: 1943; about 3.0 million people died.UPPSC
    • First advertisement of Indian cinema: The Times of India (Bombay), 7 July 1896, "The Marvel of the Century".
    • Same day (7 July 1896) the Lumiere brothers (France) gave the first cinematography show at Watson's Hotel, Bombay.
    • First Indian cotton cloth mill: 1818 at Fort Gloaster (Kolkata); it failed.
    • First successful modern cloth mill (first cotton textile mill of Bombay): 1854, by Parsi cotton merchant Cowaszee Nanabhoy Davar.
    • Baden-Powell = founder of the Boy Scouts and Civil Guides Movement.
    • 1 August 1907: Robert Baden-Powell camped with 20 boys on Brownsea Island, Dorsetshire for a fortnight; start of the movement in the UK.
    • 1908: scouting spread worldwide with first instalment of his "Scouting for Boys"; in India scouting began 1909, guiding 1911.
    • Rakhmabai case (1884-1888) was about age of consent and restitution of conjugal rights; she was a child bride.
    • Rakhmabai: one of the first practising women doctors of colonial India; her case led to the Age of Consent Act, 1891.
    • Word "Boycott" comes from Captain Charles C. Boycott, an Irish land agent; first used as a political weapon in 1880.
    • International Labour Organisation (ILO) came into being in 1919.
    • N.M. Joshi went as labour representative to the first ILO summit at Washington, 1919; B.P. Wadia went as his adviser.UPPSC
    • Whitley Commission (Royal Commission on Labour, 1929, chairman J.H. Whitley): to report on existing conditions of labour and make recommendations.
    • Whitley Commission covered industrial and plantation labour: health, efficiency, standard of living, and employer-employee relations.
    • Indentured labourers: taken from India to British colonies for fixed periods; their state was like bonded labour.
    • Gandhi helped end indentured labour: raised it in South Africa in 1894; talked with Viceroy Chelmsford; system banned in July 1917.

    • Attlee, 20 February 1947: Britain would transfer power to responsible Indians by a date not later than June 3, 1948.
    • Attlee also said: if the League did not join the Constituent Assembly, Britain would decide to whom central power should be handed.
    • Party-less Democracy in India was proposed by Jaya Prakash Narayan.
    • Louis Fischer: American journalist; wrote Gandhi's biography "The Life of Mahatma Gandhi".
    • Ras Behari Bose: revolutionary; a key organiser of the Indian National Army (INA).
    • "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" (Hail the Soldier, Hail the Farmer) was given in 1965 at Ramlila Maidan, New Delhi.
    • Quit India Movement began on 9 August 1942; Gandhi gave the mantra "Do or Die": we shall either free India or die in the attempt.
    • Bose also wrote in "The Indian Struggle": Gandhi "has rendered and will continue to render phenomenal service to his country".
    • Dadabhai Naoroji: "Grand Old Man of India"; industrialist, educationist and thinker.
    • B.S. Moonje: Hindu nationalist leader; spoke against Ambedkar's demand for a separate electorate for Dalits.
    • Lord Mountbatten (1947-48) held Jinnah most responsible for the partition of India.
    • Maulana Hasrat Mohani first raised the demand for "Complete Independence", in 1921.
    • Stafford Cripps headed the Cripps Mission (1942) and was a member of the Cabinet Mission (1946).

    1. 1542St. Francis Xavier: reached Goa in 1542; a founding member of the Jesuit Order; spread Christianity in India.
    2. 1552Xavier died on 3 December 1552 on Shangchuan Island (China), not in Goa; his feast is held in Goa every 3 December.
    3. 1849C.F. Andrews: social reformer in India, close friend of Gandhi; William Digby (1 May 1849 - 29 September 1904): British author and journalist.

    Aurobindo Ghosh

    • Aurobindo Ghose: 15 August 1872 - 5 December 1950; nationalist, scholar, poet, mystic, philosopher, yogi and guru.
    • "New Lamps for Old" (1893-94): article series by Aurobindo Ghose criticising Congress policy as out of touch with the proletariat.
    • He wrote it at the request of Cambridge friend K.G. Deshpande, in charge of Bombay weekly "Induprakash".
    • Aurobindo's political career lasted about ten years, 1901-1910.
    • He claimed India's freedom as an inherent right, not on any charge of misgovernment or oppression.

    B.R. Ambedkar

    • Ambedkar born 14 April 1891 at Mhow (now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar), M.P.; parents Bhimabai Sakpal and Ramji Sakpal.
    • Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956 at his home in New Delhi.UPPSC
    • Ambedkar got Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990.
    • First Defence Minister of India was Baldev Singh, not Ambedkar.
    • Ambedkar founded the Depressed Classes Welfare Institute (Bahishkrit Hitkarini Sabha) at Bombay on 20 July 1924 (not 1925).
    • Ambedkar founded Siddharth College and started his journal "Mook Nayak" in 1920.
    • Ambedkar did not take part in the Quit India Movement.

    Rabindranath Tagore

    • Tagore was popularly called Gurudev; poet, philosopher, musician, writer, educationist.
    • Born 7 May 1861 in a wealthy Brahmin family at Calcutta; 14th child of Debendranath Tagore and Sharada Devi (14 children, 13 survived).
    • Tagore died on 7 August 1941 at his ancestral home in Calcutta.
    • 1901: started a school at Shantiniketan; it became Visva Bharati University in 1921.
    • 1913: Nobel Prize in Literature for "Song Offerings", English translation of his poems "Gitanjali"; first Indian and first Asian Nobel laureate.
    • Tagore was awarded knighthood by British King George V.
    • Gandhi called Tagore "the Great Sentinel"; Gandhi felt Tagore gave moral force to the freedom struggle.UPPSC
    • Tagore did not favour the economic side of the Swadeshi Movement.UPPSC
    • His novel "Ghare Baire" showed the ill effects of economic Swadeshi, including the bitterness of Muslim traders.
    • Tagore sang the glories of ancient India; saw Shivaji and Guru Govind Singh as nation builders; many of his songs refute Maratha heroism.
    • Tagore emerged as a great painter at the age of 70.UPPSC
    • 1930: Tagore was the first Indian artist to exhibit across Europe, Russia and the USA.

    Jawaharlal Nehru

    • Publicity Department of United Provinces called Nehru "high priest of Communism in India" in pamphlet "Communistic Likes and Dislikes".UPPSC
    • This was Government propaganda to confuse people about Nehru's socialist views; higher authorities advised stopping it.
    • Nehru became champion of socialism; in 1933 wanted to overthrow British rule, princely states, landlordism and capitalism.
    • Nehru's socialism was shaped by Soviet socialism; he visited the Soviet Union in November 1927.
    • Frank Moraes was Nehru's biographer.UPPSC
    • Nehru was influenced by socialism, British liberalism and Gandhi; not by German nationalism.
    • Nehru's book "Glimpses of World History", articles and speeches show his socialist ideas.
    • Nehru introduced the concept of Non-Alignment for world peace and cooperation.
    • Nehru's three foreign-policy aims: preserve sovereignty, protect territorial integrity, promote rapid economic development.
    • Five founders of NAM: Nehru (India), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Sukarno (Indonesia), Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana).
    • First Non-Aligned summit: Belgrade (capital of Yugoslavia), 1961.
    • Nehru's policy in the Cold War stressed peace, disarmament and racial equality.
    • Nehru revered the Upanishads and had great faith in them; he also had a scientific outlook.UPPSC
    • Upanishads = philosophical and scientific analysis of Vedic literature.
    • Nehru is called the father of science in modern India; saw science as a tool for socio-economic growth.
    • Nehru died on 27 May 1964 in his 4th term as PM (1947-52, 1952-57, 1957-62, 1962-64).
    • Nehru represented Phulpur (near Allahabad/Prayagraj), never Rae Bareli.
    • Teen Murti Bhavan, Nehru's residence, became a memorial after his death in 1964.
    • Teen Murti Bhavan complex houses the new Prime Ministers Museum, opened by PM Narendra Modi on 14 April 2022.UPPSC

    India after independence

    1. 1941HMS founding conference included Indian Federation of Labour (1941), Hind Mazdoor Panchayat (1948), Forward Bloc unions and independent unions.
    2. 1947Goa stayed under Portuguese rule after 15 August 1947.
    3. 1948First Industrial Policy of independent India: 6 April 1948.UPPSC
    4. 1948Industrial Policy 1948 first framed the mixed economy idea; split industries between public and private sectors and clarified their roles.
    5. 1948Operation Polo: military action in Hyderabad State, 13-18 September 1948; Nizam overthrown and state joined to India.UPPSC
    6. 1948Hind Mazdoor Sabha (Calcutta, December 1948): founders Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta.
    7. 1949Privy purse: payment to former ruling families under the 1949 agreement to merge their states with India.
    8. 1953Order of events: Air India nationalised as national carrier (1953) → Imperial Bank of India renamed State Bank of India (July 1955) → Kerala communist government (April 1957) → Goa joined India (1961).
    9. 19551955: America backed Portugal's claim over Goa.
    10. 1955Post-independence order: Khrushchev and Bulganin visit (after Nehru's USSR visit, 1955) → Dalai Lama fled to India (Tibet revolt, 1959) → Chou En-lai in New Delhi (April 1960, fruitless) → Liberation of Goa (1961).UPPSC
    11. 1957First Communist government in India: Kerala, 1957 (April); Communist Party of India won by a slim majority.UPPSC ×2
    12. 1957E.M.S. (Elamkulam Manakkal Sankaran) Namboodiripad: first Chief Minister of Kerala, 1957-59 and again 1967-69.
    13. 1961Operation Vijay (Army, Navy, Air Force) freed Goa on 19 December 1961, after 14 years of patience; ended about 450 years of Portuguese rule.
    14. 1962Goa became a Union Territory by the 12th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962 and a full state in 1987.
    15. 1971Privy purse and special rights of princely states were abolished in 1971 by the 26th Constitutional Amendment Act.
    16. 1972Shimla Agreement, 1972 (June-July): Indira Gandhi and Pakistan President Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, after the 1971 war and birth of Bangladesh.
    17. 1977Morarji Desai: first non-Congress PM, from 24 March 1977, heading the multi-party Janata Party; he represented Surat (Gujarat).
    18. 1999Operation Vijay (1999): successful military action against Pakistan in the Kargil war.

    National symbols, buildings and persons

    • "Vande Mataram" was composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in both Bengali and Sanskrit (not Bengali alone); it is in "Anandamath".
    • National Calendar (Saka era): 1st Chaitra falls on 22 March normally and 21 March in a leap year.
    • National Flag design was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947.
    • "Jana-Gana-Mana", written in Bengali by Tagore, was adopted in its Hindi version as national anthem on 24 January 1950.
    • First month of the Indian National Calendar is Chaitra (March-April); last month is Phalgun.UPPSC
    • Alipore Central Jail is in Kolkata; set up in 1906; held political prisoners under British rule.
    • Writers' Building = Secretariat of West Bengal, Kolkata; designed by Thomas Lyon; built in 1777 for junior servants (writers) of the Company.UPPSC
    • Suresh Tendulkar is an economist, not a political scientist.
    • Fateh Singh Rathore: "Tiger Man"; Mani Kaul: film maker; R.S. Sharma: historian.

    World history and general facts

    1. 1789French Revolution began in 1789.
    2. 1789First US President: George Washington (1789-1797).
    3. 1910Mother Teresa: born 1910 at Uskup, Ottoman Empire (now Skopje, North Macedonia), of Albanian origin.
    4. 1929At 18 she joined the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Sisters of Loreto); came to India in 1929; taught at St. Mary's School, Calcutta.
    5. 1939World War II began on 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland.
    6. 1941USA joined the war after Japan's attack on its naval base Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941.
    7. 1945First atom bomb: Hiroshima, Japan, 6 August 1945, dropped by America; second on Nagasaki, 9 August 1945.
    8. 1945Japan announced surrender to the Allies on 15 August 1945; formal surrender on 2 September 1945.
    9. 1950People's Liberation Army invaded Tibet in October 1950; Seventeen Point Agreement (1951) gave China control, Tibet keeping internal affairs.
    10. 1952Queen Elizabeth II reigned 70 years (1952-2022) and died aged 96 (1926-2022).
    11. 1959China occupied Tibet in 1959; Tibet's autonomy ended when the PLA crushed the uprising.
    12. 1960First woman Prime Minister in the world: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka, July 1960.UPPSC
    13. 1971Bangladesh freedom movement began 26 March 1971; Indo-Pak war December 1971; East Pakistan became Bangladesh on 16 December 1971.
    14. 1984Tutu got the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 and Gandhi Peace Prize in 2005.

    16. 1991USSR broke into 15 independent republics, including Russia, on 26 December 1991.

    • Queen Elizabeth II reigned 70 years (1952-2022) and died aged 96 (1926-2022).
    • First woman Prime Minister in the world: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka, July 1960.UPPSC
    • 10 Downing Street = official residence of the British PM, in the City of Westminster, London.
    • British PM is also called "First Lord of the Treasury".
    • Present-day calendar is the Gregorian Calendar, used in most countries.UPPSC
    • First atom bomb: Hiroshima, Japan, 6 August 1945, dropped by America; second on Nagasaki, 9 August 1945.
    • Japan announced surrender to the Allies on 15 August 1945; formal surrender on 2 September 1945.
    • French Revolution began in 1789.
    • It was a revolt of the Third Estate (peasants, artisans/urban workers, bourgeoisie) against feudalism, birth privileges, corrupt bureaucracy and incapable monarchy; also described as a middle-class revolution against feudalism, class privilege and autocracy.
    • Karl Marx explained class struggle by Dialectical Materialism.
    • Marx's materialist view of history: slavery was the base of ancient society, land of feudal society, capital of bourgeois society.
    • For Marx, economic factors decide the history of society, and they carry class struggle.
    • Mother Teresa was an Indian citizen when she died on 5 September 1997.UPPSC
    • Mother Teresa: born 1910 at Uskup, Ottoman Empire (now Skopje, North Macedonia), of Albanian origin.
    • At 18 she joined the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Sisters of Loreto); came to India in 1929; taught at St. Mary's School, Calcutta.
    • Mother Teresa founded the "Missionaries of Charity".
    • China occupied Tibet in 1959; Tibet's autonomy ended when the PLA crushed the uprising.
    • People's Liberation Army invaded Tibet in October 1950; Seventeen Point Agreement (1951) gave China control, Tibet keeping internal affairs.
    • USSR broke into 15 independent republics, including Russia, on 26 December 1991.
    • Bangladesh freedom movement began 26 March 1971; Indo-Pak war December 1971; East Pakistan became Bangladesh on 16 December 1971.
    • After World War II Germany was split into West Germany (US, British, French zones) and Soviet-influenced East Germany.
    • Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.
    • World War II began on 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland.
    • USA joined the war after Japan's attack on its naval base Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941.
    • First US President: George Washington (1789-1797).
    • Richard Nixon, 37th US President: the only one to resign, over the Watergate Scandal.
    • Bishop Desmond Tutu: black bishop of South Africa, famed for anti-racism movement in the 1980s.
    • Tutu got the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 and Gandhi Peace Prize in 2005.
    • Tsai-Lun (Cai Lun) made paper in China in 105 AD; he lived at Leiyang, Hunan province.
    • Plato was the disciple of Socrates; Aristotle was the disciple of Plato.
    • Plato discussed justice and the "Ideal State" in his book "The Republic".
    • Italian Renaissance began in the 14th century; start of the modern era and end of the medieval feudal era.
    • Main cause of the Italian Renaissance: freedom to express ideas.

    Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Vidyasagar

    • Raja Ram Mohan Roy wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhiddin in Persian (one question dates it 1809).
    • Maulavi Obaidullah Al Obaidi translated Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhiddin as 'A Gift to Monotheists' in 1884.

    Note from the book UKPSC cancelled its question on the language of 'Gift to Monotheists' in the revised answer key.

    • Precepts of Jesus = work of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.
    • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820-1891): great social reformer and educationist of the 19th century.
    • Hindu Widows Remarriage Act, 1856 was passed mainly by Vidyasagar's efforts.
    • Vidyasagar wrote Bahuvivah and 'Balya Vivaher Dosh'.

    Gandhi's writings

    • Hind Swaraj was written by Mahatma Gandhi.UPPSC ×2
    • Hind Swaraj: written in 1909 in Gujarati, by ship on his return visit to Cape Town (South Africa) from India via London; first published in Gujarati in 1909.UPPSC ×2
    • British Government censored (banned) Hind Swaraj; in March 1910 the Bombay Government proscribed its circulation.
    • In reply to the ban Gandhi published his own English rendering, 'Indian Home Rule'; it was put into English to avoid the ban.
    • In Hind Swaraj Gandhi compared the British Parliament to a sterile woman and a prostitute and commented on the working of the British Government.UPPSC
    • Gandhi wrote his autobiography The Story of My Experiments with Truth in Gujarati.
    • Gokhale: My Political Guru by M.K. Gandhi: first published February 1955 by Navajivan Publishing House, Ahmedabad.UPPSC
    • 'Gokhale: My Political Guru' is an English compilation of Gandhi's earlier writings and speeches on Gokhale.
    • Gopal Krishna Gokhale: liberal nationalist and social reformer; Gandhi considered him his political guru.
    • Gandhi translated Anasakti Yoga of the Bhagavad Gita into English and wrote Anasakti Yoga in 1929 while staying at Kausani (Uttarakhand).
    • Songs from Prison: Gandhi's English translations of Sanskrit hymns and lyrics from the Upanishads and other scriptures, made in Yeravada Prison in 1932.
    • Memoir Bapu: My Mother was written by Manubehn Gandhi.UPPSC
    • The book 'Satyagrah' is by Vinoba Bhave, not Gokhale.UPPSC

    Tilak, Aurobindo and Lajpat Rai

    • Gita Rahasya (Srimad Bhagavad Gita Rahasya): Bal Gangadhar Tilak's commentary on the Gita, in Marathi, written in Mandalay jail.
    • Bal Gangadhar Tilak lived 1856-1920.
    • Indian Unrest was written by Valentine Chirol.
    • Chirol called Tilak 'The Father of Unrest in India'; Tilak sued him for defamation.
    • Aurobindo Ghosh was jailed in 1908, where he studied spiritual texts; in 1910 he retired from politics and lived at Pondicherry (Puducherry).
    • Aurobindo's works: The Life Divine, The Ideal of Human Unity, Essays on the Gita, The Synthesis of Yoga.UPPSC
    • New Lamps for Old was written by Aurobindo Ghosh.
    • The Foundation of Indian Culture was written by Sri Aurobindo Ghosh.
    • Unhappy India was written by Lala Lajpat Rai; in it he compared Indian society with contemporary USA and Britain.UPPSC
    • Printed wording: Unhappy India is by Lala Lajpat Rai, 'not Bal Gangadhar Tilak who chaired the Special Session of Indian National Congress (1920)'.

    • Deuskar used 'desh' to mean the nation (not only the region of Bengal).
    • Desher Katha records the cries of the Indian public under slavery and exploitation in the British Empire.
    • Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar: Marathi origin, born and raised in a Bengali environment; Maharashtra was his inspiration; bridge between the renaissance of Maharashtra and Bengal.
    • Deuskar: thinker of the Indian public awakening; his thinking and writing joined localism and pan-Indianness.
    • Balkrishna Sharma Naveen wrote two kavyas, 'Pranarpan' and 'Atmosarga', on Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi.
    • Balkrishna Sharma Naveen was a member of the 1st Lok Sabha.
    • Naveen's poetry anthologies: Kumkum, Rashmirekha, Apalak, Kwasi, Vinoba Stavan, Urmila, Hum Vishpaee Janam Ke.

    Plans and constitutional writings

    • People's Plan: authored by M.N. Roy, drafted by the Post-war Reconstruction Committee of the Indian Federation of Labour; a 10-year plan.UPPSC

    • Jayaprakash Narayan drafted the Sarvodaya Plan in 1950.
    • Planned Economy for India: by M. Visvesvaraya, 1934; gave his own suggestions for a ten-year plan for India.
    • Gandhian Constitution for Free India: written by Shriman Narayan Agarwal, published 1946.
    • 'Landmarks in Indian Constitutional and National Development' was written by Gurmukh Nihal Singh, (first) Governor of Rajasthan 1956-1962.
    • G.A. Natesan edited 'Congress Presidential Addresses' (1934-35), in two parts: Part 1 = addresses 1885-1910; Part 2 = 1911-1934.

    Tagore

    1. 1861Tagore lived 1861-1941; Gitanjali is his work.

    4. 1912English edition of Gitanjali was first published in November 1912.UPPSC

    • Amar Sonar Bangla was written and composed by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905 during the Partition of Bengal (Swadeshi Movement).UPPSC ×2
    • Its tune was inspired by Gagan Harkara's song 'Ami Kothay Pabo Tare'.
    • Bangladesh officially adopted the first ten lines of Amar Sonar Bangla as its National Anthem in 1972.
    • Syed Ali Ahsan translated Amar Sonar Bangla into English.
    • Tagore also composed Jana Gana Mana; he is the only poet whose compositions are national anthems of two countries.UPPSC
    • In February 1919 Tagore translated the National Anthem from Bengali to English at Madanapalle (Annamayya district), Andhra Pradesh.
    • Bengali Gitanjali was published on 14 August 1910 (31 Shravan 1317).
    • English edition of Gitanjali was first published in November 1912.UPPSC

    • 'Gitanjali: Song Offerings' was the English book chiefly linked with the Nobel; it was Tagore's own English selection / recasting, not a direct translation of the Bengali Gitanjali alone.

    World books and authors

    • Das Kapital was written by German socialist Karl Marx, 19th-century economist and philosopher.
    • In Das Kapital Marx criticised capitalism (its dynamism and tendency to self-destruction) and gave his socialist principles, called Marxism.
    • Marx's stated purpose: to lay bare 'the economic law of motion of modern society'.
    • First part of Das Kapital came out in Marx's lifetime; second and third parts were edited and published after his death by his friend Friedrich Engels.
    • Hans Christian Andersen wrote fairy tales: The Steadfast Tin Soldier, The Snow Queen, The Little Mermaid, Thumbelina.
    • Silent Spring was written by Rachel Carson, famous American biologist; it questions the use of pesticides.
    • David Copperfield: novel by Charles Dickens, published serially 1849-50 and as a book in 1850; semi-autobiographical.
    • J.K. Rowling, British author, created Harry Potter; Cornelius Fudge is the Minister for Magic in it.
    • Elizabeth Hawley, American writer, was known for writings on Himalayan expeditions, though she never did mountaineering.
    • The Audacity of Hope (2006) is Barack Obama's second book.
    • Obama's first book: 'Dreams From My Father'; third: 'Of Thee I Sing: A Letter to My Daughters' (2010).
    • The Challenge of World Poverty was written by Gunnar Myrdal.UPPSC
    • Karl Gunnar Myrdal: Swedish economist and sociologist; Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences 1974, shared with Friedrich von Hayek.
    • 'In the Line of Fire' is by Pervez Musharraf, former President of Pakistan; its actual (ghost) writer is believed to be Humayun Gohar, son of Pakistani bureaucrat Altaf Gohar.UPPSC
    • Living History was written by Hillary Clinton, former US Secretary of State and wife of former US President Bill Clinton.
    • Spare: memoir of Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex.UPPSC
    • 'Spare' set a Guinness World Record as the fastest selling non-fiction book, on its release date 10 January 2023.

    Cultural institutions

    1. 1814First Sanskrit chair was established in 1814 at College de France, of the famous Paris University (France).UPPSC
    2. 1901Pandit Vishnu Digambar Paluskar founded the first Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore in 1901 (then in undivided India).
    3. 1919Kala Bhavan: famous centre of fine arts at Visva-Bharati University, Shantiniketan, West Bengal; founded in 1919 by Rabindranath Tagore.
    4. 1922Painter Nandalal Bose became Principal of Kala Bhavan in 1922.
    5. 1952Sangeet Natak Akademi was set up in 1952 and inaugurated on 28 January 1953.
    6. 1954Lalit Kala Akademi, New Delhi: set up by the Government of India as an autonomous body on 5 August 1954; given statutory authority in 1957.UPPSC
    7. 1959National School of Drama: theatre training institution, set up in 1959 by Sangeet Natak Akademi as a constituent unit; independent entity and registered autonomous organisation in 1975.
    8. 1979Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT): set up in 1979 by Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Dr. Kapila Vatsyayan; works to link education with culture.UPPSC
    • Pandit Vishnu Digambar Paluskar founded the first Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore in 1901 (then in undivided India).
    • Gandharva Mahavidyalaya: one of the earliest institutions for organised training in classical music by a modern method.
    • Paluskar wanted to take music education out of the hereditary domain of professional musicians and open it to the wider public.
    • Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT): set up in 1979 by Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Dr. Kapila Vatsyayan; works to link education with culture.UPPSC
    • CCRT is an autonomous organisation under the Ministry of Culture; committed to holistic education: cognitive, emotional and spiritual development of children.
    • Sangeet Natak Akademi: India's National Academy of music, dance and drama; first national academy of the arts set up by the Republic of India.UPPSC
    • Sangeet Natak Akademi was set up in 1952 and inaugurated on 28 January 1953.

    Note from the book Sangeet Natak Akademi's own website gives its founding year as 1953; other sources give 1952 as founding and 1953 as inauguration year.

    • Lalit Kala Akademi, New Delhi: set up by the Government of India as an autonomous body on 5 August 1954; given statutory authority in 1957.UPPSC
    • National School of Drama: theatre training institution, set up in 1959 by Sangeet Natak Akademi as a constituent unit; independent entity and registered autonomous organisation in 1975.
    • First Sanskrit chair was established in 1814 at College de France, of the famous Paris University (France).UPPSC
    • Kala Bhavan: famous centre of fine arts at Visva-Bharati University, Shantiniketan, West Bengal; founded in 1919 by Rabindranath Tagore.
    • Painter Nandalal Bose became Principal of Kala Bhavan in 1922.
    • Shantiniketan: small town near Bolpur in Birbhum district, West Bengal.
    • Shantiniketan was renamed Visva Bharati, which Tagore defined as 'Where the world makes a home in a nest'.

    Folk culture and ideas

    • Folk culture = cultural practices of common people: expressive parts of everyday life of localised, common, tradition-bound groups.UPPSC
    • Folk songs matter most for preserving traditions, passed from generation to generation.
    • Preserving intangible cultural heritage across generations keeps the memory of one's origin and identity.
    • Cultural lag: culture takes time to catch up with technological innovations; this lag causes social problems and conflicts.
    • Religion, law and tradition are factors of cultural lag; politics is not.UPPSC
    • Ogburn: cultural lag is common because material culture evolves and changes rapidly.
    • Cultural lag is a critical ethical issue: no broad consensus on use of modern technology can break social solidarity and raise social conflict.
    • Tribhanga (tri-bent pose): standing pose in Indian sculpture, art and classical dance; one leg bent, body curved oppositely at waist and neck.
    • Tribhanga literally = three parts break: three bends at neck, waist and knee, giving a gentle 'S' shape.
    • Mimamsa philosophy stresses the doctrine of Karma; liberation is possible by performing Karma.
    • Vidushaka in Sanskrit drama is the dear one of the king and is a Brahmana; used by dramatists like Kalidasa and Bhasa.
    • Earliest reference to the magnetic compass is found in Jawamiul Hikayat.
    • Surkhi in Indian architecture was introduced by the Kushans; its use is found in Kushana-period buildings.UPPSC
    • At Mathura, Surkhi was found in the third stage (200 BC to end of 1st century) and fifth stage (4th to 6th centuries) of excavation.
    • Vichitravirya was the grandfather of Arjun; his two sons were Pandu and Dhritarashtra; Arjun was Pandu's son.
    • Pampa's Vikramarjuna Vijaya is the Kannada version of the Mahabharata.
    • Amir Khusrau was the first writer to use Urdu for poetic expression; wrote several verses in Urdu; called originator of Qawwali.
    • Sardar Puran Singh is known as the 'Tagore' of the Punjabi language.

    Festivals and fairs

    • Kumbh Mela: mass Hindu pilgrimage with a dip in a holy river; world's largest religious gathering.
    • Kumbh is held every third year by rotation at four places: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain (not Varanasi).
    • So Kumbh Mela (Purna Kumbh) comes to each of the four places every twelfth year.
    • U.P. government renamed Kumbh Mela (every 12 years) as Mahakumbh and Ardh Kumbh (every 6 years) as Kumbh, at Prayagraj.

    • Thadingyut marks the full moon of the summer lunar month Thadingyut.
    • Navarathri is celebrated as Saraswati Pooja in Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.
    • Tamil Nadu Navarathri: first three days for Lakshmi, next three for Durga, last three for Saraswati.
    • In Kerala, Telangana and Karnataka, Mahanavami is celebrated as Saraswati Pooja.
